Mr. NIXON: I would also like to protest against this very long adjournment.
Parliament has practically done nothing

It is only to Christmas; just for

for three hundred and sixty-five days,
but what is this Chrismas adjournment?
This is the 26th November, 1936, and the

adjourned until 9th March, 1937. And
that is Christmas. I wonder if Christmas
was introduced for a joke, or what was
it introduced for? It is not much of a
Christmas for thousands of poor people
in this city who are famished and waiting
for that bag of charity coal. Something
should be done for them by legislation,
although I am not despising the good
people who subscribe to the Coal Fund.
But if the people were treated the way
they should be treated by legislation promoted by the Government, there would
be no necessity for those few bags of coal,
which in the end do not do much good,
and there would be no necessity to cover
over this adjournment with the pretence
that it is only a Christmas adjournment.
The joke would be all right if there
was
not such poverty in our midst.

I may say that the solution of the unemployment problem is, in my opinion,
possible under the present system and
will eventually be achieved, but it will
involve in its solution, so far as my
understanding carries me, a
tain number of changes in the system.
There is one disturbing feature in the
present system, but it is a feature which,
unhappily, our Government has no control over-the excessive amount of saving
that goes on in periods of prosperity for
the purpose of investment. The money
that is saved cannot be genuinely invested,
because there are no new investments or
replacements to take up the tremendous
volume of money saved during that time
for the purpose of investment. The old
idea was that when money was saved it
was necessarily invested, and, therefore,
put people in work, but the new theory
is that a prosperous community can save
an amount of money altogether out of
proportion to the amount of investment
required at any time. The result of that
is that money flows into the stock markets
and is used to keep up existing shares,
and eventually it has a depressing effect.
upon industry. It is by taking note of
that fact and controlling it within the
framework of our present industrial
organisations that I believe the solution
of the unemployment problem will
largely be found.
At the same time, however, I do not
think that a complete solution of the
unemployment problem, even in our own
area, lies within the power of the Government. The hon. Member for Shankill
might just as well go to the Belfast
Corporation, harangue them, and say they
should sit continuously throughout the
year in order to solve the unemployment
problem as to come here and say that we
could solve the unemployment problem if
we sat here from week-end to week-end.
It is because I believe that a solution of
this great problem, the greatest evil of
our time, is possible that I greatly deplore
the advocacy of quack remedies. I do
not refer to the remedy suggested by the
hon. Member for Dock, but quack
remedies advocated by people who, in my
opinion, are little better than charlatans.
They never give any explanation of these
quack remedies, except that these remedies
involve the making of plenty of new
money. Such spurious remedies for our
troubles only do harm and prejudice the
minds of those people who have to be
educated to look forward to the practical
and effective changes which are necessary
if they are to be brought up to that
standard of life which we all wish to see
them possessing.
I am not at all pessimistic about the
future. Our own Government is doing
all it can. I observed the other day that
the Government at Westminster is
actually spending £400,000,000 on social
service, and our own Government, as we
know, spend a very large proportion of
the revenue derived from our people in
helping the less privileged members of
our community. In Ireland we are in a
position to make some experiments, and I
am glad to know that experiments are
being made by our Government in regard
to social service. The programme which
they have put before us in the King's
Speech has my hearty approval.
Mrs. PARKER: There are one or two
points in the Gracious Speech upon which
I should like to dwell for a few minutes.
Before doing so, I should like to reiterate
what has been said by various speakers
in this debate, and that is that the Session
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
on which we are entering will be one of
the most important in the history of our
Parliament, because our deliberations
will be carried on during the year of the
Coronation of His Majesty the King. I
think, even though it has been said often
during the debate, it would not be out
of place to once more repeat that our
hearts are full of loyalty to the one who
is taking on the burden of kingship at
a time when the international horizon is
so dark. I might also say that our hearts
are full of hope that through his personality, which is so much beloved by
all his people at home, he may be the
means of bringing about peace abroad
and in acclerating the return of prosperity
at home.
We have been told, both in the
Gracious Speech and by the Prime
Minister, that prosperity at home is well.
on its way. I think we can draw our
own conclusions from our own knowledge
in that respect. The people of Northern
Ireland and the people of Great Britain
should indeed be thankful that their lot
is cast where conditions are as they are
and not as they are in foreign countries
to-day.
In the speech made by the hon. Member for Dock (Mr. Midgley) yesterday—I
am sorry he is not here now, as I have not
previously had an opportunity of answering some of the points which he made
-he spoke about conditions of life for
labourers, both agricultural and industrial, in other countries and especially
in Russia. I should like to tell him
through you, Mr. Speaker-again I repeat I wish he were here that a friend
of mine, a distinguished writer, went to
Russia last summer. I should say that
this distinguished writer was a Socialist.
She went to Russia and was determined
to see the conditions, the real conditions,
under which the people in that country
live. She did what I think was a very
brave thing-she worked on three communal farms. I am not going to
anticipate the book which she will
publish shortly, but I can say she found
the conditions terrible, almost beyound
description. I am not going to say anything more than to state that she was a
Socialist when she went out, but she
came back a Conservative.
I do feel, and it cannot be too often
repeated, that the citizens of Northern
Ireland, as well as those of Great Britain,
ought to thank God every day of their
lives that the doctrines of Socialism and
Fascism do not flourish in their midst.
I am certain that the hon. Member for
Dock, and indeed all hon. Members
opposite, would be very far from
satisfied if the labourers in this country
had to endure the standard of living
which is the lot of the labourers in
practically every Continental country today, where not only the standard is
terribly low, but where there is no
freedom. They are nothing but slaves.
The hon. Member for Dock would have
us believe that prosperity has not reached
the individual. I would like to say that
prosperity is not to be measured by the
individual or individual sections of the
community. I believe that is where we
are inclined to make such a great mistake,
because of our too narrow outlook. We
only think of our own particular section
or of the individual we know. We will
have to learn to look upon these matters
as a whole, and think of the prosperity
of the whole country, just as we expect
the Government to consider the country
as a whole, and to endeavour to bring
back prosperity to all individuals, to all
classes, and to all sections of the community and to all districts. On that
basis we can from our own knowledge
agree that the glass is set fair, and that
prosperity is on its way.
There are one or two matters I would
like to deal with very briefly. Naturally,
like other hon. Members I am delighted
to find that a reduction of age is going
to take place in the matter of blind
pensions. I think that is a matter upon
which we are all unanimous. I am
delighted also to see that medical treatment for those under 16 years of age will
be under consideration. That seems to
me to be a natural sequel to the medical
and dental inspection of our schools, and
there I would like to emphasise the fact
that I always considered that the medical
inspection of schools was one of the most
important features of our Education Act,
and one which I would like to see used
very much more extensively and more
thoroughly than it is at the present
moment. I cannot fail to feel that this
further medical treatment foreshadowed
will be for the good of the nation and the
future of the race.
One matter referred to in the King's
Speech has received very little comment
141 Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address 142
26 NOVEMBER 1936
during the debate, and I consider it one
of the most important, that is, the
establishment of a voluntary scheme on
a contributory basis to provide pensions
for persons of limited means. I cannot conceive of any provision more
necessary or any class more deserving.
Those people of limited means, the people
to whom, I presume, this refers, are
always haunted by the fear of the future.
Unlike the lowest classes they have always
to try to keep up certain appearances,
and they have always received the
sympathy of the thinking people of the
country. This will encourage them to
save and will remove, I hope, the fear
which must be in their minds for themselves in their old age.
Reference is made in the Speech to
agricultural workers. I am confident
they will benefit by being admitted to insurance and benefit in many ways, just as
the whole community will benefit because
a prosperous farmer, as has been often
said, ought to mean a prosperous labourer
and a contented labourer may help to
create a more prosperous farmer.
I am
quite confident that gradually the whole.
standard of their life is going to be
raised. Perhaps it may seem that this
comes rather late, but I can assert that
their standard of living is being gradually
raised, and that their contentment will
naturally follow.
Housing is referred to, and I wish that
all district councils would avail themselves
of the Labourers Acts. I believe that all
rural district councils will be very anxious
to have these Acts restored, and will avail
themselves of their privileges in time. I
have heard of many actively engaged at
the present time in the necessary preliminaries. In my district council we have
something like 400 applications, and we
are now awaiting the medical reports on
the conditions of the houses. These
measures are all rather slower than the
average person realises, and it does take
time and patience for their adjustment.
In this connection I should like to ask the
Minister of Home Affairs if he would consider because it is also connected with
the beautifying of the countryside-the
adoption of the Rural Workers Housing
Act, 1926, whereby two-thirds of the
cost of repairs and improvements is given
by way of grant. I have always thought
that not only should we provide housing
for labourers, but it would be a great
advantage if we are able to assist the
farmers, some of whose houses are falling
into disrepair, in their proper repair.
It would, at the same time, be a very
great advantage in beautifying the
countryside rather than have these
tumbledown houses.
I do not wish to detain the House any
longer, but I am extremely glad that
the question of advertisements is being
considered, because these advertisements
in many cases disfigure the countryside.
I do not quite agree with the hon.
Member for the University (Rev. Professor Corkey), because, as a matter of
fact, some of the advertisements to which
he referred are among the most artistic
and ingenious of all the advertisements
which appear in the country.
In conclusion, there are a few words I
wish to say in connection with the great
work carried on by the Tourist Development Association. I understand that the
Government this year propose to give an
increased grant. Nobody would deny
that that association has done, and is
doing a magnificent work. I would like.
to make a suggestion, because I do not
think their work is thoroughly appreciated by all the local authorities. It is
most important that it should be appreciated because all the local authorities
should contribute as generously as possible.
We have a rather narrow outlook
on certain questions. Perhaps we have a
narrow outlook when it comes to our own
district. We want to encourage tourists
to come to our own part of the Province.
I suggest that, perhaps, the Ulster Tourist
Development Association might send
someone down, not just a member of the
county council, to each rural district
council to consult with the members of
those boards as to the best means of helping the locality because I am sure they
are anxious to see that no town is overlooked.
In my district I claim that we have
scenery second to none, and have advantages for visitors second to none in the
whole of Northern Ireland. I hope my
suggestion may bear some fruit. This
does not mean that I am casting any
reflection on the very great work done
for Ulster by the Tourist Development
Association. I have spoken at greater
length than I meant to, but I would once
more like to emphasise the fact that I in
common with, I think, every other Mem-
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
ber am delighted that the Gracious
Speech shows recognition of the fact that
prosperity has come back to our midst.
Mr. YOUNG: There is one item
referred to in the Gracious Speech, to
which I would like to refer shortly. It
is the one where it is observed there is
an increase in the exports of linen goods.
The hon. Member for Dock when addressing the House yesterday rather implied
that any improvement there was in trade
at the present time was almost entirely
owing to armament contracts.
really as far as the linen of Northern
Ireland is concerned armament contracts
affect it very little. I would just like the
House to hear some of these figures which
show the improvement there has been
latterly in linen.
I think
The export of linen goods for the ten
months to the end of October of this
year were 73,000,000 square yards compared with 65,000,000 square yards last
year. Then if we take the one month
of October this year,
it is 7,000,000
square yards compared with 5,500,000
square yards last year. It is of enormous
advantage to us here in Northern Ireland
that there is a decrease in imports of
foreign yarns of no less than 480 tons.
during the last ten months and
an increase in exports of 368 tons.
These figures show an improvement in
the linen trade, which is not owing in
any respect to armaments, but very
largely due to the improved condition of
things in the United States of America.
The hon. Member for Dock in his
remarks yesterday implied that the real
cure for unemployment in Northern Ireland or anywhere else was to reduce the
working hours from 48 to 40. I have
been thinking that if the trade union
leaders really had the courage of their
convictions they had many opportunities
in the last fifteen years to try out these
experiments. Trade unions have very
large capital sums at their disposal.
Unfortunately during the last fifteen
years in Northern Ireland there have been
many cases of spinning mills and weaving
factories having been put up for sale and
sold
as going concerns at absolutely
ridiculous prices. Why did not the trade
union leaders, if they believe in their
policy, buy up these concerns, get
machinery, and try the experiment of
shorter hours and higher wages? The
reason that they did not do so is that
they have not got the courage of their
convictions, and they knew perfectly well
that they would make a complete "mug"
of the whole business. They could not
run a spinning mill or a weaving factory
in spite of their organisation and their
capital.
It is not fair to be getting up here and
making those unreasonable statements
about a cure for unemployment. If they
had had the management of a mill or
factory I am afraid there would be no
employment left at all. These are the
only remarks I want to make. I challenge
the trade union leaders that if they
believe in their policy they had and still
have a chance to prove that they can
run a spinning mill or weaving factory
on co-operative lines with short hours and
high wages. We will then see where they
stand.
Mr. MURPHY: I would like in
rising to support the Address in reply to
add my tribute to the admirable way in
which it was proposed and seconded on
Tuesday by my hon. Friends. There are
very few points in connection with the
Gracious Speech that have not already
been discussed by Members on either side.
There, are, however, one or two matters
to which I would like to make reference
with special regard to my constituency.
At the outset, I would like to say that
Londonderry City will yield to no city in
the Empire in its loyalty and enthusiasm
in connection with the celebrations of our
Gracious Majesty's Coronation. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Passing from that I, like every citizen.
in Northern Ireland, rejoice to see that
the work in our great shipyard in Belfast
has been maintained during the year,
and further that in addition to that great
shipyard we are now to look forward to
an aircraft factory soon to be completed
in Belfast. I think the Government deserves the warmest congratulations of
every citizen in the Province on the
policy they have maintained through
good report and ill-report-the policy of
giving facilities to the ship-owning
companies to have their ships built in
Belfast, a policy which has enabled the
Island through desperate years of slump
and depression to maintain that great
standard of craftmanship and good workmanship that have always characterised
that concern.

Having said that, might I say a word
or two about the position of my constituency, Londonderry City? No sensible
man in that city begrudges Belfast its
success in
in shipbuilding or begrudges
it its new aircraft factory. It is
not with jealous eyes that my constituents
look at the improvement referred to in
the Gracious Speech in the position of unemployment in Belfast, but I do say that
a great many of my constituents in Derry
City look with rather wistful eyes at that
great shipyard at the Island and the new
aircraft factory. As everybody in this
House knows, Derry City at one time
possessed a shipyard. It is true it was a
small shipyard, but at one time it turned
out most excellent shipbuilding work.
Unfortunately, owing to the general conditions in the shipbuilding trade, that
shipyard is derelict, and, in fact, has
been dismantled for many years.
He
would be a bold man who would prophesy
that in the present conditions of the shipbuilding trade any firm could be induced
to start a new shipbuilding yard in Derry
or elsewhere. When one sees a great
yard with the great reputation of
Workman & Clark dismantled and treated
as a shipyard, that definitely is one of
the shipyards that must be closed in the
interests of the shipbuilding industry,
one realises how difficult it would be to
induce any shipbuilding firm to start a
new shipbuilding industry in Derry.
to
Derry possesses advantages not possessed
by a great many other cities in the
Kingdom. It possesses enormous advantages in the Foyle, and I venture to suggest that there are few cities in the
Kingdom more admirably suited
form a base for aircraft, either aeroplanes or seaplanes, than Derry and
its neighbourhood. It was not without reason that when a great flotilla
of seaplanes started out from Italy
Londonderry was selected as one of the
ports of call. I suggest that those connected with the sailing of that aerial
Armada left satisfied that in Derry they
had visited a place eminently suited to
form a landing place for seaplanes. It
would also be idle to say that there has
not been great disappointment in Londonderry at the decision, unfortunately come
to, to select another part of this island
as a terminal base for the Imperial-
American air service. I do not wish to
go into a discussion on that matter. It
would certainly not be relevant to the
present Gracious Speech. I have said
that because I do wish to emphasise the
fact that Londonderry possesses advantages for aircraft of all kinds, and is still
waiting for some development that may
bring it some additional employment.
When I say that I do not wish to suggest that it is necessary to ask the special
consideration of our Government to the
needs of Londonderry. I know—no one
knows better-of the efforts made by the
members of our Government to do everything possible to improve and better the
employment situation in Londonderry. I
am aware of the interest taken in the
matter by all the Members of the Government or those immediately concerned with
the problem; in particular, the Prime
Minister, the Minister of Labour and
Minister of Commerce, but I would once
again ask the Members of our Government
to make a still further effort in this direction, because the position in connection.
with aircraft, as we all know, is not
static. We all see the enormous developments that are taking place, and that
necessarily will take place. Amongst
other matters it seems to me universally
agreed nowadays that it is absolutely
necessary to keep our Navy up to a high
standard for the purpose of protecting our
seaborne commerce on the high seas. If
we were to be involved in the tragedy of
another war it would be essential for the
protection of that seaborne commerce to
have flotillas in the narrow waters, and
could any more suitable place for such
flotillas be conceived than Londondery?
It has got the natural advantages. I
suggest it has got every advantage in that
connection that a place could have. It
has already got in the immediate neighbourhood enormous tracts of reclaimed
land ready made for the purpose of an
aerodrome, and enormous tracts of land
at present covered by the sea at high
water, which could be most readily reclaimed, and, above all, it has got in the
Foyle a sheet of water which could not be
bettered for the purpose of the landing
of seaplanes. I would once again ask the
Members of the Government, who have
already been so active in this direction,
to make further effort to try to secure
for Londonderry city or neighbourhood
some place in this vast expansion of aircraft development. I suggest that
Londonderry city is deserving of special

Mr. POLLOCK : I hope I may
be permitted to join with my other
hon. Friends in the pæan of praise

the Address,
Address, and to
say that in

in respect to the merits and facilities

Government have always had the greatest

it was in their means and power to help

It must be remembered, so far as

will shortly come when in Northern Ireland the necessity for facilities for the
treatment of aircraft would arise. So far
they have been successful. But this is

of ours as time goes on, and as the use

We see omens of that kind now in the

for Transatlantic air liners carrying mails,

that there will be a development here in

It was very pleasing to listen to some
of the speeches delivered this evening,
particularly that of my hon. Friend the
Member for Bann Side (Mr. Young). He
gave us information in regard to the linen
trade which was cheering to our hearts.
He told us there was a very considerable
increase in the export of linen goods this
year as compared with last year. That is
something we have all to be thankful for,
because, as we know, linen is one of the
staple industries of our Province. It is
also
very pleasing to have such a
reply to the vaticinations we heard of
depression, of unemployment, and of the
deprivation of the ordinary means of livelihood of our citizens, and to learn that
one of our staple industries is progressing
in the way we have heard.
I am not prepared to talk upon the
subjects discussed in His Majesty's
Gracious Speech, because they have been
dealt with so completely by the Prime
Minister and almost every Member of
the House. It would be unnecessary
and superfluous for me to do so, but I
may touch perhaps on one or two matters.
The hon. Lady Member for South Derry
(Mrs. Parker) spoke of the development
of housing in respect of labourers'
cottages. If the local authorities had
been active during the last two or three
years there is no reason why the development of labourers' cottages should not
have been continued. Parliament has
provided the necessary means by which
the local authorities without any burden
upon them-I say that deliberatelycould have developed sufficient labourers'
cottages, so that there would have been
no need to-day. The Government not
only gave a grant of 40 per cent. of the
cost of the houses initially, or rather the
cost of the loan charges, which is the
same thing, but with derating they

from any burden in connection with
them. Between one thing and another,
with the rents that would accrue from
149 Debate on the Address

26 NOVEMBER 1936
Debate on the Address
these cottages, the local authorities would
have practically not one single penny of
obligation in regard to the building of
labourers' cottages. We have seen that
one local authority by means of the
rentals of the houses made a profit of a

year before.
My primary object in rising at this
moment is to correct what, if I want to
be polite, I shall call a misunderstanding, but what was really a misrepresentation of the financial position arising out
of the Loans Guarantee Fund, which the
night before last the hon. Member for
Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) indulged in. He
was in possession of a small White Paper
which was submitted by my Ministry in
the month of September. At that time.
I was laid up and had no knowledge that
such a paper was in existence. As I say,
I was not aware that this small slip called
White Paper had been prepared and
circulated. From the figures on that
Paper the hon. Member said there was
a sum of £1,279,546 apparently irretrievably lost in connection with loans
guarantees.
If the hon. Member had only extended
to me the courtesy generally shown in
this House and allowed me to make a
correction at the moment by intervention
I could have informed him in one single
sentence that the amount he described
as lost was covered by valuable securities,
so that this amount was actually in the
suspense account waiting for a suitable
moment when the securities represented
by this amount could be best realised.
It is not right that statements of that
kind, which have a tendency to injure.
the Province, should gain dirculation.
For the public depending upon the accuracy
of the statements that appear in Hansard
it is, of course, highly inconvenient, to
say the least of it, and not in the
interests of the Province that statements
of that kind should be circulated. Had
the hon. Member only permitted me to
give the information at the time I could
have said that the sum was represented
by securities, and that would have been
sufficient to satisfy all those listening to
him in this House that there was
practically no risk involved.
The Prime Minister was perfectly
justified when in the course of a lengthened review of the whole situation at the
opening of the debate he stated:
Of all the guarantees entered into by
the Government in connection with
shipbuilding it can be said with assurance that there is hardly one case which
admits of any doubts as to its ultimate
ability to redeem its obligation to the
full 100 per cent.-(Official Report,
24th November, 1936, vol. 19, col. 29).
I should like to repeat and confirm that
statement so that the House may be under
no misapprehension in regard to the
favourable position in which we stand in
respect to our loans guarantees, and may
I add, in conclusion, that that very
favourable result to which I have referred
can very readily be explained by the fact
that the shipping business of the Kingdom
has improved to such an extent that shipbuilding shares have now become one of
the most attractive of all the stock listed
upon the Stock Exchange. That is probably the best evidence that can be offered
that the immediate future of our shipbuilding will, at any rate, be advanced
and secured.

speech very much. I hope that at some
other time I will have an opportunity of
telling Ministers what should be done
regarding these particular matters.
will content myself by again congratulating the Members of the Cabinet on the
great work they have accomplished. It
is a source of satisfaction to think that
the same Ministers who came into office
when this Parliament was established are
still with us.
It goes to show that the
people have entire confidence in the
Ministers. In conclusion, I hope the
Member for Dock will realise, even at
this late hour, that the workers of
Ulster will never be driven to adopt
Russian ideals. If the hon. Member
wants to do good for Ulster he should
turn his head away from Russian ideals
and try to become a good Ulsterman.
Original Question put, and agreed to.
Resolved, "That an Humble Address
be presented to His Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland, as follows:-
"Your Grace,
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern
Ireland, in Parliament assembled, beg
leave to offer our humble thanks to your
Grace for the speech which your Grace
has addressed to both Houses of Parliament."

HOUSE OF COMMONS
A PROCLAMATION
BY THE GOVERNOR OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
WHEREAS it is provided by section eleven of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, as modified by and in
pursuance of certain other enactments, that the Governor
of Northern Ireland shall, in His Majesty's name, summon
the Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS both Houses of the Parliament of
Northern Ireland stand adjourned at this present time:
AND WHEREAS under an Instrument of Abdication
dated the Tenth day of December instant, his former
Majesty King Edward the Eighth did declare His irrevocable determination to renounce the Throne for Himself
and His descendants, and the said Instrument of Abdication
has now taken effect, and His former Majesty's Most
Honourable Privy Council, and others, did meet on Saturday
the Twelfth day of December, 1936, and did direct that His
Royal Highness Prince Albert Frederick Arthur George be
proclaimed King by the Style and Title of George the Sixth:
NOW, THEREFORE, I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
Duke of Abercorn, Knight of the Most Noble Order of the
Garter, Knight of the Most Illustrious Order of Saint
Patrick, Governor of Northern Ireland, in His Majesty's
name, do hereby summon the Parliament of Northern
Ireland to meet on Thursday, the 17th December, 1936, to
the intent that such proclamation of His Majesty's accession
as may be signed in the Privy Council of Northern Ireland
may be read to the Members of both Houses of the said
Parliament:
And the Senators and Members of the House of
Commons are hereby required to give their attendance
accordingly.
GIVEN this Twelfth day of December, Nineteen hundred and thirty-six.
(Signed by his own hand)
ABERCORN.

Question of Procedure.
Mr. BEATTIE: On a point of Order.
I would like to know the procedure
adopted in placing you, Mr. Deputy-
Speaker, in that exalted position in this
House. I understand that on leave of
absence to the Speaker certain procedure
must be conformed to, and I will read it
to you.
If Mr. Speaker desires to be absent
from the House on a subsequent day
he asks the indulgence of the House
and a Motion is then made that during
such absence the Chairman of the Committee of Ways and Means do take
the Chair as Deputy-Speaker, pursuant to Standing Orders.
I would like to know has that Motion
been placed before the House to exalt
you into that position which you now
occupy, and if not, why not.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: I understand that the House is notified that the
Speaker is unavoidably absent from this
day's Sitting and that the House is also
notified that a vacancy exists in the office
of Deputy-Speaker, and that then I am
in order in presiding over this Assembly.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am not taking any
personal exception to you.
Mr.
DEPUTY-SPEAKER: I am
aware of that.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am only asking the
question and I am trying to guide the
House. I have read that Motion about
leave of absence for the Speaker, that
the Clerk at the Table informs the House
and then the Chairman of Ways and
Means proceeds to the Table, and, after
Prayers, takes the Chair. That refers to
the Deputy-Speaker. You occupy the
position of Deputy-Chairman, and, therefore, it requires a Motion in accordance
with Parliamentary procedure to exalt
you from the Deputy Chairmanship to
the position you now occupy.
Mr.
DEPUTY-SPEAKER:
If that
was carried out I do not know who would
preside in the circumstances in which we
are met at present.
Mr. BEATTIE: The circumstances
under which we are met at the moment
have not appeared on the Parliamentary
records of this House before, but it is
the duty of the Clerk to put the Motion.
Mr. HENDERSON: Would I be in
order in moving that this House do
adjourn until all the Cabinet Ministers
come home from abroad?
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: No.
A Motion under this rule cannot be
made-
(a) in the House unless the Speaker
or (after the announcement of
unavoidable absence of the Speaker)
the Chairman of Ways and Means or
(after an announcement of the unavoidable absence of the Chairman of
Ways and Means also) the Deputy-
Chairman is in the Chair.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am sorry I have to
go into this again. I think we will all
accept the authority of this book which
I hold in my hand. It is the key book
of the late Deputy-Speaker, Mr. Thomas
Moles, and the authority is the right
hon. Evelyn Denison, Speaker of the
British House of Commons from April
30, 1857, until February, 1872. Parliamentary law is founded on the rulings
given during that time. I am prepared
to accept the Clerk of the House as the
authority to put the Motion, and failing
the Clerk putting the Motion I am
opposed to the Deputy-Chairman accepting the Motion on his own behalf to exalt
him to the position of Deputy-Speaker.
Mr. NIXON: I do not want to make
your position more difficult. As a matter
of fact I would like to make it easier.
But apart altogether from the Standing
Orders the House is met under the
shadow of a loss on both sides and I
know that your position is difficult.

Oral Answers to Questions.
FLOODING IN DONEGALL ROAD
AREA.
1. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state if it is a fact that an Act of Parliament of 1911 authorised the Belfast
Corporation to construct a culvert to deal
with the flooding in the Donegall Road
area, and can he state the reason for the
delay in carrying out the proposed
works.
Mr. HANNA: In the unavoidable
absence of the right hon. Gentleman I
have been asked to reply.
I am informed by the Belfast Corporation that the Belfast Corporation Act of
1911 authorised certain works for the
prevention of flooding, including the construction of a culvert from Donegall Road
to the Lagan (Culvert No. 4), and the
construction of several other flood prevention works. Certain of these works
were put in hand before 1914, but during
At
the period of the War practically all
works of this nature were suspended.
the termination of the War it was evident, as a result of the enormous increase
in cost, that further loan sanctions
would be necessary to enable the proposed
works to be completed, and the statutory
powers conferred by the Act of 1911 for
carrying out the scheme had then lapsed.
The Corporation have under consideration at the present time the promotion of
a Bill to obtain the necessary powers to
enable them to proceed with the construction of this culvert.
Major McCORMICK: Arising out of
that answer may I ask the hon. Gentleman to explain why the Government has
not insisted on this corporate body
putting this measure in force since the
delay is causing thousands of pounds
damage in the district.
Mr. HANNA: I would inform the
hon. and gallant Gentleman that the
Act of Parliament was passed in 1911
and it could only be operative within a
period of either three or five years. This
Parliament was not in existence at that
time.
Major MCCORMICK: Is the order
not renewed for another five years?
OBSTRUCTION ON THE LAGAN.
2. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state when the obstruction on the Lagan
caused by the works of the proposed weir
and locks now under construction by the
Belfast Corporation will be cleared so
that normal traffic will not be impeded.
Mr. HANNA: I am informed by the
Belfast Corporation that the works
referred to by the hon. Member are now
completed and the contractor is removing
the plant.

Adjournment of House Moved.
move
Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to
"That this House do now adjourn." I
fully recognise that this privilege is only
allowed by the House in cases of
emergency. I do not think that an
emergency such as has arisen to-day has
ever occurred before in the history of
this House. The emergency relates not
only to the business of the House and its
good conduct, but to the proper control
of State affairs in the Six Counties. You
will fully appreciate that in moving the
Adjournment I mention no date. That
is a privilege reserved to the mover of the
Motion. If he feels disposed to mention
a date after the Motion has been considered and decided upon he can do so.
Why do I ask for the Adjournment of
the House? I have several reasons for
doing so. I am not allowed to refer to
a Motion standing on the Order Paper,
but I can make certain indirect statements which will lead members to realise
the condition we are getting into as a
representative assembly in this area.
We are at the moment the second
highest unemployed area in Great
Britain and Ireland. We are now being
compelled, through circumstances over
which we have no control, to be part and
parcel of a great rearmament scheme
which is likely to cost the nation and
taxpayers anything in the region of
fifteen hundred million pounds. That
being so I think it is the duty of every
representative in this House to see that
the return for that money is equivalent
to the returns made to the other countries
which compose the British Empire. We
have heard of outside controversy which
we are not permitted to mention in this
House. We have heard of controversy
with local authorities and with certain
Members of the British House of
Commons, and we can make up our own
minds as to what we think of the case
as it has been presented through the
Press. But we are not to take cognisance
of what appears in the Press as to the
position here. What we have to take
cognisance of is the real state of
Northern Ireland, and ask ourselves is
the Government carrying out the affairs
of the State in accordance with the requirements of the people. That is the
point on which I rely to move the
Adjournment.
I feel disposed to say now that the
administration by the Government of this
Province is sadly neglected. It has been
neglected to such an extent that we have
people suffering undue hardships due to
controversies over financial arrangements
between one authority and the Government and between the British Exchequer
and the Government of Northern Ireland.
We are overburdened with taxation, and
the Minister of Finance cannot exempt
himself from the position in which he has
placed Northern Ireland. He came to
this House five years ago and told us
that he was compelled by the British
Chancellor of the Exchequer to have a revaluation of this Province. We asked at
that time that the correspondence be
placed on the Table of this House, but
up to the moment the Chancellor of the
Exchequer here has failed to put it on
the Table, because no mandate ever came
from the Chancellor of the Exchequer
in Great Britain to revalue Northern
Ireland. As a result of all that we have
great hardships imposed on Northern
Ireland, and especially on working-class
tenants.
The next point is that the Minister
himself put to this House the point of
view of anomalies existing in Northern
Ireland, and said that the Measure which
the House was asked to pass was only an
anomaly Bill. The Measure was passed
in the expectation that the anomalies
which we
were all aware of would be
remedied. Instead of these anomalies
being put right more anomalies were
created, and the result of the whole work
of the Minister of Finance has been to
over-value Northern Ireland. The Minister of Finance is solely responsible for
the position in which overburdened ratepayers and taxpayers find themselves. I
think it is necessary that this House
should get down to real business, not in
an assembly of this kind, but in some
other way whereby we can bring greater
benefits to the people than we are doing
Adjournment Moved
Adjournment Moved
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
under the procedure we are attempting
to-day.
We are now working in an area which
I would call distressed-if not distressed,
then necessitous-due to unemployment.
We are paying the British Exchequer
our contribution towards distressed or
necessitous areas, and what are we getting
in return? Absolutely nothing.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Almost a million.
Mr. BEATTIE: I do not wish to

a million. If we are receiving a million

Fourteen factories are going to be

Mr. BEATTIE: The only thing is to
apply to applicants who are legally
entitled to receive their benefit the same
conditions as operate in Great Britain.
The law may be the same here, everything may appear to be the same, but
the administration here is not the same.
How many cases appear at the Courts of
Referees under the name of "misconduct." These cases of misconduct are
all turned down for a period of six
weeks. They would not be considered in
Great Britain as illegalities under the
Act. Not only that but you have increased the fees of the legal gentlemen
who sit in the chair at the courts. You
have reduced the number of claimants
at each court, and owing to the brainwave of some fanatic in the Department
a full statement that would take one
and a half hours to complete has to be
made out on each claim; while people
like myself have to wait in court for a
period of three or four hours in respect
of three or four cases. That is pure
waste. You say it is economy.
If that money was paid to the applicants instead of being paid to the legal
profession and for administrative costs,
I think the unemployed worker would be
greatly benefited. The legal gentlemen
have other ways and means of making a
living without recourse to that position.
An opportunity has been afforded to me
now to refer to the lamented death of

position at the beginning of the House
to what we would be at the end, owing
to the emergency that has arisen.
If you accept that ruling you will find
that it will not put you wrong, and if
you proceed with your ruling as outlined
by the Assistant Clerk, I certainly will
have to conform to it, as I do not want
to be obstreperous. I say again there is
an emergency, and I say with all the
emphasis at my command, that it is an
emergency to the extent that there are
over 80,000 people unemployed. As far
as our employment figure is concerned it
is supposed to be at its highest peak since
1929. We are supposed to be getting our
fair share of the money which is being
spent in Great Britain.
How are we receiving our fair share
with 80,000 people unemployed? Are
we receiving the same consideration in
connection with widows' and orphans'
pensions as they are in Great Britain,
and are we receiving the same consideration under the Unemployment Insurance
and Unemployment Assistance Acts as
they are in Great Britain? Therefore,
there has arisen in Northern Ireland an
emergency which requires immediate
attention and which requires the consideration of this House and their vote
upon it.
I would like to say that to me the
absence of the Prime Minister is a want
of respect to this House. If I were a
follower of his I certainly would have a
vote of censure passed upon him for his
continual absence from the business of
the House every year about this period.
I do not think it is fair to the Members
of his own party, but that is a matter not
for me but for them. I do not want to
proceed any further in regard to this
matter, and I will finish up on this point.
The Minister of Labour has said we are
getting a million pounds. There is to be
a half-crown and a shilling per head given
to the unemployed during Coronation
week in Great Britain, but we have not
heard of anything of that nature being
suggested in Northern Ireland. I would
request that that should be put into
operation here.
I would ask the Minister of Labour to
economise and not pay that million
pounds to the legal profession by making
the unemployment insurance administration cost twice as much as it did previously,
both in Great Britain and in Northern
Ireland, owing to the procedure which
has to be followed by the chairmen of
courts of referees because some head of
the Ministry of Labour gave instructions.
that it must be followed. No useful purpose is gained beyond the spending of the
money. We should go into the Lobby
and allow the Government to retire to
make up their mind as to what they are
going to do for Ulster and the Ulster
people. We will not mention a date for
meeting again until we are satisfied as to
what the Government are prepared to do
for the unemployed and the remainder
of the people in the Six Counties Therefore I move, "That this House do now
adjourn."

Question of Privilege.
a
Mr. MIDGLEY: May I raise
question of privilege. It concerns a communication sent out by the Magistrates'
Association of Northern Ireland. I
should like to read you an extract from
it and ask your ruling on the question of
privilege. The document, which
sent out from Donegall Square East,
dated 8th February, 1937, makes amongst
other statements the following :-
was
a
Ulster's Parliament consists of fiftytwo M.P.s, and the law cannot be
changed except by a majority. Ulster
is nominally at all events
democracy, yet this Bill, which changes
the most ancient part of our Constitution, was passed by only twenty M.P.'s,
the majority of whom were senior and
junior Ministers, and therefore bound
to obey the official Whip, otherwise
their highly-paid jobs would have been
endangered.
The only two men who dared vote
against the Government on this Bill
were Mr. Rowley Elliott, M.P., and
(in the Senate) Senator Leslie, and
these gentlemen were pilloried-at
least by a junior Minister-as unfit for
Parliament. All the others, about
thirty M.P.s, afraid of the electors on
the one hand and of forfeiting bureaucratic favour on the other, were too
cowardly to vote either for or against.
They were dumb, and thus on that
occasion their constituencies were disfranchised.
I ask your ruling as to whether that
constitutes a breach of the privileges of
this House.

Mr. Pollock's Tribute
9 MARCH 1937
I have received the King's Command
to convey to the Commons of Northern
Ireland the thanks of His Majesty and

Death of Rt. Hon. Thomas Moles and
Mr. J. J. McCarroll.
MR. POLLOCK'S TRIBUTE.
Mr. POLLOCK: I would crave the
indulgence of the House for a few short
moments if I may to pay a brief tribute
to the memory of one of our outstanding colleagues in this Parliament who
has recently passed on. I refer to our
late Chairman of Ways and Means, Mr.
Thomas Moles. I am sure hon. Members will expect me to express how deeply
we deplore the loss of one who played
such a lengthened and important part
in the proceedings of this House, and
who, if I may say so, enjoyed the confidence of all its Members in no small
degree.
Mr. Moles's conduct of the proceedings
as Chairman of Ways and Means and
also as Deputy-Speaker was characterised
with a fairness and impartiality which
won the respect of all parties of the
House; whilst his admonitions and
rebukes were always tinctured with a
vein of humour which immediately disarmed any feelings of irritation.
Might I strike a personal note? It has
been my privilege to have been brought
into close association with Thomas Moles
in many phases of his long and varied
public career, and it affords me a
melancholy satisfaction to-day to be permitted to bear testimony to his bold,
courageous and manly character, his
sympathy with the weak and suffering,
and his abhorrence of all meanness or
chicanery. I feel that his passing is a
distinct loss, not alone to this House,
but to the whole Province of Ulster, of
whose rights with voice and pen he was
such a sturdy and valiant champion.
I would be very remiss in my duty if I
did not also refer to the further loss
sustained by the House through the death
of the hon. Member for the Foyle
Division of Londonderry. In politics the
late Mr. McCarroll held views diametrically opposed to my own and to those
held by the majority of hon. Members
of this House, but nevertheless, his
modesty of bearing, fairness in debate,
and unfailing cheerfulness won the
respect of each of us. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
I feel sure that I will be expressing
the sentiments of hon. Members when I
say that we deeply regret his passing,
and that our heartfelt sympathy goes
out to his sorrowing relatives and friends.
Mr. HEALY: I should like to add my
tribute to that which the Deputy Prime
Minister has paid to the two distinguished Members of this House who
died during the recess. I think it will
not be out of place if I recall three coincidences in connection with their careers
which are of more than special
significance. Firstly, both were particularly well informed, having at their
command statistics and facts bearing on
discussions in this House and outside it.
Mr. Moles, as is well known, had made
himself familiar with the rather intricate
procedure of another assembly, and
although a layman and not a lawyer he
was recognised as an authority on the
procedure here for a very considerable
time. Although the Opposition found it
necessary on one or two occasions to
question his ruling and his methods-I
suppose the Opposition in all Parliaments
do the
same on occasions we never
doubted his honesty and his desire to be
fair to all.
The second coincidence in connection
with their career was that both should
have found as a common training ground
for their public life the profession of
journalism. To the last, notwithstanding their great interest in public affairs,
the two hon. Gentlemen never lessened
in their attachment to the profession in
which they were engaged. They differed
in their political outlook and in their
ideals, but I know that each of them
very sincerely admired the ability with
which the other conducted the great
newspaper over which he presided.
The third coincidence was that these
two departed gentlemen began their
careers in the Primatial City of Armagh
Deceased Members-
Business of the House
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Healy]
under rather humble circumstances, and
both rose to eminence and success in their
professions within a comparatively short
period.
As an associate and colleague of Mr.
McCarroll from the first moment he
entered this House, I know how firmly
he held his views. Honest in his own
faith he never questioned the honesty.
of others who differed from him. In
regard to the criticism which he uttered
in this House and the principles on which
it was founded he always refrained from
either uttering a bitter word to an
opponent or attributing to him a wrong
motive. He saw the way clearly and he
walked it fearlessly. Mr. McCarroll
loved Ireland very much and particularly
his own Province of Ulster, which he
served with all the intelligence and
ability with which God had endowed
him. I know, too, that some of the
ideals which he hoped to see realised in
his lifetime have been left over for other
men and for other times, but I think that
an occasion of this kind is one that should
broaden our political views no matter on
which side of the House we sit, should
show us the need for tolerance in our own
lives and greater charity in dealing with
each other.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I should like
to associate myself with the Motion
which has been so well spoken to by the
Deputy Prime Minister and my hon.
Friend the Member for South Fermanagh. I knew the late Mr. Moles for
40 years. During eleven very strenuous

So far as Mr. McCarroll is concerned,

deceased
as the relatives of the two

Business of the House.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That notwithstanding anything contained in Standing Order No. 1 (Sittings
of the House) the proceedings on Government Business, if under discussion when
the said business is postponed this day,
be resumed and proceeded with, though
opposed, after the interruption of business; That until the Easter Recess
Government business be not interrupted
under the provision of any Standing
Order regulating the sittings of the
House, may be entered upon at any hour,
though opposed, and after the conclusion.
of this day's sitting shall have precedence
at every sitting."-(The Minister of
Finance.)
Mr. MIDGLEY: I rise to oppose this
Motion. I do so because the Opposition.
point of view ought to be sufficiently
obvious without requiring any great
argument. There is a tremendous
amount of business to be done, not only
by the Government side but by the
Opposition in drawing attention to paradoxes and anomalies in regard to the
administration of our affairs, and it is
straining the credulity and the patience.
of the people to a great extent to ask us
to come here in the month of March,
after the House has been adjourned since
December of last year, and then in the
name of pressure of business ask us to
subordinate all our individual rights to
the requirements of the Government.
One thing I said this about a year ago,
and I repeat it because my words were
prophetic, as they usually are that it
makes the name of Parliamentary
institutions stink in public estimation the
way those in control handle them at the
present time. One thing that causes
people in Northern Ireland to look with
suspicion upon their Parliamentary
institutions more than anything else is
the way those who control Parliament
abuse the power placed in their hands
by a trustworthy people in years gone
by. The Government claim now that
from this time to the Easter Recess they
will require a first lien on business, that
is for the transaction of Government
business.
Business of the House
Business of the House
9 MARCH 1937
We, on the Opposition side, claim that
by our knowledge of the unemployment
problem, the suffering in agricultural
districts, and the depression generally at
the present time-these are subjects we
will raise, perhaps, more specifically on
the Supplementary Estimates-we claim
that on these grounds we are entitled to
have at least the same consideration as
any other section of the House. If it could
be demonstrated here to-day that
through some cause over which the
Government had no control they were
unable to provide the necessary time then
they would be able to put forward an
unanswerable case, but I submit that
those in control of this Parliament, even
though some Cabinet Ministers are not
present, could have spread the time that
this House meets over the year better
than they are doing, so that all aspects
of public affairs could be adequately
dealt with.
The hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr.
Nixon) has a question coming up, and
it is one that will require a good deal of
attention. I believe it is the intention
of the Government to give time for discussion. It is a question which deserves
every attention.
But I want to protest here and now in
the name of the working classes in
Northern Ireland who want to see this
Government functioning in the fullest
sense of the term with regard to social
service I want to protest against the
growing practice of this Government
having long intervals of inactivity, long
intervals during which so far as Parliament is concerned, the people may be
cast into the melting pot while the
Government hybernates for several
months. This practice, I repeat, is
bringing the name of our Parliamentary
institutions into disrepute, and as one
who believes in Parliamentary institutions I wish to lodge a protest against the
Government adjourning in December
and then meeting again in March and
asking that, owing to the shortness of
time, precedence should be given to
Government business. In days gone by
we have had examples in this Parliament
of Measures being rushed through without adequate consideration.
To-day we are called together and get
Supplementary Estimates and other
questions banded to us, and they are
going to be dealt with in the most severe
manner possible by the Government,
while questions of unemployment, questions of anomalies in pensions, questions
of how agricultural workers are being
treated by the Court of Referees and how
they are being compelled to accept
employment under rotten conditions, are
all going to be relegated to the background. I have said what I think is the
right attitude towards the Government,
and I am going to protest against the
Resolution submitted here, because I
think it is a travesty of Parliamentary
Government for the Government to ask
us to give up all our time to their requirements while they themselves have
deliberately misused their capacity or
misused their opportunity to the extent
of shutting us out from excess to Parliamentary Government for several months
past.

Business of the House
Business of the House
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Captain Dixon]
Member for Dock knows perfectly well

through important Measures of a financial character affecting the public
interest it has to put down a Motion of

In conclusion, I want to say definitely

Mr. NIXON: The statement made by
the Chief Whip does remove a good deal
of what is irritating in this Motion. If
he says that private Members will be
given time to discuss their Motions and
will be enabled to raise matters on the
Motion for the Adjournment there is no
harm done.
At the same time, I disagree with the Chief Whip when he says
that this is the usual procedure in all
Parliaments. It is a most unusual procedure at the opening of a Session, and
after the Government have been idle for
months and months, to bring in a Motion
like this. Such a Motion is usually only
tabled at the end of a Session when there
is something important the Government
wants to get out of the way, but it is
most unusual to bring it forward at the
beginning of a Session.
However, the statement of the Chief
Whip, if carried out and I have no doubt
he will carry it out-has taken away
the effect of what was a most irritating
Motion on the part of the Minister of
Finance. He is getting to that stage
when it will be very difficult for us to
stand it much longer. ("No, no.") We
have a good deal of sympathy with him,
but there comes a stage-and we will all
reach it, I hope, in the course of
years when no man has a right to
impose his peculiarities on the House.
("Shame.") A stronger word could be
used, but it would not be allowed. He
gets the notion that no one should at all
question what he does. For years in
this House he was treated with great indulgence and great sympathy, and I hope
we will see no more of these Motions. We
know that this Motion has not the

We get nothing in this House that we

There was another point made by the

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I am sorry the

Business of the House

There are a whole lot of questions I
hope to be able to debate in this House
before this Session of Parliament ends.
For instance, in some of the smaller
towns like Ballymoney and Portrush they
are very anxious to get houses for the
very poorest of the working classes, and
I hope to have an opportunity given to
me to put a reasonable case forward to
the Government on behalf of those
people. Then there is another question
which the Member for Mid-Antrim (Mr.
Minford) and I are interested in, and
that is the question of a minimum price
for flax. There is also another question
that has been hanging fire too long, and
that is the question of leaseholders.
Probably the most important of all the
questions, and one that this House
might devote even a week to, is that of
adult education. I am sure the Leader
of the House and the Chief Whip will
give us full opportunity to discuss in
this House all these important questions.
In the meantime, realising that it is in
the interests of the unemployed that this
money should be voted as quickly as
possible, I for one have no hesitation in
saying that I will vote for the Resolution
moved by the Minister of Finance.

He has to pay at least 5s for his lodgings.
How can he live on the 5s that remains

233 Unemployment Assistance Bill

9 MARCH 1937
Adjournment
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Assistance (Temporary
Provisions) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE: By
the permission of the House I beg to
move the Second Reading of this short
but very important Measure. As hon.
Members are aware, the effect of the postponement from the 1st March, 1935, of
the Second Appointed Day under the
Unemployment Assistance Act, 1934,
was that local authorities had to continue
to bear the cost of assisting the ablebodied industrial unemployed, a large
proportion of which would have been
borne by the Unemployment Assistance
Fund as from the 1st March, 1935, if this
postponement had not taken place. Let
me remind hon. Members that two
previous Measures of an almost identical
kind have been passed by this Houseone in the year 1935 and one in 1936.
The Unemployment Assistance (Temporary Provisions) (No. 2) Act, 1935,
and the Unemployment Assistance (Temporary Provisions) (Extension) Act,
1936, made provision for grants to local.
authorities for the year 1935-36, which
were calculated to put the local authorities concerned as nearly as possible in the
same financial position as would have
obtained if the Second Appointed Day
had not been postponed. The purpose of
the Bill now before the House is accordingly to empower the Government to continue to compensate the local authorities
for the year ending the 31st of the present.
month.
That is why it is so urgent and necessary
that this Measure should reach the Senate
on this day week, and it is also the reason
I am troubling the House at this hour of
the evening. It follows, therefore, that
this is the last occasion on which it will
be necessary to present a Bill of this
kind.
The only change in the present Bill, as
compared with similar previous Bills, is
that the amounts of the grants to individual authorities have been altered in
such a way as to conform more closely
to the expenditure incurred by each
authority. This redistribution will result in larger grants to Newry, Derry
City, Derry Rural District and Strabane
Urban District, while smaller grants will
be payable in other instances, notably
Belfast. I understand that the proposals
meet with the approval of the local
authorities concerned.
I do not think it is necessary to go
through all the details, and I ask the
House
Bill
to give the
a Second
Reading.

Bill committed to a Committee of the
whole House for to-morrow.

to attack as any port in England or
Scotland.
What has the Prime Minister of England done? There the whole country is
being fortified, and that work is creating
employment for people who would otherwise be idle. What is happening in
England, Wales, and Scotland to-day?
Through the great interest that the
Prime Minister of England is taking in
the matter, industries are going full
steam ahead; they are working night
and day on the manufacture of armaments for the protection of the civil
population. The coast of Great Britain
is being fortified. All those things are
being done to protect the people of Great
Britain from invasion and the possible
consequences of air attacks, and they are
providing work for the people.
What have you done in Northern
Ireland in the way of protecting the
people? Nothing. The Prime Minister
goes away too often. I contend that the
salary he receives now is quite big
enough for the small time that he spends
in this country. I do not want to be
disrespectful at all; I am only trying to
tell the truth. No other country in the
world would tolerate such a state of
affairs for five minutes. No other
Cabinet in the world would tolerate what
is taking place. There never was more
need for the presence of the Prime Minister at home than at present. Instead
of that the Prime Minister is away, and
not one solitary Member of the Cabinet
is looking after the interests of the
people in the way he ought to do. A
thousand and one things could be done
by the Prime Minister and the Cabinet
if they would only do them. Why is the
Prime Minister not at home to-day? Why
is he not in England demanding the
justice that Northern Ireland is entitled
to? The Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour have failed miserably to
cure unemployment. I know the Minister of Labour is broken-hearted about it.
I know that he realises that his Department has not the brains to solve this
important and growing problem.

too little concerned about the people.

contend that the place for the Prime

per

the time has come when the Government
should take other aspects of the question
into consideration rather than those they
had in mind when this Parliament was
first set up.
I am told by old Parliamentarians that
when this Parliament was first set up-
I was living in Belfast at that time, but
I did not see anything from the insidethe predominant feeling was that we must
keep up the standards and traditions of
the British Parliament. This Parliament was modelled more or less upon the
lines of the British Parliament although
we are only approximately one-thirtyseventh of the British Parliament in
regard to population, and I assume with
a taxable capacity of only one-thirtyseventh of that of Great Britain. We
ought to realise that our administration,
though not necessarily on the basis of
one-thirty-seventh, ought to have some
sort of proportion to our population,
the amount of our finances, and the
onerous duties people are called upon to
perform.
The Minister of Commerce to-night
spoke about public officers. Let me tell
him this. I completed thirteen years'
voluntary service two months ago in connection with the Belfast Corporation. I
have given far more service to the Belfast Corporation than ever I believe I
would be privileged to give to this Parliament. A tremendous amount of
labour is given voluntarily in the North
of Ireland about which people do not
know very much. If our services were to
be rewarded upon the basis of our value
to the community a far better case would
be made out for paying local government
representatives than any other kind of
representatives because of the enormous
amount of work done. The Minister of
Commerce might discover some individual
secretary who is paid more highly than
the officials here, but generally speaking
with the exception of Belfast, and
Belfast is 50 per cent. of the whole areawe have practically speaking a population
of half-a-million and we represent about
50 per cent. of the taxation resources of
Northern Ireland-the standards are not
nearly so high as those existing here in
Parliament.
I know certainly there are representatives in the Corporation who give services
which would make the services of some
of the Cabinet Ministers pale into
insignificance if a true comparison were
made. I know what it means to give
public service, and I like to see people
giving public service in proportion to
their capacity. Because of that I think
the Government should accept the spirit
of those who agree that the time has
arrived when something ought to be done
to reassure public opinion in regard to
this old, bad condition of things under
which masses of the people are living
perilously near the verge of poverty
whilst those at the top are in receipt of
incomes which under a reconstructed
society might not represent vast wealth
but in our present condition of society
represents wealth beyond the dreams of
avarice. I want the Committee to keep
that comparison in mind and to try to do
something in their time to effect an
equalisation which will bring to the masses.
something more in the shape of purchasing power. I do not want anybody to be
under the impression that I think all the
economic evils of society can be solved by
reducing the salaries of highly paid
officials. I know they cannot, but we
can do something to convey to the people
that an effort is being made to improve
the conditions of those at the bottom of
the social scale.

MINISTRY OF FINANCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £6,800 be granted to his Majesty for
the service of the year ending on the 31st
March, 1937, to defray the salaries and
expenses of the Ministry of Finance."
Mr. BARBOUR: I think I should
make a few remarks in regard to the increases shown against the Works Division.
I think hon. Members will agree that the
case of our technical officers is in a rather
different position to that of the usual
civil servant. It was found that many
of these officers had been recruited at
times when the remuneration in the particular profession was low as compared
with the salaries now obtainable in outside
employment; and that the attractive posts.
now on offer both in the British Civil
Service and in industry were likely to
deprive the Northern Civil Service of men
who could ill be spared. It, therefore,
became expedient to have the rates of
remuneration for professional and technical officers re-scaled in an upward direction and this has been done. The amounts
required under Subheads D and J are due
to under-estimating. It was not possible
to state exactly the amount of the costs
of the education levy Privy Council appeal
at the time the original Estimate was
framed. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I notice considerable
increases in this Estimate. In a speech made
by the hon. Speaker of this House in the
year 1921 when these offices were under
consideration he warned the Government
of that time to be very careful not to be
having a horde of highly-paid officials.
He also said:
I myself if it came to a division
would not vote against the Government
because they are placed in a very
difficult position, but I do feel that the
body of opinion is for Heaven's sake
practice economy and keep your staff
of officials as low as possible consistent
with efficiency.
These were very wise remarks, but have
they been followed in the Estimates we
are considering now? We are told by the
right hon. Gentleman, who introduced
the Estimate, that they must keep the
salaries of the civil servants up to a high
standard because of the highly technical
services required and outside competition.
I should like to ask has any permanent
head been angled after by any private
firm in this country since the establishment of the Northern Government? There
has only been one case where an official of
the Ministry of Home Affairs was allocated
to an office because of his able manipulation of a Bill that was passed into law.
In that case, however, no private firm
applied for his services, and, according
to public criticism, he is a most inefficient
official. I am not concerned with that
public criticism, but I can prove beyond
the shadow of a doubt that the public
do not appreciate the high qualifications.
of the heads of some departments in the
same way as the right hon. Gentleman.

officials receives £40 a week and she receives about 30s. She probably has to
keep four or five children on that miserable pittance, and she is not paid for her
holidays. The officials with £40 a week
get three weeks' or a month's holiday;
in fact, according to the hon. Member for
Pottinger, their whole life is a holiday,
because there is nobody here for nine
months in the year to worry them.
Then I want to speak about the
messengers in the Department of the right
hon. Gentleman. The right hon. Gentleman must remember that the messengers
in the Ministry of Finance are men who
Supplementary Estimates-

served in the Ulster Division.
Where is
the gratitude of this Government to the

The Minister of Finance has given great
service to this country in the past. We are
very proud of him, and I am sure the
Government are proud of him, too. But
what are the facts? The right hon.
Gentleman, who has received a huge
salary for many years, and who is responsible for this increase to the officials with
£40 a week, had been responsible for the
revaluation of Belfast, which has practically ruined many shopkeepers and
business men. I want to point out that
the right hon. Gentleman and these
gentlemen with £2,000 a year are the
people responsible for inventing the revaluation and increasing the rates of the
overburdened ratepayers of Belfast.

Mr. HENDERSON: It is not often I !

Assistance Scheme. Let me deal with

to increase the Fund's reserve. As to

meet the payments to those obtaining un-

wish to criticise the officials severely, but

are as many inspectors as would be able
to inspect the whole of Ireland. The
Department is overstaffed, and it must
be carefully looked after in the future.
This is one of the most important Estimates that could be placed before any
assembly. It would take a week to
criticise the Estimate properly, and yet
we are only devoting a short time to it in
debate.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.

the policy of the Government to foster
existing industries by the application of
derating to such industries. I am not
aware that the benefits of derating
enjoyed by any industry in the Province.
which satisfies the statutory conditions
have been withdrawn. In any event, I

statutory machinery exists whereby industrialists may appeal against any decisions.
of the Commissioner of Valuation.

4. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Acting

a resolution requesting the Government

to introduce schemes of superannuation

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
I have received a copy of the resolution
to which the hon. Member refers, which
would seem a somewhat extraordinary
one to come from the Belfast Corporation,
in view of the fact that that body has
had power to introduce a Contributory
Pensions Scheme for its own employees
since 1924, but has not yet done so, and
indeed has recently rejected a scheme of
this character. There would appear to
be no general demand for such powers
from other local authorities, and the
Government would hesitate to impose a
burden on the industries of the Province
which would handicap them as compared.
with their competitors in other parts of
the United Kingdom and elsewhere.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I beg to give notice
of my intention to raise this matter on

GAS ATTACKS FROM THE AIR.
5. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state what steps the Government are taking to protect the citizens of Northern
Ireland against a poison gas attack from
the air.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As the hon.
Member is aware, the question of air raid
precautions in Northern Ireland has been
the subject of consideration by a
mittee presided over by my hon. and
gallant Friend, the Member for East
Down, and as copies of the Report of that
committee have been circulated to all
Members of the House, the hon. Member
is no doubt acquainted with the recommendations which have been made. He
will, however, appreciate that in a matter
of this kind any action taken in Northern
Ireland must necessarily conform to the
arrangements for air defence in the
United Kingdom generally, and the
Report of the committee to which I have
referred is at present under the consideration of the Imperial authorities.
I may say, however, that so far as the
supply of gas masks is concerned, the
hon. Member may rest assured that
Northern Ireland, in common with the
rest of the United Kingdom, will receive
the necessary numbers of gas masks as
soon as the supply which is at present in
process of production is available.

I may also say that arrangements have
been made by the Ulster Joint Committee
of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem

Civil Anti-Gas School at Falfield, and at

these organisations are actively engaged
in carrying out the training of their

Mr. BARBOUR: In moving this Vote
on Account, I propose to depart from
the usual practice of merely moving it
formally and to avail myself of the opportunity to deal with a matter which
appears to be of considerable public concern, namely, the financial relations
between the Exchequer and the ratepayers of Belfast. It seems to me that
I may with all Parliamentary propriety
deal with the matter in this way, as the
sums to be voted contain substantial
payments to the Belfast Corporation.
The issues in question are five-fold;
firstly, the question of unemployment
costs; secondly, the education rate;
thirdly, the comparison between the Government grants made to the city of
Belfast as compared with the grants made
to county areas; fourthly, the recent
proposals of the Government in regard
to grants in aid of mental hospitals, and
lastly, the suggestion that each local
authority might claim to be credited
with the proceeds of the motor licence
duty collected within its area,
a suggestion which, I agree, would be of
immense benefit to the ratepayers of
Belfast.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
Before dealing with these particular
issues in detail, may I state with a full
sense of responsibility that there is no
justification for any statement that
Belfast is heavily penalised as compared
with the other local government bodies
throughout the whole of Northern Ireland, as the statement which I propose
to make will clearly demonstrate.
As regards unemployment costs, I am
sure that hon. Members will agree that
too much has already been written and
said on this subject. The plain fact is
that after 1st April next if the Government proposals are approved by this
House the Exchequer will be bearing in
respect of Belfast an expenditure on
unemployment assistance of £850,000,
and the ratepayers £127,000, including
a contribution of £56,000 towards State
expenditure on this service. As the proposal to levy this payment of £56,000
will have to be confirmed by a Bill, I
consider that its merits or demerits can
well remain over for debate after the
Easter Recess when that Measure is
introduced.

persons in receipt of distress relief in

I have no reason to believe that the

I now come to the second point,
namely, the effect which revaluation has
had upon the education rate. This subject was dealt with at a conference held
at Stormont on the 24th September, 1935,
with representatives of the various local
authorities in Northern Ireland. The
conference was the outcome of the statutory undertaking in the Valuation Act
of 1932 that before revaluation took
effect the Government would review the
capacity of the local rates, based upon
the new valuations, to bear the expenditure required by the law then in force
to be defrayed out of those rates. The
discussion at that conference mainly
centred on the effect which revaluation
would have in reducing derating grants,
but the representatives of the local
authorities also pressed that the
education rate should for all time be
related to the old valuations.
1s
The question of derating was satisfactorily settled by compromise, but in
regard to education my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, explained
that he could not agree that is on the
new valuations was in any way an
exorbitant contribution by local authorities towards the cost of the Government's
educational expenditure. He agreed,
however, contemporaneously with the
increase of the produce of the education
rate he would per contra increase the
Government's grant in aid of the
expenditure of local education authorities
by relating the Government's maximum
