This was accepted by all representatives
present as a reasonable solution. It is
regrettable that the Belfast Corporation
were not separately represented at this
conference, but the Government cannot

to be present. The result of the arrangement is that the education rate in
Belfast, which will next year amount to

leaving the net increase to the Corporation at only £15,680, equal to less than
ld in the £.

The last point, namely, that Belfast

These issues, however, are very minor
ones, but minor issues often obscure the
main issues, and in view of the publicity
which has been accorded to them I feel
impelled to focus attention again upon
the major question of the incidence of
expenditure in Northern Ireland
between rates and taxes, not only as
regards unemployment relief and educational expenditure, but expenditure on
other services. My right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Finance, has emphasised,

appreciated even as yet-that in Northern
Ireland not only is the burden resulting
from derating relatively much greater

of educational expenditure and police

per cent., and in the case of the police

of the thousands of agricultural labourers

put some of the great business firms of

We
We are all very proud of these men, and

497 Unemployment Assistance

11 MARCH 1937
Supplementary Estimates
The taxpayers of the country are
clamouring for you to reduce your Estimates, which every year are increasing
instead of diminishing. It is not due to
legislation which is of any benefit to the
taxpayer. Therefore, I appeal to the
Government to put their house in order
so that when the Minister of Finance
presents his next Budget he will be able
to announce that expenditure has been
greatly reduced, and that the taxpayer
will get the benefit of that reduction.
Question put, and agree to.
Resolution to be reported on Tuesday;
Committee to sit again on Tuesday.
Unemployment Assistance (Temporary
Provisions) [Money].
Resolution reported:
That for the purpose of any Act of
the present Session being an Act 'to make
provision, as respects the twelve months
ending on the thirty-first day of March,
nineteen hundred and thirty-seven, for
the financial adjustments necessary by
reason of the Second Appointed Day for
the purposes of the Unemployment Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934, having been
postponed until the first day of April in
the said year; and for purposes connected with the matter aforesaid' it is
expedient to authorise the payment out
of moneys provided by Parliament of
any grants which may become payable
under the said Act of the present Session
to the County Borough Councils, Urban
District Councils and County Councils in
the said Act mentioned, such grants
being of the amounts in the said Act
specified."
Resolution agreed to.

Mr. MIDGLEY: In pursuance of
notice given in this House yesterday, I
now rise to direct the attention of the
Minister of Labour and of the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Labour to the question contained in the
private notice which I gave to the
Minister yesterday. I asked the Minister the following question:-
Whether it is a fact that wages in
the retail drapery trade in Northern.
Ireland are deplorably low, and that
those employees who are desirous of
organising as a preliminary to negotiations for improved wages and conditions
are being dismissed by certain employers and thrown on to the Labour
Retail Drapery Trade Wages
Adjournment-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
Exchange, and, if so, whether he is
prepared to take immediate steps to
stop this victimisation and call a conference of employers' and workers'
representatives in the trade on the
lines of the conference convened by
the Minister of Labour in Great
Britain.
This is a matter of grave urgency so far
as the workers of Belfast are concerned,
and I wish to ask for an assurance from
the Minister. I know that the right
hon. Gentleman has had to go, because
of another pressing engager ent, but the
Parliamentary Secretary will answer in
his stead, and I make a very strong
appeal because of the urgency of this
matter. I want the intervention of the
Minister along the same lines as the
Minister of Labour in Great Britain. I
want to quote my authority for making
this statement. Here is "The Drapers'
Record," dated 20th February, 1937. It
states:
As long ago as December 30, 1933,
retailers were urged to face up to the
situationthat refers to wages and conditions—
..
The only way in which wages can be
raised with fairness to all concerned
is to give them statutory status
All the old arguments against interference with business by regulating
wages may have been true in their day,
but times have changed, and store
leaders must change with them.
As the latter have refused to change,
Government pressure is now being
do so.
exerted to compel them to

trade associations cannot or will not

is no doubt whatever.
That is a comment upon the dispute at
Messrs. Lewis's, Ltd., in regard to a
wages' agreement covering all their
shop assistants.
The same journal dealing on page.
with the same question-this is an employers' journal-said this:-
The significance of the agreement
cannot be overrated, especially as regards its probable influence on the
course of the conferences proceeding
(at the instance of the Minister of
Labour) to discover whether it is possible to establish machinery
voluntary wage regulation.
for
That
aspect of the matter is clear from the
speeches at the signing of the pact last
week.
The pact referred to was the agreement
between Messrs. Lewis's, Ltd., and the
shop assistants. The head of Messrs.
Lewis's, Sir Frederick Marquis, remarked
that:
"The Minister of Labour convinced
me that it was of the greatest importance that somebody should seek to
enter into an agreement with the trade
unions in order that there should be
some basis for subsequent discussion."
There is still in several quarters the
strongest possible objection to anything
that savours of "Unionisation"; but,
sooner or later, everyone will have to
recognise that if effective voluntary
machinery is to be set up the employees' side must be represented.
Those who object to meeting the trade
unions on principle will have to face
up to the reality, which is that the
alternative is a trade board or some
other form of statutory regulation.
I just want to read another quotation.
At the annual meeting of the Drapers'
Chamber of Trade there was a contribution to the discussion by Mr. W. L.
Barber, Fulham, a member of the
Chamber. He also revealed that negotiations were in progress with the Ministry
of Labour and he said this to the conference:
It was not a bit good of sitting on
the fence, as they had been doing,
waiting to see what other people did
to-morrow. The Chamber should give
a lead. Either it would have to come
forward on its own initiative and make
suggestions to the Ministry, or that
Department would step in without any
consideration from them whatever.
I represent, along with my colleague.
in Belfast, a section of the organisation
that is responsible for the distributive
workers in Great Britain, and in pursuance of the policy that is being carried
out in Great Britain at the present time
between the employers, the Ministry of
Labour and the trade unions, we looked

upon it as our special prerogative to see
to it that the same machinery should be
brought about here. We were not guided
in this decision by any malice or ill will,
nor was there any intention of placing
obstacles in the way of legitimate transactions in business on the part of any
trader in the city of Belfast. All we
proceeded to do was to try to get information as to what their desires were in
this matter. We found there was
clamant demand, so far as the workers
were concerned, for this kind of a situation to be developed and we proceeded
to hold meetings at which the workers
could attend or not, just as they decided, and they could join the
organisation if they liked. We made
a
representations to certain employers and
in some cases our overtures were received
in the spirit in which we intended them.
Just within the past few days a serious
development has taken place. One of
the leading firms in Royal Avenue,
Belfast, trading under the name of
Sinclairs, which firm is owned
Councilor F. Collier, Belfast, who is not
unknown to some of those sitting in this
House, has decided to take up an attitude of bitter and unreasonable hostility
to the organisation of the workers.
by
Mr. GRANT: Is he a member of the
Belfast Corporation?
Mr. MIDGLEY: He is a member of
the Corporation. I am sorry my influence has not had a good effect on him.
I think he sits for Pottinger Ward. I
raised this matter yesterday and the
Minister's reply was as follows:-
No representations on this subject
have been made to my Department by
any interested party. If the hon.
Member has evidence which he would
like to bring to my notice I will carefully consider it.
I am making the representations now
because I am interested. I am doing this
on behalf of the organisation and on
behalf of my colleague who is in direct
touch with all the employees in the retail
drapery trade. I want to bring to the
Minister's notice some facts which will
make him act with all convenient speed.
Mr. Collier has been interviewed twice
this week by Mr. Kirk, of the National
Union of Distributive and Allied
Workers, and myself. For the purpose of brevity the organisation is
known as the "Nudaw." We are going
to amalgamate with the Shop Assistants'
Union, which carried out this agreement
with Messrs. Lewis's, and our organisation will have a membership of
approximately 250,000. The Ministry on
the other side is making a concerted
effort in this trade to get some machinery
brought into being where no machinery
has hitherto existed. It is because our
industrial policy is largely a reflex of
the industrial policy on the other side
that I am sure it will be the desire
of the Ministry that some such effort
should be made here as is being made
in Great Britain. The Ministry have
established trade boards where there is
a trade organisation and sweating
conditions. In the retail drapery trade,
which is a sweated industry, there is an
utter lack of organisation and an overwhelmning case can be made out for some
kind of protection 'or negotiating
machinery. In order to get that
machinery we must appeal for the cooperation of all interested. The main
obstacle in Belfast is Councillor F.
Collier. He is a law unto himself. He
is a mental anachronism, an intellectual
anarchist, who owes allegiance to no law
nor to any code of ethics except what he
thinks ought to be done. His conception
of what ought to be done is to barter
with the unemployed to the detriment of
those employed in his firm, and who are
employed at the lowest rates of wages.
We have got some statistics and
reliable data. We have the names and
addresses of the people concerned. Case
No. 1 is that of a man, 28 years of age,
a skilled drapery assistant, having served
eleven years in the firm, and his wages
are 22s 6d a week. Case No. 2-25 years
of age, ten years' service, an exceptionally
skilled man and supposed to be one of
the most outstanding men employed by
Mr. Collier, and he enjoys the magnificent
sum of 30s a week. Case No. 3-26
years of age, eleven years' service, a man,
30s a week. Case No. 4-28 years of
age, thirteen years' service, 35s.
No 5-23 years of age, eight years'
service, having served his complete
apprenticeship and since acted as a
journeyman, wages 20s. Case No. 6-a
lady this time, 21 years of age, five
years' service, wages 15s a week.

Mr. MIDGLEY: Case No.
years of age, ten years' service, 15s a

Collier, we find that girls from 16 to 20
years of age are paid from 6s to 10s per
week-6s, 7s 6d, 9s and 10s. The
average wage of the adult female
assistant in the firm-I want you to think
of this of all ages, experience, and
length of service works out at 12s 6d a
week. It might be said by someone subsequent to this that he also pays a commission. He pays a commission of 3d in
the £, but I want to give the conditions
under which that is paid. It only
becomes operative after each assistant has
sold £14 worth of goods, and the 3d
becomes operative on the first £ above
£14. This 3d in the £ is not payable
upon credit trade or upon clubs, and it
is not payable upon sales to members of
the staff. This 3d in the £ commission
is not paid upon credit trade, and every
Member of this House knows how credit
trade is growing in the shape of drapery,
and how clubs are carried on. They must
be transactions outside these three
categories. It is only paid after
assistants have £14 of trade to their
credit. As from 70 to 80 per cent. of
Mr. Collier's trade is done by clubs that
means that 70 or 80 per cent. is excluded
from the operation of the 3d in the £
commission. These facts are an epitome
of the conditions which prevail in that
firm.
What are Mr. Collier's reactions to an
attempt by goodwill to solve the situation? I know the man by contact in the
Corporation, but this is the first time I
have come into contact with him in his
own business. In order to get him to
discuss the question we went to the firm.
We discussed it twice this week at
separate conferences. We pointed out
that certain things were taking place in
his firm. We pointed out that he was
carrying on a policy of hostility to the
workers exercising their constitutional
right under the Trades Disputes and
Trades Union Act. We told him we had
no desire to cut his jurisdiction or do
anything that would lessen his authority
in the firm. We indicated what was
being done in Great Britain by
the Imperial Ministry. He remained
adamant. Every person who, of his own
volition, has joined the trade union as a
preliminary to negotiating machinery,
has been dismissed and has become a
charge on the public funds.
On Monday night last, in the
Y.M.C.A., Wellington Place, I went
round after the League of Nations meeting to give my colleague some assistance.
At that meeting Councillor Collier had
two understrappers who would get 28 6d
a week extra for practising all the
duplicity that Councillor Collier wants
them to practise. They were there in
their capacity as spies to report to
Councillor Collier on Tuesday the
number of people from his firm who
attended that meeting. The workers
themselves told us on Monday night
about what had happened. They knew
of the presence of the two gentlemen concerned, and that the likelihood was that
they would be dismissed at the week-end.
Since then we have been informed that a
list of all the people who have taken an
interest in the trade union and were
present at that meeting, has been made
out by Mr. Collier, and that he intends.
to put into operation the same principle
that he put into operation last Saturday night and without warning dismiss
all the men who had joined the union
up to that time.
Mr. GRANT: Shame.
Mr. MIDGLEY: That has created a
feeling of dismay through the trade
union. It is a remarkable tribute to the
workers and I want hon. Members to
bear this in mind-that despite the fact
that almost every employee in Councillor
Collier's place would be better off in
receipt of unemployment benefit than
they would be in receipt of the wages
from the firm-despite that fact, so great
is the desire of the people to remain at
work that they are prepared to sacrifice
almost anything. That is a striking
tribute to the working classes. He dismissed all the men-magnificent workers
about whom we have had tributes paid.
We interviewed Mr. Collier and pointed
this out. I taxed him directly on the
grounds I have alleged. He said he
would take some time that day to consider the matter. He rang up the office

I am appealing through the House of
Commons, as the mouthpiece of the
nation as the sounding board of the
nation to the Minister responsible for
good conduct in industrial affairs in the
relationship
between employers and
employees here. I have indicated what
has been and is being done in Great
Britain, and I am sure it is the wish
of the Ministry that some sort of
machinery should be provided here.
Something has got to be done. I say
this without malice or bitterness. When
one comes up against such an unswerving
enemy as Councillor Collier, against a
man with such distorted ideas, such
peculiar notions and such disordered
mentality with regard to his rights in the
community, one is almost driven beyond
the verge of rational action. Here is a
man who is spreading dismay and
demoralisation in the trade. We have
exhausted every possible avenue of
negotiation and hope. We come to the
Ministry now and ask them,
immediate step, to prevent this man exploiting the unemployed, to deprive this.
man of the right to do what he is doing
at the present time-paying women
wage which is a direct incentive to
prostitution. I allege that men like
Councillor Collier, who pay these wages,
are responsible for a great deal of that
problem, not only in Belfast, but
elsewhere.
as an
a
In face of these facts I ask the Ministry to take the earliest possible opportunity that is to-morrow-of bringing
influence to bear on Councillor Collier to
desist from this course of action, which
is not only immoral but scandalously
inhuman, a degradation and disgrace,
which ought to fill any rational man
with shame. I ask the Ministry, in protection of their own economic interests,
to prevent him exploiting this policy.
At the same time I ask the Ministry to
bring pressure to bear on him to do what
other employers have indicated, and that
is, to recognise the creation of some
machinery to bring about that better
understanding in industry which has
already been created in the majority of
other industries not only here but in
Great Britain.
I feel strongly on this point, because
I have, in the course of my life, as an
negotiator and individual, to come in
contact with some of the results of the
Labour Exchange on this policy. Other
Members can speak with extensive
knowledge also. I feel it is a burning
shame that in 1937 we have such a case
after the progressive social legislation we
have had, after the expressions of
opinion we have had throughout the
British Empire in regard to the efficacy
of trade unionism to bring about sweet
reasonableness in industry generally. I
have quoted Mr. Baldwin as saying that
without trade unionism industry and
commerce would have been reduced to a
state of chaos. I quoted the opinions of
the Minister of Labour, the Parliamentary Secretary and Cabinet Ministers,
that it was the desire of the Cabinet, as
Mr. Baldwin desired, to see trade
unionism develop right through industry.
But Mr. Collier is living in the long
past. He is living in a condition, so far
as ideals are concerned, that bears
absolutely no relationship to the economic
problem or to ordinary methods of to-day.
I am going to ask the trade unions in
Belfast and the transport service to give
us the moral and material assistance to
which we are entitled in trying to have
the grievances of these people redressed.
I make a final appeal to the Parliamentary Secretary to set the wheels in
motion to-morrow, so that the problem
will be dealt with as a matter of extreme
urgency.

ings mentioned by the hon. Member.

Mr. Collier will be made to realise that

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 16th March, 1937.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Papers Presented.

Oral Answers to Questions.
TEACHERS' ECONOMY CUT.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he is prepared to
restore the economy cut of 1931 to all
public elementary teachers in the forthcoming Budget.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): It is not the present intention
of the Government to make any alterations in the reconstituted and stabilised
salary scales of public elementary school
teachers recently promulgated.
Mr. BEATTIE: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman whether it is the
intention of the Government to put in
their own pockets part of the economy
cut of 1931 taken from the public
elementary school teachers, and whether
that is a proper distribution of the prosperity wave which has been outlined by
the right hon. Gentleman in speeches he
has made outside?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is a very large
question and it is not one that it is
competent to discuss by question and
answer.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman whether he is
aware that the public elementary school
teachers will not sit quietly in future as
they have done in the past while treatment of this kind is meted out to them.
CONTRACTORS AND THE FAIR
WAGES CLAUSE.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he is aware that Government contracts have been given out
to the woodmaking firms of Messrs.
Flanigan, Rowntree & Glendinning, of
Richhill, and Messrs. C. Rowntree,
Stoneybridge, and Messrs. Donaghy, of
Portadown, in Richhill and Portadown,
who are not observing the Fair Wages
Clause, and what action he is prepared
to take
against these firms for the
irregularity.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am aware that my
Ministry has placed contracts for the
supply of furniture, after open competition, with the three firms of Messrs.
Flanigan, Rowntree and McDonagh (not
Donaghy). No contracts have been
awarded to any of the other firms
mentioned in the question.
Representations have in recent years
been made to my Ministry alleging noncompliance with the Fair Wages Clause
by the firms mentioned, and the matter
has been exhaustively discussed with
representatives of the Belfast Furnishing
Trades' Joint Committee. As a result
the Ministry came to the conclusion that
in all the circumstances no evidence had
been produced of specific infringement of
the Fair Wages Clause.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask,
is it not a fact that the Joint Furnishing
Trades have tabled figures proving beyond a shadow of doubt that the Fair
Wages Clause is not conformed to by
firms receiving these contracts, and in
view of that state of affairs is he prepared to withdraw these contracts from
these firms mentioned in the question?
Mr. POLLOCK: No. I may add
that no complaints have been received by
those who are engaged by my Ministry
from the workpeople employed by the
firms mentioned. There is no standard
rate of wages in Richhill district and,
accordingly, there is no fair wage in the
ordinary sense. Belfast Trade Unionists
some years ago engineered a strike
among the workers in these areas, without success, and consequently there have
been large defections from their unions.

Oral Answers
16 MARCH 1937
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman's attitude really not to give
standard wages? Is he prepared to take
immediate action to make the firms in
the furnishing trade keep up the
standard?
THE LOANS GUARANTEE ACTS.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is prepared to insert
a Clause in the Loans Guarantee Acts
that all work covered by this Act must,
as far as possible, be carried out by
workers in Northern Ireland.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is unnecessary to
introduce a Clause in the Loans Guarantee Acts on the lines suggested by my
hon. Friend seeing that the agreements
entered into between the Ministry, the
shipowners and the shipbuilders under
that Act already embody a provision
almost in identical words with those suggested by the hon. Member.
I might remind the hon. Member that
our guarantees cover in general not more
that 60 per cent. of the contract price,
and it would be entirely wrong for this
Government to impose onerous conditions
directed against Great Britain in
relation to any part of the balance of 40
per cent. where the shipbuilders are
satisfied that on economic grounds certain
work can best be carried out in their
establishments across the water or by a
sub-contract to firms in Great Britain.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that 70 per cent. of
the finished work for these ships is
covered by the Loans Guarantee Acts;
is he aware that the work can be as
economically carried out by Northern
Ireland workers as where it comes from.
In view of Northern Ireland workers
being assured work under the Loans
Guarantee Acts, I think the right hon.
Gentleman is entitled to give cover to
these trades who are suffering by this
Motion.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am certainly sure
that the shipbuilders are the best authorities in regard to this matter and I do
not care to interfere with them.
NORTHERN IRELAND
INCOME TAX.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Finance whether, owing to the
general revaluation, the income tax
yield from Northern Ireland has been
at least £500,000 in excess of the total
in the last year of the old valuation.
Mr. POLLOCK: As I have already
informed the hon. and learned Member
in my reply to his question of the 27th
February, 1936, and in a letter sent to
him on the 4th June, 1935, I regret
that it is not possible for me to give him.
the information which he desires as the
Imperial Authorities concerned inform
me that for various reasons it is not possible to give estimates of the yield of
income tax under the various schedules.
If, however, the hon. and learned
Member will refer to my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Commerce's
Budget speech of 14th May of last year
he will find that the estimated increase
in income tax and sur-tax for the current
financial year
is given at the figure of
£445,000; £130,000 of which is due to
the increase of 3d in the standard rate
of income tax; and the remaining sum
of £315,000 is due partly to an expected expansion in income tax consequent on improved trade and partly to
an expected increase in income tax consequent on revaluation. From these
figures the hon. Member will appreciate
that his figure of £500,000 as the increase
in income tax yield consequent on re
valuation in the current year is very
wide of the mark.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the
Minister what is the secret of this strict
economy in giving information on this
point?
Mr. POLLOCK: The British Government is the best authority on that matter,
and I have entire dependence on them
for the returns of income tax. I have
no direct means of assessing income tax.
Mr. NIXON: Does the Northern
Government get credit from the Imperial
Government for income tax collected
here?
Mr. POLLOCK: Exactly.

Mr. CAMPBELL: Would the right

ACCOMMODATION FOR
DISPOSSESSED TENANTS.
com-
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state what
provision he has made for the tenants
who are likely to be put out of their
homes due to the opening of the by-pass
road running through Foundry Street
and district; whether he is prepared to
safeguard any disturbed tenant from an
increase of rent in the accommodation
provided; and whether he is prepared to
guarantee that the houses provided will
be in the same area.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The hon. Member
may rest assured that every care will be
taken to ensure that no hardship will be
suffered by these persons as a consequence
of the construction of the by-pass road.
I am not yet in a position to say what
arrangements it will be possible to make,
but the hon. Member may take it that
the point which he has raised will be most
carefully borne in mind.
GLENARD ESTATE HOUSES.
have
6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
the houses on the Glenard estate contain
a large quantity of highly inflammable
material known as plasterboard; whether
he is aware that several fires
already occurred in the district, that
many of the houses are flooded underneath the floor board of kitchens and
sculleries to a depth of two feet from
which a foul odour emanates, and that
over £100,000 has been granted in subsidies; and, in view of the health of the
residents, whether he is prepared to hold
a public inquiry into the conditions of the
houses on this estate.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am advised
that the plasterboard used in these
houses is similar to that used elsewhere
in non-subsidy houses and in public
buildings, and that it is not more highly
inflammable than many other materials
used in the construction of houses. There
have been five fires in houses on the
estate, but in only one case was the house
seriously damaged. In no case does it
appear that the pasteboard-I beg your
pardon-plasterboard had anything to
do with the outbreak.
I have already received representations
regarding water lying under the floors of
some of the houses and have brought these
to the notice of the Belfast Corporation,
which is the sanitary authority, so that
any necessary action may be taken. As
I have no reason to suppose that the Corporation will fail to carry out its duty I
see no grounds for holding a public
inquiry into the matter.
I may add that the amount of the
subsidy paid by Government in respect
of houses on this estate was £37,925.
your
Mr. BEATTIE: I agree with
designation of pasteboard in this case. Is
the Minister aware that grave dissatisfaction exists amongst the public, the
tenants, the builders and agents, and in
view of that dissatisfaction will he have
a public inquiry held to give all sides the
opportunity of proving their case?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have explained to the hon, Member that I have
brought to the notice of the Belfast Corporation certain defects in the property,
and I have no reason yet to suppose that
the Corporation will not take steps to
have these defects, in regard to the
sanitary arrangements, made right.
LICENSED CLUBS.
7. Mr. CRAWFORD (for Mr. Elliott)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state the number of
licensed clubs in existence, respectively,
for the years 1930, 1931, 1932, 1933,
1934, 1935 and 1936.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The particulars asked for by the hon. Member
are as follows:-1930, 77; 1931, 76; 1932,
77; 1933, 78; 1934, 77; 1935, 78;
1936, 78.

NEW LICENSED HOTELS.
8. Mr. CRAWFORD (for Mr. Elliott)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state the number of new
hotels which have been licensed since the
passing of the 1927 Licensing Amending
Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Licences have
been issued to 12 new hotels (including
one provisional licence) since the passing
of the Intoxicating Liquor and Licensing Act (N.I.), 1927. The number of
such new licences would, however, include
licences granted in respect of re-opened
hotel premises where a licence had
previously been in existence but had been
allowed to lapse.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN
DERRY.
9. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
if any labourers' cottages have been built
in Derry rural district during the past
15 years; whether he will consider the
appointment of a Commission to expedite
the building of such cottages in that and
other districts; how many decrees for
possession have been issued during the
past two years in the city of Derry against
persons living in cellars, stables and
overcrowded tenements; how many closing
and demolition orders have been made by
the Derry Corporation during the same.
period in respect of old houses, and how
many tenants have been evicted therefrom without any provision for the housing of such tenants; and whether
Government grant or
or a long-term loan
can be made available to facilitate the
acquisition by the Corporation of slum
areas with a view to the building thereon
of decent working-class dwellings.
a
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer
to the first part of the hon. and learned
Member's question is in the negative,
but I would remind him that for a
number of years past the operation of the
Labourers (Ireland) Acts has been
suspended. Since the passing of our
recent Act, enabling the resumption of
such operations to be commenced, the
Council of the Derry rural district has in
process of preparation a scheme for the
building of 125 cottages, and all the other
rural district councils in Londonderry,
and most of the rural district councils
elsewhere, are also preparing schemes. In
these circumstances I see no grounds for
appointing a Commission as suggested.
I regret that in the time available it
has been impossible to obtain the other
information asked for by the hon. and
learned Member, but with regard to the
last part of his question, I may say that
under the Housing of the Working
Classes Acts the Government grants longterm loans to all urban authorities for
the purpose of financing housing schemes.
ROAD ACCIDENTS.
10. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
how many road accidents happened in
Northern Ireland during the operation
of the Locomotives on Highways Act,
1896, with a maximum speed of 14 miles
an hour for motor-cars; how many during
the operation of the Motor-Car Act, 1903,
with a maximum speed of 20 miles an
hour; and how many since the abolition
of a speed limit; and during this latter
period how many of these accidents have
been fatal, and whether he proposes to
introduce a speed limit for built-up areas.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I regret that
I have no information whatever as to the
number of traffic accidents which occurred
in any year prior to the year 1922, and
that I am, therefore, unable to give the
hon. and learned Member the particulars
which he desires. Such statistics were
not regularly compiled by the Ministry
before the year 1927. The hon. and
learned Member will, however, appreciate
that such statistics, even if available,
would offer no basis for comparison with
conditions at the present date.
As regards the last part of the hon.
and learned Member's question, I may
say that I am not satisfied that the introduction of a speed limit for built-up
areas, on the lines of the system adopted
in England, would secure the desired
result, but we are at present considering
the imposition of a speed limit in certain
towns where this would seem to be likely
to prove effective and capable of satisfactory enforcement.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to give
notice that I will draw attention to this
matter on the Adjournment of the
House.

NEWTOWNARDS ROAD POLICE
BARRACKS.
12. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware of
the unsuitability of the Newtownards
Road Police Barracks from a health point
of view, and whether he will take
immediate steps to provide new accommodation in this area at the earliest possible
date.
aware
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am
that the accommodation at the Newtownards Road barracks is generally unsuitable, and the question of providing
alternative accommodation is receiving
the consideration of my Ministry in consultation with the Department of my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, and I hope that we shall shortly
be in a position to provide better accommodation than the existing barrack,
which I quite agree is not suitable.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the Minister also
survey the outlying police barracks convenient to this area and provide new
accommodation?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am continually doing that, and I hope before
long the police in Belfast will be properly
housed.
DEVONSHIRE ACCORDION BAND.
13. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the regulations governing the
marching or parades of bands through
the streets, and whether he will state the
circumstances in the case of the Devonshire Accordion Band, which was not
allowed to play loyal music in certain
thoroughfares of Belfast by the action of
the police on a recent occasion.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There are no
regulations or bylaws governing the
parades of bands.
Under the common law it is the duty
of the police, where they anticipate that,
as a result of the action of any individual
or body the public peace may be endangered, to take such steps as they consider necessary to prevent such a situation
arising. It was in accordance with their
common law duty that the police took the
action referred to by the hon. and gallant
Member in his question.
I am glad to say that in the vast
majority of cases the bands cordially cooperate with and assist the police in falling in with any arrangements which have
for their object the preservation of the
peace in the city.
Major McCORMICK: Are there no
regulations governing bands parading
streets? May I also say that the Devonshire Band on this occasion did get a
permit
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order. The
hon. and gallant Member can ask a
supplementary question. He must recollect that I cannot allow him to make a
speech.
Major McCORMICK: Is the Minister
aware that this band got a permit from
the local police barrack and afterwards
that permission was taken from them?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
aware of that.
Major MCCORMICK: Owing to the
unsatisfactory nature of the answer I will
raise this matter on the Adjournment.

NORTHERN TRANSPORT BOARD'S
SUPPLIES.
14. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that the Northern Transport Board
does not advertise for tenders for plant,
machinery, oil, vehicles, etc., in the local
Press, and whether he can state the
reasons, if any, why Belfast and Ulster
firms do not have this opportunity
afforded them through public advertisement of supplying material required.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
aware whether the Northern Ireland Road
Transport Board advertise for supplies in
the local Press, but the matter is one
entirely within the discretion of the
Board, and is not one in which I have
any authority to interfere.
I have, however, no reason to suppose
that the Board do not make use of local
facilities as far as is possible, but I would
suggest that the hon. Member should
address to the Board any inquiries which
he wishes to make regarding the matter,
and I am quite certain, having regard to
the composition of the Board, that every
information will be given to the hon.
Member.
Mr. NIXON: Is the House to understand that it is competent for this Board
to give contracts without advertising
locally?
MANUFACTURE OF GAS MASKS.
15. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Acting Prime Minister whether he can state
the names of firms in Northern Ireland
who were approached by the Government
to start the manufacture of gas masks
for the protection of the civil population,
and who refused on the grounds that they
were too busy, and, in view of the large
number of unemployed in Northern
Ireland, whether the Government will
take steps to ensure that a number of the
mills which are idle in Belfast and
district at the present time will be used
for this purpose.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply. The hon.
Member will appreciate that it would not
be proper for me to mention the names of
firms who have been, or now are,
in communication with Departments of the
Imperial Government in regard to the
manufacture of articles under the scheme
of national defence. As regards the latter
part of the hon. Member's question, he
may rest assured that no opportunity is
being lost of taking steps designed to
secure further employment within
Northern Ireland in connection with rearmament work.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Minister tell
us what is the cause of the secrecy, in
view of the fact that the Imperial Minister stated everyone will have a gas mask?
BENEFITS FOR PENSIONERS IN
CORONATION WEEK.
16. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is prepared to grant
the same financial assistance to recipients
of old age pensions and widows and
orphans pensioners as suggested for
recipients of unemployment benefit during
Coronation week.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) So far, additional payments.
during Coronation week have been
promised in Great Britain only to those.
in receipt of unemployment assistance.
In accordance with the policy of the
Government of Northern Ireland, the
Unemployment Assistance Board will
authorise additional payments to the same
class here.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the Minister pay
financial assistance to the old-age
pensioners and widows and orphans?
That is the point in the question I have
asked.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am quite prepared
in this matter to follow Great Britain.
For obvious reasons we cannot leave
Great Britain.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman not make a special effort for
Northern Ireland on the point raised in
the question?
Mr. ANDREWS: The hon. Member
knows perfectly well that it is not
possible.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
CLAIMS BEFORE COURTS OF
REFEREES.
17. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware of the undue delay at the hearing of claims before
the court of referees under the Unemployment Insurance Act, due to instructions being issued to the chairmen to take
a detailed statement of the applicant's
case in writing; whether he is aware of
the additional cost of this procedure, and,
in view of the heavy cost, whether he is
prepared to revert to the procedure that
operated so successfully from 1912-1937.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am satisfied that
there is no unnecessary expenditure of
time by courts of referees in the hearing
of unemployment benefit claims.
The Act provides that a court shall
record its decisions in writing and shall
include in the record a statement of the
findings on material questions of fact, so
that in the event of an appeal to the
umpire, authoritative information on the
matter may be available for all concerned.
I am sure that the hon. Member will
agree that this is a most important consideration.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister aware
that the procedure from 1912 to 1937
acted more successfully, and will he state
the reasons for the change? Is he aware
that where I spent one hour at the Labour
Exchange I have now to spend three
hours, and the number of cases I do is
less than when I spent one hour there?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have already
explained to the hon. Member, in answer
to his question, the reasons for the
change. It is for the purpose of getting
authoritative information to place before
the umpire and for all concerned to know
exactly why the claim has been refused.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman whether he is
aware that the old practice of the clerk
taking the full statement should be conformed to, or whether the position should
be raised to that of a higher grade officer.
Mr. ANDREWS: I heard the old
arrangement seriously criticised, even in
this House.
Mr. NIXON: Does the new procedure
involve the payment of an additional
chairman ?
Mr. BEATTIE: It does.
Mr. ANDREWS: It does not.
Mr. SPEAKER: Unless any Member
gives notice at the Table to the contrary
the remaining questions will be circulated in the Official Report.
Written Answers.
PERCENTAGE OF UNEMPLOY-
MENT.
Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Labour whether the percentage of
unemployment for Northern Ireland in
1936 was 22.7; whether the percentage
for London was 7.2; and whether the
rate for Northern Ireland was the
highest for any depressed area except
South Wales.
Mr. ANDREWS:
The average percentage rate of unemployment in the
London Division during 1936 was 7.2,
the lowest in any of the Ministry of
Labour Divisions in Great Britain, and
whilst the average percentage rate for
Northern Ireland was 22.7, the rate for
Wales was 29.4. In the depressed areas
of South Wales to which the hon. and
learned Member refers, the rates of
unemployment are unfortunately even
higher than the rate for Wales as a
whole. There are areas where the unemployment is over 40 per cent., and in
one town the rate is as high as 52.3 per
cent.
REVIVAL OF OLD AND INTRO-
DUCTION OF NEW INDUSTRIES.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Labour whether the Government propose to introduce legislation
similar to that now being discussed in
the Imperial Parliament, for the purpose of reviving old industries, or introducing new industries, into distressed
villages, such as Shrigley, thus ensuring
that permanent work will replace the
various forms of relief schemes which
are now exhausted.
Written Answers
Written Answers
16 MARCH 1937
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply. I
presume the hon. and gallant Member
refers to the measures under discussion
in the Imperial Parliament for the relief
of unemployment in the special areas in
Great Britain.
It is the Government's intention at
an early date to introduce legislation in
the hope of achieving, if possible, the
objects which the hon. and gallant Member has in mind.
RECLAMATION OF COUNTY
ANTRIM FORESHORE.
Mr. HENDERSON asked the Minister
of Labour whether, in view of the large
number of unemployed men in Belfast,
the Government will introduce legislation to enable them, or the Corporation,
to carry out the scheme of reclaiming
the County Antrim foreshore, and thus
give much needed employment for at
least five years.
Mr. ANDREWS: The responsibility
for putting forward schemes of improvement within their areas and for promoting Bills to obtain such additional
statutory powers as may be necessary
rests with the local authorities.
As I have previously stated in this
House, I am prepared to give sympathetic consideration to any application
which may be put forward by the
responsible authority for an unemployment relief grant in respect of a scheme
of this kind, if it complies with the usual
relief scheme conditions.
FLOODING OF LOUGH ERNE.
Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he has had any report
yet from the engineers appointed some
months ago to make a report with
regard to the flooding of Lough Erne;
whether he is aware that many of the
Loughside farmers have sustained serious
losses by having their lands covered with
water, rendering it unfit for cultivation
this year; and whether he can indicate
what steps the Government intend to
take to deal with this urgent matter.
Mr. BARBOUR: The Ministry's
engineers have seen no reason to alter
their views as communicated in a report
sent to the Lough Erne Drainage Board
two years ago that a lowering of the
statutory level of Lough Erne unless
coupled with heavy expenditure in clearing the channel between the upper and
lower lakes would be for all practical
purposes valueless. I can well understand that serious flooding has occurred
this winter, but the problem from a
financial point of view is almost intractable.
A letter has, however, been recently
received from the Drainage Board asking
for an interview on the whole subject,
and the Ministry is in communication
with the Board in regard to it.
NEW INDUSTRIES
(DEVELOP-
MENT) ACT, 1932.
Major HALL-THOMPSON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether it is the
intention of the Government to introduce legislation to replace the New
Industries (Development) (Northern
Ireland) Act, 1932, the operation of
which expired on 31st October last.
Mr. BARBOUR: The reply is in the
affirmative. I hope to bring the Government's proposals in this matter before
the House at an early date.
ARMAGH FRUIT GROWERS.
Mr. HENDERSON asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he has seen the
report in the Press of the 9th and 10th
March of a meeting of the Armagh fruit
growers at which statements were made
that thousands of tons of apples were
rotting in the orchards of Northern Ireland, and, if the statements are correct,
what steps will be taken by the Government to help the fruit growers in
Northern Ireland.
Mr. BARBOUR. I have seen the
Press reports of the meeting on the 9th
instant of the Armagh Rural Council at
which it was stated that "thousands of
tons of apples were lying rotting this year
because of the Ministry's restricting
regulations." These statements are not
correct.
There is a small residue of low grade
apples of last season's crop at present on
the hands of Northern Ireland growers.

Mr. CAMPBELL: I am very glad to
find that there is at least one Motion
which will commend the support of all
Irishmen. I take it that the Motion
brought forward to-day by the right hon.
and gallant Gentleman, the Chief Whip
of the party opposite, is a reminder, a
rare reminder, and a rather refreshing
reminder, that we are still in Ireland,
and that in itself is a very welcome
declaration coming from the Chief Whip.
It is almost as good in its own way as an
oasis in the Sahara is to a thirsty
traveller. It is a gesture which every
honest Irishman will welcome. I take it
the right hon. and gallant Gentleman
means to remind us that we are still
Irishmen, proud to be Irish, and I am
sure that to-morrow he will sport the
shamrock. I hope he will honour and
observe our national festival in the
proper spirit. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Question put, and agreed to.

Major HALL-THOMPSON: I would
like to draw the attention of the Acting
Minister of Agriculture to the fact that
in my opinion the charge for milk to institutions might be amended, and that
where a large quantity of milk is taken
by one institution there might be a considerable diminution of price. I have in
mind a secondary school which has been.
using Grade A milk for almost twelve
years. Prior to the introduction of the
Milk Board they paid 1s 3d per gallon
for their milk; to-day they pay 1s 10d.
Now, their consumption is 38 gallons per
day, and there are, roughly speaking,
250 school days in the year. That results
in the school paying over £250 a year
more for their milk to-day than they
paid for the same class of milk, Grade A,
in 1935. It is being appreciated more.
and more that the rising generation
should have plenty of good milk. I do
not see how they are being encouraged in
that when these institutions and schools
are being made to pay almost as much

however, he does not feel free to refuse
the transfer, because there is an onus
thrown upon the local authority to provide alternative accommodation, and
there is not sufficient accommodation provided by the local authority, or any other
authority, to warrant the medical officer
embarking on a general scheme of what
might be termed slum clearance or the
abolition of slum property.
That brings me to the responsibility of
the Government. I think the time has
arrived when the Government of
Northern Ireland-I am sure the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Commerce will be very sympathetic-should
consider the advisability of setting up
some kind of housing commission, a coordinated housing authority, to deal with
the situation that has been brought about
as a result of generations of inaction and
apathy. Dr. Thomson, the medical officer
of health for Belfast, intimated a week
or a fortnight ago that although he has
not completed his investigations in
Belfast, 1,680 houses so far have been
reported to him as completely unsuitable
for human habitation, and he has another
substantial part of the city to explore.
The medical officer of health and many
other people in the Public Health Committee are reluctant to take action under
the Public Health Act until they feel
they have some machinery to put in
motion to provide the people affected with
alternative accommodation.
Alternative accommodation implies not
only houses, but houses under certain
conditions. The pressing nature of this
problem of slum property in Belfast was
evidenced this morning by the hesitancy
of the medical officer to renew a licence
in respect of a lodging-house in a certain
quarter of the city. He agreed to recommend a transfer of the licence only on the
distinct understanding that as soon as
possible that is, as soon as alternative
accommodation is available—he would
suspend that licence. I want to tell the
Health
Government that the Public
Committee decided not to accept the
advice of the medical officer, but rejected
his proposal to transfer the licence from
one person to another.
That being so, we are now face to face
with this position, that the person who
now is the licence holder for that lodginghouse, and who is desirous of transferring
it, can either curtail his proprietorship or
continue to exercise it. He can continue
to hold the licence, even though somebody else is actually running the business,
and there seems to be no legal way of
dealing with the matter. Yet I am
satisfied that in respect to that lodginghouse and many others, an overwhelming
case has been made out by the sanitary
and medical authority for the scrapping
of the property. That is the civic point.
of view. I have dealt with 1,680 houses.
Now I come to the country point of
view. In answer to a question this
afternoon-I think with reference to the
County of Derry-the Minister of Home
Affairs said that no labourers' cottages
had been built for the past 15 years.
think it is simply an appalling state of
affairs that in a big county like London-

slums. I know that that is a matter

In regard to the rural districts, I want

questions in reference to this point, and
I wish to emphasise it again. A few

Labour Exchanges. One way out is for
the Government to establish an Agricultural Wages Board. I commend the
idea again to the Government. I believe
the Government are likely to be converted ultimately on this question,
though it may take a long time. I know
A
that that requires fresh legislation, and
that I cannot deal with the question now.
An Agricultural Wages Board is in
operation in England and Wales.
united recommendation has been made in
Scotland in favour of an Agricultural

should not sympathetically consider the

of the present time removed.
I have said before, and I say again,
one thing Northern Ireland is suffering
from at the present time is a general
poverty level that is positively alarming.
Some people may not believe that, but I
want to tell you that I got statistics
supplied to a local employment committee
the other day, and I think I am correct
in saying that there were over 33,000
unemployed persons registered in Belfast
on that date. Those 33,000 unemployed
persons are being exploited and used by
many of the employers in Belfast as a
lever by which to cut down wages, with
the result that thousands of people in
the city have a very depressed standard
of life.
I have already drawn attention-and I
do not want to repeat my observations
because the matter is under consideration
-to certain trades, but the general level
for unskilled and semi-skilled workers is
perilously near the destitution line at
the present time. Proper housing, the
tightening up of conditions in regard to
housing, and the provision of support for
the local authorities in the matter of slum
clearance these things should determine
the Government to make a five or a ten
years' plan, or whatever they like to call
it, if they think this too revolutionary
a title, to wipe out slums and unsuitable
property in Northern Ireland. That
would give a fillip to industry generally.
I am not copying anybody else's
economics or political philosophy. I
said this 20 years ago, when I was a
good deal younger than I am now. That
is the kind of policy for the Government
to undertake in order to try to deal
with economic depression and poverty
generally.
Seeing that this Motion provides a

of the Ministry of Education in this

House to the notices which have appeared
in the Press recently with regard to the
inadequacy of the provision for higher
education in Northern Ireland. When I
think of all the boasts that we make
with regard to educational opportunities
for the working classes of Belfast and
Northern Ireland generally to take

absolutely sick at the criminal apathy
not only of the people in Government
circles, but of people outside who are
satisfied to maintain working-class
children in a position of inferiority as
compared with the children of England,
Scotland, and Wales. I have made my
allegation in regard to this matter as
strong as I can. I say, challengingly, to
the Minister of Labour that in the whole
of Great Britain we are the most poverty
stricken section of the community in regard to facilities for higher education.
Compared to England, Scotland and
Wales, we ought to burn with shame at
the indifference we display. I know this
is not a revolutionary question, it does
not create thunders of applause from the
street corners; it does not cause people
to gather round street corners and talk
and it does not excite the imagination so
easily as other questions. But it is a
very important question and strikes at
the root of representative Government
and the right of our people to enjoy the
full fruits of representative Government.
I say that compared with England,
Scotland and Wales our people occupy a
position of complete inferiority from
which they ought, if they had any pride
or spirit of independence, emerge with all
possible speed and I think the Government ought to take the matter up.
Local authorities at the present time
are doing a great deal with regard to
technical instruction, but with regard to
secondary education we have not the
facilities, and if we had the facilities
there is not the machinery in existence,
because the existing secondary schools
could not accommodate the people who
desire to go and who could profit from
higher education. These are a few
fragmentary criticisms.
I want again to say that I conceive
the function of the Government to be
this, that it should apply its power
and ability to the question of ensuring
that as many of the people in Northern
Ireland as possible should be relieved of
the burden of poverty. Too many of
them are groaning under the burden of
poverty; too many are deprived of the
social amenities that they ought to enjoy.
Unemployment continues to be a very
grave problem because we have over
30,000 registered unemployed in Belfast
alone. It will continue to be a grave and
pernicious problem as long as we have
the existing social order. When people
get wise and realise that they cannot deal
with unemployment without changing
the economic structure of society, then
we shall get something done. I heard
a member of this House the other day
say and it is a homily for everybodythat the cause of unemployment was
machinery, new inventions and other
things. That is sheer piffle. Machinery
and inventions in themselves do not
cause unemployment and economic hardships. It depends upon how you use
them. If machinery and inventions were
applied for the benefit of the community
they could be welcomed by every section
because every machine and every new
invention applied to
to industry that
resulted in increased productivity would
go to enrich the nation, provided the
nation controlled the machinery and the
inventions.
It is wrong to condemn machinery.
It leads to the productivity of mankind;
makes it easier to produce that potential
supply of riches that all might enjoy.
Do not let us decry inventions and
machinery. Do not let us think that the
remedy for unemployment is to go back
to the Guild age, because we have got
to go on. The age is marching on, and
that the Government of Northern
say
Ireland must accept its share of responsibility in an age of potential bounty and
plenty. If there are thousands of people

I
and I submit there are-if thousands are

by initiating machinery to bring both

a small amount compared with what re-

SPEED OF MOTOR-CARS.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Arising out of the
reply of the Minister of Home Affairs
this afternoon to a question of mine dealing with the speed of motor-cars on the
highways in Northern Ireland, I intimated that I would raise this question,
which is one of public importance, on
the adjournment of the House. The
question of the speed of motor-cars in our
area is one of increasing gravity. It is
almost 40 years since motor-cars first
began to be familiar on our highways,
and I do think had Parliament at the
time it was legalising speed limits on the
highways been able to foresee the long,
long trail of death and mutilation that
would follow the introduction of this
weapon on the highways a silence would
have fallen upon the assembly as tragic
as that which fell upon those at Belshazar's feast. There is no hope of any substantial improvement in the dangers to
which the public are exposed, or any substantial hope of security for the public,
by way of piecemeal dealing with this
topic.
The records of the Minister of Home
Affairs is not satisfactory in this respect,
it is a record of inefficacy. The deaths
and the grave injuries are going on from
week to week and month to month.
They are being repeated with clock-work
regularity. The Ministry's attitude is
really one of inertia, an attitude of
sluggish inertia. Some efforts have been
made I know to try to minimise the
danger, but little progress has been
achieved. There have been steps taken
to educate road users to have more care.
Drivers and pedestrians have been told
to be more discreet and wise in their use
of the highways. That will do some
little good, but not much good. I think
it can be compared to the free distribution of revolvers, dangerous weapons,
and then the issue of instructions to the
people who are the possessors of these
revolvers showing how to use them with
Adjournment-
Speed of Motor-cars
16 MARCH 1937
the least possible danger to themselves
and others.
I admit that speed is not the sole
cause of these distressing calamities that
are shocking so many of our people, but
I do submit for the good judgment of
the House that speed is a tremendous
factor and is contributing to these distressing results. The same roads are being
used for vehicles that are travelling at
60 miles per hour as are being used for
vehicles travelling at 15 miles per
hour. The same roads are being
used for pedestrians and motor-cars
which are really being treated as if they
were
a kind of accelerated horse
carriages. They are nothing of the kind;
they are dangerous weapons of powerful
potency and are a very grave risk to the
public. I think the danger is complicated by the fact that there is a minority
of what I would call motor speedmen
who seem oblivious to the danger to which
they are exposing the ordinary public.
They are without manners and certainly
do not lack callousness, and they are a
very grave danger to the public. They
act as if the absence of a speed limit in
our area were a guarantee to them that
they can go at any speed. They rush
along our main highways, they dash past
stationary trams, and they seem to regard
the ordinary pedestrian on the highway
as something that can be brushed aside.
When the railways were legalised in this
island 100 years ago very strict precautions were taken to ensure public safety.
Legislation of the most drastic character
was introduced and safeguards of every
kind carried out. Certainly the legislators of those times had at heart the safety
of the travelling public. In England I
know there is a speed limit of 30 miles per
hour in built-up areas, but the view is
taken by very many wise heads that that
is not low enough for a speed limit, and
that the very utmost speed limit that is
compatible with public safety is one of 20
miles per hour. In this connection the
very first speed limit put upon motor-cars
when they came to be in any kind of
general use on the highways was 14 miles
per hour.
Ten years later motor-cars became more general, and became more
powerful, and Parliament then put on a
speed limit of 20 miles per hour. A man
can now career along the highways so long
as it is thought he is not careering to the
danger of the public. There is no maximum. The reply of the Minister would
indicate that so far as a general scheme
is concerned it is out of the question.
There may be a partial alteration and beyond that the Ministry will not go.
think that is unsatisfactory and indicates
a want of due regard for the gravity of
the situation.

I do feel those who prove themselves
unfit to hold a driving licence should be
disqualified for life and put off the roads
altogether. Where it is a case of driving
under the influence of drink, or a case of
callous disregard for the safety of the
public I say that is not a case for mercy
or compassion; it is a case for rigid justice.
In many quarters these offences are looked
upon with a kind of levity. I do not for
a moment disguise the fact that a responsibility rests upon foot wayfarers, for they
must exercise care. I would like to say

high-powered engines, and they are not

worst sufferers from this motor-car traffic
It is a shocking and sad thing that the

I am sorry that the Minister seems

Britain, 516. Per 100 miles of road-
Northern Ireland, 18.3; Great Britain,
131. However, that does not mean that
I am a bit satisfied to allow the present
condition of affairs in Northern Ireland
to obtain, but I do say this-that we are
far ahead of Great Britain in regard to
the management of the roads, and in the
prevention of accidents. I do not know
whether the hon. and learned Member is
a practical motorist, but if he is he will
realise that even at fifteen miles an hour
a motorist may be driving to the danger
of the public.
Mr. BEATTIE: Or less.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Or even at a
lesser speed, as the hon. Member
remarks. There is a tendency on the
part of certain motorists to feel that if
they drive within the speed limit they
are not guilty of the more grave offence
of driving to the danger of the public.
Anyone who has acted as official timekeeper at a race meeting will realise how
difficult it is to ascertain the exact speed
at which a car is travelling.
I would like to take this opportunity
of saying, as I have said before, that the
vast majority of motorists
are lawabiding people who are anxious to avoid
accidents. On the other hand, there is
a certain element this does not apply to.
There is first of all the individual without any road sense. Then we have the
road hog, and we have the drunken
driver, and they all contribute to the toll
of the road. But I am glad to say that
these are in the minority, because if they
were not the toll of the road would be
absolutely appalling.
As I have said before, I believe the
real solution of this problem is that those
individuals who do not realise their
responsibilities, who do not realise that
they are in charge of what you might
describe as a dangerous weapon, and
those who are guilty of either dangerous.
driving or of indulging in too much
liquor, should be put off the road. I
think the hon. and learned Member will
recognise that the various measures
have passed in this House, which have
gone far beyond what has been done in
the Imperial House, have all
have all been
directed to that end. If I am not wrong
we

Speed of Motor-cars
16 MARCH 1937
in my recollection I think that in one
of our earlier Acts I went so far as to
press this House to impose a minimum
penalty on any individual who was found
drunk in charge of a motor vehicle, and
the House agreed to do so. That penalty
also puts such person off the road for a
minimum period of twelve months.
There is no use fining a well-to-do man
£10, or £20, or £30, because it is nothing
to him. I am not at all sure that the
hon. and learned Member opposite did
not oppose in another place the suggestion of a minimum penalty.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Do you speak from
recollection?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am open to
correction. One of the objections to having a speed limit is this: that you are
really providing an excuse for the unscrupulous driver to drive up to that
limit, which may be thirty miles per hour,
and he may have the idea that he will
get away with a prosecution for committing a technical offence. There is no doubt
that if a motorist is trying to make his
passage and he finds there is a speed limit
in a certain area he will risk exceeding
it if he thinks he will be fined only 10s
or so for exceeding the speed limit, but
if there is no speed limit he will think
twice before driving to the danger of the
public when the penalty may mean losing
his licence for a period.
I do not want to close the door in regard
to a speed limit, but I will never go the
length of imposing a speed limit such as
has been imposed in England, and which,
according to the official figures, has proved
a failure. There is one town in Northern
Ireland in which we have imposed a speed
limit, the town of Antrim, and it is an
extraordinary thing to find that since the
speed limit was imposed there the number
of accidents has actually increased. Looking round for the cause I believe the explanation is this: that the pedestrians
seem to think they can take quite a liberty
in crossing the road. The fact remains
that we imposed that speed limit, and the
result is a greater number of accidents.
Personally, I believe that the solution,
so far as pedestrians are concerned, is to
ensure that the younger members of the
community shall be taught to appreciate
the dangers that may arise by reason of
neglect on their part to take care.
condition of affairs has arisen.
A new
We have
got motor-cars, and we cannot put them
off the road; but I do think a good deal
more might be done to get the young to
appreciate the dangers. The hon. and
learned Member for Central will remember
that in the old days there used to be a
great game of "Last across the road,"
just seeing how far they could go to the
horse's head. That does not do with
motor-cars. So far as the Government is
concerned we are endeavouring, through
the teachers, who, I am glad to say, are
co-operating with us, and through the
training school to bring it home to the
children through the teachers the risks
they run through not taking care.
In conclusion, may I point out an
extraordinary thing to the hon. and
learned Member, who, I know, takes a
great interest in animal life. While the
casualties among human beings have increased since the introduction of the
motor-car, the casualties amongst animals
are steadily decreasing. Perhaps that is
due to the fact that more generations of
animals have passed since the motor-car
was introduced, and the present generation of animals has, perhaps, a more acute
sense of how to avoid accidents. I throw
out that suggestion to the hon. and
learned Member, because if he were a
practical motorist like the Member for
Pottinger he would realise how hard it is
to kill a dog, a hen, or a duck on the
road.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the Minister
suggest that animals are more sacred than
human beings?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, I do not.
I am only referring to children, and I
suggest that that is one of the ways of
dealing with the problem. Already we
have a good many police patrol cars, and
we hope to increase the number at a very
early date. It is only by that means that
you can get hold of the road hog to whom
I have already referred. We are also considering the advisability of bringing over
an expert to still further train our police
patrols to distinguish between really
dangerous driving and driving without
due care.
But if the hon. and learned
Gentleman has any practical suggestions
to make I am perfectly prepared to consider them. But I will with great respect

of the net in question, the certificate
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
described the net as a fixed draft net, and
it was proved in evidence before the court
that until a few years ago the net fished
under the authority of that certificate
had always conformed, both in regard to
its construction and to the manner in
which it was operated, to the accepted
construction and method of operation of
a fixed draft net. Latterly, however,
certain alterations had been made in the
form of the net and in the method of
operation. In the opinion of the court
these alterations were such as to put the
net outside the category of fixed draft
nets and to render its use, in its later
form, illegal.
The point at issue in this case is of particular importance, inasmuch as similar
alterations had been made in other fixed
draft nets held under corresponding
certificates.
Whilst it is not disputed
that a fixed draft net is not only less
effective, but more difficult to operate
than other types of net which it would be
possible to devise, the Government must
have regard to the principles upon which
the Act of 1863, to which I have referred,
was based. That Act established a
balance between the competing interests
in sea and inland salmon fishing, which,
in the considered view of the Government,
cannot with safety be disturbed even at
this date. For this reason I regret that I
cannot hold out any hope of fresh legislation designed to legalise the type of net
which was the subject of the recent
proceedings.
COST OF CRAIGAVON BRIDGE.
9. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
if the contract for the building of the
Craigavon Bridge in Derry was advertised
for; what was the contract price, and
what was the exact cost of the bridge
when completed.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Advertisements were not issued inviting tenders
for the building of the Craigavon Bridge,
but in accordance with well-established
practice, a number of firms of high standing (actually 15), who were known to be
skilled in the execution of such works,
were invited to tender. Eight of these
firms submitted tenders, and the lowest
tender, that of Messrs. Dorman, Long &
Co., Ltd., was accepted. The contract
entered into covered both the erection of
the new bridge and the removal of the old
bridge, the price being £255,510.
The contract price did not include
engineers' fees or certain minor road
works, etc., which were carried out subsequently as part of the general scheme.
The total gross cost of the entire scheme,
including these latter items, amounted
approximately to £285,000.
I may add that the Road Fund contributed approximately £267,000.

Mr. HENDERSON: Will those Members opposite who are holding a Committee meeting stop and allow the hon.
Member for Falls to speak?
Mr. BYRNE: No person will be
prouder than I am to know that Ulster
is prosperous and in a good financial
position. The reason I rose to speak is
that I meet so many people who are
unemployed, and the little assistance
they are getting is insufficient to provide
them with a bare existence. The Corporation recently have been making
some change with regard to the recruiting of labour, and I, as a representative
of the working people, am called upon
from day to day to intercede with the
City Council in an endeavour to get
some of those people employment. I
must say I am distressed to listen to the
stories I have to listen to.
There are 73,000 people unemployed
in Northern Ireland. I quite admit
that the Government have recently increased the grant to the local authorities
from 60 per cent. to 75 per cent., but
when that is brought up in the Corporation the Corporation say the loans to be
raised are such that that grant does not
amount to a very large percentage of the
work. I would appeal to the Government, if at all possible, to return to the
50-50 basis. Under that system the
Corporation took up a lot of work, and I
believe they would do so again. There
is much necessary work to be done in
connection with streets in the city, and
there are thousands of unemployed
people appealing for assistance on the
Lisburn Road. It would be a pleasure
to all of us to know that those people
were in employment. The employment
of the working people is one of the things
in which I take a very deep interest, and
I sincerely hope that at no distant date
something will be done to relieve those
people.
The Minister of Finance to-day has
said that Ulster is in a prosperous
position, and I have said we would all
be glad to know that. He has also
quoted New Zealand, but in New
Zealand people get a pension of £1 a
week, and when they are unemployed
they get a larger sum than the people.
in this country. If Ulster is so prosperous,
why not treat the people 1ere in the way
the inhabitants of New Zealand are
treated? Why not endeavour to give increased pensions to widows? I should
like to see the Government bringing in
a Measure to provide pensions for all
widows. It would not cost so very much
money to do that. The widows of men
who were insured already receive
pensions.
The subject of education is a very
delicate one, but, on behalf of the people
I represent in this House, I should not
be doing my duty if I did not point out
the difference made between us and the
other section of the community in the
matter of educational grants. In the
Free State no difference whatever is
made on the ground of religious belief.
The Free State gives the same contribution to Protestants as to Catholics,
whereas
in Northern Ireland the
Catholics are severely penalised in

schools to any local authority. Why not
give the Catholic schools the same treatment as the Protestant schools? I think
that would be only reasonable, and it
would be a great relief to my people,
who are the poorer section of the community. It is my duty, representing

Oral Answers to Questions.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN
DERRY.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received a
Resolution passed by the Committee of the
Derry Tenants' and Rural Workers'
Defence League calling upon the Government to build labourers' cottages on
not less than one acre of land of suitable quality, and protesting against the
arbitrary attitude of the farmers in
trying to withhold such land, and, if
so, what action he intends to take.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): No such Resolution
has been received from the Committee
of the Derry Tenants' and Rural
Workers' Defence League, but a Resolution somewhat to the same effect has
been forwarded by the North Antrim
Labour Party.
With regard to the request that the
plots attached to cottages should be not
less than one acre, I would point out
that the matter is one to be determined
by the local authority, which should be
in the best position to decide upon the
quantity of land required.
I have no information that farmers
are trying to withhold land required for
the purposes of a labourers' cottage
scheme, but in any case if a farmer is
unwilling to sell land for the purpose,
the local authority has statutory power
to acquire the necessary land by compulsion.
RATES IN DERRY CITY.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he has received a Resolution passed by the Derry
Tenants' Defence League protesting
against the high rates in the City of
Derry, which tend to increase the cost
of living, discourage new factories, and
inflict serious hardship on the working
classes, and, if so, what action he is
prepared to take.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have
received the Resolution referred to by
the hon. Member. The fixing of rates
is a matter for the Derry Corporation
who must strike a rate adequate to meet
the annual expenditure of the County
Borough, and no action on the part of
my Department is called for.

on the by-pass road will be commenced.
