DONEGALL PLACE FLOWER
SELLERS.
6. Mr. BEATTIE: asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he has approved
of the action of the Belfast Corporation
in transferring the flower sellers from
Donegall Place to the front of the City
Hall.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, Sir.
The Corporation submitted
to my
Department for confirmation certain
by-laws which prohibited street trading
altogether in a number of streets-Donegall Place and Donegall Square amongst
others. The Ministry protested that
these by-laws did not appear to have
been drawn upon any logical foundation,
and pointed, in particular, to the case
of the traders to whom the hon. Member refers, suggesting that interference
with them was uncalled for.
The Corporation, however, pressed for
the confirmation of the by-laws, and as
the question was purely one of local
opinion and not one having any bearing
on local government administration
generally, I felt bound to yield to the
views of the local authority in the
matter.
The Ministry had nothing whatever
to do with the fixing of the present
"pitch" for these traders and was not,
in fact, consulted in the matter.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Might I ask the
right hon. Gentleman if an individual
member of the Corporation like myself
moves an amendment at the next
monthly meeting disapproving of the
action of the Corporation, can we rest
assured we will have his support?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member must not ask me a hypothetical
question. I have tried to explain the
exact position in regard to the matter.
Mr. GRANT: Arising out of the
right hon. Gentleman's reply, am I to
understand that Donegall Square North
is a street in which street trading is
also prohibited and that the flower
sellers have as much right to Donegall
Place as they have to their new pitch?
Sir DAWSON BATES I have
already told the hon. Gentleman in my
reply that Donegall Square North is
included.
Mr. GRANT: Does that mean that
the Corporation are deliberately contravening their own by-laws?

TEACHING OF IRISH IN SCHOOLS.
9. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the
number of public elementary schools in
Northern Ireland and the number of pupils
therein who are learning Irish; the number of secondary schools and the number
of pupils who are learning Irish; the
number of junior technical schools and the
number of pupils who are learning Irish;
the number of pupil teachers in Stranmillis Training College, Belfast, and St.
Mary's Training College, Strawberry Hill,
respectively, and the number who are
learning Irish in each of these Training
Colleges.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): On 31st
December, 1936, the number of public
elementary schools was 1,753, and the
number of pupils therein who were learning Irish was 9,358.
As regards the secondary schools—the
number of which during the current
session is 73-the Ministry has no information as to the number of pupils who
learn Irish, but the subject was taught
in 28 schools, and, of the 3,581 candidates
at the certificate examinations last year,
922 offered Irish as a subject.
On the 31st December, 1936, there
were 13 junior technical schools, and,
whilst I have not exact information, it is
estimated that the number of pupils in
those schools who were learning Irish was
approximately 240.
The number of students in Stranmillis
Training College in the current session is
225, none of whom learn Irish. At St.
Mary's College, Belfast, there are 72

DEATH OF THOMAS ARCHER,
MOTOR LORRY DRIVER.
the
10. Mr. MIDGLEY asked
Attorney-General whether he is aware
that considerable dissatisfaction prevails
in County Tyrone arising out of an
inquest which was held on Thomas
Archer, a motor lorry driver, who was
killed on 29th January, 1936, following
a collision between his lorry and a bus at
Coalisland, and also from a widely held
opinion that certain material facts were
withheld from consideration by the
Coroner's Court; that the manner and
method of arranging the inquest were not
in conformity with the dictates of justice,
and so cast aspersions upon the capacity
and integrity of the deceased; and
whether, in view of these facts, he will
institute an inquiry into the matter with
a view to allaying the misgivings which
exist at present.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): I am not aware that any
dissatisfaction prevails in County Tyrone
as a result of this inquest, and if any
misgivings exist I am satisfied that they
are unfounded. No material facts were
withheld from the Coroner's Jury. The
inquest was opened on January 25, 1936,
and adjourned indefinitely because
William J. Latimer, a passenger in the
lorry driven by the deceased, was in the
Royal Victoria Hospital, Belfast, suffering
from very severe injuries and unable to
attend. A statement was taken from
Mr. Latimer by the police as soon as he
was able to be interviewed, but in June it
was ascertained that he would not be able
to attend for a further indefinite period,
and in fact he was not discharged from
hospital until October, 1936. As other
necessary witnesses were about to leave
the locality and some of the jurors had
left the county, the police very properly
proceeded with the inquest. Latimer's
statement was, by consent of the coroner,
read to the jury at the hearing, which
lasted for almost six hours. Mrs. Archer
was informed of the resumed hearing in
good time and was allowed to telephone
to her solicitor from the police barracks.
No unjustifiable aspersions were
upon the integrity or capacity of the
deceased. The jury exonerated the driver
of the bus from all blame, and I am
satisfied that the inquest was carried out
with complete propriety and that no
inquiry into this case other than that
made by me on receiving notice of this
question is necessary.
cast
Mr. MIDGLEY: I should like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman whether it is
a fact that the lady concerned, Mrs.
Archer, the mother of the deceased man,
only received notice of the resumption of
the inquest on the morning on which it
was to be held, and is it not a fact that
the solicitor for the deceased person protested in the court against the conditions
under which the inquest had been
resumed, the short notice given to the
people concerned, and the manner of
taking evidence?
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: It is
true to say that the solicitor representing
this lady did protest, but I am satisfied
that he had no reason for protesting.

inquest in this case was conducted by

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Advertisements Regulation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill has
been introduced to meet representations
made from time to time by Members of
this House and by local authorities outside, who have complained of the disfigurement of the countryside caused by
the indiscriminate exhibition of advertisements. Since the Bill was published some
further representations have been received
and the Government will be prepared to
give sympathetic consideration to these
at a later stage.
At present local authorities have somewhat limited powers under an Act passed
in 1907, under which they can make
by-laws for regulating the erection of
hoardings over 12 feet in height, and for
preventing the exhibition of advertisements in such a way as to affect
injuriously the amenities of a public park
or pleasure ground or so as to disfigure
the natural beauty of the landscape.
In England the power of the local
authorities was extended by an Act
passed in 1925, which did not apply to
Northern Ireland, and under it they
could make by-laws so as to prevent the
obstruction of a view of rural scenery
from a highway, railway, or other public
place, or the destruction of the amenities
of any village or place of historic or
public interest.
In the Bill now before the House it is
proposed to do two things. In the first
place, it is proposed to extend the control.
of the local authorities to all hoardings,
whether or not they exceed 12 feet in
681 Advertisement Regulation Bill- 23 MARCH 1937

Second Reading
height. It will be conceded, I think,
that serious injury is as likely to be
caused by the fall of a hoarding of seven
feet or eight feet high as by any accident
to one over 12 feet in height, and there
is no apparent reason why hoardings of
less than 12 feet in height should not be
subject to regulations to ensure that they
are securely constructed and not likely to
cause injury to passers-by or to obstruct
the view of persons driving vehicles.
or
In the second place it is proposed to
apply to Northern Ireland, with some
slight extension, the powers given to
local authorities by the English Act of
1925. This should give them practically
all the powers necessary for preserving
the amenities of their districts, but, in
order to deal with special areas, it has
been thought advisable to give local
authorities the further power of making
bylaws prohibiting the erection
exhibition of advertisements in such
areas, or their erection without the consent of the local authority. It should be
noted that the power of making such
by-laws can only be exercised for the
purpose of preserving the amenities of the
area, so that an area scheduled for total
prohibition under sub-clause 3 would
have to be one in which it could reasonably be held that the exhibition of any
advertisement of any kind would cause
disfigurement. Hon. Members will
realise, therefore, that any such area
would necessarily be a very restricted one.
It will not, therefore, be open to the
local authorities to prohibit arbitrarily
the exhibition of advertisements, and
there is the further safeguard that the
by-laws have to be approved by the Ministry of Home Affairs. If advertisements
are erected contrary to a by-law the
council is empowered to require the owner
to remove them on fourteen days' notice,
and if he fails to do so the council may,
itself, remove the offending advertisement. The maximum penalty for erecting an advertisement which does not
comply with the bylaws is £5, with a fine
of 40s for each day during which the
offence continues. This is the penalty
prescribed under the existing Act of 1907.
In order that there may be no hardship, it is proposed to allow advertisers.
to continue to use existing hoardings for
a period of five years, and to require the
local authority to pay a reasonable compensation for any loss sustained by reason
of any by-laws which they may make.
It will be observed that the premises of
any railway, harbour, or similar undertaking are exempted from the operation.
of the section of the Bill dealing with
amenities. This is in accordance with the
existing Acts. For the purposes of determining whether by-laws made by a local
authority should be confirmed the
Ministry of Home Affairs may hold a
local inquiry at which those interested
can be represented.
The local authorities concerned with
the administration of the Bill are the
county councils, the councils of county
boroughs, boroughs, urban districts and
rural districts. In county boroughs,
boroughs and urban districts the council
will be the local authority to the
exclusion of any other authority. In the
counties it is intended that the primary
authority should be the county council.
The latter is, however, authorised to
delegate its functions to a rural district
council but with power to cancel the
delegation at any time.
The expenses of administering the Act
in county boroughs, boroughs or urban
districts will be borne by the borough or
urban district. In counties they will fall
upon the county, excluding the boroughs
and urban districts, and in rural districts the expenses will be a charge on
the rural district. As certain local
authorities already have considerable
powers for dealing with advertisements
under local Acts, a provision has been
inserted in the present Bill to preserve
any such powers so that the powers given
to these authorities by the present Bill
will be in addition to and not in substitution for any of the powers they
possess at present. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

Local Government (Postponement of
Elections) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This is a short
Bill and is practically self-explanatory.
As hon. Members are aware, the Local
Government Act (Northern Ireland),
1934, fixed the date of the Local Government Elections as the 15th May. This
year this date falls within the week of
the Coronation, and it would be obviously
most inconvenient if local government
elections were to be held during that
week. The purpose of the present Bill is
to postpone any elections which would
normally have taken place on the 15th
May until some date later in the year,
to be fixed by Order in Council and not
to be later than the 1st December.
A consequential requirement of the
postponement of the elections is, of
course, the postponement of the election
of the lord mayor, mayors, and chairmen
of councils, and also of the high sheriffs.
I am quite sure that this Measure will
meet with general approval from both
sides of the House. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time.'
Mr. BYRNE: The holding of elections
in November or December would cause a
good deal of confusion, and I suggest
that the right hon. Gentleman should
postpone the elections for one year.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Why not postpone
the elections altogether, and let the
existing occupants hold their seats?
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for Tuesday, 13th April.

Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to move the
Second Reading of this Bill. I hope to
be able to show that it is a Measure that
no Member of this House will object to.
No good master whom a faithful servant
served for 51 weeks in the year would
grudge him the remaining week as a
Eight-Day Holiday Bill-
Second Reading
23 MARCH 1937
holiday with pay. For that reason I ask
the House to sanction the Second Reading of this Bill, and to sanction the
principle of an annual eight-day holiday
with pay for employees. There are other
reasons. The Parliament at Westminster
has already affirmed by a large majority
the principle of this Bill. It must be
clear to anyone conversant with modern
life that a reform of this kind would be
beneficial to the health of working
people, and would add to the productivity of industry and commerce.
The
It may be said, "Why cannot the
working classes themselves make provision for a holiday as they ought to
make provision for a rainy day?"
answer I give to that question is that the
wages earned to-day by workers living
at a standard of subsistence befitting
human beings are not enough to enable
them to provide for a holiday such as this
Bill contemplates. Great numbers of the
salaried class already have holidays each.
year with pay. Great numbers of
Government and municipal employees
already have holidays each year with
pay. But far greater numbers of ill-paid
workers in mills and factories, in
foundries and shipyards, in shops and
elsewhere, have annual holidays without
pay. When they take those holidays they
take them with the thought running
through their minds of the privations the
holiday will entail upon them or upon
their dependents.
Members of Parliament get very long
holidays every year, Cabinet Ministers
get very long holidays every year, and
they all get their holidays with pay. I
do think this House will agree that the
holiday would be less pleasurable both in
anticipation and in actual enjoyment if
it were a holiday without pay. To-day,
when wealth is flaunted on every side of
us, we know that just as it has always
been, to him that hath shall be given,
and to him that hath not even the little
which he hath shall be taken away. We
hear that a trade wind of prosperity is
blowing in our area. That, at least, is
the inference I drew from a recent speech
of the Minister of Finance. I am sure
we would all be glad to feel a wind of
that kind blowing in our midst, and I
hope it will continue.
Last year, according to the report of
the Commissioners of Inland Revenue,
a
there were 49 more millionaires and
2,030 more persons in receipt of incomes
above £2,000 a year, than in the previous
year. The number of persons in that
highly-privileged state in Great Britain,

85,449, and those people drew

Those are very remarkable figures. At
the same time, alongside that immense
accumulation of wealth, there is widespread want and distress, which for tens
of thousands in our own area makes the

one almost from the cradle to the grave.
I venture to say that if a plebiscite were
taken for and against this Bill in Northern Ireland there would be an overwhelming majority in favour of it.
Progressive employers give their work
people holidays with pay. Backward
employers are reluctant to give their
workers that privilege, and the only
remedy is to educate the backward
employers by law to act as the progressive
employers do. Progressive employers
who have experience of the benefit of an
annual holiday with pay for their
workers state that they would not go
back to the old system. They find that
the annual holiday with pay, instead of
being a charge to the cost of production
actually benefits their balance sheets. By
reason of what? By reason of the more
willing, more zealous, and better and
more efficient service given by more contented employees during the rest of the
year. Those employers deserve to
prosper, and I hope they will continue to
do so.
A point may be made of the cost of
this to industry. I submit that the most
this concession would increase a wages bill
by would be 1/52, or less than 2 per cent.
in the year. It would not be even so much,
because in many establishments the
higher-paid people get holidays with full
pay, and the only extra cost to be

this to the ordinary workpeople.

our

again we cannot ignore the fact that we
are part of the United Kingdom, existing in this part already under certain
disadvantages due to the fact that we do

have to import the greater part if not the

Now we have got to be careful if
I may say so, very careful, that in
endeavouring to help our workers in

for our employers to compete with other

with an additional burden of somewhere
between £30,000 and £40,000 a year.
Now when these firms estimate, this sum
would have to be included in their
estimates, and it would mean that
when they were competing with firms
across the Channel also estimating for the
same work they would be at such a disadvantage that instead of the work
coming here it would be carried out
elsewhere.
I am always slow to mention special

that orders have been frequently

We frequently in this House discuss

bearings. We all regret unemployment,

The working class in Northern Ireland

the enthusiasm into the struggle for
decent social services that, at the present
time, they put into illusions or things

do that they will get paid for holidays.
Coming up here this afternoon I felt that

in eight in Great Britain, and one in
twelve in Northern Ireland, are already
in receipt either by statute, or practice, or
tradition of holidays with pay.
What is being done at the present time

treatment to the workers and equality of

got to sell their commodities in the same
market. At the present time the workers
do not get holidays. They get enforced
periods of idlenes. They are pushed out

The resolution he enclosed is as follows:
(Private).
Erection of Labourers' Cottages in
Rural Districts.
Resolution passed by the Unionist
Members of the Omagh Rural District
Council on 6th June, 1936 :-
That we, the Unionist members of
Omagh Rural District Council, would
strongly urge upon the Minister of
Home Affairs, through the Ulster
Unionist Council, the advisability of
abolishing the present system whereby
representations are made by labourers
for the erection of labourers' cottages
in rural districts, and that the Minister
make such changes in the regulations
as will obviate the necessity for representations.

Adjournment--
Labourers' Cottages
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Healy]
That rural district councils be
empowered to formulate schemes of
their own for the erection of cottages
without representations being made;
and that at the inquiry by the Inspector
of the Ministry general evidence of the
demand and necessity for the cottages
be accepted, instead of evidence by individual labourers.
We would point out that in certain
districts cottages are required by
Unionist workers, but we hesitate to
invite representations, as we know there.
would be a flood of representations from
the Nationalists' side, and our political
opponents are only waiting the opportunity to use this means to outvote us
in divisions where majorities are close.
If the Minister would be good enough
to change the regulations as suggested
this council and all the other Unionist
councils in the country could erect
cottages and let them to the most
deserving applicants without being
under an obligation to accept any particular tenant. We would also like to
point out that a great number of applicants for cottages in County Tyrone are
either Free State Roman Catholic
labourers or the families of such
labourers who are definitely hostile to
the Unionist Party and to the Northern
Government.
That a copy of this resolution be sent
to Sir Wilson Hungerford, M.P.,
secretary of the Ulster Unionist Council
for communication to the Minister of
Home Affairs, and that copies be sent
to all Unionist M.P.'s and Senators in
Fermanagh and Tyrone, with the
request that they will use their influence
to have the regulations amended as
suggested; to the chairmen of the rural
district councils, and to the secretaries
of all Unionist associations in Fermanagh
and Tyrone.
I want to draw the attention of the
House to the fact that that resolution was
passed in June of last year. Since then,
although I addressed two questions to the
Minister of Home Affairs on this subject,
the right hon. Gentleman has always
referred me to the local councils-in other
words, he has taken his instructions from
this secret society in
in Tyrone
Tyrone and
Fermanagh. You may laugh at the idea:
it would be very laughable if it were not
for the fact that it is no laughing matter
for the poor people in Fermanagh who
cannot get a single house erected. I say
it is a most disgraceful thing that anybody
professing the Christian religion should
draw that line between one applicant and
another. It an unchristian and inhuman thing for anybody in this Northern
Government-this Protestant Government for a Protestant people, as the Prime
Minister has announced-to be guilty of.
I wonder what excuse the Parliamentary
Secretary has to urge, what reason he has
to advance for not a single cottage having
been erected in Fermanagh since this
Government came into power.
To my
mind that is what has been behind the
whole matter from June, 1921, to this
minute this intimidation, this blind
bigotry, this intolerance, for which a
parallel could not be found in any place
in the world.
Mr. HANNA: I do not know exactly
what the hon. Member is complaining of.
The Home Office gets copies of all sorts of
resolutions that are passed at all sorts of
party meetings, but does the hon. Gentleman suggest that the Government have in
any way attempted to do anything to alter
the law as it stands, and as it stood, under
the Labourers' Act? Does the hon.
Gentleman imagine that the Minister of
Home Affairs can, while the law remains
as it is, give any other answer than the
answer he has already given to the hon.
Gentleman on the two occasions on which
he has put his questions?
Under the Labourers Act schemes for
labourers' cottages are initiated either by
the rural district councils themselves
or following representations made by
labourers. There was a time when the
operation of the Labourers' Act was sus
pended because of the impossibility of
getting money. I am now glad to say
that in nearly every part of Northern
Ireland, at the request of the Minister
of Home Affairs, the rural district councils are again taking steps to secure
cottages.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Has a single cottage been built in Fermanagh since that
time?
Mr. HANNA: The right hon. Gentleman answered that question to-day.
The answer is "No," but for the hon.
Member to suggest that the Government
have any responsibility in that regard
is absurd.

Mr. HEALY: Could the hon. and
learned Gentleman tell us of the inquiries
that were held before this Government
came into power?
Mr. HANNA: No Government ever
held any inquiry under the Labourers
Act unless it had had representations
from the rural district councils.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member for
South Fermanagh has had an opportunity
of expressing his views and he must now
allow the Parliamentary Secretary to
make his case.
Mr. HANNA: The resolution is pure
nonsense, and those who are responsible
for it-if it ever was passed-show that
they do not appreciate the true position
of the Labourers Act at the present
time. I say with great respect that the
hon. Member himself has shown that he
too does not appreciate it. For instance,
there is a reference to asking the Minister
of Home Affairs to change the regulations.
Impossible! There are no regulations
except those statutory conditions laid
down within the four corners of the Act,
and they could not be changed without
the Government coming to this House
and asking that they should be changed.
Does the hon. Member suggest that the
people of Northern Ireland generally
have been unfairly dealt with in the
matter of labourers' cottages? The
position of affairs is this, that of all the
thousands of labourers' cottages that
have been built far more than one-half
are occupied by members of the hon.
Gentleman's faith. Does the hon.
Gentleman challenge that?
Mr. HEALY: How do you know that?
You say you have no record of the religion of applicants.
Mr. HANNA: No inquisition is made
by my Department in relation to this
matter, but the hon. Gentleman is not so
foolish as to imagine that it is not our
duty to make ourselves familiar with conditions of that kind. We have no official
figures, and I am sorry to be placed in the
position to have to make an observation
of this kind, because neither I nor any
of my colleagues will ever be a party to
passing an Act of Parliament, or administering an Act of Parliament, in
favour of one section of the community
as against another section. In spite of
all the resolutions that are passed and
the observations that are made in this
House and outside it our record in that
respect is perfectly clean and honourable.
Now that the rural district councils are
applying themselves with a great deal of
vigour to this question, which had its
origin, if it had an origin at all, in June,
1936, it is a pity it should have been
placarded in the way it has been either
outside or inside this House.
I have pointed out that no attempt
has been made to alter the law, and none
will be made. I would like it to be wellknown and appreciated that rural councils may initiate schemes without any
representation from any labourers, and
that they can be forced into action by
representations made by labourers on the
proper form.
Those labourers who make
the representations are entitled, under
the provisions of the Act, to a preference
when it comes to the allocation of the
houses. They have not an absolute right
to get houses, but, all other things being
equal, the preference goes in their
favour. I am very glad and proud to be
able to say, speaking with the knowledge
I have of the Home Office, that that
section of the Act has never been
departed from except for very good
reasons that are entirely outside the considerations that have been mentioned in
the debate to-night.

Mr. ANDREWS: There was a mistake

:

has been passed

PENSIONS ON NEW ZEALAND
BASIS.
8. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Prime
Minister whether, in view of the statement of the Minister of Finance on the
18th March, 1937, that "Northern
Ireland is richer than New Zealand," he
will take steps to ensure that old age
pensions, widows' pensions, orphans'
allowances and wages in Northern Ireland
will be brought up to the New Zealand
standards with all convenient speed.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply to this
question.
The answer is in the negative. I firmly
believe that it is in the best interests of
the workers of Northern Ireland that
social standards should be maintained on

Kingdom.

Northern Ireland to non-European
countries was 48,557. I regret I have no
information regarding the migration of
foreign nationals. The statistics I have
given are taken from the "Board of
Trade Journal."
COPIES OF CENSUS RETURNS.
10. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
it is a fact that members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary are taking a copy
from the census forms for the purpose of
compiling a household register; whether
the Registrar General of Northern
Ireland assured the citizens that the
census form was private and confidential,
and, in view of this assurance, will the
Minister issue an instruction that all
copies of the census returns in police
barracks must be destroyed.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact
that, owing to a misunderstanding, census
forms were made use of at certain police
barracks to check and bring up to date
the householders' register which is kept
at all barracks. Immediately upon this
matter being brought under notice.
directions were issued drawing attention
to the provisions of Section 10 (4) of the
Census Act (Northern Ireland), 1936, and
any records of the particulars taken from
the census forms have been expunged.

CLAUSE 1 (Power of local authorities to make bylaws for regulating
advertisements).
(1) Subject to the provisions of this
Act, a local authority may make bylaws
for the regulation and control of
hoardings and similar structures used
or intended to be used for the display
of advertisements.

and similar structures in use for
advertising purposes at the time of the
making of the bylaws, and of any
advertisements exhibited at that time,
for such period, not being less than
five years from that time, as they may
think fit.

As hon. Members are aware, this Clause
is directed to secure the safety of hoardings and other structures used for the
display of advertisements. Under the

authorities to make bylaws for this purpose was limited to hoardings exceeding

preventing the erection of any advertisements whatever. The object of the

does not do more than carry out the
intended purpose of providing for structural security.

If within the district of a local
authority any advertisements are
erected or exhibited in contravention of
any bylaw made under this Act, the

which such advertisements are erected
or exhibited a notice in writing requir

the service of the notice) as may be
specified in the notice, to remove such

intoxicants.

Rev. Professor CORKEY: I beg to
move, "That the Clause be now read a
Second time." Legislation dealing
with advertisements is not very common,
but it is not unknown. A few
years ago in the House at Westminster
a man very famous in Northern Ireland,
Lord Carson, introduced legislation
limiting the power of moneylenders to
advertise the boons and blesssings which
they were prepared to offer to the community. That Bill which limited the
power of this class of people to advertise was accepted and adopted by this
House and is now the law in Northern
Ireland. This new Clause which I propose to be inserted in the Bill seeks to
limit in the same way the powers of
those who are interested in the sale of
intoxicating liquor to advertise their
wares. There are three or four facts I
would like to mention in justification of
this new Clause.
First of all, I would remind the
House that for centuries the legislature
in this country has regarded intoxicants
as a peculiar kind of commodity requiring special regulations. Only a limited
number of people are allowed to sell intoxicants at all and they have to be
licensed to do so. They are only allowed
to be sold on certain days of the week
and during certain hours of the day. In
Northern Ireland they are not allowed
to be sold where groceries are sold on
the same premises. These are only a
few of the regulations which the legislature has laid down for the handling
of these particular commodities. The
Amendment goes just one step further
and suggests that those regulations
should extend to the advertisements

is not a point of order. I rule that the

Mr. STEWART: May I remind the

The CHAIRMAN: As far as Parliamentary procedure is concerned that

The CHAIRMAN: I have already

The CHAIRMAN: I have given my

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: You have

I was
Mr. ELLIOTT: I quite agree.
not referring to any Member of this Committee when I made my statement that
the finished product of the brewers' business is the drunkard. On one occasion I
heard of a shoemaker who lived beside a
public-house. Before closing time there
was a man on the licensed premises who
was the worse of drink. The publican
came to the bootmaker next door and
asked him to come inside and give him a
hand to put out the drunk man. The
bootmaker said when he finished a pair
of boots he put them in the window, and
why should the publican not do the same
thing-put the man in his window. I
do not for a moment say that all those
who partake of intoxicating liquors are
going to be drunkards, but it cannot be
denied that a number of people who partake of them go down to drunkards'
graves every year. I am sure those interested in the trade do not want to hear
that, but I am dealing with facts, and I
put them as I know them.
The hon. Member for Woodvale in a
very slighting way made some reference
to the Irish Temperance Alliance. I do
not make any apology for being president
of that body. All through my life I have
been a strict teetotaller. I defy anyone
to say they have ever seen me taking
liquor or being under the influence of
liquor in any place. I do not see why
people who come here as temperance
reformers should not express their views.
I think there is nothing dishonourable
in that. We stand for our principles and
intend to carry our principles into the
Division Lobby in support of the Clause.
We ought to be allowed the liberty which
hon. Members on the other side claim
for themselves. We temperance people
ask for nothing more. We believe these
advertisements are dangerous to the
young people of the community. In the
best interests of the community we ought
to oppose liquor advertisements being
allowed to be put on hoardings in our
countryside. One advertisement I see
often is, "Guinness is good for you."
Mr. STEWART: So it is.
Mr. ELLIOTT: It is good for Guinness
because he gets big dividends out of it.
Guinness never says it is good for him; he
says it is good for you. Many of the
advertisements we see are not true to fact
at all. They do not give the truth, the

whole truth, and nothing but the truth.
They proclaim statements that cannot be

deal has been said about the revenue
derived from strong drink. One would
think these men in the liquor business
were engaged to bring revenue to the

It is a fact which I know does not go

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON : I do not
intend to adopt the lines of the last

advocate, in my opinion made the most

man standing on the same platform as he
does I would get off it. I stand as an
ordinary person who drinks beer and
thinks it is good for him. Coming down
to bed-rock this Clause appears to me to
be aimed at restraining what is a perfectly
legitimate trade in the eyes of the law.
It is proposed in this Clause to prohibit
the advertisements of the drink trade
which is a legitimate trade as much as, let
us say, shipbuilding, linen manufacture,
or any other trade. All trades existing
in this and other countries are subject to
certain restrictions as to hours of work
and so on. The liquor trade is subject to
a great many more restrictions, but that
does not prevent it from being a legitimate trade.
If this Clause were accepted by this
Committee-but I know it will not be
accepted-you will find people coming
along and saying, "You should not be
allowed to smoke. Advertisements about
smoking should be prohibited," and so
on. This is only the thin end of the
wedge of these people calling themselves
temperance people who when they get on
their feet use most intemperate language.
If the hon. Members who support this
Clause are really keen in their intentions
why do they not submit a Bill to stop the
display of ladies' underwear? The hon.
Member for the University might as well
object to a picture of a lady dressed in a

I am not going to support any Clause to
restrain a perfectly legitimate trade
which has just as much right as anybody
else to advertise.
Mr. HANNA: I was rather anxious

Mr. CRAWFORD: Cannot be trusted.
Mr. HANNA: From the beginning to

NEW CLAUSE (Bylaws as to advertisements on trees).
Subject to the provisions of this Act
and without prejudice to the operation
of any bylaws made under Section one
thereof, a local authority may make
bylaws for the purpose of providing
that no advertisements shall be affixed

Brought up and read a First time.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON : I beg to
move, "That this new Clause be read a
Second time." Anybody who takes an
interest in the country or who drives
through it will find a great many advertisements nailed to trees. These advertise
somebody's mineral waters or some other
commodity; but it does not matter what
the advertisements are, they are an eyesore and disfigure the countryside. The
Act which applies to Scotland goes a good
deal farther than my new Clause. There
local authorities are empowered to make
bylaws for preventing the affixing of
advertisements upon any wall, tree, fence,
gate or elsewhere on private property,
without the consent of either the owner
or occupier previously given in writing,
or except by virtue of some other sufficient
legal authority. I am doubtful whether
we could apply that Clause here in full,
but I do ask the Committee for the sake
of the countryside and the development
of the tourist traffic to prohibit the spoiling of our countryside with these horrible
tin advertisements on trees. I hope this
new Clause will be accepted.

Mr. MIDGLEY: I do not like to be
interrupted when I am speaking, and,
consequently, I am waiting until the élite
have departed. In pursuance of the
notice I gave at question time this afternoon I wish to raise the matter of the
wages paid in the drapery trade, and
respectfully to draw the Minister's attention to another angle of this question.
For the purpose of getting down to the
point which I have particularly in mind,
I also wish to refer to the question
I addressed to the Minister of Labour this
afternoon. The question was:
Wages in Drapery Trade 802
Adjournment-
13 April 1937
To ask the Minister of Labour
whether, in view of the fact that
thousands of workers in the wholesale
and retail drapery trade are being
scandalously underpaid, and that as he
has repeatedly declared the Government's policy is to keep in step with
social improvements in Great Britain,
and that as the British Minister of
Labour agreed to meet representatives
of the employers and workers in the
English and Welsh Drapery Trade in
London on the 18th March, 1937, and
of the Scottish employers and workers
in Edinburgh on 8th April, 1937, for
the purpose of fostering machinery for
the regulation of wages and working
conditions by negotiation, he is prepared to take similar steps in Northern
Ireland.
I now wish to inform the Minister that
these conferences were held under the
jurisdiction of the Imperial Minister of
Labour, and that it was decided, as a
result of those conferences in London and
Edinburgh, to set up a Joint Council of
the wholesale and retail drapery trade
for the purpose of fixing agreed rates of
wages for various classes of workers in
the distributive trade. The Imperial
Minister of Labour also gave an undertaking to the people concerned that is,
to both sides-that it is his intention to
promote a Bill to legalise those rates as
and when they are agreed upon. That
is a very important point.
The Minister of Labour for Northern
Ireland intimated to this House, in reply
to my question, that he had received a
resolution from the Chamber of Trade in
Belfast in reply to representations which
the Minister himself had made. I now
wish to express my personal appreciation,
and the appreciation of all the people in
the trade concerned, of the steps that the
Minister has already taken in this matter.
I am sure that it has not been an easy
task, in view of the lack of tradition in
this respect, and I should be very sorry
to do or say anything to-night that would
place any obstacle in the way of the right
hon. Gentleman consummating the good
work which he has already undertaken.
The right hon. Gentleman has intimated that a representative of the Ministry of Labour will meet a committee of
the Chamber of Trade on Thursday.
What I now wish to do is to appeal to
the Minister to inform his representative
that it is absolutely imperative in deciding upon a committee to consider wages
and conditions in the distributive trade,
both wholesale and retail, that the
workers are kept in mind, and that no
committee will be deemed to be suitable
to cope with this question in all its comprehensiveness unless there are representatives of the workers upon it. I have
indicated to the Minister and to the
House what has been done on the other
side of the Channel, and I am sure the
Minister of Labour in this area is just
as desirous personally of doing as much on
this side of the water. The conditions
may not just be analogous throughout,
and it may be that some aspects here may
present more difficulties than were
encountered across the water. I came to
the House this afternoon with the mass
of evidence which I hold in my hand, in
support of the question which I had put
down. This is a mass of evidence as to
wages and conditions in the distributive
trade, drawn from a variety of firms in
the city of Belfast. I am not, however,
going to deal with this evidence now,
because it is not necessary at this
juncture.
I do want to indicate to the Minister
that already partial machinery exists on
the workers' side for dealing with this
question. What we want the Minister
to do, through his representative, is to
ask the employers to note that a committee of that kind cannot be regarded
as complete if the employers deem it to
be a committee of themselves only. To
get the job done thoroughly and impartially provision must be made for representation of the workers in any
machinery which is provided. It is the
basis of our civilisation, so far as working
conditions at any rate are concerned, that
there must be mutuality of contract and
recognition of that in all phases of industry. Already that has been provided in
the large industries of Great Britain and
Northern Ireland by the trade union
organisations, and in some respects by
trade boards. But here is a vast field
of distributive work in which no adequate
machinery exists at the present time, and
the employers are being asked to take the
first step to provide the machinery. At
this juncture I do not wish to go any
further than to make an earnest appeal
to the Minister to use his best efforts, and
to use the best possible methods, to ensure

Petroleum (Transfer of Licences) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The provisions of this short Bill are similar to
those of the recent Imperial measure
bearing the same title, and have for their
object the remedy of a technical flaw
in the previous enactments which, while
dealing with the issue of licences for the
storage of petroleum spirit, failed to
make provision for the transfer of such
licences if the premises in respect of
which they were issued were sold or
transferred to new ownership. The
result of this has been that where the
annual licence fee prescribed under the
Act of 1929 has been paid, a new owner
of the premises has in some instances had
to pay an exactly similar fee for a new
licence within a few months after the
first fee has been paid.
Under the provisions of this short Bill
the transfer of a petroleum spirit licence
may be granted by the local authority
who originally issued the licence, or by
the Minister of Home Affairs, in cases
where the licence was issued by him, and
in respect of such transfer a fee of only
2s 6d will have to be paid.
I do not think there is anything
further I need say about this short
measure, which I am sure will commend
itself to every Member in this House. I
beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.
Horse Breeding Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): As this is
short amending measure it will not b
necessary for me to trespass upon the
time of the House except for a very
brief explanation.
The Ministry's powers of licensing the
ownership or control of stallions are at
present governed by Section 1 of the
Horse Breeding Act (Northern Ireland),
1926, which provides for the licensing
of stallions of three years old and upwards. We are however, satisfied from
reports received that animals of a low
grade between two and three years old
are being used for stud purposes. This
practice presents an appreciable obstacle
in the way of the Ministry's efforts to
secure and maintain an improved standard
of horses bred in Northern Ireland.
Powers are, therefore, sought to enable
the Ministry to exercise licensing control
over all stallions of two years old and
upwards. This proposal is in accordance
with a strong recommendation made by
my Ministry's Horse Advisory Committee and endorsed by the Ministry's
Law Reform Bill-
Second Reading
14 APRIL 1937
Consultative Committee. If the Bill is
passed the Ministry's powers of regulation in this respect will again be brought
into uniformity with those at present
vested in the responsible Departments in
Great Britain and the Irish Free State.
I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.
Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: This is
a Bill which embodies a number of
Statutes recently passed in England,
reforming the general law in very important directions. It is, as Members
will see, highly technical, being altogether of a legal nature, and in order
to understand the ramifications of these
provisions it is necessary to have a very
complete knowledge of our law. Notwithstanding that, in moving the Second
Reading I will point out in as simple
language as possible exactly what these
provisions are intended to do.
Before I do so might I say a word
about the general position of the law in
Northern Ireland. I think that Members of the House will agree that it is
an important thing that so far as possible the general law of the land should
be uniform with the law in England.
For instance, to take an example which
comes out in this Bill now before the
House, it is an anomalous thing that,
supposing there is a motor accident and
injuries are received, persons would have
a right of action in England that they
would not have if the accident took
place in Northern Ireland. It is a
matter which affects the rights of the
public and I think the House will agree
that the public in Northern Ireland
should have the same rights and the same
protection as people on the other side
of the water. And that is also an important consideration from another point
of view, because, to take the same
example, the insurance of persons in the
use of vehicles upon the highway is
almost entirely carried out by companies
that have their headquarters across the
water and it is important that the same
rights should apply to their policy holders
in Northern Ireland as apply to policy
holders in England. If that were not so
differences would have to be made in the
policies to meet the varying conditions in
this country, and, in addition to that,
there would probably have to be a
variation in the tariff rates which would
operate in an unfair manner against our
people.
There is also another reason for trying
to keep these provisions of the general
law uniform with the provisions of the
law in England. It is important that
persons on both sides of the water should
have as complete a knowledge of the
general law as possible, and the more
uniform the law is kept the easier it is
for lawyers in England, as well as our
own lawyers here, to be familiar with
the rights of their clients. And that
suggests another line of thought, and
that is, that as this country is very small,
and it is very difficult to have textbooks
dealing with these very complicated
matters, if the law is the same in Northern Ireland as in England the textbooks
published by the great English publishing
houses will be the authorities for our
people.
When we remember that the ultimate
appeal in all these matters is the Supreme
Court of Judicature and then the House
of Lords, which is the same tribunal that
tries the appeals from the courts in
England, it will be seen that it is
obviously of great advantage to have the
law uniform in the two jurisdictions.
This Bill now before the House is an
attempt to put the law in Northern
Ireland and in England on a uniform
basis in one or two very important
matters.
As the House will see, the first portion
of this Bill deals with the establishment
of a "real representative." In technical
language this means that where real
estate is being dealt with in the courts it
is to be dealt with for the purpose of
administration in the winding up of the
estate as if it were personal property.
This reform has been overdue for
many years,
because it has been
the law in England since the Land
Transfer Act, 1897, but has not yet been
put on the Statute Book in Northern
Ireland. The necessity for it is thisthat where an estate is being wound up
which comprises both real and personal
Law Reform Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Attorney-General]
property, it is absolutely necessary to have
somebody to represent the real estate.
There have been numerous cases in which,
owing to the difficulty of ascertaining who
was the heir-at-law, the winding up of
the estate has been greatly protracted,
and very serious costs occasioned to the
persons interested in the property. This
part of the Bill will obviate that, because
we have adopted the provisions of the
Land Transfer Act, 1897. Under this
Bill as it stands, freehold land in
Northern Ireland is to devolve upon the
personal representative instead of the
heir-at-law.
The provisions are based on the Land
Transfer Act, 1897, and our Local
Registration of Title Act, 1891. It was
suggested that some of the provisions
should be taken from the new English
Property Act, but on consideration it was
decided that it was better to keep to the
Land Transfer Act, 1897, especially
having regard to the fact that the greater
part of our land now devolves under the
Local Registration of Title Act, 1891, and
in that way not only devolves but is
administered. I think this particular
section of this Bill is one which is long
overdue. It has been submitted to the
various bodies of the legal professionthe Incorporated Law Society and the
General Council of the Bar-and so far as
I know it has received the approval of
these bodies.
The second part of this Bill is, perhaps,
better understood by the public. It deals
with the capacity and liability of married
women and the liability of husbands.
Under it the last fetters of married
women are to be swept away. It follows
the English Act of 25 and 26 Geo. V,
chap. 30, which was passed a year or so
ago, and was based upon the interim
report of the Law Revision Committee,
which was presided over by Lord Hanworth. If hon. Members will turn to the
first of the Clauses in this Part 2 they
will find in Section 9 it provides that:
A married woman shall be capable of
acquiring, holding and disposing of any
property; be capable of rendering herself, and being rendered, liable in
respect of any tort, contract, debt or
obligation; be capable of suing and
being sued either in tort or in contract
or otherwise; and be subject to the law
relating to bankruptcy .
That puts her in the position of control
over her own property. It makes her
liable for her own contracts and debts.
Section 10 goes on to deal with the
property of a married woman, and it
provides that her propertyshall belong to her in all respects
as if she were a feme-sole, and may be
disposed of accordingly.
What is known in the law as restriction
upon anticipation is taken away by the
proviso in Clause 10. Then the corresponding provision in respect of the
husband comes under Clause 11. Under
it the husband of a married woman is
to be relieved first of all from being
liablein respect of any tort committed by
her whether before or after the
marriage, or in respect of any contract
entered into, or debt or obligation
incurred, by her before the marriage.
He is no longer to be liableto be sued or made a party to any legal
proceeding brought in respect of any
such tort, contract, debt or obligation.
That, I think the House will agree, marks
the final emancipation of women.
Husband and wife will be able to look
over the table at each other knowing that
she is entitled to use her personal
property for herself, while the husband
will realise that he will not be responsible
for the consequences of any indiscretion
committed by his wife.
The third part of this Bill deals with
the effect of death on certain causes of
action. It is based on the English Act
of 24 and 25 George V, which was passed
in Westminster after the Law Revision
Committee had sat upon it and had gone
into the matter in very great detail.
Under this part of the Bill what is known
as the main actio personalis moritur cum
persona disappears. I will explain
exactly what that means. Supposing that
a person is injured in an accident and he
brings an action in respect of personal
injuries. He may proceed right down to
the hearing and incur very heavy costs
and expenses. The parties may actually
get into court, but before a verdict is
given or any judgment is entered the man
may die, and the result is that under the
law as it stands at present the right of
action disappears with the death of the
party.
Law Reform Bill-
Second Reading
14 APRIL 1937
Under the provision in this Bill the
right of action is to survive. Clause 14
provides that
All causes of action subsisting against
or vested in him shall survive against
or as the case may be for the benefit
of his estate.
If a man dies there is a right of action
which is a subsisting right of action
which he could have brought in his lifetime, and it will be possible to carry on
that right of action for the benefit of
his estate. If on the other hand he is
liable to some action in respect of some
personal cause of action it can be continued against his personal representative
by the person to whom he would be
liable if he were alive. This is a rule
which I think most lawyers regard as a
very just one, because as the matter has
been applied up to the present it has
given rise to a great injustice in a number of cases. It will also be noticed by
Clause 15 that there is an amendment of
the Fatal Accidents Act which is known
as Lord Campbell's Act. That was one
of the exceptions to the rule in main
actio personalis. By statute children.
or dependents were entitled to bring an
action in respect of the deceased if they
could prove dependency, but that did
not apply to illegitimate children or
adopted children. It has now been
applied in England to illegitimate
children and children of adoption.
Accordingly that same provision is made
in Clause 14 to apply here. I think the
House will agree that it is a just and
proper Clause.
The last part of this Bill deals with
amendments as to tort-feasors and
interest on debts and damages. This also
follows the Act of 25 and 26 George V,
Chap. 30, in England, and it is based on
the interim report of the Law Revision
Committee. As the law stands at present
if a number of persons commit a tort
which injures another party that party
must sue them together. He cannot sue
one and afterwards sue another. The
result of that very often is that it is
impossible to know originally who
exactly of all the persons who may be
liable are liable. Under this Clause in
the Bill it is provided that a judgment
recovered against one person liable for
tort shall not be a bar to action against
others who are equally liable. The
House will, however, find in Clause 16
certain provisions preventing the multiplicity of actions against a number of
tort-feasors. This is a provision which,
I think, is long overdue. There is hardly
anyone practising at the Bar who has
not at some time or other found the
present rule to work harshly in certain
cases.
Under the Clause as it stands it will
be possible for a person, who has been
held liable along with a number of other
persons, to pay a contribution towards
the damages and costs awarded against
him the same as the other persons liable
with him. As the law stands at present
that cannot be done. I have known cases
in which persons have been sued for a
tort. Some of them have been people
against whom the plaintiff had got a
certain amount of animus and they have
got a judgment against them all, but
levied the whole of that judgment against
one of the number. That has worked
with great injustice and has been what
I may describe as a medium of blackmail, because some of the tort-feasors in
order to get out of the liability agree
with the plaintiff that they want a test
action and costs and judgment are not
levied against them. This will put an
end to any possibility of that sort and
will make the contribution as between
all the persons who have done a wrong
equal and equitable.

In England, owing to the great increase

the powers of the courts over arbitrations,
and facilitated the holding of arbitrations.
in very many respects. Notwithstanding

advisers of the Government of Northern

bringing our arbitration law up to date
we found there was then sitting a Commission, known as the McKinnon Commission, which was going into this
question of arbitrations in England in

commercial community. We have been
waiting for some years for the outcome

1934 its deliberations were embodied in
the English Arbitration Bill. But instead of revising the law of arbitration
as a whole they merely amended the Act
of 1889 by the Act of 1934, and that
is the way in which the law in England
stands now.
This Bill is based upon the two English Acts thrown into one, and from a
drafting point of view it is perhaps preferable to the two English Acts, because
it is more coherent. Since 1856, when
the Common Law Procedure Act for

and engineering concerns have always

their disputes-

Looking at it from the practical point

There is here no proper system of having

matters that arise in the course of arbitration proceedings in a way that people wish
them to be dealt with nowadays. As the
Attorney-General has told the House, a
comprehensive and modern Act was
passed in England in 1889. It was not
applied to Ireland, and I am not sure of
the reason why, but I think the reason
probably was that arbitration has
developed more in commercial communities than in communities which are
largely agricultural.
In the nineteenth century England
became a characteristically industrial
community, and arbitration did develop
there, and they eventually got an up-todate arbitration code. In Ireland, on the
other hand, there was not as big a commercial community in the northern part
of the country, and in the rest of the
country there was no great need felt for
amendment of the law, with the result
that nothing in particular was done. We
in Belfast, which is a characteristically
commercial city, have always felt the need
for the law to be brought more into line
with the English law. That is what is
being done in this Bill. Arbitration was
greatly extended during the latter part
of the nineteenth century and the early
years of the present century.
Take
Commercial men have got the idea into
their heads-and there is much to be said
for it that many commercial disputes
can be better dealt with by an arbitration court than by a court of law.
the case of two merchants in the grain
trade who have a dispute about a contract. They feel that it is better to refer
the dispute to an arbitrator who is
acquainted with the grain trade and its
8 25
Size of Classes in P.E. Schools 826
Arbitration Bill
14 APRIL 1937
technicalities, and the practice that goes |
on in buying and selling, and who will
be able to get down to the net point in
dispute. They feel that a matter of that
kind, which might occupy a court for
some days, can be dealt with by an
arbitrator in a short time, perhaps after
perusal of the correspondence and the
hearing of one witness on each side.
The same thing applies to engineering
disputes. Suppose that Belfast Corporation goes in for laying a large system of
sewers, or that a waterworks undertaking
decides to build a new reservoir. They
have to employ an engineer, and very
many matters are sure to come up in the
course of such contracts which might lead
to differences between the owners of the
works on the one hand and the contractors on the other. It is now the
invariable practice to insert an arbitration clause in such contracts, for this
reason, that the fighting out in a court
of law of the differences that might arise
would be interminable. An engineer of
some eminence is always appointed as
arbitrator, one who is au fait with the
technicalities of the contract and of the
work, and who can deal rapidly, and with
the necessary technical knowledge, with
the points in dispute. Those immediately
concerned feel that in that way disputes
are much better dealt with than they
would be in the ordinary way before a
judge and a jury.
Arbitration, therefore, has grown up
particularly among the commercial community here, but we have been working
under an old-world, out of date code, a
code that is full of holes, if I may say so,
full of imperfections and all sorts of
technicalities that have to be watched.
The commercial community has been
pressing for a more satisfactory code.
this Bill we have got a code that is based
on the English legislation of to-day, and
which, in view of the practitioners in
England, gives great satisfaction. This
will be a great acquisition, particularly
in a commercial city like Belfast. It will
also have this advantage, that if we adopt
the English system here we will have the
benefit of the English text books. Here
we have no text books on the Irish law of
arbitration. We have to go to the law,
to the statutes, and to the collected
decisions, and to as much of the English
text books as we find applicable. Now
we will have the advantage of the English
text books, and of the decisions that are
given from year to year with regard to
the various matters that arise in
arbitration.
We in Ireland, in considering points,
have always had to look at the English
decisions, and to decide—and it is a very
difficult matter to decide-whether the
English decisions are applicable or not.
We have been working here in this unsatisfactory way and in this state of uncertainty, and I think the Government
have taken a step which is in the interests

of the community generally.
branches of the legal profession heartily
welcome this Bill, not so much in the

Motion for Adjournment.
SIZE OF CLASSES IN
ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.'
(Sir Wilson Hungerford.)
Major MCCORMICK: I wish to raise
the question, of which I gave notice, of
the size of, or the abnormal number of
pupils in, classes in elementary schools.
The answer that the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education
gave me last week was of such an indefinite or non-committal kind that I considered it most unsatisfactory in view of
the importance of the question. I took
it in effect as an answer in the negative.
I hope, however, I am wrong in that
deduction, and that I will have the help
of the hon. and learned Gentleman in
settling this matter. In any case, I feel
so strongly on this matter that I may
be allowed to bring to the notice of the
House facts that will show the injustice
that is being done to both teachers and
pupils in schools where there are these
large classes, which are beyond the
capacity of any teacher to manage, let
Size of Classes in P.E. Schools 828
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major McCormick]
alone teach. There is the waste of the
pupil's time, and no attention is possible
to the backward child.
This question has been raised here on
many occasions, and I have taken the
views of both parents and teachers in
order to voice them in this House. I
hope to show the Parliamentary Secretary, by evidence, that this injustice is
greater than he thinks. The House will
admit that we owe a great deal to the
elementary school teachers, and will
allow that in the main they all are
anxious not only to fulfil their duties
satisfactorily, but to get the very best
results possible out of their classes.
I tried to find a public elementary
school with classes of from 35 to 40
pupils, to which I could send a boy of my
own. I went to many schools in order to
find such conditions, but I could not find
one in which the classes consisted of under
60 pupils. I may add that my boy is
now going to a country school, where
there are 38 pupils in the class. As a
parent I object to these large classes that
I have mentioned, for the children's time
is wasted and the teachers are under a
great disadvantage. The teachers are
disheartened by the size of the classes,
and the result is that they concentrate on
the clever pupils who can enter for
scholarships and so on. Teachers cannot
do the impossible. I admit that they do
everything that is humanly possible.
I have a list here which can be verified.
Some 30 schools are concerned in which
there are 45 classes and over 50 pupils
in each class. I am now speaking of
infant as well as adult classes. In one
class a few weeks ago there were 87
pupils, but that number has been now
reduced to 74. In another class there
were 82 pupils. There are classes with
from 60 to 65 pupils and no teacher can
be expected to manage such a large number of pupils. It is admitted that in
classes of 50 or upwards the dull
children, those whose mental ability
develops later in life, have not a fair
chance. The teacher's time is spent in
controlling the class instead of teaching
it. In English schools we find that
classes of 40 are common, but even then
the educational authorities are being
asked to reduce the number to 35. In
England, if there are more than 40
pupils in a class, the teacher must report
this fact to the Director of Education.
I do not know what system our
inspectors have here, but I say in all
seriousness that perhaps they feel it is
hopeless to do anything. It is apparently
useless for the inspectors to report such
large classes seeing that they are so
common. If I am informed that I am
wrong I shall be glad. Owing to the difficulty of teaching classes with over 50
pupils, scholarship classes of 40 are being
formed in many of the new schools and
this gives only the brilliant pupils a
chance. The answers given by the Parlia
mentary Secretary in reply to previous
questions on 20th February and 26th
November, 1936, are very much the
same. In view of the figures now given
I would ask him what he proposes to
do. Can he give us some hope that this
matter will be rectified, or will he tell us
what action has already been taken!
This question must be raised again and
in a much stronger form. If the matter
is gone into-I am speaking particularly
with regard to the Belfast Education
Authority-it will be found that there
are fully 100 classes in each of which
there are from 50 to 60 pupils. The
answer previously given by the Parliamentary Secretary was as follows:
I would refer the hon. and gallant
Member to my replies to his questions
on this subject on 20th February and
26th November, 1936. The Ministry
is not aware that abnormally large
classes are so common as is implied in
the question, but inquiries are being
made and the matter will be carefully
watched.
When this information was given to
the right hon. Gentleman he did not seem
to worry much more about it. So far as
I know the figures given are correct. It
seems to me that the policy of laisser
faire is followed in regard to this matter.
If the difficulty is one of finance surely
the House will help him out. We can
find the money for the extra teaching
staff that is required. He informed met
on a previous occasion that whilst he
would not admit the existence of a class
of 72 pupils, he would accept my
assurance that there was a class with 72
pupils in it. I have discovered a larger
class, one with 80 pupils. As this is
such a serious matter the Ministry must
Size of Classes in P.E. Schools 830
Adjournment-
14 APRIL 1937
be aware of it, and also of the school in
which it exists. If the Parliamentary
Secretary states that there is no regulation governing the size of the classes
then I say that commonsense should be
exercised by the Education Authority.
In view of the difficulties which teachers
have to face, the loss by the pupils in
regard to education is great.
Our reputation-that is our National
School reputation-so far as elementary
schools are concerned is going down.
Can you tell me how a class of 80 can
be taught the three Rs? The clever
pupils are gaining all the knowledge
while the backward children remain at
the bottom. It is a serious matter that
instead of the pupils who need more
attention receiving it, consideration is
given to those who least require it. I
understand that has come about through
schools being amalgamated and a false
idea that economies can be effected in
the teaching staff because fewer teachers
are required. It does not seem that that
system has been a success. The high cost
of our educational system is well known.
Over two millions is spent annually. In
my opinion and that of many others this
scandal of large classes has lowered the
standard of education, and national
school education has lost the great
There is no
reputation which it had.
excuse for such large classes unless,
perhaps, it is a question of finance.
In answer to a question I was informed
that there are 87 teachers unemployed.
These teachers could be brought in and
thus in some way relieve the situation.
Can the education of these children be
considered satisfactory? Teachers no
doubt try to get through a weary day's
work and do their best, but many conscientious teachers feel the strain of trying to do the impossible. What of the
pupils? One teacher told me that they
will get pushed through to the next class
whether they are fit for it or not. I
cannot, however, accept that statement
as being right. Surely our national
school education has not come to the pass
that because of large classes the pupils
who are unfit are pushed on into the next

another teacher. A teacher cannot
manage a class of 80 children, let alone
teach them. The days of miracles are
past, and the teachers cannot do it.
Whether they do it or not they get their
salaries.
I should like this matter to be taken
up and if it is necessary to employ more
teachers by all means let us do so. There
are close on 100 teachers unemployed at
the present time, and surely the money
can be found to have some of them
employed in the schools. If this were
done it would help to remove this
scandal.

The standard staffing of our schools,
according to our regulations is this, we
start with five pupils, and as against five
pupils on the rolls we allot a principal to
the school. Then for every subsequent
45 pupils we allot one assistant teacher,

rooms for practical subjects there is an

for every 220 pupils. Working that out
in no case should there be under any

The hon. and gallant Member said one
thing that disturbed me. He said that
the progress of pupils in elementary
schools in the three Rs, as he called
them, at the present time falls far short
of that to which pupils attained say 30
or 35 years ago. This is a question that
was investigated by a Committee of
which I was Chairman a few years ago,
and we asked one of our inspectors what

Commissioners of National Education
exactly 30 years before the date we were
speaking and in it exactly the same
charge in the same words was made.
However, he went a little further than
that. He reminded us that 30 years ago
it was usual in connection with what
was then in existence, the famous
"results system", to have the pupils in
the elementary schools examined once
every year regularly by His Majesty's
inspectors on set papers in arithmetic.
The complaint has always been that in
reading, writing and arithmetic the
present generation falls far behind that
of 30 years ago.
He said it was very
difficult to test reading and writing, but
it was quite simple to test arithmetic. He
happened to have a set of these arithmetic cards which had been abolished
some 30 years ago and taking them out
of a drawer he selected cards suitable to
the standard and the age-I think he
said 12. This inspector said he took these
cards and went into the classes of pupils
of the corresponding age in two schools
in Belfast and one school in Bangor, Co.
Down. He said they were not selected
schools in any way: he went into them
on chance. The cards were cards in
arithmetic and they were calculated to
occupy the pupils on an examination that
would last for one hour and a half. The
result was this, that instead of taking one
and a half hours to do this test the pupils
had the test done in half an hour and
the percentage of correctness was over 90
per cent. Is not that a complete answer
to those who say that present day pupils
are not instructed as thoroughly and as
well in the subject of elementary arithmetic as the pupils of 30 years ago?
The charge is constantly made.
Personally I do not believe it. I cannot
say any more than that. I have given
you one test that was applied quite
recently, quite deliberately, and quite
honestly by a person in a position to
know what he was doing. Those are the
results. In face of that, how any person
persists in propagating what I believe to
be an untrue assertion with regard to
our present day curriculum and teaching
I cannot understand.

that is required. Has the Parliamentary
Secretary ever visited some of the overcrowded schools in agricultural areas?
Mr. ROBB: Yes.
Mr. HENDERSON: Are you proud
of what you saw?
Mr. ROBB: No.
Mr. HENDERSON: No, and I do not
think any citizen could be proud of the
condition of the schools in agricultural
areas. There are children who may be
future Cabinet Ministers in Northern
Ireland, and why should they be crowded
like herrings in these schools? The
mother of a pupil in a Crumlin Road
school told me that when she went into
that building she was flabbergasted at the
terrible conditions of overcrowding existing. The children had no forms on which
to sit. Time and again the educational
authority have appealed to the Ministry
for permission to employ additional
teachers, but they get no reply. The
question of cost should not be taken into
account. There is no question of cost in
connection with the running of the Agricultural Department. Here is a Department that requires every farthing that
can be spent on it. The Parliamentary
Secretary is starving education in
Northern Ireland. He speaks about a
million pounds. What is a million
pounds in a country like this? Why,
the Minister of Finance has stated
that this is the richest country of its size
-richer than Australia and New Zealand.
In New Zealand they pay their pensioners
15s to £1 a week, and it is a poorer
country, and we only pay them 10s. You
can easily get the money if you set your
mind to it. The money can be got to
build new schools and employ additional
teachers.
The most important factor in connection with this question of overcrowding
is the question of the effect on the health
of the children. Their health is bound
to be impaired by these large classes. I
appeal to the Parliamentary Secretary to
take this matter up in a more serious way.
Instead of going to teachers' conferences
let him pay a little attention to the
