Adjournment-
[Mr. Henderson]
elementary schools. Let him do the same
as the Minister of Labour does-visit the
storm centres and evil spots in the
country. He can then come back here,
and if he has the courage of his convictions he will tell the Prime Minister
that no matter where the money comes
from it must be got for the building of
schools and the provision of work for unemployed teachers. I have a high regard
for the Parliamentary Secretary, but he
does not pay attention to the work that
he ought to. It may be that he is overworked at something else. At Lambeg
the condition of affairs is little changed
since I visited it two or three years ago.
The overcrowding there was abominable.
There were 40 or 50 children grouped in
a small thatched lean-to. I have repeatedly, at the Corporation, drawn
attention to the condition of things in the
north end of the city. There are very
large classes in some of the schools. I
know classes comprising between 70
and 80.
That state of affairs should not exist
in modern schools. We had a great deal
of trouble with the Ministry in regard
to the appointment of an additional
teacher for that school, and I think that
before we got confirmation of the
appointment we had to wait two or three
months. I hope the hon. and learned
Gentleman would pay a little attention
to the delay that takes place in his
Department. I do not want to place
the blame on him, but I suggest that
he should take a few lessons in regard
to these matters from the Minister of
Labour. If the Corporation, the Board.
of Guardians, or even the horrible Harbour Board, send a letter to the right
hon. Gentleman they will have
acknowledgment the next day, but when
we applied to the Ministry for sanction
of certain plans in regard to the building of new schools we had to wait two
or three months. I could have had as
voluminous notes as the hon. and
gallant Member for St. Anne's had; in
fact, if I had all my complaints they would
be as thick as a volume of Hansard.
an
This is a great injustice, in the first
place, to the children from the point of
view of health, and in the second place
to the teachers who are doing their best.
They are very competent teachers, but
they cannot do things that are utterly
impossible. I am sure the hon. and
gallant Member for St. Anne's will be
able to convey to the Parliamentary
Secretary a list of the schools in which
overcrowding takes place. The hon. and
learned Gentleman should not allow the
question of money to keep him back.
If he is stuck for monev let him call
upon his friend the Minister of Commerce, who will use his influence with
the Minister of Finance and he will provide the money for new schools and
teachers' salaries.
In Belfast we are prepared to spend
any money that is necessary for new
schools. I appeal to the hon. and
learned Gentleman to go round the
various schools in Northern Ireland, and
when he comes back to this House and
reports what he has seen, I believe he
will say he is shocked with the conditions existing in many of the public
elementary schools and he will make a
special effort to get something done. If
there is anything we in the Opposition
can do to help the hon. and learned
Gentleman to improve the conditions
existing, we will do it.
I would not be doing justice to the
people who elected me if I did not protest against the overcrowding allowed in
these schools. If the hon. and learned
Gentleman has inspectors it is his duty
to see that the persons responsible for
these large classes are reported to the
proper authority and that definite steps
are taken by the Ministry. They can
stop it if they like, and if they do not
stop it they are neglecting their duty.
Epidemics may break out in the schools
in the Shankill Division owing to there
being 20 or 30 more children in a classroom than should be there. If a classroom is built for 45 pupils the Ministry
should not allow 70 to be crammed into
it. That is what is taking place, and
I hope, following the very able criticisms levelled by the hon. and gallant
Member for St. Anne's, something will
be done to stop this terrible condition
of affairs in Belfast.

1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister

that the Relieving Officer in Dungannon.
is also an insurance officer for a private

Guardians he endeavours to further the
interests of the insurance company by
which he is employed; whether it is in
order for an employee of a local authority
to also hold office with a private company; and what steps he proposes to
take to ensure that no employee of
a private company shall be placed in

capacity.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am not aware
that the Relieving Officer in Dungannon
also acts as an insurance agent. Under
the regulations a Relieving Officer must
not engage in any retail trade, but insurance work would not appear to come
within the scope of this prohibition.
I am, however, drawing the attention.
of the Guardians to the hon. Member's

If the hon. Member will furnish me

instance in which it is alleged that the
Relieving Officer has in fact abused his
position, as suggested, I shall immediately
cause the matter to be investigated.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of that

that the official in question has given
entire satisfaction in the performance
of his duties not only to the pblic but
also to the Board of Guardians that

Sir DAWSON BATES: I would like
to say that up to the present time I have
had no complaints.
BELFAST CITY BIRTH RATE.
2. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the cause of the declining birth
rate in the city of Belfast.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This matter
has been, and is still, the subject of
discussion and inquiry in scientific and
medical circles, and various theories have
been propounded in explanation of the
position, but no definite conclusion has
yet been arrived at.
I am afraid I am not in a position.
to offer any expert opinion on a matter
that is still exercising the minds of
scientists, and on which there must necessarily be a divergence of opinion, and I
can only refer the hon. Member to the
various treatises which have been published dealing with the subject.

throughout Northern Ireland; and also

labour is to be provided from Exchanges
unless this wage condition is guaranteed.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have no power to issue regulations or to withhold the facilities of
the Employment Exchanges, as suggested, but local authorities have been
requested to apply the provision of the
Fair Wages Clause to all persons in their
employment, including those employed
under contracts.

NUMBERS OF UNEMPLOYED MEN

5. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Labour whether he can state
the number of unemployed men and
women, and boys and girls in Northern
Ireland, and what steps the Government
are taking to place these unfortunate
people in useful employment.
Mr. ANDREWS: There were registered at the Exchanges on the 15th
March, 54,386 men; 17,986 women;
2,270 boys, and 982 girls.
The majority of those unemployed
return to work after relatively short
periods; for example, nearly one-half of
those registered on the 15th March were
unemployed for less than three months.
The Government has stated on several
occasions the steps that are being taken
to increase the opportunities of employment where possible, and I am glad to
say that the average number of persons
at work is steadily increasing.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Arising out of that
reply I should like to ask this question:
If it is true that half have returned to
work within a certain time, would it be
true to say that the figures have never
consistently fallen below 70,000 ?
Mr. ANDREWS: No. I do not think
that follows.

CHEAP MILK FOR SCHOOL
CHILDREN.
11. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked
the Minister of Agriculture whether he
can state when he proposes to introduce
a scheme to enable regional committees
to supply cheap milk to school children,

to introduce such a scheme.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers

HOUSE OF COMMONS
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I regret that
I have not hitherto felt justified in
incurring out of the Milk Fund the large
expenditure which would be involved in
a scheme for the supply of cheap milk
to school children in Northern Ireland.
As the hon. and gallant Member is
aware, the scheme which operates in
Great Britain is heavily subsidised out
of public funds. Any scheme in Northern Ireland would, on the other hand,
have to be defrayed entirely from the
Milk Fund, the first charge against
which is the payment of equalisation and
bonus payments to producers who send
their milk to creameries. Through the
operation of the Milk Assistance Grants
which have been received from the
Imperial Treasury the Northern Ireland
Milk Fund has hitherto been relieved of
the amount required to meet equalisation payments to creamery suppliers, but
the legislation authorising these payments from the Imperial Treasury
expires at the 30th September next and
I am without knowledge of what the
position may be after that date.
In view of the uncertainty of the financial contribution for this purpose which
may be received from the Imperial
Treasury after the 30th September next
I have deemed it prudent to conserve the
largest possible balance in the Milk Fund
until such time as the present temporary
policy with regard to milk produce has
been replaced by a permanent policy.
My difficulty at the present time in using
the Milk Fund in order to subsidise the
supply of milk to school children becomes
thus apparent. Moreover, as I pointed
out to the hon. and gallant Member in
my reply to him on this subject on the
8th October, 1935, the urgency of this
problem is vastly less great in Northern
Ireland than in Great Britain, as the
Joint Milk Council by its price determination enabled milk to be supplied to all
consumers who collect it at a rate
very slightly above the rate at which it
is supplied to school children in Great
Britain. Further, regional committees
may also, under the determination of the
Joint Milk Council, purchase milk at the
wholesale price, and are thus in the same
favourable position as hospitals.

849 Death of H. M. Pollock

15 APRIL 1937
Death of H. M. Pollock
Death of the Rt. Hon. H. M. Pollock.
TRIBUTES BY PRIME MINISTER
AND OTHER MEMBERS.
The PRIME MINISTER: The duties
that devolve upon one in my position
from time to time are very varied and
sometimes very painful. The staggering
blow which has been dealt Ulster to-day,
the knowledge of which only reached me
a few minutes ago, has prevented me
even collecting my thoughts in order to
present to the House a proposition in
respect to the memory of our lamented
dear friend. I am sure that all sides of
the House will sympathise with me in
the situation in which I now find myself.
Words fail to convey the feelings entertained at any time when a close friend
departs this life, but here something
larger is at stake. It is not only a
question of a close, personal and very
dear friend, but one of the most distinguished sons of Ulster who has
suddenly left us. Only a very short time
ago he stood at this Bench addressing
the House with his usual vigour.
was a man who possessed the courage of
a lion and at the same time the tender
heart of a woman. He was a man who
was perhaps more responsible than anyone else for the establishment of our
Constitution, the setting up of our Parliament and all the Civil Services that
go to make the community in a federal
State such as ours.
He
From the very first day he had to face
a great deal of difficulty, and, naturally,
he met with a considerable amount of
criticism. He lived to a ripe age, and
through it all he never flinched from
doing what he considered was his duty
in the long run to the Ulster people.
I know that this magnificent building in
which we carry on our deliberations, the
Royal Courts of Justice in the city of
Belfast, and many other of those new
structures which go to beautify our part
of the country were due to his great
anxiety that we should possess in Northern Ireland nothing but the bestmonuments to the progressive age in
which we live. I was naturally in very
close association with what lay at the
back of his mind. His high artistic
sense, coupled with a financial genius,
which is very difficult to find in any
part contributed very largely to the
success of many of our undertakings,
because we here, as Members of this
House, doing all we possibly can for the
good of our community and of the
Empire as a whole, have to be led. There
is hardly any action that does not require
leadership, and if there was one high
quality possessed by Mr. Pollock it was
that of admirable leadership. He led
the people in what he thought was the
right way. He asked them very often
to make heavy sacrifices. He did not
promise them any reward, but we all see
the reward to-day in the improved
position in which we find ourselves.
How much of that is due to his foresight and genius perhaps only posterity
will be able to explain, but in the meantime with this dark shadow resting over
us, with the memory of a great man
so fresh in the minds of all of us, I
think it will be felt by a wide circle, not
only in Ulster itself but far beyond its
bounds, that a gap has occurred that
will be very, very hard to fill.
Immediately the sad intelligence reached
me, I got into communication with Mr.
Neville Chamberlain, with whom Mr.
Pollock dealt for many years on matte's closely associated with the joint
financial relations between the two
countries. Knowing how deeply he
would feel the loss we have sustained
and knowing his sympathy with everything that had to do with Ulster, I got
into touch with him and he desired me
to read to the House the following
message:
I am deeply distressed to hear of
the death of Mr. Pollock, with whom
I have long had such friendly and
helpful relations. I had the greatest
respect for his abilities and public
spirit, and I should like to express
my heartfelt sympathy with you and
the Government of Northern Ireland
on the great loss which they have
sustained.
hard
In these few words it is
very
for me to cover very much of the ground.
I know many opportunities will be
afforded to all of us to say what we
think, what is in our hearts regarding
the deceased gentleman, but I do know
that at any rate he died a death which
I am sure he himself would have wished
-he died in harness, I am glad to say
without any pain. He died with his last
thoughts centred
future of

Mr. BEATTIE: In trying to pay a
tribute to the late right hon. Gentleman
I have some difficulty in finding words suitable to express the feelings that animate
me at the moment. When I arrived at
this House to-day shortly after two
o'clock I was startled by the news of
the lamented death of the right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Finance.
That being so, I am unprepared to pay
him the compliment which I feel he is
entitled to receive from those on this
side of the House. The first compliment
I would pay, and which I think everyone would approve of, was as to his
outstanding qualification, and that was
his character. That was pronounced in
every part of the late Minister. The
second thing is that he was a very keen
but very clean fighter. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) He lived a very useful
life. A great part of that life was
given in the service of the Province
which he loved so much. As the Prime
Minister has said, the speech he made not
so long ago from that Bench in defence
of Ulster showed the spirit and sincerity of his love for the Province. I
had many years association with the late
right hon. Gentleman as a political
opponent and I can say from my experience that he was an expert in finance.
He was very keen for the Province in
so far that he never desired that any
word spoken in this House or outside
it should be used against the Province.
His whole ambition was for his fellowcountrymen, and I was thinking as the
Prime Minister was speaking that if ever
a monument was required to the memory
of the late right hon. Gentleman we
ought proudly to point to the Belfast
shipyards. (Hon. Members. Hear,
hear.) I know he did a great amount of
work on behalf of the finances of Northern Ireland without much public
attention being focussed upon it, and I
know the difficulties he had to contend
with, but this is not the time for me
to place that matter before the House.
All I can say is that as a humble Member of this House I looked to him when
I entered it first to set me a fatherly
example, and if I can only follow the
example which he set me, and if I can
leave this House and this Province in
the same way as he has left them, those
who remain behind me will have
regrets. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
no
I would like to say, in passing, that

have the memory of his character before

I am
sure he could at all times seek

but to every Member on this side of the
Hou..
Ulster has lost a true friend,
and Ulster will mourn him in a way
which I believe will do credit to his

Mr. BYRNE: On behalf of those I
represent in this House I wish to join

death will be a great loss generally. Personally I feel his passing very much. He
was approachable on all occasions, and if
he was not able to comply with any request made to him, at least he extended
the greatest friendship and consideration
853 Death of H. M. Pollock

15 APRIL 1937
Death of H. M. Pollock
I am sorry that more of my colleagues
are not here to-day to pay their tribute.
The passing of Mr. Pollock has been
a very great shock to me. I only heard
at ten minutes to three o'clock that he
had passed away and I have not had
time to prepare what I should have
wished to say concerning him. This I
can say, that for many years I had
known Mr. Pollock and had been associated with him on Joint Committees. In
1922 when the Education Bill was about
to be introduced I was on a Joint Committee with him, and on that occasion,
as well as on other occasions, I found
him to be a true gentleman. I join
sincerely in the sympathy expressed here
to-day on the great loss that this House
has sustained through his death.
Mr. HENDERSON : Like all the
other speakers I feel at a loss for words
with which to pay a tribute to this great
statesman. Coming up to the House this
afternoon none of us realised that we
would never again have the pleasure of
the company of the right hon. Gentleman. Like the Prime Minister, we on
this side deeply deplore the loss of the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Finance. It is quite true we often
crossed swords on the floor of the House,
but if there is one thing that can be
said about him it is that no matter how
harsh were the words used against him,
which sometimes he may have thought to
be untrue and words that ought never
to have been spoken, he never bore any
malice. If one met him afterwards in
the corridor he was the same friendly
man there that he was inside.
The position of the Minister of Finance
will be very hard to fill. It will be very
difficult to get a Minister of Finance who
will do the work in the same manner as
the late Mr. Pollock did it. We are
sorry to hear that the Prime Minister
has lost such a great friend. We all
realise how very sincere are the references to Mr. Pollock, and I desire to
associate myself with the remarks of the
hon. Member for Pottinger and the hon.
Member for Falls. Ulster has lost one of
her greatest sons. His work will live
long after him, and I am sure that any
tribute that may be proposed will be
supported by every Member on this side
of the House.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I rise to express a
few sentiments on this very sad occasion,
and I do so with some reluctance because
I think the spirit of the House might
have been well expressed had it been
possible to have followed the example of
the Prime Minister and have the perfect
harmony that might have prevailed on
such a solemn occasion, but owing to the
disposition of the forces in this House
that has not been possible of achievement in the course of two or three
minutes. I should like to pay a personal tribute, as one who did not know
the late gentleman for as long a period
as the majority of hon. Members, to the
greatness of the man from a national
point of view. From the little I did get
to know about him I realised that in Mr.
Pollock Northern Ireland had a gentleman who stood for her defence constitutionally, economically, and in every other
way, at a time when if he had chosen he
might have had a much easier life for
himself.
The late gentleman was called upon-
I am not now obtruding myself into
realms into which I ought not to govery often to bear a heavy cross, and
still bearing that cross he chose not the
path of least resistance but the path of
very stern and strict duty, and he gave
service to this part of the world in no
unstinted fashion. He gave that service
to the extent of 100 per cent.; he gave
all that he had to give, and deprived
himself of many of the joys, and
pleasures, and outlets of life that an
ordinary person is tempted to enjoy from
time to time, in order that he might
render greater and more efficient service. Mr. Pollock was a man after my
own heart in that he did not sit on the
Front Bench to serve as a kind of political ornament or statesmanlike ornament.
He had a point of view and he believed
in putting that point of view firmly,
with dignity, and with great force.
There was something in his nature
that appealed to me, because to my mind
he was a representative of that sturdy
stock about which we hear so much in
Northern Ireland. I know he was a
past master in his work. Time and time
again when various points were expressed
in this House in regard to the financial
relations between Northern Ireland and
Great Britain he revealed an insight into
855 Death of H. M. Pollock

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Death of H. M. Pollock
[Mr. Midgley]
the whole position and a knowledge that
were unsurpassed throughout the whole
community. We on this side of the
House realise that although we had
political differences he was actuated by
a desire to serve the generation to which
he belonged, and we believe to-day
quite sincerely that he served that
generation in his day so well that future
generations will reap the fruits of his
labour.
I would like to express the same sentiments as the Prime Minister and other
speakers as to the suddenness of the news.
When I came here at three o'clock and
heard that Mr. Pollock had passed away
I was absolutely stunned, because, just
a few days ago, on the last occasion on
which I saw him sitting on the Front
Bench, I thought, without having inner
knowledge, that he would be with us for
many years to come. He was a man of
wonderful physical and mental vitality,
and I thought he was destined to remain
in his place for years. His end, as the
Prime Minister said, was perhaps the end
he himself would have chosen, in full
possession of his mental vigour. We can
look back upon
him as a giant from
every point of view in the service of
Northern Ireland, and we can only pray
that God in His infinite mercy will pour
out that comfort which He alone can
pour out to those who are bereaved and
sorrowing this afternoon.
Mr. GRANT: As other hon. Members have already stated, it is not easy on
an occasion like this to find the words
one would like to use to express the sad
loss that not only this House but the
people of Northern Ireland have sustained. We who knew Mr. Pollock very
well realised that his one desire was to
further the interests of the people of
Northern Ireland. On the last occasion
on which I spoke to him privately he
had just returned from London after his
most successful visit in connection with
the Loans Guarantee Act. That was one
thing for which Mr. Pollock was responsible in spite of many adverse criticisms.
As the hon. Member for Pottinger and
the Prime Minister have stated, the
people in the shipyards of Northern Ireland always appreciated what Mr.
Pollock had done for them, and on their
behalf to-day I would like to express the
deep sympathy they feel in the sad loss.
they have sustained. He was a real
friend to the people of Ulster. Ulster
has lost one of her most distinguished
His memory, unlike that of many
other people who have passed away, will
always be revered in this Province, and
on behalf of the workers in the shipyards, who always appreciated wholeheartedly the efforts that Mr. Pollock put
forth in their interests, I should like to
express their deepest sympathy.
sons.
When I asked Mr. Pollock if he would
give me permission to announce what
had been done he said, "No," and then
I thought foolishly I might touch his
personal pride and said, "I should like
to get you a little credit for what you
have done." He said, "What do I care
about credit? So long as we can provide work for our Ulster people who
deserve it, I am amply repaid for anything I have done." That was characteristic of the man, and that is the
memory of him that will always remain
with those of us who have been so closely
associated with him. On behalf of those
whom I represent I join with the other
speakers in this expression of our deep
sympathy, and in saying how much we
feel to-day the sad loss we have sustained
in the death of one of those good old
Ulster people that sometimes I feel we
are not breeding at the present time.

Oral Answers to Questions.
LURGAN GUARDIANS'
EMPLOYEES.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether his attention
has been directed to the conditions of
employment imposed upon employees
under the control of the Lurgan Board
of Guardians; whether he is aware that
a fireman has to work 17 hours per day
for seven days a week; whether the
working fireman, who is a qualified
engineer, is compelled to work 84 hours.
per week for a wage of 63/- per week;
whether the working week in this district is one of 47 hours and the recognised district rate is 66/9; whether these
conditions of employment are a violation
of the fair wages clause, and, if so,
whether he will take steps to have this
injustice ended and direct the Lurgan
Board of Guardians to immediately
recognise the working week of 47 hours.
with full district rate of wages of 66/9.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been informed of the case referred to by the
hon. Member.
The man in question was not employed
as an engineer but as a working fireman,
and his duties were to attend to the
plant generally and to supervise the
firing of the boilers when necessary.
The nature of the duties required that
he should be ready to give his services
at any time irrespective of any fixed
hours. Normally the work would not
be continuous, and, moreover, the person
employed gets holidays with full pay,
and receives a superannuation allowance
when he retires on account of age or
ill-health.
The post is, therefore, not at all comparable with that of a working engineer
in an industrial concern.
I understand that the hours and rate
of pay mentioned are those claimed for
engineers throughout Northern Ireland
and not in the Lurgan district specially,
but that they are not universally
recognised.
The fact that there were 23 applicants for the post would appear to
indicate that the remuneration and conditions of employment are not unsatisfactory, and, in the circumstances, I am
not prepared to interfere with the discretion of the Board of Guardians in the
matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman say whether a 17-hour day
for a seven-day week for a fireman in
the Lurgan Board of Guardians is. a
reasonable day for employment with so
much unemployment in the district?
I
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir.
certainly would not like to work 17 hours
a day.
A TRANSPORT BOARD
APPOINTMENT.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
why the Northern Ireland Road Transport Board did not advertise in the local
Press for an assistant manager at £1,000
a year, and whether their policy is to
consider no local applications.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am informed by the Transport Board that the
advertisement referred to was inserted
in the general technical papers, including the local technical paper, and that
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
the policy of the Board is to consider
all applications, with a view to appointing the man who is, in their opinion,
most suitable for the position.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask whether
the right hon. Gentleman can say if this
is not an unusual practice for any company or business concern operating in
Northern Ireland to ignore the public
Press of Northern Ireland in regard to
advertising appointments to positions?
Sir DAWSON BATES: From the
inquiries I made from the Board they
are only too anxious to get the best man.
With that object they inserted the
advertisement in different technical
papers, one of which circulates specially
in Northern Ireland. I do not think
there is any idea of excluding the
ordinary general Press, but it was felt
that if the advertisement was inserted in
a technical paper it might attract more
applicants.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is not the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the best qualified
persons in that respect reside in Northern Ireland, and in view of the failure
to advertise in the local Press these
gentlemen may be excluded?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not
think that is possible. I am assured to
the contrary.
Major MCCORMICK: Will the right
hon. Gentleman assure the House that
where the applications are proper an
Ulsterman will have preference for the
position?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
prepared to adopt the slogan of Ourselves
Alone or Sinn Fein.
PRISON OFFICIALS' PAY.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
if it is a fact that the rates of pay of
the prison uniform staff are based on
entirely lower rates than those in the
prison service of England and Wales;
whether a class 1 chief warder's pay is
lower by 7/6 to 10/- per week; chief
warder, class 2, by 5/-; principal
warders by 2/6 to 5/-; engineers by 2/6
to 5/-, and warders by 3/- to 4/- per
week; whether it is a fact that many
years ago the rates of pay and conditions
of service in Ireland generally were
assimilated with those obtaining in England and Wales by the British Government; and whether these officers are
protected in this respect by the Government of Ireland Act, 1920.
year
Sir DAWSON BATES: The facts as
stated by the hon. Member are correct.
In the
1919 the rates of pay
and general conditions of the prison service in Ireland were assimilated to those
then in force in the prison service in
England and Wales. I regret that it
has not been possible in our prison service to grant further increases of salary
to the same extent as have been since
granted to the prison service in Great
Britain. It is a fact that officers who
were "existing officers" within the meaning of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, were accorded certain safeguards
to protect them against any less
favourable conditions of service arising
from the establishment of the Government of Northern Ireland, but this does
not imply that the scale of pay in Northern Ireland must necessarily follow
exactly the correspondir g scales in Great
Britain.
If, however, any officer to whom the
Government of Ireland Act applies considers that his present conditions of
service are, in fact, less favourable than
those to which he was entitled at the
date of the transfer of the prison service to the Government of Northern
Ireland, he has a statutory remedy as
provided in that Act.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman say whether his answer
conforms to the step-by-step policy outlined by the various Cabinet Ministers
on political platforms in Northern Ireland, and whether he is prepared to set
up a committee to investigate the
conditions of service of these men under
the 1920 Act?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The step-bystep policy, as I understand it, applies
to the maintenance of exactly the same
social services in Northern Ireland as
in England.

DUNDONALD'S WATER SUPPLY.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware
that a supply of pure water has been
withheld from the residents of Dundonald for this past week; and whether
he will inquire into the reasons for the
failure of the water supply, in the interests of public health.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not the
case that a supply of pure water was
withheld from the residents of Dundonald during the past week. A pump
at Dundonald village appears to have
been slightly out of order, but water
could always be obtained from it.
With the permission of the hon. and
gallant Member for East Down, I propose to take this question and the one
standing in his name together.
As already intimated to the House in
reply to a previous question by the hon.
Member for Shankill, the whole
question of air raid precautions is engaging the close attention of the
Government, and some headway has
already been made in the training of the
civil population through the agency of
the Ulster Joint Committee of the
Order of St. John of Jerusalem and the
British Red Cross Society.
The Government has decided to take
such further steps as may be considered
necessary for bringing our air raid precautions in Northern Ireland to a proper
standard of efficiency, and the hon. and
gallant Member may rest assured that
no avoidable delay will take place in
the suggestions
tained in the Report of the Advisory
Committee of which he was chairman.
I might, however, point out that
Dundonald is not
implementing
now dependant on
pumps for its water as the Rural District Council a year ago introduced a
proper pipe system, and any resident
can have the supply for his house from
this.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman say when the extension of
the boundary of Belfast is going to take
place and bring in this area?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would like
to refer the hon. Member to certain
Members of Belfast Corporation who
may be able to enlighten him.

civil population of Ulster is adequately
protected in event of hostile air raids.

6. To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether the Government has adopted the
Air Raid Precautions Committee's Report, and whether he can make a statement as to the procedure to be adopted
to give effect to the decisions arrived at.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been

so that the necessary organisation by the

PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

QUALIFICATIONS FOR PUBLIC
ASSISTANCE.
9. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the total
number of stamps under the National
Health Insurance and Widows', Orphans'
and Old Age Contributory Pensions Acts
that an applicant must show to qualify
for public assistance under the Unemployment Act 1934, Part 2, Section 31;
whether voluntary contributors' stamps
count as a qualification; whether stamps
received from relief work by the Belfast
Board of Guardians will be accepted in
the calculation of the total stamps
required; whether he is prepared to
inform the House what "normally insurable" means in Northern Ireland and its
application to Part 2 of the 1934 Unemployment Act.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Act does not lay down
any contribution test for determining
whether an applicant for unemployment
assistance is normally occupied in employment insurable under the Contributory
Pensions Acts. The question has to be
decided in each particular case in relation
to the individual's industrial record as a
whole.
The duty of interpreting the condition
laid down by Parliament, and of applying it to the widely differing types of cases
which arise, has been placed by statute
on the officers of the Unemployment
Assistance Board in the first instance, and
from their decision there is a right of
appeal in every case to the chairman of
the Appeal Tribunal.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of that
answer, which is very unsatisfactory, I

aware that I have perused all the

National Health Insurance and Widows
and Orphans Acts; is he also aware that
the "normally insurable aspect,"
applied under Part 2 of the 1934 Act, is
a new incursion for the purpose of turnas

COST OF PROVIDED SCHOOLS.
12. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the total
education
expenditure by the local
authorities on the building of provided
schools; the reconstruction of transferred
schools; and the current repairs of each
class; the number of provided, transferred
and 4-and-2 committee schools and voluntary schools; and the number of pupils
on their respective rolls.
Mr. ROBB: Up to 31st December,
1936, the expenditure upon the building
of provided public elementary schools was
£995,390.
as
In regard to works of reconstruction
and repair, the details of the expenditure
of the local authorities are not segregated
as between reconstruction and repairs or
between provided and transferred
schools. I understand, however, that up
to the present it has not been necessary
to do more than minor repairs to the new
provided schools, and I think it may be
taken that expenditure upon work costing £100 or over in each case has been
chiefly upon the enlargement or improvement of transferred schools; up to
31st December, 1936, this expenditure
amounted to £384,889.
Within the year 1936 the expenditure
upon works costing less than £100 in each
school has amounted to £4,526; this
includes both provided and transferred
schools.
On 31st December, 1936, there were
129 provided schools with 31,201 pupils
on rolls; 512 transferred schools with
61,489 pupils; 63 voluntary schools under
"4-and-2" committees, with 8,553 pupils;
and 1,049 other voluntary schools with
96,110 pupils.
APPOINTMENT OF ELEMENTARY
SCHOOL TEACHERS.
13. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether his attention has been
called to the resolution of the Ulster
Teachers' Union at its annual meeting,
calling for drastic changes in the method
of appointing elementary teachers by
local committees, and for the suppression
of the system of canvassing, and what
steps the Ministry propose to take to ensure that appointments are made on merit
and not through intrigue.
Mr. ROBB: I have seen the resolution
referred to, which suggests that a short
list of not more than six candidates for
each appointment (in a public elementary
school managed by a local education
authority) should be prepared by the
Ministry of Education, and the final
appointment by the school management
committee and the education authority
limited to candidates on this list.
I would remind the hon. and learned
Member that the present procedure is laid
down in the Education Act of 1930 and,
whilst the Ministry strongly deprecates

public appointments, there is not evidence
to show that the present procedure is

CLASS I. No. I.
HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £15,446 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending on the 31st day of March,
1938, to pay the salaries and expenses of
the Senate and of the House of Commons,
including a grant-in-aid." (Note
£7,500 has been voted on account.)
—
Mr. BARBOUR: There is an increase
of £675 on this Vote due to normal
increments of salary of the staff of both
Houses and to a full year's provision for
the restoration of the economy cuts in the
salaries and allowances of Members of the
Senate and of the House of Commons, to
which I referred when moving the
Supplementary Estimate on this Vote
for 1936-7.
Hon. Members will also notice that in
accordance with the undertaking given in
this House the views expressed by hon.
Members in regard to the salary of the
Chairman of Ways and Means have been
carefully considered, and the Government
has decided to invite Parliament to
sanction a salary of £1,000 per annum,
i.e., a reduction of £500 per annum in
the salary hitherto applicable to this post.
I beg to move.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I wish to make one
or two remarks of a short character in
regard to this Vote. Before I do so
perhaps the Committee will give me leave
to pay a passing and very sincere tribute
to the late Minister of Finance, as this
is the first money matter we have dealt
with since his death. The late Minister
had in the prime of his manhood known
and shared sympathies with leaders of enlightened and progressive Ulster thought,
who fought as fellow soldiers in memorable causes and campaigns common to
their people and to the minority in Ulster.
In his later years his was the acutest
intellect enlisted in the service of the
Ulster Unionists, but he never quite forgot the broad outlook of his early days,
and against that minority he never
uttered a wounding word. Let that
justice be done to his memory. I remember when he was over four score
years
he walked a long journey
behind the hearse which bore the
remains of the late Joseph Devlin to the
grave. It was the kindly act of a kindly
man.
Men schooled in public life learn so to
comport themselves as not to forget that
they are gentlemen. The dead Minister
never forgot that lesson. He was a man
of unabated cheerfulness; of joyous yesterdays and confident to-morrows. He had
the gift which is given to very few, of
saying in the fewest and strongest words
all he had to say on any given subject,
and that was joined to a rare lucidity of
thought and speech. By universal consent he was a fair, and square, and aboveboard fighter, free from any taint of
rancour or malice. I rejoice to think
that, unlike many public men, in the
eventide of his life he was not alone,
because he made troops of friends. Men
who stood in contradiction and protestation against almost all that he stood for
were numbered among his friends, because
of his intrinsic personal worth and
because of the gentleman he was upon all
occasions. His party will miss his
garnered wisdom, and all will miss the
charm of his eloquence and his old-time
and fascinating courtesy. (Hon Members: Hear, hear.)
In regard to the Vote itself, it is the
first Vote we are dealing with, and it
indicates an increase in expenditure. It
is the beginning of a long series of increases. In this Province at the present

time we are faced with a population not
able to bear these burdens, and I rise to
enter a protest against the increase in

Mr. BEATTIE: I notice that the
Estimate is something similar to those.
of years gone by with the exception of
the salary of the Chairman of Ways and
Means. On a former occasion I had
down a Motion which gathered a large
volume of support to the effect that as
this position was a spare-time job for 63
days in the year, on an average for
three hours a day, the cost to the taxpayers should not exceed £500. The
Government in their wisdom have
thought well to fix the salary at £1,000,
thus making a reduction of £500. Might
I ask is that £1,000 free from incometax, and if not, why? I am not an
advocate of cheap labour, but I like to
get down to bedrock from the financial
point of view. I have read our Hansards
and I have found the volume of work is
not decreasing so far as the Chairman of
Ways and Means is concerned. His
duties are ever increasing, and when I
put down that £500 it was my estimate
of the value of the position as I found it
then, but the duties attached to the office
are such that the services of the Chairman of Ways and Means are called upon
when the House is not sitting.
I should like to know if this £1,000
is free of income tax. I would like an
explanation of what the sum paid for
this position really amounts to. It is all
right to put down here £1,000, but I
may have £1,000 in my hand, and it
may not be of that value to me at all as
someone may come along and say, "I am
entitled to receive a percentage of that".
I would like to have this position.
clarified. I feel that you, as Chairman of
Ways and Means, have done credit to
yourself up to the present, and a
clarification of the position will, perhaps,
give the outside public a clear understanding of the salary allowed for the
position. That is all I wish to say.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): Perhaps I can answer the
hon. Member's two particular requirements. He is not quite right, I am sure
he will realise, in merely counting the
work of the Chairman of Ways and
Means as the work done here-
Mr. BEATTIE: I tried to correct that
and to show that I made a miscalculation in naming £500.
The PRIME MINISTER: The fact
of the matter is that anyone who occupies
such an important position has to be at
the complete service of Private Bill
Committees and also has duties in connection with the Divorce Bills that come
before this House; in other words, there
is really more work behind the scenes
than there is actually in the Chamber
itself. That is the first remark, and the
second one is that the salary being voted
is not free from income-tax. It bears
income-tax the same as everything else
except where the money received is
entered on the Estimates as expenses.
The salaries of Members are free of
income-tax because the money is looked
upon as necessary expenses, but in the
case of the salaries of Ministers, of Mr.
Speaker, and of the Chairman of Ways
and Means the ordinary income-tax is
deducted.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Even at the risk of
being misunderstood in this matter by
some people who do not look at the thing
from the same angle as I do, I would
like to associate myself with some of the
sentiments expressed by the previous
hon. Member. I think on the day this
matter was debated, in our pursuit of
economy certain elements in the whole
case were not presented as fully as they
might have been, and the presentation of
those points, and especially the elaboration of some of them by the Prime
Minister, somewhat alters the position.
I put forward a point of view the other
day to which I stick in principle to-day,
and that is that on the question of
general finance there should be a revision
of the whole position. I certainly am not
going to stand for the revision of one
position apart from any general financial
question, more especially in view of what
the Prime Minister has said.
I do not believe it is good policy to
take the first opportunity when the
position of any individual Member
happens to be raised to try to effect a
drastic economy upon that particular
Member which bears no relation to
general finance and is not taken upon a
question of the general economic principle. Furthermore, what the Prime

Minister said about this salary not being

a very substantial reduction. When you calculate

Mr. HENDERSON: There is a matter
which I have always raised on this
Estimate, and I wish to raise it once
more. I protest in the strongest possible
manner-this is not a personal matteragainst the salary and allowance of the
Serjeant-at-Arms who receives £739 and
£200 house allowance. Then you have the
assistant who somes in here to relieve
him for his tea, that is Black Rod, who
is in receipt of £575. It is preposterous
in a Parliament that meets only two or
three weeks in the year to pay those
salaries. The last time I raised the question of the Serjeant-at-Arms I was told
that this gentleman had nothing to do
when the House is not sitting, and
during the ten years I have been here I
have never seen him do anything. If
he was writing ballot tickets he would
not earn enough to keep him in
cigarettes. To have such a position is a
bad policy, and I hope the Prime Minister will take some steps in regard to it.
No Member of the House can justify it.
If he were an ex-Serviceman I could
see the sense of his receiving this sum,
but the fact is that this gentleman is
in receipt of a pension of £800. That is
a bit thick in Northern Ireland where
there are 80,000 people unemployed.
That a gentleman with a pension of £800
should have an official salary of £739
with a house allowance of £200 would
not be tolerated by any other Parliament
in the world. This position is not as
important as that of mace bearer. The
Lord Mayor's mace bearer in the city of
Belfast gets £4 5s a week and he works
52 weeks in the year. His duties are
more arduous than those of this gentleman. The only thing I ever see the
Serjeant-at-Arms doing is sitting for two
or three hours wearing knickerbockers.
That is the only uncomfortable thing he
does for his salary. It would be
different if the position was given to
some disabled ex-Serviceman. I move a
reduction of £200 to see what the noble
Lord will do in connection with this
matter.
The CHAIRMAN: Is the hon. Member moving this reduction in regard to
this particular item or in regard to the
whole Vote?
Mr. HENDERSON: The whole Vote.
I cannot allow this to go on unchallenged,
especially in view of the fact that when
we on this side protest we are abused on
the hustings outside. The Prime Minister
will be justified in agreeing to this
reduction of £200 because he has placed
too high a figure for this post. The Road
Transport Board are going to give £1,000
for a technical expert who must know
everything about motor transport on the
roads, but this is a job with a salary of
almost £1,000 for doing absolutely
nothing. I take it that the Prime
Minister will tell us why the Serjeant-at-
Arms is paid so large a salary, in view of
the large number of ex-Servicemen who
are in destitution at the present time and
who are capable of filling this job. This
House sits only five or six weeks in the
year. I would not mind so much if this
gentleman was employed for 52 weeks in
the year. I do not wish to be personal,
but when this job becomes vacant we
will move a greater reduction than that
named in the present Amendment.
Another matter that requires some
explanation is the payment to Members
of this House for attendance at its committees or at joint committees of both
Houses. I want to know who is going to
receive the £260 set down in this
Estimate. I want also to draw attention
to the scandalous treatment meted out
to the under dog, the door-keepers of this
House. Has the noble Lord ever been
in any of the corridors when 70 or 80
people from all parts of the Empire were

all night, some of these men have to take

sat late for two or three nights in the
week, they would have to devote all their

service these men have rendered to the
country and to this Government, something ought to be done to increase their
wages, wages which are a disgrace.
other Parliament in the world would pay
men of this grade so little. The same
thing applies to the ladies who clean.
Stormont, they are paid a scandalous

the Corporation than they receive from.
the Government. I feel that the Prime

The PRIME MINISTER: If I may
answer the hon. Member-
Mr. NIXON: I was going to second
this reduction.
The PRIME MINISTER: The Motion
for the reduction does not require a
Seconder. Hon. Members will understand that if one passes by this and every
other matter raised the attitude of the
Government might be misunderstood. I
have great pleasure in explaining to the
Committee that in Ulster, with the
exception of two positions, we are far
behind the other side. In the whole of
Great Britain there are a large number
of posts-I could not say how manythat are looked upon as being somewhat
out of the common, and distinguished
sailors, soldiers, and airmen are very
often placed in those positions not only
as a reward for their distinguished
services, but as an honour to the branch
of the fighting services to which they
belong. We here have in our patronage
only two such positions one of these is
that of the Sergeant-at-Arms, a very high
position; in England he is one of His
Majesty's own personal servants—and
the other is that of Black Rod in the
Senate. The way the hon. Member
referred to Black Rod, who belongs
chiefly to the other House, was in my
opinion not in very good taste, because,
after all, one man could not sit through
the debates of this House without having
someone to relieve him occasionally.
That answers that part of the hon. Member's criticism.
The answer to the second part of the
Hon. Member's speech is this. When
these appointments were made in 1921,
it was decided after consultation with
the Speaker of that time and others to
place the salaries of the Serjeant-at-Arms
and Black Rod in the category in which
they now stand. I cannot make any
complaint whatever, and I am sure no
Member of this House can make any
complaint, about the conduct of either
of those distinguished ex-Servicemen.
Nobody desires to do that; they have
carried out their duties faithfully and
well. I wish to dispel the idea that when
the Serjeant-at-Arms is out of the House,
from the point of view of the sittings,
his work is done. He has complete control of the whole of this building from
the point of view of the arrangements
for the preservation of good conduct on
the part of everybody inside this building, whether actually in this Chamber
or in other parts of the House.
I am not prepared to say that the
salary which is attached to his position
bears any relation whatever to what he

They
may have earned in the Service itself.
The policy that is pursued here is that
followed on the other side of the water.
I have known several Serjeants-at-Arms
during my time at Westminster.
were ex-Servicemen and had their pensions in the ordinary way either from
the Navy Vote or the Army Vote. I
think the salary is almost £2,000 a year
and a house. I know that the work at
Westminster is extremely heavy, and
that the Serjeant-at-Arms has a very
large building to look after and so on.
At the same time these are the only two

who have rendered conspicuous service to
their country-and when I say their

Empire. This shows Ulster's appreciation of what these men have done, and
I hope, therefore, that the Committee.
will refuse to accede to any reduction of

Mr. NIXON: As the Chairman of
Ways and Means is mentioned in this
Estimate, the first thing I have to do is
congratulate you, sir, on sitting in that
Chair, and also on the manner in which
you have done your work since you took
office. You know when to speak and
how to speak, and what you say does
not hurt. May you be long spared to
sit in that Chair at your present salary.
I hope that you will permit me to
welcome the hon. Member for Ballynafeigh. I know that that is not in the
Estimates, but I had the pleasure of
sitting with the hon. Gentleman in
another place for five years-on a most
important Board-and only on one
occasion did we find it necessary to have
a vote. On that occasion I was in the
minority. Looking back on that period.
of five years I think the hon. Member
for Ballynafeigh was 80 per cent.
right. He himself thinks he was 100 per
cent. right. I admit he was 80 per cent.
right, and I hope that he will do as well
here as he did there. If he does he will
be a credit to Ballynafeigh. In fact, I
do not think he could do badly, because
he has no axe to grind.
The hon. Member for Shankill referred
to a famous speech in which the hon.
Member for Bann Side warned the
people to beware of Independents. I may
say that an Independent Unionist means
just what the word independent means,
a Unionist in this House who wants
nothing from the Government, and who
gets nothing. A unionist who is here to
get something for himself or his son or
his brother is not independent, because
he wants something. A Unionist who
can keep sixteen guns without a permit
is not independent and could not be. I
am satisfied that the salary paid to the
Serjeant-at-Arms is outrageous. At the
same time I want to say that I agree
with the Prime Minister when he states
that nothing personal could be said
either against the Serjeant-at-Arms or
Black Rod. I am sure no one in this
Committee would say anything personal
against either of them. At the same
time, the salary of the Serjeant-at-Arms
is outrageous for what he does. He is not
in charge here when Parliament is closed.
Mr. Gibson does all the work when
Parliament is closed. All the work the
Serjeant-at-Arms does here is to carry
the Mace three days a week for three
months in the year, and to sit watching
it for a couple of hours on each of those
days. A salary of £739 for that work is
outrageous in a small community like
this.
It is no wonder that Sir Lynden
Macassey in his letter the other day said
Ulster had a very bad Press in London.
How could you have a good Press in
London where the newspapers are
independent, not spoon fed, not tied in
any way, and not subsidised by something
approaching a grant. Lord Dufferin told
us the opinion of some of the people in
high places in Great Britain-and he
associates with the very highest-and the
cause of that is the hole and corner way
things are done here in the interests of
favourites. The Prime Minister spoke
about distinguished ex-members of His
Majesty's Army, Navy and Air Force
holding positions in Great Britain. We
appreciate that. No people in any part
of the world stand more for the Imperial
connection than we do the Member for
Shankill and the Member for Woodvale.
We are proud of that fact. What we do
object to is men who have great influence
coming in and getting these jobs to the
exclusion of deserving people. I have
great pleasure in supporting the proposal
that this Estimate be reduced by £200.
One man would be quite sufficient.

HOUSE OF COMMONS

We are fortunate in having a very
capable man in the Library-Mr. Gibson.
When required he sits there and does the
job very well. Any time you 'phone to
this House or any time you come up to
the House you will find him here.
I am
very glad to see him here, because he is
an Ulsterman whom we know, and he is
the son of a man whom we all respect.
I do not believe in inventing jobs for
people who are well enough off and who
are appointed not on their merits but on
other considerations. That is a thing

Ulster. The Prime Minister told us that
this salary was fixed in 1921. That is 16

held that position at £979 a year

should get a rest. In 1921, when this
extravagance was started, we had not the

we have to-day. I was speaking to a
business man the other day and mentioned
the figures issued by Glengall Street. He
said he did not bother his head about
those figures, but he contrasted the
amounts he had to pay in 1921 with the
amounts he has now to pay, and be knew
the difference to his sorrow.
I have a little message for the hon.
Member for Mid-Antrim, and it is in this
Estimate. There is a sum of £260, that
is two guineas to Members attending
committees. I have no objection to that.
I have not got a penny of it and I do
not want it. But one of the hon. Member's constituents in Ballymena has
written to me on the matter. Well, I
did not receive any of that money, and
the Chief Whip will see to it that I do

I hope the House will save this £200.
We could save the whole £979 and the
duties would be done as efficiently. The

House to pass this Vote, and we know
they will. But he has not justified this

the House would they give any man this
salary for carrying the mace three days.
each week for three months in the year?
The Chairman of Ways and Means has
more to do than just sit there. It takes
a very able man to carry out the duties in
connection with unopposed Bills and
things like that. He has to see that they
are in order. He has to make himself
acquainted with the Standing Orders,
and has to give decisions in a way which
will not hurt the feelings of any person

the House. The salary for that office
has been reduced to £1,000. I do not
think that amount is too much. Would
anyone outside this House give the salary
that is being paid to the Sergeant-at-
Arms. If the Prime Minister is sincere

Mr. Baldwin states that he is retiring

out very
onerous duties over certain

As one who has been working on Acts
of Parliament of this description since
1912, and as one who has during all these
years endeavoured to define the word
"normally" I must admit that I have
failed to arrive at a definition of what
the word really means. I have found
various definitions-the legal definition,
the humanitarian definition, and the
politician's definition. I will now give
you the Oxford Dictionary definition.
It is:
Right, rectangular, standing at right
angles, perpendicular, according to or
squared with a room, conforming to,
not deviating or differing from a type
or standard, regular, usual, national
school, a school for the training of
teachers.
Those are many and varied definitions of
the word "normal". It goes on and
says:
A straight line at right angles to
the tangent or tangent plane of any
point of a curve or curved surface, the
average or mean of observed quantities,
the usual state or condition, normal
temperatures.
There is the most up-to-date definition
of the word "normal" given to the world
authoritatively. I should like to have
the great assistance of the Minister in

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. ANDREWS: I would like to express my appreciation of the reasonable
and moderate way in which those responsible for this Motion have just expressed
their opinions. I would also like to thank
the hon. Member for Pottinger for the
graceful way in which he referred to the
chairmen of these courts and indirectly
paid me a compliment, because, after all,
I was responsible for their appointment.
The Act of 1934 has been criticised on
many occasions. It was criticised when
being passed through this House, and it
has been criticised to-day. I would like
very briefly to summarise the enormous
benefits which that Act has conferred upon our unemployed people. In the
first place, the rates of benefit to unemployed have been increased, and many
thousands
in
Northern Ireland are
enabled to obtain unemployment benefit
for considerably longer periods than formerly if they have good industrial
records. Then the contributions have
been lowered, an advantage to those
workers who are employed as well as to
employers and State. In the next place.
the waiting period has been halved, a
benefit which the Government has frequently been asked to confer, and which
I and my colleagues are particularly
gratified it was possible to confer a few
weeks ago.
As regards Part II of the Act, which
has been under special criticism to-day,
I would like to point out at the beginning of my remarks in this connection
that the position of no one has been
worsened; in other words, the position of
those taken over from the poor-law
authorities has been substantially improved, and that of those who unfortunately have to remain, at any rate for a
time, under the poor-law authorities will
be as it was formerly. The Guardians
will be responsible for them. I would
like to explain to the House what has
happened in recent days. The Second
Appointed Day only came into operation
on 1st April, and the work has not yet
been completed. Many people have been
given an opportunity to appeal who have
not yet had their appeals heard, so that
we are not in a position to say definitely
at the moment the numbers who have
been taken over or will be taken over,
and the numbers who will be rejected,
but I can assure the House again, as I
did a short time ago, that not only is the
legislation the same in Great Britain, but
the intention of all my colleagues and
myself, as well as, I believe, every
Member on this side of the House, is that
the administration, speaking generally,
shall be exactly the same.
Hon. Members opposite realise the
difficulty of dealing with particular cases,
because, as they have said themselves,
where you have different persons giving
final decisions there may in particular
cases be a difference in the decision either
way; in other words, there may be cases
where men would be brought within the
scope of the scheme here who would be
rejected in Great Britain, and vice versa.
That is inevitable, but I may say that the
aim and object of the Board, whom I
wish to congratulate on the way in which
they have performed their responsible
duties now for several years, is to carry
out the policy of the Government,
namely, one
of
equality, but the
main responsibility rests, of course, with
the officials of the Board. Parliament
has laid that heavy responsibility upon
them, and it is a heavy responsibility
for them to have to review all cases in
the first instance. Their aim is to conform to this similarity to which I have
referred, and it is only in certain cases
that the chairman will be called upon to
give his views in connection with the
matter and state what the decision is
to be.
Between April, 1935, and April, 1937,
the number of persons in Belfast alone
obtaining special outdoor relief fell by
3,095, and the cost to the Guardians fell to
the extent of £3,133 per week; and during
the same period the number of persons in
Belfast who obtained assistance from the
Board increased by 5,640, at a cost to
the Board of £9,807 per week. I think
those figures indicate very clearly the
vast change-over that has taken place
between the old position and the new,
and therefore I venture to suggest to my
hon. Friends opposite that they should
take a more cheery view of this situation
than they have done up to the present.
Now, let me speak for a moment of
Northern Ireland as a whole. On 31st
March, 1937, there were 21,166 claimants
under the Board's scheme at a cost of
£24,876 per week. The position to-day
is that there are 25,000 claimants receiving assistance at a cost to the Board of
Normally Insurable Conditions 911

£30,000 per week. That shows the
enormous change-over there has been.
Mr. MIDGLEY: It means you have
taken over only 4,000.
Mr. ANDREWS: It means that up to
the present we have taken over 4,000,
which has improved the position to a
very important extent. But, further, I
would like to point out to hon. Members
that between the First Appointed Day
and this Second Appointed Day a very
large number of those who were on the

as the hon. Member knows. Therefore,
I feel great satisfaction in the knowledge
that this Act of 1934, which, as I have
said, was so severely criticised some years
ago as well as more recently, has now
proved its value, and that that value is
appreciated very generally throughout
our area. It has always been the wish of
my colleagues and myself to do everything humanly possible to help our unemployed. We grieve that we have not
been able to do as much for them as we
would have wished to do, but at any
rate we can always find satisfaction
in the fact that we have maintained their
position in step with their fellow-citizens
across the Channel.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I rise to submit to
the House that there is a great deal of
misapprehension abroad with regard to
the scope of unemployment assistance.
When the Act was passed in 1934 the
idea in the mind of the ordinary man in
the Province was that benefits would be
conferred upon all the unemployed
classes who did not fall within the scope
of unemployment insurance. That is not
the case, as there is a very large body of
unemployed for whom there is no State
assistance at the present time. They are
not within the scope of the poor-law relief code. The poor-law relief code was.
never intended for the assistance of ablebodied industrial workers; it was only
intended for those rendered infirm by
illness or causes of that class. The idea
abroad certainly was that all unemployed.
would get assistance other than under the
unemployment insurance code and the
unemployment assistance code.
Now they find that is totally contrary
to the facts, and we have a very large
number of workers in Northern Ireland
who are denied work, who are honestly
anxious to get work, who do not fall
under the poor-law relief scheme, the unemployment assistance scheme, or the unemployment insurance scheme. They are
out in the cold. This is a problem of
dire distress and poverty. It is a problem that sooner or later must be faced.
The answer of the Minister of Labour,
I think, will be that he cannot go beyond
what has been done in Great Britain,
and that he is bound by some code, by
some fetters, so that some of the workers
in Northern Ireland now find themselves
denied all assistance while others are
getting assistance not in a very remarkable measure, but in some degree. Many
of those who are out in the cold, who are
outside State protection and the machine
of State assistance, are a very deserving
and very worthy class of the community.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I do not
want to make a long speech on this
Motion, but I hope the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Labour will
be able to clear up some points about
which I am in doubt. I say frankly, I
do not quite understand these regulations under the Unemployment Assistance Board. I am informed that young
men who register at the exchanges and
who never applied before are being taken
over by this Unemployment Assistance
Board and their cases are not being
turned down, and, on the other hand, I
am informed that people who have been
insured and are out of insurance, owing
to lapse of time, are not being taken over
by the Board. I have great difficulty in
explaining this fact in places like
Shrigley, where a mill has been closed
for some time, and there has been no
chance for the older people to get work.
I hope I will get an explanation, because the position is that if you are young
you are taken on by the Board, and if
you are old and have been out of work,
as the Shrigley people have been out of
work for six or seven years, you are not
taken on. I cannot understand how the
regulations work. Those are the only
remarks I have to make, and I hope that
the Parliamentary Secretary will explain
the matter so that these people will
understand. It is very hard for anybody
who has been out of work to understand
why he is not taken over while young
people are taken over.

UNEMPLOYED.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the Government's policy in regard to the
thousands of able-bodied unemployed
who will not be taken over under Part
II. of the Unemployment Assistance Acts.
and who reside in areas where the local
authorities refuse to pay outdoor relief
to the able-bodied destitute.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The position of able-bodied destitute
persons who do not come within the scope
of Part II. of the Unemployment Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934, remains
exactly as it was before the passing of
that Act.
I may say, however, that the possibility of hardship arising in certain
instances has been brought to my notice
and the whole matter is at present under
the consideration of the Government.
am not, yet, however, in a position to
make any definite statement on the point.
I
Mr. MIDGLEY: May I ask the Minister does the latter part of his reply mean
that the Government are considering
taking some action to compel these.
authorities to bring in payment for ablebodied destitute which they are not
doing at the present time?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. I think
the answer is perfectly plain. What I
indicated was that so far as the Government is concerned no change has been
made. The hon. Member suggests that
certain hardships have taken place. I
was trying to point out that no hardship
has taken place. If there were hardships
the Government were prepared to consider them.
Mr. MIDGLEY: In view of that
reply, I beg to give notice that I will
raise the matter on the adjournment.
INFANTILE AND MATERNAL
MORTALITY IN BELFAST.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he is aware
of the public alarm and apprehension at
the infant mortality rate in Belfast rising
higher than in any city in Great Britain.
except Glasgow, and at the maternal
mortality rate rising higher than in any
city in Great Britain, and whether he can
state what the Ministry has done, or proposes to do, to reassure the public.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that the infant and maternal death rates
in Belfast are causing concern, and I
may inform the hon. Member that I have
appointed a committee to take into consideration the conditions under which
maternity work is carried on in Northern
Ireland and I trust that it will be able
to make recommendations which will
have the effect of reducing the death
rates from these causes.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN
CASTLEWELLAN.
3. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether it is a fact
that the local authorities decided ten
years ago that 40 labourers' cottages
were a necessity in Castlewellan, and if
since then no cottages have been built;
whether a number of occupied houses
there are wholly unfit for human habitation; whether in several two-roomed
houses eight or ten persons are living;
whether there has been an outbreak of
diphtheria consequent on the unsanitary
Oral Answers
Estimates
21 APRIL 1937
conditions; and whether the Ministry is
powerless to expedite building in this and
other neglected areas.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would
remind the hon. Member that the
operation of the Labourers Acts was
suspended for a number of years until
the passing of the recent Act of 1935.
I am
aware from the report of my
Ministry's inspectors that there are a
number of unsanitary houses in Castlewellan, but I have no information as to the
number of persons living in such houses.
I regret to say that there were six cases
of diphtheria in Castlewellan last month.
The Downpatrick Rural District
Council has, however, a scheme of building now in contemplation in which the
needs of Castlewellan will be considered,
and I trust that this scheme will be
proceeded with at an early date.
CASTLEWELLAN-ANNSBOROUGH
FOOTPATH.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether the public
authorities have asked the Down County
Council to make a footpath along the
road from Castlewellan to Annsborough;
whether this road has been the scene of
repeated motor vehicle and bicycle
collisions with pedestrians; and whether
he can state when this footpath will be
provided.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand
that no representations have been made
to the Down County Council by any
local authority regarding the necessity
for a footpath along the public road
between Castlewellan and Annsborough.
Inquiries which I have made, both
from officials of the County Council and
from the police, do not reveal that any
serious accidents have been reported, but
I understand that a few minor accidents,
only four or five in number, occurred
during the past two years.
The provision of a footpath is a
matter entirely for the County Council,
who will, I have no doubt, give every
consideration to
any representations
which may be made to it on the subject,
and I, myself, propose to bring the
matter under the notice of the County
Council.

Turning now to the individual subheads, there is a full year's provision

proposed increases in their salaries to
which I referred in introducing the

were, in

Owing to the pressure of work it has

collection of land purchase annuities by

1937, £972,375 was due to be collected,

and another clerk in the Accounts

directions, but more particularly in the

I now
come to the Works Division,
which is responsible for the major increases in staff; these include four
additional clerks, one staff officer and one

additional architects, and a technical
assistant and two additional clerks for the
Bann Drainage site staff. These increases may seem large, but I can
assure the Committee that they are
essential if the present rate of progress
in our works programme is to be maintained, and, apart from unemployment
considerations, I am sure that no member
of the Committee would like to see any
retardation of the Government's efforts
to improve the standard of accommodation in schools, police barracks, and unemployment exchanges, work which accounts
for a large proportion of the present
activities of this division. An extensive
Post Office building programme also
accounts for much extra work, but the
cost of this is reflected in increased
appropriations-in-aid.
In addition there is a considerable
amount of work still to be done in connection with the completion of the R.U.C
Depot at Enniskillen, while the additional
Departmental accommodation to be
erected on the roof of the building in
which we now are is to be commenced this
year. As regards the Bann drainage
staff, I gave a description of the progress
made on this work when introducing the
Works and Buildings Vote.
The increased works programme is also
reflected in the additional provision for
the travelling expenses of the technical
staff, although, on the other hand, it has

in the travelling expenses of the other
staff. Legal charges show a reduction,
due to the fact that last year we had to
provide for the legal costs arising out of
the Belfast Corporation's appeal to the
Privy Council on the subject of the education rate.
The increased expenditure on photo
prints, tracings, etc., in sub-head F is
another indication of the activities of the

There is an additional executive officer
in the Registrar-General's office, an office
whose activities, as its records gradually

which was published in August of last
year. He notes in that report that there

Certain incidents of the vital statistics,
as deduced from the registration records,
may be of interest to hon. Members. In
particular, the steady increase in the
marriage rate over the past five years is
most marked, the rate for 1936 being the
highest recorded during the present
century, with the exception of those for
the years 1919 and 1920. Coincident
with the increase in marriage rates in
recent years the birth rate has been maintained at a comparatively steady level,
and is indeed the highest of each of the
four main parts of the British Isles.
Coming now to the recent census of
population, the provision made for the
year 1937-38 is designed to cover the
major part of the costs of extraction and
tabulation of the details from the census
taken on the 28th February last. The
actual enumeration process, for which

estimates, has been carried out smoothly—

as was not the case in previous censuses,
had to carry out their distribution and

preliminary statement of the results is
already in the hands of hon. Members.
It will be seen that the present population of Northern Ireland is approximately
1,279,000; this is the highest recorded
figure since the census of 1881. In the

reasonably comprehensive preliminary

will be prepared and published. Thereafter, however, there will unavoidably be

Sub-head M, receipts appropriated in

Hon. Members will notice a considerable reduction in the receipts from Great
Britain in respect of legal services performed for the Treasury. This is due to
the completion of land purchase in

the Supreme Court of Northern Ireland
