Suggested Amalgamation of Cabinet
Offices.
POSITION OF PRIME MINISTER.
Mr. CAMPBELL: We have now
come to this Vote of the Ministry of
Finance, and I submit to the Committee
that there is really no good reason why
the Minister of Finance should not take
over the Department of the Prime Minister. I know of no reason, and
many
others know of no reason why the two
Ministries should not be amalgamated
in one Ministry. Efficiency and economy
would necessitate that course. The
Minister of Finance does perform certain
specified functions in the public interests,
but I do submit to the Committee that
there is no distinctive, definite public
service of that Ministry that could not be
performed by the Department of the
Prime Minister. We can find an analogy
across the Channel. The Prime Minister
of the United Kingdom functions also as
the holder of another office and draws his
salary in this latter capacity. The same
practice prevails in the case of the British
Dominions.
Mr. Baldwin, the Prime Minister in
the United Kingdom, said quite recently
that there must be some term to the
period during which any man could continuously bear the burdens of his office.
I do not know whether the Prime Minister of Northern Ireland, as a result of his
political experience during the last
fifteen years, has arrived at the same conclusion, but there can be no comparison
possible between the duties of the Prime
Minister at Westminster and the Prime
Minister at Stormont. It does seem
Estimates-
Ministry of Finance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
strange that we have in this area two
Prime Ministers. Mr. Baldwin must
necessarily be Prime Minister of Northern
Ireland as an integral part of the
United Kingdom. It is a constitutional
anomaly. It is an anomaly without precedent in British constitutional
annals. It is an anomaly that some
day will create trouble and demand
clarification.
I submit to the Committee that the
Parliamentary duties of the Prime Minister are not of an onerous character. This
House does not sit all the year round.
We sit, as a matter of fact, for about
four months a year. We are elsewhere
after that. The Prime Minister's interventions in the proceedings are infrequent.
His extra Parliamentary duties are
mainly of a social character. Surely in
an area smaller than Yorkshire, and with
a population equal to that of Glasgow, it
is in the public interests that the dual
offices of Prime Minister and Finance
Minister should be amalgamated. The
multiplicity of Cabinet offices serves the
same purpose as that for which Admiral
Byng was shot many years ago. You will
remember that that very distinguished
and very gallant sailor was court
martialled for not bringing his battleship close up in line with the French
battleship. Admiral Byng was then court.
martialled at Portsmouth and shot.
Some people said that the French
admiral could have been court martialled
for the same thing, as his battleship did
not come close up in line with the English
vessel. A certain Frenchman, after the
English court martial result, said that
that was just done to encourage the
others. In the same way the multiplicity
of Cabinet offices in Northern Ireland
must serve to encourage the others.
In this House we have 52 Members, 37
of whom form the majority. We have
seven Cabinet Ministers. At Westminster there are 620 Members, and in
the same ratio they ought to have at
Westminster 84 Cabinet Ministers. They
have not arrived at that stage yet. We
have a stationary population. We have
almost a declining population. The
population in this area since 1911 has
only gone up a matter of 26,000. That is
very little more than a thousand a year.
In reality we are reaching a stage when
the population is stationary. We have
a rising cost of living and a growing toll
of taxation. The position must be
regularised in face of all these facts.
Details of expense are, of course, matters
one does not care very much to trouble
about, but if hon. Members will look at
the figures they will find that in the cost.
of the Prime Minister's Department
there is a sum of £9,480 set apart for
wages and salaries, £720 set apart for
travelling and subsistence allowances,
£325 for postage, telegrams, and telephones, £70 for incidental expenses,
making, all told, £10,865 a
roughly over £200 a week. That is the
way the figures stand. One would like
to congratulate the Minister of Labour
on his appointment to the office of Minister of Finance, and also to congratulate
the hon, and gallant Member for Central
Armagh (Major Shillington) on his promotion to the very onerous position of
Minister of Labour.
year,
The late Minister of Finance was not
a member of an Institution which is very
powerful in this area, but the new
Minister of Finance and the new Minister of Labour are members of that
Institution. I suppose that in the eyes
of the Prime Minister membership of
that Institution is an open door to promotion. I refer to the Loyal Orange
Institution. Queen Victoria, a queen
whose memory you all honour, at one
time was embarrassed and perplexed by
the close association of the then Prince
of Wales, afterwards King Edward VII,
with a member of the Hamilton family
of Northern Ireland, and she wrote to
the Prime Minister of the day saying
she feared the heir to the Throne was
being inoculated with Orangeism. She
added in the letter to the Prime Minister
that this was a disqualification for any
Irish responsibilities. The Prime Minister of Northern Ireland does not share
that view. That was her view, but the
very opposite prevails to-day. It is no
disqualification to-day, but rather in the
eyes of many in this Northern area an
indispensable qualification for responsibility in the Six Counties.

£ s. d., loyalty to vested interests. We

Elsewhere public spirit pays, elsewhere

pays, elsewhere talent pays; here the test

The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon) I could not help when
listening to the hon. and learned Member
reflecting that it was entirely owing to
his own party that this question arose at
all. He mentioned that the Prime Minister of Great Britain was Prime Minister
of Ulster as well. That is quite true,
but how did all this change take place?
It took place entirely by the action of
the party to which the hon. and learned
Member belongs. He and his predecessors fought for years to bring this
about. Their cry for Home Rule was
satisfied. It was none of our doing. We
fought Home Rule, and the only
difference between the hon. and learned
Member and ourselves is that having got
what he asked for he now does all he
possibly can to upset it, and when we
got what we did not ask for, out of
patriotism and a desire to help the
British Government through a very
severe crisis we took it very much
against our will, and we are now doing
our best to make a success of the selfgovernment of the Ulster area. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
That is my first comment. My second
comment is that he says-and of course
I am very loath to cross swords with one
who quite rightly holds a high position
in his own profession as I am not a
lawyer-that there is no constitutional
precedent for having such a position as
Prime Minister of Great Britain and
Prime Minister of an area within Great
Britain, or, in other words, within the
federal constitution. He must know that
there is a Prime Minister for Australia,
and there is a Prime Minister for each
of the six federal States within Australia.
The same is applicable to Canada. There
is a Prime Minister of Canada, at present in London representing the great
Dominion at the forthcoming Coronation, and he has left behind him, I think,
nine Prime Ministers of the Federal
States forming the Canadian Commonwealth. Therefore, I am right in refuting the statement the hon. and learned
Member has just made that there is no
precedent for having two Prime Ministers
for Northern Ireland.
Then he came to the suggestion that
nowadays it would be better if we were
to combine the office of Prime Minister
and the office of Minister of Finance.
The longer I am at this box the more,
perhaps, I look at things from a statesman's point of view rather than from
the shorter angle, and the longer that is
so the more convinced I am that the way
in which we conduct our business here is
in the best interests of the future of the
Province. I will tell the hon. and
learned Member why. He had a question
on the Order Paper to-day, and in order
to show him that I was indeed rather
pleased to have a debate on this subject
I will read my answer, which is very
applicable to what he has said:
"The proposal received my careful
consideration on a former occasion,
when I came to the conclusion that
such amalgamation would be detrimental to the best interests of Ulster.

""
I read that to the House in order that
the hon. and learned Member may be
assured I am quite prepared to deal with
the matter from an argumentative point
of view. First of all, there is an implied
compliment in the suggestion, because he
imagines that I would be able to hold
the position of Minister of Finance,
which, if I may say so, I feel very
diffident about myself, and certainly
when it comes to the matter of a choice

so very kindly undertaken his new duties,
and myself there is no comparison
possible. He has spent all his life as a

widespread, and, without touching on

here, I would say he is a very worthy

office, and I am sure that not only this
House but the whole country will feel

Hear, hear.)
Having said that let me go a little
further. What are the functions laid
down for the Department of the Prime
Minister? May I just read them out of
that very
admirable book, which all
Members ought to have in their hands,
The Constitution, by our draughtsman,
Sir Arthur Quekett. If they will look at
page 36 they will see it laid down that:
"The Department of the Prime
Minister is the channel of communication between the Governor and the
Cabinet of Northern Ireland, and
between that Cabinet and the Ministries of Northern Ireland, and forms
the Cabinet Secretariat.
"The Ministry of Finance administers the financial business of the
Government of Northern Ireland,
discharging functions corresponding
generally to the functions of the
Treasury of the United Kingdom. It
also administers the business of the
Government in connection with taxation, and has various administrative
functions taken over from the following Irish authorities: Treasury Remembrancer, Superintendent of the
Teachers' Pension Office, Irish Land
Commission, Stationery Office, Development Commissioners, Commissioners of
Public Works, Registrar General,
Commissioner of Valuation, Commissioners of Charitable Donations and
Bequests."
Needless to say, since the establishment
of the Government of Northern Ireland
the duties attached to all the Ministries
have very much extended, and the work
carried on in the Ministries is very
heavy work indeed, covering as it does
practically every penny that is collected
and distributed. In the first instance it
is a work which requires the whole time
of the Minister in charge.
I think it is quite right what the hon.
and learned Member said, that the Prime
Minister of Great Britain
was not
recognised officially as such up to very
recently; in fact, I think he had no precedence up to recent years. He was
simply looked upon
as one of His
Majesty's Ministers, and he had no status
as Prime Minister at all. He was paid
his salary and emoluments, and he
received his position as First Lord of the
Treasury. In other words, he was
classed as First Lord of the Treasury
before he was classed as Prime Minister.
Here the Minister of Finance is really
Chancellor of the Exchequer, whereas
the Prime Minister in Great Britain,
although he is First Lord of the Treasury,
is not Chancellor of the Exchequer.
There is a nice distinction there which
I am sure will be appreciated on both
sides of the House.

assure the House that, having in mind

stonesand there are many-may be thrown at

All our documents and Acts of Parliament are placed before this House in a
complete form, but before they reach that

I think that is perhaps one of the most

Then the question of the Prime Minister is often raised. I know it is a rather
nebulous sort of phrase, and it is far

Now I just want to refer to the valedictory remarks of Mr. Stanley Baldwin
a few days ago in his constituency of
Bewdley. I remember being rather
sneered at many years ago when I said
that one of the most necessary qualifications for the position of Prime Minister
was that the holder should be able to sit
down and think. People did not seem
to put much value on the word
"thought." But if the head of the State
is to have a continuity of policy, and if

Ministry of Finance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
Mr. Baldwin said that one of the most
important points he wished to stress that
day was to have time to think. Such a
long time has elapsed since the day I
made that observation-I think it was
made in this House-that I am sure Mr.
Baldwin, when he made his speech the
other day, was not in any way thinking
of any similar remarks I might have
made, although I am glad to be able to
claim him as a very old personal friend
of mine. At the same time, the fact of
the two remarks having been made with
such a long interval of time intervening,
shows that what was passing through his
mind was passing through mine some
time ago.
I would just like to say in conclusion
that, no matter what may be said outside,
what I may call the outward and visible
sign of the Prime Minister having charge.
is also very important. It may not be
translated into pounds, shillings, and
pence, but if Ulster is to take her proper
position on great occasions such as the
crowning of a sovereign, or a jubilee such
as we had the year before last, and on
all occasions of ceremony of that sort, it
is important that she should have her
representative there, not for any personal
reason whatever, but because Ulster
must be given her proper position. Some
people talk about giving Ulster a place
on the map. You cannot give Ulster a
place on the map if you are going to
lower her status in any way. You want
always to uplift her position and take a
pride in the position she occupies, and
the Prime Minister can materially contribute towards that end. I doubt if it
would be possible for me to combine my
position as Prime Minister with that of
Minister of Finance if the work of the
Finance Ministry is to be as properly
and conscientiously carried out in the
future as it has been in the past by our
late lamented friend.
Therefore, I hope the hon. and learned
Member for Central will, on due reflection, realise that it is far better to carry
on as we are doing to-day rather than to
ask someone-it might even be my successor-who is not an expert in finance
to occupy the two positions. On the
other hand, such a person, although not
a financial expert, might be well fitted for
the ordinary duties of a Prime Minister,
to discharge the class of work which
brings him into contact with the British
authorities, and affords him opportunities to maintain friendly relations with
Ministers on the other side, for arranging
matters of various kinds for the benefit
of the community as a whole, and for
doing the hundred and one things that
are necessary to keep us where we are
to-day, in the satisfactory position of
which I am more than proud. I think
that on the whole the hon. and learned
Member will agree that that is far better
than attempting to amalgamate the two
offices, and placing such a large amount
of detail on the shoulders of the Prime
Minister that he would not be able to
discharge his other duties in a proper and
efficient manner.

The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
The
hon. and learned Member for Central
has raised the question of the amalgamation of the Prime Minister's office with
that of the Minister of Finance.
He
started the observations which he
addressed to the Committee this afternoon by saying that he could see no
reason why these two offices should not
be amalgamated. Well I think if he had
a little more knowledge of the duties
attaching to these two offices and the
difference between them he would not
have put his question in that form. He
then went on to ask why they should not
be amalgamated. I think it is most
appropriate to ask what reasons can be
advanced for their amalgamation.
I
listened very carefully to the speech of
the hon. and learned Member and I
must confess I could not gather one
single reason from his remarks which
would justify the Committee in accepting
his proposition. The Members of the
Committee will realise, if they reflect for
moment, that
one of the
important things in our Constitution is
that the Minister of Finance, or whoever
handles the finances of the Province,
should be absolutely independent.
a
most
When I say independent I do not mean
independent in the ordinary colloquial
sense of the word; I mean independent
of all the entanglements of the Government, because one knows from experience, even those who have a very
limited knowledge of the working of
governments, the Ministries and other
public departments, that there are constantly coming along to the Minister of
Finance claims for increased expenditure
and quite legitimately so. The Minister
of Home Affairs wants to increase and
improve the accommodation for the
police force, and everybody sympathises
with that. The Minister of Education
wants to equip the Province with new
schools and a large body of the public,
almost all the public I should say, are
in sympathy with that. When all these
matters have been put forward by the
various Ministries and parties outside
the Government altogether, they have
got to be assessed by somebody who is
independent of all the Ministries, and
that person can only be the Minister of
Finance. If he is also in the position of
Prime Minister, to whom a lot of these
personal claims are made by various.
bodies for bridges, improvements in the
equipment of the police and a number of
other matters it will readily occur to
every Member of the Committee that the
Prime Minister may think that these are
very necessary matters which would be
of great advantage to the Province if
undertaken, and rightly so, but before.
he can make up his mind as to whether
they should be undertaken he has to go
to the Minister of Finance and say "Will
the Ulster Budget stand this additional
expense". Members of the Committee
can readily imagine that if these offices
are held by the same man he is placed
in a most invidious position, that is if
his duty as custodian of the purse is at
variance with his position as Prime
Minister representing the public of the
Province.
I
as
The Minister of Finance is really to
some extent in the same position as His
Majesty's judges; he is independent of
all the other branches of the executive,
and he has to look at everything that
comes before him from a strictly
financial point of view. I think Members who understand the onerous duties
which fall upon him do not envy him
the decision he has sometimes to make.
Then the hon. and learned Member said,
or at anyrate suggested, that the position
of the Prime Minister is a sinecure.
think that everybody who knows the
amount of work the Prime Minister has
to do knows quite well it is no sinecure.
Somebody in every Government has got
to lead the country, and somebody has
ultimately got to make decisions
between the various Ministries that look
after the country's affairs. That falls on
the Prime Minister and it can only fall
on him. If you take up the Act of 1921
under which these Ministries were set up
you will see set out the duties assigned
to each. You can see that these duties
are very often of a conflicting nature as
between the various Departments of the
State. At the same time, although their
duties are conflicting, all the offices are
bending their energies towards the same
end as members of the same Government
and members of the Cabinet, namely, to
see that Ulster gets the best possible
Government and the best administration
which can be provided by human ingenuity. When they differ, the only
person who can settle the differences is
the Prime Minister, and it would be
Estimates-
Ministry of Finance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Attorney-General]
impossible, in my opinion, to carry on
without a Prime Minister. You might
have somebody designated under another
name, but the duties which the Prime
Minister carries out, and to which, as
he said this afternoon, he has devoted a
great deal of thought, can be carried out
by him and him alone.
To suggest that the duty of the Prime
Minister is a sinecure is a cry which
might appeal to some people, but to anybody who realises how the Government is
carried on it must be apparent that the
ship of State cannot be steered without
somebody at the helm, otherwise you
will run on to the rocks and you will
have one portion of the crew pulling one
way and the other portion another way.
Therefore, you must have a helmsman to
ensure that the ship of State is properly
steered. The only person who can do
that is the Prime Minister, whose position
is no sinecure because it is an absolutely
essential part of the administration, and
you could no more get on without a
Prime Minister than you could get on
without a Minister of Finance. You
could no more amalgamate those two
offices than run the country without
either.
I wondered when I listened to the
argument put forward by the hon. and
learned Member for Central whether he
was putting it forward in the interests
of Ulster, as something which was going
to benefit her financial position. It
seems to me that it was advanced rather
for the purpose of decrying this Parliament and suggesting that our affairs are
so petty and so small that it is unnecessary to have both a Minister of Finance
and a Prime Minister. I think that
argument will not hold with the majority
of the Members of this Committee, and
I am quite sure it is not an argument
that will hold with the people of Ulster
outside this House. It is an argument
designed not in the interests of our
Government or this Parliament, but in
order to whittle away its prestige.
Might I say another thing that has
often occurred to me. You cannot run
a Government like a business. I have
often heard people saying that if this
Government was run by business people
the thing would be different. You cannot run a Government like a business
because a business is a personal matter.
A man engaged in trade takes risks
which a Government could never take.
If the worst befalls him he can make a
tour through the bankruptcy court and
begin again, but people running a
Government cannot allow that Government to get into the bankruptcy court;
they have got to run the business of the
country on much more conservative and
prudent lines than any businessman runs
his affairs. That is why in the main the
staffing and management of a Government is always necessarily more expensive
than the management and staffing of a
business house. I think hon. Members
should remember that when dealing with
a Government you are bound to see that
everything is run on such a basis that
will not land the country in disaster; it
must be run on lines such as the present
Government runs the affairs of Ulster.
Reference was made to some difficulty
in the Law Courts by the hon. Member
for Pottinger. I do not know very much
about the merits of this very petty dispute, but I know, so far as I am informed,
that the custodianship of the Law Courts
is in the Lord Chief Justice, because the
High Court is a reserved service. In that
building is also housed a number of
departments of the Ministry, or portions
of the Ministry, and some arrangement
had to be made to ensure that there
should not be any confusion as between
persons attending the Ministries and the
members of the public attending the Law
Courts or attending the various offices
attached to the Courts. Accordingly
there are two main entrances to the
Courts and there are two subsidiary
entrances to the administrative portion
of the building to which you can get
through the medium of a lift. But in
order to ensure that there should be no
confusion the Lord Chief Justice, I
understand, gave instructions that a
certain door should be closed. You have
probably come across that door just as I
have. The only objection I have to it is
that on a wet day instead of walking
out through the front door I have to
walk round two sides of the square to
get from my office as Attorney-General
down to my place in the Courts. I have
to do that much more often than the
hon. Member for Pottinger, but up to
the present I have not felt much disturbed by the arrangement.

There is just one other matter of a
general nature to which I should like to
refer. That is the question of comparing
Ministers here with Ministers in
England. I think if Members of the
Committee knew a little more about the
work of the Ministers here they would
realise that there are a great many
matters dealt with by them which would
not be dealt with by Ministers across the
water. They have more elaborate staffs
on the other side, and although, no
doubt, a Minister in Whitehall does
probably a great deal more than a Minister here, at the same time the difference
is not so great as one might imagine,
because a great deal of the departmental
work here is done by the Minister, and
in the larger Ministries the Ministers are
occupied practically the whole time.
The curious thing about this argument
which is put forward year after year on
the Estimates is that it deals only with
the salaries of Ministers. The various
Ministries must be
run pretty well
because the sole argument which the
Members of the Opposition have to advance is this personal one about salaries.
We hear very little criticism about the
running of the Departments, which so far
as the arguments in this House are concerned meets with the approval of all
sections of the House. I think we owe
a deep debt of gratitude to the efforts of
our Minister of Finance, and we also owe
a great debt of gratitude to the Prime
Minister for his management of the
Province. I hope it will be a very long
time before these two positions are
amalgamated by a decision of this House.

have accepted their work as very satisfactory. No one will say that the work
of the Commissioner of Valuation has
produced good results. It has been
proved beyond the shadow of a doubt
that his basis of working is wrong. He
has adopted a basis of working which
should never have been applied to this
part of the world, and which was not
practicable. He ignored the standing
charges on the people who have never
owned any ground, and until he is prepared to prove his worth in the
Department I am not prepared to give
him the salary set out in these Estimates.
I have many places in my mind at the
present moment which are a standing
disgrace to the Commissioner's Department. The unfortunate part of it is that
the whole of the Department is blamed
for this unsatisfactory work. The unsatisfactory work should be laid solely at
the door of the Commissioner himself.
What has he done? He has treated the
people with contempt; he has laughed
and gibed at their desperate plight, which
is due to his unsatisfactory work.
every occasion when I visit a home as a
representative of the working classes and
hear of the increased rent and the reduced
purchasing power, I feel that the Commissioner of Valuation is responsible. He
set out on a job which was limited in its
scope with the full instructions and
approval of this House. He exceeded
those instructions, and proceeded to
impose upon the people a burden that
On
they could not bear. I agreed to a
certain extent with the necessity for revaluation-revaluation to end anomalies.
An assurance was given that the Government were concerned only with the
anomalies that existed. If the anomalies
had been righted and those who are
escaping the payment of income tax had
been brought to book I would have been
satisfied, and I would have said that the
head of this Department had done a good
day's work for Ulster. Instead of that
he has besmirched the name of Ulster,
and valuation in every area throughout
the Six Counties stinks in the nostrils,
because the people know they are unable
to pay the rate he has set down. We
were never treated in our lives with the
same class of scorpion as we have been
treated with on the last occasion, and on
the last occasion we were supposed to have
been dealt with by locals. Take the
valuation and the standards set up by the
Imperial Government. When we were
under the Imperial Government they
treated us more leniently. They treated
us in accordance with our ability to pay.
We get a local or native Government and
have native officials placed in these high
positions. When they got into these high
positions they put the whip on the people
of Northern Ireland. The welts left by
these whips will not wear off in a few
days, they will remain until an opportunity is afforded to the people to raise
their voices against treatment of this
kind. I do not want to say anything
which would in any way reflect on the
late Minister of Finance. He cannot be
charged with this. He gave the officials
a free and unfettered hand and he
expected a good job in return, but when
they had finished the position was worse
than it was before. Until such times as
we get an assurance from the Government that the right man is in the right
position I will always move against this
amount of money being paid to the Commissioner of Valuation.
Question put, "That a sum not exceeding £33,860 be granted to His
Majesty for the said service."
The Committee divided: Ayes, 19;
Noes, 2.

Mr. BEATTIE: I have tried every
year to get from the right hon. Gentleman an account of the way in which this
money is really spent. I notice at the
bottom of the page it is stated:
This expenditure will not be accounted
for in detail to the Comptroller and
Auditor-General. Advances will be
made by the Minister of Finance to
other Ministers, who will render
accounts to the Minister of Finance
with a certificate to the effect that the
sums expended have been necessarily
disbursed on public services.
certificates will be furnished to the
Comptroller and Auditor-General.
These
This Secret Service is really a menace to
the honesty of the people of Northern
Ireland, as part of this money is used
for the Secret Service branch of the
Ministry of Labour, the Secret Service
of the Ministry of Home Affairs, Secret
Service in the Civil Service, and Secret
Service in the police, so that there might
be carried to the authorities those voices,
perhaps of discontent, that may be heard.
It is time this Vote was abolished. I
have known homes to be visited by individuals drawing unemployment benefit
or public assistance, and their visits, to
me at any rate, have proved beyond the
shadow of doubt that they are in the
secret service of the Ministry. I say that
is a real menace to persons working in
the Civil Service, the police, or the
Home Office, or who are in the ranks of
the unemployed.
The object of this Vote is not to give
the Government service in connection
with an infringement of the 1920 Act,
it is not to give them knowledge of gunmen in Northern Ireland, it is not to
give them knowledge of how many Republicans there are in Northern Ireland,
or how many people wore Easter lilies on
Easter Sunday. No, that work is performed by the various departments in
the different Ministries. This Secret
Service money is really paid to those who
are prepared to carry tales about their
fellow-workers to the heads of the departments in which they are engaged. That
is really the class of secret service covered
by this Estimate, and I am going to
oppose it every year. It is not a secret
service to preserve the country against
unconstitutional acts; if it was I might
say it was necessary. I know that is not
how this money is spent because this
amount would not meet one quarter of
the requirements in the direction I have
outlined.
It is used for every Tom, Dick, and
Harry in the departments who may express themselves in the presence of a man
who is getting £1 or £2 a year extra.
That knowledge is conveyed to the heads
of the departments who then know how
to act. We have heard of many changes
taking place in the police force. There
have been very heavy charges for transfers. We have heard of many changes
taking place in the Civil Service. Hon.
Members ask why nobody is able to explain. I am explaining now; it is because
of the openness of the expressions of some
members in the various departments-

Mr. HENDERSON: Might I ask the
Prime Minister-and I am not doing it to
cause him any embarrassment-whether
it is the custom of the Prime Minister of
any Parliament to divulge to the Press
changes in Cabinet offices before Members
of Parliament are acquainted with the
information. When we opened our newspapers this morning we read that the
Prime Minister had been at Hillsborough
Castle, and that he had appointed the
Minister of Labour as Minister of Finance
and the hon. and gallant Member for
Central Armagh as Minister of Labour,
and that was the first intimation we
received of the changes. Is it not the
custom of Prime Ministers to keep these
Cabinet secrets from the Press until they
have first been divulged to Members of
the House?
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the Prime
Minister if he is now in a position to state
the date of the introduction of the
Budget.
The PRIME MINISTER: With
regard to the question of the hon.
Member for Shankill, he will, of course,
realise that constitutional practice was
faithfully followed, and until his Grace
the Governor had signified his approval
of the appointments no announcement
could be made. On the other hand, of
course the Press, as usual, very correctly
prognosticated what would happen, though
the information was not given to them
by the Government. But their knowledge
of what goes on is perfectly wonderful,
as I am sure the hon. Member realises.

Oral Answers to Questions.
NUMBER OF NEW INDUSTRIES.
1. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he can
state the number of new industries
established in Northern Ireland since
1935, and what these particular firms
manufacture, and the number of men,
women, boys and girls employed in
them.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): So far as I have been
able to ascertain at least seven industrial
undertakings have been established in
Northern Ireland since 1935. These are
engaged in the spinning of jute yarns for
hessians, and of woollen yarns for carpets, the manufacture of power fruit
spraying machinery, nicotine, biscuits,
millinery, and inedible waste meat products. Together they afford employment
at the present time to approximately 140
men, 95 women, 15 boys and 67 girls.
This statement does not profess to be
exhaustive, nor does it include the aircraft factory of Messrs Short & Harland,
Limited, at present in course of erection.
PROTECTION OF PETROL AND
OIL DEPOTS.
2. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state how it is proposed to protect
the petrol and oil depots on the Harbour
Commissioners property in the event of
enemy air raids; and whether he is
making representations to the Imperial
authorities to have an anti-aircraft
detachment stationed in this area.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The hon. Member's
question appears mainly to relate to the
question of defence, which is one entirely
for the Imperial Authorities, but I may
inform the hon. Member that the
question of the protection of oil tanks.
is at present engaging the attention of
technical experts. Much research work
has already been done and certain basic
principles have been laid down by the
Air Raid Precautions Department of the
Home Office, London, for the guidance
of the appropriate authorities.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the right
hon. Gentleman aware that the Air
Raids Committee in London are doing
nothing for Ulster?
CABINET MINISTERS AND.
DIRECTORSHIPS.
3. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister whether he is aware that
all Members of the British Parliament
who hold the rank of Cabinet Minister
must resign their directorship of private
companies during their tenure of office,
and that the same law applies in every
Government throughout the world; and
whether he will apply this principle to
the Cabinet Ministers of the Government of Northern Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER: Whatever
may be the practice elsewhere, I am of
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
22 APRIL 1937
opinion that in the best interests of
Ulster it would be unwise to limit the
choice of Ministers by the prescription
suggested. Experience covering the past
sixteen years has amply shown that the
public interest has in no way suffered,
but on the contrary has benefited by
the system we have adopted here.
SUGGESTED GENERAL ELECTION
4. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister whether he is aware that
there is a growing discontent amongst
the people of Northern Ireland due to
the introduction of the Road Transport,
Revaluation and other Acts that have
seriously interfered with their business
and have resulted in an increase in the
rent of every working man's home; and
whether he can state if, in view of this
discontent, the Government are prepared.
to have a general election at an early
date.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am
aware that certain ill-disposed persons
are engaged in stirring up discontent
among the people not only in connection.
with the subjects mentioned, but in
other directions. The hon. Member
may rest assured, however, that the great

Sir DAWSON BATES: In presenting the Estimates for the Home Office,
I propose, following the usual course, to
give a brief survey of the operations of
the various services for which the Home
Office is responsible, and if there are
any points on which hon. Members
desire elucidation, I shall be only too
happy to give them any information
which I possess.
With very deep regret I should like
to refer to the loss which the Ministry
has sustained by the death of the chief
medical officer, the late Doctor Norman
Patrick. Doctor Patrick was well
known by every Member of this House
and by every member of the local
authorities, and while the Home Office
will sadly miss him, he will be especially
missed by the various local authorities,
who received such valuable assistance
from him in the arduous duties which
they have to perform in connection with
public health.
With regard to the services falling
under the head of public health, I should
like to take this opportunity of expressing my indebtedness to the various
local authorities throughout the country.
As the result of their operations, backed
and assisted by the Government in every
way possible, while we would still like to
see further progress made in connection
with this all-important subject, we can, at
all events, claim that during the past 16
years an enormous improvement has been
witnessed in the public health of the
Province. One has only to deal with
matters such as hospital work, medical
services, water and sewage, cleansing and
supervision of food, to see the wonderful
improvement that has taken place in our
midst.
Take hospitals. When this Government was formed there was only one
district hospital in Northern Ireland.
Now there are 11. On visiting one of
these district hospitals one is struck with
the contrast to the old workhouse
hospitals, which in many cases were
managed by indifferent nurses, and had
the services of one part-time medical
attendant, who, in no sense, could be
called a surgeon. These district hospitals
now have some of the ablest surgeons in
control, and they employ fully qualified
nurses.
May I here remind hon. Members that
since the Government was formed a
Nursing Council has been established, and
this has had a most salutary effect in the
type of nurses appointed to public
institutions.
Ministry of Home Affairs 990
Estimates-
22 APRIL 1937
These hospitals have up-to-date equipment. In most cases they have X-ray
apparatus, so that they are in a position
to deal with the most difficult surgical
and medical cases. This has had the
effect of doing away with the unfortunate
practice which existed in the old days
where poor persons might have been
driven in an ambulance for many miles
before they could get proper attention.
Apart from this there has been an
enormous improvement in the workhouse
hospitals that have not been converted
into district hospitals. The same sign of
improvement is shown in all other
hospitals, and the county infirmaries, I
am glad to say, are by degrees being
brought up-to-date. The mental hospitals
-we do not now use the old term
asylum-also are improved out of all
recognition.
Take another all-important questionthe question of water and sewage. Very
considerable progress in this service has
been made, and the cities of Belfast and
Derry have now water supplies which are
second to none. Other towns, like
Coleraine, Donaghadee, Portstewart,
Holywood, Ballycastle, Dromore, and so
forth, either have, or are engaged in
providing pure water supplies. In regard
to sewage, people are now beginning to
realise that with the amenities which we
enjoy sewage is of first importance. A
question was asked the other day in regard
to the situation in Dundonald and Newtownbreda areas. I am glad to say that
these two important areas have recently
been supplied with a water supply and
efficient sewage services.
Mr. BEATTIE: All except the police
barracks.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure
isolated cases will be looked after. After
all, considering what we have already
done, I think the police barrack will also
be dealt with. I find that in regard to
the expenditure on this particular branch
of our work, something like 1 million
pounds has been sanctioned by the local
authorities.
The housing question has been dealt
with so often that I feel I need not say
very much on the subject, but I should
like to remind the Committee that no
fewer than 38,500 houses have been built
with the aid of Government subsidy,
involving an expenditure of no less than
3 million pounds—not a bad sum for this
Province of ours. I believe that we are
rapidly approaching a period when the
supply will be equal, if it does not exceed,
the demand. We are getting back to the
old days when Belfast used to take credit
for being the cheapest and best housed
city in the three Kingdoms.
Unfortunately, owing to financial
stringency we had to suspend the operations of the Labourers Acts, but this
suspension has been withdrawn by our
1935 Act, and every encouragement has
been given to the various local authorities
to proceed with schemes. There are 26
schemes at present in contemplation,
involving the erection of 4,000 cottages.
The question has been raised from time
to time in this House as to the advisability of extending the operation of the
Labourers Acts to
urban districts,
especially those situated in non-industrial
areas. The mere application of the existing Labourers Acts to urban districts will
not in itself solve the various problems
which arise. One difficulty which presents itself, and which I think will be
apparent to hon. Members, is the difficulty in getting vacant land in certain
urban areas.
This matter was raised in the House
some time ago by, I think, the hon. Member for North Antrim and the hon. Member for South Derry, and I should like to
take this opportunity of assuring them
that I hope shortly to be in a position, in
conjunction with the Minister of Finance,
to arrive at a solution.
I am glad to be able to inform the
Committee that there has been a steady,
but very decided improvement in the conditions in reference to the maintenance of
law and order. While I say this, and
while I am glad to realise that there is a
marked absence of organised crime, I
wish I could feel satisfied that this
absence of what I have described as
"organised" crime, was the result of
change of heart on the part of those who
have always been on the watch for any
weakness on the part of the Government
or on the part of the police, ready again
to plunge this Province into disorder.
am sorry that I cannot but feel that the
Province would not be in its present
peaceful condition if the vigilance of our
Ministry of Home Affairs 992
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
police forces were to be relaxed. If this
vigilance were relaxed I believe that
attempts would again be made by certain
individuals to press forward their political
views by means of criminal methods.
As regards ordinary crime, hon. Members, I am sure, will be gratified, as I am,
to see from time to time the remarks
made by His Majesty's Judges. One of
the most satisfactory features contributing largely to this result has been the remarkable success that has attended the
police forces in the detection of offences.
At the recent City Commission no less
than 68 per cent. of the cases of housebreaking had been cleared up by the
police. This result is, I consider, highly
satisfactory, and will, I am sure, compare
favourably with the results in any city of
a similar size or type in the United
Kingdom, and I should like to take this
opportunity of congratulating the police
on the marked success they have achieved.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Apart from this satisfactory condition
of affairs, we have, unfortunately, still
a very large amount of crime among
juveniles, and hon. Members will recollect
that a committee, under the chairmanship of my hon. Friend, the Member for
North Antrim, is now studying the whole
question. I understand that that committee will shortly be in a position to
report, and I can assure the Committee
that no time will be lost in putting forward a Measure for the consideration of
this House with the object of dealing
with one of the most serious aspects in
our social life.
There is, perhaps, one other instance
to which I might refer. It will be in the
recollection of hon. Members that, for
some years past, smuggling was very prevalent from the Irish Free State into
Northern Ireland, with serious loss to
the Imperial revenue. This had undoubtedly a most demoralising effect on
the inhabitants of Northern Ireland,
especially along the Border. I consider
that the arrangements made were not as
satisfactory as they might have been,
and as a result of representation made
by our Government to the
the Imperial
Government, new arangements were
entered into under which our police force
as a whole was responsible for dealing
with the infringement of the Smuggling
Acts instead of a limited number of
specially selected members of the force.
As a result of this new arrangement I
am glad to say, in the space of something
like a year smuggling has been reduced
to a non-paying proposition, and it is
practically non-existent.
In connection with this matter, I
should like to express my appreciation of
the way in which the Imperial Government met our Government, and I should
also like to point out that the financial
burden of carrying on this work does not
fall upon the finances of Northern Ireland. Hon. Members will see that an
appropriation-in-aid in respect of this
service has been made.
Mr. BEATTIE: What do the Committee get out of it?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member will see that by the Estimates.
Towards the end of 1936 the police depot
was moved from Newtownards to the
newly reconstructed premises of the old
military depot in Enniskillen. Hon.
Members will appreciate that if it is
desired to give a proper training to our
police, proper quarters must be provided, and I am glad to say that we have
every reason to believe that the good
accommodation now provided for our
recruits will redound to their efficiency.
Before I pass from the police forces
I should like again to refer to the
efficient way in which the Royal Ulster
Constabulary have carried out their
duties. The time was-now many years
ago-when there was always an element
of hostility between the civilian population and the regular police forces of the
Crown, but I am glad to think that this
has long since disappeared, and I believe.
in our Royal Ulster Constabulary we
have a force second to none, and one in
which the civilian population take the
greatest possible pride. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I should also like to bear tribute to
the wonderful work carried on by the
"B" Special Constabulary. As the
Committee are aware, this force is
entirely a voluntary one. During the
past year I am glad to know that we are
recruiting many of the younger generation, thereby relieving the older members
of the burden which they so efficiently
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs

carried in the past. One item which will
appear on the Estimates is the provision
of new clothing for the "B" Special
Constabulary, I have always felt very
strongly that, when men are prepared to
give their services free in the defence of
law and order in their country, they
should be provided with proper equipment. I am sure this statement will give
much gratification to many Members of
this House who are also members of that
force.
As regards prisons, I am glad to be
able to tell the Committee that the administration of our three prisons-
Derry, Armagh, and Belfast-has been
most efficiently carried out. The discipline of the staffs has been excellent
and the conduct of the prisoners good.
Perhaps I should refer to the improved.
salary scale of pay which has been introduced for prison staffs, with effect from
the 1st April, 1936. The details of the
new scales and a comparison with the old
will be found in the appendix on page
75 of the Estimates. I cannot imagine
anything more arduous or more distasteful than the duty of a prison.
warder, and I should like here again to
bear testimony to the valuable services
they have rendered. We read of troubles
in prisons in other parts of the world,
and the Government feel they are under
an obligation to our prisons staffs for
the work they have done.
In dealing with prisons I cannot
refrain from referring again to the criticisms which have from time to time been
levelled at our prison administration
because on a per capita basis the cost
appears somewhat high, and I would
again like to point out the fallacy of
this argument. In the first place, our
prison population is, I am glad to say,
small, and it is hardly necessary
explain that in a service of this kind a
very considerable proportion of the overhead charges must necessarily remain
constant, and consequently the smaller
the number of prisoners, the larger the
per capita cost appears to be.
to
Again, in our limited area we are also
under the necessity of providing for
the various classes of prisoners in one
prison. In England there is a prison for
each class of prisoner, but in Belfast
there are no fewer than six or seven
different types of prisoner-convicts
serving long terms, prisoners undergoing hard labour, contempt of court
prisoners, prisoners on remand and
awaiting trial, juvenile adults, etc. In
order to provide so far as possible for the
necessary segregation of such classes
under the varying conditions applicable
to the various classes, a relatively greater
amount of supervision is required than
if all the prisoners were of the same
character. I think that will be perfectly
clear to every Member of the Committee.
It would, no doubt, be cheap and easy
if we could deal with prisoners as in
the old days-herd them in dungeons,
feed them with a minimum of bread and
water, and give no consideration whatever to the question of their moral welfare either in prison or after their
discharge. Would any hon. Member who
wishes to criticise these Estimates desire
to-day to put back the hands of the clock
in this respect?
A prison, while primarily a place of
punishment, cannot be regarded as a
purely penal establishment. The whole
trend of modern thought is to stress the
reformative aspect of our prisons, so
that those who are unfortunate enough
to be confined therein may not during
their period of imprisonment become.
hardened and embittered but will be
given an opportunity of realising the
error of their ways and leave the prison
gates behind them with a determination
to turn over a new leaf. It is, therefore,
necessary to preserve a judicious balance
so as to secure that prisoners are made
to realise that although their wrongdoing must be expiated by punishment,
this is no vindictive revenge, but rather
a reformative discipline for their own
good.
As regards the Borstal Institution at
Malone Training School, this institution
continues to perform a very useful and
efficient service. Hon. Members are
aware that since we took over the old
Malone Reformatory it has been used
partly as a Borstal Institution and
partly as a Reformatory for boys. The
premises were not altogether suitable for
the dual purpose, but, having regard to
the financial stringency, we have had to
do the best we could. I am glad to say,
however, that I have arranged with the
Ministry of Finance for the school to be
reconstructed, which will not alone
improve the amenities of the premises
generally but will also enable us to pro-

Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
vide for a more effective segregation of
the reformatory inmates from the
Borstal boys, the necessity for which, I
am sure, the Committee will appreciate.
I think anyone who has taken any
interest in this institution must admit
that the success of the school under its
present Governor, Mr. Watson, has been
most remarkable.
Many people are inclined to sneer at
Borstal treatment simply because certain
offenders revert to their old life of crime,
but outsiders seldom hear of the number
of boys who have made good. I can
assure the Committee that the percentage
of boys who have made good in after life
has been most remarkable. I am prepared at any time to show figures to hon.
Members if they are interested. One has
only to remember the difficulties which
these boys have to encounter when young
to appreciate the fact that under proper
training there is no reason why the
majority should not make good.
should like here to express my indebtedness to the Borstal Committee, which
includes many Members of this House,
for the wonderful work they have done.
I
Mr. BEATTIE: Only Members from
one side of the Committee.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I will with
pleasure issue an invitation to every
Member on the Opposition side to join
the Borstal Committee. Not alone do
they visit they school and take a personal

have been instrumental in getting

wonderful results we have attained are

I now come to a matter which gives me
a great deal of anxiety, and that is what
is referred to as "the toll of the road."
When one realises that last year we had a
total of 2,021 accidents and 127 fatalities
in a comparatively small community like
ours, it must make not alone the general
public, but motorists themselves, realise
the seriousness of the situation. We have
one crumb of comfort in the fact that
taking into account the increase in the
number of cars on the road, there is a
downward tendency, and our accidents in
proportion to those in England are considerably less. The number of accidents
per thousand vehicles in Northern Ireland
in 1935 was 47.1, while in 1936 the figure
was 43.1. The comparable figures in
Great Britain were 76 and 66.
As I have said before, I believe the vast
number of the motoring public are careful
drivers who would be horrified if anyone was to suggest that they were
indifferent to human life. On the other
hand, there are a certain number of
motorists who, by their conduct, seem to
be absolutely indifferent-who risk not
alone their own lives, but the lives of
other motorists and the public generally,
and I am more than ever convinced that
the most effective factors in bringing
about a reduction in the number of road
casualties is the rigorous enforcement of
our motor legislation in respect of the
suspension of driving licences. Motorists
who do not realise their responsibilitiy,
and carelessly and recklessly drive a
vehicle-which is, when SO driven,
nothing less than a dangerous weaponor who so indulge in alcohol when in
charge of a car as to bring themselves
within the clutches of the law, should be
put off the road. It is an interesting
factor in considering this problem to
notice that those who have had their
licences suspended by our courts frequently appear again on similar charges
-in other words, they never seem to have
learnt their lesson. Leniency is no good.
Hon. Members are aware that as
regards serious offences, such as the
offence of driving when incapable
through drink, or driving to the danger
of the public, or driving without an
insurance certificate, our legislation is
more stringent than that which exists in
England, and it is an appalling fact that
no fewer than 461 individuals had their
licences suspended in 1936 for such
offences.
I have been impressed, as I think most
of the public will have been, by the satisfactory operations of the Police Traffic
Branch of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
in connection with the prevention and
detection of motoring offences, and I may
say that the system of police patrol cars
has proved so satisfactory that we are
arranging for an increase in their number.
I am glad to think that much more
friendly relations exist to-day between
Ministry of Home Affairs 998
Estimates
22 APRIL 1937
what I may describe as the decent motoring public and our police. I think the
motoring public are beginning to realise
that the police are not their enemies, that
the police are only there for the purpose
of protecting, not alone the public, but
the decent motorists from the
"road
hog." At the same time, may I say this,
that I believe that, without the cooperation of the general body of decent.
motorists, whose interests and whose
safety is dependent on the decencies of
road traffic being preserved, it is
impossible for the police to do more than
touch the fringe of the problem.
I am afraid, however, there are still
entirely unwarranted prejudices on the
part of motorists as a class, against taking
any steps, either by giving information to
the police of breaches of the traffic laws
which they may observe, or in bringing
under notice the delinquencies of their
fellow motorists. The Government can
do much in providing safer roads-they
can provide for white lines they can
provide for stop signals, but what good.
are all these if motorists deliberately drive
over the white lines coming round corners
or refuse to stop when emerging from a
side road. After all, the road hog is perfectly indifferent to the safety of others,
and the only thing that stops him is the
knowledge that the police may be on the
spot, and what strikes me as a rather
peculiar thing is the practice amongst
certain motorists, if the police are
stationed at a dangerous corner to try
and ensure that accidents will be avoided,
of signalling all down the road that
the police happened to be stationed
there. After all, the decent and careful
motorist has nothing to fear from the
police the police are only there for the
purpose of trying to ensure that the
motorist may return to his home in safety.
I will go further and suggest that those
motorists, by assisting potential criminals,
are defeating the ends of justice and are
themselves guilty of a criminal offence.
The Government, as I said before,
spend large sums of money in trying to
secure the safety of the motorist, but if
the decent motorist is not prepared to
co-operate with the police these accidents
will still continue. I can draw no distinction between the individual who risks
destroying life simply because he happens
to be a motorist, and the other type of
criminal who may risk destroying life with
any other instrument, but because they
are motorists the same disgrace does not
seem to fall upon them as other offenders.
After all, do not forget this, the motorist
who is convicted for a serious offence has
a right of appeal to the county court
judge if he thinks he has been wrongly
convicted, and while it is not for me to
dictate to any of the great motoring
organisations who have done so much to
promote the motor industry and to assist
motorists, I do suggest to them, with
great respect, that they should consider
whether or not these road hogs, who endanger life and take life, should have the
benefits of membership of their organisations when the law has removed their
licences on grounds that they are unfit
to drive. The Government's policy has
been to avoid, so far as possible, the introduction of legislation involving a new
code of offences, but what I do appeal
to the motoring public for, as I said
before, is that there should be greater cooperation with the police and greater
friendliness, and the realisation that the
police are there to help them.
I may add that, with the view of assisting to bring this about, I have arranged
with the Inspector-General that where the
police see a motorist driving badly, or
committing some other act which, while
not in itself sufficient to justify a prosecution, might if persisted in result in
accident, the police should give a written
warning of a friendly character to the
motorist, pointing out the defects which
are shown in his driving, not with the
view of a prosecution, but with the object
of bringing home to him that further
care should be exercised by him. I feel
that a written warning of this character
might do more to impress upon motorists
the necessity for the utmost care while in
charge of a car.
In conclusion, I may say that I shall
be only too glad to deal with any matter
arising on these Estimates to which I have
not referred and about which hon. Members may desire information. I beg to
move.

take it, subject to correction, that,

to grant outdoor relief to able-bodied unemployed instead of restricting it to those
who are sick. I looked down the local
grants to see if anything was paid, but
having read this Act I am satisfied the
responsibility for payment under it
devolves upon the local authority. That
is where the fly is in the ointment. I
think that is one of the difficulties the
local authorities do not seem to be getting
over. I am now appealing through this
Committee to try to rouse the social
conscience of Northern Ireland in regard
to the gravity of this problem.
I think, with the exception of three
local authorities in Northern Ireland—
the Parliamentary Secretary will correct
me if I am wrong-no local authority pays
outdoor relief to able-bodied unemployed,
which means that vast masses of the unemployed population are almost derelict
at the present time. The other day I
quoted the case of a constituency represented by an hon. Member opposite, where
the maximum standard of outdoor relief
is 5s a week. That standard is only paid,
under the Local Government Act, to those
who are sick. I am not now raising a
question that requires legislation, I am
raising a question of what can be done.
I know it is a very moot point whether
the governmental authority ought to
interfere with the functions of a democratically elected local authority, and I know
the people who have returned that
authority look to them to carry out the
law in accordance with the mandate they
received.
I have distinct and vivid recollections
of a joint deputation that left part of
County Down a little over a year ago and
made overtures to the Minister of Home
Affairs and the Minister of Labour regarding the possibility of doing something
in that area to make it less backward and
less depressed economically than it was
at that particular time. Speaking from
memory, I think the figure quoted that
day to the Ministers was that of the total
working population, or workable population, if I may use that term, some 85 per
cent. were unemployed, and distress relief,
or relief to able-bodied unemployed, was
not being given there. I have quoted one
area this afternoon where the maximum
outdoor relief given is 5s, and in that and
other areas no relief is paid to able-bodied
unemployed.
Ministry of Home Affairs 1016
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
Many of these people, as was revealed
by the statistics given the other day, have
had their cases heard by the tribunals
set up under the Unemployment Assistance Act, but will not be taken over
under Part II of that Act. As they will
not be taken over they will be left in the
position they were in before. A number
of these men have been tightening their
belts and enduring this hardship in the
hope that they might be taken over under
Part II, and that is where the Ministry
of Home Affairs must come in. The
Minister of Home Affairs, in reply to a
question put by me yesterday, said they
were keeping their eyes very carefully
upon the problem, and if any indication
of distress was forthcoming they would
take some action. I asked him what was
the policy of the Government in regard
to these people, and he said their policy
remained unchanged; in other words, he
was going on as heretofore, despite the
fact that Part II will not be applied to
these people.
I wish to submit my views in no narrow,
cavilling spirit and with no desire to
besmirch the reputation of Northern
Ireland. That is not my purpose, because
I join with every other person in this
Committee in desiring Northern Ireland
to be the place it ought to be, one of the
brightest jewels in the whole community
of nations. I want to see Northern
Ireland governed and administered in
such a way that the humblest in the community, intellectually, can look up with.
pride to the community to which he
belongs in which is achieved the highest
standard of life. I have a sense of civic
and national pride, and I appeal to the
Parliamentary Secretary and to his Minister to take up the consideration of the
situation in Northern Ireland where, at
the present time, thousands of people in
the areas I have indicated are living a
very precarious and tragic life, and where
literally thousands of the dependants of
those adults are compelled to go without
sufficient food, and many are suffering
from malnutrition, which is depriving
them of taking full advantage and enjoyment of the education which is being
given to them under the Education Act
of Northern Ireland.
Those are aspects of the poverty
problem which press upon me spiritually
very heavily at the present time.
I
should like to have an assurance this
afternoon that before the Government
think of doing anything else in regard to
the tightening up of the conditions upon
any section of the community, that those
areas in Northern Ireland that have
damnably failed to do their duty,
whether through criminal neglect or
because they do not understand, which is
intellectual impotence, and indicates that
they ought not to be there, will have
overtures made to them by the Government to the end that we may remove this
cruel paradox in the year 1937, under
which hundreds of our people are being
insufficiently fed and badly clothed. That
is the tragedy of the poverty problem at
the present time.

Under the Act of Parliament we have
power to do something. If the local
elected authority does not do it the Minister knows what to do. When local
authorities in by-gone days prove recalcitrant from other points of view,
necessarily from that of poverty, the
Ministry of Home Affairs came down in
the exercise of their authority, and said
that as long as they would not conform
to the law the Ministry would be compelled to relieve them of some of their
responsibilties. I am not in favour of
dictatorships either from the Right or
from the Left. I believe in democratic
government, but nevertheless I believe
that when democracies, such as we have in
local authorities, deliberately or
ignorantly neglect the power a beneficent
State has vested in them, the time has
arrived when every right-thinking man
and woman should protest against the
perpetuation of the scandalous conditions.
revealed in those districts.

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask

to-day without the Government having
extended to the Members of this House
the usual courtesy of first making the
this House. The
announcement in
appointment of the Financial Secretary

officially notified to the House by the

the House the order of business for
Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday
next.
The PRIME MINISTER: I have not
seen the Press to which the hon. Member refers. With regard to the business
of the House for next week, on Tuesday
it is proposed to take the Committee
stage of the Horse Breeding Bill, the
Petroleum Bill, the Law Reform Bill,
and the Arbitration Bill, and, if time
is available, the Advertisements Regulation Bill; on Wednesday the Estimates
of the Ministry of Labour group; and on
Thursday the Ministry of Education
group.

did not read the Press.

say that. I said I had not seen the

was issued from Stormont Castle. The

wish to take this opportunity of congratulating the Member for Duncairn.

of police forces in all parts of the Empire

admit will probably never be excelled.
It will be one of the greatest parades that
have ever taken place in the British Empire, and for the Royal Ulster Constabulary, one of the most loyal forces serving
His Majesty the King, not to be recognised shows that there is something

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am
glad to hear the Member for Shankill
say these pleasant things about the police
force, but I think there is a certain
amount of misunderstanding in regard to
this matter. We are still part of the
United Kingdom. It is true that the
Dominions are sending detachments of
police and soldiers to represent their
particular Dominion at the Coronation,
but we are still part of the United Kingdom, and the arrangements for the
Coronation are such that they are not
drawing police either from Scotland or
this country. Personally, I would be
only too glad if our police force could be
represented, and I made representations
with the object of trying to ensure that
our force would be represented. Unfortunately, if they decided to invite a detachment of our police force they would also
have to draw police from Scotland and
Wales and other parts of the United
Kingdom.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of

Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order. This

some special arrangements ought to be

of men represented at the Coronation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: By leave of
the House I should like to say that
nothing would give me and other Members of the Government greater satisfaction than that the police should be
represented on this occasion, and I can
assure hon. Members that we have taken

from police forces in Scotland and other

up to the present time I have not been

but if we can arrange it even at this hour
nothing will give me greater pleasure.

1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether, in view of the

The MINISTER OF LABOUR
(Major Shillington) (who was received

CONDITIONS OF EMPLOYMENT
IN THE IRISH PEAT COMPANY.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the
wages paid and the hours worked by the
employees of the Irish Peat Company,
Derryane.
Major SHILLINGTON: I am sorry
I am not in a position to furnish the

UNINSURED ABLE-BODIED
UNEMPLOYED.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the
total number of able-bodied unemployed who are excluded from the
operations of the Unemployment Insurance Acts, and who will have
their claims considered under the Unemployment Assistance Board; whether
he can state the number of cases already
dealt with and the number allowed; and
whether upon this basis he can state
the total (approximate) number likely
to be taken over under Part II of the
Unemployment Assistance Act.
Major SHILLINGTON: It was only
on the Second Appointed Day, that is
to say, the 1st of this month, that the
Unemployment Assistance Scheme came
fully into operation, and up to the 23rd
April the total number of applications
received from persons who were outside
the scope of the Scheme before the
Second Appointed Day was 8,340. Of
these, 4,846 have been found to come
within the scope of the Scheme and
2,494 have been found to be outside its
scope, while about 1,000 applications are
still under consideration. Additional
applications are being received daily.
and it is, consequently, impossible to
state yet the total number of persons
likely to be taken over by the Unemployment Assistance Board. From the
figures I have given, however, it is
obvious that the number will be considerable, and as the majority of applicants have dependants, the total number
of persons who will benefit by the extension of the scheme will be very large.

PROTECTION OF "THE DAWN."
4. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is true that
police protection-day and night—had
to be provided in Enniskillen for a film
called "The Dawn"; whether he can
state who asked for the protection and
who will meet the cost, and whether this
film has already been exhibited in Northern Ireland; whether he can state the
names of the areas where it was shown,
and whether police protection had to be
provided in such cases.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): While the film to
which the hon. Member refers was being
exhibited in Enniskillen the police were
informed of a rumour that an attempt
might be made to steal the film, and in
these circumstances the police considered
it advisable to take precautions to ensure
that this did not take place. Apart
from this, no special protection was
afforded.
So far as I have been able to ascertain, this film has also been exhibited
at Cushendall, Newcastle, Downpatrick,
Strabane, and Londonderry. No police
protection was either sought or afforded
at any of these places.
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that there is no need
for police protection in Enniskillen for
the showing of a film dealing with
Ireland's fight for freedom; also that the
public of Enniskillen of all creeds and
classes believe in toleration, unlike the
public of Belfast, where civilisation has
no made such headway?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
must not take the opportunity to make
a speech.
FILM CENSORSHIP.
5. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether there are any
general rules governing film censorship
in Northern Ireland, or whether every
local authority is a law unto itself; and
whether, in view of the anomalies being
created by the unregulated use of the
power of censorship by various authorities, he will define the standards which
ought to be applied in considering films.
The following question also stood on
the Order Paper in the name of Mr.
Midgley:-
6. To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state why some films
made in Great Britain have been
banned, whilst other films of a
provocative nature have been exhibited
in various parts of Northern Ireland.
more
Sir DAWSON BATES: I propose,
with the hon. Member's permission, to
answer these two questions together.
A censorship of films is exercised by
the British Board of Film Censors
whose certificate embodies a classification
stating whether the film in question is
suitable for universal exhibtion or for
adult audiences only. Local authorities
have the power to refuse a licence to any
place of entertainment at which films
are exhibited which have not been passed
by the British Board of Censors.
In addition to this censorship, every
local authority has the right to refuse
to allow any film to be exhibited within
its area, even although such film may
have been passed by the British Board
of Film Censors. Parliament has given
a discretion to local authorites in this
matter, and each local authority uses
its discretion in what it considers to be
the best interests of its particular community. In the exercise of this discretion certain films have been banned
in Northern Ireland and other films
allowed to be exhibited, but I do not
think that the hon. Member would expect me to discover for him the reasons
for the actions of the local authorities
in this matter of film censorship.
As regards the general banning of
films, a regulation was made on 2nd
May, 1930, under the Civil Authorities
Act, empowering the civil authority to
make an Order prohibiting the possession or exhibition of any cinematograph
film. This regulation applies only in
the case of films which are considered
subversive of law and order.

HOME FOR ULSTER
EX-SERVICEMEN.
10. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister whether he intends to
have established in Northern Ireland a
home for Ulster ex-Servicemen similar to
the Chelsea Hospital in England.
The PRIME MINISTER: Chelsea is
open to qualified ex-Servicemen throughout the United Kingdom, including
Northern Ireland. A movement has been
afoot for some time past to start a home
here on somewhat similar lines, but as,
under the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, public funds cannot be made available for assisting such a project, it must
be established and maintained on a purely
voluntary basis; consequently, I have no
authority to answer questions in this
House as to what is being attempted by
private effort, but I will be glad to supply
the hon. Member with any information
in my possession if he will approach me
unofficially, and needless to say, if someone takes the initiative in establishing a
home of the kind in our midst, I will be
only too happy to render every support
and assistance in my power.
Mr. BEATTIE: When is the right
hon. Gentleman's pledge to provide a
home for ex-Servicemen, as a memorial to
the fallen in the Great War, to be put
into operation?
The PRIME MINISTER: I answered
that question of the hon. Member once
before, and I explained to him, as I do
to the House to-day, that I was speaking
entirely in my own private capacity.
Owing to the generosity of the Ulster
people there was raised a sum of £60,000,
and that was handed over to an organisation, a voluntary committee, which
is doing immense good for our ex-
Servicemen in our midst.
