ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Ancient Monuments Bill [S.].
Order for Second Reading read.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
was
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon) (who
received with general cheers): This Bill
is brought forward as an amendment of
the
Ancient Monuments Act of 1926,
and embodies administrative changes
which have been found desirable in
working the 1926 Act, and various
suggestions put forward in the interests
of learning by the Ancient Monuments
Advisory Committee. Very appropriately, it commences by recognising
the very extensive and valuable work
done by that body for the study and
the preservation of the antiquities of
Ulster, culminating in its completion of
an illustrated descriptive survey of all
the noteworthy antiquities of the
Province which will be published by this
Ministry shortly. This work was undertaken voluntarily, one may say
labour of love, by the Committee, under
the chairmanship of the Dean of Down,
and the extent of it may be judged from
the fact that the monuments to be
described will number nearly a
thousand. Therefore, though it may
only be small, recognition is given in
Clause 1. The title of the Committee is
to be changed to the "Ancient Monuments Advisory Council."
By the same Clause, permission is
taken to include in the Council curators
of approved museums in Northern Ireland. Where a well-conducted museum
exists, its curator is a most suitable
appointment for such a council, and we
may hope that before long each county
and considerable town in the Province
will have a
The
worthy museum.
curator of the Belfast museum, Mr.
Deane, has, from the outset, been a
valued member of the Committee, and
the House will be glad to hear that a
county museum, the first of its kind in
Ireland, is being opened to-morrow in
Armagh. From his previous work the
curator will be an extremely valuable
member of the Council, his appointment
to which will follow as a matter of course
on this Bill becoming law.
Turning to the Clauses of the Bill,
Clause 2 allows powers of entry to officers
or nominees of the Ministry of Finance
for
the purpose of inspection of
antiquities, subject to restrictions which
would prevent them being exercised in
an obnoxious manner. These powers are
necessary because it is conceivable that
an obstructive person on whose lands an
antiquity of very great importance was
discovered might, relying on his ownership, debar all access and deny information.
Clause 3 requires a person intending
to make archæological excavation to
1061 Ancient Monuments Bill-

27 APRIL 1937
Second Reading
obtain a licence for that purpose from
the Ministry of Finance. This is intended to prevent the ignorant amateur
or untrained excavator from ruining a
monument by ill-advised or ill-conducted
excavation, thus destroying its evidence
for all time.
Clause 4 has excited a little concern
in another place, and has received considerable amendment there. It takes the
place of Section 18 of the 1926 Act
which only required a report of
the circumstances of finding of an
archæological object. Now, deposit of
the find for not more than twenty-one
days with the secretary of the Ancient
Monuments Advisory Council, or with
a police officer, who would, of course, get
into touch with the secretary, is
required. The intention of this is to give
opportunity for proper examination of
the object, which may entail its submission to different experts and its inspection by local museums which may
wish to purchase. To prevent defeat of
the ends of the Clause by immediate
private sale, and consequent disappearance of the find, the Bill restricts
the finder from disposing of it and any
other person from obtaining possession of
it within twenty-one days.
the
I would like to explain to the House
that this Clause will operate to the benefit of the finder, who is often a simple
countryman, quite unaware of
nature or real value of his find, and only
too ready to dispose of it for a trifling
sum in ready cash to the first person that
offers, often a private collector or dealer.
In future if his find is worth purchase by
a museum, he will get a much fairer
price for it, and, if it is not, he will
be at liberty as before to make
what bargain he can, with the advantage that meantime he will have been
informed of the real nature of his discovery. This much outweighs the inconvenience of a short delay. The whole
purpose of the Clause is to ensure that
in the interests of science every
archæological find shall be adequately
reported and examined. To this the
Ancient Monuments Advisory Committee attaches the utmost importance.
The only person likely to be incommoded
is the less scrupulous kind of dealer or
collector, and with him the House will
have little or no sympathy.
Clause 5 enables the Ministry to assist
in the repair of monuments which are
not in its own custody. The purpose of
this section is to encourage private
owners to repair structures which,
though often of considerable local interest, are not sufficiently noteworthy to
merit their maintenance by the State. A
private owner or local antiquarian
society might often undertake such work
if the burden of the cost was alleviated
to some degree. I may add that, under
the Act of 1926, the Ministry is able to
give skilled technical advice in such cases
and there seems to be an increasing
desire on the part of owners to avail
themselves of it.
Clause 6 merely allows a monument to
be transferred from the Ministry to a
county council. Under existing legislation, transfer is only permissible in a
contrary direction. The Ministry looks
forward to a time when, as in other
countries, local authorities will take a
pride and delight in maintaining many
such structures.
Clause 7 enables the Ministry to erect
a sign giving some description of a monument which, though still remaining in
private custody, has been scheduled under
the 1926 Act as being of national interest. It has been found in the case of
the monuments which are in its com..
plete charge or ownership that the
erection of such descriptive tablets is
much more effective in securing a respect
for the structure than putting into force.
penalties. Though held in reserve as a
means of dealing with the destruction
the Ministry is always reluctant to
exercise these powers. Often, for
instance, when the country people know
that what they have always thought was
a heap of old stones is classified and
recorded as an elaborately constructed
monumental grave some 4,000 years old
it will be regarded locally with quite
other eyes and safeguarded from
ignorant destruction. Such a result is
well worth the two or three pounds
which it costs to erect a descriptive
tablet.
Clause 8 is a mere matter of
machinery.
Though some of the provisions of this
Bill may seem somewhat novel the House
can be assured that similar enactments
will be found in the legislation of the

As an illustration of how material of

us, I have in mind the ancient castle of
Con O'Neill at Castlereagh, the site of
which is within sight of this Parliament
House. It is said that some worthy
people, wishing to preserve the ruins of
the castle, which contained many fine
beams of Irish red oak and other relics,
took steps to have a wall built round the
site. Legend recounts that a wall to
enclose the castle, and to keep it from
further harm, was built from the stones
of the ruin itself. To-day no trace of
the castle exists. The site is known
only by the wall and the group of trees
forming a conspicuous landmark that
can be seen from many parts of the city.
I think the site is worthy of a notice
giving a description of the castle, and I
hope steps will be taken to provide one.
I mention this merely to show the great
advantage that the Ancient Monuments
Act can exercise in preserving antiquarian objects from the hands of the
vandal.

occasion. He went out to-day when I
spoke about the Pope's picture, but he
would not be missing on that day.
There is another thing you might get,
and that is the Mountjoy, the boat used
for the gun-running. I do not suppose
she is in commission now. You will
recollect that in England they had the
Nelson's flagship. If they can have that
ship, why shouldn't we have the Mountjoy?
Mr. MIDGLEY: And the Lady
Hamilton picture.
Mr. NIXON: We owe our position
here to the gun-running exploit. I am
very sorry that two Protestants in my
constituency lie in jail for having a little
handful of ammunition, some of which
was brought here in the Mountjoy. They
got three years for a handful of ammunition and the people who got the whole
cargo got seats here for sixteen years.
The thing did not work out equitably
somehow or other. It did not work out
satisfactorily for everybody.
But notwithstanding all that the
Mountjoy in years to come would be a
relic of great history in Northern Ireland
and elsewhere, and there might come a
time when a future generation would look
on it in that way. That is the way at
the present time a good lot of trophies in
our great museums in London, that were
taken in battle on the Continent from
enemies, are looked upon. People from
those countries can come forward and
have a look at them and enjoy them. If
we had the statue of King William and
the Mountjoy to commence with we would
have a good foundation and a good start
in connection with something to preserve.
But I do not by any means recommend
the retention of the Pope's picture. It
occupies a room in this House, and for
more reasons than one I do not recommend its retention. As a matter of fact,
no plaster ever fell from the ceilings of
this House till you had it, and it will
never keep from falling until you get
rid of the picture. I know that, so, as I
said before, get the Free State Government to give you the statue of King
William and let them have the Pope's
picture with all its nasty commercial and
other implications.
1073 Ancient Monuments Bill-

27 APRIL 1937
Law Reform Bill
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON (by leave of
the House): In replying to the debate on
this Bill may I start with saying "thank
you" for the personal references made by
Members to me when I first stood up.
As regards the remarks of the hon. Member for Fermanagh, I should like to say
for his information that lectures are given
on these antiquities and archæological
subjects in Stranmillis and also in St.
Mary's for the instruction of pupils there,
and other people can attend. With
reference to the remarks of the hon. Member for St. Anne's, I might mention that
in the original Bill there is a Clause which
says if any interference takes place with
somebody's land compensation is to be
paid. That is carried forward in this
Bill. As to the O'Neill Castle at Castlereagh, Members will see that the Clauses
of this Bill are exactly to stop what
happened there. I think the House
knows what happened there. The O'Neill
of the day wrote to the agent and asked
him to erect a wall around the castle at
Castlereagh to preserve it from being
pulled down. What the agent did was
to pull down the castle and build a wall
out of the ruins of the castle. The Bill
is to try to stop that sort of thing-unauthorised, ignorant destruction of
ancient monuments.
The hon. Lady for South Derry made a
speech which showed a great deal more
knowledge than I have of this matter.
What she said is quite right, that this
Bill is based on the experience gained in
the working of the past Act to prevent
unlettered and untutored excavation.
The idea is that the people who want to
excavate must obtain licences so that they
may not do any harm, and the Clause
which allows the ancient monuments to
be transferred from the Ministry to the
county councils is one which is intended
to stimulate the interest of those in
authority in the counties in this matter.
I hope this will help in that way.
As regards the remarks of the hon.
Member for Woodvale, I would like to say
that any expenditure under this Bill will
be accounted for in the normal, usual way
before the Public Accounts Committee,
and as far as I am aware the Bill proposes no posts or appointments or what
he calls jobs. I must thank the House for
their reception given to this Bill on its
Second Reading.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I tried to

which was passed by the Imperial Parliament-control in regard to advertisements the railway companies took care
to ensure that all advertisements
erected on their premises were of a proper

objected during all these years to anything that is done by the railway companies in regard to the erection of
advertisements. If anybody had suffered

erected the railway company is in a position to pay. I am sorry to have to say
that although under the 1905 Act the
local authorities here had powers to make
bylaws they did not exercise the rights
they had. On the one side we had the
railway companies apparently exercising
care and precautions, and on the other
side the local authorities not doing so.
I only hope as a result of this Bill which
gives still wider powers that the local
authorities will exercise the powers that
are conferred on them by it. It would
be a most ungracious and unnecessary

hope when this Bill comes into operation
the local authorities will at least exercise

exercised without being compelled to
do so.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR
(Major Shillington): In rising to present the Estimates of the Ministry to
which I have SO very recently been
appointed, I am sure I shall have the
sympathy of every Member of this
House. May I also crave the indulgence
of the House for a few moments to refer
to one or two matters which, while not
directly concerned with the Estimates
we are about to consider, have led up
to my finding myself in this position?
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Shillington]
I am glad to have this opportunity
of joining with others in paying a
tribute to the memory of Mr. Pollock.
First, speaking as one who has had the
privilege of being a Member of this
House since our Parliament was established it is difficult to find words to
express my admiration for the manner
in which he carried out his very arduous
duties. Secondly, may I pay a tribute
as an ex-Serviceman. My last close
connection with Mr. Pollock was a comparatively short time before his death,
when he presided at a meeting of the
Thiepval War Memorial Committee, of
which I have the honour to be a member. The interest Mr. Pollock took in
this memorial will never be forgotten by
the ex-Servicemen of Ulster or their
dependants and relatives. Ex-Servicemen will remember with gratitude the
legislation which Mr. Pollock introduced and passed through this House
to ensure beyond any doubt that this
memorial to the memory of the fallen
sons of Ulster should be preserved for
all time in that manner which they
would wish. They also appreciate the
leading part he took in securing, in
regard to the Government Services, that
as much employment as possible should
be found for those men who served
their country and were unable to get
into
suitable occupations on their
return to civil life.
And now I should like to say something about my predecessor. I have
been asked to step into the place of one
who has had the unrivalled experience
of, I may say, laying the keel of the
Ministry of Labour and of navigating
the ship for 16 long and arduous years.
We have all admired the sagacity and
courage he has shown. But there are
two qualities in his administration that
particularly impressed us on the Back
Benches. First, there was the constancy
with which he held fast unfalteringly
to the course of complete equality of
social standards throughout the United
Kingdom. The wisdom of this course is
unchallengeable. It has enabled us to
weather the heaviest seas. So long as
I have the honour to stand at the helm
of the Ministry of Labour I will hold
as firmly to that course as did my predecessor. Secondly, we Back Benchers
came to see very clearly that the motive
underlying the administration of the
Ministry of Labour, and the principle
actuating not only the Minister but the
whole staff, was sympathy with the men
and women of our Province, to serve
whom the Ministry exists. I would like
to assure hon. Members that it is my
chief desire that this sympathetic consideration should continue to be the
mainspring of the administration.
In this great new task I am
glad to know that I shall have
the unfailing support and unstinted cooperation of my old friend, the Parliamentary Secretary. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I am happy to have him
with me as an honoured colleague. His
experience, I realise, will be invaluable
and I am reassured by knowing that our
desires and aims as regards the administration of the Department are identical.
I am looking forward to a happy partnership with him, and between us we
will do our best to carry on the
traditions that my right hon. Friend,
who is now Minister of Finance, has
created for the Ministry of Labour.
Hon Members will recall that they
have had the advantage in previous years
of hearing a very explicit and interesting survey of the many activities of
the Ministry of Labour by my predecessor. These surveys were so clear and
comprehensive that I feel there is no
necessity for me on this occasion to go
into matters so fully, nor do I think
that hon. Members would expect me to
do so, as I have not had the opportunity
to make myself personally acquainted
with all these difficult and complicated
are, however,
some
matters. There
points to which I must refer. In the
first place I would like to say that I
think one of the most important services
that the Ministry can render and is
rendering to the public is the preservation and fostering of good relations
between employers and their workers.
One of the foundations of our social
structure is economic stability, and to
secure this it is essential that there
should be freedom from the dislocation
caused by trade disputes.
I think it is a great advantage. to us
in Northern Ireland that we are a compact community, and that in general
employers and workers here stand in a
closer relationship than is perhaps possible elsewhere. In consequence, when
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
28 APRIL 1937
differences arise, as they inevitably do
in all human affairs, the spokesmen on
either side can meet as neighbours who
can appreciate each other's qualities and
difficulties. Mutual consideration of the
other viewpoint makes the adjustment of
questions at issue so much the easier. In
the past, both sides have shown a degree
of reasonableness and commonsense and
good feeling that is most creditable, and
I have every reason to believe that this
attitude will endure. It is to this cause,
I think, we can attribute our happy
immunity from serious industrial trouble.
I would like to assure hon. Members and
the public whom they represent that it
will be the constant endeavour of myself as Minister and of the staff of my
Department to place, as heretofore,
freely and frankly at the disposal of all
concerned our experience and facilities
for helping employers and trade unions
to maintain the reputation of Northern
Ireland for good and harmonious
relations in industry. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Next, I would like to refer to the
employment situation. The turn of the
year, as usual, showed a high figure of
registrations at the
the employment exchanges. The volume of employment
had lessened as the orders for the
Christmas trade had been worked off,
and there was the usual seasonal
diminution of occupations out-of-doors.
At the same time it must be remembered
that registration is much more complete
than ever it has been-the inclusion of
juveniles in insurance, and the bringing
into operation of agricultural insurance
and unemployment assistance have all
led more people to register at the exchanges. For three months in succession.
now, however, I am glad to say that
the number of persons registered has
fallen, the total on the 19th April being
4,359 less than it was in March. The
wholly unemployed figure is 65,622, and
the total of temporarily stopped and
casually unemployed persons has fallen
to 5,643.
The improvement has taken place in
every exchange area save three, and is due
to resumption of work in all outdoor
occupations and in farming, and to
increased employment in the shipyards
and the linen and making-up trades.
think it should be constantly borne in
mind that a large number of those who
register are not permanently out of work
-their periods of unemployment are
relatively short-and there is a constant
turn-over throughout the months.
For some years now there has been a
steady increase in the number of persons
for whom our industries are finding employment. This is proved conclusively by
the regular growth of the contribution
income, not only of the Unemployment
Fund, but of the Health Insurance and
Pensions Funds as well. The estimated
average number of those employed in the
industries insured under the general unemployment insurance scheme has risen
year by year from 181,000 in 1933 to
about 206,000 to-day. In addition, of
course, there are those employed in agriculture and in occupations outside the
unemployment insurance scheme, but
insured under the health and pensions
schemes.
Our industrial employers are not unready or unwilling to embark on new
enterprises when opportunity arises. The
new aeroplane factory of Messrs. Short &
Harland is a case in point, and there are
other examples. Thus, Harland & Wolff
are developing their steel girder and
locomotive branches; the spinning of
woollen yarns for carpet manufacture has
commenced at Newry; a new dyeworks has
begun operations at Kilbroney; biscuit
manufacture is progressing; a fertiliser
works has just started outside Lisburn;
two new firms have opened up as manufacturing chemists; and we all wish sucto the new furniture factory at
Glenarm. It may be said that some of
these new ventures may not at present
give much employment, but every venture
must have a beginning.
cess
To give further encouragement to local
authorities and public bodies to undertake useful schemes which will give employment, the Ministry has recently
increased the rates of grant from the Unemployment Relief Vote to 75 per cent. of
the wages of men engaged through the
exchanges. I am glad to say a number of
schemes, which will give valuable employment and prove of lasting benefit to the
community, have recently been approved.
At the same time, I am looking forward
to a considerable extension of the
facilities for useful instruction to young
people when they are out of work. A
representative committee, under the able
Estimates--
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
on
[Major Shillington]
chairmanship of the Vice-Chancellor of
Queen's University, is engaged
examining this question, and I hope to
have its report before many weeks are
past. The needs of those of maturer
years are also not being overlooked, and I
would like to express my indebtedness to
the technical education authorities for the
assistance they have been giving the
Department and the unemployed.
example, in Belfast the Technical College
has provided instruction in working from
blue prints and in the use of micrometers
and vernier gauges to unemployed fitters,
and this instruction has been of real value
to the men in securing employment.
For
Turning to the insurance schemes, the
unemployment scheme continues to show
the advantages derived from its reconstruction by the Unemployment Act of
1934, and its linking up with the Great
Britain scheme through the Reinsurance
Agreement. As a result it was possible
to reduce the rates of contribution as from
July, 1936, and last month to halve the
"waiting" period. Moreover, we have
been able to increase the number of
additional days of benefit for which those
with good industrial records may qualify.
The agricultural insurance scheme
began last May, and it was extended to
include private gardeners in February.
Altogether, some
some 27,000 workers are
insured under this scheme, and benefits
amounting to £36,000 have been paid up
to 16th April.
There have been two important developments in unemployment assistance, as
hon. Members know. In November last
the new assistance regulations came into
force. They have raised some of the standard allowances, simplified and improved
the procedure for dealing with rents, and
increased the amounts of earnings which
may be allowed for personal requirements
in taking account of available resources.
In April, 1936, there were some 18,700
persons receiving almost £21,000 a week.
In March, 1937, the number has grown
to about 22,800 and the amount to
£27,000 a week. The total sum paid in
allowances during the year was over
£1,125,000.
The second part of the scheme began to
operate at the beginning of this financial
year, and the effect of the enlarged scope
of this service can best be shown by the
fact that the number of applications.
authorised for allowances has grown from
22,800 before the Second Appointed Day
to over 27,600 on the 17th of this month.
To give advice and assistance in the
administration, the Unemployment Assistance Board has established nine advisory
committees, and I understand the Board
are confident that these committees, composed of those who are familiar with the
conditions prevalent in their areas, will be
of great help.
Of the two pensions schemes I need
only say that the number of those who are
assisted by them continues to grow. It is
now 96,140.
I would like to say a little more, however, about national health insurance.
The unemployment arrears scheme, with
which we are in a common pool with Great
Britain, and which allows full excusal of
arrears of contributions due to unemployment, and thereby secures full rates of
cash benefits, is proving of great value to
insured persons in times of illness. Even
more important in my opinion, however,
than the cash payments is the provision of
medical treatment. Almost 386,000
people are entitled to medical attention,
and about 520 doctors are co-operating
with the Department in this service. I
would like to pay a tribute to the conscientious way in which the medical profession is helping in this matter. May I
quote from a letter recently sent to the
Ministry:
"I am writing these lines regarding
the attention of two insurance doctors.
My father was faithfully and wonderfully attended by them. He had been
on.
ailing for four years with a serious
disease, yet these doctors never
grumbled at how often they were called
Father could not have got better
attention had he been paying heavy
fees." (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Before I pass from this subject I must
refer to a very helpful report on the
development of the arrangements for the
visiting of insured persons in times of

The other services for which the Ministry is responsible-its industrial conciliation activities, the administration of the
Factory and Workshop Code, the Trade
Boards, the administration and audit of
public utility schemes, etc.—will cost, it
is estimated, about £9,400.
The recent committee has
worked out a plan for including Belfast,
and I shall recommend the acceptance of
these proposals to the National Health
Insurance Joint Committee, which, as the
Committee is aware, is the body responsible for the co-ordination of health
insurance in the United Kingdom, and
for the supervision of societies which have

are concerned with National Health
Insurance will wish, I am sure, to join
me in thanking and congratulating my
hon. Friend on the outcome of the committee's deliberations. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
If Members will please turn to page
86 of the book of Estimates they will see
a summary there of the total amount required for the Ministry of Labour during
the current financial year. As regards
Vote 1, which is the one that the Committee is now considering, it will be
observed that the net Vote shows a
decrease of £170 on last year's estimate.
The gross Vote is £11,778 higher, due to
the necessity for increased provision for
temporary staff in consequence of the
operation for a complete year of both the
agricultural insurance scheme and the full
unemployment assistance scheme. These
increases, however, are more than offset by
the higher appropriations-in-aid. I feel
that I need not detain the Committee at
this stage by going over the details of the
other Votes, which will come up for consideration in due course.
It is estimated that this year the
amount that will be paid out in benefits
of all kinds under the five social services
for which the Ministry is responsible will
be about six million pounds-to be more
accurate £5,990,000. No portion of this
great sum will be diverted from benefits
to administrative expenditure. The cost
of administering these services, including
the cost of the Ministry of Labour, the
Unemployment Assistance Board, other
Government Departments such as the Post
Office and the Works Service, the
approved societies and all the other bodies.
which take their part in the administration will be about 7.5 per cent (£450,000)
of the expenditure on benefits. I am glad
to say this is a lower proportion even than
last year. It should be borne in mind
too that the administration of the social
services is not merely a matter of the disbursement of money, but necessitates
I think hon. Members may conclude
from these figures that these great services
for the benefit of the people of Northern
Ireland are being administered with every
regard to economy.
But, whilst the observance of economy
is of the highest importance, hon. Members and the public have the right to
expect that the administration should
also be sympathetic and considerate. As
a private Member I have had long experience of finding that these services are
administered sympathetically, and I have
no doubt that my experience has been
shared by very many.
The provisions
laid down by Parliament itself must be
observed, but, subject to statutory requirements which are binding on the
Ministry as well as on the public, the law
is carried out, I believe, with the fullest
regard to these other aspects.
I had a striking illustration of this a
few days ago, before I had the honour to
become Minister. It was my duty, as a
member of a Civil Service Board, to interview candidates for permanent appointments, following an open competitive
examination. One of the candidates had
but a few weeks before secured a temporary engagement in an employment
exchange. Her duties, she told us, were
connected with applications for unemployment assistance. She was asked how
long it took to deal with an application.
She said that it depended on circumstances, but individual applications might
take as long as twenty or thirty minutes
to complete. She explained that this was
because it was desired to give applicants
every assistance to show that the necessary
conditions were satisfied. She was asked
what she regarded as the most important
qualification for her duties. Her reply
was most significant-patience.
Twenty or thirty minutes for a single
application-what a waste of time, may
say the rigid economist, and time means
money. But these minutes may mean a
world of difference to an unhappy man or
S
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Shillington]
woman, out of work and in misfortune,
and its value cannot be expressed in the
terms of a balance sheet.
If a new recruit to the Department,
holding a very junior post, can feel so
soon that the essential need for her work
is patience and consideration for those
who require help, I leave it to hon. Members to realise that this spirit must permeate the service and influence their
whole outlook. It is the attitude we all
want to encourage.
It is the one my
right hon. Friend, the first Minister of
Labour, has done so much to establish.
It is the one I shall endeavour constantly
to make my own. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Now I come to two matters which I
approach with more confidence and with
particular pleasure. I am glad to have
this early opportunity of expressing my
thanks to all those men and women
throughout Northern Ireland who have
given such valuable public service voluntarily to my Ministry. They have
sacrificed time and trouble in acting on the
numerous committees connected with the
work of the Department. I can speak
with a certain amount of personal experience in regard to this matter, as it
was my privilege at different times since
our Parliament was set up to act myself
on some of these committees. I need not
refer to all these bodies by name, but
hon. Members may be interested to know
that those I have in mind are the local
employment committees, the King's
National Roll Committee, the Belfast
Juvenile Advisory Committee, the
Medical Benefit Council and the several
committees connected with medical
benefit, the Dental Benefit Council and its
reference committees, the members of the
panels of courts of referees and local
pension courts, and the advisory committees connected with the Unemployment Assistance Board. The members of
these committees deserve the respect and
thanks of the whole community, and I
trust we shall never be wanting in securing the co-operation and assistance of
members of the public, ready to help to
make the work of the Ministry run so
much more smoothly.
Now I come to the second point. I
have no false ideas of the magnitude of
the duties of the post to which I have
been appointed. I am approaching them,
however, with more confidence by the
knowledge that I am taking over a
Department which is manned by a staff
which has already won the confidence of
our people in Northern Ireland. As a
back bencher I think I can say I came
more in touch with the staff of the Ministry of Labour than with that of any other
Department, and in all matters that I
had to bring before them I was always
met with the greatest possible courtesy
and consideration, and I am confident
that this is the experience of every Member of this Committee.
By the kindness of my predecessor I
have had the privilege of being with him
when he paid his official farewell to the
permanent head of his Department, and
a number of his principal officers. I am
happy to think that I have enjoyed the
friendship of the present Permanent
Secretary of my Department since it was
established some sixteen years ago, and
who has since then given of his best to the
work of the Ministry of Labour.
I could easily realise the feeling of these
officers in saying "Good-bye" to a chief
whom they had learned not only to respect
but to esteem, but I am satisfied from
what I know of them that they will be
only too anxious to give the same loyal
and devoted service to anyone who is
appointed to the important post of
Minister of Labour. I hope by the
manner in which I carry out my duties
that I will, in course of time, come to
secure at least some degree of that affection which I know they had for my predecessor in this office.
As I started on a more or less personal
note, may I be permitted to end in a
similar way.
I have already asked for
your sympathy; this, and also your
patience, I hope will be extended to me
for some time until I become more
acquainted with the details of my duties.
I have always liked to have my time fully
occupied, either at work or at play. I
am quite willing that there should not be
much of the latter for some little time,
and so I have no qualms about the work
in connection with the ordinary routine
duties of my office. But I must be quite
frank with the Members of the Committee, and say that it is not altogether
with equanimity that I am looking forward to what I saw was recently described
as the "rough and tumble" of the House
of Commons. However, I am sure that

disease or the complaint may have made

one.
I hope that the Minister and those

heard it asserted by medical men in the

pronouncement ought to be made by the

I wish now to direct attention to the
question of unemployment. I hope that
all you people who believe that unemployment can be cured within the ambit
of the capitalist system will listen to
this. On the unemployed register at the
present time we have, according to the
Minister, 65,622 persons, to which must
be added for calculation purposes the
people who are employed only for part of
the time or for a short period, 5,643,
making a total at the particular date
mentioned by the Minister of over
71,000 persons registered as unemployed
in Northern Ireland. What have I got
to say about that? Only this. I do not
expect anything nowadays but a kind of
stability in unemployment. It is the
most stable thing we have in life under
existing conditions. There is nothing so
firmly set or fixed as the continuous unemployed problem. After sixteen years
you have to face up to a position in
which there are over 70,000 persons unemployed, many of whom will not come
into contact with the beneficence of your
social scheme for unemployment in any
of its phases, many of whom are destined
to be shut out from unemployment benefit and Part II of the Unemployment
Act.
You have got to face up to the fact
that there is a large problem of poverty
and unemployment in Northern Ireland
at the present time. I hope that people
will get away from believing that I am
trying to besmirch the fair name and
reputation of Northern Ireland. Personally I can give the House the
assurance that I desire to uphold the
dignity and reputation of Northern Ireland as far as I possibly can. I draw
attention to the question of poverty and
destitution in Northern Ireland because
I think it is better to do so. It is better
that you should know of the ramifications
of the social evils that exist in your
midst, and thus be able to do something
for them. The Minister will have to
give his attention to this matter in conjunction with the Minister of Home
Affairs and, as I will indicate later, the
Minister of Agriculture. There is
scarcely a problem affecting the Ministry
of Labour which does not either directly
or indirectly affect the Ministry of Home
Affairs or the Ministry of Agriculture in
some way or other, as some of the services are concomitant or coincident.
I wish to point out that the Minister
of Home Affairs stated this week in reply
to a question that unemployed persons
in Northern Ireland, who are shut out
from Part II. of the Unemployment Act,
have the right to get outdoor relief even
if they are able-bodied unemployed persons. I do not think that the right hon.
Gentleman meant to mislead the House,
but he certainly did succeed in misleading some people, and in creating the
impression I have indicated. That statement was wrong. There are only three

places, so far as I know, in the North

British Press and from some of the

I state that in that way in order to

about half-a-dozen are already blushing

unemployed permanently in the sense.
of statistics. It does not matter whether

So they are, if they only knew it. How

year? You speak of the unemployed in
the same way as you would ask a man
in the wholesale drapery trade how often
he turns over his stock in the year.
We have the Minister's assurance that
there are 65,000 permanently unemployed people, and although the personnel may change to the extent of a
few thousands, so far as I can see, even
under improved conditions, there will be
a large permanent body of unemployed.
What are you going to do? As long as
you are content to believe that this old
system is the best of all possible systems,
and that it has been definitely ordained
by the Lord that this system should prevail, you are going to have no fundamental change. But, if you really believe earnestly that you ought to try to
deal earnestly with the unemployment
problem from the point of view of
making as many as possible of the 65,000
potential wealth earners for the community, you should ask yourselves what
is standing in the way of your doing
that. If you approach the question
from that angle you will find that those
people are unemployed because it is not
profitable within the existing order of
things to employ them. In order to
employ them you must change the
structure of society from the so-called
competitive basis to the collectivist basis.
I put it no more strongly than that.
So long as you are content to pay out
money under the Ministry of Labour
Estimates for the maintenance of a permanent army of unemployed, you may as
well face up to it, and tell the people
quite frankly at the
the next General
Election, that it is impossible to solve
the problem in the existing social order.
That is what it amounts to if you are
to be frankly and completely honest
with the electorate. The Minister,
although I know he understands this just
as well as I do, is like the rest of the
Front Bench, hidebound by tradition; he
is tied to the chariot wheels of the old
social standards and he cannot get away
from them. But a new generation, even
in his own family, just as in the family
of the Imperial Prime Minister, may
break with tradition and try to bring
about social changes. We are waiting
on those changes being brought about.
I want to ask the Minister to consider

Affairs, so as to ensure that not one
man or one woman in Northern Ireland
should be denied access to a certain
amount of income per week. Why
should they be? If any man or woman
in Northern Ireland is willing to work,

access to a certain standard of income?
If they offer their services and they cannot be put to work they have no right
to be denied an income. When you deny
a man or woman an income you deny
them a share in the national wealth of
the country. The national wealth
ought to be enjoyed. On the basis of
the figures given yesterday in reply to

to be taken over under Part II-the

The Minister of Labour this afternoon
drew attention to the total cost of the
social services and gave the amount this
year as £5,990,000, almost £6,000,000.
The cost of administration is £450,000
or 7.5 per cent. I wish to draw the attention of the House and the people of
Northern Ireland to this problem, and
to ask them to look upon this not from
a
narrow political point of view but

there is not, and that a great deal of the
talk indulged in by people nowadays, no

speaking, what the Yankees call ballyhoo-so much trash to mislead the
people. Our social services both from

point of view have been built up on a

the present in a way that reflects great

Civil Service.
I take courage from that to hope and
believe that what is being done in regard

Acts, under Part 2, what is being done in

With an extension of these things, and
with good administration, we can bring
better security to our country and greater
economic joy and hope to the people.
I trust the Minister will keep in mind
the question of pensions, and that he
will not be satisfied with saying that we

standard all the time. The British
standard is a good standard, but I hope

an age in which it has become harder for
widows and old-age pensioners to exist
than at any time within the last two

The Cabinet is not tackling the job,

The proportion of unemployment in
Northern Ireland is higher than any

Mr. NIXON- -would never rest until

thousands of families whose only prospect

unemployment is worse in no part of the

Distress, when it is brought about by unemployment, over which the people have
no control, is something for which they

The proportion of unemployment here is

Kingdom, and altogether more than 25

Everybody knows now that the Government made no effort to press their claims
on the British Government for some of

There they are getting it in areas which

There is only one area worse, South

It is very easy to move from one part of

They tell us about the Loans Guarantee Act. I never belittled that Act, but
we got orders in the shipyards before that
Act was passed. That Act, like some
other things, is very much misunderstood.
There are people who actually think that
it gives a grant or subsidy for shipbuilding. It does not do that. It is only a
guarantee to the bank advancing the
money that if the company for whom the
ship was built did not pay the Northern
Government would pay. I do not object
to that; I supported it. It has been useful. Money has been guaranteed which
will never be recovered, but you must
take a risk. If you had not taken a risk
I suppose I would have attacked you for
it. But you did take the risk. You had
to pay something, and you may have to
pay more, but I would support you again.
But do not make too much of it, because
there are any number of firms building
ships without it.
I may tell you
that the late Minister of

gives an opportunity of raising some

have been raised to-day which I am

I would like to make a few observations

am a minister in another sense, and I

It is a matter of great gratification to
everyone, or ought to be, that there is
such a Ministry in Northern Ireland,
and that this Ministry has at its disposal such a vast sum of money to dispense every year for the alleviation of
need, for bringing opportunities
recovery of health to those who are in
sickness, and to enable them to tide over
periods of anxiety. It is a tremendous
fact that sometimes we forget that thirty
years ago none of this money was available, and that at the present time we
in this small area have at our disposal
every year about £6,000,000 for social
services. It does not need very much
calculation to indicate what that means;
that this Ministry, on the average, is
able to disburse every week for the social
wellbeing of the people the tremendous
sum of about £100,000. I think that is
a matter on which we should all congratulate ourselves; that our Christian
community is in this way expressing
genuine Christian sentiments and is
administering Christian love in a
moderate and effective way by putting
at the disposal of this Ministry such a
tremendous sum of money from the
Exchequer every year.
The Minister of Labour is in a very
happy position to-day inasmuch as
practically no criticism at all has been
directed towards the way he and his
predecessor have administered the Department for which they were responsible. There have, however, been
questions of policy raised, and it has
been suggested that the Ministry might
do a great deal more. Much of the
criticism directed towards the Ministry
of Labour comes chiefly from two
directions. Hon. Members opposite
generally suggest that the Ministry does
not go far enough; that they ought to
spend a great deal more money; and
that, indeed, they ought to go beyond
the pace that is being set on the other
side of the channel. They suggest that
it is not enough to keep step by step
with Great Britain. The Ministry
think, and I agree with them, that we
in Northern Ireland, being a comparatively poorer area than England, are
doing well to take advantage of the
social services on the other side of the
channel, and that we should do our very
best to live up to the social services
which they have discovered to be
practicable for them.
Estimates
Ministry of Labour
28 APRIL 1937
May I remind Members that this policy
will this year mean that our unemployed
will have available for them about
£1,000,000 more than they otherwise could claim by reason of
the arrangement made by the Ministry
of Labour with the Government in
England in regard to balancing the
account. That is one amongst other
advantages which we in this area enjoy
from this policy of keeping in step with
the Government at Westminster in regard to the social services.
It has been said, and said with truth,
that this Ministry has not succeeded in
solving the problem of unemployment in
Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland,
and Belfast in particular, has been unfortunate perhaps in having concentrated its efforts on two great industries,
the linen and shipbuilding industries.
During the depression both these
industries, being dependent on foreign
trade for their prosperity, were hit with
great severity, and it has not been possible yet for this area to recover the
position which it occupied before this
depression set in. I am afraid it will
be a considerable time before the unemployed are absorbed in industry again in
Northern Ireland, but I am quite sure
that we have very able men in the
Cabinet who are doing their very best to
bring new industries to this Province,
and to see that as many as possible of
our
unemployed are absorbed into
industry. I consider the Prime Minister a very able negotiator, and I do not
know that anyone could do more than he
has done in the way of winning advantages for the people of Ulster, whom he
lores so well.
There is another direction from which
criticism is hurled at the Ministry. It
is said, on the one hand, that they do
not spend enough money, and, on the
other hand, it is said from outside
sources that they spend too much. The
question is sometimes asked, "Where is
it going to end? We are spending
£6,000,000 a year on social services, and
that cannot go on for ever.' I have no
fears in that direction. I have come to
the conclusion that it is part of the
nature of the system of industry under
which we work that a great deal of the
wealth consumed must, for the stability
of the system, be consumed as it is produced. The great defect of our system
in the past, so I am told, has been that
consumption did not at all come up to
the standard which was necessary to
secure the stability of the system.
an
Perhaps you will allow me to use an
illustration. There is a little device
known as a gyroscope which is used at
the launching of ships. It has a number
of weighted wheels which are made to
rotate rapidly, and by rotating rapidly
they are able to keep the ship on
even keel as it slides down the slip
towards the water. In industry we
require an even keel, and if on the one
hand too much is spent the ship of State
will tend to diverge. If, on the other
hand, too much is saved you will have
disaster in another direction. Our
system of private enterprise has tended
to the accumulation of too large amounts
of savings, with the consequent slumps
and unemployment. I know this is
rather remote from the subject, but perhaps you will allow me to say this. I
observed in a letter to "The Times,"
which came to hand to-day, figures
which are very interesting in this connection.
The CHAIRMAN: I do not think I

Professor CORKEY: I do
not think it necessary to pin my faith
to any particular system for the solution.
of this problem of unemployment. We
are at the moment operating within our

systems. We have our Electricity
Board, and nothing can be more akin

time we have in our hands a Bill for

system as we have it to-dav has in it
the elements of all systems, and it would
seem to me to be the wise thing to experiment along the various lines for the

maintaining so far as we can the advantages of individual initiative and private
enterprise so far as they are wholesome

and good, and adopting other systems in

In regard to the means test I would

There are just two other observations

favour of the applicant. It is quite

The only other observation I want to

sure hon. Members
understand that this question of unemployment affects the whole Province. It
affects not merely the city of Belfast;

can only say this, while I understand

Mr. BYRNE: I should like to join
in the congratulations that have been
extended to the new Minister of Labour.
Every Member of this House congratulates him, and will give him his
entire support. I should also like to
refer to the former Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews). I am one of those
people who are mixed up a good deal
with the working people. It was my
duty on many occasions to approach the
right hon. Gentleman and I always
found him very kind and considerate. I
should also like to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Labour (Mr. Gordon), and I am sure he
will give the new Minister of Labour the
cordial support that he gave the former
occupant of that office. As one who
represents a working-class constituency,
I know the responsibilities which the
new
Minister has assumed, and I
sincerely hope that during his term of
office a great industrial improvement will
take place, in order that the very large
number of unemployed persons will be
reduced. It is a very serious matter that
there are 70,000 unemployed people in
this area.
I should also like to refer to Part II
of the Unemployment Act which came
into operation on 1st April, and to say
how very much disappointed I have been
to find that many hundreds of people are
outside its scope. I understood-it was
reported that when Part II of the Act
came into operation any person who was
ready and willing to work, and could not
get work, would be given unemployment
assistance. It has been my duty to
attend at the Employment Exchange as
the nominee of some of the applicants,
and I was very much disappointed to
find a large number of these people
turned down.
They had been looking forward to the
coming into force of Part II of the Act,
and were in consequence bitterly disappointed when their claims were disallowed. There is one case fresh in my
mind. It is that of a man with a wife
and four children; he was getting 26s.
a week. That man had to pay 10s. a
week for rent, and the balance was all
that was available to maintain him, his
wife, and children. That man has been
signing continuously at the Employment
Exchange for four or five years. He had
attempted on several occasions to obtain
employment, but without success. I
understand that that man's claim has
been turned down. I sincerely hope that
the Government will do something to
bring these people to whom I refer within
the provisions of the Act.
I should also like to refer to pensions.
I sincerely hope that during the new
Minister's term of office something will
be done to increase the pensions. I think
that all widows should come within the
provisions of the Widows', Orphans' and
Old Age Contributory Pensions Act. I
am satisfied that 10s. a week is an insufficient sum to maintain any person at
the present time. We know that the cost
of living is increasing day by day, and I
hope that an increase in these pensions
will be granted so that the people concerned can be kept out of the workhouse.
I read a recent speech delivered by the
Prime Minister. The noble Lord said
that he would like Ulster to lead, and
not only follow the lead of the people
across the water. I would suggest that
the noble Lord should give a lead in
this very important matter of increasing
the pension by at least 5s. a week.
There is nothing that this Government

I wish to congratulate the new Minister of Labour on his appointment.
have known him since I came to this

Major HALL-THOMPSON: I should
like to congratulate the right hon. Gentleman upon his appointment as Minister of
Labour. I wish him many years of
happiness and success in that office, an
office for which he is particularly well
qualified in view of the 16 years he has
spent in this House and the experience of
the social services which he has gained on
the committees with which he is connected. As one who has been intimately
associated with labour and National
Health Insurance questions for the past
16 years, I can say it is a matter of sincere
regret to those who are voluntary
workers that they have lost the services
of Mr. Andrews as Minister of Labour,
under whom it was a privilege and joy to
serve. No Minister could have brought
more energy and sympathy to his job than
he did, and we certainly wish him every
success in his new and difficult post.
I appreciate the difficulty of Northern
Ireland getting out of step with Great
Britain in the social services, but I should
like to ask the Minister of Labour to bring
a fresh vision to the problem. It should
be possible to take risks and
make
experiments in a small community such
as Northern Ireland, with an unemployed
population of 65,000, which it would not
be possible to take on the other side of
the Channel where the unemployed population represents something like a million
and a half. There are many other things
I would ask him to press upon the Unemployment Assistance Board. One is the
necessity of maintaining the unemployed
mentally and physically fit to take up
work when it is available. It is very easy
for a man who has means to make
interesting use and probably good use of
his time if he is unemployed, but it is a
very different matter to be unemployed
with practically nothing to live on and
to be only able to get the bare necessities
of life. You cannot blame that type of
man if he deteriorates morally, mentally
and physically. It is our duty to the
community to try to provide for these
persons, particularly those who are receiving benefit from the Unemployment
Assistance Board because we must assume
when they get to that stage their chances
of obtaining employment are gradually
getting less and less.
In my opinion up to the present the
Board have not appreciated their responsibility in that direction. I myself have
tried to impress it upon them, and it is
many months since the Advisory Committee, of which I am a member, also
tried to impress upon them the same
point; yet nothing has been done. Perhaps the Board's modesty is such that
we are not yet aware of what action they
have taken on this question. Although
there are many things they might
do which might not meet with the approval of the Opposition I maintain that
it would be in the best interests of the
community to insist that where a man
gets-I do not know what the proper title
is what used to be called extended benefit he should give some service in return;
not with the object of getting service from
him but with the object of keeping him
mentally and physically fit.
I sympathise with the Member for
Dock in deploring the absence of the
Opposition on an important occasion like
this. I could not help but notice that
during the whole of this important debate
on questions which they claim, or a few
of them claim, to be of particular interest
not more than three members of the
Opposition at any one time were present

The physical fitness of the man
spoken of by the last speaker is not being
considered. It is being decided on a
legal interpretation of words. And I
might say from the first day I entered
into that grade of work it never has been
so rigidly interpreted. I do not blame
those appointed to interpret They are
legal men, and, as I said before, highly
qualified legal men, and all young men.
But there is no basis of instruction set
down to them as a guide, not only to the
legal interpretation, but always to remember the human side of the question.
I have now felt disposed to say that in
England and Scotland the older chairmen who had had the pleasure of working on the Courts of Referees, under the
Unemployment Insurance Act, and who
are
now appointed to the new
Part 2 of the 1934 Act, are giving that
humanitarian side weight, and perhaps
cases that would be disallowed in Northern Ireland are being allowed across
the Channel. There is no use in asking
for step by step unless we have it in the
administration. And how is it possible
to get two legal men to come to the same
decision on the same words? Is not that
how lawyers live? By disagreement on
the law. One's interpretation is that,
and the other's that. That is how
lawyers make their living. Now, a profession which is not inclined to bring the
humanitarian side of the "normally"
aspect into being and apply it, is not,
I think, just the fit and proper body
to be doing the work, and the only way
to get the basis of interpretation uniform
is this, that if you have a "scope" to
work to that is the "scope," which is
private and confidential, but is not so
private and confidential that one cannot
get a copy when one desires to have a
copy-the "scope" is very large, and
the wording of the "scope" on the
"normally" aspect, in my opinion, could
fit in far better under Part 2 than it is
doing. And if your endeavour to fit it
in to make it work successfully, then you
will have a guard against exploitation;
that is, after you qualify you will have
to go before a tribunal again under
Schedule 5 on the family means test;
that is, the allowances required for the
family needs. There is a guard against
any exploitation of the fund.
That is the first thing to make the
"normally" aspect more suited to the
present conditions of our unemployment
market, and to give the applicant the
advantages of all the periods of years
that he was out of employment through
no fault of his own, and to try to bring
that spirit of help-one-another into
Part 2, instead of having the rigid
position presented to the applicant as
presented at the present moment. I feel
this point very sorely, because I have
been working under unemployment
insurance on the "normally" when we
discarded the thing as unfit to find a
place in any Act covering unemployment.
We also discarded the "not genuinely
seeking work" condition as not being
proper wording fitted into an Act covering unemployment. But with the resurrection of the "normally" the "not
genuinely seeking work" has returned.
It is not actually in words. Not normally
is there, but not genuinely seeking work
is in actual practice, because I had a
case where the applicant was turned
down in 1932 as not genuinely seeking
work, and that was standing against
him under the "normally" aspect in
1937. Therefore, while it is not in the
Act, it is in actual operation against
the applicant. When they make a case
against an applicant they discover that
he has been 3, 4, 5, 6 or 7 years out of
employment. The whole trend of the
questions is, was he seeking work?
Questions are put and, if his answers are
not highly satisfactory, they come to the
conclusion that this man has not been
genuinely seeking work, and he is not a
normally insured person under subsection (2).
That is not the way we intended
Part 2 to work. The way we intended
it to work was to take the able-bodied
from the local authority and relieve the
rates and accept a national responsibility.
When this Bill was mooted first we
understood that there would be about 10
per cent. of the tramp and vagrant class
who would not be taken over, that is, 10
per cent. of all those drawing outdoor.
relief or being assisted by the boards of
guardians. What do we find to-day?
We find the percentage taken over is
little over 40. Now, that spirit has not
been fulfilled when the percentage is so
low. I make these comments with the
object of getting the right hon. Gentle-

I am under no illusions about national
health insurance. The hon. and gallant
Member for Clifton has talked about the
voluntary service given under national
health insurance. I say national health
National
insurance is badly managed.
health insurance means national control,
not control by approved societies or big insurance companies. National health insurance means each for all and all for
each. What do we find to-day? We
find approved societies paying their
members minimum benefits, and the big
companies, who have been able to select
"lives," paying a very high figure with
additional benefits. That never was the
intention of Mr. Lloyd George in 1912,
or of the delegation that went to
Germany before the first Act was passed.
The word "national" was placed in the
title of this Act with the intention of
having national control similar to unemployment insurance. I oppose strongly
the distinctions that are being made in
national health insurance, although all
are paying equal contributions. Men,
women, boys and girls, if insured under
the National Health Insurance Act, pay
the same contributions. If you get into
the big approved societies you will get
£1 and additional benefits, while the
poor individuals, such as mill workers,
whose lives are supposed to be "poor
lives," will not be accepted.
The sooner amalgamation of national
health insurance takes place the better
for all concerned. You can amalgamate
national health insurance without interfering with the step-by-step policy, because by amalgamation all the amounts
paid out to approved societies will go into
a common pool. Every man, woman,
boy and girl will have equal rights in
that common pool. You would make
huge savings on behalf of national health
contributions if you took on a scheme of
national ownership and control. It
should never have been given into the
hands of the approved societies. I am
not exempting even trade unions.
including everything. Trade unions make
a profit out of it.

I would like to say a word in regard to
the officials at the Labour Exchanges.
passed this afternoon through Antrim,
where there is a new Labour Exchange
in course of erection. I would like to
compliment the officials in the Labour
Exchanges. I know our own Exchange
in Belfast, and I know the highlyefficient standard of the officials there.
I want to point out that in the last rearrangement of salaries in the Civil
Service a certain number of Exchange
officials did not get their just reward.
They have been serving the public and
the Ministry faithfully, but in the readjustment of salaries they did not get
the reward that I expected they would
get. Those officials come into personal
contact with the public. Personal contact means many things. It means that
an applicant can go away dissatisfied and
grousing and grumbling, or it means
that he may go away satisfied and feeling
that everything possible has been done
for him.
The remuneration of these people with
the personal contact is the smallest in the
Estimate. Why is it that the man with
the most difficult job receives the lowest
salary, while the man with the smallest
number of difficulties attached to his job,
as far as the personal touch is concerned,
is in the higher grades? I made an
appeal in this connection to the former
Minister of Labour, but he had not time,
I suppose, to review the position, and I
think I am justified in repeating it and
asking the new Minister for his assistance
in seeing that these lower grades are
given their rightful position. I will
give an illustration. Assuming the
clerks who sat at the table in Courts of
Referees in 1912 had said, "We are only
clerks here for the purpose of taking
notes," the Ministry would have had to
employ very able advisers. They would
have had to reduce the number of claims
appearing before the courts, because the
chairman could not have adjudicated on
all the claims. They would have had to
do many things that would have cost
money.
Those clerks saved them that money.
They were experts in the working of the
Act. They knew the administration and
were able to give advice which expedited
the work of the courts to the extent that
the courts did 50 per cent. more work
than they could have done otherwise.
Still no recompense has been given to
them in the revision of grades. That
refers to one class. Then there is the
interviewing section. I could go over
several grades in the Labour Exchanges
which have certainly not got compensation in accordance with the value of the
work they perform. The Civil Service
Association are not satisfied with the last
arrangement. They are partly satisfied,
but many things are outstanding, and
most of them are in the Ministry of
Labour.

TREATMENT OF HAY FEVER.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether any steps are
being taken to encourage in Northern
Ireland the new treatment for hay fever
as practised in some of the London hospitals.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The treatment to which the hon. Member refers
is, I understand, being tried experimentally in one of the London hospitals.
I cannot, however, associate myself
with any implication to the effect that
Government action is necessary to ensure
that any up-to-date method of proved
worth will be afforded in our local hospitals, as that is the business of the
medical profession-whose reputation I
think every Member of the House will
agree stands second to none-which, for
my part, I have no doubt they faithfully
discharge.

MINIMUM FAMILY INCOME.
5. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Labour whether his attention has
been drawn to Mr. Seebohm Rowntree's
estimate published last week, of the
family income needed to supply the
bare necessities of a civilised existence
on current prices and standards of needs,
namely, that the physical necessaries of
a healthy life cannot be provided at less
than 53s a week for an urban worker
with a wife and three children, or 41s
for an agricultural labourer with the
same family; and whether the Ministry
will shape its policy towards enforcing
such a minimum by means of trade
boards and family allowances.
Major SHILLINGTON: My attention
has been drawn to Mr. Rowntree's survey, and, in pursuance of the Government's general policy on matters
affecting the United Kingdom, close
touch will be maintained on the subject
between my Department and the
Ministry of Labour in Great Britain.
The hon. and learned Member will, no
doubt, agree with Mr. Rowntree that
the matter is one of great difficulty,
as it would be easy by ill-advised and
precipitate action to raise prices to an
extent that would annul any increases
of wages and so provide no real remedy.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the Minister
approve of family allowances?

FLAX CULTIVATION.
6. Sir ROBERT LYNN asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether in view
of the alarming decrease of the area
under flax in Northern Ireland the Government intends to take any steps which
will encourage the farmers to grow this
crop.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): So far as
its limited resources permit, the Government has been doing everything
practicable to encourage flax production mainly by increasing the supply
o pure line seed available for sowing.
As the hon. Member is, no doubt, aware
the best of such seed gives yields which
exceed those obtained from ordinary
commercial seed by as much as 50 per
cent. Largely as a result of these efforts,
it is estimated that pure line seed was
available this year sufficient to sow upwards of 12,000 acres or about one-half
of the total flax area.
Once again, however, I must emphasise that flax acreage in this country is
dependent entirely upon price.
Experience indicates that if a satisfactory
price is assured the farmer will not be
slow to respond. It must, however, be
remembered in considering this matter
that the farmer has normally other, and
probably more profitable, alternatives,
and like everybody else, he will naturally concern himself with what pays
best.
At the same time, the Government
fully realise that at the present time
there are wider considerations than
purely agricultural ones, and I can
assure the hon. Member that in regard
to this aspect of the question representations have been made to the appropriate authorities.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Arising out of
that reply, will the right hon. and
gallant Gentleman say whether he can
facilitate the supply of the new seed to
farmers at as low prices as possible.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: That is
rather a difficult question, because the
production of seed is in the hands of
farmers in Canada, who sell it in this
country on a commercial basis.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Is the right
hon. Gentleman aware that the farmers
would sow the new seed only for the
fact that it is so much higher than
the ordinary seed in price?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am aware of
that.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that
at the Ottawa Imperial Conference both
the Minister and Mr. Lewis Gray,
chairman of the Flaxdressers' Association, influenced the Government to
remove the duty on Russian flax to the
disadvantage of Northern Ireland flax
growers, and were they not publicly
complimented by the Prime Minister for
their successful efforts in that direction?
a

Gentleman consider guaranteeing

EXTERNAL TRADE OF NORTHERN
IRELAND.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state the value
in 1935 of the external trade of Northern
Ireland and the method by which his
figures are computed, and whether goods
in transit to and from the Irish Free
State passing through the ports of Belfast,
Londonderry and other ports in Northern
Ireland are included in the figures given.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The estimated values of
the imports into and the exports from
Northern Ireland during 1935 were
£47,110,000 and £45,055,000 respectively.
making a total combined value of
£92,165,000.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
29 APRIL 1937
In the case of trade passing direct
between Northern Ireland and places
other than Great Britain, details of
quantity and value are obtained from the
Commissioners of Customs and Excise.
In the case of trade passing between
Northern Ireland and Great Britain,
details of quantities, but not of value, are
obtained from the various port and
harbour authorities in Northern Ireland.
The value of each class of goods is then
assessed in the Ministry on the basis of
the available information regarding
average prices.
It is not possible in the case of either
imports or exports to distinguish between
goods passing through Northern Ireland
to or from the Irish Free State and those
for consumption in or originating in
Northern Ireland. For this reason the
figures which I have mentioned as being
the value of Northern Ireland's external
trade are inclusive of the value of goods
in transit to and from the Irish Free
State.
Mr. NIXON: Are the figures recently
given on behalf of the Government only
an estimate instead of an ascertained
fact?
Mr. BARBOUR: I have already stated
that the values are estimated according to
the standard figures kept by the Ministry
of Commerce. I may say that they may
be considered as absolutely reliable.
STOPPAGES IN ELECTRICITY
SUPPLY.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether there were serious
stoppages of electricity in Northern
Ireland during the past year; whether he
would impress on the Electricity Supply
Board the importance of improving the
efficiency of the undertaking under their
control, and whether all serious stoppages
took place outside the jurisdiction of the
Belfast Corporation.
Mr. BARBOUR: I assume from the
question that the hon. Member has in
mind interruptions on the Electricity
Board's system. During the past year
there were two interruptions affecting considerable areas. The first of these, which
extended for 45 minutes, affected certain
towns in County Down and was due to
damage by gale to a main trunk line.
The second was caused by the abnormally
severe snowstorm in March, when certain
sections of the Electricity Board's system
were
temporarily out of commission.
I understand, however, that the resultant
dislocation due to the snowstorm was
much less serious, both in extent and
duration, than that in certain districts
in Great Britain served by overhead
transmission lines.
In regard to the second part of the hon.
Member's question, I am satisfied that the
Electricity Board are taking all practicable steps to maintain continuity of
supply and to localise the effect of any
faults which may arise. I am glad to say
that the supply system of the Belfast
Corporation has been singularly free from
interruptions.
Mr. NIXON: Would the experience of
the Minister and Board suggest that as
far as possible underground high tension
cables should be laid and used?
Mr. BARBOUR: There is a very
severe limiting factor, and that is the expense involved.

of Education whether he can state if any

NORTHERN IRELAND'S ECONOMIC
POSITION.
11. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he has read the Midland Bank's review of the economic
position in Northern Ireland, which
appeared in the Press on 2nd April, 1937;
whether he has any comment to make on
the statement that "The proportion of
unemployment in Northern Ireland is
higher than in any other division of the
United Kingdom except Wales, and is
more than double the average for the
country as a whole"; whether over 25 per
cent. of the working population in
Northern Ireland are unemployed; and
whether the time has not arrived for the
Prime Minister to redeem his promise
regarding unemployment.
Major SHILLINGTON: I have been
asked to reply to this question by my
right hon. Friend, the Prime Minister.
The position is as stated in the publication to which the hon. and learned Member refers, but the review goes on to state
that there has been a substantial revival
in the shipbuilding industry; that there
are sufficient orders to keep spindles in
the spinning trade busy for many months,
and that for many descriptions of linen
goods manufacturers have been offered
more orders than they can deliver in the
desired time. The review also records
improvements in the clothing and rope
and twine trades.
The better state of trade is reflected,
I am glad to say, in the unemployment
returns for April, which show that the
number on the register on the 19th of this
month was 4,359 less than a month ago.
The Government has the general industrial situation here under constant consideration and will continue to take every
possible step to promote employment.
Mr. NIXON: Everything the Minister
says with regard to improvement is
correct. I know that to be so, but what
does he expect the position will be when
the boom passes over?
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask is it a
fact that 25 per cent. of the working
population in Northern Ireland are unemployed?
Major SHILLINGTON: I have stated
that the report in the paper was at that
time accurate. The figure, fortunately,
has been considerably reduced since then.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
the figures as quoted by "The Times "
show Northern Ireland to be the second
highest unemployed area in Great
Britain; and whether the Minister has
made no arrangements to take into indus-

AGRICULTURAL WAGES IN
LIMAVADY DISTRICT.
12. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister whether he is aware that
agricultural labourers in the Limavady
district are working for farmers who are
only paying 10s to 15s per week, and
would he state whether he is prepared to
recommend the Government to introduce
an Agricultural Wages Bill to set up a
Board to stop this exploitation of agricultural workers.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
According to information collected by
my Ministry the average rates of wages
(including perquisites) paid to married
men in the Limavady rural district in
1936 were 21s per week for ordinary
labourers, 24s per week for ploughmen.
Single men receive about 3s per week less
than these rates. Cash wages such as those
mentioned by the hon. Member are sometimes paid, but in addition labourers
receive various perquisites such as a free
house, free meals, coal and milk.
With regard to the establishment of an
Agricultural Wages Board, I would refer
the hon. Member to the replies given to
the hon. Member for Dock on the 18th
March and 15th October last.
