CORONATION OF KING GEORGE VI.
Address to His Majesty.
our
The PRIME MINISTER: I am sure
everyone in the House will share with me
in the pleasure of a slight interlude in
ordinary Parliamentary activities
while I have the great honour and privilege of moving the Resolution of loyalty
to His Majesty the King that stands upon
the Order Paper. His Majesty the King
and Her Gracious Majesty the Queen
have come to the Throne at a comparatively young age, and we in this part of
his Dominions realise that a message of
encouragement would be welcomed at the
moment almost of the important celebration of being crowned at Westminster.
On a former occasion I had the honour of
moving a Resolution of loyalty from this
box, but some little time has elapsed
since then, and during that period I
think the whole country has appreciated
what His Majesty has been able to do
the whole country has appreciated that
the old traditions of the Monarchy are
going to be upheld in a perfect way by
1161 The King's Coronation-
Address to His Majesty 1162
29 APRIL 1937
him and by Her Gracious Majesty the
Queen. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Under those circumstances I feel quite
confident that this House and this part
of the United Kingdom, which will
shortly have the great honour of paying
their respects and showing their loyalty,
will demonstrate to the world that no part
of His Majesty's Dominions will be more
delighted to see him than Ulster.
I am sure there will be a universal
feeling of gratitude that he has graciously
consented to visit us in person so soon
after the ceremony of being crowned
King of these vast realms. It is indeed a
great compliment, and I am sure he will
be able to judge by its intensity the loyal
welcome which will be accorded to him,
and he will go away, I hope, feeling that
at any time he will be welcome to pay a
return visit to this Ulster of ours. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We all realise
in the circumstances of the case that his
visit is obliged to be a short one. It will
follow very much, we hope, along the
lines of that of his revered father, but
although it is a short visit I am certain
the Ulster people will, by the intensity of
their greeting, show him that if he had
stayed here for any length of time it
could not be more sincere.
With these few words on behalf of this
House and of those whom hon. Members
represent outside this House, our
message to both the King and Queen is
that God may spare them for many long
years to reign over us, and that during
that time they may experience the very
utmost of happiness amongst their people.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Question proposed :
"That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty as follows:-
"Most Gracious Sovereign,
"We, your Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to renew, on the
occasion of Your Majesty's Coronation, the assurance of steadfast
devotion to the Crown and Person of
Your Majesty which we tendered at
Your Accession.
"The happiness and prosperity of
the United Kingdom and of the whole
Empire have been Your Majesty's constant concern. The solemnity of Your
Majesty's Coronation cannot fail to
create a fuller understanding of the
meaning and value of the Crown, and
strengthen the bond of loyalty between.
the Sovereign and his subjects in
Northern Ireland and throughout the
Empire.
"To Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth
we desire also to express our loyalty
and devotion, rejoicing that the heavy
responsibilities of the Throne. are
shared by one who already holds a
place in the affection of the Ulster
people.
"We offer our heartfelt good wishes
for Your Majesty's reign, and we
pray that, under Divine Blessing,
there may be granted to Your Majesty
and to Her Majesty the Queen,
health, strength and happiness."
Mr. NIXON: On behalf of thousands

Markets and Fairs Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In submitting this
Bill for a Second Reading, I should like,
in the first instance,
to say that,
although for reasons of Parliamentary
convenience the Second Reading is being
taken to-day, there is no intention of
proceeding with the Committee stage of
this very important Measure until
all the local authorities and other
interested parties have had full and
ample opportunity to examine its provisions and to submit any representations
which they may think desirable, which,
I need hardly say, will receive my most
careful consideration.
Perhaps I may be allowed to preface
my remarks by referring briefly to the
position which markets have occupied in
the past. They are very ancient institutions and must have arisen out of a
need which would very early be felt of
arranging safe places where people
could meet. As violence and robbery
were prevalent in these early times
the merchants would meet where they
had the protection of some powerful
man and would pay him for his protection. Later, markets were recognised as a very convenient means of
raising revenue, and the grant of the
privilege of collecting tolls, etc., was one
way by which a ruler could reward a
favourite. Then some of the more
important towns, either by favour or
by purchase, got the right of holding
their own markets. There has, therefore, grown up a great variety of conditions under which markets are carried
on, some belonging to private individuals, some to public trustees, some
to local authorities, some held by
Charter from the Crown, some under
Act of Parliament, and some merely by
customary right, and each market has
its own regulations and its own scale of
charges. The accommodation provided
varies greatly also.
The want in
many cases of proper
accommodation and the charging of tolls
without rendering any service in return
as well as the variations in the tolls
charged have long been grievances
with people using markets, and when
the subject came under discussion in
connection with the Agricultural Marketing Bill in 1933, the Government
decided to appoint a
a Commission to
inquire into the position of markets and
fairs in Northern Ireland and into the
tolls or other charges made by market.
authorities in respect of marketable
commodities and marketable animals
and to make recommendations with
regard thereto.
The Commission furnished an interesting and informative report in 1934 and
made a number of recommendations for
the amendment of the existing law
relating to markets most of which the
1173 Markets and Fairs Bill-

29 APRIL 1937
Second Reading
Government has endeavoured to incorporate in the Bill.
The principal recommendations of the
Commission related to the reorganisation of markets
on a more or less
uniform basis throughout the whole of
Northern Ireland, and to the application of some uniform principle of
charging tolls. There were several other
recommendations of less importance to
which I need not refer at present.
The reorganisation of markets would
certainly appear to be very desirable
having regard to the variety of conditions to which I have referred and
the proposals put forward by the Commission, which involve placing practically
all markets under the control of the
local authorities, appears to be well calculated to remedy the present chaotic
state of things and enable improvements
to be effected in the conditions under
which markets are carried on. The
Commission recommended that in all
urban districts the urban council should
be obliged to acquire any market within
its area, and that in rural districts the
rural district council, while not obliged
to acquire markets, should have power
to acquire them if it so desires. These
recommendations have been incorporated in the Bill, and I think that there
could be no doubt that the placing of
markets in the hands of the local
authorities should lead to a great
improvement in the accommodation and
in the general conditions under which
markets are held.
With regard to the manner of
charging tolls, the Commission recommended that no toll should be charged
in respect of any commodity unless some.
service other than weighing facilities is
rendered by the market authority in
connection with the sale of that commodity, or unless tolls are necessary to
make the market self-supporting. These
conditions seem quite fair, but the
Commission recognise that there should
be some considerable latitude in defining
what constituted service. It recognised
that there might be cases where it was
difficult to point to any specific services
that the market was rendering in
respect of any goods, but yet that the
market might be a benefit to the
neighbourhood indirectly by providing
a centre to which persons came,
and
in which, therefore, they would be
likely to do business.
For the same reason, while the Commission considered that normally a
market should not be a charge on the
rates, it agreed that although a market
might not be self-supporting it might
distinct
nevertheless be conferring a
benefit on the community, and in such
cases the rates might be expected to
contribute to some extent towards the
cost. Generally speaking,
speaking, however,
their view was that markets should be
self-supporting and that tolls should be
collected only on goods in respect of
which the market provided some specific
service.
An
In connection with this matter of tolls
a much-vexed question has been the area
within which the tolls are leviable.
attempt has been made to protect the
market authority from undue competition by forbidding the sale of tollable goods within certain limits outside
the market or by requiring toll to be
paid on all such articles when bought
within these limits. The principle
appears to be equitable and is being
retained in the present Bill.
It is proposed that the articles on
which toll may be levied and the amount
of the toll shall be approved by the
Ministry of Home Affairs, in consultation with the Ministry of Agriculture.
In this way, therefore, although for
various reasons it is unlikely to be possible to have one uniform list of charges
throughout Northern Ireland, a much
greater amount of uniformity should be
obtained than exists at present.
Several other minor recommendations
of the Commission for the improvement of
the law relating to markets have been
inserted in the Bill. One of these is the
concentrating in the Ministry of Home
Affairs of all the powers of Government
Departments relating to markets. The
principal power affected by this recommendation is that at present exercised by
the Ministry of Agriculture under the
Markets and Fairs (Weighing of Cattle)
Act, 1887, which deals with the provision
of suitable accommodation for weighing
cattle. Another is the transfer from the
Governor of Northern Ireland to the
Ministry of the power to alter the date
of fairs under the Fairs (Ireland) Act,
1868.

Other suggestions included in the Bill

necessary, the duty of local authorities to
provide accommodation or other facilities
for marketing boards in connection with
any market belonging to local authorities,
and the empowering of local authorities
to employ auctioneers for the purpose of
conducting auctions.
Mr. BEATTIE: Do the local authorities
want it?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is a
matter which I am sure the hon. Member will deal with when he comes to speak.
As I have already pointed out to him, we
appointed a very representative committee and also representatives of various
authorities and various interests, and on
this occasion they produced a unanimous
report. As I said in the earlier part of
my remarks, I propose we should not take
the Committee stage of this Bill in the
meantime, as it is a very important and
very complicated Measure. I propose to
invite the views of all those who are
interested in the subject, as I want to try
to get a Bill which will suit the needs of
all. I can only say that this is an
attempt by the Government to remedy
what everyone must admit is a most unsatisfactory state of affairs. The Government in framing the Bill has endeavoured
to keep in view and to provide for the
interests of all parties as impartially as
possible, but in dealing with a matter of
such complexity it is almost impossible
that some things should not have been
overlooked, and the Government is only
too willing to receive suggestions for its
improvement. I shall, between this and
the Committee stage, be only too glad to
receive any recommendation from anybody interested in this particular matter.
In the meantime, I beg to move.

Oral Answers to Questions.
THE BY-PASS ROAD TO
HOLYWOOD.
1. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state if any further developments
have taken place in regard to the construction of the by-pass road to Holywood, and whether the Government will
take steps to have the work expedited
as much as possible.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
Negotiations have been and are still
being carried on with the appropriate
authorities regarding the difficulties
which the Minister of Home Affairs
mentioned in his reply to the hon. Member's question on the 23rd March last as
having arisen owing to the proximity of
the route of the proposed road to the
Belfast Harbour Commissioners
aerodrome.
new
I think I may now say that these
difficulties have been removed and I can
assure the hon. Member that every effort
will be made to have the work of constructing the road commenced with the
least delay possible.
CANCER IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
2. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state what steps the Government are
taking to combat the scourge of cancer
in Northern Ireland.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
A Commission set up by the British
Government has been investigating the
subject of cancer for some years past
and has issued reports from time to time
which are available for the guidance of
medical men and hospital authorities in
Northern Ireland.
Research work is also being carried on
in the Queen's University.
The medical profession and hospital
authorities in Northern Ireland are fully
aware of, and make use of, the latest
methods of treatment and it does not
appear that any action on the part of
this Government is required at present,
but I need not say that it will be only
too happy to render any assistance in its
power if asked by the responsible
authorities.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Money Resolution
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): The Resolution
now before the House sets out the Government's proposals for the amendment
of the provisions of Section 40 of the
Unemployment Assistance Act (Northern
Ireland), 1934, which provided for the
payment by local authorities of contributions towards the expenses of unemployment assistance. The passing of
the Resolution is the preliminary to the
introduction of an amending Bill during
the present Session which will, apart
from details of machinery, contain little
more than is set out in this Resolution
itself.
It is important at the outset to recognise that no new principle is involved,
and that these proposals arise from the
fact that provision was made in the 1934
Act for the payment of contributions
only up to the 31st March, 1937, after
which period the contributions were
again to be calculated and determined by
Parliament. It will be remembered that
owing to the postponement of the Second
Appointed Day until the 1st April of
this year the provisions regarding the
payment of contributions never became
operative; instead, in order to meet the
expense to which local authorities were
put because of their continued responsibility for certain insurable able-bodied
unemployed, grants on a generous scale
were made to local authorities from the
Exchequer.
may
It
be desirable to restate the
position generally as to the
provision which was made under the 1934
Act regarding the contributions of local
authorities. This Act provided that from
the Second Appointed Day, in view of
the relief to be afforded to local authorities through the Unemployment Assistance
Board taking over a substantial number
of the able-bodied poor from the Board
of Guardians, contributions were to be
paid for the three years ended 31st
March, 1937, as follows:-
Belfast, 11d in the £ on the rateable
value.
Londonderry County Borough and
boroughs and urban districts, 2d in the
£ on the rateable value.
Rural areas, 1d in the £ on the rateable value.
Owing to the existence of a special
distress relief order in Belfast it was
possible to make a fairly reasonable
estimate of the expenditure of which the
rates would be relieved, and the Belfast
Corporation, through their spokesmen in
this House, while objecting to a contribution related to poundage, did not raise
any real objection to the amount itself.
In the case of the remaining local
authorities there were no distress relief
orders in existence except in one or two
urban districts and, therefore, it was not
possible to make as accurate a division as
in Belfast between ordinary poor law
relief and distress relief. In the light
of such information as was available
amounts related to rate poundage were
inserted in the Bill, and they passed the
House, almost without comment.
The Government has given very careful consideration to the question of the
contributions now to be fixed, and these
are now embodied in the Resolution
before the House. It is proposed to fix
the contributions for a period of five
years, and, in view of the improved conditions of the employment situation, and
of the hope of possible future improvement during the next five years, to reduce the contributions as laid down in
1934 by approximately 25 per cent., and
at the same time to express the result,
not in terms of a contribution based on
valuation, but in definite amounts.
The proposals have been communicated
to all local authorities. Suggestions
made by the county councils in regard to
the machinery of collection and appropriation of the money will be met in the
Bill. For example, the money, unlike
the education levy, will not be paid to
the Exchequer, but appropriated in aid
of the relevant Vote and, in the case of
will
urban districts,
be contributed
direct and not through the county
councils.
The Belfast Corporation, which is the
local authority mainly concerned, has
made representations for a reduction of
the contribution of £56,000, but the
Government has been unable to agree
with the basis of the Corporation's contention, which is that the numbers of
able-bodied poor still left to be dealt
with by the Board of Guardians are in
excess of those estimated by the Government. The Government, therefore,
1185 Unemployment Assistance-

after giving most careful consideration
to the Corporation's representations, is
satisfied that the figure of £56,000 is
fair.
As regards the urban and rural contributions, seeing that the original
figures in the 1934 Act passed almost
without comment, I apprehend that the
local authorities concerned are not likely
to criticise the modest sums which it is
sought to impose on them. I beg to
move.

Any members of the Belfast Corporation on this Committee are free and unfettered from the entanglements of the

is concerned. I had a long talk last

Londonderry.
I am not going to repeat anything I

I feel that the Government are trying to

who were taken over under Part 2,
because the majority of the Belfast unemployed who were taken over were that
class who had paid into the Unemployment Insurance Fund since its inception,
or from the year 1920. This section of

outside the Unemployment Insurance
Acts. Belfast has been left with a very
heavy burden to bear as regards the
able-bodied unemployed. The ratepayers are now asked to make a contribution towards the upkeep of those taken
over, and accept full responsibility for
those who are left outside.

the workhouse or giving them some other
class of treatment; secondly, the Minister to be responsible for the able-bodied
unemployed, whether insured or uninsured. That was the Minister's own
statement. Now we find that the per-

for Mid Antrim. We are not speaking

speaking on the basis of ordinary
common
sense. The Belfast representatives who have approached this question do submit that in view of the whole
of the facts and the allocation of these
charges they have established a prima
facie case for a reduction of this contribution of £56,000 by 33 per cent.
In other words, the contribution of
the city of Belfast ought to be reduced
by £21,000. That is made out on the
following basis. The total cost of distress relief for the ensuing year is based
on the figures available at the 31st
March, 1937. Assuming that cost to be
£130,000, and that the Corporation will
continue to pay 60 per cent. of that
figure as the equivalent of the 11d. rate
contained in the Unemployment (Northern Ireland) Act, 1934, which represented 60 per cent. of the total cost, the
inclusive charge for the Corporation
would be £78,000. From that figure
must be deducted the amount to be
defrayed by the Government, 33 per
cent. of £130,000, or £43,000 approximately. Therefore the minimum cost for
which the Corporation ought to be
responsible on the 60-40 basis would be
£35,000, or a reduction of the present
amount by £21,000. I do not think this
case can be controverted.
The impregnability of the Belfast
position--if I may use that term-is seen
by taking a survey of what is to be paid
by the other local authorities in Northern Ireland. This is outlined on the
Order Paper of to-day. All the other
areas in Northern Ireland will pay the
sum of £6,990 per annum. Belfast will
pay £56,000. Do you think that is a
fair allocation. Let me take it from
the point of view of unemployment.
Approximately there are 70,000 unemployed in Northern Ireland at the
present time. I think I am correct in
saying that the city's proportion of the
unemployed would be 35,000 out of a
total of 70,000. Unemployment in
Northern Ireland is split up in this way
-Belfast represents 50 per cent. of the
unemployed population, and the rest of
Northern Ireland represents the other 50
per cent.
Yet here is how the charge for distress
relief is being allocated-£6,990 from
the whole of Northern Ireland, excluding
from the city of
Belfast; £56,000 from
Belfast.
Do you think that is a fair
allocation? I say it is not. I say nobody
could defend that, nobody except the
cock-eyed, lopsided Government that has
got the queerest conception and most distorted vision of how the finances of this
country ought to be administered. I use
that phrase in no vulgar or personal
sense. I am merely using it as a film
term, in order to bring the spiritual
complex of the films into this assembly.
Those of you who are familiar with film
terms will appreciate the significance of
what I say. The man who could defend
this in the name of good government is
defending something which is iniquitous
and unjust to the city of Belfast.
Let me say that in making out this
case-very imperfectly I must admit-on
behalf of the city of Belfast we put it
forward without prejudice to our contention that unemployment ought to be
a national charge. It is because I
argued, have argued, and will continue.
to argue, that unemployment ought to
be a national charge that I did not proceed to take advantage of a parliamentary loophole this afternoon to move an
Amendment which the Chairman ruled
out of order. Had I been as dexterous

Amendment in another way. I could

I know on my Motion I cannot wander
over the whole Resolution, but if the
Government wanted a certain amount of
money the proper way would have been
to calculate what poundage would bring
in that sum in Northern Ireland. If
that had been done everybody paying

pay their share. That, however, did not

occasion. They have not told us how
they arrived at the figure of £56,000 for
the city of Belfast. They could not tell
us. No man in the world could tell why

£900. I do not know what was in the
mind of the Government when they
brought forward this proposal. I do not
wish to drive in a wedge between the
people in the city of Belfast and those
living in the country. It is far too small
a Province to do anything of the kind.
The prosperity of the country is the
prosperity of Belfast, and the prosperity
of Belfast is the prosperity of the
country. When things are prosperous in
Belfast there are better markets for the
people in Co. Down and Co. Antrim.
Nobody has attempted to explain how
the Government arrived at the figures
put before us this afternoon. The reason
for that I do not know.
The Minister of Finance at one time
said that capital was a very timid bird.
The Government have persistently
frightened capital out of the city of
Belfast and the Province until now they
resort to all sorts of means of collecting
money to balance their Budget. This is
probably the last straw.
When you
crush Belfast you crush the country. I
remember the hon. and gallant Member
for St. Anne's stating that when it rains
on the mountains it is the valleys which
become flooded. Government extravagance is raining on the only city of
consequence in Northern Ireland-
Belfast-and they are apparently doing
their best to put it down and out.
Belfast has to pay £56,000 and the city
of Londonderry £900.

longer.

considerable numbers, and

Let me, for a moment, deal with the

It is remarkable how much the city ratepayers
are being relieved of. In 1933-34 the

1215 Sale of Ice-Cream Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
Bill ordered to be brought in by the
Minister of Finance and the Minister of
Labour.
Unemployment Assistance (Finance) Bill,
"to amend the provisions of the Unemployment Assistance Act (Northern
Ireland), 1934, with respect to the contributions to be paid by local authorities
for the purposes of that Act," presented
accordingly and read a First time; to
be read a Second time to-morrow, and
to be printed. (Bill No. 14).
Sale of Ice-Cream Bill [S].
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I do not
propose in moving the Second Reading
of this Bill to say very much in regard
to those provisions which are of a purely
sanitary nature. I am sure that all
Members will agree that it is desirable
that ice-cream should be manufactured
and sold only under the most hygienic
conditions, and should not be exposed to
any danger of contamination or infection.
Likewise there will be no dispute that
ice-cream should not be sold which contains any harmful preservatives.
Clauses 4 and 7, which deal with the
regulation by sanitary authorities of the
manufacture and sale of ice-cream, are
similar to provisions which have been in
operation for a number of
years in
several urban areas in Northern Ireland
where they have been found to work
satisfactorily. The representative associations of the sanitary authorities have
been consulted in regard to these provisions and have expressed their general
agreement.
Clause 3, however, contains a very
important new provision which will be
of great value from the public health
point of view. It has in the past been
customary from time to time for samples
of ice-cream to be taken for bacteriological examination in order to check
whether the conditions in which it was
being produced were satisfactory. It is
now proposed to institute a statutory
bacteriological standard, and thus to
afford the public a further degree of
protection against the purchase of contaminated ice-cream.
I now turn to one or two aspects of
the Bill with which hon. Members may
be less familiar, but with which I, as
Minister of Agriculture, am more nearly
concerned. The first is the question of
the nutritive value of ice-cream. Icecream is consumed largely by the
younger members of the community, and
it is, therefore, desirable that those who
purchase this commodity should receive
something which is not merely pleasant
to the taste, but is also wholesome and
nutritious.
Clause 1 of the Bill enables the Ministry of Agriculture to prescribe minimum
standards of milk fat and of solids,
including milk fat, with which all icecream sold in Northern Ireland must
comply. The Clause also seeks to prohibit the sale of ice-cream which contains
any fats other than milk fat, e.g.
vegetable fats. These provisions, which
are the basis of local legislation which is
in operation in the County Borough of
Londonderry and the Borough of Bangor,
are designed to ensure (1) that ice-cream
shall not be sold in this country unless it
contains a reasonable proportion of food
values, and (2) that these food values
shall, as far as possible, be derived from
fresh whole milk.
Clause 3, to which I have referred
before, contains a further novel provision
-novel, that is to say, so far as this
country is concerned, though I believe
there is similar legislation in parts of
the United States. This Clause seeks to
provide that ice-cream shall comply
with a prescribed standard governing
the relation between the volume and
weight of ice-cream. This Clause may
require
The
some explanation.
ingredients out of which ice-cream is made
are, during manufacture, submitted to a
process of aeration or swelling, which has
the effect of increasing the volume of the
final product without, of course,
reducing the proportion of milk fat and
other solids which are calculated upon
the weight basis. Thus, of two portions
of ice-cream equal in volume, and both
complying with the standards prescribed
under the first Clause, one may have a
considerably higher food value than the
other. The object of this provision is to
protect those who produce the former
type of ice-cream. A certain amount of
swell or over-run is essential in order to
1217 Sale of Ice-Cream Bill-

4 MAY 1937
Second Reading
produce a palatable ice-cream, but it is
considered desirable in the public interest that some check should be placed
upon excessive over-run, since otherwise
the standards prescribed under Clause 1
might be largely ineffective. It is, moreover, probable that those manufacturers
who rely mainly upon fresh milk for the
manufacture of ice-cream subject their
ice-cream to a lesser degree of aeration
than their competitors. It is believed
that by restricting over-run it will be
possible in effect to give a certain advantage to those manufacturers who use
fresh whole milk as one of the main constituents of their ice-cream.
This reference to the use of whole
milk in the manufacture of ice-cream
brings me to the agricultural aspect of
this subject. The manufacture of icecream, taking place as it does mainly
during the summer season, forms a useful
outlet for the surplus of milk which producers find on their hands at that time of
the year.
At present ice-cream manufacturers in Northern Ireland use
approximately 300,000 gallons of milk
per annum, and it is desirable that they
should receive every encouragement to
continue to use fresh milk of good
quality and to increase the quantity so
used.
and
I have already referred to two clauses
which have a bearing upon this matter,
namely, Clause 1, which provides milk
fat standards for all ice-cream,
Clause 3, which will, it is hoped, conduce to the sale of ice-cream containing
higher food values. I now come to
Clause 8, which is primarily intended to
encourage the use of fresh milk of good
quality in the manufacture of ice-cream.
Under Clause 8 the Ministry of Agriculture seeks authority to provide for the
sale of ice-cream of high quality under
the designation "Premium". It will be
a condition of licences issued under
Clause 8 that licence holders who
manufacture ice-cream shall, for the
purpose of providing the milk fat for
such ice-cream, utilise fresh whole milk
of a standard quality of not less than
Grade C. These provisions will, it is
hoped, incidentally conduce to the consumption of ice-cream of a higher nutritive value.
It will be observed that in Clause 13
there is provision whereby contributions
may be made from the Milk Fund
towards schemes for encouraging the
purchase of ice-cream in the manufacture
of which milk of Grade A, Grade B or
Grade C has been used. This will enable
"Premium" ice-cream to be advertised,
and such publicity to be carried out as
will give an advantage to those ice-cream
manufacturers who use fresh milk in the
manufacture of their ice-cream.
In conclusion, may I say that in addition to consulting the local authorities in
regard to those provisions of the Bill
which are likely to affect them, we have
been in consultation with representatives
of the ice-cream trade, and these representatives have expressed their general
approval of the Bill. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be

Unemployment Insurance
(Additional Days and Waiting Period)
Order (Northern Ireland), 1937.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Major
Shillington): I beg to move: "That the
Order in Council made by the Governor
of Northern Ireland on the 22nd March,
1937, under Section 65 of the Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern Ireland),
1936, for increasing the maximum number of additional days of benefit other
than agricultural benefit, payable in a
benefit year, and for reducing, in relation
to benefit other than agricultural benefit,
the number of days at the beginning of
a continuous period of unemployment
after which benefit becomes payable, be
hereby approved."
On the recommendation of the Unemployment Insurance Statutory Committee, an Order was made in Great Britain
on the 10th March, providing for two
modifications in the general insurance
scheme in favour of applicants for benefit. The first reduced from six to three
days the waiting period during which
benefit is not payable at the beginning
of a continuous period of unemployment.
The second increased the number of
"additional days" of benefit for which
applicants with good employment records
may qualify.
Under Section 65 of the Unemployment Insurance (Northern Ireland) Act,
1936, His Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland is empowered to apply to
Northern Ireland by Order in Council
the provisions of any Order made in
Great Britain on the recommendation of
the Statutory Committee in order to
secure that any modifications so made in
the Great Britain scheme may be brought
into operation in Northern Ireland.
That Order in Council was made on the
22nd March, 1937, and it has been presented to Parliament. The Northern
Ireland Act of 1936, however, provides
that the Order will cease to have effect
unless approved by both Houses of Parliament within 12 months from the date
upon which it came into force.
The reduction of the waiting period
under the general insurance scheme will
be welcomed, I am sure, by all Members
of the House. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) When unemployment insurance
was first made statutory in 1911, the
waiting period was fixed at six days, and,
with the exception of a short time after
the scheme was extended in 1920, it has
remained at six days, until this Order
came into operation on the 25th March.
It has been possible now to reduce the
waiting period to three days because of
the financial strength of the Unemployment Fund in Great Britain, and the reinsurance arrangements letween the
Exchequers of the United Kingdom and
Northern Ireland.
Unlike the waiting period, which has
been a feature of unemployment insurance since the beginning, "additional
days" of benefit under the general insurance scheme for persons with good
employment records were introduced for
the first time by the Act of 1934, the
1229 Unemployment Insurance-
Resolution Agreed to
4 MAY 1937

provisions on the subject contained in
that Act being reproduced now in
Section 32 of the Consolidation Act of
1936.
Under the law as it existed before it
was altered in the applicant's favour by
the Order which the House is now considering, a person who had been five years
in insurance at the time of his application
for benefit and had had a good employment record might become entitled to
"additional days" of benefit over and
above the normal period of 156 days'
benefit in a benefit year. The Act laid
down the formula for calculating the
number of these "additional days."
Paraphrasing the legal language of the
Act, the formula provided that three
"additional days" benefit might be added
for every five contributions paid in the
previous five years, less a discount of one
"additional day" for every five days'
benefit drawn. Under the terms of the
Order, the discount for benefit already
received is changed from one "additional
day" for every five days' benefit drawn
to one "additional day" for every eight
days' benefit drawn.
The effect of this change in the case, for
example, of a man who has worked for
an average of 42 weeks in each of the five
years before he claims benefit will be to
qualify him for 20 more "additional days"
of benefit. Taking another example,
a man who has worked on the average for
34 weeks in each of the five years could
not qualify for any "additional days"
under the old formula, but under the
Order he is entitled to 38.
Since the general insurance scheme
was remodelled in 1934 it is significant
that it has been possible in Great Britain
and (thanks to our re-insurance arrangements) in Northern Ireland also, to
amplify the provisions of the scheme
under no fewer than four heads. In
October, 1935, the allowance for a dependent child was increased from 2/- to 3/-;
in July, 1936, the contribution rates for
persons over 18 were lowered by 1d all
round, and this year we are able to halve
the waiting period and secure an increase
of the number of "additional days" of
benefit. I am sure that these continuous
improvements in the scheme will be
gratifying to all Members of the House,
and I am happy to think that my first
duty as Minister of Labour in connection
with the scheme is to move the approval
of this Order. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)

Unemployment Insurance
(Private Gardeners Inclusion) Order
(Northern Ireland), 1937.
Major SHILLINGTON: I beg to
move, "That the Order in Council made
by the Lords Justices for the Government of Northern Ireland on the 22nd
January, 1937, under Section 65 of the
Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern
Ireland), 1936, for the inclusion of employment as a private gardener among
insurable employments as employment in
agriculture, be hereby approved."
When the unemployment insurance
scheme was extended to agriculture,
gardeners employed in a trade or business, or by a local authority, were
covered, but private gardeners were excluded from its scope pending consideration by the Unemployment Insurance
Statutory Committee of the question of
their inclusion. The Committee reported
that it was desirable that they should
be brought into insurance under the
same conditions as agricultural workers,
and an Order providing for their inclusion was laid before the Parliament
of the United Kingdom and approved
by resolution of both Houses.
1233 Unemployment Insurance-

4 MAY 1937
Adjournment
Section 65 (1) (b) of the Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern Ireland),
1936, provides as follows:-
"In the event of an order being
made at any time under the Unemployment Insurance (Agriculture) Act,
1936 (passed by the Parliament of the
United Kingdom) for the purpose of
including any class of employment as
a private gardener among insurable
employments as employment in agriculture, then in that event there shall
apply to Northern Ireland so much as
the Governor of Northern Ireland by
Order in Council declares applicable
of the provisions contained in such
statutory order."
An Order in Council was made on
22nd January, 1937, including employment as a private gardener amongst
employments insurable under the Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern Ireland), 1936, as being employment in
agriculture, and the Order came into
operation on the 1st February, 1937the same date as that on which the corresponding Order in Great Britain came
into force. The Order in Council was
duly presented to Parliament, but it is
necessary that a resolution approving it
should be passed by each House, as provided for by Section 65 (4) of the Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern
Ireland), 1936. The inclusion of private
gardeners in insurance has been welcomed
by many employers, as well as by the
gardeners themselves.
The number of
insurance books issued to private
gardeners up to the 1st May is 1,164.

CLASS VII. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £14,521 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the

will come in course of payment during

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): It has been my practice
each year, in presenting the Estimates of
the Ministry of Commerce, to review in
brief the general trade position of Northern Ireland. The effects of the trade
depression have been so long-lived as to
mar at times the picture which in recent
years it has been my duty to present
to the Committee. To-day, however,
the outlook is sufficiently bright to make
my task in this respect much more congenial than on any previous occasion
during the life of the present Parliament.
Since the prosperity of Northern Ireland is necessarily bound up with that
of the United Kingdom as a whole, it
may be relevant for me to mention that
during 1936 the value of imports into
the United Kingdom increased by 12.3
per cent., and the value of exports by
3.5 per cent. over the figure for 1935.
During the same period industrial production in the United Kingdom is calculated to have increased by 9.7 per
cent., while the average number of
insured persons in employment in Great
Britain rose by 5 per cent.
Preliminary estimates of our own external trade during 1936 indicate that
Northern Ireland enjoyed its full share
in the increased activity of industry and
trade. The value of imports rose by 9.5
per cent., and of exports by 7 per cent.,
over the figures of the previous year,
with the result that our total external
trade is estimated to have approached in
value £100,000,000, as compared with
£92,000,000 in 1935. Further evidence
of the advance in economic activity is
provided by the fact that the two records
for the tonnage of vessels cleared and for
the tonnage of goods passing through
the port of Belfast, which I mentioned in
presenting last year's Estimates to the
Committee, were both broken during the
year 1936.
Furthermore, the average
number of insured persons in employment in Northern Ireland in 1936 exceeded the 1935 figure by 12,537 and the
figures for April of this year indicate
the probability of further improvements
during 1937.
The tonnage of vessels launched from
our shipyards during 1936 did not indeed attain the high level of 1935, but
the new orders which have been
announced during the last few months
are likely to maintain and even to increase the activity of our shipbuilding
industry for some considerable time.
Hon. Members will be aware that rearma-
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
5 MAY 1937
ment contracts have made no small
contribution towards this fortunate state
of affairs. Moreover, a new and kindred
industry has come amongst us, namely,
the aircraft industry, and I am confident
that the skill and enterprise of our
people will lead us on to triumphs in
this new field of activity comparable
with those we achieved on the sea. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
The outlook of the linen industry is
brighter than it has been for a number
of years. The value of linen exports of
all kinds from the United Kingdom in
1936 was the highest recorded since 1930
and showed an increase of £838,984,
representing 13 per cent. over the figure
for '1935. Last year I drew attention to
the expansion in British markets overseas which had been largely responsible
for the improvement in the linen export
trade. During 1936, while the position
of British markets was maintained,
foreign markets began to expand, particularly the United States, exports to
which reached the highest level for any
year since 1929. This progress in
foreign markets has been achieved in the
face of the several barriers which stand
to-day in the way of international trade,
and provides an indication of the
benefits likely to accrue to the linen
trade from any relaxation of these restrictions which we can secure.
While hon. Members of the Committee are, no doubt, familiar with the
commercial services undertaken by my
Ministry, I would like to remind them
that in times of trade expansion, as
well as of economic depression, my
Ministry is constantly watching for
opportunities to secure the advancement
of our linen trade, and, indeed, of the
overseas trade in any of the commodities
which are produced in Northern Ireland.
I am glad to be able to tell the Committee that not only the linen trade,
but
many other branches of trade in
Northern Ireland realise that the
Ministry can be of real service to them
in smoothing the way of export trade
and overcoming the many difficulties.
that beset it.
During the year under review the
Imperial Government, in pursuance of
its policy of promoting bilateral trade
agreements, entered into negotiations
with a number of foreign countries, and
•
in every case the Ministry has been
enabled to keep in touch with the progress of events and to put before the
Board of Trade the special desiderata of
trade in Northern Ireland. As an
example of the concessions which have
been gained in response to representations made by the Ministry, I may
mention that within the past few weeks
agreement was reached with the Cuban
Government for the removal of a
charge of 30 per cent. on the duty on
certain types of linen goods of United
Kingdom origin.

Hon. Members will recall that I have
alluded on previous occasions to the
benefits which Northern Ireland industries have derived from the Empire
agreements concluded at Ottawa.
Committee will be glad to learn that
not only are the benefits to be maintained, but also, as a result of a trade
agreement recently concluded with

affecting dress linens, cotton handkerchiefs, union goods, cigarettes and
certain types of soap, have been granted.
The examples I have quoted are such

will appreciate that Northern Ireland.
industries will derive indirect benefit

of
One of the major difficulties
restoring trade has been an increasing
tendency on the part of a number of
countries to regulate the volume of imports by means of quota restrictions. It
has been the constant endeavour of the
Ministry to obtain wherever possible
relaxation of these restrictions, and I am
glad to be able to tell the Committee
that our efforts, especially in the case of
flax yarns, have met with a considerable
measure of success.
So far I have spoken of our manufacturing industries. I might venture at
this stage to draw the attention of the
Committee to a source of income none
the less important because it is not a
product of the machine. I refer to the
tourist industry, which is growing from
year to year and the assets of which are
imponderable, consisting, as they do, of
the scenery and the natural charm of
Ulster. The extent of this industry has
hitherto passed unrecorded, but, with
the co-operation of the transport and
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
shipping companies, my Ministry has
recently been able to form some estimate
of its value. In 1936 its value is
calculated to have been in the region of
£1,500,000, roughly equal, for example,
to the value of the eggs exported from
Northern Ireland during the year 1935.
These figures indicate the importance of
the industry to all sections of the community, and it is in consideration of the
growth of the tourist traffic that the
Government has decided to recommend
to this Committee that the Tourist
Development Association should be
enabled to extend their activities
through an increase in the amount of
their annual grant.
As any Member of the Committee who
may have visited Olympia will have seen,
Northern Ireland was again fittingly
represented at the British Industries
Fair this year, and our stand had the
honour of a visit from their Majesties the
King and Queen. The reports reaching
me leave no doubt that both this exhibit
and
similar
a
one at Manchester,
organised last autumn in collaboration
with the Ministry of Agriculture,
achieved useful propaganda for our
produce.
I should add that the Ministry also
collaborated last year with the Linen Industry Research Association in staging an
exhibit at the Imperial Institute in
London, which covered the whole range
of linen manufacture from the seed to
the finished article. The exhibit, which
was educational in character, fulfilled
the useful purpose of demonstrating the
great diversity of uses to which linen can
be put and the high artistic standards
which science, linked with modern industrial practice, has made it possible to
achieve.
As a
matter of administrative convenience, arrangements have been made
for my Ministry to take over on behalf
of the Ministry of Agriculture the
organisation and display of exhibits in
Great Britain, which were formerly
staged by the latter Department.
Accordingly, in the Estimates now before
the Committee, provision has been made
not only for the normal exhibition
requirements of the Ministry of Commerce, but also for other exhibits such as
those at the Imperial Fruit Show and
the Fat Stock and Dairy Show, in which
the Ministry of Agriculture has in the
past been wont to participate.
Turning to fisheries, I regret that the
improvement in herring fishing which I
was able to report in presenting the
Ministry's Estimates for last year was
not wholly maintained during 1936.
Fortunately, from the point of view of
the fishermen, the falling-off in quantity
was largely offset by the higher average
price realised for the fish. As contrasted
with the total of some 38,000 cwts. of
herring landed in Northern Irish ports
during 1935, the landings in 1936 were
rather less than 27,000 cwts., that is to
say, there was a decrease of just a little
under 30 per cent. in the quantity of the
fish landed in the latter year. On the
other hand, the total value of the
herring landed in 1936 was £13,000, or
only some £1,700 less than the value of
the landings in 1935. From a monetary
point of view, therefore, the results in
the two years were not dissimilar,
although the share of the landings in
1936 attributable to boats belonging to
Northern Irish owners was markedly less
than in 1935.
The returns which have been made to
me show that, whereas out of the
£14,725 represented by the whole of the
landings in 1935, £12,453 represented
the earnings of Northern Irish boats,
only £7,581 out of the total of £13,008
represented by the 1936 landings are to
be attributed to locally-owned boats.
The balance of the total receipts in each
of the two years is accounted for by the
landings of visiting ring net boats. In
this connection I should, perhaps,
remind the Committee that, in consonance with a recommendation made to
it by the Northern Ireland Area Committee the Herring Industry Board
issued a direction at the beginning of
the herring fishing in Northern Ireland
last year prohibiting the landing in
Northern Irish ports up to 11th July of
any herring caught by ring nets.
The purpose of the Board's direction
was to protect our local drift net boats
from outside competition in the local
fresh market during the portion of the
season when the herring are unsuitable
for curing, and when the fishermen can,
therefore, only look to the local market
for the disposal of their catches. After
11th July, when the prohibition of landings from ring net boats came to an end.
Ministry of Commerce 1242
Estimates-
5 MAY 1937
Scottish ringers, some of which had
previously been landing their catches in
the Isle of Man, commenced to land at
Ardglass, where the fish found a ready
market amongst the curers. These ring
net boats, I should like the Committee
to bear in mind, conducted their fishing
operations not in the waters immediately
adjoining the Northern Irish coast, but
in those lying only a few miles off the
Manx coast. A few of our own boats,
which had hitherto fished only the traditional type of net known as drift net,
equipped themselves with ring nets
during the latter part of the season. The
results derived by them were, I am sorry
to say, rather disappointing.
The question of the comparative merits
of the drift net and the ring net is one
which time alone can properly decide.
The experience gained during the past
two years has, undoubtedly, shown that,
given the herring shoals in sheltered
waters, the ring net can be used much
more effectively than the drift net. Conditions, however, are incalculable in
advance and it may be that the final
solution of the problem for our fishermen
will prove to be equipment of the boats
for both types of fishing, leaving the
selection of the type on any particular
occasion to the circumstances of the
moment. Beyond this problem of the
net, however, there is the further
problem of finding a market for large
catches during the early part of the
season when the herring are unsuitable
for curing, and may only be disposed of
in our local market. In the view of the
Northern Ireland Area Committee this
second problem can best be met by a
repetition of last year's ban on the landings from ring net boats, and the committee has made a recommendation to
the Herring Industry Board that such
landings should be prohibited up to 12th
July this year. That recommendation
was an unanimous one on the part of the
committee, which is comprised of representatives of fishermen, curers and
freshers, and I am informed that the
Herring Board have adopted the recommendation.
Although, as I have said, the 1936
season was a relatively disappointing one
in so far as our summer herring fishing
was concerned, its shortcomings in this
respect were, to some extent, offset by
the exceptionally favourable results
experienced by Northern Irish boats in
the Maryport herring fishing from the
middle of October to Christmas last year.
I am informed that the earnings of the
twenty-six Northern Ireland boats which
engaged in that fishing amounted in the
aggregate to a sum of £8,000, which,
spread over the entire number, averaged
approximately £40 per man. These
earnings formed a very much needed
supplement to those derived from the
summer season.
Apart from herring fishing the year
1936 may be regarded as satisfactory in
so far as our sea fisheries are concerned.
The total value of the sea fish, including
shell fish but excluding salmon, landed
during the year was approximately
£51,000 as compared with £40,000 in
1935. This increase of £11,000 is
attributable to increased landings of
whiting in County Down ports and of
plaice and cod by fishermen working
from ports along our Northern coast. It
is true, however, that a share in the landing of whitings must be credited to a few
Scottish boats which fished from
Ardglass during the early part of last
winter. Measured in terms of weight the
comparison between the two years is
even more favourable since the total of
22,000 cwts. in 1935 was increased by 50
per cent. in 1936.
The statistics available in regard to
the capture of salmon and trout do not
admit of an exact comparison as between
one year and another, but they do disclose a slight decrease in 1936 as compared with 1935. Against this, however,
can be set an increase in the export of
eels which rose by approximately 30 per
cent, over that in the previous year.
The past year has seen further considerable progress in the supply of
electricity to the public throughout
Northern Ireland and the results indicate that the policy of the Government
in promoting the co-ordination of such
supplies has been more than justified.
Returns for the year 1936 furnished
by statutory undertakings show that
approximately 169 million units were
sold as compared with 142 million units
in the previous year, representing an increase of over 27 million units or 19 per
cent. The extent of the development
during the past five years is strikingly
illustrated by comparison with the num-

are
The functions of my Ministry with
which I have dealt up to this point
are those which are best known and the
effect of which are probably most readily
felt by the body politic. There remain
other statutory functions which
carried on from year to year, I am glad
to say, with benefit to the public
generally. It may be of interest to the
Committee to learn that during the year
1936, 83 new companies were registered,
having a nominal capital amounting in
the aggregate to
to £1,071,900. These
figures indicate to some extent the
revival in commercial activity since the
year 1934 during which 76 new companies were registered with a total
nominal capital of only £299,100. The
total number of joint stock companies on
the Register at 31st December, 1936, was
1,716 with a total nominal capital of
£68,272,000.
Another indication of the improvement in the economic position may be
found in the remarkable extension of the
activities of the building societies. These
societies have been largely responsible
for the increased number of the smaller
type of privately-owned dwelling-house
which has brought a great boon in the
form of healthier and more attractive
surroundings to the city worker. During
the year 1936 the crosss-Channel building
societies, which have been in the van of
progress in recent years, advanced in
Northern Ireland the sum of £1,145,475
as compared with £701,929 advanced
during 1935, and by the end of the year
1936 the amount outstanding on loans
for house purchase had risen to
£2,342,369 from £1,570,477 at the end
of 1935. It is interesting to recall that
in 1922 the amount outstanding on loans.
made by building societies for the construction or purchase of houses in Northern Ireland was £253,000.
Finally, I wish to refer briefly to the
functions assigned to the Ministry under
the Industrial Assurance Acts. Industrial Assurance Acts provide cheap
and efficient machinery for the settlement of disputes between policy holders
and the companies and societies which
transact industrial assurance business in
Northern Ireland. The importance of
this form of small-scale saving to the
community is illustrated by the total
amount of the premiums usually
amounting to a few pence per weekcontributed during the year. The
figures for 1935, for example, reached
the very large total of £1,075,636.
During the year 1936 no fewer than 835
disputes were referred to the Commissioner, representing an increase of
213 cases as compared with the previous
year. The volume of work involved has
increased steadily from year to year, and
this increase is proof of the confidence
reposed in the system of arbitration provided. Provision is therefore made for
the continuance of the arrangement
whereby the assistance of a practising
barrister is secured in order to deal with
the large number of cases presented for
adjudication. I beg to move.

Mr. CHRISTIE: If I am in order I
would move a reduction in this Estimate
of £100, in order to draw the attention
of the Committee to the fact that the
seaside resort of Castlerock is being
denied a supply of electricity by the
Antrim Supply Company. I listened
very carefully to the right hon. Gentleman's remarks on the electricity question,
and I was particularly struck with one,
that was that the Antrim Company and
the subsidiary company are responsible
for County Antrim and South Derry.
He left out North Derry. That is
exactly the case. They are ignoring
North Derry, and particularly the seaside resort of Castlerock, a residential
area with a very good tourist influx in the
summer. The valuation of Castlerock
to-day is over £3,200, which, with new
valuations on some houses that are being
built and on the Orange Hall, when completed, will bring the total valuation up
to £3,500. Are we living in an age of
progress or are we not?
Mr. BEATTIE: No.
Mr. CHRISTIE: The supply is within
two and a half miles of this resort, and
yet the company, who have the exclusive
right to go into Castlerock to supply it
with electricity, refuse to do so unless
they get a guarantee from the residents
that it will be a paying proposition. I
had quite a lengthy correspondence with

Can you imagine the Borough Council
of Coleraine going to the residents of
Portstewart and saying, "We will not
put gas in Portstewart unless you give
us a guarantee that it will be a paying
proposition." Can you imagine any
shopkeeper going into Castlerock and saying, "I will start a drapery or grocery
shop, or even a public-house if I can get
a licence, on condition that you,
residents of Castlerock, will guarantee me
a return commensurate with my outlay."
The thing is absurd. The Minister, in
the course of his remarks, referred to the
exhibitions at Olympia. Unfortunately
I did not see the exhibition at Olympia
this year, so that I can neither praise nor
criticise it, but I saw a previous exhibition at Olympia, arranged by his Department, that would have been a disgrace to
a country shopkeeper. I mentioned it at
a meeting of the Agricultural Committee
of the County Council of Londonderry
when I returned from Olympia.
I regret that no mention was made by
the Minister in his speech of the sugges
tion put forward by that eminent Ulsterman, Sir Lynden Macassey, with
reference to the appointment of a High
Commissioner for Ulster in London. We
are living to-day in an age when business
does not come to any concern. We have
to go out and look for business, and I
hold that Ulster would be well advised
to go out and look for more business than
they are at present enjoying. I think
the proposal put forward by Sir Lynden
Macassey should be taken full advantage
of by the Government of Northern
Ireland. It is said that such an appointment will interfere with our relations
with the Imperial Parliament. I fail to
see how it would. Scotland has its office
in London, and the Dominions have
offices in London pushing their wares.
But first we want in the Ministry of
Commerce-
Mr. BEATTIE: More light.
Mr. CHRISTIE: Not more light, but
more energy and more thrust. It is all
very well for the Ministry of Commerce
to be run by civil servants, for whom I
have every admiration, but there are
things they do not know, and I think it
is a business man you want to look after
business. I quite realise that the Minister is one of the outstanding men in
commerce in Northern Ireland, but I also
realise he has not the time to devote to
the duties of the Ministry of Commerce.
In my opinion it should be a whole time
job. It is a matter of regret to me that
the Minister saw fit to decline the office
of Minister of Finance, or even to carry
on his post as Financial Secretary to that
Ministry, but if he had not the time to
discharge those duties I fail to see how he
has the necessary time to devote to the
Ministry of Commerce. I would like to
see him devoting his whole time and
energy to the Ministry, and if he did so
our electricity, whether supplied by the
Board or the Antrim Company, and our
fisheries, whether salmon or deep sea,
would bring Northern Ireland the
prominence in the commercial world that
it deserves.

Mr. NIXON: The Minister, as has
already been stated, is certainly well
qualified to speak on commerce and
industry. He painted a very rosy picture
of the position of Northern Ireland.
Everything has improved, and as the
prospects are so good, according to the
Minister, I am quite sure the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education will have a good message for
the teachers to-morrow. There is one
industry on the Government benches that
the Minister did not mention. It has
been very progressive lately. There were
never more vacancies for positions since
I came into Parliament than there have
been recently, and the right men have
got there every time. That is an industry the Ministry did not tell us about.
There is still a vacancy, and I have heard
of a man who is fighting for it until he
is black in the face. However, we will
pass over that.
What I often wonder at when things
are so rosy, and when there is an improvement in trade, as we know there is, is
that neither the Minister of Commerce
nor any other Minister has ever thought it
worth his while to explain to this House
and to the country why it is that the proportion of unemployed in Northern
Ireland at the present time is more than
twice as much as the proportion in Great
Britain, notwithstanding the rosy picture
that has been painted. Why is it higher
here than in any other part of Great
Britain except Wales. I would like the
Minister to reconcile that well-known and
admitted fact with the very rosy picture
he has painted here this afternoon of
conditions in Northern Ireland.
The Minister referred to the tourist
traffic, which is undoubtedly increasing,
but I think he is stretching it too far
when he asks us to believe that the
Government is in any sense responsible
for that increase in tourist traffic. For
one thing, they have not the same transport facilities when they come here that
they used to have, owing to the Road
Transport Act that was introduced and
passed by this Government. There are
certainly more tourists coming here, first,
because the population of England is
increasing, and secondly, because there
is more prosperity in England and more
money to spend on tourist traffic, but this
Government has nothing to do with that.
They are not giving the encouragement
they should give to tourists.
When I was making a tour to Australia
some time ago I never saw anything about
Ulster in any tourist literature or book
except one very good article by the Minister of Commerce, which I saw in a book
on the ship. I saw advertisements about
Norway, Sweden, Germany, and other
countries, but no literature about
Northern Ireland except this one very
good article by the Minister of Commerce in one book. I have suggested
before that if the Government were to
get pictures of the Giant's Causeway and
other famous beauty spots of Northern
Ireland and send them to hotels in
America, the Colonies, and England they
would be glad to show them, and nothing
would bring home to the people in those
countries the attractions of Ulster more
than a picture of the Giant's Causeway
and other outstanding places like that.
There is no use in the Government pretending, as they are always pretending, that
everything that happens is due to their
efforts. I said once before that if a hen
laid an egg with two yokes the Government would pretend they got it to do so,
and they would cackle more about it than
the hen itself.
With regard to electricity, I am sorry
to tell the Minister that his speech was not
fair. Every speech the Minister has
made since the Electricity Board was set
up was not fair, and I have heard that
commented upon. Only for the Belfast
Corporation where would your electricity
undertaking be. Is not the Belfast Corporation responsible for generating most
of the electricity you buy?
Mr. BARBOUR: And they do it
admirably.
Mr. NIXON: Yes. The Belfast Corporation are responsible for purchasing
the machinery, for all the engineering
work, and for supplying the electricity,
and all the Electricity Board do is to purchase it at the cost of production.
Eventually, the cost of production had to
be fixed according to what the Department thought right, and not according to
what the Corporation thought right.
Tell me of any other wholesale firm in the
Ministry of Commerce- 1252
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
world which compels the producer, by
Act of Parliament, to sell at cost of production, and then takes credit for the
way they are distributing it. Furthermore-and I have never said this before,
because I was a member of the Electricity
Committee, and I am not now-the members of the Electricity Committee of the
Belfast Corporation receive no pay of any
kind or description. All they do get is
abuse. The members of the Electricity
Board are paid for not doing half as
much. I do not mean the permanent
officials; I mean the members of the
Board.
I read where one member of the Board,
who is getting two hundred guineas a
year for attending a meeting occasionally,
was patting himself on the back because
at some little ceremony at Dungannon he
gave the people present a cup of tea out
of his own pocket. Although I never
personally spent a penny on such
a thing, there was always someone else
who could better afford it who was big
enough to spend money in this way. That
includes the present chairman of the
committee, and he was not always patting
himself on the back for giving a cup of
tea to people, like the member of the
Board who did so at Dungannon. He
did not tell us what he was getting out
of it.
I supported the Bill for setting up this
Electricity Board, and I said it was time
it was set up. I think it was time to
take them over and co-ordinate them. I
am not condemning that. I would say
the Board did pretty well. But the
Minister gives them too much praise at
the expense of Belfast Corporation, the
body that laid the foundation of the
whole thing. It was laid long before my
time. One of the principal men at laying the foundation was the great Lord
Pirrie himself, and it was through his
instrumentality that the power station
was put where it is. Every expert that
I have spoken to on the subject says it
could not have been put in a better place.
The Corporation Electricity Committee
never bring across experts to advise
them. They rely upon their own engineers, and they have not made any mistakes up to the present. There was a
time when they did bring across experts,
but they became wise and appointed
proper engineers themselves. I think it
would be a good thing for the Minister
to consult his own engineers. I happen
to know, not of my own knowledge, but
from what I have heard people say, that
the Ministry have very good, reliable,
and competent engineers, just as good as
could be got across the water at very
high figures. I have heard that in
London, I have heard it in Bournemouth,
and I have heard it in other places.
Sometimes these men who are brought
across the water have a spurious reputation; you may have just as good men
at home. I do not want the Minister
to take it that I am belittling the work
of the Department. I am not. But I
future
think that in the Minister's
speeches he should be a little more
generous to the much-abused Belfast
Corporation. If the Minister had to
start the electricity scheme from the
foundation, without the power station at
the harbour, he would be a very long
time in building it up.
Mr. BARBOUR: I never said anything reflecting on the Electricity Department of Belfast Corporation.
Mr. NIXON: I hope I did not charge

What I charged him with was giving all

have gone to the Belfast Electricity

from that matter now.

the Chairman were here he would rule

for the

week or so much a year." What those

As to the progress that the Minister

advanced by the hon. Member for Woodvale (Mr. Nixon). I was impressed by

to take the activities of the building

I regard that view with considerable
misgivings on other points as well as on
those advanced by the hon. Member for
Woodvale in regard to the exploitation

the building societies. I should like to
put this forward-that as the Minister.
of Commerce the right hon. Gentleman
is charged with the responsibility of
seeing that protection is given to the

of the value of which the building
society makes itself responsible, leaving
the unfortunate person to find the

The Government, in my opinion,

Estimates--

certain commodities in Northern Ireland,

Imperial connection. The Minister has

a
are

I am afraid the rural areas are not going

the

Next I should like in particular to deal
with the electricity supply to Castlerock
which was raised by the hon. Member for
North Derry. As I tried to bring out
in the course of the debate the various
areas in Northern Ireland are served by
different undertakings. The Corporation
of Belfast look after the electricity requirements in their own area, the Electricity Board the requirements in its own
area, and then Antrim and South Derry
are looked after by the Antrim Electricity
Supply Company. The Special Order
granted to the Antrim Electricity Distribution Company, Limited, provided for
the development of all the principal
towns and villages in the extensive area
granted to the company. The company
is still proceeding with the carrying out
of this programme of development,
which, however, does not include the
village of Castlerock. Had there been
a demand for a supply to this village at
the time the application for the Order
was being made, it would have been open
to the residents to make representations
with a view to securing the inclusion of
the village in the company's programme
of initial development. Under the
Electric Lighting (Clauses) Act, 1899,
the company's obligations with regard to
villages and districts not specially provided for in the Special Order are that
they must provide a supply if and when
they are offered a gross return of not
less than 20 per cent. for a period of at
least three years on the capital cost involved. I should explain that this 20
per cent. return is intended to cover not
only the cost of extensions, but also the
cost of the current at the generating
station, as well as the cost of transmission and transformation.
I am informed that the company
recently carried out a canvass in the
village of Castlerock, and out of approximately eighty premises within a reasonable distance of the most suitable site
for a sub-station, only thirty-five owners
indicated their preparedness to take a
supply, and the estimated revenue from
these applicants is approximately 13 per
cent. on the estimated cost of extending
the company's main transmission line
from Coleraine and providing the necessary sub-station and distribution mains.

With regard to the suggestion that
Castlerock should be supplied from a
small local generating station, there are
both legal and practical difficulties.
Since the passing of the Electric Lighting Act of 1909 it is not lawful for any
local authority, company, or person, to
provide a supply in the area of an
authorised undertaker unless empowered
by Parliament to do so. The cost of
obtaining the necessary powers would be
relatively high, particularly if the
application were opposed. It is obvious
that such a scheme would not be in the
interests of the Castlerock residents in
the long run, since it could only provide
for electric lighting, and could not hope
to give the inhabitants the benefit of a
full electric service for heating and cooking, such as is being given by the Antrim
Company or the Electricity Board.
Moreover, the creation of a vested
interest in Castlerock at the present time
would not enhance the prospects of the
provision of such a comprehensive service
in the future.

was

the
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can give
House information as to the ownership
and control of the cinema which is
carried on in the Town Hall, Enniskillen; whether it is registered in Northern Ireland or elsewhere; and whether
the manager of this concern also acts
as hall-keeper and janitor to the Enniskillen Urban District Council, and, if
so, whether he can state the amount of
time this man devotes to his duty on
behalf of the local authority and to the
cinema company; whether his job with
the local authority is pensionable, and,
if so, whether it is in order for such a
person to hold a dual appointment;
whether he is aware of the fact that
allegations have been made as to the
low standard of wages paid in this firm,
and if this, in conjunction with the facts
already submitted to the House regarding various other firms, would not
warrant a full investigation being held,
with a view to some definite action being
taken by the Minister for the creation
of negotiating machinery for the regulation of wages and working conditions
throughout the whole cinema industry.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Major
Shillington): I am informed by my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Home
Affairs, that the cinema which is carried
on in the Town Hall, Enniskillen, is
owned and controlled by the Dundealgan
Electric Theatre Co., Ltd., which has
registered offices in Dundalk, and that
the manager of the cinema also acts as
hall-keeper and janitor to the Enniskillen
Urban District Council, but it is not
known how much time he devotes to his
various duties. He is not, so far as the
Ministry is aware, a pensionable officer
of the local authority. It is understood
that the present manager has been acting
in that capacity as well as hall-keeper
and janitor for many years and the
Minister of Home Affairs sees no
objection to his holding the dual appointments.
As regards the latter part of the hon.
Member's question which relates more
specifically to my Ministry, I have no
information as to the rates of wages
paid by the firm mentioned. On the
general question of wages and other conditions in the cinema industry, I have
nothing to add to the answer given to
a similar question by the hon. Member
on 27th April of this year.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Is the Minister
satisfied that it is the correct policy to
be followed by the Government that a
gentleman should act for the local
authority and also act for a private firm
in a dual capacity?
Major SHILLINGTON: Of course that
matter really comes more under the control of the Ministry of Home Affairs. I
understand this man in question is the
servant of the local authority there.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I will raise this
matter on the Adjournment.

INFIRMARY.

whether two relieving officers were recently suspended and dismissed; whether

suspension and what action was taken

tenders for supplies to poor law and
infirmary institutions have also to submit samples; whether he can state what
becomes of these samples, and give the

samples are eventually removed.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The former
workhouse master was indicted and convicted in respect of sums totalling
£474 6s 6d. I understand that the
Guardians have made good the losses
where these have been substantiated.
Two relieving officers were recently
suspended and dismissed as a result of
irregularities in connection with the distribution of small sums ordered by the
Board of Guardians as extra Christmas
relief. The intended recipients subsequently received the sums due to them.
In certain cases persons tendering for
supplies to poor law and similar institutions are required to lodge samples.
These are taken into stock if the tender
is accepted, or if the tender is not
accepted, are returnable to the tenderer.

hon. Gentleman have an inquiry into it?
