RIGHT TO VISIT
BELFAST INFIRMARY.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if
the Belfast Board of Guardians have
recently passed resolutions restricting
the right of Guardians and Protestant
missionaries from visiting old-age pensioners ill in the institution except by
special authority of the master, or otherwise, and whether he will state the
object of placing difficulties in the way
of these people.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The admission
of visitors to inmates in poor law institutions is covered by regulations made by
the Poor Law Commissioners many years
ago. The operation of these regulations
has been found entirely satisfactory in
practice, and I am furnishing the hon.
Member with a copy of them for his
information.
The only resolution recently passed by
the Guardians having any bearing on the
matter imposed no new restrictions of
any general character, and operated only
to instruct the master to exercise his
discretion under the rules to refuse
admission to a particular individual who,
in their opinion, had been making a
habit of visiting at irregular hours without legitimate business and creating
disturbance.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not only by visiting at irregular hours and at night that
larcencies and frauds can be detected,
and does not a missionary living in Irwin
Avenue, in the right hon. Gentleman's
own constituency, who never did anything worse in the institution than read
the Bible, have to make special application to visit a pensioner he wants to
see?
I
Sir BASIL BROOKE: That is
entirely a domestic matter. During the
influenza epidemic the Guardians,
understand, took steps to prevent any
person visiting the institution. I think

and will supply a copy of the rules.

MINISTRY OF EDUCATION.
Motion made, and Question proposed:

The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): When I
presented the Education Estimates to
the Committee a year ago, I was able to
point out that the total of Votes 1 and 2
amounted to just over £2,000,000. The
announcement made a few days later in
last year's Budget concerning the
partial restoration of the cuts in
teachers' salaries necessitated the presentation of a Supplementary Estimate
in the autumn, amounting to £42,400,
so that the full sum voted by the Committee last year for education came to
£2,045,775. In order to ascertain the
net amount borne by the Exchequer the
education levy must be deducted from
this total, that is, a sum of approximately £140,000 last year, so that we
arrive at a net total contribution from
Parliament for education equivalent to
£1,905,775. That figure gives us the
cost for 1936-37.

TELLER FOR THE NOES-

This year I have to ask the Committee
for a substantially larger sum, the full
amount being £2,155,849, that is,
£69,247 for Vote 1 and £2,086,602 for
Vote 2. This is an increase of £110,074
on last year's figure, including the
Supplementary Estimates. The greater
part of the increase is due, firstly, to
the balance still to be paid in the partial
restoration of the "cuts," "about £40,000,
and, secondly, the increased grant to the
education authorities, amounting to
£57,000; the increase is, of course, consequent on the revaluation of the
Province, which has raised the yield of
the eightpenny rate very considerably.
Against this, of course, I must offset the
amount contributed by the ratepayers in
the education levy of one shilling in the
pound on the new valuation, the total
of which has risen from £140,000 to
£235,000. If this amount be deducted
from the sum of the present Estimates,
the balance, £1,920,849, represents the
net contribution from the Parliamentary
Vote to education. This, being compared
with the figure I have given above for
last year, shows an increase of only
£15,074. If we add to the amount of
the education levy the estimated amount
to be raised this year from the rates,
omitting £64,000 of derating grants,
and deducting receipts from students'
fees, etc., about £48,000, we arrive at a
figure of approximately £340,000 to set
against the net amount falling on the
Exchequer. Thus we see that the contributions from public funds to education are approximately 85 per cent. from
the Exchequer and 15 per cent. from
the rates. The average rate for education
over the whole Province, including the
education levy, is equivalent to 1s. 5d.
in the pound.
Turning to Vote 1, the salaries and expenses of the Ministry of Education, I
may say that the sum required this year
Ministry of Education
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
is £69,247, which is an increase of
£3,081 over last year's Estimate. The
extra money is due chiefly to reorganisation of the salaries and the normal effect
of progressive awards of increments to the
staff.
Since the beginning of October
last the Ministry has moved out of Stormont to new offices in Ormeau Avenue,
which were previously occupied by certain
departments of the Ministries of Finance
and Labour. This change has led to an
increase of the number of individuals
whose salaries are borne on this Vote.
Hon. Members will observe that the total
staff now consists of 145 individuals
instead of 134, an increase of 11. These
11 are made up of four engaged in
typing, two messengers, and five cleaners.
With the exception of one messenger, all
these persons were included in last year's
Estimates of the Ministries of Finance
and Labour, but the Ministry of Education is now responsible for the provision
of all the typing, messenger, and cleaning services accommodated in Tyrone
House, a portion of which is still occupied
by officials of the Ministries of Labour
and Finance.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I take it that
these people have been absorbed by the
Ministry of Education?
Mr. ROBB: Yes. The posts formerly
included in the Estimates of the other
Ministries are now more appropriate to
this Ministry, and their cost has been
transferred to this Vote, but recovered,
as appears at the end of Subhead A4,
page 110, from the other Ministries concerned. The provision of money made in
our Vote is confined, therefore, to the
proportionate part cost of these services,
which are given to the Ministry of Education. The only actual increase in the
numbers of the staff is a messenger, this
post being in respect of a door-keeper at
the main entrance of Tyrone House.
Vote 2, amounting to £2,086,602, for
educational services, is, of course, the
main expenditure of the Ministry, and,
as I have already intimated, it shows an
increase over last year's Estimate of
£106,993. Whatever the causes of this
increase, some hon. Members will, no
doubt, be inclined to express surprise
and perhaps even dismay, and we may
hear charges of extravagance and wastefulness. I have, therefore, made a rough
analysis of the items on which this large
sum is expended. If we begin by deducting from it, first, the amount of the
university grant, which has stood at the
uniform figure of £40,000 for a number
of years, and secondly, the amount of the
grant made under Section 76 of the
Education Act of 1923 to local education
authorities, amounting to £237,000, we
have left a sum of £1,812,802. A careful analysis shows that practically the
whole of this sum, 97 per cent. of it to be
exact, is distributed in payment of
teachers' salaries in all grades of
recognised schools and in contribution
towards teachers' pensions. If, therefore, economies are to be effected, this can
be done in practically only two ways,
that is, either by reducing the number of
individual teachers on the pay roll, or by
reducing the amount of their emoluments. I take it that, in view of the
representations made to me recently in
this House regarding the size of some of
the classes in our schools, no hon. Member wishes to see the numbers of the
teaching staffs reduced, nor do I think.
that another cut in teachers' salaries
would meet with a favourable reception
from hon. Members, but apart from
these two courses, I can see no other
method whereby any appreciable
economies can be brought about, for I
assume that nobody would desire to see
the university grant reduced or to cut
down the grants to the local authorities,
and thereby throw an increased burden
on the rates. Unless, therefore, some
other way of economy can be found, and
I am not aware of any other courses open
to the Ministry, I am not clear how any
substantial economies in this Vote can be
effected.
I had occasion last year to refer to a
decline in the school population, and I
must tell the Committee that, notwithstanding the increase in the total population of the Province disclosed at the
census recently taken, the number of the
child-population indicated by the enrolment in the public elementary schools has
not moved upwards since. The average
number of pupils on rolls in 1936 was
199,692, which was a decrease of 3,633 on
the figure recorded for 1935. Happily,
however, owing to an improvement in
regularity of attendance, the average
attendance of pupils has not diminished
Ministry of Education 1294
Estimates-
6 MAY 1937
in proportion, the drop being only one of
1,562 pupils. I may
say that the
relative decline in child population in
Northern Ireland, while it appears to be
substantially less than has recently been
recorded in the Irish Free State, is
almost exactly the same as that reported
for Scotland over the same period, but
for the reason I have given, our drop
in actual attendance is relatively much
smaller. The percentage of regularity
of attendance for last year for elementary
school pupils of compulsory school age was
86.79, compared with 85.8 in 1935, and
while this improvement is gratifying as
far as it goes, it ought, in the opinion of
the Ministry, to be much higher, and I
would again call the attention of school
attendance committees and others concerned to the need for increased efforts
to improve the attendance. I may point
out that an increase of only one per cent.
in regularity of attendance would fully.
make up for the diminution in the child
population to which I have referred, and
afford employment to those teachers who
find difficulty in securing posts after
leaving the training college.
Turning to the different heads of the
Estimates, I may state that the sum required under Subhead Al for training
colleges shows a slight increase over last
year of £475, due altogether to the
restoration of the cut in salaries inflicted
on the teaching staffs in 1931. As the
greater part of the expenditure is in
respect of the numbers of students at
present in the colleges, any savings that
may accrue from a diminution in the
number to be admitted next session will
not take practical effect until next year's
Vote. The position as to the employment of male ex-students remains unsatisfactory, but the measures taken by
the Ministry to increase the proportion
of men assistants in large schools, as well
as the new departure in regard to the
need for employing substitutes in cases
of teachers absent through illness will, it
is hoped, lead to increased demands for
the services of teachers now unemployed.
There is also a possibility that the establishment of classes for unemployed juveniles
under the Unemployment Act, which is
at present under the consideration of a
committee set up by the Minister of
Labour, will lead to a demand for new
teachers. The Ministry is keeping a
careful watch on the situation, and will
take every practicable means to make it
easier for these young men to find suitable employment.
The special refresher courses for
elementary teachers, held at Stranmillis
College during the summer holidays last
year, were very well attended and proved

continued this year, and arrangements
have been made for courses in ten subjects, to be given by professors and
lecturers of standing. Owing to a change
in the regulations for maintenance of
teachers attending courses, a saving of
£200 is estimated under this head.
Owing to the slight decline in the numbers of pupils at school, allowance is made
in the subhead for teachers' salaries for
a small decrease in the number of
teachers. Allowing for this, provision

has been made for an increase over last
year of £30,000, the greater part of which
is due to the partial restoration of the
cut." The Committee will probably
remember that the restoration took effect
from 1st July last in the elementary
schools, so that the amount required for
a whole year was not included in the
Supplementary Estimate voted last
autumn. The increase in the capitation
payments, paid annually in arrear, comes
altogether into this year's Estimate, and
there is a balance of four months' salary
at the revised rates to be included.
sum of these increases is about £29,000.
The new provision for the employment
of substitute teachers is estimated to
require £6,000. Under arrangements
agreed upon with the representatives of
the teaching profession, substitutes for
sick teachers will now be required to take
up duty after a week, instead of a month,
of consecutive absence. The whole cost,
formerly borne by the sick teacher who
was unable to attend his school, will now
be shared by the Ministry, who will pay
two-thirds of the substitute's salary,
while the teacher will be responsible for
the other third only.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does this apply
only to teachers in primary schools?
Mr. ROBB: Yes, to primary school
teachers only. This measure will, it is
believed, make for greater efficiency in
the school work, which has, in the past,
been interrupted seriously by the prolonged absences, through illness, of mem-
Ministry of Education
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
bers of the staffs, and it will, at the same
time, create greater opportunities for
employment for teachers just out of the
training college. The hardship imposed
upon teachers laid aside by serious illness
in the necessity of providing substitutes
entirely at their own expense, which has
hitherto been the rule, will be greatly
lessened by this new arrangement.
Apart from these measures for improving the staffing of the schools when
teachers are laid aside by sickness, the
Ministry has not been unmindful of the
more general question of the sufficiency
of the number of teachers employed in
the schools. This question has for many
months past been the subject of conferences with representatives of the
teaching profession. The building of
large schools of 600 to 1,000 pupils in
the last few years has accentuated the
difficulty of the problem. When our
elementary schools were much smaller
and rarely exceeded 300 pupils in average
attendance, the arrangements for staffing
were tolerably sufficient to secure
efficiency, but the establishment of these
very large schools of over 600 pupils, and
particularly of schools confined to senior
pupils, has brought out the fact that a
more
generous system of staffing was
needed. While the proportion of 45
pupils to each assistant teacher has continued in force, the Ministry has provided additional assistants in schools,
where practical subjects such as woodwork, cookery, etc., are taught; a change
has also been made whereby the number
of assistants on the staff has been related
to the yearly, instead of the quarterly
average, with the possibility of recognising additional temporary teachers should
the numbers show an unexpected increase
in the course of the year. The measures
were adopted experimentally, and the
Ministry is not assured that a satisfactory
arrangement has yet been discovered;
the question of further measures is at
present under consideration.
In this connection I should like to
refer to the question of unduly large
classes in some of the Belfast schools,
which was pressed upon me some days
ago by the hon. and gallant Member for
St. Anne's (Major McCormick), as well
as by other hon. Members. I then
promised to inquire into any cases he
might give me of unduly large classes,
and the list which he was kind enough to
communicate to me has been the subject
of a special report from the director of
education for the city. I do not propose
to weary the Committee with the explanations received in each of the cases put
forward, but I shall be happy to supply
the hon. and gallant Member with a copy.
Suffice it to say that the director's report
shows that all such cases of abnormally
large classes are mainly due to the fact
that the Belfast Education Committee
has not yet completed its programme for
the provision of new school accommodation in the city, and that there is still,
unhappily, a good deal of overcrowding
in many schools. It is scarcely appreciated by the public to what extent the
school provision in Belfast has been reorganised in the last few years, and I do
not think that people are aware of the
complex nature of the problems set before
the Education Committee by the adjustment of the attendance to the new conditions. It must be remembered that,
according as these fine new buildings are
completed, the old inferior accommodation is withdrawn by the closing of the
former schoolhouses, so that the opening
of new schools does not usually mean an
actual increase in school places available
for the population. Hence, conditions of
attendance and distribution of pupils are
still abnormal, and here and there overcrowding and inconvenience must still
continue. In addition to providing new
accommodation to replace obsolete buildings, the Committee has had to meet the
demands of the rapid growth of the
suburbs. The migration of the population from one part of the city to another,
according as subsidy houses are built,
adds to the problem, and already several
new or reconditioned schools have had to
be enlarged on this account. I would
ask, therefore, for a little indulgence and
patience on the part of the parents in this
matter of unduly large classes. Every
effort is being made to adjust the numbers as well as the circumstances of each
case admit, and, as I have already said,
the Ministry is studying the question of
making a change in the general conditions
of staffing.
As regards the quality and attainments of the teaching staffs, two important changes in regulations have been
made recently. In future all new
candidates for the post of junior
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
6 MAY 1937
assistant mistress must have been trained
in a recognised training college, instead
of merely passing an examination in
some specified subjects; and secondly, all
members of religious communities wishing to become teachers must have
complied with a similar condition of
training. In both cases due allowance
will be made for the rights of existing
teachers and suitable transitional
measures have been adopted to meet the
cases of persons in process of qualifying
under the rules hitherto in force. I
need not stress the fact that this improvement in qualifications is calculated
to increase the efficiency of the work
done in the schools.
During the past year also an important
series of conferences has taken place
between the higher officials and
inspectors of the Ministry and representatives of the Irish National Teachers'
Organisation on the method of inspection
and reporting on the work of the elementary schools. The chief object was to
see whether, without setting aside the
main principle on which the present
system is based, that is, the giving of
reward and encouragement to teachers
who do the best work, it was practicable
to introduce any
alterations in the
methods of inspection which would make
the operation more effective in its workto the
ing and more sympathetic
teachers. I am pleased to bear witness-
I presided myself at these meetings-to
the excellent spirit of friendliness and
goodwill in which the conferences were
carried on and the harmony that prevailed. The result of the meetings has
been embodied in a published report,
and the consequent changes in the system
recommended by the conference have
been adopted by the Minister and came
into operation on the first day of last
month. Broadly speaking, the new
method aims at a wider interpretation of
school work and a giving of greater
importance in the assessment of results to
those sides of education which are concerned with the training of the pupils in
character, address, good manners and
intelligence. At the same time the
importance of the acquisition of knowledge is not to be overlooked. While I
do not claim that the changes made will
reconcile all our teachers to the necessity of being inspected, I am hopeful
that the new system will be found to
work more smoothly and give rise to
little friction. It tends certainly in the
direction of greater freedom for teacher
and pupil and a broader outlook towards
school activities.
Our secondary education system continues to expand, and the part restoration of the "cuts" as well as the cost of
increments to teachers and an increase
in capitation rate, due partly to a rise
in attendance, are responsible for the
Estimate at £192,400, being £11,600 in
excess of the amount voted last year.
The expansion of secondary education,
amounting to an increase of 50 per cent.
in the attendance since 1927, is one of
the surest signs of educational progress.
I do not claim that our secondary education has become as accessible to the
poorer classes of the community as it is
at present in Great Britain, but it is
moving steadily in that direction, and a
comparison of the sums voted for it
to-day compared with a very few years
ago is most significant of the tendency.
A great deal of its increased popularity
rests naturally on the scholarship
system which has now been in force for
a dozen years. Experience has caused
the Ministry to criticise some of the
means devised for the giving of scholarships, and a committee representative of
all grades of education, including the
University, is at present sitting to discuss in what way the system of scholarship awards by the local education
authorities can be improved. I anticipate
that many useful suggestions will be
found in the committee's report, which
is expected at an early date.
I am gratified to observe that many of
the education authorities are giving increased attention to secondary education
by making grants for the erection of new
secondary school buildings, and in other
ways. I would particularly mention the
regional committees in County Antrim,
where measures are being taken to aid
the erection of new premises for the
secondary schools at Larne, Ballymoney
and Ballyclare, at an estimated cost
exceeding £30,000. Last week the fine
new Dungannon High School for girls.
was opened by Her Grace the Duchess of
Abercorn; it has been built by the
Dungannon Regional Education Committee. A new school building is projected for secondary education in
Ministry of Education 1300
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
Limavady. There is also activity of a
similar kind in County Down.
The direct grants for technical education,
which amount to £72,100, show
an increase over last year's Estimate of
£2,450. The greater part of this sum
represents the increase in salaries and
increments, due partly to the restoration
of the "cut". The method of paying the
"attendance grant", which stood at a
gross uniform sum of £40,000 for the
past five years, has been altered, and
this grant is now based for the next
three years on a system of assessment,
whereby the value of a so-called "unit"
of technical instruction is fixed at twelve
shillings, without prejudice to any increase in the payment that might arise
through an expansion in the number of
pupils or classes. It is expected that this
change will facilitate committees in
giving increased effect to their programmes.
I have already referred to the increase
of £57,000 in the grants to local education authorities, consequent on the increased yield of an eightpenny rate on
the new valuations. The grants are now
estimated at £237,000 for the current
year, and the increase will result in
reducing the average rate levied for
education over the Province to a sum of
five pence in the pound. The effect of
this relief in assisting the education committee to provide for the needs of their
area is obvious, and it will, I am sure,
be some consolation to ratepayers interested in education for the increase of
the education levy to know that the
education committees will have larger
sums at their disposal from the
Exchequer for the improvement of the
schools.
The policy of the Ministry in promoting the reorganisation of school
supply by encouraging the education
authorities to build new schools and to
concentrate them when practicable so as
to enable small and unsuitable buildings
to be closed continues to bear good fruit,
and at the end of last year the total
number of public elementary schools.
was 1,753. This is a reduction of 22 on
the previous year, and compares with a
total of 1,948 ten years ago. The great
majority of the schools that have been
struck off were situated in Belfast and
other urban centres, and in nearly all
cases they have been replaced by larger
and excellently constructed new buildings. During the past year 14 new provided schools were completed with
accommodation for over 2,900 pupils,
bringing the number of provided schools
in the Province to 129. The cost of these
new buildings was approximately
£81,000. In addition to this sum, over
£20,000 was expended by the regional
and borough education committees on
repairs and reconditioning of transferred
schools. Nor have the voluntary school
managers been behindhand in this most
necessary work of improving the school
buildings. During 1936 the Ministry
sanctioned grants to the extent of
£26,000 for the building of six new
voluntary schools, with places for 1,595
pupils; nearly £10,000 was granted for
enlargements and improvements to other
existing voluntary schools, and taking
into account some supplementary grants
made in cases already under construction, the total sum granted for voluntary school buildings comes to over
£38,000, representing a total expenditure of double that amount, that is,
£76,000.
I submit to the Committee that this
evidence of activity in building shows that
the good work of bringing the school
accommodation of the Province up to a
high standard is being successfully continued, and I trust that hon. Members
who are still aware of schoolhouses being
used which are unsatisfactory or unsanitary
will realise that all that is still necessary
cannot be done in a moment. The
Ministry will spare no efforts to
encourage education committees and
school managers to improve the accommodation wherever it is needed. It is a
source of gratification to me to be able
to congratulate all concerned on what
has been accomplished in this respect.
The committees generally continue to
show great activity in the promotion of
education and in the execution of the
powers and duties entrusted to them.
An efficient system of medical inspection
is gradually being brought into operation
all over the Province. Every year shows
an increase in the number of full-time
medical officers employed, and the benefits of this service are appreciated by the
parents to an increasing extent. It is
believed that the number of parents who
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
6 MAY 1937
object to their children being examined
by the school medical officer is diminishing, and that it will not be necessary for
the Ministry to promote measures of
compulsion to prevent pupils being
withdrawn from the medical examination.
on
The provision of meals for necessitous
children continues to be carried
extensively in Belfast and in County
Down, the former spending £4,300 on
this service in 1936-37, and the latter
£1,829. The Lisburn and Belfast
Regional Committee has also adopted a
scheme for meals, and spent £121 last
year.
In half-a-dozen other regional
areas, Coleraine, Cookstown, Ballymena,
Larne, for example, meals are supplied
to some extent through voluntary
agencies, the committees usually making
grants of the necessary equipment. It is
satisfactory that this matter is
beginning to receive more general attention, but very much yet remains to be
done, and I would urge the education
authorities who have not yet co-operated
in this work to devote attention to it.
The Ministry's special school at Haypark for mentally deficient children has
now been in operation for over twelve
months with beneficial results to the
pupils. The numbers now consist of 20
boarders and 64 day pupils, which is a
considerable increase on those enrolled
last year, especially in day pupils.
Parents in country places are still slow
to permit children to go to the school,
and I would appeal to all interested, as
I did last year, to point out the advantages of the school with a view to
removing the parents' objections.
In making this review of the year's
progress I have not found it necessary to
say much about the general state of
education in the schools, which shows
little alteration from year to year. The
Ministry has not made any spectacular
or drastic changes in the year, nor are
such necessary or practicable. We have
aimed at steady progress and the gradual
elimination of defects as far as possible.
We are quite aware of the new developments in educational services in Great
Britain, and we hope to adopt all such
measures of improvement so far as they
seem adaptable to our requirements and
are possible, having regard to the extent
of our purse.
We are taking steps to
give some assistance to nursery schools
under suitable conditions, and regulations on this matter were laid on the
Table a few days ago. We are preparing
to take measures to deal with the question of the extension of the schoolleaving age, which, I may observe, does
not take effect in Great Britain until
1939, and we are making inquiries into
the existing facilities in Northern Ireland for physical training and recreation,
so that we may see in what way this most
important social service can fittingly be
extended and encouraged in our midst,
not only through the schools but by the
agency of voluntary youth organisations.
We should like to see greater use made
in our schools of such modern aids to
education as wireless lessons and the film,
and no opportunity has been lost for
drawing attention to the possibilities
afforded to education by these inventions.
Our relations with the education authorities and the teaching profession continue to be most harmonious, and we
acknowledge the co-operation and
assistance we have invariably received
from them in the pursuit of our joint
aims. We do not pretend that our
system is perfect or nearly perfect, or
that there is still not a great deal of
leeway to make up, but we think we can
point with justification to a great deal
that has been achieved in the past fifteen
years. I beg to move.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I rise to discuss
these Estimates because I happen this
year to have the honour to occupy the
chair in one of the largest sub-committees
under the control of the municipality
that is interested in the question of
education, and because for thirteen years
I have been an active member of the
local education authority. I have been
interested from year to year in the
question of the co-ordination of the work
of education throughout Belfast and the
North of Ireland as between the Ministry of Education and the education
authorities. That must be my justification for intervening this afternoonbecause of the standing I enjoy in the
educational world through the local
authority, and which, I think, entitles
me to take a leading part on the question
of education. I should like to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary, in the
first place, on ably upholding the
tradition he has created in presenting
Ministry of Education 1304
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
these Estimates year after year. He is
the one Gentleman in this Northern Parliament who adds lustre year by year
to the presentation of the facts in regard
to the Department under his control, and
I should like to express my own individual appreciation as well as the appreciation of many others of the very
lucid
and able manner in which he presents
the various aspects of educational development.
Many of the things the Parliamentary
Secretary said this afternoon would compel attention, and sympathetic attention
at that, from every section of the community, but there are points upon which
one must disagree in view of one's varied
experience. The Parliamentary Secretary deals essentially with the educational problem from the Government
point of view. Other people perhaps see
it from the local point of view, where
the decisions of the Ministry and the
ordinances of the Ministry have to be
given effect. I will as rapidly as I possibly can cover the various points, some
of which I have raised from time to time
in this House and elsewhere and which
I feel compelled to draw attention to
here to-day again. In the review of
educational development in the past
twelve months the Parliamentary Secretary drew attention to what he considered
a satisfactory rate of progress in regard
to higher education. I am speaking now
of secondary education as distinct from
technical education. I will have something more elaborate to say later on in
regard to technical education, and as I
have gone to some trouble to prepare my
facts I hope, with the indulgence of the
House, I may be permitted to quote the
actual position. At the moment, I wish
to say I followed with interest a discussion in the Press recently with regard to
higher education, and certainly if the Parliamentary Secretary is satisfied I am
far from satisfied in regard to bringing.
higher education within the reach of the
masses of the people.
I was very glad to hear him say this
afternoon in regard to the local authorities the one he mentioned was Antrim
Regional Committee-being likely to
embark on an extended scheme of increased facilities for higher education in
the near future. As a member of a
local authority that is not doing as much.
as it ought to do I am very pleased to
hear that. I trust it will get the prominence it deserves, and will create an
incentive in the minds of the people of
the Belfast education authority to follow
the example of the Antrim authority in
developing the facilities for higher
education. I think it is true to say that
roughly only about 7 or 8 per cent. of
our school population of Northern Ireland have full access to higher education.
That is, in my opinion, absolutely unsatisfactory from the point of view of
the whole body politic. When you again
concentrate attention upon the number
of people with access to free places you
find that many of the working-class
people the masses of the people-are
shut out except in those privileged cases
where scholarships of one kind or another
operate the masses of the working-class
people are shut out from access to the
higher education which ought to be within their reach.
Again, in this connection, I want to
say I am not in agreement with the
point of view of holding fast to the
principle of scholarships. Of course I
speak as a layman and subject to the
limitations a layman must suffer from,
—but, after all, a layman who is worth
his salt at all and who has had experience ought to bring ordinary commonsense to bear upon the result of his
observation. And my observation
teaches me to recognise that many
people have not got the examination
complex, and for that reason, while the
general mental standard is good enough
to enable one to say they would profit
by having access to higher education,
because they are not able to overcome
some temperamental difficulty or some
reason which it would take a psychologist to cure, these children are precluded
from having access to the education to
which they are entitled because of
their general mental condition and
attainments and from which they are
precluded through adverse economic circumstances.
I believe a better policy, taking the
long view, would be a policy in which
the education authorities would be
instructed throughout the whole education year to watch carefully the trend
of development in the students, and that
promotion and facilities ought to be provided on the basis of the general intel-

lectual attainments of the child and
definite indications of promise in the
child. In my opinion that would be a
better way to increase the steady flow of
children from the bottom class right to
the higher ranks, speaking educationally
and speaking of education not in the
wage-earning sense or profit-making
sense, but from the cultural and humanitarian aspects. A rich mind is better
than a rich man.
That is what I believe. I approach education from that
point of view. A good, rich mind is one
of the noblest things. It enriches the
community. A rich man does not
always enrich the community. In fact
he sometimes beggars the community;
he may have made his money in that
way. But a rich mind casts a radiance
throughout the community with beneficial results to all concerned. Speaking
of education in that way I am of opinion
that a new policy should be developed.
are
Now, there are three aspects of this
question, but I have only a limited time
and I want to go on to the question of
the deficiency in the education system
of Northern Ireland. I think the Ministry ought to give attention at the earliest
possible date to the provision of facilities for acquiring degrees in veterinary
surgery in Northern Ireland. At the
present time in our Province the parliamentary area that we here have under
our control-we develop an agricultural
complex in our outlook because we
mainly agricultural. Already the Government, in its various Departments, has done
a great deal with regard to the development of agricultural schemes, not only
under the auspices of the Ministry of
Agriculture, but also partly under the
auspices of the Ministry of Educationdairymaids, poultry, and we have fine
judges of the achievements of the whole
Province in these two directions. But it
might come as a surprise to some Members of the House to know that if any
Northern Ireland pupil wants to become
a veterinary surgeon he has got to go to
Dublin, Edinburgh, or to the college at
Liverpool in order to get his degree, and
no facilities exist at the present time
for the acquisition of that degree in
Northern Ireland. That defect ought to
be repaired, more especially in view of
the greater utilisation of the veterinary
knowledge throughout the North of Ireland.
The last big scheme in Northern
Ireland in which their high skill, to a
very great extent, was put into operation
by the Government, was in connection
with the milk question, under which the
inspection of milk passed out of the
hands of the local authorities into the
hands of the Ministry. There was a
greater demand for this training
throughout the area, and consequently a
new incentive was created to attract
people into the profession, and the fact
that no facilities exist at the present
time for allowing students of Northern
Ireland to satisfy their aspirations in
that direction is something that can be
pointed out as a flaw in our educational
system. If we have already premises in
Elmwood Avenue, Belfast, for the
presentation of facts in regard to aspects
of agricultural life, why cannot we go
a step further, and in co-operation with
Queen's University, Belfast, make the
provision which ought to be made to
enable students, on the basis of equality
so far as machinery is concerned with
students all over the country, to acquire
this degree?
I have a small complaint in passingso small that I was reluctant to mention
it, but the accumulated effect of small
things sometimes becomes difficult. One
thing the Ministry should deal with is
the question of expediting correspondence
and plans from the local authority. At
the present time I know considerable
delay takes place when local authorities
submit plans, from the time the local
authorities present these until the reply
is received by the local authority. In
these cases there are feelings of irritation.
I think the Ministry, generally speaking, has done very well and is doing
very well. In fact it is one of the best
Ministries in Northern Ireland. There
is not the slightest doubt about that.
It is doing so well, generally speaking
subject to a few reservations, that the
Ministry ought to be at pains to overcome some reluctance the local authorities feel at the present time about
approaching them. I pass that on in
the sure and certain hope that it will
be repaired.
I want now to touch briefly on something on which I wish to enlist the support of the Ministry and hope the
Ministry will make a great big bold
pronouncement. I regard myself as a

pioneer. Eleven or twelve years ago, on
my own initiative-of course I nearly
always do things on my own initiative.
That is why there is no result for ten
or twelve years and then somebody else
comes along and gets the glory. Ten
or twelve years ago, when I began
listening in, I realised the possibility of
education from wireless. I realised it
just by listening to experts in the realm
of education and general knowledge,
such as history, music, and various other

language. I used to listen to correct
pronunciation-at least, the professor
said it was correct pronunciation.
although they changed it subsequently.
and I do not know which is correct.
use
I want to ask the Minister of Education to try to speed things up to the end
that the local authorities will make the
use of wireless in education that they
could make. It is being made
of in Great Britain to a considerably
greater extent than it is here. At the
time I presented this point to the local
authority-it is more a point for the local
authority than the Ministry, as they have
the power-they were, of course, hesitant
about embarking on any new policy such
as wireless, which ten years ago was not
so good as it is now. There was bad
selectivity, it was not distinct, and it was
subject to disturbance. After trying it
in one or two places, the local authority
was not sympathetic towards the venture.
I believe the Ministry, armed with the
data which it can get from the other side
and also utilising its power sympathetically to impress its mind on the local
authority, could bring about a great
change in regard to the development or
utilisation of wireless, with beneficial
results to all concerned. If it was accompanied by a declaration on the part of
the Ministry that they did not seek to
ask local authorities to do anything which
was going to overload the curriculum or
daily work, that would be an important
psychological factor in bringing about a
desired change of heart and mind in
regard to this question.
These are only a few points I am referring to as I go along. I was delighted
to hear the reference of the Parliamentary Secretary to two aspects of
educational life. One is with regard to
nursery schools and the other is with
an
regard to the consideration of the school
leaving age. I know that the Ministry
has already done something as to giving
assistance to nursery schools. This is a
question in which I have taken
interest for years in the local authority.
I have been trying to get them to embark
on a policy of the development of nursery
schools, as they have power to do, but
unfortunately they seem to hold the point
of view firmly that until they make up
the leeway in regard to the provision of
elementary schools it would be wrong to
carry on the other matter. I think they
are wrong in that stand. They could do
the one
as a counterpart of the other.
They could develop both together. The
action of the Ministry is in the direction
of supporting that policy, because the
Ministry has done the next best thing.
In the absence of any well-considered
scheme for the development of nursery
schools on the part of the local authority,
the Ministry has given evidence of good
wishes and good faith in the work, not
only by offering to assist, but by encouraging the local authority to assist.
I am glad to say that as a result of the
development of this new policy in the
city of Belfast, nursery schools are being
carried on voluntarily. And to the
ladies in charge I would pay the highest
possible tribute.
Mr. ROBB: Hear, hear.
Mr. MIDGLEY: They are amongst
the noblest women in Ulster. They have
done a tremendous amount of good work.
To those Members who do not know anything of nursery schools I would throw
out an invitation to go and see these
ladies at work under their voluntary
system, and what they have sacrificed in
order to develop a new mental outlook
in the children as regards questions of
hygiene and what I might call children
citizenship. They have succeeded to a
remarkable extent. Those ladies deserve
every consideration and appreciation
from the community, because of what
they have already done. I hope the time

that one of the important

As regards the College of Technology

Robertson Commission emphasised the

Technology he brought forth a COordination scheme which was acceptable
to the University authorities, which was

recognised by the University authorities

the honorary degree of LL.D. on the
author of the scheme. Under this scheme
the whole of the work of the Faculty of
Applied Science and Technology, most of
the work of the Faculty of Commerce,
and some of the work of the Faculty of
Engineering is carried out at the College
of Technology.
But more than that, under this coordination scheme a young man working
in the shipyards or other industrial
activity in the city during the day can,
by assiduous work at the evening classes
in the College of Technology, obtain a

facilities of the University classes are

Education.
Then I would point out that the

At present about 12 per cent. of the

to provide higher technical education for

there are failures here and there then

The danger of allowing education to
degenerate into routine is something that
we ought to guard against. We in
Northern Ireland possess many, very
many, admirable qualities, but I wonder
who would be bold enough to suggest that
we are really a highly-educated people?
Education is more important to-day than
ever it was in the history of mankind.
Perhaps fifty years ago it did not matter
so much when people had to work longer
hours. People have more leisure to-day
and, therefore, we should be making
some provision, so that men who have
more time on their hands will know how
to spend it.
To-day, what have we to offer to
people? They go to the dogs or to football matches. Beyond those two things
what really have we to offer them? We
take the children into the schools at five
years of age, and we teach them from
five to fourteen. When they leave
school, at the age of fourteen, how much
do they know? They may know how to
read and write and do a little arithmetic, but so far as history, economics
and the other forces that play such a
large part in the life of a nation are concerned, the vast majority of them know
little or nothing. I suppose that I know
as many teachers in Northern Ireland as
any Member of this House. I have
watched their work with sympathy and
interest for a great many years. I think
we must blame the system which throws
children out into the world at the age of
fourteen and lets them sink or swim,
without making provision for the continuation of their education. For the
vast majority of these children I think
we have done little or nothing. Education must be adjusted to the stage of
development which the child's brain has
reached. Those who are interested in
education know very well that a young
girl of eighteen can learn more in six
months than it is possible for her to learn
in six years before she is eighteen. The
best teachers in the world cannot teach a
subject unless the child is able to digest
the knowledge that is imparted.
My hon. Friend, the Member for Dock,
has raised the question of the school age.
Personally I have no objection to the
raising of the school age. As one who
has taken some interest in education, I
do not believe that the raising of the
school age to 15, or even 16 years of age,
is going to solve our problem. Take the
United States of America, where it is
compulsory for children to remain at
school until they are sixteen. In France,
on the other hand, the children can leave
school at thirteen, or under special
circumstances, at twelve. Compare the
children of those two countries and disillusion will follow with regard to the
value of the extended school age. What
I plead for is a change of system which
will keep the children under some sort
of educational control until they have
reached the age of eighteen. I know that
there are economic difficulties in the way,
but I do think this thing could be
worked out.
I think I am right in saying that in
every Continental country in Europe
there is conscription, and the young
people have to serve two years in learning how to kill their neighbours. Would
it not be possible to spend two extra years
in learning how to develop oneself and to
make oneself a more useful citizen? I
think if we look at it we will find that
this is a problem that can be solved. If
we had some system that would take the
child up to eighteen, we would then have
taken it to the threshold of adult education. Sir Richard Livingstone, who was
until recently Vice-Chancellor of Queen's
University, has pointed out that adult
education is the solution of our educational problem. That is an aspect of
education which I do commend to the
sympathetic consideration of the Ministry and to this Committee.
If a model is wanted for it, you have
one ready to hand in the case of
Denmark. The Danish folk have a high
school system which has been in operation for a great many years, and it has
done good work. I believe that the
future lies with adult education. The
present system is wasteful both in money
and in energy. It always reminds me
of the man who starts to build a house
and stops after he has got two or three
courses laid. Going through the country
one sometimes sees a house that has been
half built, and it is generally referred
to as so-and-so's folly." Is it not
really a folly to spend so much money on
education of children up to fourteen, and

There was a statesman at one time who

Party, a man who led and educated that
party. I refer to Disraeli. His memory
is perpetuated on banners in July. The
hon. Member for North Antrim is
smiling; apparently he has seen his

regard to Bible teaching. Speaking on
the English Education Act, 1870,
Disraeli said:
Although no creed or catechism of
any denomination is to be introduced,
the schoolmaster is to have the power

the Holy Scriptures when he reads.
Now he cannot do that without drawing inferences and conclusions, and
what will those inferences and conclusions be but dogmas . . . You will
not entrust the priest or presbyter with

Scriptures to the scholars, but you are
investing and establishing a new sacerdotal class.
The hon. Member for the University will

What then shall we have, the Bible
without note or comment? Not so, for

Testament who do not require to have

Disraeli, who was clear-sighted if not farsighted, did not see that the day would come
in England when teachers would sap the

Rev. Professor CORKEY:
I rise
simply for the purpose of making
a very few observations on this
Estimate, and also for the purpose
of congratulating the Ministry on the
high way in which it carries out this
great work that has been entrusted to it.
It is undoubtedly a very valuable bit of
work, and a very intricate task involving as it does primary education, secondary education, and technical education;
and it is made even more difficult by the
fact that those in charge of it have got
to do their best to reconcile a great
number of conflicting interests in the
community, as may be gathered from the
interesting speech which has just been
made by the Member for Central. I
think that the Ministry achieves its task
with very great success considering the
difficult nature of the task and the conflicting interests in the community with
which they have to deal.
It is, perhaps, unfortunate that all
these interests cannot be absolutely satis
fied. But I think that in carrying out
the work of education the Ministry has
been true to the principle of British freedom and British justice. Those who wish
to have their children educated in a
peculiar way are given the opportunity
to have them so educated, and I think
that is right. I think every man ought
to have an opportunity of living his own
life in his own way, provided that in living his life he does not make himself a
nuisance to other people. And those
who desire to have voluntary schools are
given the opportunity of having voluntary
schools, and even those voluntary schools
are subsidised to a tremendous extent, perhaps to 97 per cent. or 98 per cent. of
the entire cost of those schools. Compare
that situation with the situation that
exists in America, a great free country
where the people who wish to have voluntary schools can have voluntary schools,
but where they have got to pay the entire
cost of those schools out of their private
purse. I think the same is true of
elementary education in Australia.
fact I do not know any country in the
world where those who desire special
In
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
6 MAY 1937
educational facilities for themselves are
met in a more handsome way by the Government than in Northern Ireland.
I would like to reiterate some of the
ideas which were suggested by the
Member for North Antrim. I think we
should attempt to keep in step with Great
Britain as far as possible, not only in our
social services, but also in our educational practice, and I am sure that the
Ministry will have seriously before them
in the near future the question of keeping in step with regard to the raising of
the school age. I would be glad to see
Northern Ireland going a little further
than Great Britain in that respect.
I would feel great satisfaction if our
Ministry could devise some method of
taking hold of a number of young people
throughout the city who have left school
but are not able to find any occupation,
and who are at a loose end most of the
time. If a dictator were in power in
Northern Ireland these young people
would not be allowed to hang round uselessly and idly at street corners pitching pennies and shuffling cards. They
would very soon find something to do. I
do not, of course, suggest that we should
establish a dictatorship to deal with this
matter, but I think it is a question of
great concern. These young people are
spending the best part of their youth
doing nothing and earning nothing. They
are getting no opportunity to develop
their muscles or exercise their minds or
prepare themselves for earning a livelihood; in fact, they are just in training
for spending all their lives at the cost of
the rich. I would be very glad to see
some scheme for the part-time education
of these people at any rate worked out,
which would bring to bear some authority
or educational influence on boys up to
the age of 18. It would be of tremendous value to them and to the community. Possibly our system of technical
education might be developed to some
extent for the benefit of this particular
class. There are great potentialities in
the system of technical education, which
I hope will be explored and developed in
the years to come.
Those who are in touch with the educational work carried out by the Ministry
feel great satisfaction at the value of the
medical services of which these voung
people have the benefit. Probably we
could all cite cases of young people whose
lives were handicapped unwittingly
by the fact that in their early years they
had no glasses. It was thought they
were dull and stupid, whereas the fault
was purely physical. It is a tremendous
boon to have medical inspection of school
children as we have it, and I would be
glad if the authorities would go further
and follow up some of the reports which
are given to the parents in regard to the
children. I understand that at present
when the medical inspector discovers anything amiss the parents are notified in
the case of eye defects or dental trouble.
I notice in a number of cases that the
matter is neglected. Such reports should
be followed up and inquiries made from
time to time as to whether action has been
taken in regard to the suggestion made
by the school doctor.
In conclusion, I would like to express
a word of appreciation of the great work
that is being done by our day school
teachers, not only in their secular
education department, but also in their
work for religious education. This is a
very fine work in spite of the deprecatory
remarks made by the last speaker. I do
not say that it is without difficulty. These
people have got in their hands for half
an hour a textbook, which is one of the
greatest pieces of literature in all time.
Those who handle it for the benefit of
children have to do their best to detect
the substance in the passage before them,
and emphasise the substance for the
benefit of the moral and religious insight
of the children. I do not think it is
such a phenomenally difficult task as was
Sigested. I do not agree with the idea
put forward that
that it is practically
impossible except for the trained
ecclesiastic. I believe from my own
experience it is being done by these dayschool teachers. They are handling this
matter in a very wise way, and with
keen interest, so far as my observation
goes, and at a time when in some
countries in Europe the trend is away,
not only from Christian belief, but from
Christian morality.
I think we should all be very grateful
that we have in our schools a body of
men who are prepared to face up to the
task of putting before the young people
of the country the elemental principles
of our morality and the elemental
principles of our Christian belief. I
think we would all agree that unless

New Industries (Development) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In asking the House to
give a Second Reading to this further
Measure for the attraction of new industries to our area, may I remind hon.
Members for a few moments of the chief
features of the earlier Act, particularly
as some of the proposals which I am
about to submit to the House have been
conditioned by the shortcomings which
the working of the earlier Measure
revealed.
The New Industries (Development)
Act of 1932, which expired in October
last, authorised the grant of a free site,
and complete exemption from local rates
for a period of 20 years, to any person
or company establishing an undertaking
for the manufacture or production of
goods of a kind not being manufactured
or produced in Northern Ireland on or
before 31st October, 1931. Unfortunately, the Act belied the hopes
reposed in it. Small grants, amounting
in all to some £300 per annum at the
present time, have been made to eight
industrial undertakings employing in the
about
aggregate
The
200 people.
application of one large industrial undertaking has still to be considered, but,
apart from this, the operation of the
Measure cannot be said to have broadened
materially the basis of industrial life in
Northern Ireland. This failure may, of
course, be ascribed in part to considerations entirely independent of the Act and
its provisions.
We know, for example, that the years
of the Act's operation coincided with a
period of considerable hesitancy and uncertainty in industrial circles, that it
covered a time when industry was concentrating for the most part on the maintenance and consolidation of its position
rather than on the launching of fresh
enterprise. We must recognise, however,
that in two respects the Act proved
inadequate to the purposes for which it
was intended. Experience showed that
the site rent, even when coupled with
exemption from the balance of local rates
to which industry was liable, was small
in relation to the other charges which a
1349 New Industries Bill-

1 JUNE 1937
Second Reading
new undertaking would be called upon to
meet. Furthermore, the rigid limitation
of the scope of the 1932 Act to "new"
industrial undertakings effectively debarred several promising enterprises from
consideration.
In framing the Bill now before the
House, the Government has been guided
not only by the experience gained in the
working of the earlier Act, but also by
the special measures now being adopted
in Great Britain for the stimulation of
industry which, as the House will be
aware, is being fostered by Government
action and private benefaction in the
special areas, and by local authorities and
development organisations throughout the
country as a whole.
The problem which faces the Imperial
Government in the special areas in Great
Britain is one of great magnitude, and
the position here is happily one neither
of such difficulty, nor of such complexity.
My colleagues and I feel, however, that if
this Measure is to stand a reasonable
chance of attaining the end which we all
desire—namely, the broadening of our
industrial basis
greater and wider
financial inducements must be offered.
The new Bill, then, is framed from
somewhat wider concepts than the old.
No longer is an enterprise to be debarred
from its facilities merely by reason of the
fact that some small scale production of
similar goods, possibly for quite a
different purpose, is being carried on.
What we want is more employment for
our people, spread over as wide and as
varied an industrial field as possible. We
want to welcome over here industries that
will provide it. We want to get them
established and giving employment, and
we do not want in the future to be
obliged to split legal hairs as to whether
this industry or that industry can be
considered a "new" industry within the
meaning of the Act, and eligible for its
benefits.
Having said that, let me make it quite
clear to the House that we do not intend
that this Bill should be used for the
indiscriminate subsidising of new industrial undertakings, whatever their nature
may be. Clearly, the Bill would be
defeating its own purpose if it merely
succeeded in transferring employment
from one industrial establishment to
another, in raising up, as it were, State
subsidised competitors of existing industry. To obviate this, as hon. Members
will observe if they turn to Clause 1 of
the Bill, we have laid it down that the
Ministry of Commerce and its Advisory
Committee shall be guided in this matter
by three considerations: they must be
satisfied, firstly, that the applicant undertaking promises to make an addition to
the existing sum total of employment;
secondly, that that addition will be a
substantial one; and, thirdly, that this
additional employment will not be
ephemeral but continuing. I am sure
that the House will agree that any new
industrial undertaking which can satisfy
these three tests will, by its establishment, confer industrial benefit upon
Northern Ireland.
In
So much for the principles upon which
the Bill is based; now let me turn to the
facilities which we propose to offer. I
would first call the attention of the House
to the distinction between grants and
loans. The 1932 Act, hon. Members will
recollect, provided for out-and-out grants
only. Those grants related exclusively to
the site on which the undertaking had
been, or was to be, established, and did
not cover the rent of the premises.
the present Measure it is proposed to
repeat the 1932 Act in so far as a grant
in respect of the site is concerned and,
where premises are rented by the applicant, to substitute for a grant in respect
of the site a grant in respect of the rent
of the premises. Hon. Members will
note, however, that whereas a site grant
may be made throughout a maximum
period of twenty years, a grant in respect
of premises is restricted to a period of five
years, reckoning from the date on which
the undertaking is established.
The effect of these provisions is to free.
the recipient completely of all rent
charges for a maximum period of five
years and, thereafter, to leave him to
conduct his undertaking entirely on his
own resources without the obligation to
repay any grant which may have been
made to him under the Act in respect of
such rent charges. These provisions
cover the case of rented premises, but it
is also necessary to provide for premises.
which, though rented by the applicant,
require to be adapted to the particular
needs of the undertaking as well as cases
in which entirely new premises have to

cases of these kinds the Bill proposes that
the Ministry of Finance should be empowered, on the recommendation of the
Ministry of Commerce, to advance loans
up to an aggregate of £200,000, either
out of the Consolidated Fund of Northern
Ireland or out of the Government Loans
Fund, and that such loans shall, during

may determine.
In effect, therefore, the Bill provides
financial accommodation for an applicant
who either rents existing premises which
require adaptation, or who builds
premises suitable to his own particular
needs, the accommodation thus provided
being free of all interest for a maximum
period of five years. Let me take a few
examples, illustrating the working of the
Bill:-Applicant A proposes to
rent
premises which do not require any
structural alteration or adaptation. Provided he satisfies the Ministry of Commerce on the various points attaching to
the sanction of his application, the Ministry may make an out-and-out annual
grant to him over a period not exceeding
five years of a sum not exceeding such
amount as the Ministry may consider to
be the equivalent of a reasonable annual
rent of the premises.
Applicant B proposes similarly to rent.
existing premises which, however, let us
suppose, require alteration or adaptation. In his case the Ministry may make
a corresponding out-and-out grant in
respect of the rent of the premises and,
in addition, the Ministry of Finance may
lend to him free of interest for a period
not exceeding five years whatever sum is
required to carry out the structural

the end of the interest-free period the

Finally, applicant C proposes to erect
entirely new premises for the purposes
of his undertaking. In this case no
question of a grant in respect of rent of
premises can arise, but in addition to an
out-and-out grant in respect of the site,
the Ministry of Finance would be empowered to lend to the applicant free of
interest for a period not exceeding five
years a sum equivalent to the cost of the
buildings. In this case also the applicant
would be required to repay only the loan
together with interest for any period
subsequent to five years in such instalments and within such a period as the
Ministry of Finance might fix.
I have endeavoured, as briefly as
possible, to explain to the House the Bill
in its general aspects. There are, however, a few points to which I should also
like to draw attention. Only concerns
established after the passing of the Bill
will be eligible for its benefits. Here the
Government's view is that the object of
the Bill is to attract new industries
offering new employment and not to
subsidise those already established.
Again, grants or loans may only be made
where the application is made to the
Ministry of Commerce within a period
of five years reckoning from the date of
the passing of the Act.
Another point is that, in determining
whether to accede to any particular
application or the extent to which an
application might be granted, the Ministry of Commerce shall be entitled to have
regard to any circumstances which may
render it desirable that the undertaking
should be established in some particular
district in preference to another.
It is also proposed to repeat the provision in the 1932 Act empowering local
authorities to exempt from the payment
of rates any undertaking in respect of
which a grant or a loan has been made
under the Act, the period of exemption
not to exceed the period of the currency
of the grant or, in the case of a loan,
the period between the date on which the
loan is made to the applicant and the
date fixed for the repayment of the final
instalment thereof to the Ministry of
Finance.
I am confident that hon. Members
appreciate the many attractions which
Northern Ireland already offers to the
industrialist seeking a fresh outlet for
his enterprise. Foremost amongst such
advantages stands a supply of skilled

Second Reading
labour, reinforced by cheap power, commodiously and conveniently situated
harbours and efficient transport. Clause.
5 makes provision for the expenditure
necessary to make known the special
facilities proposed in the Bill.
Much
can, and will, be done by the dissemination of information through His
Majesty's commercial representatives
overseas, through Chambers of Commerce
and other trade associations at home, and
by articles in journals that circulate principally in industrial circles.
While we hope that, as a result of this
fresh attempt, we may see established
here new industries whose products, like
those of our existing major industries,
will find a ready market far beyond our
own shores, we shall also welcome new
industrial units catering primarily for
the local market. So far as the home
market is concerned the Ulster Industries
Development Association, which has done
so much in the last few years to assist
the home producer, should be of great
assistance.
In order that that association may be in a position to maintain a
continuity of policy, I propose, in due
course, to ask the House to agree to the
continuance for a period of three years
of the grant which it at present enjoys.
I beg to move.

find work. Under the Act which was
passed before, we found that very few
industries were attracted here. Few
firms came forward to start, owing to the
few facilities that we can offer. The
question was asked whether we did offer
them sufficient inducements as regards
suitable sites and transport facilities.
The aim of the Measure is to employ more
of our people, and we hope it will attain
the object which it has in view, and that
many people in Ulster will find employment through its means. It is an
attempt to bring about increased prosperity to industry and employment to
our people, but we cannot expect, in view
of our experience in regard to the last
Bill, that firms will come here simply
through the passing of an Act. I should
be glad, and I am sure every Member of
the House will be glad, to hear what
opportunities are to be given in regard
to propaganda, and what action will be
taken by the right hon. Gentleman's
Department in order to induce those
firms, which I take it are largely across
the Channel, to come here and make use
of the facilities which we are offering.
It is believed in a general way that
new industries bring more employment,
but we have not found that that is so
to the extent we thought in recent years,
owing to the fact that machinery and
labour-saving devices are coming more
and more into use. Very few people,
indeed, are employed in a great number
of cases.
Knowing the state of our unemployment and the large numbers of
able-bodied men whom we have to help.
either through unemployment benefit or
by means of outdoor relief, I think this
problem of unemployment should be
boldly faced by the Government itself.
and it should aim at large schemes of
employment. When I say that I am
speaking of the employment of 10,000 or
20,000 of our unemployed. That would
make these people more happy and contented. We have many such opportunities of work in our Province. I would
recommend to the right hon. Gentleman
the reclamation of land, and I would
recommend drainage and other useful
works which a future generation would
benefit by. The cost of those works
might be passed on to that generation.

I recently read in the papers of an
English Member of Parliament, a wellknown doctor, who went through the distressed areas of England and Wales. By
observation he came to the conclusion
that through unemployment there was
a lower mentality among the people, more
inmates of mental institutions, and more

of this? Therefore, a Bill of this kind

thousands of motor-cars used in this part

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): In rising to open my first
Budget my thoughts are naturally mainly
centred at the moment on my distinguished predecessor-a very great
Ulsterman, a "Companion of Honour,"
and a very dear
and
colleague
friend of mine. Since I have
been endeavouring to grasp during
the last few weeks our financial
affairs and the widespread work of the
Ministry, I have appreciated even more
than ever before how much Ulster owes
to his wisdom and work.
Sixteen years ago he established his
Ministry on a sound and enduring
foundation, and he has left it a very
efficient Government department. During
all these years he was able to provide for
the ever increasing demands of our ever
expanding social services, which mean so
much to our people during times of
adversity, and also the large sums required in connection with our building
programme, including improved housing
conditions for our people. He was also
able to provide adequate Sinking Funds
where necessary, with the view to securing our financial position for posterity.
Then again (notwithstanding the depressed industrial conditions through
which every country in the world has
been passing) he balanced each of his
Budgets, besides providing for
Imperial contribution of varying substantial amounts, and, in addition, he
secured that our relations with the
British Treasury are of an extremely
friendly and satisfactory nature. This is
a prolonged record of public service
which has seldom been equalled in our
time. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
an
Following the usual practice, I would
like to say just a few words as regards
our industrial position because of its
close association with our financial one.
We are united in this House, I am sure,
in desiring the welfare of our native land
though we differ as to how that can best
be brought about, and I am glad to be
able to state that every test that can
be applied points to a gradual improvement, although it is true that, as yet,
our progress has not been as rapid as
that in Great Britain owing to circumstances beyond our control. Hope, however (based on actual facts) is on the
ascendant. Our present harbour returns
are
a record both as regards our out-
Minister's Financial Statement 1386

Our
going and incoming shipments.
people's investments in Savings Banks,
Post Office and Ulster Savings Certificates year after year show a very substantial increase, and, generally speaking,
social standards have been raised.
Agriculture, our chief industry, is on
a sounder basis than for many years,
largely due to the Imperial Government's
tariff and quota policy formulated in cooperation with our Government and the
substantial subsidies which are being
paid in order to encourage the production
of various farm produce and the rearing
of cattle, and to the various Boards which
have been set up by our Minister of
Agriculture in order to ensure as far as
possible that farmers get a reasonable
return upon their capital and labour.
It is also gratifying to know that our
textile industry, which for several years
has been passing through a particularly
difficult time, is now in a much better
position, and, as a consequence, almost
all our spindles and looms are well
occupied for months ahead. While I
regret to say that the shirt and collar
trade of Derry is suffering somewhat
from a temporary shortage of cloth the
prospects for the industry are satisfactory. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
un-
Again, we find that our shipbuilding
and engineering industries are
doubtedly in a better position, and the
prospects are more encouraging than for
a considerable time past. I am gratified
to be able to state that this improved
industrial position is reflected in the fact
that there are nearly 43,000 more persons
now working than in December, 1930,
and almost 8,000 more than at the
beginning of this year, whilst the fall in
the live register in the past two months
was 7,694. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Expenditure, 1936-37.
I shall now follow the usual practice
of reviewing the figures of the past year
before considering the problems of the
future. Hon. Members will find the
figures to which I will be referring in
Tables I., II. and III. of the White
Paper in their hands.
CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
Dealing first of all with the expenditure, we find that Consolidated Fund
services, apart from the Road Fund and
the self-balancing item of the Milk
Industry Assistance Grant, accounted for
£699,789, or £180,789 above the Estimate.
This large increase over the Estimate
is partly due to the decision to resume
the normal annual Sinking Fund payment towards our Terminable Revenue
Sinking Fund, which, as hon Members
may recollect, was not provided for in
the last Budget. It was, however, explained by my right hon. Friend that the
final balance emerging from last year's
Budget Statement would be subject to
a claim that we would make to the Joint
Exchequer Board in respect of this
charge. Later in the year, owing to
certain changes in circumstances, the
Treasury agreed with our views on this
matter: it was not, therefore, necessary
for us to formulate a claim to the Joint
Exchequer Board, and we were able to
set the usual sum aside from our annual
revenues. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Secondly, owing to the satisfactory
state of our revenues at the end of the
financial year, we were able to allocate
a substantial sum towards the liquidation
of money borrowed in previous years for
meeting payments that had fallen due
under the Loans Guarantee Acts.
INTEREST ON BORROWINGS.
From Table II the Committee will
observe that the Exchequer issues in
respect of interest on temporary borrowings are about £12,000 under the
Estimate. The very high point at which
Northern Ireland credit stands is made
clear beyond doubt by the fact that
nearly all Northern Ireland Treasury
bills issued during the past financial year
only cost the Government approximately
the same rate of discount as is paid in
connection with Treasury bills issued by
the Imperial Government. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) During the year
Northern Ireland Treasury bills, to a
total amount of £6,385,000 were issued,
and the average rate of discount worked
out at about only 12s per cent. per
annum. It will be realised, therefore,
that the bidding for these bills in London
is exceedingly keen. A few years ago
the Northern Ireland rate exceeded the
London Treasury rate by about 5s per
cent., whereas the two rates are now
virtually identical-of course, very
satisfactory state of affairs. (Hon. Mema

TAX REVENUE-TRANSFERRED TAXES.
The revenue from transferred taxes,

own Government, produced £1,235,300,
which is £242,300 more than the Budget
Estimate.
This large increase in the yield of
transferred taxes over the Estimate is
almost entirely due to the rise in the

receipts from estate duties.

My
the appreciation in capital values.
right hon. Friend in his Budget Speech

It is satisfactory to know that our people

and on other forms of amusement and
recreation.
Motor taxation produced £714,080.
Another good sign.
REVENUE FROM RESERVED TAXES.
The Budget Estimate for reserved
taxes, that is, the taxes such as income
tax and customs and excise duties
imposed and collected by the Imperial
Government, was £8,620,000. The
receipts are shown at the same figure, but

The transferred and reserved taxes
