NON-TAX REVENUE.
The financial value of our Imperial
connection, apart from other outstandingly important considerations, is
emphasised by three items of non-tax
revenue, to which I desire especially to
draw the attention of the Committee.
First, the milk industry grant made by
the British Government, amounting to
over £100,000, all of which reached our
farmers; secondly, the £95,000 of interest
received from the Capital Fund; and
thirdly, the £1,039,000 parity payment
received under the Unemployment Reinsurance Agreement an agreement
which is of immense value to our working
people, because it enables us to maintain
our social services on the same basis as
those in Great Britain. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) It is really our workers'
charter.
-
The interest on the Capital Fund to
which I have just referred is also the
direct outcome of the Reinsurance Agreement. Until the new Agreement was
made this interest was being retained in
the Fund, which was being accumulated
in order to liquidate the old Unemployment Fund Debt. The Capital Fund was
released from this liability under the
new Agreement, and we were able to
resume the transfer of its annual income
to the Exchequer, a practice which was
suspended in the year 1930.
Other items of non-tax revenue are set
out in Table I, and are, in general, so
close to the Estimates that it is unnecessary for me to weary the Committee by
quoting items and figures in detail.
In all, the non-tax revenue, including
the self-balancing items in respect of
local loans repayments, "new" land
purchase annuities, which we collect for
the Imperial Government and pass on to
that Government through the medium of
our residuary share of reserved taxes, and
the Milk Industry Assistance Grant from
the Imperial Government, amounted to
£3,652,789, bringing the total revenue
available from all sources last year to
£14,222,169.
If we deduct from this total the expenditure for the year already mentioned by me, namely, £13,667,219, we
are left with a balance of £554,950. Of
this balance £500,000 is the provisional
amount of our contribution towards the
Imperial services last year. Ulster is
proud of her Imperial connection and
deems it a privilege to be able to contribute towards its cost. It is, therefore,
a matter of much gratification to my
colleagues and to me and, I am sure, to
our people generally, that our finances are
in a position to continue to bear a share

SUPPLY SERVICES.
The Estimates for the expenditure on
Supply services, after deducting the
estimated local contributions towards the
cost of the Education and Unemployment
services, total £10,010,000, which represents an increase of approximately
£92,000 over the actual expenditure on
Supply services last year. This increase
is partly due to the anticipated higher
costs of the Education and Unemployment services, and partly to an anticipated increase in the Exchequer liability
likely to mature in the year in respect of

In referring to grants to local authorities, the Committee will be interested
to learn that as from the 1st January
last the interest rate on new loans made
from the Government Loans Fund was
reduced to 3 per cent. This reduction
should be of considerable value to local
authorities in financing necessary schemes
of public utility. I might add that the
rate of 3 per cent. is the lowest local
loans rate recorded since the establishment of our Government, and it is now
the same as the corresponding British
rate.
I should also mention in this connection that recently the Government increased the amount of the percentage
grants made to local authorities in
respect of approved schemes of public
utility. Formerly, as hon. Members may
be aware, the Government made grants
to local authorities of 60 per cent. of the
labour costs of such schemes which were
not revenue producing undertakings, and
Minister's Financial Statement 1394
The Budget-
2 JUNE 1937
of 50 per cent. of the labour costs of
schemes in respect of revenue producing
undertakings. Now the Government
makes grants of 75 per cent. of the labour
costs of all approved schemes of public

That is done with a view to encouraging our local authorities and other public
bodies to undertake useful work which
without a grant they would not be able
to do. It is hoped by the Government
that much additional employment will

RESERVED SERVICES.
The last category of expenditure is that
relating to the cost of Reserved services,
that is the services administered by the
Imperial Government, the total of which.
is £1,935,000, an increase of £23,000
over the Budget Estimate of last year.
The increase is due to an expected rise in
the cost of the revenue departments,
namely, the Inland Revenue Department
and the Customs and Excise Department.
The "new" land purchase annuities and
the pre-1921 local loans, which we collect
as agents of the Imperial Government,
are £300,000 and £54,000 respectively,
making a total of £354,000. The total
estimated expenditure for the year is,
therefore, £13,499,000.
Revenue, 1937-38.
I now turn to the estimated revenue
for the current year showing how I propose to provide for this very considerable
expenditure. At the outset I might
inform hon. Members that the buoyancy
of our reserved revenues has made the
task of preparing my Budget Statement.
a relatively easy one as compared with
that which sometimes faced my predecessor. In making this statement I do
not desire hon. Members to infer at once
that I am in the happy position of
making wholesale concessions. I feel,
however, that the Committee will agree
when they have studied the figures I am
now about to reveal that our finances are
in a satisfactory state. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
During the past few weeks through
anonymous letters and otherwise I have
had protests about the burden of taxation
in Northern Ireland. I think I should
say frankly at this stage that it is not
possible to have lower rates of taxation
here than in the rest of the United
Kingdom, unless we were prepared to
reduce our social standards and allow this
part of the United Kingdom to drag
behind, which is, of course, unthinkable.

I now come to that part of my statement which I am sure hon. Members have
been patiently waiting for, namely, such
concessions as I am in a position to propose to the Committee.
Hon. Members will recollect that my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Commerce, in his Budget Speech of last year,
announced a restoration of half the cuts
in teachers' salaries made in 1931. I
propose to restore the teachers' salaries
fully to the scales in force immediately
prior to 1931. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The restoration will take effect
as from 1st July in respect of the salaries
of public elementary school teachers, and
from the 1st August in respect of the
Minister's Financial Statement 1398
The Budget-
2 JUNE 1937
salaries of secondary and technical school
teachers. The cost of this proposal in a
full year will be approximately £54,000,
and £32,000 in the current year.
In addition, of course, our teachers will
continue to receive the benefit of the
scheme on the lines which have operated
from last year, under which they receive
a lump sum on retirement in addition to
their pension.
I also propose to take steps to have the
pensions of teachers who have retired
since 1931 re-calculated in accordance
with the new scales of salary, so that the
temporary financial sacrifice which they
willingly made in 1931 in the national
interest will not adversely affect their
pension. This proposal will cost the
Exchequer about £2,000 per annum.
The actual details of the restored salary
scales will be brought to the notice of
the House in due course by means of the
presentation of the usual Statutory Rules.
I am sure that our teachers, feeling
satisfied, will devote themselves unreservedly and happily to their important
task of educating the young people of
Ulster to be loyal, worthy and helpful
citizens.
our
My next proposal should give considerable satisfaction to all classes of motorists.
It has always been a matter of regret to
my colleagues and myself that
financial position during the past few
years has compelled us to maintain our
motor vehicle duties at a higher level
than that obtaining in Great Britain.
We are, therefore, gratified that the
financial position in general, and that of
the Road Fund
Fund in particular, has
improved to such a degree as to enable
me to make the proposals which I now
wish to reveal to the Committee.
I am
not in a position to announce, as I should
have liked to do, that it is possible to
reduce these duties to the British level
in all cases, as to do so would endanger
the financial stability of the Road Fund,
and place it in such a position that the
existing standard of grants to local
authorities for road construction and
maintenance might not be preserved. At
the same time I think hon. Members will
agree that, keeping in mind the interests
of our local authorities, I have tried to
deal fairly and sympathetically with all
classes of motorists.
I propose to reduce the horse-power tax
on private cars and motor-bicycles to the
same level as that obtaining in Great
Britain. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The loss to the Road Fund in a full year,
consequent on the adoption of this proposal, will be £33,000, and the loss to the
Exchequer £11,000 in respect of the
luxury tax. The reduction of the tax
will, however, operate only from the 1st
January next, as will be the case with
the other motor taxation proposals I am
about to make, and I, therefore, estimate
the loss to the Road Fund, consequent on
the reduction of the horse-power tax on
private cars, to be £16,000, and the loss
to the Exchequer £5,000 in the current
year.
I also propose to reduce the fee for
driving licences to the Great Britain
level. The loss to the Road Fund
involved by this proposal is £17,000 in
a full year and about £5,000 in the
current year.
I propose to reduce by approximately
one-half, the existing difference in the
rates of duties between Great Britain and
Northern Ireland on goods vehicles. The
cost of this proposal to the Road Fund
in a full year would be £22,000, and in
the present year £11,000.
I also propose to reduce, by approximately one-half, the existing difference
between the rates of duties in Great
Britain and Northern Ireland on hackney
vehicles, that is, buses, taxi-cabs, etc.
The loss to the Road Fund involved in
this proposal in a full year is £8,000, and
in the present year £4,000.
My next proposal will afford relief to
our farmers. I propose to reduce the
duty on agricultural goods vehicles to the
same level as that obtaining in Great
Britain. The loss to the Road Fund in
a full year involved by this proposal will
be £1,800.
The total cost of all these motor taxation concessions in a full year is estimated
at £93,000, of which £82,000 will be
borne by the Road Fund, and £11,000 by
the Exchequer. In the present year the
total cost is estimated at £42,000, of
which £37,000 will be borne by the Road
Fund, and £5,000 by the Exchequer.
I am also glad to be able to say that
I propose to sanction improved rates of
pay for certain officers of our prison

Politicians during their lives get

Oral Answers to Questions.
ANTRIM SCHOOL ATTENDANCE
OFFICER.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state if it is
a fact that the Antrim Regional Education Committee recently appointed an
attendance officer at a salary of £90 per
annum; whether there were 38 applicants for the position, amongst them
being farmers, unemployed ex-Servicemen, University Graduates, etc., whether
the person appointed is an extensive
farmer with no family who is at present
employed as a rate collector; whether this
person is a relative of the present clerk
of the Antrim Union; and whether,
having regard to all the circumstances,
he is satisfied that this appointment is
in conformity with equity and justice
having regard to the abnormal unemployment problem; and whether it is in
order for an employee of the local
authority to hold dual positions.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
OF
TARY
THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The Antrim
Regional Education Committee have
appointed a part-time school attendance
officer at a salary of £90 per year. There
were 38 applicants for the post, but I
am not aware of their occupations or
qualifications.
The regulations made by the Ministry
under Section 4 of the Education
(Administrative Matters) Act of 1935
require the Ministry's concurrence only
in the case of certain major appointments of a local education authority,
but in other cases under Section 84 of
the Education Act (Northern Ireland),
1923, the Ministry's approval is limited
to the question of the numbers and remuneration of the officers and does not
extend to an investigation of the qualifications of the individuals appointed.
In the case referred to by the hon.
Member, the appointment arose owing
to a vacancy in the staff already
authorised and as no change is involved
in the remuneration, and as the post
does not come within the regulations
above referred to, the Ministry is not
called upon to interfere with the discretion of the Committee as to the person selected for the appointment.
Provided that the duties of the two
offices do not conflict, I am not aware
of any legal obstacle to the posts of parttime rate collector and part-time school
attendance officer being held by the same
person.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Does the Parliamentary Secretary not think that in the
interests of justice it would be better to
give £90 a year to an unemployed man
than to give it to a man already employed with a good family income?

SECRE-

TARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF

CARRYING FIREARMS BY
POLICE.
3. Mr. BYRNE (for Mr. Campbell)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he considers it necessary for the
Royal Ulster Constabulary to carry firearms on ordinary duty.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The answer is in

SPEED LIMIT IN BUILT-UP
AREAS.
4. Mr. BYRNE (for Mr. Campbell)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he has considered the statement
in the annual report of Sir Philip Game,
Commissioner of the London Metropolitan Police, that in London the speed
limit on motor vehicles in built-up areas
has been an outstanding example of
successful measures for reducing materially the severity and number of
accidents.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have seen
a newspaper reference to the report
referred to by the hon. Member. I have
not, however, seen any evidence that
demonstrates clearly that a general speed
limit would have the value which the
hon. Member attaches to it, but I notice
that Sir Philip Game considers that the
obstruction of streets by standing
vehicles is a much more serious matter
than the speed at which vehicles travel,
and I thoroughly agree with his remark
that the reduction of accidents is mainly
in the hands of road users themselves,
and that without their willing and intelligent support there is little hope of
any large-scale improvement.
To emphasise this, I might remind the
hon. Member that last year in Northern
Ireland pedestrians caused 791 accidents
out of a total number of 2,022, and that
cyclists caused 411. That is, 60 per cent.
of the accidents were caused by the
people whom one would expect to be
most careful.
It might also interest the hon. Member to know that although there was a
12 per cent. increase in the number of
motor-cars in use as between the years
1935 and 1936 the number of accidents
increased only by 2.3 per cent.
These figures do not seem to indicate
a need for a general speed limit, but
rather a need for the education of the
public in the art of exercising elementary
caution.
I have already indicated in a speech
which I recently made in the House the
Measures which I am taking, and I trust
the hon. and learned Member will not
think I am unmindful of the necessity
of doing everything possible to reduce
still further the number of accidents on
our roads.

EMIGRATION TO CANADA.
7. Sir ROBERT LYNN (for Mr.
Crawford) asked the Minister of Labour
whether his attention has been drawn to
figures issued by the Canadian Immigration Department showing that 12,023
emigrants were admitted into Canada
during 1936 and of the number 2,264
were of British origin and only 262 Irish;
whether he will take steps to find out if
foreign countries are getting preferential
treatment in this matter, as during the
same period the number from the United
States was 5,113 and from other countries
4,646; whether, with a view to reducing
the number of unemployed here he will
endeavour to get the restrictions removed
so that unemployed persons desiring to
emigrate to Canada may have an opportunity of doing so.
Major SHILLINGTON: All matters
relating to emigration within the Empire
are dealt with by the United Kingdom
Government, and further legislation on
the subject has recently been passed at
Westminster. Northern Ireland as an
integral part of the United Kingdom
comes within the scope of that Measure
and any schemes arranged between the
United Kingdom Government and the
Governments of any of the Dominions
will be available for persons living in
Northern Ireland who may wish to take
advantage of any facilities offered, as
fully as for persons living elsewhere in
the United Kingdom.
I am informed that no preferential
treatment is given by the Canadian Government to immigrants from foreign
countries.

him. But the right hon. Gentleman acts

Economy is not a subject that is popular in the country. People will subscribe.
to economy as long as you do not ask
them to economise themselves. It is a
desirable thing they admit, but they
have no desire to practise it. In bulk
we are all economists. Then when it

does not make for economy. If a Member suggests that we should save £100
here or £1,000 there he is met at once

economically and I do think that we
ought, where it is at all possible, to

Now, I gathered from the speech of

I should be delighted to go round his

and point out to him these little whitewashed cottages with their earthen floors,
dilapidated roofs, no sanitation, and no

The Budget, in my opinion, is

If you think you are doing the right

Never in the history of this country was

I am going to finish now. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I ask you in all

to go and see these slaves at work. They
get a chew of tobacco a day for giving

It makes me sad to think that men are
still slaves in loyal North of Ireland.
If this continues I will kick up such a

Are you satisfied to allow this to continue? Are you satisfied to allow widows

would like to see the Minister of Agriculture and Minister of Finance collaborating to give to the producer of flax a

We would all like to see pensions

would really mean an increased expenditure of something like two-and-aquarter millions a year, even if the age

Let us look at things from a practical

including the Imperial contribution, this
year amounts to just over a million
pounds. Even if our whole surplus was
used for paying increased pensions it
would not go half-way to meet the cost.
Besides, it is unthinkable that the Joint

as our contribution in order to pay

are paid in the rest of the United Kingdom. Now I could speak on that subject

Oral Answers
8 JUNE 1937
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 8th June, 1937.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
CLAIMS FOR PUBLIC ASSISTANCE
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the total
number of claims received by the Public
Assistance Board since the 1st April,
1937, the total number allowed assistance and the number disallowed;
whether he can state the total number
of cases received under the "not normally insured" conditions; the total
number allowed and the number
disallowed.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR
(Major Shillington): The number of
applications received by the Unemployment Assistance Board from the 1st
April to the 4th June, 1937, both dates
inclusive, was 14,296, all of which were
subject to the "normal occupation"
qualification under Section 31 of the
Unemployment Assistance Act, 1934.
The total number of applications
received from the new classes of persons
coming within the scope of the scheme
as from the Second Appointed Day was
9,246, of which 3,734 were held to be
outside the scope of the section.
The number of persons receiving unemployment assistance allowances in the
week that ended 28th May was just
under 27,000.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman inform the House what percentage passed the normally insured
test of the 3,000 who had to qualify on
these conditions?
Major
SHILLINGTON: I presume
the hon. Member refers to those who
only came in on the Second Appointed
Day. The percentage of disallowances,
those held to be outside the scope,
worked out at 40.
AN AGRICULTURAL WAGES
BOARD
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state on
what date an Agricultural Wages Board
is to be established in Northern Ireland
governing wages and conditions similar
to those operating in Great Britain and
the Irish Free State.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I would
refer the hon. Member to the replies
given to the hon. Member for Dock on

(Sir Dawson Bates): No, sir. Reports
made to my Ministry from time to time
by inspectors are of a private and confidential nature, and are furnished for
the sole reason of assisting my Department in determining matters coming

as

The Rural District Council received
295 representatives in respect of unsanitary dwellings (which includes
crowded houses), but as a result of
inspection decided that only 74 were so
bad that they could not be put into
habitable condition. They are, accordingly, proposing a scheme for the erection

on the owners of such of the houses as are

type in the Baronscourt area.
VENUE FOR PARLIAMENTARY
NOMINATIONS.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state why
the venue for receiving nominations and
declaring the result of elections in connection with the Parliament of Northern
Ireland has been changed from Belfast
City Hall to an office in High Street;
whether he will state the extent of the
accommodation in the High Street offices
for the candidates, their friends and supporters, and Press representatives, and
whether, in the case of future elections
and by-elections, the convenience of
candidates and all concerned will be considered in arranging the venue for
nominations and poll declarations.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The determination of the place at which nominations will be received and that at which
results of elections will be declared is
entirely within the discretion of the
Under Sheriff.
I am aware that on some occasions in
the past arrangements were made for the
use of apartments in the City Hall for
these purposes, but I understand that on
some recent occasions the Under Sheriff
did not consider that the heavy expense
of hiring these apartments for uncontested
elections was justified, and that he used
his office in High Street instead.
I have no reason to doubt that due
consideration has been given to the convenience of candidates in the past, or that
it will continue to be given in the future.
Mr. NIXON: Does not the question
of confidence, without reflecting on anyone, outweigh the question of expense in
cases of this kind?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a matter
for the Under Sheriff. This is the first
time anybody has suggested that any
sheriff is acting in any way improperly.
Mr. NIXON: Nobody has suggested
that.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The first plans
were selected after competition in August,
1934, and the final plans were ready in
May, 1936.
The total cost incurred to date is
£7,889, but all the accounts have not yet
been settled.
As regards the views of the experts
regarding the suitability of the site, the
resident medical superintendent of the
sanatorium considered it suitable, but the
committee's chief tuberculosis officer was
not examined. The one expert from
Great Britain examined considered the
site suitable. The two other medical
witnesses differed on the point.
The Ministry of Home Affairs, after
inquiry, refused to sanction borrowing for
the expenditure on the ground that the
site was not suitable and that provision
had not been made for all classes of cases.
With regard to the latter part of the
hon. Member's question, I understand
that the committee have now completed
their inspection of suggested new sites and
hope to be able to come to a definite
decision at an early date.

COLLECTIONS FOR CORONATION
ARCHES.
12. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether any applications to
the Commissioner of Police for permission
to make outdoor collections for Coronation arches in the city of Belfast were
refused.
Sir DAWSON BATES: One such
application was received and, in accordance with the policy which has been in
force now for some years, under which
permits are restricted to those collections
which have been carried out annually for
a considerable time, the application was
refused.
I am aware that there is a large body
of opinion against the continuation even
of the existing street collections, and I
am in entire agreement with the police
authorities in refusing to extend the list
of well-known charities which at present
benefit from such collections.

With regard to the hon. Member's
point concerning the Government of
Ireland Act, 1920, he will appreciate that
the privileges granted by that Act apply
only to officers who were in the service in
1920 and cover the public services as a
whole. I am informed, and believe, that
the safeguards provided for such officers
by the 1920 Act are generally regarded
as adequate and even generous.
It is
open to any officer, who considers that his
conditions of service have been altered to
his disadvantage, to apply to the Civil
Service Committee to be allowed to retire
from the service, and if successful in his
application he will receive the compensation for which the Act provides.

8 JUNE 1937
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): The Resolution
now before the Committee is being moved
in substitution for a Resolution passed
earlier in the present session for the
amendment of the provisions of Section
40 of the Unemployment Assistance Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934, which provided for the payment by local authorities of contributions towards the expense
of unemployment assistance.
that
Hon. Members will recollect
during the debate on the original Resolution my right hon. Friend promised to
reconsider the amount of the contribution
to be paid by the Belfast Corporation.
In accordance with this promise further
discussion has taken place with representatives of the Corporation, and
I am glad to say that a satisfactory
settlement has been arrived at. The
Resolution now before the Committee
amends the contribution from £56,000
to the agreed figure of £45,000. I beg
to move.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I rise to take exception to one thing that has been said by
the Financial Secretary of the Ministry
of Finance. He stated that this represents a satisfactory settlement. I say it
does not. It does not represent a satisfactory settlement from the point of view
of Belfast or of Northern Ireland, and I
wish to state that in terms which will not
be misunderstood. It would not be wise
and it would, perhaps, be uncharitable
to suggest that all local representatives
in Belfast are not appreciative of the fact
that one of the first acts of the new
Minister of Finance was to meet the local
authority in Belfast and re-discuss the
matter, with the result that a reduction
of £11,000 has been brought about in
the contribution which has to be paid by
Belfast.
I want the Committee to appreciate
thoroughly two points of view. The first
is that the Belfast Corporation does not
accept this as a satisfactory settlement of
the question. We are still called upon to
pay £45,000 a year under this settlement
in discharge of a responsibility which we
in the Belfast Corporation do not accept.
I repeat now the words I used the last
time I spoke on this question. When I
say the Belfast Corporation I do not
mean
a small elected group of people,
who may like parliamentarians politically
abuse their authority, but I speak in the
name of the whole body politic, the
citizens of Belfast. I speak in the name
of the intelligent people of Belfast who
have tried to study this problem, and I
wish to point out that there are in Belfast
thousands who are quite capable of
taking some cognisance of this problem of
unemployment, especially in regard to the
able-bodied unemployed. Those people
believed for a long time, and they believe
now, that the onus of responsibility so
far as the able-bodied unemployed are
concerned must rest in the first place
upon the Government. The care of the
able-bodied unemployed should first and
foremost be a Government charge and a
Government responsibility.
In the second place, I was just in process of counting up the total payments of
all the other bodies as compared with the
Belfast Corporation when I had to rise,
and I want those Members who are interested in this problem of unemployment to think for a moment about this.
According to the amount of idle gossip
that goes on in this Committee you would
think that the Members were interested
in nothing of a public nature, and I want
to draw attention to that. Every Member ought to be interested in unemployment, and any man cognisant of what
unemployment means at the present time
ought to be doubly interested in it. We
want to try to focus attention upon the
disparity between the contributions the
local authorities have been called upon
to pay.
The Antrim County Council is called
upon to pay £535, and each urban
council in the country is called upon to
pay such part of £1,280 as is apportioned
to it. The total that the Armagh County
Council is called upon to pay is £180,
and each council of each urban district
such part of the sum of £675 as is apportioned to the council; Down County
Council, £610; by each council of each
borough or urban district such part of
the sum of £1,560 as is apportioned to

involved in the giving of the site grants,

facilities now to be made available succeed in attracting new undertakings.
The additional facilities-this is the
important part provided by this
Measure are set out in paragraph (d) of
the first part of the Resolution and in
part two. It will be noted that they
include two forms of assistance, one by
way of annual grant for five
based
years,
upon either the rents of existing premises

actual or constructive, of the premises.
for five years.

any final cal upon the Exchequer in

CLAUSE 26 (Penalty for perjury).
Any person who wilfully and corruptly gives false evidence before any
referee, arbitrator or umpire shall be
guilty of perjury, as if the evidence
had been given in open court, and may
be dealt with, prosecuted and punished
accordingly.

TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The Ministry's Estimates for the current year show

I have used the words "net increase".
because hon. Members who have studied
the details of the Estimates will notice
that in many directions there has been
considerable expansion in the services
rendered by the Ministry to the several
branches of the industry. These services have been undertaken at the direct

as
With regard to the net increase of
£8,000 in the two votes, this is mainly
due to three factors: first, the regrading
of work and the stabilisation of salaries
in accordance with the recent general
scheme; secondly, to the increase in
wages to forestry workers and agricultural workers at the farms controlled by
the Ministry; and thirdly, the increased
cost of purchased feeding stuffs on those
farms.
In view of the importance of the agricultural industry to Northern Ireland,
and having regard to the developments
and great progress which have taken
place, it is a matter of some satisfaction
to me at any rate to think that out of a
Budget of £10,000,000 I am only asking
the Northern Ireland taxpayer to find
£191,000 for agricultural purposes.
In introducing the Estimates last year
I stressed the fact that contrary to what
has happened in most countries we had
pursued unswervingly a policy, despite
many serious difficulties and disadvan-
Estimates--
Ministry of Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
tages, of increasing production and doing
everything we could to lower costs of
production and eliminate waste and
inefficiency. Hon. Members will, I am
sure, realise that such a policy is one
which is not only in the interests of
producers, but in the interests of consumers. These two interests, producers
and consumers, are not, as is often
thought, opposites: they are, in fact,
identical. I have always so considered
them and will continue so to do.
Hon. Members are already familiar
with the remarkable development which
has taken place in our production of
pigs. I would, however, point out that
the policy we have pursued has resulted
in building up in little more than three
years an industry which had a value to
us of slightly over £1,000,000 to one
which is to-day worth something in excess of £3,000,000 per annum and is still
growing, or if you would like it in
numbers, from an output of 282,000 pigs
per annum to 710,000 pigs in 1936. I
would have the Committee realise that
this achievement has brought not only
a
measure of prosperity to producers,
but it has been of great assistance to the

distributive and transport undertakings,
and has brought a substantial increase
in prosperity and employment to our

been accomplished without any increase
in cost to the consumer.
I know that the temporary breakdown of the scheme in England and
Scotland must be a source of anxiety to

Ministry.
the

by creameries. These are

Ministry of Agriculture
9 JUNE 1937
On the liquid side of the milk trade
substantial progress has been made.
Until the present organisation came into
effect we had no means of measuring
what was happening. During the past
year our consumption of liquid milk has
increased by 8 per cent. or approximately
1,000,000 gallons, and I have good reason
to suppose that the present year will
witness a further increase in liquid consumption. It may interest the Committee
to know that of the liquid milk sold to
the public the approximate position is:
12 per cent. Grade A, 60 per cent. Grade
B, and only 28 per cent. Grade C.
Whilst this is a revolutionary change I
am not satisfied and I hope before long
to be able to report to you a very substantial increase in the production of
Grade A.
I am
aware that in certain quarters
an effort is being made to attack the
Milk Council on the question of the
price of milk. So completely misleading
are the statements which are made, so
devoid of knowledge are the opinions
expressed, that it almost looks as if those
who are responsible for them desire to
raise the bogey-and it is a bogey-of
consumer versus producer. Nothing
could be more unfortunate, especially in
Northern Ireland. I welcome criticism
and would plead for constructive criticism. To those who wish to criticise I
would say: "Do not believe what you
hear, get the facts." It will not help
the interests they have at heart and will
do great harm to the country generally
to make statements which arouse
prejudice and which have no solid
foundation.
As there has been some uninformed
criticism as to the price of milk to the
consumer it is desirable that I should
tell the Committee some of the salient
facts. In July, 1936, the price of milk
to the consumer was fixed for the year
commencing 1st September, 1936. In
fixing the all-the-year-round price the
Council had regard to the fact that
winter milk was dearer to produce than
summer milk, and in particular it took
cognisance of the then existing price of
feeding stuffs. Uunfortunately, owing
to
causes which none of us can
control, the price of feeding stuffs
began to rise, and in October the farmers
sought a reconsideration. This application was refused by the Council on the
grounds that the increase in the cost of
feeding stuffs might be only temporary
and the position was not then too difficult. But the rise in feeding stuffs continued, and by the end of last year a
ration which cost £7 per ton had risen
to about £10 per ton.
Supplies of milk were unquestionably
decreasing. The Council wisely, in my
view, decided to grant a temporary increase of 2d. per gallon for the three
months, February to the beginning of
May, after which the price reverted to
the original determination and SO
remains at present. I would point
out in this connection one additional
fact, namely, that our in-calf heifers
have decreased by 16 per cent., a fact
which shows quite clearly that the supply
position was in danger owing to the
relatively unremunerative nature of milk
prices. Nevertheless, I hope the consumer in Northern Ireland will bear in
mind and give to the Milk Council and
the Ministry this credit, that even during
the three months, February to May, when
the price was temporarily increased
Northern Ireland still had a much
cheaper milk supply than any part of the
United Kingdom. Finally, I would
make this point. I have heard no agitation at the increase in the price of bread
or beef and countless other commodities.
Can it be that in these cases the critics
have no organised public body to shy at?
I would merely remind them that as the
Minister of Agriculture I am more interested and concerned than even they
are in securing fair treatment to the
consumer, because I want the consumer,
in the national as well as the agricultural
interest, to consume much more liquid
milk than at present.
I have reviewed the position with regard to milk and pigs at some length
because they are two important branches
of the industry in which at the moment
most development is taking place.
Progress in other directions has, however, been equally satisfactory. The
potato crop in Northern Ireland, like the
rest of the United Kingdom, was not so
great owing to climatic conditions as it
was in the previous year. Whilst,
therefore, the shipments to Great Britain
will not reach the record level of the
previous year they are well above the
general average. The price has been
substantially better and the income from

potatoes as a consequence substantially

The poultry industry, as Members

here we have plenty of room for continued expansion, and although the industry has recently been hard hit by the
increase in the cost of feeding stuffs

Even the much maligned Fruit Act.
has, as it was intended, borne fruit in

season, we have shipped over 3,700 tons of

In the
five years since the Act came into operation we have shipped an annual average
of 6,100 tons to Great Britain, compared

for the five years before the Act came
into operation. Needless to say, the Act
alone is not entitled to all the credit.
What has made this development possible

horticultural staffs and the Ministry's

There are naturally many other

In effect, the scheme means this: If the
market price of oats falls by 3s to, say,

18s. an acre in respect of every acre of

the
in question under the Wheat
year
Act. The scheme, as my right hon.

the cost will not fall upon our own
Exchequer. What I should like to say
to our farmers in this connection is that
I hope they will grow much more barley
than in the past. The assistance I have
mentioned will be given to both oats and
barley, not to one or the other. It would
be a great asset to Northern Ireland if

accomplished in making us independent

Finally, there is one other piece of
advice I should like to give with all the
emphasis possible. I hope our farmers
will at once put a stop to the exceedingly
stupid and unwise policy of fattening
their heifers for beef. It is a suicidal
policy. What we need, and for many
years to come, is an increase in our cattle
breeding stock and a consequent increase
in our milk supplies. I beg to move.

We come to an important point in
regard to milk. The hon. Member spoke
about the consumers' representatives on
the Board. The consumers have
representatives on the Board-that is no
reflection on the hon. Member-and never
had, because you cannot have a representative on anything unless you have a
voice in the appointment of a representative. The consumers never got an opportunity of appointing representatives.
That does not reflect in any way upon the
character of the gentlemen who represented the consumers; it is only an attack
upon the system of appointing representatives. This is a representative Government, because everyone here, whether on
this side of the House or on the other,
has been selected by constituents who had
a voice in his selection and had a vote.
It is Hitlerism to nominate people and to
say to them, "You are the representatives of the consumers." The consumers
do not know who they are, and have no
voice in their appointment.
Even these so-called representatives
had practically no voice on the Council,
for we have had it established here today by the hon. Member who resigned
his seat (Mr. Grant) that the majority
does not rule there, that the Ministry's
representatives rule there, that officialism
rules there, and that Hitlerism rules
there, and in practically every other
sphere in this country at the present
time. Nothing that I could say would
be more severe than what has been said

Lt.-Colonel MITCHELL: I have listened with interest to the speech of the hon.
Member for Duncairn (Mr. Grant).
When I was appointed a member of the
Milk Board I took it that the Act of
Parliament passed by this House had
four different objects in view. The
first was to secure a supply of pure, safe
milk; the second was to secure an
adequate supply of milk for the consumption of the public of Northern Ireland; the third was to secure a
reasonable but not an exaggerated
reward for the producers of that milk
for the labour they had expended on
its production; and the fourth was to
see that milk was supplied to the consumers at the lowest reasonable cost.
The difficulties of the milk question are
not confined to Northern Ireland; they
have also occurred in England. A Commission was appointed to inquire into the
working of the milk business in England.
Here is an important recommendation
by that body:
The necessity for ensuring to the
consuming public an ample supply of
clean, safe milk at a reasonable price
must be the overriding consideration.
One essential condition of achieving
this object is that the producer shall
be fairly treated; otherwise the milk
required would not be produced. But
the interests of an individual section
must not be permitted to override the
general interest.
I think it is only right to let this House
know what really occurred. It is true, as
the hon. Member has said, that the price
was fixed for a year. When that price
was fixed the farmers stated that the
price of feeding stuffs was rising, and
that if the price continued to rise they
could not carry on on the terms fixed.
The chairman of the Milk Board, a most
valuable member-I do not question

no evidence before the Council that the
price would continue to rise, but that
if it did continue to rise it was open to
the producers to have another meeting
called for the consideration of the
position. The price did continue to rise,
and the producers did ask for a meeting
of the Milk Council. They put their
figures before the Council, and I confess

an hour. That was done, and I said to

representatives of the Government as
usual."
Eventually they stated that
they would never be able to agree.
As a matter of fact the farmers said
that as some sort of compromise they
were willing to take 1s 4d.

supply of milk from the point of view of
safety than they ever got before. Before

this milk question for the past fourteen

years ago. It has been the aim of the

water supply of the country is now being
given to milk, so that the people will get

can be a constructive case put against itthat the people in Northern Ireland,
thanks to the extensive schemes to safeguard the public health interests, are
now actually getting that quality of milk
to a much greater extent than hitherto.
While on that subject I want to ask

prepared to consider the advisability of

the Ministry adhere to that policy. I

the House to a very important consideration. In many countries, thousands of
miles away, pasteurisation is compulsory

of the finest cities in the British Empire,

in Great Britain but elsewhere, that
In one

Ministry of Agriculture 1548
Estimates--
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
pasteurisation is destined to play a big
part in safeguarding the public so far
as milk is concerned, and I think the
time has arrived when our Ministry of
Agriculture should depart from their
policy of unbridled opposition to pasteurisation.
I should like the House to listen to
this report by the medical officer of
Bournemouth, where there was an outbreak of typhoid. It is the report of
the late Dr. Vernon Shaw, of the British
Ministry of Health, who was appointed
to inquire into the cases of typhoid
which occurred in Bournemouth, fashionable Bournemouth of all places. Dr.
Shaw in his report states:
The outbreak was first brought to
the notice of the Ministry on August
21, 1936, and Dr. Shaw began his investigations on the following day. On
arrival he was informed that thirty
cases of enteric fever had been notified
during the preceding 24 hours and
that medical practitioners in Bournemouth and Poole reported that they
had a very large number of other
patients, who would probably prove
to have enteric fever, under observation.
The Ministry of Health investigated the
matter, and what did they find? That
this disease, this outbreak or epidemic
was caused by a contaminated milk
supply. The first thing they did was
this. The distributor of this milk, acting on the advice of Dr. Shaw, of the
Ministry, decided, on the day after Dr.
Shaw arrived and before they had traced
it to its proper source, to begin pasteurisation of the whole supply in order
to safeguard himself. This measure
was immediately successful, and it is to
be noted that up to the time this was
suggested by Dr. Shaw not one pint of
this man's milk had been pasteurised.
There is documentary proof here and I
will leave it on the Table for the Minister's perusal. This policy was successful
in terminating the outbreak. They explored the whole situation and Dr. Shaw
concluded that the milk was infected for
a period of about thirty-one days preceding August 22, prior to the time
that pasteurisation was begun, and that
the approximate number of persons who
had contracted the disease was 718, of
whom 518 were residents and 200
visitors. The deaths of residents numbered 51. I submit that that is an
alarming enough picture to focus
attention on the matter.
I am not going to weary you by reading lengthy extracts, but the doctor concluded his report by recommending to
all local authorities this consideration,
which is participated in by our Own
medical officer in Belfast:
In the present state of our knowledge, where large milk supplies and
commensurate risk are involved, the
only practical way to reduce the risk
of such outbreaks to a minimum is by
pasteurisation.
I speak with the authority of an organisation that has always pasteurised its
milk. What is the attitude of the
Ministry to that and other similar
organisations on the question? It is
this. We used to produce a Grade A-
I want people to understand that we did
produce a Grade A milk-baby milk
drawn from tuberculin tested herds.
That milk was sold at a halfpenny per
pint more than the ordinary price. It
was Grade A, but pasteurised. I am
not a medical man and speak subject to
the limitations of a layman. I have read
a good deal on the subject and there
are medical men in this House who can
keep me right. The safest milk in Northern Ireland at that particular time
was Grade A pasteurised milk. Not only
was it Grade A, not only did it come
up to expectations, but subsequent to
that it was pasteurised and that was an
additional measure of security.
A civil servant-I was amazed at the
abysmal ignorance of the man because
he was the first I heard using this argument. As a rule civil servants are fairly
intelligent and charitable in their outlook, a complex they develop by having
to advise Ministers-this civil servant
said to me when I was dealing with the

any misunderstanding let me say he did

at all, it is something that has been

by that and he said pasteurised. I said
there was a difference between pasteurised
and doctored, but he said, "Ah, but the
worst of it is all the vitamins, all the
health-giving properties in the milk are

people like the Mayo brothers,

connection with the milk supply. I am

that is not inspected at the present time,

The hon. Member for Woodvale also
accused the Government of having,
through their officials, ruined two industries in Northern Ireland, namely, two
bacon factories, in connection with which
negotiations are at present taking place.
I would like the Committee to realise—
I will put it very shortly, because an
explanation of the position would take
a very long time-that there are only
two solutions to this problem. One is to
increase the price of bacon in England.
That, of course, I am not able to do. The
other solution is to decrease the price
paid to the producer. I want to warn
the Committee that we are now on the
borderline. The pig producer in this
country is only just able to make his pig
production pay, and if the price is reduced the pig production will drop
straight away. Nothing can drop more
Sows
quickly than the pig population.
will be fattened and sent off and panic

short time, instead of having 700,000 pigs
we may drop to 500,000 or an even lower
figure. Those are the only two solutions
of the present difficulty, putting the
matter in a very short way.
I should like people outside this Committee and hon. Members to remember
this. The present Minister of Agriculture in Great Britain has made a definite
statement that the pig situation will not
be allowed to deteriorate into the position
in which it was before. He is to make
a statement shortly, and I am optimistic
enough to feel that, if by some mischance, by some wrong action, the pig
population of this country is allowed to

be in a position to take advantage of the
scheme when it is rebuilt, and the curers,
two of which are already established and
two more are coming-that will be four
Wiltshire curers in addition to our home
curers would not be in a position to take
advantage of the scheme which will be
introduced very shortly in England.
Surely that is a reason why, at the
moment, I cannot do anything more than
is being done, except to adjust minor
questions of price. I am optimistic-I
say that feeling it-that the whole of
this difficulty will, in a short time, be
solved.

The position, as I saw it last autumn, is

the requirements of this country.
Roughly, by the time the plant is installed, I am speaking from memory, it
would cost somewhere in the region of
£1,300. The cost of the production of

£7 a ton, and there are other matters

With the very heavy overhead costs of
the machine and the cost of working it
there is a temptation for those using the
grass-drying plant only to cut the grass
in the vicinity of the machine in order to
avoid the cost of haulage.

As Minister of Agriculture, I was

I might have been expected to answer.
That made it considerably simpler for me.
One of the great difficulties that must arise
where you have a body such as the Milk
Council or the Pig Development Council
is that the various interests concerned
have to fight their own corner. That is
bound to happen. It happened in this
case. The consumers' interests, to a
certain extent, clashed with the other
interests. But, if I did what the hon.
Member for Duncairn has suggested, and
altered the constitution of the Council
so that it would give its decision by a
majority, I am sure he will realise that
it is quite conceivable-I am not talking
in
a personal way that two of the
parties could bargain at the expense of
the other. It might happen that the
consumers and the distributors would
decide to bargain at the expense of the
farmers.
The most dangerous possibility is that
two interests should by some arrange.
ment bargain in such a way that the

The hon. and gallant Member for the

Here you

business, what is going to happen?
Suppose that he is compelled to accept

He produces and the other buys. I do

and who cannot buy milk, can be helped.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: That is a
matter which I cannot discuss with the
hon. Member now. He may know the
technical points. Perhaps he would be
good enough to come up to discuss this
matter with me some time, and we may
come to an understanding. There is just
one other point I should like to mention.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Minford), I think, is of the opinion that
the Potato Marketing Board has accomplished nothing in regard to prices. If
he will forgive my saying so, the hon.
Member is not right in that opinion.
What has happend is this. Normally
speaking, England produces 95 per cent.
of its requirements. It took some time
for the Potato Marketing Board in England to arrive at a working method
whereby they could control the potato
areas in England. I should point out
that in England there is a definite control of the areas; there is no control in
Northern Ireland. The only extent to
which we dovetail into the English
scheme is that the grading of potatoes
leaving this country is exactly on the
same basis. There is no question about
it but that for the restriction of the imports of foreign potatoes into England
the price of potatoes in Ireland this year
and last year would have been very
considerably lower. Although the
potato scheme is an extremely difficult
and complicated one, it has accomplished
a very great deal.
So far as drainage is concerned, I am
very glad to be able to announce, after
discussion with my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Finance, that the cost
will be borne by the Government to the
extent of 75 per cent., and that the
valuations in respect of which grants are
available has been increased from £60
to £75. That is very satisfactory.
Mr. GRANT: What about the black
scab?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I regret that I
omitted to refer to that question. So far
as black scab is concerned many farmers
in that particular district may feel that
they have been badly treated because of
the fact that although black scab has not
appeared for many years they are still
restricted and in a black scab area. I
do not know whether or not the Member
for Duncairn knows that black scab is
one of those peculiar diseases that
remains in the ground for twenty years.
It has been proved that although ground
has been left clear of potatoes for twenty
years, at the end of that time potatoes
have been replanted and black scab has
reappeared. But the real point is this;
that if we were to open a doubtful area
for potatoes it would mean an immediate
stoppage of buying by the importing
countries. Unless we can give them a
definite undertaking that the potatoes.
they are receiving are taken from parts
of the country that are not in the black
scab area they will not buy them. If
we open an area which is at all doubtful
these importing countries will simply
say: "No. No more potatoes from
Northern Ireland". I think that possibly the solution is-and the Ministry
are working along these lines-to try to
find immune varieties which correspond
in quality to the non-immune varieties.

make was that I understand they are

WIDENING OF DEE STREET.
1. Mr. BEATTIE askel the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
date on which work is to be started on the
widening of Dee Street roadway and footpaths at the railway bridge, as promised
by the Minister in his answer to my
question nine months ago.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The widening of the
roadway and footpaths at Dee Street is
closely bound up with the scheme for
providing a by-pass road, and if it is to
be executed economically and effectively,
must be carried out as part of that
scheme.
As the hon. Member is possibly aware,
work on the by-pass road cannot be commenced until negotiations which are in
progress with the Belfast Harbour Commissioners have been completed, but I
hope that it will be possible to make a
start at an early date, and I can assure
the hon. Member that when the scheme,
as a whole, is being executed no avoidable delay will take place in carrying out
the Dee Street improvements.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman is he aware
that the portion of Dee Street I refer
to has no connection with the by-pass
road. It is pedestrian traffic passing
through the railway arch-numbers of
school children.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg the
hon. Member's pardon. It is the railway bridge I am speaking of. I think
the Dee Street Bridge is most important.
The widening of the railway bridge will
enable all forms of traffic to get into the
by-pass road.
WIDENING OF HOLYWOOD
ARCHES.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
date upon which work is to be started on
the widening of the Holywood Arches as
promised some time ago.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Over a year
ago the Belfast Corporation submitted to
the Ministry a proposal for widening the
Newtownards Road between Connswater
Street and the Holywood Road, and also
for widening the roadway under each of
the two bridges.
The scheme was prepared with a view
to relieving congestion of traffic at that
place, but I considered that it would go
only a very small way towards solving the
traffic difficulty on the Newtownards
Road and that to gain adequate relief
it would be necessary to construct a bypass road which would take away from
the Newtownards Road and continually
increasing traffic from Holywood and
Bangor.
As the hon. Member is aware, steps
are being taken to provide such a road.
The proposals for widening the Arches
were a part of the scheme for widening the
Newtownards Road. I am of opinion
that the construction of the by-pass road
will render the road widening unnecessary, but while this is so, I cannot but
think that traffic requirements may
necessitate a modified scheme for widening the Arches.
If the Corporation, as the highway
authority, consider that some such
widening is necessary the matter will be
carefully considered when proposals for
effecting the improvement have been
submitted to my Ministry.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
there is no footpath under the two arches,
one leading to Upper Newtownards Road
and the other to Bangor, and is it not
a fact that many accidents happen there
due to lack of footpath accommodation
for pedestrians?

PRISON REFORMS.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether, in view of the
recent prison reforms announced by the
British Home Secretary, he is prepared
to institute similar prison reform in
Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have read
with interest the announcement to which
the hon. Member refers. He will, however appreciate that the changes which
have been made must be regarded as of
an experimental nature and that the
question of their application to our own
prisons cannot be summarily decided
without carefully considering the implications of these reforms in relation to
local conditions. My hon. Friend may
rest assured that I will give the matter
careful attention, and that on this subject the aim of the Government is identical with that which I am
sure has
impelled him to ask the question, namely,
that the punishment of criminals shall
be reformatory and not vindictive.
TRANSPORT FACILITIES IN
LARNE.
4. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
has seen the statement that '1,200 tourists
were landed on Sunday morning in Larne
and that no transport was available to
take these people to the town, and
whether, if the facts are as stated, he
will make representations to the Transport Board to have arrangements with
the shipping companies so that transport
will be arranged to meet tourists coming
to Larne and other seaside places.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
in communication with the Transport
Board in regard to the hon. Member's
question and I have been informed as
follows: :-
This boat did not arrive in
Larne in the morning as suggested in
the question, but at 3 o'clock in the
afternoon. Last season for several Sundays the Board provided a number of
special buses for the purpose of conveying passengers arriving at the quay in
Larne to the town, but they found that
these buses were not availed of at all.
Apparently the great majority of the
tourists coming in these boats preferred
to walk to the town instead of going
by bus, as they are only on shore for
about three hours.
After half the season had expired, on
finding that there was no demand for
the buses and that the tourists were not
using them, the Board discontinued the
provision of buses for this purpose and
no complaint whatever was received last
season.
Acting on past experience the Board
did not provide buses to take people
from the boat to the town on Sunday
last, but on that day as on every
occasion last season, they did provide a
sufficient number of buses for those
tourists who desired to occupy their time
on shore by taking a run through the
country.
Mr. NIXON: Could not the Transport Board, by a little intelligent inquiry, have found out the number of
persons leaving on the Stranraer boat?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If the persons
running the boat do not inform the
Transport Board we cannot blame the
Transport Board for not knowing.

Board want business that would be the
It
businesslike way of doing things.
would attract visitors and encourage

held on weekdays.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Under the
provisions of Section 48 of the Weights.
and Measures Act, 1879, the powers of
weights and measures inspectors are
limited to the examination of weights
and measures or machines used for
trading purposes. In these circumstances I am afraid it is not within my
province to implement the suggestions
contained in the hon. Member's question.
Mr. NIXON: In the absence of a
legal decision, is not boxing promotion
a recognised legal trade at the present
time?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I entirely
agree that boxing is recognised, but I
would suggest to the hon. Member that
the Boxing Control Board which is an
entirely impartial body, is operated in
Northern Ireland by a properly constituted council, with powers delegated to
them, and I can hardly suggest that
these gentlemen who control boxing in
Northern Ireland are not prepared and
not competent to look after their own
machines and to ensure that justice is
done.
Mr. NIXON: Are not the Boxing
Board of Northern Ireland all selfappointed and do they not largely
emanate from Glengall Street?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, Sir. The
Boxing Board is appointed from Great
Britain, which controls boxing.
Mr. NIXON: Do the clubs of Northern Ireland appoint a single one of them?
FIRING AT MOTOR VEHICLES.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the
number of shots fired by people in Northern Ireland at motor vehicles which
failed, or refused, to halt when called on
by the police to do so; whether police
instructions are that all firing must be
with effect; and, if so, whether he is
satisfied that this policy is in the
interests of good government; and
whether, in the event of fatal consequences consequent on the police carrying out orders, the Government will
vindicate the police.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member does not indicate in his question
the period in respect of which he desires
this information, but in any event I do
not consider that the time and work involved in making such inquiries would
be justified. The police are fully aware
of their legal rights in this matter, and
I am satisfied that they have not abused
those rights.
The Government will support the
members of the police force wholeheartedly in any action which they may
find it necessary to take, in accordance
with their legal rights, in enforcing the
law and will, of course, be responsible
for the consequences of any such acts.
Mr. NIXON: Have motorists as a
matter of fact been fired on for failing

sure

Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of

harbours. The Bill as originally drafted

for the regulation of advertisements in

rural areas require protection under the

Amendment agreed to.
Senate Amendment: Clause 2, page 3,
line 19, at end insert "or, without the
consent in writing of the owner and
occupier, upon any wall, fence or
building".
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Amendment is an extension of the by-law making
powers with reference to trees in Clause
2 to advertisements put on
any wall,
fence, or building, without the consent
of the owner and occupier. The hon.
and gallant Member (Lieut.-Colonel
Gordon) who moved the insertion of
Clause 2 in the Bill pointed out that the
Clause as moved by him did not, in his
opinion, go far enough, and that in addition to authorising local authorities to
make bylaws relating to advertisements
to be affixed to trees, he thought local
authorities should be empowered to deal
by bylaw with advertisements on any
wall, fence, or building. He did not,
however, press for any addition to the
Clause. Accordingly, the Clause was
accepted as moved by him, applying to
trees alone. In another House the
matter was taken up again, and it was
felt that a great injustice would be done
if we were to preclude the putting up of
advertisements, provided it is done with.
the consent of the owner or occupier, on
any wall or building. Hon. Members
will appreciate that if this Amendment
had not been put in by the Senate,
auctioneers' advertisements or advertisements for bazaars and so forth would
have been precluded. I think this is a
reasonable Amendment.
Amendment agreed to.

HARVESTING AS RELIEF WORK.
2. Major ROBINSON asked the
Minister of Labour whether he will consider the advisability of giving a grant
to farmers towards the employment of
extra labour during the harvesting period
and thereby help to alleviate unemployment.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply,
this being a matter which concerns my
Department. As farmers must, in any
event, employ the necessary labour for
harvesting operations it is not likely that
the payment of grants to them in respect
of such labour would have any appreciable effect upon the numbers of men
engaged for harvesting work. I understand that at present farmers find
considerable difficulty in securing the
services of agricultural workers and that,
therefore, the hon. Member's suggestion,
if practicable, would not increase the
number of agricultural workers.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's reply, while it may not increase the number of working men employed, would it not be a great thing
for the large farmers for the Government
to pay their labourers and workers?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am sure the
farmers would like it.
LIME FOR FARMERS.
4. Major ROBINSON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether it is the
intention of the Government to introduce a scheme of assistance to farmers
for the purchasing of lime and slag on
the same basis as is foreshadowed in
Great Britain, and, if so, whether he can
state when the scheme will come into
operation.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I regret that
I cannot at this stage give the hon. and
gallant Member a specific answer to the
first part of his question, as negotiations
are still in progress as to whether the
scheme referred to should be on a United
Kingdom basis or whether a similar but
separate scheme should operate in Northern Ireland. I can, however, assure the
hon, and gallant Member that in either
event similar facilities will be available
in Northern Ireland as soon as they are
in Great Britain.
ULSTER TOURIST TRAFFIC.
5. Major ROBINSON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether any complaints have been made to him regarding
the non-fulfilment of arrangements made
by tourist agencies bringing visitors to
Ulster, and, if so, whether he is prepared to take steps to protect the Ulster
tourist traffic.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. J. Milne Barbour): I am glad to
assure the hon. and gallant Member that
in general the arrangements made for the
reception of tourists coming to Ulster
have proved satisfactory, but from
inquiries made I understand that it is
alleged in one case that there was a
failure on the part of a private individual to fulfil his obligations in the
matter of accommodation and transport
as advertised by him.
The standard of hotel accommodation
and of catering generally, with particular reference to the tourist industry, has
recently been the subject of investigation.
by a representative Committee set up by
the Ulster Tourist Development Association, and
and in the discussions now
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour.]
proceeding with my Ministry as a result
of the Committee's deliberations any
matter such as that to which the hon.
and gallant Member has drawn attention
will be borne in mind. It would, however, be a matter for regret if failure on
the part of one individual were to be
allowed to reflect in any way on the
general efficiency and integrity with
which the tourist traffic is being handled.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Would the Minister undertake to promote the tourist
traffic of Northern Ireland by giving
more reasonable facilities for obtaining
refreshment to tourists from England
and Scotland?
Mr. GRANT: The House has to do
that.

July holidays. The final report will be
prepared and published in sections, but,
as the hon. Member will realise, a considerable time must elapse before these

AFFAIRS OF THE NORTHERN
IRELAND TRANSPORT BOARD.
8.
Mr. CAMPBELL asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state the revenue, the expenditure
and the profits of the Northern Ireland
Road Transport Board since the establishment of the Board, and how, on the
average, fares and rates for the conveyance of passengers and the carriage
of merchandise on the public service and
goods vehicles of the Board compare with
the fares and rates in operation
immediately before the establishment of
the Board.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As the hon.
Member is aware, the accounts of the
Board cannot be made up until the
Pooling Scheme is completed and
approved by the Transport Appeal Tribunal. The preparation of the scheme is
being actively pressed forward, but it is
a matter of great complexity and
involves the examination of a large
number of figures.
With regard to the second part of
the question, I am informed that passenger fares are, on the average, lower
than the fares in force prior to the
establishment of the Board.
So far as freight rates are concerned,
even if it were possible, which is doubtful, it would involve enormous expense
to ascertain what was the average previously charged.

Mrs. PARKER: There is a matter to
which I should like to refer on this Vote,
and it is of great importance to our local
authorities at the present moment.
refer to the item of grants to local
authorities under head B, in relation to
the Labourers Cottages Acts. This
matter has been exercising the minds of
all rural district councils which have
schemes under consideration. We were
most grateful to the Minister when he reintroduced the Acts which enable the
local authorities to undertake labourers'
Some of the district
cottages schemes.
councils had been waiting for this permission for a long time. Some of us had
already schemes arranged for; others have
taken up schemes since then. We are
most anxious to put this point before the
Minister. When this permission was
given the cost of building was considerably lower than it is at the present
time. The concession consisted of a 40
loan
per cent. grant on the annual
charges, and I think this applies to a
house costing £350. Since the concession.
was given the cost of building has
increased tremendously, and this is going
to act extremely hard on district

in a certain way in order to meet the
increased outlay. The district councils
would be very glad if the Government
and Minister would reconsider this

on loan charges to cover the reasonable
cost of building each cottage.
I am not going to suggest any particular figure, but £350 is really too low
for the present cost of building. There
are a great many other things, such as the
purchase of land, to be considered. The
cost of building has gone up, and it makes
it very hard for the local authorities to
go on with their schemes. In my own
case we are most anxious to undertake a
scheme of cottages. We are not a rich
district, and we have had applications for
a great many cottages. We are ready to
undertake a scheme for building 211
cottages. When the plans finally came
to us and we examined the estimate of
cost we found that it will mean something very heavy on the rates, especially
as we have undertaken an extensive
water and sewerage scheme, costing something like £85,000. That is a large expenditure for a small rural district. This
increased cost makes it almost impossible
for us to carry out labourers' cottages

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): In presenting
this very comprehensive Estimate I will
not go into detail but simply propose to
go through the subheads explaining those
items which are of particular interest.
The provision of £300 in Section 1 is a
token figure to cover the internal painting and ceiling repairs in this building
which are still under discussion with the
Office of Works. The amounts in this
section of the Vote are, as the note shows,
recoverable from the Imperial Government.
Subhead A, New Works, shows a reduction of £8,135. The reconstruction of
Government House after the fire is now
completed and His Grace the Governor
has resumed occupation. The provision
of £6,400, which is a revote, is to cover
the contractors' final accounts. I think
that the Ministry's architects and
Resolutions agreed to 1602
Estimates-
15 JUNE 1937
engineers as well as the contractors are
to be congratulated on the great improvements which they have introduced into
the layout of the building and its
internal decorative treatment-not an
easy task in reconstruction of this kind.
At the same time they have kept the
cost within the total sum paid by the
insurance companies in respect of the
fire.
The next item of interest to the Committee is the money for providing shelters
for the public on the Stormont estate.
An improved scheme for this purpose has
been put forward, involving the construction of four shelters at a cost of £900.
Owing, however, to the open nature of
the ground there has been some difficulty
in arriving at a suitable design for the
shelters and their positioning has also had
to be very carefully considered so as to
avoid interference with the amenities of
the estate. What is hoped will be a
suitable design is now nearing completion
and I expect that we shall soon be in a
position to start the actual construction.
The amount provided last year for the
laying of a sewer from the Ministry of
Agriculture's buildings on the Stormont
estate to the Newtownards Road is revoted as owing to unforeseen developments
the work was not begun last year. The
work is now being carried out by the
rural district council as part of a general
sewerage scheme for the district, and the
Government proposes to contribute a sum
of £500 towards the cost.
A sum of £16,400 is revoted for the
Royal Ulster Constabulary Depot at
Enniskillen. The main building has been
completed and is now occupied by the
police. This year's provision is to cover
the contractors' final account for the
main building as well as the cost of a
house for the instructor, married
quarters for sergeants on the staff, rifle
range, and other incidentals. The cost of
the depot is being met out of Capital
Fund No. 2, and hon. Members will,
accordingly, notice an appropriation from
that fund of £16,400 in subhead I.
The Committee will be interested to
hear of the progress made with the
Government's policy of improving the
standard of accommodation at employment exchanges. The new exchange at
Antrim has been completed and is now
in use, but it was not found possible to
commence work last year on the new
exchanges at Bangor, Newtownards, and
Cookstown. Provision is now made for
the work which it is expected will be
carried out this year. £600 is provided
for purchasing the site of the proposed
new exchange at Newtownards, and provision is also made for improving the
buildings at Carrickfergus and Strabane.
There is a sum of £3,550 provided for
the decoration and illumination of
Government buildings during the Coronation celebrations. This includes the cost
of floodlighting Parliament Buildings,
the Law Courts, Telephone House and
the Royal Ulster Constabulary Depot,
Enniskillen.
I now come to the largest item
of expenditure under this subhead, the
provision of accommodation on the top of
the building we are now in. As the Committee is aware, this has been made
essential by the
the
expansion of
activities of the departments, especially

will shortly be invited for this work,
which will end the present overcrowding

There is an increase in subhead B due

barracks; £600 is also provided for

remembered that it covers the requirements of some three hundred buildings in

c1
Resolutions agreed to 1604
