HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
to the interest charges on the growing expenditure on the county councils' share
of the Bann drainage scheme expenditure
and to provision being made for the completion of the channel improvements in
the River Quoile including the underpinning of the road bridge at Downpatrick.
I now propose to inform the Committee
of the progress made in connection with
the Bann drainage scheme. I would ask
the indulgence of hon. Members as since
I became Financial Secretary I have not
had time personally to visit these
drainage works, but I hope to do so as
soon as the present Session ends, in order
to make myself fully acquainted with the
work so that next year, if I am here, I
shall know more of the drainage system.
This report, which is prepared by the
technical officers of the Ministry, gives
the Committee full information regarding this work. Approximately twentyfour miles of river channel have now been
improved. The quantity of dredging still
to be completed is approximately threequarters of a million cubic yards. All
rock excavation under the contract is
completed, the maintenance period has
expired, and the reaches thus improved
have been taken over. The three
batteries of sluices at the Cutts, Portna
and Toome respectively, with their
accompanying fish passes and other
fishery protection works, have been completed and the maintenance period for
the last, that is Toome, expired on the
31st December last. The sluices have now
all been taken over and are operated by
the Ministry's engineers.
I will now deal with the practical
results of the scheme. What is generally
referred to as the statutory or summer
level of Lough Neagh is 52.00 feet O.D.,
and flooding of the low lying lands
surrounding the lough, due to a rise in
water level, does not commence until the
lough reaches a level of 53.5 feet O.D.
The highest recorded lough level this
winter was only approximately 1-inch
above the commencement of flood level,
and only continued for one day, the 25th
of January.
It is estimated that the pre-contract
level of Lough Neagh under similar
weather conditions would have been
above flood level for a period of nine
days in November; the lough would have
risen to flood level again on the 15th
December, and from that date onwards
until the end of March would have
remained consistently above that level.
In fact, continuously from the third
week in January until the end of March,
the lough level would have been round
about 55 feet O.D. or over, which is at
least 18 inches above the commencement
of flood level.
A spell of very inclement weather culminated in the blizzard on Friday, 12th
March, with a following wet thaw, which
gorged all streams and rivers, and caused
a considerable amount of flooding in the
Province.
The highest level attained on the Bann
during this spell was some 5 inches below
the commencement of flood level, and it
is calculated that in pre-contract days
the lough under similar conditions would
have risen to a level of 55 feet O.D. on
the 6th March, and would have remained
at that or a still higher level until the
end of the month, with resultant serious
flooding on the low lying lands surrounding the lough. Such local flooding as did
occur in the neighbourhood of Portadown
due entirely to the incapacity of
tributary streams and drains to deal with
the volume of melted snow and was not
attributable to Lough Neagh levels.

The Ministry's control of the sluice
gates is not at present unrestricted,
because care has to be taken not to create
current velocities which would hinder the
contractor's dredging operations
endanger his craft; if such restrictions
had not existed the levels of Lough
Neagh would have been lowered still
further.
Rainfall conditions last winter were
such that in pre-contract days very
severe and prolonged flooding would have
occurred; and I am glad to say that the
Ministry's engineers are entirely satisfied with the benefits effected by the
measure of control so far possible.
A sum of £2,200 is provided this year
for afforestation on the River Bann.
Over 200 acres between the Cutts,
Coleraine, and Kilrea have been planted
under this scheme and it is estimated
that a total area of about 600 acres will
ultimately be planted at a total cost not
exceeding £10,000. The scheme should
be completed by the end of 1939.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The amount

joint scheme for improving the property

Council adjoining Carrickfergus Castle.
The work is approaching completion,
and a large part of the grant has been
paid, so that provision need only be
made now for a small revote.
The work of the Ancient Monuments
Department is steadily expanding.
During last year, the early seventeenth
century structure of a manor house type
called Castlecaulfield, in the village of
the same name, was accepted from Lord
Charlemont, our Minister of Education,
who accompanied his gift with a donation
towards the cost of repair and preservation. There are few surviving specimens in Ulster of unfortified mansions
erected at this period, and Castlecaulfield, besides being handsome and imposing, still retains most of its architectural
features. Sketterick Castle, that familiar
landmark on Strangford Lough, is also
being handed over by its owner to the
custody of the Ministry.
Another remarkable acquisition was
the group of holy wells at Struel, County
Down, which came by gift from Mr.
Robert Brown. Here the main archæological interest lies in the structures
placed over the wells, and particularly
the ancient bath house which local
tradition ascribes to the seventeenth
century, but which may be of even
earlier date if architectural evidence is
taken into account.
Grants of 60 per cent. of the costs of
unemployed labour used in archæological
investigation were made in the case of
investigations conducted by accredited

Roads Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That the Bill be now read a Second
time."

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The main purpose of
this Bill is to enable the Ministry of
Home Affairs to undertake the construction of new roads. I might point out,
however, that this is not a new power.
It was one which was vested in the old
Road Board, and subsequently transferred to the Ministry of Transport, whose
duties and functions are now vested in
the Ministry of Home Affairs. As hon.
Members will readily appreciate, however,
modern conditions are very different to
those which obtained in 1909, when the
old Road Board was created, and accordingly it has become necessary to modernise
the provisions of the Development and
Road Improvement Funds Act, 1909.
Roads Bill--
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
of
Extensive improvements have,
course, been effected in the roads of
Northern Ireland, and many sections of
roads have been widened, but road widening is usually a costly proceeding, and
where the road runs through a densely
populated area it is neither a satisfactory
nor an economic way to afford additional
facilities for traffic. Motorists, in fact,
will not use roads which have been constructed through congested parts of an
urban area, for the numbers of streets of
small houses opening on to such roads
result in the likelihood of pedestriansboth children and adults stepping
into the traffic at any moment, and the
driver of a motor-car feels that he can
progress almost as quickly, and with very
much less strain, by choosing a route.
through ordinary city streets.
In the rural areas, moreover, there are
many small towns and villages in which
the streets are narrow and tortuous, and
in such cases the obvious course, if there
is much traffic passing through the town
or village, is to by-pass it.
con-
No by-pass roads have been
structed in Northern Ireland, although
they form a regular feature of modern
road systems in other countries.
It
would appear, however, that the time is
not far distant when by-pass roads may
become a necessity in certain areas here,
and the Government recently determined
to promote a scheme for the construction
of such a road to by-pass the congested
area at Connswater, and as that road
would lie within the areas of three local
authorities, it was decided that the construction of the road should be entrusted
to my Ministry.
I wish to emphasise that the purpose of
this Bill is simply to modernise and make
more convenient procedure for which provision already exists, as it has been stated
in a leading article in one of the papers
that until this Bill becomes an Act work
on the by-pass road, to which I have
referred, could not be commenced, and
that the delay which has taken place in
the commencement of this work is, in
fact, due to the Government having overlooked the absolute necessity for this Bill.
Such a statement is absolutely misleading
and only shows a complete and entire
misunderstanding of the whole situation.
If this Bill were never passed into law
it would still be possible, though with
some inconvenience to all concerned, to
construct the by-pass road under provisions that already exist in the 1909 Act
and, in any event, the particular provisions of that Act, to which amendment
is now sought, will not be put into operation for many months after the work is
begun-in fact, they may never be required at all. Time alone can tell.
Briefly, then, the Bill will provide suitable procedure to enable my Ministry to
construct any new roads which are needed
to facilitate traffic, and which it is
appropriate should be provided by the
Government rather than by local authorities. The cost of such roads will be
defrayed out of the Road Fund, either
directly or by means of money borrowed
on the security of that Fund.
Every new road made by the Ministry
will become a public road and, on completion, will be vested automatically in the
council of the county, county borough or
urban district in which it is situated, and
it will be eligible for assistance from the
Road Fund for maintenance purposes.
It will, however, differ from other public
roads in one important respect, inasmuch
as communication between it and any
other roads, paths, lands or premises will
not be permitted except with the approval
of the Ministry of Home Affairs.
An important aspect, in which the Act.
of 1909 is unsuitable, is that relating to
the compulsory acquisition of land. It
is, in fact, very defective in this respect,
as it incorporates, without modification,
the Land Clauses Acts, which are so complicated and so difficult to apply, that it
has been necessary, from time to time, to
make extensive exceptions and amendments in enactments which incorporate
these particular Acts.
The Bill empowers the Ministry to
acquire land needed for the construction
of new roads and to take it compulsorily
if it cannot be obtained by agreement. In
this respect it follows closely the procedure sanctioned by Parliament in recent
years for enabling local authorities to
take land for the improvement of roads
and for other local government services.
In fact, it simply adapts the appropriate
provisions of the Local Government Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934, so that they
can be utilised by the Ministry.
Roads Bill—
Second Reading
15 JUNE 1937
In Clauses 4 and 5 the Bill contains two
provisions which are not connected in any
way with the construction of new roads.
Where a public utility undertaking,
whether for the supply of water, gas,
electricity or some other service, opens a
road to lay or repair a main or pipe it is
obliged to restore the road and to do so
thoroughly.
For some inexplicable
reason there is one exception to this rule.
A sanitary authority may open a road to
lay or repair a sewer, but it is not obliged
by statute to reinstate the road, and
frequently, when the road is one for the
maintenance of which a county council is
responsible, difficulty is experienced in
having the road suitably repaired. In
fact, I know one case where a sanitary
authority relied on this particular defect
in the Act and refused to repair a road
which they themselves had cut up, and
the expense, therefore, fell upon the
county council.
Clause 4 is designed to remedy this
defect by obliging sanitary authorities
who break up county council roads for
sewers to repair them to the satisfaction
of the county council, and it provides
that, in the event of failure to repair a
road properly, the work may be undertaken by the county council at the
expense of the sanitary authority.
Clause 5 deals with an entirely different
matter. It gives to courts of summary
jurisdiction the duty of assessing the compensation to be paid for any damage done
by a county surveyor or by a contractor
when obtaining materials for the repair
of roads if the compensation cannot be
determined by agreement. At present
the matter is determined by three substantial householders, selected in the
manner prescribed in the Grand Jury
Act of 1836, but the procedure is too slow
and cumbersome for modern requirements.

Government is concerned we are doing
our very best with the local authorities,
and I will say this, that they, on the
whole, respond to our request that the
roads should be made safer. Anybody
who remembers the roads 15 or 20 years
ago will realise the enormous improvement that has taken place since that
time, but, at the same time, Rome was
not built in a day, and the local authorities, even if they do get 72 per cent.-
Mr. CHRISTIE: Sixty per cent.
was
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member suggests that Coleraine
singled out to get only 60 per cent., but
at all events these authorities, even with
the aid of the Government Road Fund,
are reluctant to put a greater burden on
the local rates. All I can say is with
regard to the local authorities that the
Government is, I am glad to say, on the
best of terms with the various councils
and we are doing our very best to encourage them to improve the roads and
make them safe. With regard to this
particular by-pass road this is a peculiar
case. There is only one town that I
know of in Northern Ireland where a bypass road is necessary. Belfast is a
peculiar city. It is, may I say, the
centre of a sort of cart-wheel. Traffic
coming from every side is absolutely
congested. One hon. Member suggested
that what we should do is improve existing roads. There is no use in doing that
because the roads are not wide enough to
carry the increasing traffic into that part
of Belfast. But that road is not for the
benefit of Belfast. It is for the benefit
of the people coming in from the country
into Belfast and not for Belfast's inhabitants at all, and therefore I do think
the construction of a by-pass road there
will do much not alone to make the road
into Belfast from the outskirts safer, but,
at all events, will expedite traffic and
make it safer for people coming in from
the country.
Mrs. PARKER: I just wish to say a

the money out of both rates and Road
Fund.

cut away the dangerous corners. The

Mrs. PARKER: I never alluded to

Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is

Lady as Mrs. Parker, and secondly, his

Mrs. PARKER: I seem to have raised
a storm, which I had no intention of
doing. I had no wish to misinterpret
any Member. I only pointed out that
instead of giving the impression, which I
certainly think we got, that the local
authorities might do more to put the
roads in good order, and that our Ministry could do more to help the local
authorities, it would be better to give the
impression that our roads are in excellent
order, that the local authorities do everything possible with the grants at their
disposal, and that the Ministry has been
proud to help the local authorities in this
concession. I was trying to point out
that visitors coming over from England
are agreeably struck by the main and
second-class roads. If the hon. Member
(Mr. Minford) would care to pay me a
visit in County Devon he will see what
narrow roads are like. I think we have
reason to be proud of our roads. Being
a member of a district council-I am not
actually a county councillor-I am sure,
from my knowledge of the district
councils, that they would be only too glad
to take all the money the Ministry would
give them and do their best to put the
roads in more perfect order.
As I say, I think we have every reason
to be proud of the roads we have got.
They bear comparison with English roads
and with roads nearer to us. Of course
this Bill is primarily, as the Minister
pointed out, for the purpose of assisting
one particular by-pass road which, as far
I understand, is very necessary.
Much as we would like the whole money
spent in the Province, it does not seem
right to grudge money towards the
making of a road which will benefit those
who come from the country as much, if
not more, than those going the other way.

connected with the matters aforesaid, it

Mr. Andrews.)

Queen's Bridge is not a suitable roadway
to meet all the traffic there. He will have
to discharge the idea of using the Queen's
Bridge as a crossing over the Lagan for
the purpose of meeting the traffic which
is proceeding in three different directions.
There is only one solution of the
present difficulty and that is to build a
bridge at Queen's Square or a little
further down the quayside. It would be
a blessing in disguise if the Minister did
this because the coal depot is an eyesore
to many people, especially visitors, who
are faced with it as they emerge from
the centre of the city. It is an exaggeration to say that if the coal depot is removed from near Queen's Bridge it will
mean an increase in the price of coal to
the consumer. The cost of cartage from
Queen's Bridge would be exactly the
same as it would be from a hundred
yards further down the quayside. By the
construction of a bridge over the river
there to Middlepath Street the new road
would proceed in a straight direction.
That road would then suit the traffic
coming from Antrim Road, Shore Road,
and Lisburn Road. It would form a
central position and relieve in a practical
way the congestion on the two roads that
we are trying to relieve. As the right
hon. Gentleman knows, this new road will
run through my division and partly

certain extent.

We are all agreed that the outlet across
the Lagan for the traffic coming from
County Down is not sufficient, and I
I would like to inform the hon. Member
that we are exploring the best way of

road will be an enormous success and that

to construct it. We are not going to be

Oral Answers to Questions.
HOUSING OF LABOURERS IN
MOIRA DISTRICT.
1. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
forty-three labourers, including ex-
Servicemen, have applied to the Moira
Rural Council for cottages and that up
to now no action has been taken.
The MIINSTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): From the information received by my Ministry, it appears
that 62 representations have been submitted to the Moira Rural District
Council to date. The Council has these
under consideration and it is to be presumed that as a result they will, in due
course, formulate a building scheme.
COST OF PLANS OF LABOURERS'
COTTAGES.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
the cost of preparing the original model
plans for labourers' cottages; whether
these plans were prepared without consultation with local authorities and have
now been scrapped, and, if so, for what
reason.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The fee paid
to the architect by whom the model plans
and specifications for labourers' cottages,
first issued by the Ministry, were prepared was £250. This covered the
preparation of five different sets of plans
These
to meet different requirements.
plans have not been scrapped, as suggested, and, as a matter of fact, are
being used by some of the rural councils
for their cottages and are available for
use by any others who find them suitable
to their requirements. A number of
Councils, however, desired to modify these.
plans to a very substantial extent and,
as the Ministry did not consider that the
plans lent themselves to modification,
they issued as an alternative, sketch plans
providing for a more simple type of
cottage which Councils can modify within wide limits at their discretion.
WAGES OF FARM LABOURERS.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether a farm labourer
named Robert Gilchrist was sent by the
manager of Banbridge Labour Exchange
to work for a farmer named Robert J.
Morton; whether the wage offered was
24s per week, and whether upon refusing
to accept such a wage, the man was informed by the farmer that the Exchange
manager had requested him not to pay
more than 24s a week; whether the Exchange manager is a farmer and is thus
directly interested in this matter, and
whether it is in the best interests of
justice that a local farmer should also
act as Exchange manager, and whether
he will take steps to ensure that this
practice shall cease.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Major
Shillington): I am informed that a
vacancy for a farm labourer at a wage
of 24s per week was offered through the
medium of the Banbridge Employment
Exchange by the employer, and refused
by the worker named in the hon. Member's question. I am satisfied from
inquiries I have made that the employer did not inform the worker that
he had been requested by the Exchange
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Shillington]
manager not to pay more than 24s per
week, and that no such request was in
fact made by the manager.
The Exchange manager does not engage in farming operations, and has no
private interest in the rate of wages paid
to agricultural labourers.
Dr. WILSON: Arising out of that
question, might I ask the right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Labour,

occasion on which the hon. and gallant

Mr. SPEAKER: That is hardly a

4. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware that farm
labourers in certain districts, particularly
Banbridge and Downpatrick, are being
asked to work for at little as 2s per day,
with food, and in the event of refusing
such offers of employment are being disallowed unemployment benefit, and, if
so, whether he will take immediate steps
to ensure that Labour Exchanges shall
not be used to supply sweated labour.
Major SHILLINGTON: I am aware
that the rate of wage mentioned by the
hon. Member is currently paid to agricultural labourers in parts of Northern
Ireland. Where this rate is prevalent
claimants accustomed to work on these
terms have in some instances been disqualified for benefit by the courts of
referees for refusing further work under
similar conditions.
With reference to the concluding
portion of the question, as the hon.
Member is aware, the facilities provided
by the Employment Exchanges are available for all members of the public, but
it is not the function of the Exchanges,
nor have they any power, to fix rates
of wages.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The right hon.
Gentleman says Labour Exchanges have
no power to fix the rate of wages, but is
it not a fact that Labour Exchanges have
power to withhold labour from people
who pay
lower than the proper rate of
wages?
Major SHILLINGTON: That is a
matter decided by the courts of referees
and eventually by the umpire if any case
of that sort arises.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not the duty of
the Labour Exchanges before supplying
any labour to see that the wages are
reasonable in accordance with the regulations in the district?
Major SHILLINGTON: They do try
to do that.
Mr. HENDERSON: Would the right
hon. Gentleman be kind enough to inform
the manager of the Exchange that he
should refuse to give labour to these
people who starve the agricultural
labourer?
THE OPPOSITION.
5. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Prime
Minister whether, in view of the fact

House has refrained from accepting the

of the House who are bona fide representatives of other opposition parties will
be consulted upon matters which affect
the interests of all sections of the House.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am glad
to be able to give an undertaking that
if the Leaders of the various Opposition
parties will communicate the names of
their Whips to my right hon. Friend,
the Chief Government Whip, he will consult them regarding the business of the
House.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg leave to say
that the Nationalist Party have never
sought any arrangement or consultation
or understanding.

Adjournment of the House (Summer).
Motion made, and Question proposed:

do adjourn until 12 noon on Wednesday,
the 7th July, and that after the report

Houses, Mr. Speaker do adjourn the

duly adjourned to that date, and at its

satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the Government, that the
public interest requires that the House
shall meet at any earlier time during the
Summer adjournment, Mr. Speaker may
give notice that he is so satisfied, and
thereupon the House shall meet at the
time stated in such notice and shall
transact its business as if it had been duly
adjourned to that date."-(The Prime
Minister.)

is becoming a mutual admiration society,

What is the aim of all this one-sided,
top-heavy administration? It is to
depress, and, if it can be achieved, to
degrade one section of the community.
In no other country that I know of does
a Government foment and perpetuate
religious discord as a main plank in its

of man.
Here that brotherhood is conspicuous in what way? It is conspicuous

employment all those who are seeking it,

land, I do not think it would be possible

I also ask the Government to bear in

Government we will find we have been

millions. It is controlled by a Socialsit
corporation similar to London, and

here the only shipping centre in which is

cent. Is that an equal distribution of the

partners with that great combination?
I think I might quote the speech made

Now in that shipbuilding controversy

is not a trade or calling which a man can

made in finding work for the able-bodied
comes in in another way. If we could
possibly reduce the pensionable age from
65 to 60. That is an end of the business
that will have to be tackled sooner or

fit industry into our available numbers,
because that would cut down wages and
give starvation conditions to service in

at least 16. That will be confining industrial employment from 16 to 60.
And remember that would only be the

be the finished article, because industry
is eliminating every year the human

age for entering industry will be 18 and
the age of leaving 55. And it is bound
to come to this as anyone who reads the

employed. A reduction of hours does not

took a leading part in it, proved that by

to produce three tons head
per
per

Therefore, shorter hours do not

We have less employment in shipbuilding

hours and lower production. Twelve
mean
thousand is about the total number

22,000 were employed and the tonnage

have got to go into employment not only

[Mr. Beattie]
I may be told that it cannot be done,
because the limited finances at the disposal of the Government would be a
hindrance to the application of the
theory which I am now propounding. I
have not such a short memory as to forget that the New Zealand Government,
within twelve months of taking over the
reins of office, was able to institute a
revolutionary change in that country.
The population of New Zealand is equal
to the population of this country, and
her wealth is not any greater.
I mean
the developed wealth is not greater; the
undeveloped wealth is much greater. In
New Zealand you have a Government in
power which has given itself a task that
is going to relieve the economic pressure
on the working classes in that country.
In our area we have a Government which
is only prepared to accept the old
orthodox methods of dealing with matters
and allowing things to go on as they are.
What was good enough for my grandfather is good enough for me.
Present
day requirements will not tolerate that.
You have got to renew your house and
get into your minds ideas more suited to
present day conditions.
What do the New Zealand people say?
They set out a code and they give a man,
on his retirement from industry, 22s 6d
a week at the age of 60. They give to
his wife 22s 6d a week, and they claim
that that amount is the sum that is required to keep them in decency in accordance with the cost of living. The cost
of living is a factor in the make-up of the
amount. If we take all the factors that
go to make up the cost of living into
account we find that we in Northern
Ireland are not much lower than they are
in New Zealand. The cost of living in
New Zealand is set down as 60s against
55s here. That is only a difference of
5s. I think if New Zealand, which is a
young country, is able to find ways and
means of getting their people comfortably situated we should copy their
example and give a lead to Britain. We
are returning to Britain over a million
pounds as an Imperial contribution. I
am satisfied in my own mind that Britain
does not want you to impoverish the community which you govern and pay them a
contribution of over a million pounds.
I want to remind the Minister of
Finance that when he was Minister of
Labour I asked him to allocate a proportion so that old-age pensioners would
receive an enhanced amount during
Coronation week. I was refused that
request. Then I read in the English
newspapers that various amounts of
money had been allocated to old-age
pensioners during Coronation week. I
was certainly very much disappointed
with the answer I received from the
Minister of Labour. We failed in our
obligations to the old-age pensioners and
unemployed during that week. We are
continually failing the unemployed. They
are getting hopeless. They are now dispairing because they can see that there is
no real effort being made to find useful
work for them to do. If this question is
not handled in a proper way it may turn
out very serious for all concerned. It is
galling to a man that the labour he was
previously employed on can be got in
abundance in England but cannot be got
at his own home. England and Scotland
are taking as much skilled and unskilled
labour as possible from here. Why are
we being made a market for the supply of
labour to other countries? We should be
a productive market ourselves and keep
intact the family life of our own workers.
We are supplying labour at present
and breaking up the family life. We are
taking fathers away from the mothers
and children. That is not the way to
encourage the people in this area. You
are asking them to work under conditions
of labour equal to those of the Englishman in the country in which he was born.
The man sent over from here has a dual
responsibility. His first responsibility is
to pay 25s a week for lodgings, and then
he has to pay for washing and other
necessary things. The amount remaining
he sends to his wife and family. The
family income is cut down and there is
the break up in the family life. That is
a wrong policy. It might be suitable in
a period of exceptional distress, but in a
period of prosperity such as we are
passing through, that policy should not be
continued. I hope the right hon.
Gentleman who now holds the important
position of Minister of Labour will try
to get industries and work suitable for the
people we are driving across the Channel.
We want to find work for them at home.
There are just two points I want to
make and I will finish. They deal with
the condition of affairs existing at present

Minister of Finance, because we know

Having said that, and having thanked
the Minister for what he has done
already, I am going to ask him to try to

[Mrs. Parker]
do a little more to help the Province in

done in the way of subsidies has, I am

and country would like to see. There the

will be seen that very few houses like that

have already said in this House, I know
of one public-spirited man in my neighbourhood who built a considerable number of houses to let at 3s 6d a week.
Then the Government have reintroduced the operation of the Labourers'
Cottages Acts, and as we know, large
schemes are contemplated by the district.
councils. I am quite sure, but I am not
going to deal with this point, that more
and larger schemes will be undertaken if
the Ministry can see their way to make

day ago and in regard to which he held
out hope and said he would consider the
matter. If he does favourably consider
that matter there will be a great deal
more done by the district councils in the
future for their labourers.
It is very much easier to give instances
which affect oneself. The council of
which I am a member in considering a
labourers' cottage scheme asked in the
ordinary course of events for representations and received something like 411
representations. They then asked for the
medical officers' reports on the cottages in
which the applicants lived, and I may
say we were horrified at the conditions
revealed by those reports. We realised
we were not able to build all the houses
we would have wished to build, and we
decided to try to help those who lived in
cottages which were designated as not fit
for human habitation, and were impossible to repair, or where the cost of
repairing was prohibitive.
We selected a certain number of these
applications and then we turned to the
ones we were obliged to reject. Here we
found something like 200 cottages, mostly
belonging to farmers, which were in a
terrible state but were capable of repair.
If we took action to insist on the repair
of those cottages, we knew from experience that most of the owners could
not possibly afford to put them in repair.
Something like 84 per cent. of the
farmers of this country have holdings of
under 50 acres. They are small farmers,
and I think I am correct in saying that
many of the farmers in my district, and
of course I speak for the whole rural
district, live themselves in houses which
if the details were known would probably
be labelled as in extremely bad repair,
probably in just as bad repair as the
cottages of the applicants. Therefore, to
ask them to put those houses in repair, or
failing that to close them and condemn
them, simply means that there is going
to be an even greater shortage than at
present. That would hit the employers
of the labourers very hard.
At the present time the rents of the
cottages to which I am referring are
something like 1s 6d let to agricultural
labourers. As I say, it would be
extremely hard on the farmers and would
definitely not be of very much assistance
to the labourers to condemn those
cottages because, after all, there are
limitations to what a district council can
do.
We have to consider the ratepayers
in our district, and no matter how urgent
certain reforms may be, there is a time
when we have to say stop, when it is a
matter of the rates rising beyond a
certain level.
I now want to make a request to the
Minister. I want to know if he will consider the application or introduction of
a Measure similar to the English and
Scottish (Rural Workers) Housing Act,
1926, because I believe if he would consider the introduction of a Bill on those
lines, with modifications, of course, to
suit the conditions in Northern Ireland,
he would be conferring a tremendous
benefit on the rural district councils who
are anxious to help the labourers in their
districts, and, of course, on the labourers
themselves and on the farmers. Under
that Housing Act, as far as it applies to
England, local councils are empowered to
give grants up to two-thirds of the cost
of reconditioning farmers' houses let to
agricultural labourers. This Act would
have a great bearing on the condition, to
which I have referred-these miserable
houses which can be put into repair at a
certain cost and which belong to farmers.

It has always been a principle of all
educational systems that those who insist
upon maintaining control of their schools
should pay for that control. The
teachers' salaries, of course, are paid out
of public funds.
With regard to the erection of schools,
the grant under our present system in the
case of a four-and-two committee is threequarters of the cost. The hon. Member
for Falls, speaking for the Roman
Catholic community in this area, said it
was contrary to their principles to accept,

by the public authority in the control of

it to accept four-and-two committees.

accepted the four-and-two committees in

cent. to which they are entitled under

in Northern Ireland for the construction

LIGHTING OF MILLISLE DISTRICT.
2.
HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that no streets or roads in Millisle
and the surrounding district have been
lighted during the past number of weeks;
whether he can state who has been responsible for this state of affairs, and,
in view of the number of visitors to this
district during the summer months,
whether he will take steps to have these
districts lighted.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am aware that
since the beginning of May no streets or
roads in Millisle have been lighted. I
understand that this is also the case
throughout the Newtownards Rural
District. Formerly the cost of lighting
villages, such as Millisle, fell upon the
local ratepayers as a localised charge.
Full urban powers in regard to lighting
and certain other matters have comparatively recently been conferred on
Rural District Councils, and the cost of
lighting has become a general charge on
the whole rural district. The Newtownards Rural District Council have
made arrangements under contract for
the lighting of the various parts of their
districts for the eight months September
to April in each year, from dusk to
11 p.m. During the months of May,
June, July and August the interval between dusk and 11 p.m. is very short,
especially in the mid-summer holiday
period, and the Council naturally concluded that no useful purpose would be
served by expending any public money
on lighting during the months in question. The Rural Council are satisfied
that
is
no appreciable inconvenience
caused thereby elsewhere in the rural
district, and do not consider that there
is any outstanding reason for according
Millisle exceptional treatment.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the shopkeepers
and visitors are complaining very bitterly
of the inconvenience caused by the lights
being turned off.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have endeavoured to point out to the hon. Member the position of the Rural Council who
are primarily responsible for carrying
out the work.

CONDITION OF MILLISLE
FORESHORE.
3. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware of the unsanitary condition of the
foreshore in Millisle; whether it is a fact
that the sewers empty on the foreshore,
and whether he can state what steps the
Government propose to take to abolish this
nuisance in the interest of the health of
the citizens of Millisle and visitors to this
seaside resort.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that the sanitary condition of the foreshore at Millisle is not all that could be
desired, but I understand that such nuisance as occurs is confined to the immediate
vicinity of four outfalls along the foreshore.
Naturally this pollution of the foreshore
will be much greater than usual during
the months of July and August owing to
the greatly increased summer population,
and the Rural District Council are alive
to the need for improving the position. I
understand that the provision of a modern
sewer in the northern part of the village
would do a great deal to remove the pollution, but, as I pointed out to the hon.
Gentleman in reply to an earlier question,
the provision of an adequate water supply
for flushing purposes is an essential precedent to the provision of an efficient
sewer. The Council are still endeavouring
to solve the difficulties about a water
supply, difficulties which the hon. Member
from his local knowledge will appreciate
are serious, and until they are solved there
is little either the Council or the Government can do to ameliorate the conditions
to which he has again drawn my attention,
Mr. HENDERSON: Are the people of

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Major

course
of preparation; and the present Calculation of Contributions Regulations, both here and in Great Britain,
are based on the provisions contained in

WAGES IN THE RETAIL DRAPERY
TRADE.
6. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is now prepared
to give a full report of the rates agreed
upon in the retail drapery trade in
Belfast, the number and names of the
firms who have signed the agreement, and
the names of any firms eligible to enter
into the agreement who have, so far,
refused to do so.
Major SHILLINGTON: The drapery
section of the Belfast Chamber of Trade
has, in consultation with my Department,
drawn up an agreement in which is set
out a minimum scale of wages for assistants and clerks employed in retail
drapery shops in Belfast. While this
agreement was still in draft it was submitted through my Department to the
National Union of Distributive and
Allied Workers, who agreed to its terms;
and I have arranged that a copy should
be sent to the hon. Member.
Additions are still being made to the
number of signatories to the agreement,
so that the number of firms who have
become parties to it is not yet complete.
It may interest the hon. Member, however, to know that 23 firms, employing
approximately 2,500 persons, have already
signed it, and so far as I am aware no
firm has yet refused to sign the agreement.
I should add that several firms were
already paying higher rates of wages to
the majority of their employees than the
minimum rates laid down in the agreement.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I should like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman is he aware that
it is alleged that some of the firms subsequent to the date of signing the agreement, or having agreed to have an agreement, reduced the amount of commission
payable to the employees, and that that
constitutes a violation of one of the
clauses of the agreement? If he will
accept my statement that that has
happened, is he prepared to have an
investigation with a view to having that
rectified?
Major SHILLINGTON : I have not
heard any complaints of the nature he
has put forward in the House. If he lets
me have particulars I will certainly be
glad to make inquiries.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman have a copy of this circular
containing the agreement circulated in
Hansard, or, failing that, is he prepared
to give a copy to any Member of this
House who may desire to have it?
Major SHILLINGTON: Certainly, it
will be available to any Member who
desires to see it.

CLAUSE 4 (Restoration of public
roads broken up by sanitary authority).
Senate Amendment:
Clause 4, page 3, line 38, after the first
"council" insert "within a reasonable
time."
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Davison): I beg to
move, "That this House do agree with
the Senate in the said Amendment."
very
This Amendment and the one following it were introduced as a result of representations received by the Government from the County Councils'
Association after the Bill had left
this House. The association apprehend
that as
of
a consequence
recent
developments in connection with the
extension of the Belfast Water Commissioners' supply area there is likely to
be a very marked increase in the number
of sewerage schemes, and therefore road
openings, undertaken by sanitary authorities and that special measures are therefore required.
the
The object of the Amendment now
before the House is to provide that repairs to a road broken up by a sanitary
authority should be carried out without
delay. The Clause, as it left this House,
merely placed an obligation on
sanitary authority to repair the road to
the satisfaction of the County Council,
but it was considered desirable in view of
the circumstances I have indicated to
provide that not only should the works
be carried out to the satisfaction of the
County Council, but that there should be
no unreasonable delay in executing such
works.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Parliamentary
Secretary, in his first speech in this House
in his new capacity, gave a very clear exposition of the meaning of the Amendment sent forward from the Senate. I
would like to know, however, what in the
opinion of the Ministry of Home Affairs
is "within a reasonable time." Each
department of the Government seems to
put a different interpretation on the term
"reasonable time." For the last fifteen
or eighteen years I have been trying to
get an interpretation of that phrase, particularly as it is used by the Ministry of
Labour, and I want now to find out from
the Parliamentary Secretary whether the
Ministry of Home Affairs place the same
interpretation on "reasonable time" as do
the Ministry of Labour. In their opinion.
would a month be a reasonable time to
allow a sanitary authority to complete its
work, or would three months be regarded
as a reasonable time.
In my opinion this Clause should lay
down a definite period in which a sanitary
authority must complete the work on a
road, and, personally, I would not agree
to any period varying from six to twelve

months. I think the Ministry should insist on the work being completed in a
month, or, at the outside, two months. I

or even two years, but in a case such as
we are now considering under this Clause
I think one month is the maximum period

""
Mr. DAVISON: If the words, "within

liked to complete their work. For this

Section, the matter shall be referred to

not be possible to fix a definite time for

nature of the work, and for the purpose of

Mr. BEATTIE: Where is this new

Mr. DAVISON: It is one of the

The PRIME MINISTER: My hon.
Friend has suggested that there might

have been circulated amongst the local

But the House will remember that the

are and always have been most helpful

They
The Member for Pottinger rather fell

Clause 4.
Senate Amendment:
Page 3, line 41, at end add the following new sub-sections:
"(2) Before a sanitary authority
acting as aforesaid proceed to break up
any such road, the authority shall,
except in a case of emergency, give
to the county surveyor seven days'
notice in writing of their intention so
to do, together with a plan showing
particulars of the proposed work so far
as it affects such road, and the sanitary
authority shall, before proceeding with
the work, consider any representations
which may be made to them by the
county surveyor.
(3) In any case where any difference
arises between a sanitary authority
and a county council as to what is a
reasonable time for the purposes of
sub-section (1) of this section, the
matter shall be referred to the Ministry
whose determination thereon shall be
final and conclusive".
Mr. DAVISON:
This Amendment
meets the point which was raised in the
debate on the first Amendment with regard to the delay by the county council
in approving of the work. They do not
approve of it; the sanitary authority
only consider the representations made by
the county surveyor, and then proceed
with the work, giving effect to them or
not, as they think fit. This Amendment is really on the same lines as the
first one, and the intention is to provide
that before a road is broken up by the
sanitary authority, in pursuance of the
Public Health Acts, they shall give
notice to the county surveyor together
with a plan showing particulars of the
work which they intend to carry out.
The county surveyor will thus be enabled
to give such advice as he thinks fit in connection with the proposed work with a
view to preventing unnecessary damage
being done to the road. The later part
of this new Sub-Clause 3 I have already
read. It provides that where there is a
difference between the sanitary authority
and the county council as to what is a
reasonable time, the dispute is to be
decided by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
I beg to move, "That this House do
agree with the Senate in the said Amendment."

the Senate in the said Amendment."

The PRIME MINISTER:
I very
readily agree to answer, as far as I can
on the spur of the moment, the questions
put by the hon. Member. In the first instance, he asked whether or not the Belfast
Harbour Commissioners had in some way
held up the making of the by-pass road.
No, sir. When the proposals for the bypass road were put forward I examined
them very carefully myself, and I am able
to give the hon. Member the very latest
information regarding the proposal to
construct a bridge over the County Down
Railway. The Government and the
Harbour Commissioners were most anxious
that the property recently acquired should
be devoted to aeroplane purposes, either
for civil aviation or for the use of the
Royal Air Force later on when the aerodrome is fully developed. Those chiefly
concerned in watching events were rather
afraid that, with the new type of heavy
machine it would be dangerous to have a
bridge over the railway at that spot. In
consequence it was immediately found necessary to devise some other plan for getting over that difficulty. I think it has
been surmounted, but, in any event, there
is plenty of work outside that particular
point, which will be gone on
with
immediately, as soon as the Royal Assent
to the Bill is obtained.
In the meantime I should like the hon.
Member to realise that there is no obstruction being put in the way by the Harbour
Commissioners. They are, indeed, pioneers
in connection with the development of
that part of their estate for aviation purposes, and the Government have been
helping them in every way possible with
the idea of having a first-class airport in
Belfast.
The second question put to me by the
hon. Member referred to relief schemes.
It appears to me that, although the hon.
Member has been in the House for some
time, he hardly realises that it is not the
Government who carry out relief schemes;
it is the local authorities. The Government help the local authorities, and are
sincere in asking those bodies to proceed
as much as possible with what I may call
works of national importance in order to
relieve the unemployment situation. But
the Government have gone a step further
this year.
My right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance has stated on many
occasions that we have actually sent to the
local authorities an intimation that instead of giving a 60 per cent. grant we
are now prepared to give a 75 per cent.
grant of the cost of wages for all the relief
work that is undertaken by the local
authorities. The hon. Member, therefore, should begin at the other end, and
if he can bring forward schemes that the
Corporation will recommend I am quite
sure that he will find my right hon. Friend
is ready to foot the bill as far as 75 per
cent. of the cost of wages is concerned.
That answers his second question.
The third question was, I think, more
general. It was as to what we have done
to help the unemployed. We have
stretched every point, as far as we possibly
can, in order to help those who cannot
find employment. In the meantime,
fortunately we are able to put our unemployed on exactly the same basis as the
unemployed in the other parts of the
United Kingdom. Nobody regrets more
than we do that there are so many people
out of employment, but we are satisfied
that nothing more can be done until we
are able to get more employment. I may
say that every attention is being paid
to the younger unemployed persons, and
if the hon. Member would some day call
in at the Juvenile Centre and see the
wonderful work that is being done there
I am sure he would be deeply impressed.

Harbour Board, of which some of his
Colleagues are Members, have inserted
in a resolution certain provisions which
must be observed before the Government
or anyone else will be allowed to interfere
with the Commissioners' right of way
either over the Lough or underneath it.
That decision was made about two meetings ago.
No matter what the Prime
Minister or the Harbour Board may say
about the benefits which the city of
Belfast is going to receive by the construction of this road, that is not the
point at issue at the moment. We must
have this road, but the Belfast Corporation have not at their disposal a mouth
to that road sufficient to deal with the
volume of traffic. The Queen's Bridge is
a very old bridge, and if we are not
going to be curtailed in our efforts for a
new aerodrome or the industry to be
carried on at Short & Harland's, we must
have either a transport bridge or a
tunnel. Those two things would have to
be on the Harbour property, and the
Harbour Board say
"No."
I support the Bill which has now been
passed, believing that in that Measure
we had power to deal with the Harbour
Board as we would deal with any other
concern that refused to give up certain
things in the interests of the community.
I say that we have to deal with the
Harbour Board on exactly the same lines
as with anybody else, irrespective of
vested interests. If the Government fail
to make provision for either a bridge or
a tunnel, they are going to spend money
foolishly on the by-pass road.
The next point the Prime Minister
made was that we are dealing with our
unemployed on exactly the same basis as
Great Britain. That is not So. The
regulations are not administered in Northern Ireland in the same way as they
are administered in Great Britain in regard to the scope of normally insurable
persons. I have proved that by testing
it. Only this morning I appeared at a
tribunal with a shipyard labourer, who
had been employed as an insured person
from he was 14 years of age until he
was 31. He has been six years out of
employment, through no fault of his
own.
He is a single man. I appeared
with him at the tribunal this morning,
and his application was disallowed on the
ground that he did not come within the
scope of the regulation, as he was not a
person who had contributed to the
Widows', Orphans', and Old Age
Contributory Pension scheme.
I know of another case, that of a
riveter, who has been unemployed for
eight years. He appeared before one of
the courts, and his claim was disallowed.
I myself paid the fare to Glasgow of his
wife and himself. They landed at
Glasgow without a halfpenny, and without one day's residential qualification.
They appeared before the Parish Relief
Committee, and on that first day they
got 34s to maintain them for a week,
and were told to come back in the following week for further consideration of
their case. In the following week he was
able to go before the tribunal under the
regulations in operation in Great Britain,
and it was held that he was a normally
insured person within the meaning
of the Act, who would make contributions to the Widows', Orphans' and
Old Age Pensions Scheme, although he had
not made a contribution of one penny
during the previous eight years.
claim was disallowed when a Member of
this House was sitting on the tribunal.
That man is now in Glasgow receiving his
unemployment assistance grant and he
has not one good word for the administration of Northern Ireland.
That
The next case to which I refer is this:
two old-age pensioners, drawing 10/- each
per week, could not exist in Belfast owing
to the smallness of their income, and I
advised them to go to Glasgow. It takes
some time to have the pension transferred, and during the period of waiting
-three weeks-the Parish Committee
allowed them 17/- a head, on the understanding that when the pension was transferred they would repay 10/- of the 17/-.
That means that in Glasgow persons who
have no resources other than the old-age
pension have 7/- a week added to their
income, making a total in Glasgow of 17/-
as compared with 10/- in Belfast. Those
are cases that I can stand over, and vet
we have been told by the Prime Minister
and by others that we go step-by-step with
Great Britain. We are not going stepbv-sten. We are far from going step-bystep so far as the social services are concerned.

similar to those fixed by the Imperial
Parliament; there is no increase whatever.

The ATTORNEY - GENERAL (Sir
Anthony Babington): May I say a word
with reference to this matter, as there
appears to be some confusion of thought
among Members on both sides of the Committee? There are two matters involved
in this, one is salary and the other is
duties. So far as salaries are concerned
I think the matter is perfectly plain.
Before 1921 all the county court judges
were on the Consolidated Fund of Great
Britain. When the Consolidated Fund
of Northern Ireland was set up and
separated from the Consolidated Fund of
Great Britain the county court judges
remained upon the British Consolidated
Fund, but they are charged upon the
revenue of Northern Ireland. Those
officers were existing officers in 1921, and
the conditions of their service and their
salaries could not be altered by this
Parliament without their consent and,
therefore, so far as their salaries were
concerned, they were stereotyped.
I think the hon. and learned Member
for Central (Mr. Campbell) is perfectly
right in saying that the salary could
have been increased, not so far as it was
paid out of the Consolidated Fund of
Great Britain, but by this House out of
our Own resources. That, however, is
purely a technical point. We could have
increased the salary, and I have no doubt
that if it had been increased the
occupants would have accepted the
increase, but we had no power to increase
it so far as it was a charge upon the
Consolidated Fund of Great Britain.
Every county court judge appointed since
1921 becomes a charge upon our Consolidated Fund.
The appointment is made by the
Government here, the duties are prescribed by this House, and the salary is
paid out of the Consolidated Fund of
Northern Ireland. What has happened
is this. Our county court judges were
upon a similar footing to the county court
judges in England. Their salaries are
now stereotyped by amalgamating the
basic salary and the bonus, and have been
raised to £2,000 or more across the water.
At the same time the salaries of our existing county court judges, that is, those
appointed prior to 1921, are consolidated
at the figure in this Money Resolution.
1773 Judges' Salaries (Money)-

Committee
Mr. BEATTIE: No increase and no
decrease?
The ATTORNEY GENERAL: No
increase and no decrease. What this
Money Resolution means is that we are
accepting the valuation put upon the
joint salary in the English Act of Parliament. Therefore, this is merely a Money
Resolution to enable this Government to
pay to the new County Court Judge for
County Tyrone, and to any other county
court judge who may be hereafter
appointed, the salaries mentioned in this
Money Resolution. The hon. Member
for South Tyrone (Mr. Elliott) is perfectly correct in saying that probably
there was an interregnum in respect of
the lately appointed county court judge,
and his salary will be fixed, not by this
Resolution, but by the Bill which will be
founded upon this Resolution and will
come before the House, I presume, in a
few days. If he has been paid-as to that
I cannot say, in the meantime and if the
salary that is ultimately fixed by this
House is less than that at which he has
been paid, there will be have to be an
adjustment as between the occupant of
the office and the Treasury. That is as
far as the matter goes with respect to
salary.
Another matter has been raised, that
is the question of duties. The Government are perfectly aware that in the
future there may be readjustments of the
county court areas. I am far from subscribing to some of the statements in the
Committee to-day as to the work done
and the duties performed by these judges.
The hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.
Beattie) said that in numerous cases these
men are constantly late. I spent over
seventeen years practising day and daily
in the county courts of Northern Ireland,
and I must say it was a very exceptional
thing indeed for a county court judge to
be late. I have no reason to suppose that
the punctuality they then observed is not
still observed in the county courts. Of
course there may be cases in which, for
some unforeseen reason, a judge may have
been detained and so may not have been
present at the time the court was
scheduled to sit.
In 1933, in order to give the Government a free hand at some future time,
if necessary, and if it was found
expedient to deal with the duties of
county court judges and to make either
an amalgamation or rearrangement of
duties, this House passed the County
Officers and Courts Act. Section 11 of
that Statute provides as follows:-
"A person appointed to act as county
court judge for any county or counties,
who has duly taken the oath required
by section three of the Civil Bill Courts
(Ireland) Act, 1851, shall, if the
Governor of Northern Ireland, after
consultation with the Lord Chief
Justice of Northern Ireland, from time
to time so directs, have jurisdiction and
authority to do and execute the duty
of county court judge for any county
or counties, or part or parts of a county
or counties, in addition to those for
which such person had been appointed,
and, if the said direction so provides,
may do and execute the said duty as
an additional judge.'
Then the sub-section reads:
"So long as any existing county
court judge continues in office, a direction shall not be given under the provision of this section, except with the
consent of every such judge affected by
the direction."
That means that the judges who were
appointed prior to 1921 cannot be called
upon by this House to undertake duties
other than those to which they were
appointed, but every county court judge
appointed by this Government under the
supervision of this House can be required
to act in either one county or two
counties or one county and part of
another county, and it gives the Government a free hand to put into force a
rearrangement of areas and a rearrangement of duties at any time it thinks fit.
When they do come to discharge those
duties the salaries will be the salaries that
are provided for here, and the County
Court Judge of Tyrone mav be asked to
do the duty of, sav, the County Court
of Tvrone and perhaps portion or the
whole of an adjoining county. If, in
the course of that rearrangement, one of
the county court judges drops out, it
means there will be one county court
judge less.
I think the Committee will realise that
these two questions are absolutely
distinct. First of all, there is the one
provided for in this Money Resolution,
and then there is the other and perhans
more important matter, namely, the

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): This resolution
is the necessary preliminary to the introduction of a Bill to implement the undertaking given by my right hon.
Friend in his Budget speech that the
motor-car driving licence duty would be
reduced from 10s to 5s from the 1st
January, 1938.
This provision could not form part
of the first Finance Bill as it was not
covered by the long title of that Bill as
presented. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: Do I understand
that this reduction will become operative
from the first of January, 1938?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): Yes.
Mr. BEATTIE: What becomes of the
10s that is paid from now till the end
of the year? Can any rebate be claimed
for the licences which will be paid for
in full?
Mr. ANDREWS: The position is that
any licences applied for since the
Budget speech are issued for a year and
then new licences at the reduced rates
from the beginning of the year.
Mr. BEATTIE: The point is that in
the Budget speech there was a notification given of a reduction of 50 per cent.
on the licences from the 1st of January,
and I want to know if there is any rebate
given on licences taken out in November
and December. A man may run a cer-

Widows', Orphans and Old Age Contributory Pensions (Voluntary
Contributors) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The
OF LABOUR
MINISTER
(Major Shillington): I beg to move,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
It gives me great pleasure to do so,
for I think there is general agreement
that one of the most valuable parts of
our social insurance code is the scheme
for widows', orphans' and old age
pensions.
At the present time 407,000 persons
are insured in Northern Ireland under
the Contributory Pensions Act. When
account is taken of their dependants it
will be evident what a very large proportion of our population enjoys the protection of this scheme. Since it came
into operation more than 88,000 persons
have shared in its benefits and the sum
paid in allowances of all kinds has exceeded £7,722,000. In addition, over
£3,882,000 has been paid to those over

years of age who have obtained an
insurance qualification under the scheme
-this sum being over and above the
further amount of £9,075,000 which has
been paid by the taxpayers under the
Old Age Pensions Act since the
year
1928. When it is remembered that this
has all come to pass during the last few
years, I think it will be realised what
a great advance has been made by the
community in affording protection to
those least able to provide adequately
for themselves and those dependent on
them.
The Bill now before the House proposes to carry the State provision for
pensions a step further. As hon. Members know, it is a condition of the scheme
at present in operation that, broadly
speaking, the contributors should be employed under contracts of service in what
are known as the "insured employments." In addition, there is a small
group of what are known as "voluntary
contributors," amounting to about
5,500, composed mainly of those who
began insurance as compulsory contributors.
Now, it is common knowledge that
there are many people not engaged in
regular wage-earning employment who
are no better able to provide for themselves than those covered by the present
compulsory scheme. It is to help them
that this Bill is designed. Examples of
those who will be assisted by this
Measure are mentioned in the first paragraph of the White Paper which is in
the hands of hon. Members, and which,
I hope, they have all read. They are
ministers of religion, farmers, shopkeepers, persons working on their own
as painters, handymen or blacksmiths,
dressmakers, private nurses, music
teachers, and many others-persons with
small incomes, whether working on their
own account or not, who have not the
qualification of insurable employment
essential under the present Acts.
The scheme embodied in this Bill is
the counterpart of the one which is to
come into operation next year in Great
Britain, and, as in the case of our other
insurance schemes, being identical in all
essentials with the Great Britain scheme,
it has been possible to arrange for complete reciprocity throughout the United
Kingdom. Contributions paid here will
rank for pensions in Great Britain, and
vice versa. Hon. Members will
1787 Contributory Pensions Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Major Shillington]
appreciate the great benefits of this
arrangement, and how essential it is that
the condition for its existence, namely, a
uniform basis in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland, should be carefully
preserved. The uniformity of structure
guarantees that a contributor can move
freely between here and Great Britain
without in any way impairing his insurance rights, and it maintains intact his
freedom of following up his livelihood anywhere throughout the United
Kingdom.
to
Now the first point I want
emphasise is that this scheme is entirely
a voluntary one. No one need come into
it unless he or she wishes to do so. If a
person thinks he can provide better for
himself in some other way or by taking
out a policy with an ordinary insurance
company, he is perfectly free to follow
that course without having to make any
contribution to this scheme. On the
other hand, if, after having carefully
compared the provisions of the scheme
with alternative provisions that may be
open to him, he decides to insure under
the scheme which I will now explain, I
think myself that he will realise that it
has great advantages, with a very solid
backing of Exchequer aid.
It may be a convenience to hon. Members if, in explaining the Measure, I do
not follow the course of making a commentary on the individual Clauses of
the Bill. The principal Clauses are
explained in the White Paper that has
been circulated. Instead, I will confine
myself to outlining in simple language.
the main structure of the scheme.
The first question, no doubt, that will
occur to hon. Members is, who can join
the scheme? The answer is, any man or
woman resident in Northern Ireland at
the date of his application who has
resided in Northern Ireland or Great
Britain for ten years before that date.
The only qualifications to this are two.
First, on joining a man's total income
must not exceed £400, or a woman's
£250, of which in each case not more
than one-half may be unearned. Total
income is the sum of the net income from
each source.
Allowances made for income
tax purposes, in respect of earned income
and for wife or family, however, cannot
be deducted, and where the applicant is
one of a married couple living together,
their joint income is to be treated as the
income of the applicant.
It is thought that those having means,
at the time they apply for insurance,
above these income limits have opportunities of providing for themselves and
their dependants without recourse to a
State-subsidised scheme.
I would like to emphasise that the
income limit applies only at the time of
entry into insurance. If, subsequently,
the insured person's income exceeds the
limit, his insurance continues unaffected.
To enable applicants to satisfy the income.
limit condition, arrangements will be
made with the Inland Revenue authorities to supply applicants with a simple
form of certificate to the effect that their
income does not exceed the limits laid
down in the scheme.
The second qualification is that an
applicant for admission during the first
year must be under 55 on the 3rd
January, 1938, and after the first year
an applicant must be under 40.
Within these reasonable limits of
residence, age and income any person may
join this scheme, provided he is not one
of the persons mentioned in the First
Schedule of the Bill.
These are people who are either already
insured or people for whose old age or
dependants' provision is already made by
Statute or other means recognised as
giving equally good security to that given
by the present pensions scheme. It
would be unreasonable that such a person
should be entitled to receive a second
pension under a State-aided scheme. On
the other hand, where the alternative
scheme does not provide the benefits of
widows' and orphans' pensions, the
person concerned, if he is not already
compulsorily insured, may insure himself for such rights under this scheme.
What can a man insure for? He can
insure, subject to what I will say later,
for a widow's pension of 10s a week with
allowances of 5s a week for the eldest or
only dependent child and 3s a week for
each other child; an orphan's pension of
7s 6d a week for each orphan; an old age
pension at 65 of 10s a week with a similar
pension for his wife at the same age, and
the widow's pension and old age pension
will be continued after 70 without any
means test. A woman, for a lower
premium, can insure herself for a "65"
1789 Contributory Pensions Bill-
6 OCTOBER 1937

Second Reading
pension, to be continued similarly after
70 without any test of means. She will
also be covered for orphans' pensions.
The allowances for children, and orphans'
pensions are payable up to the age of
fourteen, or, in the case of a child who
remains at school, until the 31st July
next, following the 16th birthday.
To secure these valuable rights, what
premiums are to be paid? During the
first year a man under 55 can obtain them
all for the very low weekly premium of
ls 3d, or, if he chooses to insure for
widow's and orphan's pension only, for
10d a week. A woman under 55 can
insure for old age and orphans' pensions
for 6d a week.
I need hardly point out that these low
premiums can only be quoted because of
the very substantial Exchequer assistance
that is being provided. As the White
Paper explains, for every 10,000 married
men under 55 who may join the scheme
during the first year, the actuary
estimates the present value of the benefits
to be £1,275,000 up to the age of 70,
and the present value of the contributions
of 1s 3d a week, payable up to 65, to be
only £400,000. The difference, namely,
£875,000, will be made up by an
Exchequer subsidy. The extent of the
subsidy to the women's insurance is also
set out in the White Paper.
Were it not for the assumption of
liability by the State the 1s 3d
premium for a man of 55 would have to be
at least 15s 1d a week, and the 6d premium for a woman of 55 would have to be
at least 8s 2d-these being the actuarial
equivalents of the value of the benefits of
the scheme, including the after-70
benefits.
During the first twelve months everyone within the scope of the scheme has
the opportunity of an extraordinarily
advantageous offer. Whilst every
additional person who joins will increase
the burden on the Exchequer which my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance has to carry, I can assure hon.
Members that nothing will please him or
his colleagues more than a real rush to
take up policies.
Of course these bargain offers cannot
remain open indefinitely, and after the
first year, which should give ample time
to everyone concerned to make up his or
her mind, the premiums will be on an
actuarial basis related to the age on entry.
The scale of premiums after 3rd January,
1939, for all benefits is set out in Part I
of the Second Schedule of the Bill. It
ranges from 1s 3d a week up to age 21
to 2s 11d up to age not exceeding 40 in
the case of a man, and from 6d a week in
the case of a woman up to 25, to 11d up
to age not exceeding 40. The scale for
widows' and orphans' pensions only is
in Part II of the Schedule, and ranges
from 10d a week up to not over 23 years
of age, to 1s 7d up to age not exceeding 40.
A very important feature of the
scheme is that an applicant has not to
make any statement of health or undergo any medical examination. Accordingly, whatever the state of a person's
health, he or she may feel free to join.
There being no selection of "lives," it
is obviously necessary, in order to keep
the liability of the taxpayers as subsidisers of the scheme within reasonable
bounds, to lay down reasonable conditions
for qualifying periods and the payment
of an adequate number of premiums.
Accordingly, for a widow's pension
with children's allowances, and for an
orphan's pension, the qualifying period
is 104 weeks since the date of entry into
insurance and the payment of 104 contributions, and for an old age pension continuous insurance for 10 years before the
age of 65 and the payment of 260 contributions. I will explain later how the
rate of pensions will be affected by the
average number of contributions paid
each year.
It may be asked, what does "continuous insurance" mean? It is this:
in any period of 12 months from July to
June at least 26 premiums must be paid
or must be deemed to have been paid.
If the number of contributions in any
year falls below 26 a person will have
an opportunity of making them up to
that number in the following year.
addition, of course, he will have to pay
at least 26 contributions in the current
year. If the opportunity is not taken,
insurance will cease at the end of the
second contribution year.

In what circumstances will actual payment of contributions be excused, and
will contributions be deemed to have been
paid, or in other words, credited to the
insured person without actual payment?
These are set out in sub-sections (5), (6)
and (7) of Clause 5 of the Bill. First,

To obtain pensions at the full rates,

year. The premiums are cut so fine

I have already

on a sliding scale proportionate to the

What about the position, however, of
persons who for some reason or another
lapse from insurance altogether? Are
they entitled to nothing for the
premiums they have paid? The scheme.
will provide for them in this way. A
person who has an average of at least
26 contributions a year for five years,
whether the contributions represent
actual payments or credits for weeks of
sickness, may be entitled to a partial
pension on the principle of a "paid-up
policy," calculated on an actuarial basis.
This "paid-up policy" will provide cover
for a widow's pension and orphans' pensions for five years after the end of the
last contribution year in which 26 contributions were credited. This does not
apply, however, to those initial entrants
who elect to be insured for widows' and
orphans' pensions only.
The "paid-up policy" may provide
further cover still in the case of entrants
after the first year. If the number of
contributions paid up to the date of
lansing has been substantial, a partial
pension may be payable at 65 to the insured person and his wife, or to his widow
at that age. The rate of pension will depend on the average number of contributions paid or deemed to have been paid.
This will be arrived at by dividing the
total number of contributions by the
number of contribution years from the
date of entry into insurance down to the
65th birthday.
Suppose a person is not able to keep
up his contributions and lapses from
insurance, may he at some future time
again rejoin the scheme? The answer is,
yes. And, if that person has acquired a
title to a deferred pension by reason of
his first insurance, the amount of that
pension will be payable in addition to
any further pension that he may earn in
right of his second insurance, subject, of
course, to the condition that the total
amount of pension may not exceed the
full rate provided in the scheme. It will
be understood that his second insurance
may result from his having entered insurable employment and having become,
therefore, compulsorily insurable under
the existing Act, or it may be by virtue
of a voluntary insurance under the
scheme of this Bill subject to the age
limit of 40. In the latter case, a reduction in the rate of contribution payable
may be made in consideration of the
value of his rights under his former insurance.
Hon. Members may wish to know how
the 5,500 existing voluntary contributors
will be affected by the new proposals.
They are not a large body, and the
subject is rather intricate. But, I will
do my best to explain it. Voluntary contributors under the existing Acts have
to insure for both national health
insurance benefits (medical benefit excepted where the income exceeds £250 a
year) and for pension rights, and they
have no option to choose one or the
other. Now that a system of voluntary
insurance for pensions is being introduced members of this class of contributors will be able to select the
insurance best suited to their needs.
They will have the option of remaining
under their present conditions of insurance for both health and pensions
benefits at the combined contribution of
ls 5d a week or 1s 8d if entitled to
medical benefit, or of coming under the
new scheme for pensions, without
prejudice to the continuance of their
voluntary insurance for health purposes.

Accordingly, in the first financial year

I think I have now covered the main

and to explain it as simply as I can. It

my opinion the terms for new entrants
