The ATTORNEY - GENERAL (Sir
Anthony Babington): This is the usual
Expiring Laws Continuance Bill. Our
temporary laws are in two parts. One
comprises those Statutes that relate to
reserved matters, and they are dealt with
in the Imperial Parliament, while the
other relates to matters which are within
the jurisdiction of this Parliament. They
Hon.
are to be found in this Bill.
Members will see that this Measure is
shrinking gradually. One of the Acts
which, up to the present, has been continued from year to year was the Courts
(Emergency Powers) Act, 1914. That
has dropped out, because the officers of
our county courts have found that there
are no longer any Orders made during
the war which need to be continued.
There are now only four Acts continued,
which hon. Members will find in the
Schedule. The question the House has
to decide is whether the Expiring Laws
Continuance Bill should be passed.
Mr. Moles, when Chairman of Ways and
Means, pointed out on many occasions,
it is not a question of the individual
Acts mentioned in this Bill, but whether
the practice of continuing these Acts in
force should still be followed. I beg to
move, "That this Bill be now read a
Second Time."
As
Mr. BEATTIE: I do not think there
is much in this Bill to comment upon,
but I would like to ask whether the continuation of these Acts serves any useful
purpose. If it does, why are they called

these Acts in force that I am inclined to

1825 Expiring Laws Bill

Adjournment-
Act, 1920. I am not familiar with these
Acts, and I would like to know from the
Harbour Commissioner who sits on the
Front Bench whether the Belfast
Harbour Commissioners have ceased to
make the increased charges authorised by
this Act, or whether they have reduced

The third Imperial Act to be continued is the Unemployment (Relief
Works) Act, 1920. That is the Act I
really want to speak about. There is
growing disappointment amongst the
69,000 unemployed in Northern Ireland
at the failure of this Act to deal with
the position they understood it would
deal with when it was first placed on
the Statute Book. I regret that much
useful work is not being done in
Northern Ireland because the local
authorities do not take advantage of this
Act. We have about 65,000, or perhaps
70,000 persons standing idle, and yet, not
very far from where we are at this
moment, road reconstruction work could
be undertaken that would reduce the
number materially. The opportunities
provided were not taken advantage of by
the local authorities, and many people
are standing idle owing to their apathy
in regard to this Act.
Why should we continue this Act? If
it is going to be ignored in the way it
has been in the past, would it not be
better to bring in a permanent law, compelling the local authorities to provide a
certain amount of useful work in the
areas under their control? There is not
a local authority that could not find such
useful work if it were willing and anxious
to do so. I would have something more
than this legislation asking them for a
return of relief work. I would compel
them to carry out work that is necessary
and essential for the well-being of the
community.

a Report from the Examiner of Petitions
for Local Bills, That he had certified
that Standing Orders have been complied
with in the following case:-
Huddleston's Divorce.
A Bill to dissolve the marriage of
Elizabeth Victoria Huddleston, of 1
Larkstone Street, in the County of the
City of Belfast, but at present resident

Oral Answers to Questions.
LEVY ON EXPORTED BUTTER.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he can state
if it is a fact that when a Northern
Ireland creamery exports butter direct
to
a merchant in Great Britain the
creamery must make a return to the
Ministry and pay a levy; whether when
a merchant in Northern Ireland imports
butter from a British. Dominion and exports the same to Great Britain he must
make a return to the Ministry and pay
a levy; whether the levy in Great
Britain is the same in amount as here;
the total sum collected by the Ministry
here since the levy was established
and the purposes for which this money
is applied.
MINISTER
OF
The
AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I assume
that the hon. and learned Member refers
to the licence fees payable by sellers of
butter and margarine under section four
of the Milk and Milk Products Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934.
Licence fees are payable in respect of
all sales of butter and margarine made
in Northern Ireland by licence-holders
to persons other than licence-holders.
Accordingly, if a licence-holder makes
a sale of butter in Northern Ireland to
a merchant in Great Britain, licence fees
are payable irrespective of whether the
butter concerned has been manufactured
by a Northern Ireland creamery or has
been imported. The licence fees are, as
I have stated, collected under a Statute
of the Northern Ireland Parliament,
and, therefore, no question of a comparison with corresponding fees payable
in Great Britain can arise.
The total sum collected since section
four of the Milk and Milk Products Act
came into operation is approximately
£176,000.
The produce of the licence fees is paid
into the Milk Fund. The purposes for
which the Fund may be used are set
forth in section eleven of the Milk and
Milk Products Act, and include the payment of equalisation payment and bonus.
to Northern Ireland creamery milk suppliers.

SCHOOL HOLIDAY FOR ROYAL
VISIT.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether it is proposed to
grant a day's holiday to all schools in
Northern Ireland in honour of the visit
of Their Majesties, or whether it is the
intention of the Ministry to refuse this
extra day to schools which were closed
during the month of July, notwithstanding the fact that many teachers of these
schools were on duty at Balmoral for the
entire day on 28th July.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The Ministry's circular of July last authorised a
special holiday on 28th July in celebration of the Royal Visit. The Minister takes this opportunity of again
expressing his appreciation of the services of the teachers who assisted at the
youth rally at Balmoral, but it is not
his intention that if a school was closed
for ordinary vacation on that day it
should be entitled to a day in lieu at
some subsequent date.
Mr. BEATTIE. I would like to ask
whether it is the intention of the Ministry to extend appreciation to the extent
of one day to those teachers who attended
from outlying districts at Balmoral,
thereby sacrificing a whole holiday.
Mr. ROBB: I have nothing to add.
Mr. GRANT: I would like to ask the
hon. Member for Pottinger would he be
in favour of those men who lost a day's
pay on that occasion getting remuneration?
Mr. SPEAKER: That does not arise.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is a pity you did
ont let me answer that question.

CIVIL SERVANTS HOLDING
OUTSIDE POSITIONS.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if it is
competent for a full-time permanent
civil servant to hold an outside
additional position at £200 per annum.
Mr. ANDREWS: General instructions
have been issued to civil servants with
regard to their outside employment.
These instructions definitely forbid the
engaging in any employment which
would occupy their time during their
official hours or which would conflict
with their duties to the State.
I have no reason to believe that either
the letter or the spirit of these directions
has been evaded by any member of the
Service, and cannot, of course, without
details express any opinion on the case
cited by the hon. Member.

A.O.H. BAND AT CASTLEDAWSON
7. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
if on the 18th August last the police,
accomunder the command of a district
inspector, prevented the band
panying the Hillhead Division of the
Ancient Order of Hibernians from
having their annual parade in Castledawson; whether this was done in such
a manner that only tact and restraint
on the part of the band averted trouble;
whether it is a fact that for many years,
atlhough Castledawson has an equally
divided population, there has not been
the slightest sectarian trouble there, that
the lodges on both sides are on the best
of terms and in the habit of lending
each other band instruments, and that on
the occasion of the parade, in accordance
with the custom observed by both sides,
no colours, emblems or deacon poles were
carried.
Mr. DAVISON: It is a fact that on
the evening of the 18th of August last
the police found it necessary to prevent
a contingent of the Hillhead Division
of the Ancient Order of Hibernians from
parading through Castledawson. I must
point out, however, that earlier in the
evening the police interviewed a member
of the Ancient Order of Hibernians and
warned him of the dangers of this parade
through Castledawson, and it was hoped
that this advice-made solely in the interests of preventing a breach of the
peace would be accepted. I am satisfied that the police acted promptly and
wisely on this occasion and not in a highhanded or discourteous manner.
I am glad to say that through the
tact and common sense of both sides in
past years there has been little sectarian
feeling in this town, but I must add
that I am also aware that on the occasion
in question
there was considerable
opposition to the demonstration, accompanied by the band, passing through the
town, and, in fact, the police have received representations from responsible
persons that such demonstrations should
not be allowed in order that the peaceful state of the town might be maintained.
I am informed that the Castledawson
Orange Lodges have never lent their
drums or any other instruments to the
Ancient Order of Hibernians.
I am afraid I am not in a position to
confirm the statement in the last part
of the question, although I have no
reason to believe to the contrary, but I
Oral Answers
Oral Answers

am aware that the Hillhead Division of
the Ancient Order of Hibernians, unlike other Divisions, do not inform the
police of their movements in advance,
and I am sure the hon. and learned
Member will agree that co-operation of
this sort is most desirable in the interests
of the peace of the community.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Are we to take it
that in future the parades in this town,
with an equally divided population, will
be confined to one party only-the party
of the right hon. Gentleman ?
Mr. GRANT: Remember Castledawson.
Mrs. PARKER: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that for one thing the
population is not equally divided, and is
he aware that there was very strong
feeling and tension existing in South
Derry owing to the outrages at the
Coronation celebrations at Swateragh
and Maghera on people carrying Union
Jacks?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
must not supply the Minister with information.

A PIGGERY IN FOUNDRY STREET.
10. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
a pig breeder who keeps a piggery at 83
Foundry Street buried the carcase of a
dead pig against the yard walls of the
residents of Kenilworth Street and Wolff
Street, thus creating a nuisance; whether
he can state has any pig breeder the
right to place manure against the yard
wall for indefinite periods; whether he is
aware that this piggery does not conform
to the requirements as laid down by the
Belfast Corporation for keeping pigs in a
built up area; whether he will make
representations to the Minister of Agriculture to have the licence for keeping
pigs in this yard cancelled.
Mr. DAVISON: The reply to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the right of a pig
breeder to place manure against a yard
wall, it depends on the situation of the
yard and the regulations made by the
local authority.
I understand that in this case the
piggery did not comply with the regulations made by the Belfast Corporation,
and on the matter being brought to the
notice of that body the owner of the
piggery was prosecuted. I may add that
the Corporation propose to revise their
bylaws relating to the keeping of pigs.
With regard to the last part of the
question, the licensing system of the
Ministry of Agriculture is intended to
enable that Ministry to keep in touch.
with the movements of pigs, and the
public health aspect of the matter
devolves entirely on the local authority.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Parliamentary
Secretary aware that a further consignment of 100 pigs was placed in this yard,
although the yard does not come up to
the requirements of the Belfast Corporation? In view of the measurements not
being in accordance with the regulations
what action is he prepared to take to
have these pigs removed?
Mr. DAVISON: I have no information with regard to that. It is a matter
entirely for the Belfast Corporation.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the hon. and
learned Gentleman make inquiries to
find out the position as it stands to-day?
Mr. DAVISON: Yes.

occupations in Northern Ireland and in

INSTRUCTIONS TO PANEL
DOCTORS.
13. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state if he will
lay on the Table of the House a copy of
the instructions to panel doctors, setting
out the number of substitutes that must
be issued to panel patients under the
National Health Acts for medical
benefits.
Major SHILLINGTON: No instructions of the kind mentioned in the hon.
Member's question have been issued to
insurance practitioners. Notes, however, for their guidance in prescribing
have been embodied in a National
Formulary prepared by the British
Medical Association in co-operation with
the Ministry of Health and the National
Pharmaceutical Union, and with the
approval of my Department. I under-
I should like to take the opportunity
to state that there is no justification for
the statements which are sometimes made
that an insured person is supplied with
medicines inferior to those supplied by
the doctor to his private patients. The
Act requires that an insured person shall
receive proper and sufficient medicines,
and it is the aim, not only of my
Department and of the Medical Benefit
Council, but also, I am satisfied, of
insurance practitioners as a whole, to see
that this provision is observed.
Mr. BEATTIE: Thanks very much.

SENDING OF UNEMPLOYED TO
15. Mr.
ENGLAND.
HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Labour whether he can state
when his Department is going to stop
sending skilled artisans to different parts
of England for employment, thus compelling them to keep two homes and in
many cases leaving their families
practically in destitution.
Major SHILLINGTON: Opportunities of employment anywhere in the
United Kingdom are brought to the
notice of unemployed persons, both in
Northern Ireland and in Great Britain,
through the Employment Exchange
service, it being obviously of advantage
to a person out of work to know where
employment is available.
If a person resident in Northern
Ireland accepts an offer of suitable employment in Great Britain, his fare to the
place of employment is paid, and, if
necessary, a repayable advance of £1 is
made through the Employment Exchange
in Great Britain on our behalf.
If, on the other hand, he refuses the
offer and the question of suspending unemployment benefit arises, the matter is
referred to the court of referees, which
takes into consideration, among other
matters, the question of the amount which
a person working away from home would
be able to remit to his dependants.
Mr. HENDERSON: Could the Minister state whether it is a fact that single
men who are anxious to go to work in
other parts of the Empire are refused
permission to do so, and that this Ministry is compelling married men to go,
with the result that many homes in
Ulster have been broken up?
I am not

18. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of assassinations in Belfast during
the past six years in respect of which no
one was convicted, and the number of
attempted murders during the period in
question.
Mr. DAVISON: The number of
murders committed in Belfast during the
past six years in respect of which no
person has been convicted was 18. There
were 27 cases of attempted murder in
Belfast during the same period, and in
eleven of these cases the offenders have
been convicted, and two persons are
awaiting trial at the next City Commission in respect of one case. The hon.
Member is, of course, fully aware that
eleven of the murders referred to occurred
during the unfortunate riots which took
place in 1935, and there is no evidence
to show that, in at any rate seven of
these cases, there was any actual intention to assassinate the particular victims.
MANUFACTURED STORIES OF
OUTRAGES.
19. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of persons in Northern Ireland
convicted during the past three years of
causing a public mischief by manufacturing and reporting stories of outrages
which never occurred.
Mr. DAVISON: Twelve persons have
been convicted during the past three years
of effecting a public mischief, and there
is at present one case in which the defendant is awaiting trial on a similar charge.
Of these six cases might be described as
relating to outrages.

Finance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. ANDREWS: The main purpose
of this Finance Bill is to give legislative
effect to the changes in taxation which
were announced in my Budget speech.
Hon. Members will observe that certain
matters of subsidiary importance, which
are embodied in this Bill, were not
specifically mentioned in my statement.
As, however, they are all concessions
designed to relieve the payer of motor
licence duty or to remove certain
anomalies in the incidence of motor
vehicle taxation, I am sure they will be
welcomed by the House. Hon. Members
will further note that one of the changes
announced in the Budget speech, namely,
the reduction of the fee for a driving
licence from 1st January next from 10s
to 5s, does not appear in this Bill. The
reason is that it has been held that the
Title of the present Bill as previously
circulated is insufficient to cover a clause
affecting the drivers' licence fee, which
unlike motor taxation is not an excise
duty. A separate one-clause Bill is,
therefore, being introduced to cover this
point.
The
Clause 1 of this Bill gives effect to the
reductions in motor vehicle taxation of
which the House is already aware.
new rates of duty are set out in the First
Schedule to the Bill. Briefly, the Bill
provides that horse-power duties
on
private cars and the duties on motor
cycles and agricultural goods vehicles.
will be reduced to the same level as in
Great Britain as from the 1st January
next; and that the duty on goods vehicles
and hackney carriages will be reduced by
one-half of the difference between the
rates of existing duties in force in Great
Britain and Northern Ireland as from
the same date.
I desire to draw the attention of the
House to certain other points in the First
Schedule of which no mention was made
in the Budget statement. This Schedule
supersedes those in the 1934 and 1935
Finance Acts, as I consider in the interests both of clarity and efficiency of
administration that there should be a
new comprehensive enactment in which
the scale of all motor taxation in Northern Ireland can be found included in a
single document; the Schedule, therefore, contains a certain amount of
repetition of the existing law which is
not altered. It also contains in addition
to the major changes those small concessions, to which I have already
referred, designed to bring the incidence
of motor vehicle taxation more into line
with that obtaining in Great Britain.
In paragraph three of the First
Schedule hon. Members will see that excavating machines and mowing machines
are to be subject only to the nominal
duty of 5s, which is at present paid on
tractors and other agricultural engines;
and that these agricultural engines when
drawing a living van shall not be liable,
as at present, to a higher rate of duty.
A further concession has been given in
sub-paragraph (6) of Paragraph 4 to the
effect that where a receptacle containing
goods can be lifted on or off a vehicle,
it will not be included in the unladen
weight for taxation purposes. This
follows an amendment of the law made in
Great Britain in the last British Finance
Act.
Clause 2 exempts invalid carriages
from the existing tax of 5s. This exemption was granted in Great Britain by
last year's Finance Act, and I am happy
to be able to make this concession now.
Clause 3 extends the exemption of road
rollers from tax to include vehicles into
which road-construction machinery is
built or to which it is attached. This
exemption should be very welcome to
Finance Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
local authorities and contractors, who
are important users of such vehicles.
Clause 4 empowers the licensing
authority to exempt from taxation those
vehicles which are used by farmers on
public roads for less than six miles per
week. Certain persons, in the main
farmers, who own land that is divided by
a public road, have, under existing law,
to pay the full rate of duty on vehicles
that are used solely for transferring
goods from one part of their land to
another, because to do so the vehicles
have to use a public highway. This
Clause is designed to remove this grievance.
Clause 5 allows licences for certain
hackney carriages and omnibuses which
are used only at holiday seasons to be
taken out for a minimum period of one
week, instead of the existing minimum
period of three months, and this concession will, I feel sure, be welcomed
both by the Belfast Corporation and by
the Road Transport Board. It is, I may
say, a concession which has no counterpart in Great Britain, but I feel it is
reasonable and desirable.
Clause 6 is designed to assist the police
and the licensing authorities in detecting
the users of unlicensed vehicles. A
similar provision is in force in Great
Britain. Hon. Members will be aware
that Section 10 of the Motor Vehicles
and Road Traffic Act, 1934, already requires that in the case of motor accidents
certain information shall be given to the
police, and it is considered that this.
Clause will materially assist the police in
detecting offences.
Turning now to entertainments duty,
Clause 7 embodies the concession in
regard to this duty, which I announced
to hon. Members in the Budget statement. The House will remember that by
the Finance Act, 1935, a lower rate of
duty became chargeable for certain
entertainments given by living performers, but owing to the wording of the
Act a combination of such an entertainment with a non-dutiable performance
attracted the higher rates of duty. The
present Clause removes this anomaly and
the opportunity has been taken to make
it clear that a display by any of His
Majesty's Forces or by the Royal Ulster
Constabulary comes within the scope of
the concession. To avoid legislation by
reference the entire Clause has been reenacted. The new Clause will have retrospective effect as from the date of the
Budget statement.
I am happy that I am in the fortunate
position to-day of being able to introduce this Measure, which will meet, I
believe, with the approval of every
Member in the House, and also of all
those whom we have the honour to represent. I beg to move.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Bill committed to a Committee of the

County Court Judges (Salaries) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE
(Lieut.-Colonel Gordon): In moving the
Second Reading of this Bill I wish to
take the opportunity to clear up the considerable amount of misconception which,
from the debate on the Money Resolution, appears to exist in the minds of
some hon. Members.
First it is necessary to go back to the
position in regard to the salaries of
county court judges as it existed prior
to the passing of the Government of Ireland Act, and indeed during the War
years. As hon. Members are, no doubt,
aware, owing to the rise in the cost of
living during the War, civil servants had
an addition to their ordinary salaries in
the way of a cost of living bonus
calculated on a sliding scale. At the outset this was only applied to the lower
grades, but subsequently was made
applicable, though in a diminishing
ratio, to all ranks up to those enjoying
salaries under £2,000 a year. The
Imperial Government decided to apply
this cost of living bonus not only to the
ordinary voted salaries which could be
varied at any time or in any manner, but
also to those salaries which were fixed by
Act of Parliament, including salaries
such as those of the Judiciary charged on
the Consolidated Fund. Under this
ruling county court judges in Ireland,
as elsewhere, who had salaries of less
than £2,000 a year received an addition
by way of a cost of living bonus. Unlike
the salaries, this bonus was not charged
on the Consolidated Fund but was borne
on votes.
After some time the British Comptroller and Auditor-General called the
attention of the British Committee of
Public Accounts to the fact that these
additions to the statutory salaries had no
warrant in law, and suggested that the
matter should be remedied by legislation.
The British Treasury agreed with the
views of the Comptroller and Auditor-
General and made note to correct the
position on a favourable opportunity.
It was the view of the Treasury, that
is the British Treasury, that the fixing
conof the amalgamated salaries by Parliament should not take place until the cost
of living figure had attained greater
equilibrium. This equilibrium was
attained in the year 1936, when the
salaries of Civil Servants were
solidated and cost of living bonus ceased
to be paid. This year, therefore, the
British Government passed a Statutory
Salaries Bill which made consolidating
arrangements for county court judges in
Great Britain and for a number of other
statutory offices to which cost of living
bonus had been applied.
The question arose in this Bill as to
how the salaries of the Recorders of
Belfast and Londonderry, the County
Court Judge of Down, and the County
Court Judge of Armagh and Fermanagh
were to be dealt with. These judges
were all appointed prior to the operation
of the Government of Ireland Act, and
under that Act their salaries continued
to be charged on Imperial funds and
could not be altered by the Northern
Ireland Legislature. What, therefore,
the British Government did was to provide in their Bill that the salaries of
these officers should be consolidated at
the amount that they were receiving in
salary and bonus combined at the date
of the passing of the Act. The Recorder
of Belfast, who received a statutory
salary of £2,000 a year, remained, of
course, at that figure as no cost of living
bonus was paid in his case. When the
Recorder has been called on to perform
extra work, for example dealing with
revaluation appeals, this House has voted
him extra remuneration.
The British Act came into operation in
the summer of this year and this Bill
follows on exactly similar lines. As I
have explained, it cannot touch the
salaries of those judges who are existing
county court judges within the meaning
of the Government of Ireland Act, that
is to say, all the judges except the
present County Court Judge of Tyrone.
As hon. Members are aware, he
was appointed to this post in the
Spring of this year, and the salary
due to be paid to him was that
fixed in the 1877 Act, viz., £1,400 per
annum. It, however, is obviously fair
that if the other county court judges
then in office were enjoying a cost of
living bonus in addition to salaries, the
new county court judge should draw a
1853 Judges' Salaries Bill-

was accordingly informed that pending

less than an accurately calculated bonus
such as the other county court judges

The opportunity of the Bill has been

I do not think that it can be seriously

a person holding the office of a county

Having regard to the fact that resident

I do not think that the somewhat higher

responsibilities.

Mr.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The scheme
of voluntary insurance for widows',
orphans' and old age contributory
pensions has already been explained to
hon. Members on the Second Reading of
the Bill, and in moving the Money
Resolution on the Order Paper I have to
explain to the House the cost to be borne
by the Exchequer.
No widows' and orphans' pensions will
be payable until two years after the commencement of the Act in view of the

have elapsed and 104 contributions must
have been paid since entry into insurance. Consequently, during this period
no charge will fall on the Exchequer.

fLieut.-Colonel Gordon]
In the case of old age contributory
pensions-65 to 70 years since no person
over 55 years of age can enter the scheme

This
It has been actuarially estimated that
on the basis of 10,000 initial entrants the
present capital value of the benefits to
men who will join the scheme is
£1,275,000, of which £400,000 represents the present value of the contributions, leaving £875,000 as the capital
liability of the Exchequer.
Exchequer liability is equivalent to an
annual charge of £46.000 for 30 years.
It is not proposed in the Bill to provide
for this exact sum each year, but to provide for payment of provisional sums
based on the amount of contributions
received from insured persons for the
first three years, ending on the 31st
March, 1940, 1941 and 1942, and thereafter for 27 years, a flat rate annuity
calculated to extinguish whatever remains
of the capital liability of £875,000,
which, however, may be revised every
tenth year in the light of experience of
the working of the scheme. The
Exchequer cost, therefore, will be nil un
to 31st March, 1939, and for 30 years
afterwards between £42.000 and £47.000.
The cost in respect of women cannot be
estimated with any degree of accuracy,
as it is not known how many may elect
to become insured under this scheme. but
an indication is given in the White
Paper that if 1,000 women enter the
scheme the cost to the Exchequer will be
approximately £2,000 per annum for 30
years.
Special voluntary contributors will be
entitled after the age of 70 to old age
non-contributory pensions irrespective of
means. As no person enters the scheme
over the age of 55, no pension will be
pavable until 15 years have elapsed, and
after that the cost to the Exchequer in
respect of these additional pensions will
rise in 30 vears' time to nearly £40.000 a
year. I beg to move.

(Mr. Barbour): I understand that,

each

Marketing of Eggs Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): This Bill is a very
simple Measure designed to amend one
section of the Marketing of Eggs Act
(Northern Ireland), 1936. I am glad to
1381 Marketing of Eggs Bill--

12 OCTOBER 1937
Second Reading
be able to inform the House that the
proposals incorporated in that Measure,
which I submitted to this House a little
over a year ago, in regard to a system
for the fixing of statutory prices for
eggs sold by producers to wholesale
merchants, will come into operation this
week. The Egg Marketing Committee,
which was established under the Act of
1936, has, during the past eight or nine
months, made an exhaustive examination
of the best method of introducing a
system of price fixing, under which the
price received by the producer will be
directly related to the prices which are
realised by wholesale merchants for the
sale of Northern Ireland eggs on the
British market and in the retail markets
in Northern Ireland. I have received a
unanimous report from the Egg Marketting Committee on this subject, and the
necessary arrangements for the introduction of the system of price fixing recommended by them have been made by the
Ministry, and the scheme came into
operation yesterday.
I should like to take this opportunity
of recording my indebtedness to the Egg
Marketing Committee for the exhaustive.
and careful manner in which they have
considered the whole question.
I can
only add that it is my earnest hope that
the system they have recommended will
prove of real benefit to all sections of the
poultry industry in Northern Ireland.
and I am confident that every member of
this House will endorse that hope.
The system of price fixing recommended
by the Egg Marketing Committee will,
however, apply only to the sale of eggs
from producers to licensed egg merchants.
Two sets of prices will be fixed, one for
eggs collected from producers and
another price, d a pound higher, for eggs
delivered by a producer to the licensed
premises of a Class A merchant. The
question of the effect of this system of
price fixing upon the sale of eggs by producers to retailers now requires consideration. Under the Act of 1936 the Ministry was empowered to make regulations
bring retailers under the same provisions
in regard to the purchase of eggs as
licensed egg dealers, if it was considered
desirable to do so. Producers are, however, accustomed to receive somewhat
higher prices for eggs purchased by retailers in the Belfast area than in the case
of eggs sold throughout the country to
I
wholesale
dealers.
It has, therefore,
appeared inequitable that retailers should
be tied to paying exactly the same price
as licensed wholesale dealers.
The
On the other hand it is extremely desirable that this section of the trade should
also be made subject to regulation.
effect of the present Bill is to enable the
Ministry to make regulations fixing the
price to be paid by retailers by reference
to the price to be paid by wholesalers.
In other words, this Clause will enable the
Ministry to fix the price to be paid by
retailers at a certain figure above the
price paid by wholesalers. At present
the Ministry has no power to do this and
can only prescribe that retailers shall pay
the same price as wholesale dealers. I
should add that this question has been the
subject of discussions between representatives of producers and of egg merchants,
and that I have received a recommendation that the price to be paid by retailers
should be 1d per pound above the standard price paid by wholesale merchants.
I beg to move that "The Bill be now
read a Second time."

Measures for the protection of the

Sir BASIL BROOKE: By leave of

Mr. BEATTIE: To your mind.
Bill
Sir BASIL BROOKE : This
does not put up the prices of eggs at all.
The fixing of prices was arranged under
the 1936 Act, and the price structure is
worked in such a way that the prices are
fixed as between producer and consumer
in accordance with statute. The attack
which the two hon. Gentlemen have
delivered with a great deal of vigour,
namely, that I am putting up the price
of eggs to the consumer, is absolute nonsense. When the retailer has to go to an
"A" licence holder to purchase eggs for
retail purposes he has to send a lorry
down for that purpose. Instead of that,
if the producer brings the eggs to the
retailer's shop it will be much more convenient for the retailer. This is merely
making statutory what has been the
practice. The hon. Gentlemen need have
no fear that this small Bill, which I
thought would have passed without any
great discussion, will put any increase on
the consumer whatever.
It is unnecessary to go into the matter
any further, except that I do want to
refute some of the statements which have
been made by the hon. Member for
Shankill (Mr. Henderson), that
poultry farmers of this country have
been crushed by the Ministry of Agriculture. It may interest him to know that
Northern Ireland is the only place in
the United Kingdom where the poultry
population has gone up, and I can hardly
see the hard-headed farmers of Ulster
producing more chickens unless it is a
fair paying proposition. The statement
that I pay no attention to the interests
of the consumers is nonsense. The hon.
Gentleman should credit me with a little
commonsense in this respect. If I fixed
prices which were unfair to the consumer
I would be doing a very stupid thing. I
hope that the hon. Gentlemen who raised
this point will realise that this Bill will
not involve any extra price on the consumer, and that I realise that the consumer has to be safeguarded. That is
one of the reasons why the Government
have retained control, so as to ensure
that the consumers will not be penalised.

Milk and Milk Products Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: It affords me
very great satisfaction to be in a position
to ask the House to give a Second Reading to this Measure. As Members will
have appreciated, the primary purpose of
the Bill is to increase the assistance
which is given to creameries so as to
enable them to pay better prices to producers who supply milk for manufacturing purposes. Members will recall that
it is now a little over three years since
the first direct financial assistance to
creameries was afforded by the Milk and
Milk Products Act of 1934. Under that
Measure creameries were paid equalisation payments sufficient to raise the
average price of milk delivered to
creameries in Northern Ireland to 5d in
summer and 6d in winter.
The funds necessary to provide the
money for this purpose were contributed
by the Imperial Treasury under the
Milk Assistance Grant, which is paid to
the Northern Ireland Milk Fund, and I
am glad to say that this assistance from
the British Treasury will continue until
the end of September, 1938. As a result
of this assistance to our creameries the
supply of milk to creameries has shown
a very substantial increase. During the
twelve months ending 31st March, 1934,
approximately 17 million gallons were
handled by creameries in Northern Ireland. This quantity increased to 182
million gallons in the following year, to
24 million in the year ending 31st
Milk Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
March, 1936, and to 25 million in the
year ending March last. The effect of
the scheme in stimulating Northern Ireland dairy production is thus apparent.
Unfortunately, during the past twelve
months there has been a tendency for
some of the increase gained during the
first years of the scheme to be lost. This
reduction in the supply to creameries
was particularly apparent during the
past summer, and the supply has gone
down from 15 million gallons to 13
million gallons during these months of
the current year— a reduction of 11 per
cent.
I have viewed with misgivings this decline in the supply of milk to our
creameries. The reasons are not far to
seek. There has since the middle of 1936
been a rapid increase in the price of
feeding stuffs, and the cost of feeding
has increased by somewhere in the
neighbourhood of d to 1d per gallon of
milk produced. In addition, labour costs
have shown an upward tendency and also
the prices of many of those requisites
which farmers have to purchase, including dairy equipment and supplies. Prices
for fat and store cattle have, moreover,
been relatively remunerative during this
period, and as a consequence there may
have been a tendency for farmers to turn
from milk production and to sell heifers
as stores or fat cattle which they would
otherwise have retained to replenish
their dairy herd.
I think that the influence of this factor
is probably less than is frequently
supposed, but farmers, like any other
businessmen, will naturally tend to
direct their production into those
channels which are the most remunerative. The net result has been a
reduction of 15,000 head in our dairy
herd this year, compared with 1936-a
loss of 6 per cent. It was clear that some
measures were necessary in order to
arrest the decline.
In the case of the liquid milk market,
circumstances during the past year have
been broadly similar to those which I
have described for the creamery industry
The necessity for an increased price to
the producer has been recognised by the
Joint Milk Council, which is responsible.
for fixing liquid milk prices, and during
the twelve months commencing the 1st
October this year, producers for the
liquid milk market will receive a price
advance of 24d per gallon compared with
the prices fixed for 1935-36, and of
approximately 1d per gallon above the
prices fixed for 1936-37. The Government has, accordingly, decided that some
further assistance is necessary for the
creamery industry, and has decided to
increase the rate of equalisation payment during the winter months so as to
bring the
average price paid by
creameries during these months up to
6d per gallon. This increase of d per
gallon during the winter months applies
to all milk delivered to creameries, and
will, I hope, prove an incentive to
farmers to increase their supplies of milk
during the winter months. One of the
difficulties with which the creamery industry in Northern Ireland has always
had to contend has been a greatly reduced supply of milk in the winter.
the winter supply could be maintained
at a higher level, it
it would assist
creameries in many ways. It would
If
enable them to reduce their overhead
costs, and it would also enable them to
keep their own butter on the market for
a longer period of the year. At the
moment the demand for Northern Ireland Premium Red Hand butter sold
under the Ministry's official grade exceeds the supply, and any step which
increases the milk supply to creameries
during the winter, and enables them to
maintain a continuous supply of Red
Hand butter on the market, must result
an improvement in the financial
position of the industry.
Under the Act of 1934 the Ministry
has been empowered to pay a bonus of
ld per gallon on all Grade C milk delivered to creameries. The present
Measure enables that bonus to be increased to 2d per gallon. The supply
of Grade C milk to creameries has shown
a steady increase since the inception of
the scheme, and during the twelve
months ended 30th June, 1937, some 37
per cent. of all milk delivered to
creameries was of Grade C standard.
An improvement in the quality of the
milk delivered to creameries is obviously
of the first importance, because it means
the creameries can sell a better article.
I am glad to say that within recent
years the quality of the butter, and particularly of the cream sold from Northern Ireland, has improved very greatly
indeed. During the past nine months

we have shipped upwards of 485,000

and in the opinion of the large wholesalers handling our cream in London
and in other markets in Great Britain,

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I can let the

Sir BASIL BROOKE: Not just at
the moment. I am satisfied that one of
the big factors in this improvement in
the quality of our dairy produce has
been the improved supply of milk to
creameries. It is for this reason that
the Government feels that the principal
assistance to creameries in the future
should be designed to encourage increased
deliveries of Grade C milk. There is
another reason why the Grade C producer deserves special consideration. He
is producing a quality of milk which is
up to the standard required for the
liquid milk market, and this milk constitutes a potential reserve for the liquid
milk market. The increase in the price
received by the Grade C producer who
can sell on the liquid milk market has
meant that without the increased bonus
payments proposed by this Measure, the
Grade C producer whose milk is to be
used for manufacture would have been
in a relatively inferior position to that
which he enjoyed during the early years
of the scheme. The present proposals of
the Ministry will mean, however, that in
summer the Grade C producer supplying
his milk to a creamery will receive on the
average 7d per gallon, and in winter 84d
per gallon. In addition, he will receive
the separated milk back, which, at
present, is worth approximately 2d per
gallon, for feeding purposes. The return
to the creamery supplier of Grade C
milk, therefore may be placed on the
average at approximately 9d per gallon
in the summer and 103d per gallon in
winter. I feel that on the basis of these
prices there should be a reasonable incentive to producers to increase their
supplies of milk, and also for an increase.
I
to take place in the number of C producers supplying milk to creameries.
The proposals, in fact, constitute,
hope, a sound basis for the future expansion of the creamery industry in
Northern Ireland. I need not elaborate
the advantages of that industry to the
agriculture in the Province. It is in
many ways the keystone of our livestock
industry, both as regards cattle, pigs and
poultry, which, it is my hope, will show
a great expansion during the next few
years.
I should, however, like to add one
word to Members of this House who
represent urban constituencies. It may
appear to them that this Measure is designed solely to assist the farming community, and is a direct subsidy to one
section of
of the community. At the
present time, however, the importance of
increasing the agricultural output of the
country commands general acceptance in
every quarter. Every increase in food
production is an added precaution in the
event of war. In the case of other
forms of agricultural production, it has
been possible to encourage an expansion
of the home industry by means of tariffs
and import regulations. In the case of
dairy produce, however, the great bulk
of our imports come not from foreign
countries, but from our own Dominions,
and the Imperial Government has felt
itself unable to give adequate protection
to the dairy industry at home by means
of duties upon imported produce. Consequently, the assistance which during
the past three years has been given to
our creameries in Northern Ireland, and
which I propose to extend to this
Measure, is a direct alternative to a
policy of tariffs on imports of butter from
overseas.
It will be observed that no provision
has been made to recoup the Milk Fund
for the immediate increased expenditure
and I propose, with some regret, that
until the end of September next the
additional expenditure involved under
this Measure shall be financed from the
reserve which has been built up in the
Milk Fund. After September, 1938, a
change in the method of financing the
Milk Fund will occur when the proposals
in the White Paper which has been
issued by the Ministry of Agriculture
and Fisheries have been implemented by
legislation. There will no longer be any

was on the enormous abuse by monopolies
in common necessaries of life by Queen
Elizabeth. So gross was the abuse that
on a list of articles subject to monopoly
being read over in the House of

not
prerogative should

It was a hazard, lightheartedly taken. The Prime Minister
and the Minister of Home Affairs took
the idea into their heads. Like Dr.
Johnson's celebrated acquaintance they
had only one idea on the subject in their
heads and it was a wrong one. Neither
is a man to hold or to bind when he gets
such an idea into his head. Their personal experience of the conditions of
everyday life in rural Ulster is not coextensive with the wisdom of Solomon.
The Six Counties enclave was viewed as
if it was an area like Yorkshire with its
teeming centres of industry. The sole
similarity is that of size. Yorkshire is
one-sixth larger in area than the Six
Counties but holds a population of over
4,000,000. The situation was viewed
through the wrong end of the telescope,
as if what is needed is buses running
services to a fixed time schedule in a
crowded area.

At a public meeting in Armagh City Hall

In various respects working people who
used to enjoy cheap services are now exploited owing to the frantic endeavours
and struggle of the Transport Board to
make ends meet. Excursions for groups
of working men cost more and are less

Belfast, in pre-monopoly days, used to

tends to check facilities for a poor child's
trip to the seaside or to increase the cost
of a child's season ticket to school does
not appeal to me, nor does a change that
increases the cost of living to a farm
labourer.

Mr. BYRNE: I beg to second the
Motion which has been moved by the
hon. and learned Member for Central
Belfast (Mr. Campbell). I think those
who have listened to his speech must be
convinced that the Transport Act should
be withdrawn. Perhaps the right hon.
Gentleman the Minister of Home Affairs
will say if he has any objection to the
withdrawal of this Measure. I cannot
understand why the Government introduced that Act. I mix a good deal with
the country people, and I know that
before this Board was set up there seemed
to be general satisfaction with the traffic
arrangements, both by buses and lorries.
The services seemed to suit all classes of
the community, and to meet the convenience of the people generally. I cannot understand why the Government
stepped in and interfered in the way
they did. Since the Transport Board has
been set up there has been nothing but
dissatisfaction all round. The bus
services are not the same as they were.
Excursion parties do not get the same
advantages; they have to pay an increase
of about 30 per cent. The working
people have been deprived of the evening
tours which they enjoyed so much in the
summer time. That is owing to the great
increase in cost.
It was quite usual for farmers to employ lorries to lift their cattle and convey
them to the sale yards in Belfast, and
since the Board took over this form of
transport there has been nothing but
general dissatisfaction. The Board has
brought cattle to the sale yards when
the sales were practically over, and in
many cases the cattle had to be sold at a
great loss. Much disappointment and
inconvenience has been caused by uncertainty as to the delivery of goods.
This dissatisfaction does not prevail only
in one section of the community; it prevails in every section. As the hon. and
learned Member for Central Belfast has
stated, even on the Twelfth of July there
was nothing but condemnation for this
Act. Yet all this does not seem to make
any difference so far as the Transport
Board is concerned.
Since the Board took over this work,
the charges have increased by from 25
per cent. to 75 per cent. That means a
great deal to the people in the country,
and to those who buy cattle and send
them to the sale yards in Belfast. I do
not see why this should continue. I know
a number of men, not possessed of much
of the goods of this world, who started
in the motor haulage business. They
worked up a trade by paying attention
to the needs of all classes of the business
community. As their trade increased
they increased the number of lorries and
gave employment to their sons. When
this Act came into operation the whole
business was taken from them and they
were not told the price they would receive
for it. Was it not a cruel thing to take
a man's business away from him and not
give him any idea of the amount he
would receive? Inconvenience took place
when this Measure came into operation.
Some employees were taken over, sons of
the owners and drivers. When they were
taken over the Board did not act with
commonsense. They should have kept
these men in the districts where they
knew the needs of the people. Instead of
doing that I understand the Board sent
the men to strange districts and put
people, who were entire strangers on the
route, in their places. This caused great
inconvenience. The Board have made

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have

traders, and the injustice to individuals,
which it suggests have come into being
as a result of the operation of the Transport Act. I am not for one moment
going to suggest that the present state of
affairs existing in transport leaves
nothing to be desired. The Government
would not for a moment make such a
suggestion and the Transport Board
would not for a moment make such a
suggestion, but to say that a grievous loss
has been inflicted on the community as a
result of the operation of the Act is
simply not in accordance with facts. I
have, on previous occasions, endeavoured
to give some figures showing the actual
result on passenger fares of the Board's
administration, and if the House will
bear with me I will repeat these now.
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps the right
hon. Gentleman will allow me. I do not

find it equally difficult. I only make the

Gentleman would speak slowly and raise
his voice as much as he can.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Thank you
for the suggestion, Mr. Speaker. Taking
590 points from Belfast, return fares
have been decreased in 61 per cent. of
them, and single fares have been decreased in 52 per cent. of them. No
change has been made in 26 per cent. of
the return fares, and in 37 per cent. of
the single fares, so that we come down
to this; that only in 13 per cent. of the

single fares has any increase been made,
and as against this the very important
am
concession has been made by the Board
in respect of monthly tickets, that these
are now available for two double
journeys a day in all cases. The weekly
tickets issued by the Board work out at
a halfpenny a mile for adults and-I
sure this will please the hon. and
learned Member, who wept for the downtrodden children-less than a farthing a
mile for children. I think that even the
hon. and learned Member will agree that,
if these figures are correct, the fares are
on the whole reasonable, and that there
is no justification for the allegation he
has made in regard to so-called increases
in fares. Monthly tickets work out at
even lower rates than these, and I think,
therefore, I am justified in saying that,
generally speaking, so far as road
passenger traffic is concerned, the public
are being carried at cheap rates, and at
rates which are not substantially in advance of those afforded even under
conditions of uneconomic competition.
The speeches we have heard from the
opposite side of the House have been
concerned mainly with the transport of
goods rather than with the transport of
passengers, but I have purposely mentioned passenger transport here, for I
think that if hon. Members will cast
their minds back they will find that what
has been said of goods transport now is
very much what was said of passenger
transport some time ago; and just as we
seldom hear complaints regarding the
passenger services now, so I hope all
cause for complaint regarding the goods
will soon disappear.
I regret that it is not possible to give
figures as regards the rates charged for
carrying goods similar to those I have
just given regarding the passenger fares,
but hon. Members will understand that
this is impossible, firstly, because of the
diversity of the traffic itself, and,
secondly, because of the diversity of the
charges made by individual operators on
given routes. But I have little hesitation
in saying that, while, no doubt, there
are grounds for complaint in the matter,
generally speaking most of the criticism
that has been put forward is founded on
a complete misunderstanding of the
situation. I should like to give the
House one very recent example of this.
I have on previous occasions quoted
similar examples, and I feel that it would
be useful and profitable if I now quote

quote that case to show that when such

I would, however, again impress upon
hon. Members, that I am not adopting
the position this afternoon that we have
achieved perfection in the matter of
transport. Were I to take this attitude
it would not only be a departure from
fact, and it would, I think, be an insult
to the intelligence of the Members of this
House. The Board, as hon. Members are
well aware. have been in operation since
Angust. 1935. In this time they have
taken over 1,111 undertakings-goods and
passenger comprising approximately
1.823 vehicles, and a very little reflection
is necessary to appreciate that with the
vastness of this task which the Board
have had on hands. it has been simply
impossible for them to devote anv large

Tt must be borne in mind that the

serious interruption of existing services,
and I think that one fair-minded person
will admit that while difficulties and complications may have arisen in certain
instances and, in fact, they did arise in
a number of instances-nevertheless, substantially, acquisition was accomplished
without any serious breakdown of
facilities. That, I think, is a great
tribute to the Board.
Hon. Members will no doubt be aware
that the Board commenced their operations with the acquisition of passenger
undertakings. At the commencement of
these operations, as was inevitable,
certain complaints were received. These
will be well within the memory of hon.
Members and were concerned mainly with
the provision of buses on what is known
as "private hire" terms-that is to say,
the running of buses for excursion parties
and that sort of thing. There was, undoubtedly, considerable cause for complaint here, but experience has shown
that this arose mainly as a result of misunderstanding. Persons who required
buses for only part of a day, or to convey
parties to their destination in the morning and bring them back in the evening.
failed to make their requirements clear to
the Transport Board, and were quoted a
higher rate than could have been quoted
had the exact use for which the bus was
needed been made clear.
We are now over the second summer of
the Board's operations, and I do not think
it is going too far to say that there have
been no complaints this year, and that
the public are now, on the whole, well
satisfied with the way in which the road
passenger trade is being operated by the
Board. Is it then asking too much of
the public that they should extend
a reasonable measure of confidence
towards a similarly satisfactory outcome
of the acquisition of the goods services
being secured an acquisition which, I
would remind hon. Members, was only
completed on the 31st July last?
Another aspect of the matter which has
been mentioned by hon. Members is that
relating to the navment of compensation.
The House will appreciate that here it
would be easy for me to overstep the
bounds of propriety by going into matters
that mav, in a sense, be regarded as being
sub judice, and matters that have been
entrusted to the safe hands of the
Statutory Tribunal, presided over by Mr.
Justice Megaw. I think, however. I may
briefly advance certain considerations in
the matter.

First of all, on the question of payment by means of "B" Stock, I do
think that there is a good deal of misunderstanding as to the actual provisions of the Act in this matter, and I
desire, therefore, to make it quite clear
that payment in this stock is only made.
in certain circumstances, and never in
respect of what I might perhaps describe
as tangible assets. Payment by "B"
Stock is only made in respect of goodwill. I think that this has a very real
bearing on the matter.
What it comes
to is this: A man has a certain intangible
asset consisting of the goodwill that may
be said to attach to his own privatelyrun business, and what is done in the
cases we are discussing is that in exchange
for this intangible asset (the value of
which must necessarily always be very
much a matter of opinion) we are giving
him what is considered by the best
opinion available to be a corresponding
share in the goodwill of a publicly-run
concern. The House will, I am sure,
realise that there is nothing of an extraordinary nature about this, but, on the
contrary, that it is the sort of thing that
is done every day in commercial life
where mergers or amalgamations of one
kind or another are taking place. That
is as much as I feel it would be proper
for me, at this juncture, to say on that
matter. It may be that there is in
practice, some little hardship involved.
This matter is being looked into, and if
we find that there is such hardship we
shall certainly proceed to devise some
method of remedying it.
The other matter to which I would
refer briefly is the matter of deduction
for managerial expenses. Here, too, I
think there is a good deal of misunderstanding as to what actually happens in
practice. It must be borne in mind that
in the great majority of the undertakings
that the Transport Board acquire they
are faced with a very great difficulty in
arriving at any basis for compensation by
reason of the fact that no proper accounts
are kept. The Board must necessarily
have some sort of basis to enable them
to arrive at a figure on which to begin.
their negotiations. A great many factors
have to be taken into account in endeavouring to arrive at such a figure, and
amongst other formulæ adopted by the
Board there is this matter of allowances
in respect of management expenses.
Sometimes it is found to work fairly
and properly, and sometimes-perhaps,
indeed, a great many times-it is found
not to work fairly and properly, and
when this is so then it is abandoned and
some other basis is sought. I would,
however, stress that practically in all
cases this item is no more than a preliminary estimate, and that before the
final figure is arrived at it has long been
lost sight of, if not, indeed, entirely
abandoned.
It is due to the absence of accounts
that negotiations are so often of a somewhat protracted nature. I may mention
that in the case of no fewer than 390
undertakings no accounts have been submitted to the Board by the claimants.
Why that is so I do not know.
Mr. BEATTIE: Does that mean that
no claim has been submitted?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes, formal
claims, but no details of what their claim
has been based on. They put down
nothing. I hope the hon. Member will

Sir DAWSON BATES: I think it is
right to stress that the Board are not the

Hon. Members will appreciate that as

claimant is also protected by the fact
that there is the Tribunal. The Tribunal
will not be convinced that a claim is just

where the workers only get one penny a

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): It was certainly
never the intention of the Government
that a motorist who in an emergency takes
in tow the car of a fellow motorist should
be liable to prosecution unless he has a
licence to use a trailer, and I think it is
hardly an example of intelligent legal
interpretation to contend that a motor
car that on an isolated occasion takes
in tow another motor car that has
broken down is a "vehicle used for drawing a trailer" within the meaning of the
Act.
I am aware that on a recent occasion
such an interpretation was adopted, but
the additional duty and fine are being
refunded to the motorist concerned and
I think the hon. Member
may rest
assured that no similar prosecution will
be taken in the future. I am obliged
to him for drawing my attention to this
case.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Acoustics of the House.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before embarking
upon the Orders of the Day I would like
to report to the House with reference to
the steps I have taken in order to try
to improve the acoustics of this House.
There have been complaints during the
past two or three years from all sides of
the House and indeed from the public
galleries that they are unable to hear
a great deal of the debates that take
place. Consequently, I took steps to
have experimental loud-speakers installed,
and the final result was that, in order
to make a proper job of it so that all
the galleries and the benches on both
sides of the House should hear distinctly
what is said from the front Government
bench and the front bench on the Opposition side, it would be necessary to install
an apparatus which would cost upwards
of £600.
Now, before embarking on such a large
expenditure and before asking the
Treasury to sanction it, I feel we ought
to give a chance to right hon. and hon.
Members on both sides to try to speak as
slowly and as distinctly as they can, to
find out whether when they do so, their
words can be heard all over the House.
Therefore I propose to proceed for the
next two weeks without any loudspeakers at all and ask right hon. and
hon. Members to give this a fair trial by
speaking slowly and distinctly. Should
that fail I would then have no other
method to adopt except to ask the
Treasury to sanction this expenditure, so
that the debates may be properly heard
by right hon. and hon. Members and by
members of the public as well.
Members: Hear, hear.)

upon
an increased subsidy to rural district

per cent. of the loan charges
capital expenditure not exceeding
£350 per cottage, and this limitation
means that the excess loan charges arising
in respect of the capital cost incurred
over and above £350 per cottage falls
wholly upon the local authority. Estimates received for new cottages indicate
that owing to the considerable increase
in the cost of materials during the past
twelve months the cost of a cottage is
likely to exceed £400. In the circumon
stances, the Government feels that it is
reasonable to recognise the increased cost
per cottage as qualifying for the 40 per
cent. grant.
Accordingly, if this Resolution is
passed by the Committee a Bill will be
introduced to raise the present recognised limit of capital expenditure from
£350 to £450. The Ministry of Home
Affairs estimate that local authorities
have schemes in contemplation for building 4,000 cottages and if they each cost
£450, the cost to the Government of the
40 per cent. loan charge grant would be
approximately £31,300 per annum. For
the purpose of this calculation interest
has been assumed at 3 per cent.
(being the rate current for loans from
the Government Loans Fund) with a repayment period of 50 years. On the
present basis of £350 per cottage, a sum
of £24,350 annually would have been
involved, so that the financial effect of
the proposal now before the Committee
is an additional charge on the Estimates
of £6,950 per annum over the loan
period. The figures I have given are of
course estimates, but they may be taken
as an indication of the cost to be borne
by the Exchequer.
ing costs. The advances for the purpose

Order read for resuming adjourned

Question again proposed.
Mr. BEATTIE: I said very little
previously on this Bill, but, as far as it
is humanly possible, I will endeavour not
to repeat anything I have already said.
I understand the object of this Bill is to
give a subsidy to the producer at the
expense of the retailer to enable the producer to supply to the creameries of
Northern Ireland liquid milk of all grades.
Therefore, it is an indirect way of subsidising the creameries, and in view of
the fact that producers of milk have
failed to rise to their responsibility to
their employees I shall oppose any subsidy being given to them, either directly
or indirectly. We are supposed to follow
step by step with Great Britain.
The
retailers of milk have got to employ men
and boys, and they are expected to pay
them a living wage. In addition to that
they are now being asked to subsidise,
directly and indirectly, the producer of
milk and the creameries by contributing
an amount equal to a penny per gallon.
In England the creamery business and
the producing business is regulated.
In England producers are controlled
by a Wages' Board, and they have got to
pay a regulated wage to their employees.
In Northern Ireland producers can pay
their employees whatever they like. The
demand for labour in Northern Ireland
is not as great as the supply. Therefore,
a market of that description reduces the
value of the labour, and in the Castlederg and Strabane district the wages are
in the region of 7s a week. To give a
subsidy to a producer who pays 7s a week
to a man with a wife and three children
is a crying scandal. If this industry of
producing milk cannot pay a living wage
to its workers we should abolish it and
call upon the Donegal farmers to supply
us with milk.
Mr. MINFORD: Shame.
Mr. BEATTIE: In Donegal they are
subject to a Wages Board, and they are
not in Londonderry and other towns.

wide of this Bill. If the hon. Member

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Oral Answers to Questions.
VACANT SHOPS AND HOUSES IN
BELFAST.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
the number of shops and controlled and
non-controlled dwelling-houses now
vacant in Belfast, and the number of
dwelling-houses built in Belfast
during the past two years.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): According to information compiled by the Rates Department of the Belfast Corporation there
were 2,696 vacant houses in Belfast on
the 9th November, 1936. No information is available regarding the number
of these which are subject to rent restriction or regarding the number of
vacant shops.
The number of new houses built in
Belfast during the two years ended 30th
September, 1937, was 7,550.
THE CHILDREN ACT COMMITTEE.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
when the report of the Children Act
Committee will be published.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand
that the deliberations of this Committee
have reached their final stages, and I,
therefore, anticipate that a report will
be laid before me some time within the
next few weeks.
EXCLUSION OF CITIZENS FROM
NORTHERN IRELAND AREAS.
3. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether any of the
Ministry's Orders prohibiting particular
British citizens or Free State citizens
entering Northern Ireland are still in
force, and, if so, in how many cases;
and if any corresponding exclusion orders
by the Government in London and
Dublin are in force against citizens of
Northern Ireland in respect of entry into
Great Britain or the Free State.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There are
forty-nine Orders made under the provisions of Regulation 23 (a) of the Civil
Authorities (Special Powers) Acts (Northern Ireland) in force at the present
time. These Orders do not prohibit the
persons to whom they relate from residing in Northern Ireland, but merely
prohibit them from residing in or
entering certain areas as specified in the
individual Orders.
I am not in a position to answer the
last part of the hon. and learned Member's question.
AIR-RAID PRECAUTIONS.
4. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state what steps the Government are
taking to protect the civil population
against attacks from enemy bombs and
gas from the air, in the event of an
outbreak of war, and to provide the
people with gas-masks.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am glad to
be able to inform the hon. Member that
considerable progress has recently been
made in connection with air-raid precautions. As I previously promised, I
sent to each local authority in Northern
Ireland a copy of the Committee's report
with an expression of the views of the
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Government that it was essential that
this matter should be given their careful attention. I am glad to say that the
County Councils of Antrim, Armagh
and Down are dealing with the matter,
and, as one of their first duties, are
helping to arrange the organisation of
local authorities into groups within their
counties. As the hon. Member is probably aware, the Corporation of the City
of Belfast is also giving the matter its
attention, and I have every reason to
hope that that body will push ahead
with the preparation of its scheme.
Some months ago I appointed to the
staff of my Ministry an air-raid precautions officer, and this officer has
already visited and lectured to a great
number of local authorities and is giving
his assistance in the preparation of
schemes.
Courses of training at the Government
Gas School in Great Britain have been
undertaken by members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary the Order of St.
John of Jerusalem, the British Red
Cross Society, and the Belfast Fire
Brigade, and these persons who have
qualified as instructors are now holding
classes. My Ministry has also obtained
supplies of the necessary equipment for
instructional purposes and these have
been issued.
Consideration has been given to the
medical aspect in conjunction with the
Medical Faculty of Queen's University
and the British Medical Association, and
I fully realise that this is perhaps one of
the most important sides of the work.
In so far as the provision of gas-masks
is concerned, I may say that the requirements of Northern Ireland have already
been brought to the notice of the Imperial Government. I understand that
the Government factory is producing gas
masks at the rate of two million a month,
but naturally in deciding where these
shall be allocated preference is given to
the more vulnerable points in Great
Britain, and it may therefore be some
little time before Northern Ireland supplies begin to arrive.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of
that reply, would the right hon. Gentleman state whether he is prepared to assist
financially local authorities throughout
Northern Ireland who are constructing
underground bomb-proof shelters?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is a
general matter, but I may assure the
hon. Member that the Government is
prepared to assist local authorities to deal
with the matter.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of
the statement that gas-masks manufactured in Great Britain will be given
to cities and towns most vulnerable, does
he not realise that Belfast is just as
vulnerable and Northern Ireland citizens
are just as loyal as any in the United
Kingdom?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not think
the question of loyalty arises at all. As
I have already indicated in my answer
these gas masks will be dealt with, so that
places most vulnerable will receive them
first.
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the right
hon. Gentleman see that Northern Ireland will get them as soon as possible
and that it will not be treated in the
same way as it was when work was given
to other parts of England? We were
treated very shabbily in that respect.

this subject requesting his observations.
and, if so, what was the nature of his
reply.

or at any rates, I can assure him that

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Major
Shillington): In reply to the hon. Member, the contributions under the National
Health Insurance Acts have been fixed
on an actuarial basis, sufficient only to
provide the statutory benefits, namely,
medical, sickness, disablement, and
maternity benefits. Societies which pay
part of the cost of dental and optical
treatment do so out of surplus funds
which they have been able to accumulate,
mainly because the claims of their members have been below the actuarial expectation. If all insured persons were to be
given a title to free dental and optical
treatment or to the other benefits which
can be given at present only as additional
benefits, it would be necessary to increase
the weekly rates of contributions considerably.
In reply to the last part of the hon.
Member's question, no memorandum on
the subject has been received either from
the Ministry of Labour or the Ministry
of Health in Great Britain, the latter
Department being the one concerned with
National Health Insurance.
Mr. BYRNE: Does the right hon.
Gentleman not feel it is unfair that some
contributors should get more benefits for
a lesser number of contributions than
others, considering that this is a National
Health Insurance Scheme.
Major SHILLINGTON: As I have
explained, if these further benefits were
made available for every member of every
society it would mean an increase in the
contributions.

Poor Relief Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Poor Relief (Amendment) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Davison): This Bill I
am
now introducing to the House has
caused a certain amount of concern
amongst the various poor law unions in
Northern Ireland who, I think, without
fully understanding its provisions, passed
resolutions against it. I think I will be
able to establish to the satisfaction of
every Member of the House that this Bill
is a perfectly proper one, and one that
ought to be passed. The real object of
it is to extend the powers of poor law
guardians to enable them in proper cases
to give outdoor relief to destitute persons
notwithstanding the fact that they are
able-bodied. The primary object of the
establishment of guardians was for the
relief of the poor. That is the reason
for their existence and practically their
only duty. Under the old law they could
only assist able-bodied persons in the
workhouse or in exceptional cases, where
the workhouse was filled up, by permission of the Local Government Board
or Poor Law Commissioners. Their
powers of giving outdoor relief
limited to poor persons who were permanently disabled through old age.
infirmity or mental defect, or where the
head of the family was unable to work
through accident or sickness, or in the
case of widows with one or more illegiti
mate children.
were
The burden upon the guardians of
maintaining the poor was lightened to a
very great extent by different Measures
passed through the Imperial House of
Commons and this House. such as Old
Age Pension Acts and Unemployment
Insurance Acts. We in this House in
the year 1928, recognising the necessity
for giving relief outside the workhouse,
passed the Poor Relief (Exceptional
Distress) Act. That enabled destitute
persons to receive outdoor relief, but only
in cases where an area was declared one
in which exceptional distress existed.
That was not followed in many parts of
Northern Ireland-I think three or four,
Belfast, Newry and the districts of Killyleagh and Castlewellan in the Downpatrick Union. Boards of guardians in
many instances were pressed with the
necessity for outdoor relief, even where
no order declaring an exceptional distress
area had been made, and did illegally give
outdoor relief, particularly during the
years after the passing of the Unemployment Act of 1934, under which unemployment assistance boards were established, to able-bodied destitute persons.
Mr. BEATTIE: Under Section 13?
Mr. DAVISON: Under no section at
all. The relief was illegally given by
several boards of guardians, who are now
liable to be surcharged upon the ground
that they had no power to grant outdoor
relief. There was a period after the Act
of 1934 was passed during which, owing
to the delay in bringing into operation
the unemployment assistance provisions of
that Act, grants were made to guardians
to cover that period and to cover the outdoor relief they gave. The Unemployment Act of 1934, setting up the Unemployment Assistance Board, is limited in
its scope
to insured persons or persons
who would normally be in insured employment, and as was pointed out to the
several authorities before the Bill was
introduced, they would still be left with
a number of destitute persons who would
not be covered by that Act. The burden
which has always existed, and which has
always been laid upon boards of
guardians, of looking after destitute.
persons would still remain as to the
residue. Boards of guardians ought to
be, and are in most cases, anxious to do
their best and in the most humane manner
for destitute persons, who need their
assistance, and they are unwilling to send
men to the workhouse. They believe, too,
that it is cheaper for them to assist
persons by grants rather than have to
maintain them in the workhouse.
This Bill will not create any new class
of persons or throw any burden upon the
guardians that does not, in fact, already
exist, though the method at present by
which they can relieve that distress is to
be changed. As I mentioned when opening, boards of guardians did pass resolutions against the introduction of this
Measure. I had the privilege of meeting
on Monday last representatives from
practically all the unions in Northern
Ireland.
