Mr. CAMPBELL: Peace with honour.
Mr. DAVISON: The Bill itself extends
existing powers given to boards of
guardians under the Poor Relief Acts to
give outdoor relief to certain able-bodied
persons who comply with certain conditions. These conditions are-residence
in the United Kingdom for a period of
seven years, registration in pursuance of
the Labour Exchanges Act for employment at an Employment Exchange within
the meaning of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1936, and that the applicant is
unable to support himself or any persons
ordinarily and actually dependent upon
him. Nothing in the Bill is to affect the
provisions of Section 2 of the Poor Relief
Act, 1862, which excludes certain
occupiers of land from receiving outdoor
relief or the provisions of paragraph 1 of
the Sixth Schedule to the Unemployment
Act, 1934, which prohibits the granting
of outdoor relief by a board of guardians
to such persons as are mentioned in the
said paragraph.
Clause 2 of the Bill re-enacts the
powers
contained in the Exceptional Distress Act,
1928. If at any time any area is an area
of exceptional distress this provision may
be made use of to relieve that distress.
Clause 3 makes provision for the borrowing by boards of guardians of any money
necessary for the giving of this outdoor
relief. It is not anticipated that there
will be a very large number of cases to be
relieved, and it is not expected that it
will upset to any great extent the finances
of the guardians. This power is
necessary one to provide that guardians
may, by borrowing, afford the relief
necessary without any disarrangement of
the financial position for the year. There
is a repeal of Section 2 of the Poor Relief
(Ireland) Act, 1847; the Poor Relief
(Exceptional Distress) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1928; and Section 38 of the

That is not a matter that necessitates

employment

Mr. DAVISON: It is intended to

Boards of guardians

One must deplore the condition of

to set right what has been done as far as
those people are concerned. Surely the
alternative to this is to urge that means
should be found to provide work for

not keen to get the dole, or exceptional
distress money, or anything of that sort.
As I say, these people are real workers.
They are the better part of the community and more deserving of help than
the habitual mendicants. The great
regret is that work cannot be found for
them. I appreciate the difficulties which
face the Government in regard to finding
work, and I would urge on the Minister
that nothing should be left undone to
secure work for them instead of pauperising them by giving them outdoor relief.

First of all, as I understand the position, the guardians at present have no
statutory power to relieve able-bodied

for example relief outside the workhouse.
Then, in addition to that several boards

that boards of guardians, and indeed all
other subordinate organisations within

been made by boards of guardians in the

A great deal could be said for making

charge, and I think it likely that the
Poor Relief Bill-
14 OCTOBER 1937
Second Reading
time will come when the relief of the
poor will be a national charge, because
only in that way will the burden of this
relief be placed upon the shoulders of
those best able to bear it. Money raised
from the rates presses heavily on everyone, even on the very poorest, but relief
which is based on taxes is spread more
equitably over the whole community and
consequently is more defensible.
Further, in the ideal times to which we
are looking forward, I think that the
relief of the able-bodied will be
associated with some form of work. It is
hardly satisfying to the conscience to pay
these people a small modicum week by
week and allow them to drift in idleness
and in all the bitterness of soul that
accompanies a sense of uselessness, and
to allow them to lapse into the moral
degeneracy to which they are very
easily tempted when they are given no
sort of useful work to do. I think one
of the greatest blots, not on this Government but on the Imperial Government,
to which in this matter we are
subordinate, is that at this period in our
history they have allowed thousands of
young men every year to pass through
their years of adolescence without having
any sort of training.

the same

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That, for the purposes of any Act
of the present Session to amend certain
provisions of the Milk and Milk
Products Act (Northern Ireland),
1934, it is expedient to authorise a
charge upon moneys provided by Parliament in respect of the payment to
the Milk Fund for each of the four
years beginning on the first day of
October, nineteen hundred and thirtyeight of a sum equal to one halfpenny
per gallon in respect of all milk produced in Northern Ireland and delivered during such year to a creamery
and used for the manufacture of cream
or butter; provided that the maximum
sum so payable for any one year shall
not exceed a sum of sixty-five thousand
pounds."
-(Governor's recommendation signified.
-Mr. Andrews).
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The policy
of the Government in regard to improving the price paid to producers by the
creameries has been fully explained by
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Agriculture, when moving the Second
Reading of the Bill. It is now necessary
for me to say a few words on the
Financial Resolution in order to explain
how this policy will affect the Exchequer.
The relevant Clause in the Bill is Clause
4, and the present Resolution is
necessary in order that that Clause may
actually become part of the Bill.
The Resolution provides for payment
from the Exchequer to the Milk Fund of
a sum not exceeding £65,000 for each of
the four years beginning from the 1st
October, 1938. The reason for the selection of this date is that it will coincide
with the start of the new long-term milk
policy of the Imperial Government.
The financial relations between
Northern Ireland and Great Britain
require that Government expenditure,
giving effect to the new conditions, should
commence to operate in both areas from
the same date.
Up to the present, and for the next
twelve months, the Northern Ireland
Government is sharing in the benefits of
the present Imperial subsidy towards
manufacturing milk. Hon. Members
may recollect that in our local Milk Act
of the year 1934 power was taken to pay
to the Milk Fund from the Exchequer
of Northern Ireland any money which
may have been received from Imperial
sources for the purpose of assisting the
milk industry in Northern Ireland. Such
receipts have been paid over to us monthly
from that date, and, if the necessary conditions are fulfilled, will continue to be
paid up to the 30th September, 1938.
They are based on producers sending milk
to creameries being entitled to receive
fivepence per gallon in
in the summer

Sittings of the House
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
months and sixpence per gallon in the
winter months.
After 1st October, 1938, the character
of the assistance to the milk industry in
Great Britain will change and will be of
such a nature that it is not possible for
Northern Ireland to make a direct claim
on Great Britain for further assistance.
The Exchequer assistance in Northern
Ireland to the Milk Fund from 1st
October, 1938, will, under the proposals
in this Resolution, be related to the
amount that will be produced by a payment of one halfpenny per gallon in
respect of all milk produced in Northern
Ireland and delivered to the creameries.
This payment is necessary in order to
assist in meeting the extra charges on
the Milk Fund which will arise under the
proposals embodied in the Bill. It is
estimated that if the Exchequer subsidy
should come into operation now the cost
to the Exchequer would be
would be about
£50,000 per annum, but it is anticipated
that in the course of the next twelve
months the supply of milk to creameries
will have increased and that, when 1st
October, 1938, comes, the annual
amount payable will be in excess of that
figure. The Resolution proposes an overriding maximum of £65,000. I beg to
move.

Oral Answers to Questions.
LANDLORD AND TOWN TENANT
LEGISLATION.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
at what date the promised Bill to regulate the position between town tenants
and landlords will be brought in.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Government
have given this matter their most careful consideration and have been waiting
deliberately for some time past to
observe whether the conditions which
gave rise to legitimate complaint have
in any way been modified. I am happy
to say that our observations lead us to
believe that the establishment of the
Committee appointed to investigate the
matter, and the threat of legislation,
have had a salutary effect, and we have
reached the conclusion that it is not at
present necessary or desirable to add to
the existing code of law dealing with the
relationship of landlord and tenant. It
is felt that unnecessary Government
interference with relationships of this
nature is objectionable and should be
avoided.
The hon. Member may, however, rest
assured that we shall not relax our vigilance in the matter and that if and when
circumstances arise calling for action we
shall not be unprepared to act.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the right
hon. Gentleman not recollect that an
important question before this Committee was security of tenure for leaseholders who hold under building leases
-leases with building covenants? Can
the right hon. Gentleman hold out no
hope whatever of any redress or remedy
for this class of tenants?
have
Sir DAWSON BATES: I
endeavoured to point out that, generally
speaking, there is no hardship in the case
the hon. and learned Member refers to.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the right hon.
Gentleman realise that nine years have
elapsed since this Committee finished its
work? Where does he expect to be nine
years hence?

statements which were made against

Sir DAWSON BATES: I regret to
say that certain unfounded statements
appeared in the British Press reflecting
on Northern Ireland, but I am gratified
to state that the great majority of newspapers gave correct accounts of the
enthusiastic reception given to Their
Majesties on the occasion of their visit
to Northern Ireland last July.
I understand that
representations
were made to the newspapers in which
malicious statements appeared expressing
the deep resentment which the people of
Northern Ireland felt, and the local
Unionist newspapers admirably expressed
in their leading articles the feelings of
all loyalists in protesting against the
unfounded allegations.

FERRY SERVICE FOR SHIPYARD
WORKMEN.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware of
the inadequate service of ferries supplied
by the Belfast Harbour Board for workmen employed in the shipyard; whether
it is a fact that the boats are small and
workmen have been pushed into the
water in trying to get aboard; and
whether he will make representation to
the Belfast Harbour Commissioners for
a proper service to be maintained in
accordance with the responsibilities of
the Commissioners for this means of
transport across the Belfast Lough.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand
this matter was brought to the notice of
the Belfast Harbour Commissioners
some time ago by a deputation of shipyard workers.
The ferry services are operated by
licencees of the Belfast Harbour Commissioners, the licencees being under an
obligation to maintain
good and
efficient service.
a
The Board of Trade supervise the
efficiency of the boats and equipment
and recently it was arranged that new
ferry boats should be placed on the
service. One of the new boats will be
brought into service almost at once and
another will be in service in the course
of a few days.
It was reported recently that a person
had fallen into the water but, on investigation, it was found that he had
attempted to jump on board the ferry
boat after it had left the stage and was
some distance away.
The Harbour Commissioners are not
under any obligation to operate these
ferries.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR
(Major Shillington): The answer to the
first part of the hon. Member's question
is in the affirmative. As regards the
latter part, I have no evidence which

conditions of those employed in the

Ministry has received, many of the

8. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he can

HOUSE OF COMMONS

state the amount of linen piece-goods exported to China and the amount of madeup linen goods re-exported from China to

The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The destination of exports and the origin
of imports are not recorded separately
for Northern Ireland, and the only
statistics I am in a position to give with
regard to the trade in linen goods between
China and this country thus relate to
the United Kingdom as a whole. United
Kingdom exports of linen piece-goods to
China were valued in 1936 at £446,389.
Imports of made-up linen goods from
China are not classified separately in the
United Kingdom trade statistics, but the
two categories in which they are included,
namely linen and union goods and embroideries of all descriptions, were
imported from China in 1935 to the
values respectively
respectively of £46,136 and
£33,629.
Statistics of the exports of made-up
linen goods from China are not at present
available, but some light is, perhaps,
thrown upon this matter by U.S.A. trade
statistics, which show that imports of
made-un linen goods into that market
from China were valued in 1935 at
£742,000.
With regard to the last part of the
question the hon. Member will appreciate
that firms interested in export trade are
under no statutory obligation to supply
the Ministry of Commerce with particulars of their overseas organisations,
and such information as is recorded in
the Ministry regarding the export
arrangements of individual Northern
Ireland firms is given voluntarily and in
confidence. I am not, therefore, in a
position to supply the particulars requested by the hon. Member.
Mr. HENDERSON: In regard to the
goods exported from China to the United
States, amounting to a total value of
£742.000, can the hon. and learned
Gentleman state whether those goods are
being sold in America as Irish linen
embroidered in Northern Ireland?
Mr. ROBB: The hon. Member would
have to give notice of that question.

possible to state the exact number

Finance (No. 2) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. ANDREWS: This Measure is
self-explanatory. It is to carry out the
suggestion that I made in my Budget
speech that the fee for motor drivers'
licences would be reduced as from 1st
January next from 10s to 5s. This will
be some advantage for some 68,000 of
our people, and is a very good example
of the fact that even small concessions
given in large numbers amount to a very
substantial sum, because this concession
will affect the Road Fund to the extent
of £17,000 per annum. We cannot
spend more than we receive; therefore,
when we make this small concession we
have to have regard to the fact that we
are liable to make difficulties in other
directions. However, I think this proposal will commend itself to hon. Members on both sides of the House.
I beg
to move.

Mr. ANDREWS: In moving the
Second Reading of this Bill, I propose to
deal first with Clauses 1 and 3 leaving
the proposals in Clause 2 to the conclusion of my speech, relating as it does
to borrowings for the Bann Drainage
Scheme, upon which I wish to make a

The effect of Clause 1 is to increase the
power to make issues of loans from the
Government Loans Fund up to
£10,000,000. This amount is a gross
amount related to the total sums issued
in loans from the time that the Fund was
established in the year 1923. Taking repayments into account, the amount
actually outstanding at the present time
is about £6,000,000, but in view of the
terms of the original Government Loans
Act it is the gross amount which the
House is asked to control.
this money
The purposes for which
has been used are, first, to enable the
Fund to make loans to the Exchequer
for the purpose of paving housing subsidies. for the reconstruction of police
barracks, for the payment of grants in
respect of voluntary schools and for the
cost of the Bann Drainage Scheme.
Secondly, for making loans to local
authorities for every purpose for which
borrowings by them have been approved.
As an example, I may mention that a
recent loan to a rural council for a
labourers' cottages scheme reached the
large figure of £155.000, and other loans
for the same most desirable and necessary
purpose are expected to total over a
million pounds. In addition, loans are
made to farmers for reproductive purposes. The Fund, with its very reasonable rates of interest, has been
substantial benefit to the community in
many directions. I want hon. Members
to realise that the Government's borrowings for this Fund are of a reproductive
character, and are adequately secured
either by annual repayments from the
Votes or by the loan instalments charged
on local rates. The terms on which
loans are made are such that the Fund
is entirely self-supporting.

I shall now turn to Clause 3. This
Ideals with the extension of Ulster

power to the Ministry to extend the life

about 41,300.
I now turn back to Clause 2, relating
to borrowings for the Bann Drainage
Scheme. The original estimate as prepared by the Ministry's engineers was for
£643,000. The present estimate for the
completion of the work is £858,000. that
is to say, an increase of over £200,000.
In general I may say that it is a matter
of extreme difficulty to estimate costs in
connection with under-water work,
because it is impossible to foresee the difficulties that may be encountered even
after the most careful survey possible of
the river bed. To some extent the risk
inherent in estimating for work of this
character can be passed on to a contractor, but, however carefully drawn, the
contract may be there must always be a
certain latitude allowed in dealing with
claims for payment where difficulties unforeseen, either by the contractor or by
the Government's engineers have arisen.
In the main, it is because of these unforeseen difficulties and of special payments made to the contractor in respect
of them that the increase has arisen.
The contract as accepted was not and
could not be a lump sum contract. It
contained scheduled prices for various
items, such as for removing rock at so
much per yard, for removing soft
material, for erecting sluices, making
fish passes, and so forth, the quantities.
estimated for removal being set out in
the specification. However, at the
the
accepted contract rates and on
estimated quantities to be removed, it was
anticipated that the work would be completed within the total of the engineers'
estimate.
But as I have already indicated, it
became necessary to meet the contractor

standpoint will be an undoubted success;
even though it is still incomplete, it has

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL
Anthony Babington): I think anyone
who has any experience of penalty
clauses in contracts of this description
will realise that to enforce them is always
a very difficult matter indeed. It is all
very well to say that all these things
should have been seen beforehand. We
all know that in contracts of this description it is impossible to foresee all the conditions that may be laid bare when the
work is commenced. We have had some
notable examples of that in the city of
Belfast within recent years.
In this particular case, as I understand it, what
happened was this, this contract was
entered into upon a certain basis, and of
course the price that was quoted by the
contractor depended upon the work that
it was expected he would have to do.
Portion of the bed and soil of the Bann
was known to be rock. The rest of the
bed and soil was of a mixed nature, which
was not fully known either to the
Government's engineers or to the contractor. It was impossible to know what
it was until the work had been
commenced.
In fact, after the rock had been
extracted and they proceeded to deal with
the rest of the bed and soil in order to
increase the flow of the river, it was
found that a large portion of it consisted
not of mixed boulder clay, as was anticipated, but of a very thin layer of boulder
clay and then an aggregate of boulders
which practically amounted to rock. The
cost of removing that was very nearly
as much as the cost of removing the rock
itself. The House will understand that
if that had been known at the time, the
original price would have been a great
deal higher, at least as much as the extra
moneys that Parliament is now being
asked to pass.
It is a pity, of course, that it was not
foreseen. I am sure no one is more
annoyed about this failure to foresee what
the nature of the bed and soil of the
Bann was than the contractor, because
from what I know about it I am pretty
sure he has made no appreciable profit
in this contract, if he has not actually
made a loss. It is quite erroneous to say

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Davison): In moving
the Second Reading of this Bill I do not
propose to deal at length with the object
of the Bill, as this was very fully explained when the necessary
Money
Resolution was introduced in this House
on Wednesday last. The Bill is introduced to implement a pledge given in
this House to reconsider the question of
the amount of assistance given to rural
district councils in the erection of
labourers' cottages under the Labourers
Acts.
As has already been intimated to the
House, owing to the increase in building
costs during the past 12 months, the cost
of erection of labourers' cottages has considerably increased. At present the
Government makes a grant of 40 per cent.
of the loan charges incurred by rural
district councils in carrying out building
schemes up to a limit of expenditure of
£350 per cottage. Any loan charges in
respect of expenditure incurred beyond
that sum have to be met in full by the
local authority. Recognising that the
increased cost of building would either
place considerable additional burden on
rural district councils or cause these
councils to hesitate in providing necessary
cottages, the Government has decided that
the amount of expenditure per cottage,
in respect of which the 40 per cent, grant
may be paid, be increased from £350 to
£450, and this Bill is designed to implement this decision.
I am glad to say that since the passing
of the Act of 1935, which renewed
facilities for the erection of labourers'
cottages, very considerable progress has
been made by local authorities in the provision of labourers' cottages throughout
the country. No less than 24 schemes
are now in process of completion, providing for the erection of approximately
3,600 cottages, and I am confident that
the additional facilities provided under
the Bill will furnish a further incentive
to local authorities to deal with the
problem of accommodation for labourers.
in a comprehensive way. I beg to move.

unduly exploited by those who deal in
building materials.
To show how alarming the increase

I said before that Northern Ireland is

the rapacity of those who would have exploited the market in regard to building
materials. This exploitation is going on

The poor local authorities of Northern

They are going to do it under conditions

Secretary that that being so it is his duty

when they are envisaging the building of

It is up
to the Government to see to it that those

Within the past few months in Belfast
the price of building materials has

Wills (Family Provision) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to move,
"That this Bill be now read a Second
time."
This is a Bill to prevent the injustice
and cruelty of a man leaving his wife
and children penniless and unprovided
for on his death. During life the law
does not allow him to fail in his obligations towards them. It makes him
responsible for their maintenance. If a
wife has means and her husband becomes
chargeable on the rates she is legally
bound to support him and her children.
The law of Northern Ireland almost
alone among the laws of civilised peoples
enables a grave wrong to be perpetrated.
This also is the law of England. Quite
different is the law of Scotland. By the
law of Scotland, derived from the Roman
law, if a man leaves a widow and
children, a third of his estate must go
to the widow and a third to the children,
and if he dies leaving a widow but no
children the widow takes half. This is
Wills Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
the law no matter what sort of a will he
may make.
The law of Scotland shields
the widow and offspring from a tyrant of
a father who would disregard his responsibilities and inflict injustice on those
who by every tie of nature should be
the last to suffer injustice from him.
This is the law of New Zealand and
Australia, of several provinces of Canada
and of most European countries.
At Assizes, actions have been heard to
set aside wills in which the testator had
disinherited his family. Such actions
failed, since the law decrees that this
wrong can be done, but judges have said
that the day would come when Parliament would prevent wills like those being
made and a man would have to leave a
proportion of his estate for the benefit
of his wife and family. Has that day
come here?
A Joint Committee of the Parliament
of the United Kingdom, which took
evidence of this question, reported thus
in 1931:-
The Committee, however, are of
opinion that it is wrong that a surviving spouse or child who is otherwise
without adequate means of support
should be left without such means of
support owing to the terms of the
deceased spouse's will and that such
spouse or child should be able to
obtain such means of support by application to the court, the amount to be
measured by the amount of the estate
and the circumstances in which the
family had been living.
Lots of cases of capricious disinheriting never find their way into the courts.
It may be said that the persons who
make unjust wills are few. That may be
so but their number is enough to justify
an endeavour to set right this defect in
the law. It may also be argued that a
man has a right to do what he likes with
his own property. Still the State takes
a large share of his property on his
death.
This Bill does not give to anyone any
part of the estate of a testator. It is
left to the equity of the court to say,
after consideration of all the circumstances, what share an applicant should
get, if, indeed, he should get a share at
all. The law of Scotland is rigid. The
law under the Bill would be flexible.
Consider the wrong which can be
wrought by a callous testator. Consider
the case where a wife has along with her
husband been the principal factor in
building up a business and has given the
best years of her life to the task. From
caprice or whim on his part in his will
she may be left out of all benefit in his
estate. During his life the law compelled him to maintain her. On his
death his estate goes free of such
obligations.
A wealthy man who did not get on
with his wife and children left all he
had for the care of cats. Another
testator bequeathed his wife 3d to buy a
halter "which I trust she may make use
of without delay." Another left his
widow one farthing, to be sent to her
by post in an unstamped envelope. Yet
another left his wife his trousers, which,
he said in his will, she had been attempting to wear throughout her married life,
and which she could now have, as he
had no further use for them. (Laughter.) Other testators imposed conditions
of forfeiture in the event of legatees
becoming M.P.'s, which to them betokened the last scene of all.
"Second childishness and mere
oblivion."
A Bill similar to this Measure has
already been given a Second Reading in
England, and a petition, signed by
representatives of all parties in the
House, has been presented to the Prime
Minister asking that facilities should be
given by the Government for the passing
of the Measure. That indicates a very
widespread measure of support. Enlightened opinion would welcome this.
change. Very soon the law of England.
will enshrine this reform. Very soon
the law will check callous or vindictive
testators from perpetrating palpable and
patent injustice. There are cases where
women are the wrongdoers and widowers
and children suffer from their unjust
wills. Caprice is not the privilege of
one sex only. There are cases, too,
where exclusion of surviving wife or
husband or children is quite reasonable.
The parties excluded may have been
otherwise provided for. This Bill in no
way affects such cases. The Bill will
deter testators from making flagrantly
inofficious and unjust wills when they
know that a court can set right such
wills.

This is a grave wrong-the righting of

This
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
question as to the right of every individual to do what he likes with his own
property is one which has been discussed
at great length by lawyers for a great
many centuries. It might assist the
House if I drew a distinction between
this Bill that the House has before it
now and the law as it stands in other
countries such as Scotland.
The main principle seems to be this.
Are there to be any restrictions upon
persons testamentary powers or are
there not? There is no doubt that it
took some time in England before this
question was settled, as it is now settled
by the Wills Act of 1837, by which the
principle, as we know it now, was established that a man is entitled to dispose
of his property as he thinks fit, and if
he thinks fit he can disinherit both his
wife and his children. That was not so
at one time, because there was a time
in England when the present Scotch law
of legitim applied under which, as the
hon. and learned Member has stated,
there are three parts as they call them
in Scotland-the wife's part, the bairns'
part, and the dead part. Those parts
are fixed by law, and the only portion of
his property which a man can, therefore, will is the third part, which is
what is called the dead share. That is
absolutely fixed. There is no disposition
Clause; there is no power in the courts
to make a will for a testator after his
death, and the people as a whole know
exactly their rights.
The
In London, where I think this present
rule originally arose, it was always the
law, at any rate since about the middle
of the thirteenth century, that the only
restriction on a man's testamentary
power was that his widow had the right
to dower of which he could not get rid
by any provision in his will.
children were dependent upon their
father's bounty, and that principle came
under the law for England by the Wills
Act of 1837. It may be questioned which
of the two principles is the sounderthe one in practice in Scotland or the
one we find to be the law in England
and also in Ireland. There are a great
many difficulties either way because in
attempting to get rid of one injustice it
very often happens that Parliament
creates another.
With reference to the question
whether a man should be entitled to
disinherit his wife and his children I can
only say that in this country it is a thing
which very seldom happens. When it
does happen, however, it is very difficult
to assess the justice or injustice of the
particular provision. The hon. and
learned Member has referred to one or
two extraordinary cases which are to be
found in the Law Reports-the case of
the gentleman who bequeathed a halter
Wills Bill-—
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Babington]
to his wife, and that of the gentleman
who bequeathed to her his trousers. I
do not know whether either of those wills
was just or unjust; it would be impossible to say unless you knew the lady, and
presumably the person who knew her best.
was her husband.
In the thirteenth century a very great
lawyer and judge said that a citizen
would hardly amass wealth if he was
bound to leave it to an ill-deserving wife
or an idle and uninstructed child. That
was Bracton. Apparently that was the
view taken by the persons who stereotyped our law in the form we find it at
the present time. If one thinks over
that one sees the reasons for preserving
the liberty of the subject and allowing
him to do what he likes with his own.
The difficulty Parliament is faced with is
this, trying to make people do what they
do not want to do. I have no doubt that
the husband who thought so little of his
wife that he left her a halter with an
expression of the hope that she would
speedily make use of it, would, if the law
had been as it is in Scotland at the present time and he thought she was going
to get a third of his property, have taken
other means to prevent that happening.
There is, as was pointed out in the
English Parliament when a Bill of a
similar nature was being debated there,
nothing to prevent a man making a voluntary settlement to dispossess himself of
his property so that he could die without
any property and without any will. If
he did that the same object is achieved
or, failing to make any provision for his
children, he could give his property away
inter vivos. There is, in this connection,
no provision under which a will could
operate. The English people in their
wisdom adopted the rule of law which we
have at present, leaving it to the testator
to say which of his children, if any, were
entitled to benefit from his estate, and
whether his wife was entitled to benefit
also.
The modern Englishman, and I think
Irishman, are so used to this present rule
that one would almost believe that this
freedom of testamentary disposition is a
matter rooted in the individual character
of the people. Although that is not so
historical I think it is quite plain that it
is a rule which is well understood, and
which, on the whole, has not worked any
greater injustice than would be worked
under the rule which applies in Scotland.
The only rule I am aware of restricting
the testator's right to do what he likes
with his own property is the restriction
that a testator, if he is leaving his property to charities-property that consists
of land-must make his will at least three
months before his death otherwise his will
is void. That is like the old statutes of
Mortmain, which attempted to prevent
money being left to charities by testators
who made their wills upon their deathbed.
Although we have not the Mortmain Act
in force in Ireland it is one which has
been in force for many years. That
rule, like the Scottish, is a fixed law; it
is not a matter which is left to the discretion of any judge or court, and it is
a rule thoroughly well understood.
The hon. and learned Member says that
the present rule is not consistent with
modern conditions or modern ideas. I
think there is some confusion about that.
When you take up this Bill you find it
ostensibly only applies to a male testator.
Under our modern equality as between
the sexes, which was accentuated not very
long ago when this House passed an Act
which places women and men and husbands
and wives on equal footing, I cannot see
why, so far as property is concerned, this
embargo upon the testamentary disposition of a husband should be enforced and
not enforced in the case of the wife.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Might I venture to
correct the Attorney-General in his very
clear exposition. Spouse is the word used
which, I submit, covers both husband
and wife.
That
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
makes it a little more logical. It seems
to me whatever is to be the rule for the
husband must also be the rule for the
wife. Why, under modern conditions,
if the wife has got means, and the husband
has got none, should she not be liable
with him to leave something for her
children? It is a question in every case
as to what is justice, and what are the
merits of the particular case. Are those
merits to be judged by the testator, or
are they to be judged by the courts?
This has not become the law in England.
No doubt it was debated and the Bill
was given a Second Reading in the
English House of Commons, but if you
look through the report of that debate
you will find that a count took place

The Bill to me appears to contain a
very vicious principle. I can understand the Scotch system, and I can
understand Parliament saying a
must make a certain specific provision
for his wife and children. In that case
you run the risk of compelling a man to
do what he does not want to do, and
something which he ought not to do,
namely, to leave an undeserving wife or
child money which they should not get.
I think you must leave the law as it
stands at present, which gives the
testator full power to do what he likes
with his own. I do not approve, and I
do not think the House would approve,
of the particular provisions in this Bill
under which, instead of having a fixed
rule of law as to the testamentary
succession or disposition, you leave it to
the court, after the decease of the
testator, to have a roving inquiry into
the justice of his testamentary disposition. Not only is the disappointed child
or the disappointed wife entitled to have
a roving inquiry under this Bill, but if
there are any variations in the circumstances of the applicant, or any variations in the estate of the testator, it can

to his children, with the knowledge that
they will see that she is kept in a proper
state. If a man in those circumstances
makes such a will, it would be very
disastrous if after his death his widow
was in a position to make an application
to the court-it would bring the whole
matter before the public in open court.
In cases such as that it is far more desirable that the disposition of his property
should be left to a man's own private
judgment, which is nearly always a sane
and reasonable judgment. He is better
acquainted with the circumstances than
anyone else.
Take the case of a man who has a son,
who is the black sheep of the family. If
he leaves any money to that boy he knows
that it will be spent in drink or gambling.
In present circumstances a man may exercise his judgment and cut out that child.
If such a Bill as this were passed into
law, there would be an invitation to the
son to make application to the court, in
the sure and certain hope that if he did
so all the rest of the family, in order to
hush
up the scandal, would him some
pay
money which his father did not wish him
to get.
Take another instance, where a boy is
not a black sheep in the ordinary sense
of the term, where he has not squandered
his money, but is a lazy fellow. The
father recognises that it would be more
in the boy's interests to leave him nothing; that it would be disastrous to leave
him money.
That is a thing you cannot
discuss before a court. The one person
who can form a shrewd judgment in a
matter of that kind is the testator himself.
It would seem to me that in 99 per
cent. of the cases in which a man disinherits his wife or children it will be found
that he has good reason for doing so; but,
unfortunately, in a great many of those
cases it is a reason which is best known
to the testator himself and on which he
has exercised a competent and sane
judgment, but of which no court could
of necessity have the material to exercise
judgment.
The hon. Member for Dock (Mr.
Midgley) says that the State interferes
with the private affairs of individuals,
but it interferes for the general good of
the community. My judgment is that if
the State interferes with testators making
wills as they like, as suggested in this
Measure, it will not be for the benefit of
the community. It might benefit the
widow and children in those cases-about
one per cent.-where the testator had
done something whimsical or capricious,
but compare that one per cent. with the
remaining 99 per cent. I think there
would be great danger of the court being
invited to interfere where it could not
possibly have the material before it, and
where the court by its interference would
defeat what was probably the sane, considered, sensible disposition of the testator, acting on facts which were very
well known to him, but which could not
from their very nature be fully known
to the court which would have to discuss
the matter after his death.

a large family. Nearly all the children

the others, they may come into court

The making of a will is very often left
to the last moment. Many people have
an idea that the making of a will is like
signing their own death warrant, and

if

The hon. and learned Member who
introduced this Bill knows well that in
a large proportion of wills in country

this Bill were passed a greater injustice
would be perpetrated on the son or relative who has managed the farm during
the lifetime of the testator. I do think

have been led to believe.

Government and Unemployment.
The following Motion stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr.
Henderson: :-
That in the opinion of this House,
notwithstanding the statement made
by Members of the Cabinet that they
would find a cure for the unemployment evil in Northern Ireland, the
Government have failed completely to
grapple with this growing menace
which has brought much unhappiness
to the loyal people of Ulster, and that
no effective steps have been taken by
the Government to secure new industries in order to provide employment
for the 65,000 unemployed in the Province, and, further, that the Government have not secured for Northern
Ireland an adequate share of the armament contracts which are at present
being allotted by the Imperial Authorities.

for vagrants and paupers. Why is it not
there for the able-bodied unemployed?
Do you want them to become human
wrecks? Our experience of the poor law
in Northern Ireland is such that we have
no confidence in the boards of guardians
as at present constituted. I am not
speaking from outside information. I
had some most kindly persons on the

ratepayers, was always sufficient to put

bring out the worst of the individual,
making him vote against assistance which
they themselves would have liked to
grant.
We have only one
resource at the
moment, in view of the changed circumstances brought about by the Parliamentary Secretary at the instigation of
boards of guardians coming to Stormont
and using intimidation. "If you do not
do as we say we will not vote for you at
the next election," is what they said.
You know very well the coming election
has great influence to change Clause 1,
and we are not going to stand idly by
and allow the Clause as passed now to
stand, and we ask you by vote to insert
the word "compel" and not be giving
any help to those guardians who, we all
know, do exist, whether they are
Unionists or not.

the working class and have an interest in

CLAUSE 2 (Powers of Ministry of
Home Affairs and guardians as to exceptional distress).
(1) Where the Ministry of Home
Affairs is satisfied, either on representations made to it by the board of
guardians of the union or otherwise, that
exceptional distress exists in any union,
that Ministry may, if it thinks fit, by
order authorise the board of guardians
of the said union, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed (either
generally or in such order), to grant
outdoor relief during any prescribed
period to poor persons resident in the
said union who would, apart from the
order, be excluded from receiving outdoor relief by the operation of section.
two of the Poor Relief (Ireland), Act,
1862.

Mr. MIDGLEY: I beg to move in
Clause 2, Sub-clause (1) after "board of
guardians of the union" to insert the
words "or any substantial body of the
citizens."
I want those words included as a safeguard. If you allow the Clause to remain
as it stands representation may be made
by the board of guardians "or otherwise."
It does not specify what "or otherwise"
means, so instead of those vague words
I want to include the words "or any substantial body of the citizens." I am sure
that the legal gentlemen in this Committee will appreciate my efforts. Somebody may ask what I mean by "any substantial body of the citizens." I will
ask you to come back with me into a
little Belfast history in order that I may
show you what is meant.
A few years
ago a question affecting poor-law administration arose, and as a result of the
activities of the churches, social bodies,
trade unions and associated bodies public
demonstrations which had the backing of
every denomination were held in the city.
I would submit that in such circumstances
those people would represent a substantial
body of the citizens.
Take another case. Not very long ago
in East Down, the constituency of the
Financial Secretary of the Ministry of
Finance (Lt.-Col. Gordon) a set of
adverse conditions arose in which the
trade depression was felt very keenly.
The overwhelming majority of the insurable population were out of work, and
there was no likelihood of their finding
any. All sections of the community in
that constituency with the concurrence
and support of the hon. and gallant
Gentleman himself, met to make representations to the legitimate authority. I
take it that these words "or any substantial body of the citizens' would cover
a situation like that which arose in East
Down. Those are two concrete examples.
I do not think it is sufficient to leave
the matter to the goodwill or initiative of
the board of guardians. Consequently
you must have some machinery by which
the expression of the peoples' will will
be made known apart altogether from
representations by boards of guardians.
I submit that the spirit of what I am
proposing now ought to be accepted by
the Parliamentary Secretary. If he does
not agree with the precise form of words
I will be satisfied if he will undertake
on behalf of the Ministry to put in a
form of words which will give substantial
bodies of the citizens the right to make
these representations which have to be
made from time to time, and which they
will make whether you put that in or not.

section of the community would have a

that the order be issued. I appeal to the

to all concerned that even if a board of

NEW CLAUSE (Amendment of s. 2 of
the Act of 1862 as to outdoor relief).
The following section shall be substituted for section two of the Poor Relief
(Ireland) Act, 1862:-
2. Any person who is in occupation
of any land of a net annual value
greater than four pounds as shown in
the valuation lists for the time being
in force under the Valuation Acts
(Northern Ireland), 1852 to 1932
(whether any person is liable to pay
rates in respect of such land or not),
and who is considered by the board of
guardians to require relief, shall be
relieved by them in the workhouse and
not otherwise.
Brought up and read a First time.
Mr. DAVISON: This Amendment is
really an extension of the powers of the
guardians. The Poor Relief (Ireland)
Act of 1862 excluded an occupier of more
than a quarter of an acre from being
relieved otherwise than in the workhouse.
Our own Local Government Act of 1934
substituted land of a net annual value
greater than £3, and we now propose to
extend that to £4. That suggestion was
made by the boards of guardians at the
conference, and I was rather surprised at
their generosity in extending the amount.
Still that was done, and I do not think
we should try to baulk their good intentions. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Clause.
be read a Second time."

Oral Answers to Questions.
COST-OF-LIVING FIGURE.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the total
number of questionnaires sent out to
householders in Northern Ireland for the
purpose of arriving at the cost-of-living
index figure; whether 80 per cent. of
those communicated with failed to make
a return; whether the Ministry paid
2s 6d for each return, and whether the
Minister can state the cost of living in
Northern Ireland as against Great
Britain.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR
(Major Shillington): My Department
ascertained by means of personal visits
whether persons were willing to compile
budgets, and I am glad to say that a
very satisfactory measure of public support has been received. Complete
returns from all exchanges are not yet
available, but the figures for 14 centres,
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
21 OCTOBER 1937
including Belfast, show that the number
of persons who declined to co-operate was
only 7 per cent. of the total number
visited. The payment of 2s 6d to which
the hon. Member refers will be made
only to those persons who send in completed budget forms.
The cost-of-living figure is one for the
United Kingdom as a whole, and separate
figures are not ascertained for the several
areas of the Kingdom.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it a fact that 500
questionnaires were sent out and 80 per
cent failed to reply?
Major SHILLINGTON: There were
500 questionnaires distributed, but the
suggestion that 80 per cent. did not reply
is not in accordance with the information
I have.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Minister has not
replied to the last part of my question,
which is important, namely, can he state
the cost of living in Northern Ireland
as against Great Britain? Can he give
us the real cost-of-living figure here?
WORKING-CLASS FAMILY
EXPENDITURE.
2. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Labour whether any arrangements have
been made for the inclusion of Northern

family expenditure which is being undertaken by the Ministry of Labour in Great
Britain to provide a revised basis for the
official cost-of-living figure for the United
Kingdom.
Major SHILLINGTON: I am glad to
inform the hon. Member that my Department is co-operating with the Great
Britain Ministry of
Ministry of Labour in the
inquiry which he mentions. The inquiry
entails the collection of a series of four
budgets each covering expenditure for a
period of one week at stated intervals
throughout the year, and arrangements
are now in progress through the employment exchanges for collecting the first
group of the quota of budgets allocated
to Northern Ireland. I am pleased to
say that the work is progressing satisfactorily and my Department is greatly
indebted for the help given by a number of voluntary workers who are assisting in the arrangements for the collection
of budgets.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the Minister at
some future date take upon himself the
responsibility allocated to his office?
Major SHILLINGTON: I do not understand the question.
Mr. BEATTIE: Get an index figure
in Northern Ireland for yourself.
UNEMPLOYMENT ASSISTANCE
SCOPE REGULATIONS.
-
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is prepared to lay
on the Table of the House a copy of the
Scope Regulations as drafted by the Unemployment Assistance Board and given
to their administrative officers for their
guidance; whether the said Regulations.
are in conformity with the Unemployment Assistance Act; whether it is a fact
that the interpretation of this Act is less
sympathetic in Northern Ireland than in
Great Britain; and whether he is prepared to see that the administration of
this Act follows the step-by-step policy.
Major SHILLINGTON: There are no
Scope Regulations. The conditions
under which a person may be admitted
as within the scope of the Unemployment
Assistance Act are laid down in Section
31 (1) of the Northern Ireland Act of
1934. The interpretation of these conditions under Section 31 (3) of the Act is
a matter, in the first place, for the
officers of the Unemployment Assistance
Board, and, in the second place, on
appeal, for the Chairman of the Appeals
Tribunal.
It is not the practice to lay office instructions on the Table of the House, but
the Board informs me that, through the
courtesy of the British Unemployment
Assistance Board, it received copies of
the British instructions on the point and
before the "Second Appointed Day"
under the Act circulated them to all
area officers in Northern Ireland with
the direction that they were to be
followed. The machinery for testing the
decision of these officers by appeal is
identical with that in Great Britain.

[Major Shillington]
I have no power to interfere with
decisions of the Statutory bodies, to

is most anxious, so far as lies in its power,
to implement the Government's policy of
proceeding step by step with Great
Britain in the social services, and I can
find no reason for thinking that the interpretation of the scope conditions of the
Act are less sympathetic here than in
Great Britain.

BRITISH LEGION CAR
ATTENDANTS, LTD., AND
EMPLOYEES.
4. Mr. BEATTIE: asked the Minister
of Labour whether it is a fact that the
Directors of the British Legion Car
Attendants, Ltd., held meetings of their
employees in groups on Thursday, 14th
October, in a hall in Belfast, and
endeavoured to dissuade them from
joining a trade union; whether it is a
fact that following the meeting the men
were coerced into taking part in what
purported to be a ballot vote, and that
each man was compelled to sign his name
to the ballot paper; whether the directors
retained the votes without revealing the
result of the ballot to the men; whether
he can state the result of this so-called
vote; whether this treatment is in
accordance with the principles of freedom.
for which these disabled ex-Servicemen
fought, and, if not, what steps he proposes to take to protect these men from
such treatment and the likelihood of
victimisation.
Major SHILLINGTON: Meetings of
the car park attendants were held as
stated in the question. I am informed
that no coercion was used to dissuade the
men from joining a trade union if they
so desired, and that a letter stating that
there was no objection on the part of
the company to the men doing so was
sent to the trade union concerned on
Tuesday last. The names were signed
to the papers for record purposes and
the result of the voting was also notified
to the trade union.

The

TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The total

from milk producers and distributors

CONSUMPTION OF MILK IN
BELFAST.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state how the
quantity of milk consumed in Belfast
since the introduction of the Milk
Marketing Act compares with the
quantity consumed prior to the introduction of the Act, basing the comparison, as far as possible, on
consumption per head of the population.
a
answer
the
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I regret that
I am able to give the hon. Member only
partial
to
this question.
Reliable statistics of urban milk consumption in Northern Ireland have only
become available since the Milk and Milk
Products Act, 1934. These cover the
consumption of milk by the whole of the
non-farming community and it is not possible to extract sales in Belfast alone.
From these figures it is estimated that
urban consumption has increased between
the financial years 1936 and 1937
by apporoximately half-a-million gallons.
There is reason to believe that this increase has taken place chiefly in Belfast.
GRADING OF FAT CATTLE.
8. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware that
dissatisfaction prevails amongst the cattle
feeders of Ulster owing to the fact that
the grading of fat cattle is not carried
out in accordance with the Act, and
whether he is prepared to appoint three
men as referees who are not officials of
the Ministry, selected from butchers,
auctioneers and farmers.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have no
doubt that certain farmers consider the
standard for super subsidy to be too high,
but I am not aware that dissatisfaction
exists as to the application of the
standard in Northern Ireland. Furthermore, I am satisfied that the grading is
carried out in this Province in accordance with the Act. It should be obvious
to the hon. Member that the suggestion
in the latter part of the question is
neither desirable nor practicable.
Mr. MINFORD: Would the Minister
tell us why they do not adopt the same
procedure as is adopted in Great Britain
in connection with the Live Stock
Improvement Act, whereby referees can
be called in in cases of dispute?

"A" SPECIAL CONSTABULARY
AND PENSION RIGHTS.
10. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he has considered the
demand of the ex-members of the "A"
Special Constabulary for equal treatment
with men who joined the Royal Irish
Constabulary at the same period in
respect to pension rights.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply
to this question.
The claim being made by former members of the "A" Special Constabulary
to pensions has been fully considered and
formed the subject of a deputation of exmembers of the "A" Force who waited
on the Prime Minister in July last.
It was then pointed out that the members of the Royal Irish Constabulary
possessed permanent status and, therefore, on disbandment automatically
became entitled to the compensation laid
down by the Constabulary (Ireland) Act
of 1922, and that there could be no
possible analogy between the conditions
of service of these men and those of the
"A" Special Constabulary, as the latter
were definitely appointed on a temporary
basis, the terms of which included the
payment of a bounty in lieu of pension.
Every member of the "A" Special Constabulary on joining that Force accepted
the prescribed conditions of service, and
subsequently on disbandment of the
Force each man was granted two months'
leave on full pay and a free travelling
warrant to his home. The Government
is, therefore, unable to accept the suggestion that the contracts made with the
members of the "A" Special Constabulary
were in any way broken or that the members have been unfairly treated.
Mr. NIXON: In view of the fact that
the Government have just passed a Bill
to give £200,000 more than his contract
price to the contractor for the Bann
drainage, would the right hon. Gentleman introduce a Bill to give something
to the Special Constabulary?

seen the

Mr. ANDREWS: In reply to the hon.
Member, I have seen the correspondence
to which he refers. As regards the suggestion in the latter part of his question,
that holders of long leases were excluded
from the Land Purchase Acts, I would
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
21 OCTOBER 1937
point out that the provisions of the
Redemption of Rent (Ireland) Act of
1891, were extended by the Northern
Ireland Land Act of 1925, so as to render
the consent of the lessor or grantor unnecessary, thereby giving liberty of purchase to the lessee, and again by the
Northern Ireland Land Act of 1929, by
which the fact that a holding had been
purchased under the Land Acts prior to
1903 did not disqualify the lessee from
obtaining the benefits of the 1891 Act.
It was open to agricultural leaseholders to take advantage of these provisions until the Northern Ireland Land
Purchase (Winding Up) Act came into
force in the present year.

Mr. ANDREWS : The British
Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1927
informed my predecessor that the British
Government intended to legislate in their

enabling them to revalue property in
Northern Ireland for income-tax purposes; the late Mr. Pollock succeeded in
having this proposal postponed, but it
was revived by the succeeding Chancellor
at the close of 1929, and a Clause to be
inserted in the British Finance Bill of
1930 was actually supplied to the Ministry of Finance. Mr. Snowden eventually,
owing to Mr. Pollock's influence, postponed the inclusion of this Clause, and
as an alternative our Government undertook to carry out a revaluation for rating
purposes, which the British Government
would be prepared to adopt for income.
tax assessments.

ALLOWANCE TO "B" SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
16. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether, now that all
cuts in salaries and allowances of Cabinet
Ministers, Members of Parliament, civil
servants and teachers have been restored,
he will consider favourably the question
of restoring the allowance paid to members of the "B" Special Constabulary to
the original amount of £10 (ten pounds)
per annum.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The economy
cuts imposed in 1931 on the amounts paid
to the "B" Special Constabulary were
fully restored in 1936.
The hon. Member is, I think, under a
misapprehension in suggesting that the
allowance of £10 per annum, payable to
the "B" Special Constabulary, has been
reduced. This allowance was payable to
the members of the Force at a time when
it was necessary to require them to perform 36 drills and 36 night patrols per
annum. As conditions improved it
became, I am glad to say, no longer
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
21 OCTOBER 1937
necessary to insist upon the performance
of so much active duty, and the Special
Constabulary was re-organised on the
basis of three categories according to the
nature and extent of the duties to be
performed, members of the Force being
allocated to the appropriate category as
the requirements of the moment rendered
expedient, viz. :-
The patrol category, in which, as
formerly, an allowance of £10 per
annum is payable in respect of not
less than 36 drills and 36 night
patrols per annum ;
the drill category, in which an
allowance of £3 per annum is payable in respect of not less than 48
drills per annum ;
and the reserve category, in which a
purely nominal allowance of 10s
per annum is payable in respect of
three drills per annum.
In the event of mobilisation the members of the Force will, of course, receive
payment at the rate of 7s a day.

Sir DAWSON BATES: There has been

the scheme for the provision of labourers'

NORTHERN IRELAND AS A
DISTRESSED AREA.
Mr. BEATTIE (by private notice)
asked the Prime Minister whether he is
prepared to make representation to the
British Government to declare Northern
Ireland a distressed area, entitling it to
the special grants that are given in Great
Britain; whether he is aware that
Northern Ireland is the second highest
area for unemployment; whether English
workmen when transferred to centres in
England receive grants from the Distressed Area Fund to assist them to send
home sufficient money to keep their wives
and families in decency and comfort
during their absence; whether large
numbers of workmen are being sent to
Great Britain to work and, owing to the
increased cost of living, lodging expenses
have been increased and that the amount
left to be sent home has been reduced;
whether, in view of these circumstances,
the Minister is prepared to treat
Northern Ireland workmen in a similar
manner to that accorded to English
workmen ?
Mr. ANDREWS: The question
whether Northern Ireland should be
declared a distressed area is one not for
the United Kingdom Government but for
this Government to determine. The
Government believe that such a course
would be most injurious to the interests
of the workers and industries of Northern
Ireland generally, and would give an
entirely erroneous impression of our
economic position, for, notwithstanding
the regrettably high rate of unemployment prevailing at present, the volume
of employment has been steadily rising.
The areas which have been listed for
special treatment in Great Britain are
those which had been suffering for several
years from acute industrial depression
due to serious dislocation of one or more
basic industries on which they were
wholly dependent, and they are not comparable to Northern Ireland. I would
like to point out to the hon. Member that
Liverpool is not a special area, and yet
the percentage of unemployment there is
higher than in Belfast.
As regards the payment of subsistence
allowances in Great Britain, the payment
is for a temporary period only, and is
restricted to men who are willing to
transfer their families from depressed
areas under the industrial transference
scheme.
For Northern Ireland workers who
avail themselves of opportunities of employment in Great Britain brought to
their notice through the Employment
Exchange service, arrangements are in
force for the payment of a free fare and,

are
Is there any nearer approach to

Mr. CAMPBELL: I rise to express
my feeling of dissatisfaction at the complacency with which the Members on the
Ministerial side of the House are adjourning until 9th November, the Lord
Mayor's Banqueting Day in London.
They do not seem to realise the position
of Northern Ireland at the present
moment, or if they do realise it, they are
supremely indifferent to it. We have in
the North of Ireland between 60,000 and
70,000 people who are destitute for the
want of work. Unemployment does not
seem to concern the Government very
much; it is looked upon as a matter
almost of routine in the life of this
Province. We have in Northern Ireland a percentage of unemployment
which is twice that in practically every
other area of importance in the United
Kingdom. This problem of unemployment has been hanging over this
Province, heavy and frowning, for the
past 16 years. It has hardly been lessened
and no one who knows Ulster at the present time can say with truth that he sees
the least blink of blue sky.
no
Vast sums of money are being poured
forth on armaments in England, but
Northern Ireland is getting practically
none of that money which is pouring-
I do not know whether we should call
them fertilising springs or not-in great
swelling streams in nearly all the great
industrial centres of Great Britain. We
in Ulster are outside those streams of
immense public wealth. There are
new industries in our Province. Any we
have got are mere flashes in the pan.
The Acts passed in this Parliament have
come to nothing. Quite recently a former
Prime Minister of Great Britain, Earl
Baldwin, then Mr. Baldwin, said that
any government could be tested by one
great test, how it dealt with its unemployment problem. They dealt with it
in England to some extent, I suppose
artificially, by the armaments boom. If
you test the Government of Northern
Ireland by that standard, what is to be
said? Nothing has been done to solve
the unemployment problem. On that subject the Government has been a ghastly
failure, and the position would be worse
were it not for the subsidies that come
across from London. The whole thing is
dark enough and tragic enough as it is,
but it would be very much more tragic
without the British help which comes here
in various ways.
We here in Northern Ireland are
parading, strutting about as peacocks as
if this were a paradise. The man in the
street in Belfast, and the man in the

a vast amount of suffering and a vast
amount of destitution in many areas in
Northern Ireland. Yet we are parading
as if we had a paradise. The English
people have got the idea into their heads

area. Pride will not let us admit that.
We must face realities, stark staring
realities which any one with eyes in his
head cannot avoid seeing. Why are we

England these distressed areas are getting

ORDER OF THE DAY.
Poor Relief (Amendment) Bill.
As amended considered.
CLAUSE 2 (Powers of Ministry of
Home Affairs and guardians as to exceptional distress).
(1) Where the Ministry of Home
Affairs is satisfied, either on representations made to it by the board of
guardians of the union or otherwise,
that exceptional distress exists in any
union, that Ministry may, if it thinks
fit, by order authorise the board of
guardians of the said union, subject to
such conditions as may be prescribed
(either generally or in such order), to
grant outdoor relief during any prescribed period to poor persons resident
in the said union who would, apart
from the order, be excluded from
receiving outdoor relief by the operation of section two of the Poor Relief
(Ireland) Act, 1862.

four months for being a dangerous

I should like to draw attention to the
way the Government have exploited the
skilled workers of Northern Ireland who
have been sent to England, with the result that all over this area a great deal
of hardship prevails. Many homes have
been broken up owing to the fact that
husbands and fathers who have had to
go across the water have been able to
send home only 25s a week. Skilled
craftsmen are paid £3 3s in some cases in
Great Britain. When they pay 26s or
27s for their board and lodging, and pay
their contributions to their trade society,
they have only about 25s to send home
for the maintenance of their wives and
perhaps four or five children. It is
rather strange that the Government
should allow that to take place, and then
to pretend that everything in the garden
is lovely.
The policy of the Government in that
respect has been wrong. These men who
are working in England are no longer an
asset to this country, but their departure
has reduced the unemployment figures of
Northern Ireland. The cream of the
craftsmen of Northern Ireland has been
exported to England, and thereby the
unemployment figures of this area have
been reduced by thousands. The right
hon. Gentleman cannot be very proud of
reducing the unemployment figures here
by exploiting the skilled craftsmen of
this country. The families of those who
are working in England are practically
in destitution. There is no glory attaching to the statement of the right hon.
Gentleman that £1 is given to every
skilled craftsman towards the expense of
his going to England when he has to pay
the money back. Is it not rather strange
that men in England can go from Liverpool to London under the same scheme,
get a certain sum of money for their expenses, and that that money is not taken
from them? This is an allowance which
is not granted to workers of Northern
Ireland, but is given across the water.
In any case this exploitation of Northern Ireland workers is a very serious
matter. The people who are left behind
are living in houses rented at 12s or 14s
a week, and there may be four or five
children. They get about 25s to keep
their homes and feed their families. If
we had been in power we would have
made it our business not to export
our skilled craftsmen, but we would have
utilised our brains and the wealth of this
country to keep them at home, as that is
the only way the country can be made to
prosper. I hope the right hon. Gentleman will see that something is done to
give these men a grant. I do not know
whether the Speaker will allow me to
mention this matter, but I notice that
right hon. Gentlemen have suggested that
unemployment here could be reduced by
people emigrating to other countries.
do not stand for that. The Lord Mayor
made that statement, and I believe right
hon. Gentlemen will follow suit.
I
Another matter of vital importance is
the need for suitable hospital accommodation. May I take the opportunity provided by this Motion to point out that the
Ministry of Home Affairs are neglecting
their duty to a very considerable extent in
this connection? When a letter is written
to that Department on behalf of the tuberculous people who are dying owing to lack
of accommodation in a modern hospital
no reply is received. The Belfast Corporation have already waited two months for
a decision from the Ministry of Home
Affairs, and they have not yet received a
communication from the Government. The
Corporation have had three or four telephonic communications with the Ministry.
but they could hardly get a reply from
them. I think there is something
seriously wrong when such a state of
affairs is allowed to continue. I believe
the acting Prime Minister should get into
touch with the Minister of Home Affairs
and tell him to spend less time in France
and more in Ulster. If he does not go
back to France, it may save him when the
election comes round. When this House
was sitting the Minister of Home Affairs
was gallivanting about the shores of
France.
Mr. SPEAKER: It is quite unfair to
go into the private life of any Member of
this House. It is in order to say that the
administration of the right hon. Gentleman is not what it should be, but to go
into his private life is a thing that is
absolutely unknown in any Parliament.
Mr. HENDERSON: I do not want to
dispute your ruling, but I think the proper

place for the Minister of Home Affairs is
at home, especially when Parliament is

during the time he should be working he

object so much to the absence of the
Minister of Home Affairs if he were not
paid. In any case I want to get a little
more justice for the Ulster worker. Give

Englishman who has to travel from
Liverpool to London.
Mr. ANDREWS: It will only be necessary for me to say a very few words in
order to remove misunderstandings that
exist. In the first place, as regards revaluation, the answer which I gave to the
hon. Member earlier in to-day's sitting
was the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and I have nothing
to add on that subject.
As regards the recreation hall, that
grant was given in 1923 on the advice of
an advisory committee composed of representatives of all parties-Nationalists,
Socialists and Unionists. It was givenand I approved of its being given-in
order to provide employment which was
much needed at that time and also to provide working people with a recreation hall.
In 1923 unemployment, as the hon.
Member knows, was very much worse than
it is to-day, and everything possible was
being done then, as it is being done now,
to provide as much employment as possible. The hon. Member has said that
there are grievances all round. If that
be so, it seems to me wondrous strange
that the hon. Member has to go back 14
years in order to dig out this grievance.
Mr. NIXON: What is the hall used
for?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
for Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) in his very
strong attack upon the Government was
listened to with respect and in silence.
When the right hon. Gentleman on the

Government side gets up to reply I must
protect him, as I would have protected
the hon. Member for Woodvale if he had
required protection. I would ask the
hon. Member to allow the right hon.
Gentleman to proceed without interruption.
Mr. NIXON: I was subjected to interruptions.
Mr. ANDREWS: I did not interrupt
the hon. Member, and I am not in the
habit of doing so. I should like to say
in conclusion that the unemployed
workers here are given an opportunity of
accepting work across the Channel. Notwithstanding what the hon. Member has
stated, I know personally that very many
of our workers are happy to be able to
get such work. If they can show just
reason why they should not be asked to
go, that reason is accepted, and they are
not pressed to go. Every consideration
that it is possible to extend has been
extended by way of paying their fares
and making them an allowance to help
them during the first week or two until
they receive their wages. If the hon.
Member himself had been dealing with
this matter he could not have dealt with
it more sympathetically than it has been
dealt with. Further, the arrangements,
as I stated when answering a question,
have met with the approval of the Trades
and Labour Council in Belfast.

in the said Amendment."

and the insured population should know

CLAUSE 6 (Provisions to facilitate
prosecution of persons using vehicles
without excise licences).
(1) Where it is alleged that a vehicle
has been used in contravention of
section thirteen of the Roads Act, 1920
(which provides for the punishment of
persons who use vehicles without the
appropriate excise licences)—
(a) the owner of the vehicle shall give
such information as he may be
required by or on behalf of a
district inspector of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary or a county
council within the meaning of the
Roads Act, 1920, to give as to the
identity of the driver and of any
person using the vehicle, and, if
he fails to do so, shall be guilty
of an offence, unless he shows to
the satisfaction of the court that
he did not know and could not
with reasonable diligence have
ascertained who was driving or
using the vehicle; and
(b) any other person shall, if required,
as aforesaid, give any information
which it is in his power to give
and which may lead to the identification of the driver or of any
person using the vehicle, and, if
he fails so to do, shall be guilty
of an offence.
(2) A person guilty of an offence
under this section shall be liable on
summary conviction to a fine not exceeding twenty pounds.
