hon. Member for Duncairn, I hope that
he will use his powers in the interests of
the working men who have to go to and
from the premises of Short and Harland.
The next thing I want to speak about
is the by-pass road in my area. It is
alleged that the work of construction
has begun. This House gave the Minister of Home Affairs full power to proceed
with the work, and I had hoped that last
summer would have seen a number of
men employed in the construction.
Recently I asked a question on this subject, and the Minister replied that within
two or three weeks' time work would be
commenced at the Kinnegar end. On
several nights I have taken a walk to the
Kinnegar end to see what was being done.
I found it a very desolate place, and I
could see no signs of life to any extent
on the site of the proposed by-pass road.
I have tried to find out from Commissioners and from responsible Ministers of
this House what is holding up the work,
but I have not succeeded. We in this
House gave the Minister power to take
over lands and to proceed with the
making of the road, and I am inclined
to think that the right hon. Gentleman,
since he became a Harbour Commissioner,
has really come under the influence of
the Board. I hope he has not done so,
and that before Christmas arrives we will
have at least 500 men working constantly
on the reconstruction of that road.
Another question that should receive
attention is the need of employment and
the facilities provided for the establishment of new industries. We have many
appeals for the establishment of new
industries. My regret is that too many
of the old industries are being allowed
Adjournment--
Unemployment
4 NOVEMBER 1937
to pass out. You cannot jump up tomorrow morning with a new industry and
achieve all that is desired; but you know
the value of the old industries. If the
old industries could be reorganised and
enabled to utilise the full working power
available that might tend to relieve the
unemployment problem to a greater extent than new industries of which we
know nothing. If the Minister of Commerce in his quest for new industries
would keep in mind the reorganisation
of the old, and try to achieve both objects,
we might get something that would be
beneficial to the workers of Northern
Ireland.
I have in my mind at the moment the
fact that 20 girls were sent to England
on three occasions to a hat and cap
factory. There is a little place of that
kind in Belfast, and if that industry were
extended here it would probably employ
a large number of girls and boys. But it
could not be classified as a new industry,
and therefore it would not come under
the New Industries Act. The individual
who has this little hat and cap industry
is quite satisfied to carry on in the old
familiar way. "I am getting out of it
what will do me for my day and
generation, and I am not desirous of
spending any more money." I think the
difficulty of many of those who are interested in industry is that until there
are guarantees of better prospects it is
impossible to induce people to invest
money in development. Therefore, I
think that if the assistance of old
industries can be coupled with the establishment of new enterprises we will be able
in the near future to cater for the female
worker and the juvenile to a greater extent than hitherto has been possible.
My last remark is this-this is, indeed,
not only a distressed area, but a backward
area, which is a more hopeless position. I
claim that this is due to many factors,
with which I am unable to deal on the
Motion for the Adjournment. But I
take this opportunity of appealing to the
right hon. Gentleman to be active when
this House is not sitting in efforts to reduce the percentage of unemployment
here to the figure applicable to England.
In England the percentage of unemployment is 10.9 against Northern Ireland's
22.2. Before this Government took up
office the percentage of unemployment for
the nine counties of Ulster was 12. Today we have 22.2 per cent. in the Six
Counties, proving that instead of going
forward this area is going back. That
certainly does not redound to the credit
of this Government. I feel that it is up
to the Government, before the General
Election takes place early next year, to
show the people that, although they have
been sixteen years in office, they have at
least done something to remove poverty
and to assist those who cannot help themselves.

I must keep to the matter of administration. I was only putting that forward as a sort of argument that the
Government do less harm when the House

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Andrews): The hon. Member for Shankill,
who introduced this debate, began by
saying that the Government had been
seventeen years in office. I want to say
very definitely that they have been years
of continual progress. Any reasonable
man who viewed the position in Ulster
Adjournment-
Unemployment
4 NOVEMBER 1937
seventeen years ago and then viewed it
to-day could not do otherwise than admit
that great and sustained progress has
been made in every direction. Further,
the hon. Member said that something
must be done to help the situation. I
maintain that the Government during all
these years has done everything humanly
possible. We have encouraged relief
schemes. Only recently we have increased the grant from 60 per cent. to
75 per cent. to encourage local authorities to embark upon relief schemes.
We have encouraged industry in
every way that can be suggested. We
have brought in a Measure dealing with
new industries, and some progress has
been made in the way of establishing
new industries-Short & Harland, for
example.
Then, again, we have passed an Act
to enable local authorities to build
cottages all over our rural areas in order
that our people may be properly housed,
and that a considerable amount of employment may be made available for those
engaged in the building industry. Again,
we have maintained our social services
similar to those in Great Britain. It is
all very well for hon. Members to suggest
that pensions should be increased. They
never tell us how the money is to be
obtained. The Member for Shankill suggested some little time ago that we should
borrow in order to pay increased old-age
pensions.
Mr. HENDERSON: Get the money
out of the same bank as you got the
money for the war.
Mr. ANDREWS: I listened to the
hon. Member without a single interruption, and I ask him to extend the same
courtesy to me. We have maintained
our social services similar to those in
Great Britain. It is not possible for us
to do more, and we certainly are not
going to do less. When pensions
are increased in Great Britain they will
be increased here. As I have said before
the reason it is not possible for us to do
more is because our financial relations
with Great Britain will not permit us to
do so, and as long as I am Minister of
Finance I am not going to agree to borrow in order to do it. If we were to
embark upon a policy of that kind we
ould ruin the credit of Ulster, and as a
consequence we would do Ulster irreparable damage.
At the end of seventeen years our
credit in Ulster stands as good as the
credit in Great Britain, and that is due
to the careful way in which our finances
have been managed all along. If some
hon. Members opposite were in power I
say without hesitation that if they pursued the policy which they suggest from
time to time in this House they would
very soon place Ulster in a very serious
financial position. Unemployment is
regrettable. We all regret it. Every
Member on this side of the House
sympathises with the unemployed just as
much as do Members on the opposite side.
As I have already shown, we have done
a great deal to help the unemployed, and
we are prepared to continue to do everything possible to help them in every way.
But I venture to say this, that the
speeches that are delivered by the
Member for Shankill, exaggerating the
difficulties we have got to contend with,
and suggesting that the position is far
worse than it actually is, are detrimental
to the interests of the people of Ulster,
and especially to our working classes.
Instead of continually talking Ulster
down let hon. Members opposite
endeavour to talk Ulster up. How can
we expect new industries to come to
Ulster if we are always saying that this
is a miserable place, and if we are told,
not only in this House, but outside, that
we are drifting into bankruptcy who will
invest their money in our area. It is all
nonsense and absurd. It is the poorest
form of propaganda that I know.
almost go as far as to say it is not honest.

Oral Answers to Questions.
NEW TECHNICAL SCHOOL AT
BALLYNAHINCH.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether he can state the reasons for
the delay in erecting a new technical
school in Ballynahinch, Co. Down; whether
the Regional Committee have been considering sites for the past ten years;
whether the present premises are most unsuitable and have been condemned as insanitary, and whether it is a fact that
Ballynahinch and surrounding area up to
a radius of five miles has no representative on the Regional Committee.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The existing
premises, in which technical classes at
Ballynahinch are conducted, are most unsuitable, but I am not aware that the
local authority responsible has condemned
them as unsanitary.
The Down County R.E.C. is anxious to
provide satisfactory accommodation, but
has met with great difficulties in procuring a suitable site. During the past eight
years many sites have been considered,
but so far it has not been found possible
to secure one which is centrally situated,
suitable for building purposes, reasonable
in price, and, at the same time, free from
legal difficulties.
The question is, however, constantly
before the committee, and I understand
that it is hoped to obtain a suitable site
before long, although the difficulties are
such as to prevent an immediate decision
being made.
I am informed that none of the members of the present committee resides in
the immediate vicinity of Ballynahinch,
but this should not be taken as implying
that the committee is on that account less
mindful of the needs of the town or less
anxious to provide it with facilities equal
to those found in other parts of the committee's area.

INFANT DEATH RATE IN

a
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Labour whether his Ministry consider that there is direct relation
between the infant death rate of 100 per
1,000 in Belfast as compared with 60
per 1,000 in England and Wales, and the
unemployment percentage of 22 in
Belfast as compared with 12 for the
United Kingdom as a whole.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Major
Shillington): There are obviously so
many factors affecting the rate of infant
mortality that it would be impossible to
segregate the effect of any one factor. I
would like to point out that the hon.
and learned Member is comparing the
figure for Belfast with the figure for the
whole of England and Wales, the rate
for Northern Ireland in 1936 being 77.
The hon. and learned Member will be
glad to know that on the whole there has
been a decline in the rate of infant
mortality in Belfast; the average during
the period 1904-8 was 143 per 1,000, as
compared with 99 per 1,000 during the
period 1931-6.

that the witnesses were most of them

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The information at

The facts as to the Committee
appointed in 1928 are as he states, but I
do not agree that under existing conditions there is any such demand as he
would represent and I believe, on the
contrary, the facts are that the fears
expressed in 1928 have with the passing
of time in a great measure proved

Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the

Sir DAWSON BATES: In reply to a

BELFAST INFIRMARY-CASE OF
LEONORA PHILPOTT.
9. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he received a complaint from Charles Philpott, 41 Foreman
Street, Belfast, with regard to the treatment of his daughter Leonora Philpott,
who was sent to the Belfast Union Infirmary in January last when she was
13 months old; whether this child was
put into No. 12 ward suffering from
tonsillitis; whether after six weeks she was
put into No. 26 ward, which is reserved
for venereal diseases; whether blood tests
of the child's parents and family established that no syphilis was present;
whether the child's father has requested a
sworn inquiry to ascertain where the child
got the infection which qualified her for
26 ward; and, if she was not qualified for
this ward, why was she put there; and,
generally, what satisfaction this unfortunate man and his wife are going to get
for the present condition of their baby
daughter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: A complaint
has been received by the Ministry along
the lines suggested by the hon. Member
and has been exhaustively investigated.
among
a
The child in question was admitted to
hospital on the 11th January, 1937, on
a certificate from a dispensary doctor that
she was suffering from tonsillitis. On
admission to hospital she appeared to be
suffering from a post-influenza condition,
and she was in such a low state of health
that her recovery was regarded as doubtful. She was under the care of an eminent
specialist in eye, ear, nose and throat
diseases, but as she made poor progress
towards recovery, and as she was found to
be affected with interstitial keratitis-a
condition attributable,
other
causes, to congenital syphilis, but never
found in acquired syphilis-a sample of
her blood was submitted to the hospital
bacteriologist for examination. Owing to
the debilitated state of the child
sufficient quantity of blood could not be
obtained for a complete examination, but
gave a
the preliminary examination
weakly positive result. In view of these
facts, the child was transferred on the
19th February to the female venereal
diseases ward where the visiting surgeon,
who was satisfied that she showed clinical
signs of congenital syphilis gave her a
course of appropriate treatment. A further
examination of the child's blood on the
28th April gave completely negative results. The child's health steadily improved
and she was re-transferred to the eye
ward for further treatment. Whether or
not the child had congenital venereal
disease cannot be stated with absolute
conviction, but the treatment which she
has received, although it has not succeeded in clearing up all the corneal
opacity, has restored her to good general
health.
It will be seen from the history of the
case that by no possibility could the child
have contracted venereal disease in the
hospital. I am satisfied that the child
received every care and attention, and the
benefit of the attendance of eminent
specialists.

Session of Parliament was read by the

For Proroguing the Present Parliament

Northern Ireland, he can state the terms
of the draft amendment (supplied to his

Income Tax on property in Northern Ireland, as an alternative to the revaluation
which was carried out; whether he can

Mr. ANDREWS: A new Clause was
forwarded to the Ministry of Finance by
the Inland Revenue, but before the form
of the Clause was finally settled the
Chancellor decided to postpone it till the
following year. The draft Clause ran
into six typed sheets and was of a most
complicated character.
The revaluation was made on the
statutory basis of estimated rent, which
was the same basis as that used by Sir
Richard Griffiths for the last revaluation
of Ireland in the middle of last century,
and by Sir John Barton for the revaluation of the City of Belfast in the
beginning of this century. I may add
that all valuations are made on the basis

message was delivered by the

follows:-
as
I am commanded by the Senate to inform this honourable House that the
Proclamation of his Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland proroguing this present Session of Parliament is to be
communicated forthwith, and, further, I
am commanded to invite this honourable
House to attend in the Senate in order to
hear the said Proclamation.
The House went, and, having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the
Clerk's place at the Table): I have to
report that the House has this day
attended in the Senate, when the
Proclamation proroguing this present
WHEREAS it is provided by section.
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance
of certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern
Ireland shall, in His Majesty's name,
summon, prorogue, and dissolve the
Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern
Ireland should be prorogued to the
twenty-third day of November, one
thousand nine hundred and thirty-seven.
Now I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
Duke of Abercorn, Knight of the Most
Noble Order of the Garter, Knight of
the Most Illustrious Order of Saint
Patrick, Governor of Northern Ireland,
by this Proclamation do publish and
declare His Majesty's Pleasure that the
said Parliament be, as from the reading
of this Proclamation in the Parliament
of Northern Ireland, prorogued to Tuesday, the twenty-third day of November,
one thousand nine hundred and thirtyseven.
AND I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to
be that the said Parliament shall on
the said twenty-third day of November,
one thousand nine hundred and thirtyseven assemble and be holden at Stormont
for the despatch of divers urgent and
important affairs, and the Senators and
Members of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland are hereby required to
give their attendance accordingly.
GIVEN this ninth day of November,
one thousand nine hundred and
thirty-seven.

End of the Fourth Session (opened

Tuesday, 23rd November, 1937.
The Fifth Session of the Fourth Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to
meet 23rd November, 1937, in the First
year of the Reign of King George VI,
was opened by the Governor (His Grace
the Duke of Abercorn, K.G., K.P.) in
person.
The House met at Five minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mulholland,
M.P.) in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black
Rod (Major T. Dalby Hackett, D.S.O.)
was announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three
of the Clock, and then resumed.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sessional Orders.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon doub.e Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear
that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such bribery or other corrupt
practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime
or misdemeanour; and this House will
proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts, and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND
RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings,
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech on behalf of his Majesty to both Houses of
Palriament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The speech is
as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
The present year has been a memorable one in the history of our Empire.
The celebrations solemnising the
Coronation of his Majesty King George
the Sixth will never be forgotten by
those who were privileged to witness
23 NOVEMBER 1937
King's Speech

King's Speech
been at a higher level than has been
experienced for some time past. I
trust that certain disturbing factors
affecting the industry that have recently
arisen in international markets will
prove to be only of a temporary nature,
and that very soon normal trading
them, and demonstrated the depth of
affection in which their Majesties the
King and Queen are held by their
subjects throughout the Empire. Northern Ireland was graciously honoured by
the visit of their Majesties; and the
enthusiasm and spontaneous rejoicings
of our people on that occasion gave
abundant testimony of their love,
devotion and loyalty to the King and
Queen.
Although the improvement in trade
and employment that has been so
marked in Great Britain has not been
experienced to the same extent in
Northern Ireland, I am pleased to learn
that there has been an increase since
the beginning of the year in the volume
of employment. The estimated number
of persons in employment in all industries, including agriculture, insured
under the Unemployment Insurance
Acts had risen in October to over two
hundred and fifty-seven thousand.
During the same period the Unemployment Register had fallen by over seven
thousand, notwithstanding the fact
that the inclusion of agricultural
workers in unemployment insurance
and the enlargement of the scope of
the Unemployment Assistance Scheme
have led to a much more complete
registration of unemployed persons than
'at any previous time. During the past
twelve months some twenty-eight
thousand workers have been placed in
employment through the Exchange
service.
It is gratifying that local authorities
and public bodies are availing themselves of the improved facilities for
undertaking works of public utility that
have resulted from the increases in the
rates of grant which came into effect
last February. Since the increased
rates became operative, works involving
a total expenditure of four hundred
and twenty-six thousand pounds have
been approved.
I am pleased to observe that the present trend of external trade indicates a
continuance of the improvement which
has manifested itself in recent years. I
am gratified to learn that the value of
exports of linen goods to
Overseas
markets this year has so far been higher
than for the corresponding period of
any year since 1929, and that, in consequence, activity in the industry has
relations will be resumed.
It is equally a source of considerable
gratification to me that a high degree
of activity has been maintained in our
shipbuilding industry where, in consequence, the rate of unemployment,
though still unfortunately appreciable,
has fallen steadily throughout the year.
It was impracticable last Session to
proceed with Measures for the amendment and consolidation of the law
regulating conditions of employment in
factories and workshops, or for the
amendment of the Acts relating to
Blind Persons and the provision of
medical benefit for young persons
under the age of sixteen years who
enter insurable employment. These
matters will be brought forward for
your consideration during the forthcoming Session.
I am glad to learn that operations
under the Labourers' Acts are being
pressed forward, and that already
twenty-four rural district councils are
proceeding with the preparation of
schemes involving the erection of nearly
four thousand cottages.
The provision of suitable houses for
our working classes in Urban areas is
receiving the earnest consideration of
my Government and a measure dealing
with the matter will be submitted to
you.
I am advised that the Committees
which have been investigating the
question of the protection of the young
and the welfare of young offenders;
the law relating to the regulation of
shops in Northern Ireland; the conditions under which the organisation of
maternity services in Northern Ireland
is carried on; and the enlargement of
facilities for instruction of unemployed
young persons between the time they
leave school and the age of eighteen
years, will shortly conclude their
labours, and I am confident that the
valuable information which has been
obtained as a result of the exhaustive
examination of these questions will
King's Speech
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
prove of the greatest assistance to my
Government in dealing with these
very important matters.
The necessity for giving greater
attention to the physical training not
only of children and young persons
attending school, but also of those who
are no longer connected with recognised educational establishments, is a
matter of paramount importance at
the present time, and you will be
invited to consider proposals with this
object in view, adapted to the needs
and resources of our people.
to
Enquiries already received in regard
to the operation of the legislation
passed last Session, designed to assist
further in attracting industries
Northern Ireland, have indicated that
the effectiveness of the steps already
taken might be considerably enhanced
by widening the scope of the financial
assistance available. A Measure to
enable this to be done will be submitted for your early consideration.
I am glad to know that the state of
the finances of Northern Ireland made
it possible during the present year to
restore completely the cuts in teachers'
salaries which were made as an
economy measure six years ago.
Proposals will be laid before you with
a view to enabling teachers on retirement to surrender portion of their
pension in favour of the grant of a
pension payable to a named beneficiary
such as a wife or daughter.
A Measure will also be laid before
you for the amendment of the Act
relating to the Marketing of Potatoes.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public
Services will be laid before you in due
course.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I am gratified to know that as a
result of the assistance which within
recent years has been afforded to the
agricultural industry, combined with
the steps which are being taken
towards the reorganisation of the
methods of marketing agricultural
produce, farmers to-day are experiencing a gradual improvement in farming
conditions. It is my earnest hope that
this improvement will be continued
and that our oldest and greatest industry, which affords employment to
approximately one hundred and
seventy thousand people, may look
forward to a period of further pros
perity.
It is also a source of gratification to
know that, by an Act of last Session,
the opportunity has been afforded
many persons of small means, who are
outside the scope of the compulsory
Contributory Pensions Scheme, to
insure themselves voluntarily for
Widows' and Orphans' Pensions and
for Old Age Pensions at sixty-five,
and I trust that many will avail themselves of this means of providing for
themselves and those dependent on
them.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty
God may rest upon your deliberations.
DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.
Major ROBINSON (in
dress): I beg to move:
morning
"That a humble address be presented to his Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland as followeth :
"Your Grace,
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to
to offer our
humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament."
In moving the Address to the Gracious
Speech I would ask for the kind indulgence of the House. The outstanding
event in the history of our nation during
this year was, undoubtedly, the Coronation of our noble Monarch, King George
VI., and his Gracious Consort. Never in
the annals of our country has a Coronation taken place amid such Royal splendour
and universal enthusiasm. Representatives came from every corner of our vast
and mighty Dominions to pay tribute
and to express their devotion as well as
their allegiance to the head of the
British Empire-the greatest Commonwealth that has ever existed.
Their
fidelity was bound by the surest of all
ties the bonds of love and confidence,
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address

23 NOVEMBER 1937
which is mutual between our beloved
King and his faithful subjects.
At a later date his Gracious Majesty
was pleased to honour Northern Ireland
with a State visit, when his people here
were given a further opportunity of
shewing that love and loyalty which has
always been the pride of this the most
loyal Province in his Empire. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) At no time has
this integrity to the throne ever been
more clearly and bravely shown, than
during the dark days of the Great War,
when our Province not only gave the
greatest number of volunteers in proportion to our population in the Empire;
but also during the whole of those
terrible years our shipyards and munition factories carried on incessantly
without a strike or interruption of any
kind, doing all in their power to aid and
assist our country.
It is gratifying that the spirit of this
Gracious Speech is one of approval.
The volume of trade has, we are pleased
to say, increased in our several industries
during the year, and although Northern
Ireland has not benefited to the same
extent as Great Britain, in this trade
revival, we continue to hope that a just
proportion of the contracts given out by
His Majesty's Government mav yet be
allotted to this Province. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Whilst unemployment is still the
greatest of our troubles, we are pleased
to note that our labour exchanges have
been able to place some twenty-eight thousand workers in employment during
1937. Also, notwithstanding the fact
that agricultural labourers were insured
for the first time and are now included
in the unemployment register, this register shows an appreciable decline.
The fact that our local authorities and
public bodies have been able to avail
themselves of the increased rates of

4,000 suitable cottages in rural areas.

to supply a long felt need, relieving congestion and providing sanitary dwellings.
for our agricultural workers.

difficult to surpass.
I cannot but recall

easy to follow a man like the Right Hon.
Thomas Moles, whose eloquence we all so

sincerity commend to the House the
expression of humble thanks so fittingly
moved by the hon. and gallant Member

the loving thought and interest of the
King and Queen in every sphere they
touched upon on that memorable day.
Their Majesties won the hearts of
everyone.

Whilst it is gratifying to note that

We must not rest until the unemployment figure has been reduced to a

inducements which Northern
Ireland
offers must be broadcast not only in
Britain but in other countries, as I am

Whilst I am anxious to see this Province

There is urgent need for improvement of

I had the honour to serve
on the

A short time ago, a friend of mine

street in the centre of the city. In pursuit of his inquiries he passed through
a gateway and entered a small room,
something like an old saleroom, and
there to his surprise he came across some
twenty boys amusing themselves by playing cards. Their ages ranged from
about eighteen to twenty-two. The
place, he learned, was their clubroom,
and they informed my friend they were
there because they did not wish to be
hanging around the corners. That was
to their credit, but was the spectacle not
a saddening one?
While we welcome the intended
facilities to be given for physical training, I want to see workshops of instruction for these young men, the same as
have been established in England, so
that at least youths of this kind will
have some knowledge and be able to use
their hands when employment is forthcoming. Physical fitness, which is so
much spoken of to-day, especially

youths whose lives are shadowed by the

cannot do everything. We want to see
a new spirit arising in Northern Ireland-the same spirit that our noble
King expressed on the day of his Coronation when he said "that the highest of
distinctions is the service of others."
Our people have a splendid religious
background, but what is needed to-day
is a new spiritual awakening, so that
our Province may give a real leadership
in these days of stress and difficulty.
Ulster has led the Empire in many
matters before to-day-why not in this?
We have reason to rejoice in all that the
social legislation of this House has
achieved, is achieving, and the greater
good that it will achieve. Through the
medium of our social service, a helping
hand is stretched out to our people when
help is needed. It is good to think that
modern legislation, never before,
reflects a sensitiveness to the needs of
others. I trust that though these benfits may be largely material, the spirit in
which they are conceived, extended and
received may more and more weld our
community into one. To that end do
we reverently and fervently re-echo the
prayer that the blessing of Almighty
God may rest upon our deliberations.
I beg to second.

The first big question that should have

as
the British. They pay the same

ment surely Northern Ireland is entitled

The greatest tragedy of unemployment is
in regard to the youths in our Province,
young men and young girls who have
failed to find any useful employment.
The Government have been busy sending over all classes of tradesmen, all
classes of workers, both male and female,
to the British Isles. What for? To
carry out work they are accustomed to
for industrial firms. Instead of the
Government bringing those industries
into Northern Ireland they prefer to
send the workers to industries which have
been established in Great Britain by a
part payment from the people of Northern Ireland. That is the Government's
policy and they have failed to cope with
the position. The unemployment scales
are still as they were when the cost-ofliving figure was much lower than it is
to-day. The cost-of-living figure continues to mount higher and higher. The
index figure of the Ministry of Labour
at 1st October was approximately 58 per
cent. higher than the figure in July,
1914, and compared with 55 per cent. on
September 1, and 48 per cent. on 1st
October, 1936. That means that the
cost of living is going upwards; it is not
coming down. The rates of benefit paid
to the unemployed are not based on the
cost-of-living figure, and, therefore, the
rates for the unemployed have been considerably reduced. The Government had
not made any effort to bring the basis
of payment up to the required amount in
accordance with the cost of living figure.
That not only applies to the unemployed
scale rates but also to public assistance,
old age pensions, widows' and orphans'
pensions, and all that class of the community who can ill afford to have any
reduction in the amount they are
receiving.
The items most affected by the increase
in the cost of living, are eggs, milk,
butter and bacon--the essential things in
a working man's home. Those are the
commodities which have been increased
in price and no help is being given to
the 70,000 or 80,000 unemployed workers
who are drawing benefit of one sort or
another. Widows, orphans and old age
pensioners have not received any
increase. In every regulation brought into
this House the cost of which is going to
be borne by the members of the community, consideration should be given to
the section of the community which is
going to be hardest hit.

enthusiasm and once again Ulster people
were

had the opportunity of proving that
there are no more loyal people in the

The debate on the Address always gives
an opportunity to the Opposition to
attack and criticise the Government.
Provided that criticism is reasonable,
fair and impersonal, the Government will
accept it in good part.
Mr
NIXON: And deserve it.
Mr. ANDREWS: But it also gives an
opportunity to the Government to
express our views, to tell the House how
we have been and how we are dealing
with the various problems which so
deeply affect our country's welfare. The
Government, therefore, probably just
like the Opposition, welcome this
occasion. The hon. Member for
Pottinger has spoken and expressed his
views at some length. I cannot agree
with all that he has said, but I do
appreciate the impersonal way in which.
he spoke. He said, however, that
nothing was suggested in the King's
Speech to help the unemployment situation. As I proceed to-day I think I will
be able to show without much difficulty
that that is not so.
Again, the hon. Member said that he
objected to the fact that the social
services were not being raised in proportion to the cost of living. We would all
like to see the social services as high as
possible, but the hon. Member opposite
knows just as well as I do that the best
this Government can do, or any other
Government in this Ulster of ours can do,
is to maintain our social services with
British help similar to those in the rest
of the United Kingdom, similar to that
greater part, that wealthier part which
lies across the Channel. I think it is
really deceiving people to suggest that
better can be done, and so long as my
colleagues and I are in power in Northern Ireland worse will not be done. We
give that assurance to our people. The
hon. Member referred to the fact that in
relation to the population unemployment
is less in the Free State than here.
Mr. BEATTIE: Insured population.
Mr. ANDREWS: He said insured
population, but he forgets two important

factors. The Free State is not an industrial country at all; it is an agricultural country.
That makes a great
difference.
Mr. NIXON : What is Northern
Ireland?
Mr. ANDREWS: Another factor he
forgets is that there are not the same

Mr. ANDREWS: Just leave me as I
left you, and I will come to that later

Mr. BEATTIE: Do you mean
Great Britain?
in
Mr. ANDREWS: I mean here. There
is another practical difficulty. Many of
the industries which we have here are
fully engaged our engineering industry
for example-on their normal work for
their normal customers, and they do not
want to change their methods of work,
and probably their machinery, in order
to get a share of this rearmament work.
Those are two of the difficulties in the
way. I am, however, entitled to say
that the British Ministers, from the
Prime Minister down, are most anxious
to help in this matter.
The hon. Member went on to refer to
housing. I cannot understand his saying
that the Speech has nothing worth
mentioning about housing.
Mr. BEATTIE: City housing.
Mr. ANDREWS: City housing, as I
will show later, is referred to. The hon.
Member is rather despondent about the
position here. He is not, I admit, as
despondent as are some of his colleagues
at times, but despondency is really not
helpful. Unguarded words may do much.
harm. There is one thing that I can
point to with a great deal of satisfaction,
and that is that I have never met a
citizen of Northern Ireland who wanted
to live somewhere else. Surely that is a
sign and a proof, if proof were needed,
that this is not such a bad place to live
in after all. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
I admit that it is most desirable that
our existing industries should be extended. I also admit that it is most
desirable that new industries should be
established here, and we will welcome
help from anyone in that direction. The
Government will continue to do everything possible. Last Session the hon.
Member for Pottinger talked about
nothing being done to help our unemployment situation. Why, only last
Session, as he himself must remember, we
passed legislation for the purpose of
encouraging new industries in our midst.
We have found by experience that more
can be done in that way by widening
the scope of the financial assistance available, and a Bill to give effect to that view
will be submitted, as the Gracious Speech
says, for the consideration of Members
of this House.
The Government also, in order to provide work for our people, increased the
grants to local authorities to enable
them to carry out schemes of public
utility, and I am glad to be able to
state that beyond all doubt local authorities are taking a greater interest in the
matter than they did comparatively
recently and are putting up a great
number of schemes to my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Labour, to which
he has given, and will continue to give,
sympathetic consideration. Of course, it
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
is very easy for the Opposition, who have
no responsibility in this matter, to
criticise. We have undertaken to give 75
per cent. of the labour cost, and it is
the easiest thing for hon. Members
opposite to say we should give 100 per
cent., as I have heard some of them
say.
Mr. HENDERSON: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: They do not really
realise what that would mean. There
would be no inducement to local authorities to have the work carried on
economically unless they were asked to
bear a very small part of the cost. I do
not feel that pessimism is justified, and
I certainly do not feel that it is helpful.
Let us think of the unemployment
position for a moment. It is sad that
70,000 of our people are without employment. Hon. Members opposite always
refer to those 70,000 as if they were a
solid block that never changed, a solid
block driven to desperation. Of course,
that is not so. We turn over the number
about three times in the year. In addition, many of them, strictly speaking,
should not be included in the number.
They may work only a few days in the
week it is true, but if they happen to be
unemployed on the day the register is
taken they are counted as unemployed
persons. Take our dockers, for example.
The hon. Member opposite knows their
position. They are not driven to
desperation. In fact, they get very good
wages for a very few days in the week,
and many of them get unemployment
benefit for the rest of the week.
fore, it is not right to assume
because 70,000 people are unemployed,
70,000 people are living in misery.
Therethat
Again we find, and this is mentioned
in the Gracious Speech, that the number
of those unemployed is decreasing, and
has decreased since the beginning of the
year; also that the number of people in
work is actually increasing to a very considerable extent. These matters have to
be viewed in the broad sense if they are
to be looked at fairly. Again, it is easy
to blame the Government for the fact
that these people are unemployed, but
it is not correct to do so for the reason
that the unemployment situation is
largely affected by circumstances outside
our control. Let me give two examples
of that.
There was a back-set last month
admittedly, and unemployment went up
by about 5,000. Hon. Members opposite
will suggest that the Government were
responsible for that, but it is due
entirely to two circumstances over
neither of which the Government has
any control. One is the war between
China and Japan, the regrettable civil
strife in Spain, and the fact that
America is passing through a difficult
industrial and financial period; and the
other is the approach of the winter
season which affects our outdoor employment such as quarrying, road maintenance, etc. The Government cannot
make the sun shine, they cannot prevent
the days growing shorter, and yet those
circumstances inevitably affect the unemployment situation.
If anyone will view the situation as it
was sixteen years ago and as it is to-day
he will be bound to say there has been
progress on every hand. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) To begin with,
the social standards of our people have
been raised, our social services have been
increased, benefits have been increased
as compared with those existing sixteen
years ago, while widows', orphans' and
contributory old-age pensions have been
added. Medical benefits, unemployment
assistance, farm labourers' insurance,
and voluntary contributory pension
schemes have also been added to our
social code, and the proof that people
are being helped during times of
adversity, over which they themselves have no control, to
a greater
extent than ever before is to be
found in the fact that when I became
Minister of Labour sixteen years ago the
expenditure of the Department was three
millions and when I left it the expenditure was six millions, all of which went
into the homes of those who needed
assistance.
Yet we are told that the Government
has done nothing, has sat idle, has tried
to do nothing, and has succeeded in
nothing. It is simply not true. Again,
let me carry hon. Members a little
further to let them see the progress that
has been made. Everybody admits that
our educational system has been
improved. Everybody knows that schools.
have been built all over our area in town

23 NOVEMBER 1937
and country. The housing problem has
not as yet been completely solved, but it is
true that about 30,000 houses have been
built with Government aid.
Again, take road construction. There
is no comparison between the roads sixteen years ago and the roads now. Our
streets also have been improved. Land
drainage has been carried out in many
parts where the ground could not be
cultivated some years ago and where this
year I myself saw a fine harvest being
reaped. Agriculture has been assisted in
many ways by my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Agriculture. The farmers
admit it, though sometimes the leaders
of the farmers do not. Further, the
savings of our people have been vastly
increased since the establishment of
Ulster Saving Certificates.
—
The workhouses have been reduced to
half their former number. Hospitals
have been improved and increased in
number. Our Budgets have been
balanced, thanks to my distinguished
predecessor (Mr. Pollock). Our credit
has been maintained-a very important
consideration - and is equal to that of
Great Britain. Law and order has been
justly enforced with a firm hand, and
we have peace now that we had not 16
years ago. Our place within the United
Kingdom and the Empire has been preserved. It must be admitted that the
Government have taken a part in bringing all this about. Surely it is a record
of which we in Ulster may justly be
proud.
Yes, viewed from every standpoint,
progress has been made. But we are not
satisfied that further progress cannot be
made, and the Government are going to
see that it is made. For instance,
further schemes to help agriculture are
under consideration. A new Factories
and Workshops Bill will be submitted for
your consideration before very long.
You will be asked in a few days' time
to consider amendments to the Blind
Persons Act. A Bill to provide medical
benefits for young persons under 16 who
enter employment will be laid before you.
You will also be asked to consider the
provision of a course of physical training for children and young persons.
I come now to housing. The hon.
Member said that next to nothing had
been done in that connection as far as
our towns are concerned. In our rural
districts a great deal has been done, and
much also has been done in our towns.
I am glad to say that the local authorities, very generally, are taking advantage of the recent Measure which this
House passed in order that housing conditions might be improved in our rural
areas. In addition to that, the Gracious
Speech points to the fact that the Government are now considering a scheme of
housing for our urban districts as well.
We all want to see our people living
in healthy, suitable homes, at rents
which they can afford to pay. My
colleagues on this side of the House desire that just as much as hon. Members
opposite.
Our opponents seem to think that the
salvation of Northern Ireland lies in
calling it a distressed or special area, as
hon. Members opposite have often suggested. Tabs and labels of that kind
would neither end nor mend the situation.
There is no magic virtue in such words.
Only a few weeks ago, "The Times" referred to the special areas in Great
Britain as still areas of distress, forsaken
by industry, and economically derelict.
Surely that is not a correct description
of the position here. We are not forsaken by industry, and it cannot truthfully be said that we are. The number
of people in industrial employment alone
has risen. in four years from 181,000 to
230,000. In addition, agriculture provides employment for approximately
170,000 persons. We are not economically derelict when our credit is as good
as that of Great Britain, and when, by
every test that can be applied to our financial and trading position, growth and
expansion can be found.
are
I have said that we want new
industries, but statements such as are
frequently made by Members of the
Opposition and other public men
certainly not helpful. Who, for instance,
would invest their capital in a country
when they are told that it is drifting
into bankruptcy, that it is going down
and down, that the position is getting
worse and worse? Those despondent
views, as I have said, are not helpful;
in fact, they are the very opposite. I
therefore suggest to hon. Members-and
every business man knows it to be truethat it is only on a foundation of confidence that security and peace for development and progress can take place.

Government of a country which he knew

officially unemployed and another 20,000

Mr. ANDEWS: How do you know?

know. March the unemployed four
deep and you will find that instead of

There are thousands and thousands
leaving school who are not registering at

register because they know it is useless.
They know that their brothers and sisters
have been signing on since the war period
and have not as yet received any unemployment benefit. Can the Minister suggest
why they should sign on at the labour
exchanges? There is no reply from the
right hon. Gentleman. Frankly, and I
say this with a great deal of responsibility as one of the persons of independent thought in this country, so far as
the present Cabinet are concerned there
is going to be no hope extended to the

I expect this is the last King's Speech
which will be read in this House before
the Government go to the country. Had
I been acting Prime Minister or Prime

People in this country have suffered

to the Address, and it would not be fair
on my part to drag out this debate to
prevent Members when the amendment
comes before this House to-morrow starting with a clean sheet. All I can say
is this: there is not one solitary statement in regard to an Agricultural Wages
Bill. One would have thought that the
Government of this country would at
least have had a Committee of Inquiry
set up to inquire into the whole conditions
of the agricultural labourers of this community. But that was not done. I get
large numbers of letters from all parts
of Northern Ireland appealing to me to
raise this question in the House in regard
to the starvation conditions that exist in
agricultural areas. The right hon. Gentleman the Minister of Agriculture may be
surprised-I do not think anything would
surprise him-to learn that I had a letter
from his constituency with the names of
six men who are receiving 8s 3d a week

Debate on the Address

23 NOVEMBER 1937
working as agricultural labourers. They
have a house at about 2s 3d a week.
Where they have no house they get 10s
a week and no perquisites. You could
hardly believe that in view of the fact
that the coolies in the Malay States have
4s 6d a day. In view of that state of
affairs, which the right hon. Gentleman
must know exists, I cannot understand
his mentality, that he should allow these
conditions to prevail in his constituency
unless he does not want to hurt the
feelings of some of the prominent electors
in his Division. But something should
be done. I sent letters to the right hon.
Gentleman showing that in the Limavady
district agricultural labourers were working for 11s and 12s a week.
It is quite true that something is going
to be done for the blind persons of the
country. That would not have been done
only for the fact that the British Parliament is bringing it in. I feel terribly
embarrassed at times.
I would like to be
in a position to say that we could bring
in these social measures ourselves to better
conditions of the people, but unfortunately we cannot. With what result? We
have to wait, wait, wait until such times
as Great Britain brings them in, and
then when they are brought in in Great
Britain they are brought in here with a
flourish of trumpets.
One of the things that struck me to-day
was the statement made by the acting
Prime Minister in regard to what this
country was doing for hospitals. With a
flourish of trumpets he mentioned all the
great things the Government had done
for hospitals.
What are the terrible
conditions that prevail in agricultural
areas in regard to hospital accommodation? I think it is true to say that in
Belfast it is absolutely terrible. I am
afraid the right hon. Gentleman the acting
Prime Minister has nothing to be proud
of. In Belfast to-day you have from a
thousand to two thousand people dying
of terrible diseases. Day in and day out
these people are lying at home suffering
untold agonies too horrible for me to
describe. No one can describe the tortures these poor people go through in
their own homes. I think, therefore, you
will agree that the acting Prime Minister
has nothing to be proud about.
Would the acting Prime Minister tell
this House whether anything has been
done by this Government to increase the
number of beds at the Royal Victoria
Hospital? Has anything been done to
increase the number of beds at the
Children's Hospital? I know that every
one of the present Members of this Parliament, except about one, is anxious to do
something for anyone smitten with any
disease of any kind, but I feel there is
nothing to be proud of. I would have
felt proud if the acting Prime Minister
had meant that in future no one would
be on the waiting list who had been
ordered to go into hospital. That is not
So. The Government of this country are
not so anxious as the Free State Government is-

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
THE KING'S SPEECH.
Debate on the Address.
SECOND DAY.
Order read for resuming adjourned
debate on Question (23rd November).
"That an Humble Address be presented to His Grace, the Governor of
Northern Ireland as follows": :-
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to offer our humble thanks
to Your Grace for the speech which
Your Grace has addressed to both
Houses of Parliament.-(Major Robinson).
Question again proposed.
Mr. GAMBLE: In rising to support
the Motion before the House I would
like to offer my congratulations in the
first place to the hon. and gallant Member for Larne who proposed the Motion
and also to the hon. Member for Ballynafeigh, who seconded, for the able manner
in which they performed this, to them
I am sure, pleasing duty, and the way
they upheld the traditions
traditions of this
honourable House. I would like to say
also that although I was not present at
the State opening I was pleased to hear
that our Leader, Lord Craigavon, was
present in health and strength. I hope
he will soon be restored and be able to
take his place here as formerly.
The year 1937 has been a notable year
generally to the British Empire on
account of the Coronation of His
Gracious Majesty King George VI and
to Northern Ireland in particular on
account of the Royal visit that took
place here in July. I am sure the expressions of loyalty and devotion to the
Throne that were shown to Their
Majesties on their visit to Belfast in
July will warm their hearts to the
strength of the loyalty and devotion that
Northern Ireland citizens bear to the
Throne. The King's Gracious Speech goes
on to say that although the amount of improvement in trade and employment has
not been shown so much in Northern
Ireland as in Great Britain, yet I think
there is a considerable improvement in
trade here as shown by the number of
persons insured under the Unemploy
ment Acts that have been taken into
employment and the unemployment
register being reduced by a number up
to 7,000.
Much has been said for works of public
utility promoted since the increased
grant in February last-works which go up
to figures between £400,000 and £500,000,
and I think this shows that our Government have been trying to do what they
can to relieve unemployment and to increase the prosperity of the Province.
There are many things which tend to
lead to that. We have in the linen
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
24 NOVEMBER 1937
trade some disturbing factors at the
present moment, although that trade
has been carried on and greater activity
has been shown in it, not during the
past few years, but in the period before.
that time. Since then international
affairs have somewhat upset the linen
trade. I hope these things will soon be
removed and that the linen trade will
again enjoy the prosperity it had before.
Speaking of the linen trade, I
would also like to mention that
I hope the Minister of Agriculture, in
conjunction with the Minister of
Finance, will be able to see his way to
do something for the growth and production of flax in Northern Ireland. I
think flax is one of the vital necessities
for the linen trade, and it is one of the
crops that give employment to a great
number of people, both agricultural
workers and textile workers as well. I
hope this will be fostered to the greatest
extent possible.
I see that in the programme for the
session on which we are entered there are
measures for the improvement of factory
and workshop conditions. I am sure all
of us in this House will welcome an improvement in the conditions of factory
and workshop workers. An amendment
of the Blind Persons Act is also another
subject mentioned. I feel there will not
be a dissentient voice in any improvement we can make in the Blind Persons
Act. We all sympathise with their condition and think they should not be
allowed to depend on the generosity of
any persons, but should be looked after
by the State. The Labourers Acts are
being used throughout the various rural
districts. As many as 24 rural districts
are proceeding with schemes for the
erection of almost 4,000 labourers' cottages. I hope this thing will go on
because I think that after all what
tends to make a contented people is good
housing, houses that are hygienic and
can be let at an economic rent. These
conditions should be fulfilled in the near
future.
Agriculture is the industry which I
suppose I might say I know most about.
Of some other things I am inclined to
talk about I may not know so much.
But in the farming industry I believe
there is a gradual improvement in conditions. There are 170,000 persons
employed in that industry, and it is
not one we can look over lightly, because,
after all, a good deal depends on the
prosperity of the people on the land. If
the people on the land go down I am
afraid the people in the cities will go
down along with them. The most ought
to be made out of these measures for the
improvement of conditions amongst the
agricultural community. I am glad to
know that many people have taken
advantage of the land fertility scheme.
and lime and slag, which are now being
subsidised to a certain extent, are being
purchased in large quantities.
Whilst on that I would also like to
draw the attention of the Minister of
Agriculture and, again, I suppose I
must appeal to the Minister of Finance
-to the land improvement scheme. I
think the valuation is now £75 and anything above that would not qualify for
the land improvement grant. I would
like to see every acre in Northern Ireland, instead of being waste and growing
rushes and whins, made into arable land,
providing cheaper food for the people of
Northern Ireland to consume. If he
could see his way either to remove the
valuation restriction altogether or to increase the limit to such an extent that
it would bring in the larger farmers,
who are the greatest employers of labour,
it would be a good thing. It is a great
benefit to those under £75 valuation,
but we find the people under £75 in
many cases are people who work within
themselves and do not relieve the unemployment question by getting
scheme through and employing agricultural labourers. I believe this money
would be well spent, and if the Minister
of Agriculture could see his way to remove the bar great advantage would be
taken of it, and it would be a benefit
to Northern Ireland.
a
The oat and barley subsidy has also
given a fillip to the industry in Northern
Ireland. I think that people are doing
their utmost to take advantage of all
these Measures that have been promoted
for their benefit. There is just another
point that has been brought to my
notice, and that is as to the loans for
the building of hay sheds and other farm
buildings. It has been pointed out that
these loans that are granted are for very
short terms and that the conditions are
very hard. It appears that a man
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gamble]
requires to get two solvent sureties and
has to go through a good deal of what
the ordinary man thinks is unnecessary
formality before getting the loan seeing
that he can get the money as cheaply
from any bank or any other place with
the same security. That does not seem
to show that our Government are holding out a helping hand to enable farmers
to improve their premises in this way.
Then there is the matter of the improvement of old houses on the lands. This,
I am sure, has been mentioned before
in the House. I think if these buildings could be reconditioned by means of
a loan at a cheaper rate than the money
could be got ordinarily it would be a
step in the right direction. It would
help our farming community not only
to have better houses but to be a happier
and more contented lot.
Farmers are sometimes blamed for
being discontented. I think they have a
great deal to grumble at. There is one
thing that they are always bothered
with that does not bother other people,
and that is the climatic conditions.
Farmers are up against the weather.
We can see some of our year's work pass
away quickly from us as the commodities
are perishable. Then, again, we are
bothered sometimes with no stability of
market. Through the operation of our
marketing schemes there is a tendency
now to produce more stuff. The production
of pigs, eggs, milk, and other commodities
has gone up, showing that the people of
the country have confidence in the
Government. They believe the Government are doing their best for them and
that these marketing schemes are for
the betterment of the country. I believe
that if a plebiscite of the farming community were taken it would show that
they would not go back again to the old
days when many perishable commodities
were left in their hands.
Mr. NIXON: The first thing I would
like to say is that I was very glad to
shake hands with the Prime Minister
here at the opening of Parliament. I
was very glad indeed-and I say this
sincerely-to see him so far recovered as
to be able to come here. I would say
the same about any Member no matter
where he sits, because there is one thing
I do not like and that is to see a man
ill. Before proceeding to my Amendment may I be permitted to say that I
regret that the Attorney-General's hint
about the word "Ulster" is not mentioned in the King's Speech. Northern
Ireland is mentioned, but not Ulster.
The Speech is more remarkable for
quantity than quality. I want to congratulate the Mover of the Address, the
Member for Larne. I have not had the
privilege of knowing him very long. I
endorse everything he said about His
Gracious Majesty and the attachment of
the great majority of the people of
Northern Ireland to the Throne. There
is no constituency in Northern Ireland
where the people are more attached to
the Throne than Woodvale, which I have
the honour to represent. Furthermore,
there is hardly a family in Woodvale
that had not one or more representatives
in the Great War. They are all intensely
loyal. As their representative I am the
same and have a right to be. I am sorry
that the hon. and gallant Member who
was a soldier himself, and yesterday wore
his decorations, which I was proud to see
-I could wear a few myself which a
good many on that side could not do-I
am sorry that he had not anything to
say about
the ex-King, the Duke of
Windsor. We were all thrilled when he
came here as Prince of Wales and stayed
several days with us. We were more
thrilled when he beat "Dolly's Brae" on
the big drum at Hillsborough. That
drum was photographed and sent to
Canada. We did not hear much about
that recently; it is forgotten.
As to the hon. Member who seconded
the Address, he is an old friend. Every
thing that the words decency and
respectability could convey apply to him.
I do not admire him so much as a
politician of course. I knew him in 1926
when he entered the Corporation as a
councillor for the Cromac Ward. He
represented the ward until 1929. In
that year the association had so much
confidence in him that they nominated
him again, but the outcry about the
housing scandal was active and he renounced the nomination. He left the
Council but sailed in again for Ormeau
when the clouds rolled away. He made a
good member of the Council from that
day forward. In his speech he talked
about law and order-

Mr. NIXON: I accept the statement

It is common ground that owing to

is a common accepted ground between

us and nobody will contradict it. I submit that if there is always going to be
unemployment it would be better to give
the older people something they could
live on in some sort of a reasonable way;
let them retire from industry, and let
them be the unemployed people instead
of the younger people.
The point was made when this question
was debated the last time-would I compel the older people to retire at £1 per
week? I answered that in this way-if
you make the pension £1 a week I will
answer that right away now. I would
give no man who is working a pension.
If he did not elect to retire he would not
get his pension. There is no pensioner,
whether civil servant, teacher, policeman,
postman, or any other man,
gets his pension and his work. I do not want to be
misunderstood. Sometimes a man is permitted to serve longer than the allotted
span, but he will not get his pension.
There is always the inducement that if
he retires he will get it. On that point,
I have found working people very
generous and very fair, and I am not
a bit afraid to face that part of the issue
on any platform. There may be an odd
man who would not like it. Since I
undertook this campaign numbers of
people over the specified age came to me
and told me that if they got £1 they
would not be long in industry.
Another argument is that where an
old-age pensioner has got only 10s he
has no living. I know every Member on
that side of the House agrees. I was
talking to a man some time ago. He has
nothing in the world but the 10s. His
wife died and they had no family. When
he pays for his room he has nothing left.
That is a most miserable existence. I
am satisfied that through agitation and
the bringing forward of the question the
aim of the Amendment will be achieved.
Now I come to the strong point.
Where is the money to come from? I
know these arguments will be made from
that side of the House. I know that
when 5s a week was first granted the
predecessors of the present party asked,
where will the money come from? They
said the country would be bankrupt. If
you go into the Linen Hall Library and
read the files of the "Whig," the "News-
Letter," or the "Telegraph" of that
time you will see they all made the
point that the money could not be got to
pay pensions of 5s a week. I submit this
money can be got. You will get some
of it on what you save when a man
leaves employment.
The hon. Member for Oldpark a short
time ago made a speech across the water
in which he gave an idea of where we
could get more money, and that would
be here. The speech is reported in the
"News-Letter" of 2/11/37-that is this
month. He was speaking at some
exhibition which was got up to
advertise the linen industry-a very
good cause indeed. I want the Minister of Finance to pay particular
attention to what he said, so that his
statement may be either accepted or
contradicted and that we may not be
told something else later on. The hon.
Member holds the position of Junior
Whip, and he went over as the representative of the Government. It was a
good thing for the Government to take
part in that exhibition. He said that
since Northern Ireland became a State it
has paid the entire expenses of its

Imperial liabilities no less a sum than
£25,700,000.
That statement has either to be stood
up to or contradicted, because the
practice of those on the Government side
has been to say when it suits them, "We
got the money from Britain," and when
it does not suit them they say, “We find
it ourselves." An hon. Member listening to me told me that the Imperial
Government paid for education in Northern Ireland, while another Member
listening to me told me that the Imperial
Government pays the salaries of the
Ministers. These are both ridiculous
statements and are contradicted by the
Junior Whip, who was sent over by the
Minister of Finance. I will show you
what the Minister of Finance thinks of

said, amongst other things, that the

does not like that. I thought I was only

Minister of Finance said that the Junior
Whip was a very promising young man.

Mr. ANDREWS: That is quite true.
Mr. NIXON: I was only saying you
are all promising gentlemen, but you do
not always fulfil your promises. However, I am on the Amendment now. If
the Northern Government since June,
1921, can pay the entire expenses of its
territory and contribute towards
Imperial liabilities no less a sum than

save a little of that to make people
happy. I do not begrudge what we send
over for rearmament-I made that point
here before. I think that in a small way
I helped to start that campaign owing
to what I saw in the Suez Canal in 1935.
No notice was taken of it here, but notice
was taken across the water. I am one
of the people who want rearmament more
intense than it is now. I do not want
that point made against me, but at the
same time when we can pay £25,700,000
we can do a little more for the people who
have to live on 10s a week. No one on
that side will argue that anyone can live
on that amount.
Another way in which we can save the
money is by reducing some of the big
salaries. I was talking to three women
pensioners not long ago. They were
three loyalists. Two of them would be
for the £1 a week, but the third was
not because the country would not be
able to pay for it. Yet she admitted
she was prepared to vote £100 for people
who already had too much. I said that
if that was her view she should not vote
for the increased pension and should not
take it when it came, because it was
going to come, whether she liked it or
not. If that money was granted it would
be all spent in the shops around the doors
of the people who got it. It would not
be taken out of the country, but the
shops in the neighbourhood would benefit
more or less.
This time two years ago when I was in
Queensland I investigated the pensions
question there. At that time every
widow got a pension of 17s 6d subject
to a means test; every woman when she
came to 60 got 17s 6d subject to a means
test; and every man when he attained
the age of 65 got 17s 6d, subject to a
means test. In addition their houses
were free of rates. They had to get the
benefit. The landlord could not take
credit for the rates. You will permit me
to say, though some people think
differently, that the cost of living there
is very much lower than here. There is
nothing needed for fires in Queensland-
I am not speaking of Australia generally
-and for clothing a good suit might be
a few pounds dearer, but a cotton suit
does. You would pay £1 for cotton
trousers and a black or white woollen
shirt to take the sweat. That is all a
person wants to wear. The same thing
applies to bedding.
The reason that that pension is given.
there is that the people were intelligent
enough to vote for it. There is very
little unemployment in Queensland at
the present time. I do not want you to
think that it is a country where people
can do what they like because they have
a Labour Government. They cannot.
The binmen who work for the Corporation there, which is a Labour Corporation-I do not want to make
any
comparison-when they came
house were only two in number, and they

When they come to the age of 60 and they

Mr. BYRNE: I would like to say a
few words in support of the Amendment.
I have always in this House expressed
the opinion that 10s per week is not a
sufficient pension to support anybody.
I meet these people from day to day, and
they are continually appealing to me and
asking is there no word or sign of an
increase in the pension of 10s. They
say it is impossible for a person to live
on that amount. If one has to keep up
a house, one has to pay rent. Coal has
also to be bought and there is a very
small amount left for food. If one is in
lodgings in the city it costs 4s or 5s a
week and everyone will admit that the
balance is insufficient to keep any man
or woman for seven days. I would like
that the old age pension would be increased at an early date. So much has
been said with regard to pensions that
I do not think I need add very much
to what has been said.
I was pleased to see the Minister of
Labour expressing himself in sympa.
thetic terms. I sincerely hope, if we
ourselves cannot make any advance, that
at an early date a Measure will be introduced across the water which will
increase the pensions to at least £1 a
week. Less than that sum is insufficient
to keep any man or woman. There are
people to-day who would almost rather
get nothing at all than this miserable
10s. They have the name of getting
the pension but they get no sympathy
from those outside. I knew a man who
was a dock labourer in his time. He
went out of his society and was not
eligible for getting employment at the
dock. He went round occasionally and
everyone knew he had no pension. They
knew he was in a bad state. Although
he was not entitled to work his fellow
workers generously allowed him from
week to week to earn a few shillings and
others helped him to pay his lodgings
and get the necessities of life. I met
him after he got the 10s a week and he
told me that he was worse off than when
he was before getting it. That man
went into the workhouse and died there.
Cases such as that force me to appeal
to the Government from time to time to
make some effort to increase the pensions
of these people. Something more than
at present should be given to keep them
in a sort of comfort. I would like at
the close to express my sincere sympathy
with the Amendment, and I hope that
at an early date some relief will be
given to a very deserving class of the
community.

Oral Answers to Questions.
CIVIL SERVANTS AND
BROADCAST TALKS.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he approves of high
permanent officials in the Ministry taking
part in broadcasting and other debates
on the policy of the Government in regard to the Fruit Marketing Acts, or
other questions of policy, and if so,
whether the privilege may be extended
to all civil servants, including those who
may have views on Government policy
adverse to such policy.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The broadcast address to which the hon. Member
refers is a part of the educational policy
of the Ministry. I attach the greatest
importance to officers of the Ministry
meeting as many producers as possible
and speaking to producers through the
medium of the broadcast for the purpose
of explaining our various marketing
schemes and dealing with such difficulties
as may have arisen. The second part of
the question relates to the conduct of
civil servants generally and is thus one
primarily for the Minister of Finance,
who agrees with me that the answer is
in the negative. Such action would conflict with the elementary duty of a civil
servant.
Mr. NIXON: Is it only when they
speak in favour of the policy of the Government they are to be allowed to enter
into these debates?
CULTIVATION OF FLAX.
2. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether, in view of the decreasing acreage of flax grown in Northern Ireland, he will appoint a Committee
to inquire if means can be devised to
increase the cultivation of that crop
under conditions which will give growers
a reasonable return.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The whole
question of increasing the acreage under
flax in Northern Ireland has for some
time been receiving my earnest attention
and is still under consideration. I am
glad that the hon. Member emphasises
the need for giving the growers a
reasonable return. The difficulty is how
to devise a practicable scheme under
which the producer could be given such
assurances. I do not think that the
appointment just now of a committee
such as indicated would help towards a
solution of the problem. However, I
shall keep the suggestion in mind.
Mr. MINFORD: Would the Minister
tell the House why the committee would
do any harm and not good?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The question
of flax cultivation is being considered in
England at the present moment.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister
appoint the same committee which is
dealing with the transport question?

special levies, and whether his attention

Thomas Shaw, secretary and manager of

whether it is within the spirit of the Act
that the use of funds collected on all

be invested in a factory to compete with

under bulk contracts to all Wiltshire
curers to remain in the hands of the

factories, the Pigs Marketing Board will
