Sir BASIL BROOKE: The position
in regard to the administrative fund of
the Pigs Marketing Board is, according
to the published accounts of the Board,
as stated by the hon. Member. I have
seen only the Press reports of the speech
to which the hon. Member refers and
I am unable at the moment to say to
what extent the statements attributed to
Mr. Shaw were used by him. It is,
however, incorrect and misleading to producers to state that the Board has a sum
of £150,000 available for investment or
that it has a trading profit. In fact,
my Ministry has had to require the
Board to impose a trading levy at the
present time to cover heavy losses in
trading incurred in recent months.
With regard to the powers of the
Board to invest in curing factories it is
specifically provided by paragraph 26 of
the Pigs Marketing Scheme, which was
approved by a Resolution of both Houses
of Parliament, that the Board may invest money in any business undertaking
engaged in bacon curing. Bacon curing
companies in which the Board invests
money are, however, in the same position
as any other companies trading for profit
and in the event of a trading loss being
experienced by the factory in which the
Board has invested money, I have ample
power to prevent the Board imposing a levy
on producers to cover losses incurred by
these bacon factories, and the hon. Member may rest assured that if the need
arises I shall use these powers to protect
producers. With regard to the sale of pigs
on bulk contract by the Pigs Marketing
Board to Wiltshire curers, all curers
have the option of buying pigs on direct
contract from producers or on bulk contract from the Board. I appreciate,
however, the importance of securing an
equitable distribution of pigs among
different curers, and I am prepared to
ensure that this is fulfilled.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
National Health Insurance (Juvenile
Contributors and Young
Persons) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Major SHILLINGTON: As hon.
Members know, Health Insurance is in
many respects an entity for the whole of
the United Kingdom. Half of our
insured population belongs to Societies
which operate throughout the United
Kingdom and the members in Northern
Ireland share equally in all the resources
of the Societies with their fellow members in Great Britain. In addition to
this element of common insurance there
are essential features of the Scheme respecting which the power to legislate is
vested in the Parliament of the United
Kingdom and not in our Parliament.
As an example I may refer to the Central
Fund which is under the control of the
National Health Insurance Joint Committee.
It is almost inevitable in the circumstances, and in any case highly convenient, that Health Insurance in
Northern Ireland should be operated
under an Act of the Parliament of the
United Kingdom. I
may perhaps
remind the House that in 1924 the
United Kingdom Parliament repealed
all the earlier Acts relating to National
Health Insurance passed both at Westminster and here and re-enacted them
in the Consolidating Act of 1924 Again,
when important amendments to the
Scheme were under consideration in
1929, 1932, and 1935, provision was
made in the Bills introduced at Westminster for the extension of the Measures
to Northern Ireland on provision to that
effect being made by our Parliament.
In each of those years a Bill was passed
similar in form to the present Bill,
giving His Grace the Governor power to
make an Order in Council so as to complete the application of the United
Kingdom Scheme to Northern Ireland.
Last year the enactments relating to
Health Insurance were once more consolidated, when the Acts of the Parliament of the United Kingdom and of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland were
repealed and re-enacted in the National
Health Insurance Act, 1936, which was
passed by the Parliament of the United
Kingdom. The procedure which the
107 National Health Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Major Shillington]
House is asked to authorise on this
occasion is therefore in accordance with
well-established precedent.
Copies of an explanatory memorandum and of the United Kingdom Bill
have been circulated to hon. Members. It
will be seen that provision is being made.
by Clause 8 of the United Kingdom Bill
for the extension of that Measure to
Northern Ireland, and that the Bill now
before the House is the necessary complement of that Clause.
I am sure that the object of the Bill
will commend itself to hon. Members in
all parts of the House. We have had
Medical Benefit as part of the National
Health Insurance Scheme since 1930.
It provides a general practitioner service
with the supply of all necessary medicines for the industrial population from
the age of 16 onwards. Hon. Members
are also aware that we have had for
some time a scheme of medical supervision at Public Elementary Schools
which has been of value in safeguarding
and preserving the health of the
children. There is, however, that
undesirable gap from the time a child
leaves school until contributions become
payable for him under the Insurance
Scheme. In common with my colleagues
on the National Health Insurance Joint
Committee, I am satisfied that medical
treatment should be provided for these
young persons during the critical years
between 14 and 16, and I am happy to
be able to commend to the House a Bill
which will have that effect.
It is estimated that at least 17,000
young persons will come under the
Scheme on its introduction on 4th April
next. They will be entitled to join
Approved Societies and they will be well
advised to take that course. If, however, they do not join, they will still
receive medical benefit as juvenile deposit.
contributors. The Bill does not propose to make any provision for cash
benefits to juvenile contributors. They
will not become entitled to those benefits
until they become fully insured at age
16 and qualify in the ordinary way
under the general provisions of the
Health Insurance Act of 1936. I hope,
however, that it will be possible to make
provision by Regulations for them to
receive dental benefit in certain circumstances soon after reaching the age of
16 and power to make Regulations in
this sense is given by Clause 3 of the
Westminster Bill.
As regards financial arrangements, the
cost of the proposals contained in the
Bill will be met out of the National
Health Insurance Fund in the same way
as the cost of the other benefits under
the Health Insurance Scheme, that is to
say, partly out of contributions and
partly by Exchequer Grant. The State
contribution will be on the usual basis,
namely, one-fifth of the expenditure in
the case of girls and one-seventh in the
case of boys. It is estimated that the
liability of the Exchequer will be about
£2,000 a year.
The contribution payable in respect of
an employed juvenile will be 4d. a week
divided equally between the juvenile and
the employer. It will be payable in the
usual way by stamping a card.
The charge for medical benefit on
Approved Societies ard on the Juvenile
Deposit Contributors Fund will be on
the same basis as for ordinary insured
persons; namely, 13s. a year of which
9s. will go to the doctor as capitation fee
and the remainder will be expended on
medicines, payments to doctors for mileage, and on the administration of the
medical service. In addition, Approved
Societies will receive an allowance to
meet the cost of the additional work that
will be thrown on them by the issue and
collection of contribution cards for their
new members.
I might perhaps take this opportunity
of mentioning to the House that the
doctors' capitation fee has been fixed
by a Court of Inquiry, after recent
negotiations between the Insurance Acts
Committee of the British Medical
Association and the Minister of Health
in London, and separate negotiations on
the subject have not been necessary for
Northern Ireland.
This Bill is a further extension of our
social services, and I confidently commend it to the vote of the House. I beg
to move.

I should, however, like to make it
clear that the statements which have
been made by uninformed persons that
the Government has done nothing under
the Act which was passed last Summer
are wholly unfounded. It is not possible
to deal rashly or hurriedly with

financial assistance, but hon. Members
may be assured that, subject to all
reasonable precautions, no delays are in
fact occurring.
Hon. Members will recollect that the
existing Act makes provision for assisting new industries in three ways; first,
by way of a site and rental grant,
secondly, by way of loans towards new
construction or the adaptation of
existing premises, and, thirdly, the
concession of freedom from interest on
such a loan for five years. What the
present Resolution proposes to do is to
increase the foregoing assistance in five
ways:
-

First, to make contributions towards

a provision which has a counterpart in
the British legislation dealing with the

Secondly, to widen the scope of the

example, towards expenditure on
on the
supply of machinery, or even in some
special cases where constructional costs
are low but expenses on working capital
high to enable the Ministry to make
loans towards the provision of working
capital.
Thirdly, and under this head I shall
deviate for a moment to the existing
Act; that Act only allows assistance to
be given towards a new undertaking.
From applications received, however, it
is quite clear that this scope is too
limited because there are already in
Northern Ireland certain industries in
existence which are hampered from development by lack of power to raise
money at reasonable rates for enlarging
their premises or for increasing their
turnover by raising further working
capital. It is proposed in the Bill to
widen the scope of the original Act so
as to enable loans to be made, but in
such cases the interest-free concession
will not be granted. There are, of
course, suitable safeguards in the
original Act to ensure that such extensions are not in respect of an industry
which, so to speak, may be already overstocked with factories.
Fourthly, it is necessary to enlarge the
financial provision required by reason of
the foregoing extensions, and the increase proposed is from the sum of
£200,000 to £750,000.
con-
Finally, in view of the extension of
the scope of the Act, it is possible that
the Ministry may find it more
venient to provide the necessary finance
for the loans not by means of issues from
the Consolidated Fund or from the Government Loans Fund as originally provided, but by arranging for the undertakers to borrow the money from a bank
or other source, subject to a Government
guarantee. Accordingly it is proposed by
this Resolution to seek the necessary
authority for the issue of such guarantees.
Hon. Members will, I am sure,
approve of and willingly support this
Measure, which is proposed in order to
assist in certain approved cases existing
industries and to encourage new industries to be established here. I beg to
move.

Rev. Professor CORKEY: I do not
think that this Resolution really requires

We are all prepared to endorse it. We

delivered about twelve years ago, and
had refurbished them in the form of a
Financial Resolution, in view of the
approach of a General Election.
The establishment of new industries in
Belfast is not such an easy matter.
Although, of course, demands have been
made in general terms that the Government should take measures to establish
new industries, I have not heard any
concrete proposals from Members of the
Opposition, or from persons outside this
House, that would compare with the proposals in this Resolution. The Imperial
Government have a first claim on the
taxes of this country. They watch us in
our disposal of those taxes, and consequently a good deal of specialised knowledge and ingenuity are required on the
part of those who understand things to
devise methods for the encouragement of
new industries which will not be called in
question by the Imperial authorities, and
in the carrying out of which they will
not charge us with acting ultra vires.
While suggestions have been made for
new industries, the Government have
been very wise in devising ways and
means whereby these industries might be
encouraged. I think there is a certain
amount of reasonableness in this policy
of subsidising the establishment of new
industries in Northern Ireland even to
the extent of remitting income tax, and
for this reason: it is a well-known fact
that the savings of industry find their
way into new industries, and if in Northern Ireland new industries are not
being established it is an obvious fact
that money is not being invested in
Northern Ireland, and that therefore the
savings that accrue from the profits of
industry are being exported. Therefore
I think the Government are justified in
taking steps to have new industries
started in their midst. While the
establishment of these new industries will
be a charge upon the Exchequer, there
will be savings in other directions. As
I said before, the Resolution really needs
no support from anyone in any part of
the House; we are all in favour of it.

Mr. BYRNE: I strongly support this

to create employment in Belfast
Ulster has always had my wholehearted

unemployed. The Minister of Finance
has stated that this is the third attempt
the Government have made in this
direction. We all regret that the two
previous attempts have not done very
much for the city, and it is my earnest
desire that this attempt will be more
successful, and will be the means of
attracting new industries to this area.
I sincerely hope that it will lead to employment for the thousands of people
who to-day are in a very bad state.
New industries should get every encouragement, with the object of absorbing into industry the large number of
persons who are unemployed. From day
to day I meet large numbers of these
people in the streets; they are appealing
for work and assistance. There is no
denying the fact that to-day hundreds of
people are in a very bad way. Any
assistance they get is insufficient to support them. The average amount of
relief or assistance that these people
receive is about 4s per week. I have
great pity for them, and that is one of
the reasons why I heartily support this
Resolution. We should try to keep all
the work possible in our own city. It

buses must be built outside this area

here as in any part of the world. To
get employment large numbers of our
people have to go across the water. Is it

here?
We are sending hundreds of pounds'

should try to keep as much of that work

and buses. The Belfast Corporation are
tied down in regard to contracts. I

RATES ON SMALL TENEMENTS.
1. Mr. NIXON (for Mr. Henderson)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he is aware of the difficulty met
with in the collection of rates on small
tenements due to local authorities failing
to adopt sub-section 3 of Section 17 of
the Local Government Act (Northern
Ireland), 1934, and whether he is prepared to amend the law so that landlords must pay the rates and charge an
inclusive rent, thus relieving the tenants
by spreading the rates over 52 payments
instead of two as at present.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Davison): I am
not aware that any special difficulties
have been experienced in the collection of
rates on hereditaments of low valuation.
But if there have in fact been any such
difficulties, the local authority concerned
has in its own hands the remedy provided
for in the section to which the hon.
Member refers.
I can, therefore, see no reason for any
amendment of the law.

Mr. DAVISON: The facts stated in

the Ministry is aware, no complaints

if they are dissatisfied it is open to them

hours a day is a scandalously long time

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Major
Shillington): As the hon. Member is no
doubt aware, it is the duty of Boards of
Guardians, when assessing the amount of
allowances to be paid to individual applicants, to take into consideration

cost of maintenance, and periodically to
review the allowances granted in the
light of all relevant factors, including
the cost of living.

allowances, I understand that the Unemployment Assistance Board is following
the practice of the British Board by
using its special powers to make increases
in allowances where hardship might be
created owing to the rise in the cost of
living. In view of this position I am not
prepared to adopt the hon. Member's

an all-round increase of 25 per cent. on

Order for Second Reading read.
The
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The reception accorded.
by hon. Members on all sides of the
House on Thursday last to the Resolution
dealing with the financial provisions of
this Measure makes it unnecessary for
me to claim the indulgence of the House
in inviting it, after so short an interval,
to give a Second Reading to yet another
Bill providing facilities for the attraction
of industries to Northern Ireland.
need for a widening of the basis of our
industrial life is generally admitted, and,
both inside and outside this House, the
difficulties associated with the problem
have been widely discussed. Hon. Members will recall that in the 1932 Actour first effort of the kind-the safeguarding of the rights of existing undertakings was a cardinal feature. The Act
passed in July last was much wider in
scope and the experience gained in its
working so far has shown that its
facilities can be made available over a
much wider industrial field without
jeopardising existing undertakings.
Moreover, we cannot overlook the fact
that inducements to industrialists to
locate factories in areas of severe unemployment in Great Britain have been
considerably increased during the current
year.
Hon. Members will recollect that the
Act passed in July last made provision
for affording financial assistance in the
form of grants and loans to persons who,
during the currency of the Act, proposed
to establish in Northern Ireland an industrial undertaking which was likely to
provide and maintain additional employment to a substantial extent. Under
that Act grants were made available in
respect of the site on which the undertaking was established as well as in
respect of existing buildings leased by
the applicant for the purposes of the
undertaking. A grant in respect of
either a site or a building takes the form
of annual payments over, in the case of a
site, a maximum period of twenty years,
and in the case of a building, a maximum
period of five years.
Loans were made available in similar
circumstances in respect of buildings that
were either purchased outright by the
New Industries Bill-
Second Reading
30 NOVEMBER 1937
applicant or were built to his Own
requirements for the purposes of the
undertaking. A loan can also be made in
respect of any expenditure which an
applicant incurs in adapting to his own
requirements an existing building which
he has either leased or purchased for the
purposes of the undertaking. These
loans, hon. Members will remember, are
free of interest during an initial period
of five years, after which they are repayable with concurrent interest over
period to be fixed by the Ministry of
Finance in accordance with the circumstances of each individual case.
a
com-
The Measure now before the House is
designed to permit of additional financial
facilities being granted not only in respect
of undertakings which the applicant proposes to establish, but also in respect of
extensions which the applicant proposes
to effect during the currency of the
existing New Industries (Development)
Act. These additional facilities
prise grants in respect of any income.
tax which a new undertaking may be
called upon to pay during the first five
years of its existence, and loans or guarantees in respect of the funds which an
approved applicant may require to raise
to enable him to establish the proposed
undertaking. Under the existing Act
an applicant is not permitted to avail
himself simultaneously of assistance
under the New Industries (Development)
Act and the Loans Guarantee Acts,
except to the extent that a grant under
the former in respect of a site does not
debar him from participating in the
benefits available under the Loans Guarantee Acts. With the additional
assistance which is now proposed, however, it will be possible for an applicant
to receive either a grant or a loan in
respect of the buildings as well as a loan
or a guarantee covering principal and
interest towards the outlay which he
expects to incur in providing equipment
and other necessities. Here, however, a
distinction falls to be drawn. Loans in
respect of buildings, as I have already
explained, are free of interest for the
initial period of five years. The loans.
which are now proposed in respect of
equipment and other essentials apart from
buildings will be subject to interest during the five years initial period and
thereafter repayable with concurrent
interest in the same way as loans granted
in respect of buildings.
As I have already pointed out, the
existing Act makes no provision for
assisting those who contemplate the
extension of an existing, as distinct from
the establishment of a new, undertaking.
It is considered that this is an omission
which might prevent enterprise among
existing industrialists in cases where,
from an employment point of view, the
results would be as favourable as those
which would be expected from the
establishment of an undertaking that
was new. It is, therefore, proposed to
extend the new loans facilities to extensions of existing undertakings which
fulfil the statutory requirements in the
matter of additional employment. In
other words, a person who proposes to
extend an existing industrial undertaking and who satisfies the competent
Ministry that by doing so he is likely
to provide and maintain additional
employment to a substantial extent will
be eligible to receive either a loan or a
guarantee in respect of the capital
requirements of the undertaking.
a
The existing Act made available
maximum sum of £200,000 by way of
loans. This sum would obviously be
insufficient to cover the additional facilities now proposed. Accordingly, provision for the larger sum of £750,000
is now being made for this purpose.
Immediately after the passing of the
existing Act in July last, steps were
taken to make its provisions known not
only throughout Northern Ireland, but
in Great Britain, the Dominions and
certain foreign countries. The aggregate facilities now envisaged cannot be
too widely known, and hon. Members
may rest assured that fresh steps will be
taken to ensure this without delay.
With this end in view I have already
conferred with leading industrialists and
representatives of the public life of the
Province, and, as a result, I am securing
the co-operation of an advisory bodv
which will be known as the Ulster
Development Council, and which will
assist in devising the most effective steps
necessary to make Ulster's industrial
position and the facilities we have to offer
more widely known.
I am sure that it is the earnest hope
of every Member of this House that the
measures which I have outlined and the
efforts to make them effective may be
crowned with success. I beg to move.

Mr. BARBOUR: The first two items
in the Supplementary Estimate. now
before this Committee relate to the
Lagan Navigation, which, as hon. Members will be aware, connects Belfast
Harbour with Lough Neagh. As far
back as 1753 work was commenced on the
task of making the River Lagan navigable and extending it by means of a
canal, and for many years since that
date the navigation has fulfilled a threefold function, first, by providing a
navigable waterway from Belfast to
Lough Neagh which provides a link with
the Tyrone navigation or Coalisland
Canal and the Upper and Lower Bann
navigations; secondly, by
by providing
water supply for a number of mills and
factories situated in the Lagan valley;
and thirdly, by facilitating the drainage
of the area through which it flows.
Its first function, namely, the provision
of a navigable waterway, from which its
revenue is principally derived,
has
become far less profitable in recent years
as a result of the competition from road
and rail traffic. In consequence, the company which carries on the navigation has
now reached the end of its financial
resources and, without some form of
assistance, is likely to be forced to
abandon the undertaking. Whatever
view is taken of the merits of water
transport, hon. Members will, I am sure,
realise that the abandonment of the
navigation would give rise to serious difficulties in respect of the drainage of the
Lagan valley and the water rights
enjoyed by the various mills and factories
situated in that area. The difficulties
which might thus arise could not be overlooked by the Government, especially as
we are advised that upon abandonment
the undertaking would revert to the
Ministry of Finance as successors to the
Commissioners of Public Works, and my
Ministry is at present engaged in investigating the various aspects of this
problem. In order to facilitate its
investigations, the Government considered it necessary to obtain an
independent survey of the condition of
the navigation, and accordingly a report
was obtained at a cost of two hundred
and fifty guineas from a firm of consulting engineers.
Hon. Members will realise that investigations of this kind, involving
complicated technical and legal considerations, cannot be completed in a
short time. The condition of the navigation, however, is such that, unless certain
essential works of major repair are
immediately undertaken, there is an
imminent danger of a section of the
waterway being drained and considerable
expense would be necessary to restore the
navigation. Hon. Members may have
observed from Press reports that certain
defects in the bank of the canalised portion of the river manifested themselves
recently and urgent action was necessary
to prevent the damage from extending.
As I have explained to hon. Members,
the company is not in a position to meet
such expenditure, and the authority of
the Committee is accordingly sought to a
grant in aid of £1,500 to enable the company to proceed immediately with the
essential work of repair. This step will
not in any way prejudge the major question of the continuance of the navigation
which, as I have explained, is now being
investigated.

The question for the House this afternoon is not whether there shall be an
Agricultural Wages Board, because
that is settled, but whether we are going
to vote for its immediate establishment
or not. This question must ultimately
be a matter of tactics. I always take
my advice from people who work in the
industry concerned. If I had the full
power to do so I would put the thing
into operation right away, but, having
regard to all the interests, I would be
very considerably influenced in my
attitude by what the Minister may say
in reply, having in mind all the factors,
and especially the rights of those who
are engaged in this industry.
This question has been debated time
and time again in the North of Ireland.
Trade Union organisations have done
their best by negotiation, good feeling,
and conciliation to improve conditions,
and they have succeeded in some districts. We want to see their work
crowned by the establishment of a Board
on which all ends of the industry will
be represented, and from which we will
attempt to bring into the lives of agricultural workers in Northern Ireland
some of that joy and leisure which is at
present enjoyed by agricultural workers
across the water. In Great Britain the
minimum wage is about 32s. 6d. or 33s.
a week for a 48 hour week in the winter,
and 50 hours in the
summer, with a
regulated working day and provision for
the payment of overtime. Those facts
will indicate to you beyond doubt that
the operation of the Board on the other
side of the water has brought some rest
and some joy and hope into the lives of
the agricultural workers there. We
want to see our agricultural workers in
Northern Ireland placed on the same
plane as the agricultural workers in
Great Britain. We ask nothing revolutionary, nothing unreasonable.
We are not trying to hold the industry
up to ransom. We believe these things
can be done and will be done, and as we
have had a declaration that they are now
inevitable I await the Minister's reply
as to when they will be done. That will
mark the culmination of four years' work
on my part in this great cause, and when
it is finally accomplished I shall have the
satisfaction of knowing that I played my
part in my day and generation to bring
it about. I now await with interest a
pronouncement by the Minister as to the
earliest date on which the Board will be

along lines of reason and common sense
and not out of spite or bad temper or

Sir BASIL BROOKE: Many of the

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I will not

have got a very large acreage held by each

Ireland we have 40
per cent. more
farmers than in the whole of Scotland. I

There are very many labourers in the hon.
Member's constituency who are earning a

We have other difficulties which do not
exist in England. You have a system in
certain counties-I know it exists in my
own county and two or three others as
well-and that is a system of herds where
a man is given a house to look after an
area of land.
He has the privilege of
living in that house, and he herds the
cattle on these fields. He works in his
Own garden. He produces his own
potatoes and herding is not a very
onerous duty. The herd is quite satisfied.
He has got his own house, and he also
works in his own garden, but he gets no

Mr. HENDERSON: Slaves do that.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: They are perfectly satisfied. The man has a little
money of his own. He has a house and

else's farm. It is the system. It is not

have a system of hiring fairs which do not
exist in England. I think it does, perhaps, exist in Scotland. Hon. Members
may not be aware of it. Labourers stand
in these fairs and the farmer bargains

The
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): On behalf of
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Labour. I am sure my hon. and learned
Friend is aware that grants of 75 per
cent. of wages cost are available for

Road and Railway Transport Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: This is a short
Bill introduced to make good the
omission in the Road and
Road and Railway
Transport Act (Northern Ireland), 1935,
of the usual provision in legislation of
the kind dealing with interest on capital
money during the development period.
The provisions which the Bill proposes
to add to the Act are in no way new or
novel, and a typical precedent will be
found in the Northern Ireland Electricity Act dealing with the same matter.
Road and Railway Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Normally, interest on capital is payable out of revenue, but in connection
with newly formed undertakings, similar
to that of the Board, the initial years
are a period of organisation and development in which the full earning power
of the concern is built up, and during
which period revenue is not always
sufficient to meet interest charges in full.
Hon. Members will, no doubt, recollect
that it was three years before the
Electricity Board was in a position to
show a profit.
Hon. Members will remember that
transport stock is issued by the Board
as part consideration for undertakings
transferred to it, and that it may also be
issued as a means of raising money
needed for capital expenditure.
So far transport stock has been issued
only as part consideration for transferred
undertakings, the money required for
capital expenditure
expenditure being borrowed
under the temporary borrowing powers
conferred on the Board by Section 20 of
the Act, the loans being guaranteed by
the Government under Section 21.
As hon. Members are aware, the
undertaking of the Board was formed
by the amalgamation of a number of
road transport undertakings, most of
which were small in size, were scattered
throughout the Province, and were
inefficiently organised.
The acquisition and amalgamation of
these numerous undertakings has been
a very protracted business which it was
not possible to complete until three
months ago, and which is being followed
by a complete reorganisation of services.
The economies which should result
from such an amalgamation must, therefore, be effected gradually so that the
minimum of disturbance and inconvenience will be occasioned to the public.
Economies have been, and are being,
effected on an extensive scale, and are
being reflected increasingly in the
Board's trading results, but some further
time must elapse before their full effect
can be felt.
Hon. Members will remember that the
traffic receipts of the Board and of the
Railway Companies are to be pooled,
and that the pooled receipts are to be
divided between the Board and the Railway Companies in the proportions as set
out in the Act.
The preparation of the pooling scheme
has been a matter of great difficulty,
but I understand that the task has been
completed and that the scheme will be
submitted at an early date to the Transport Appeal Tribunal for confirmation.
The difficulties and delay attending
the preparation of the pooling scheme
have necessarily prevented the completion of the preparation of the Board's
accounts for the first year of its operation, and, therefore, it has not been
possible to ascertain definitely the
results of that year's working.
It is, however, expected that the
accounts for that year, that is, to the
30th September, 1936, will be ready for
publication before the 1st day of
January, and will disclose that the
revenue for the year was sufficient, or
was nearly sufficient, to meet the
interest charges.
It is not possible to ascertain definitely
whether or not the revenue was sufficient
until the pooling scheme has been
applied fully to the results as it is from
the Board's share of the pooled receipts
that interest and the Board's general
charges are payable.
Although they were unable to ascertain definitely the result of that year's
working the Board, appreciating the
importance of avoiding any delay in the
payment of interest, has paid the interest
on the stock for the year. Members will
appreciate that holders of the stock of a
public board naturally rely on prompt
payment of the interest to meet their
obligations.
Doubts have been raised as to the
legality of such payment, and it is
possible that, in so far as interest on the
stock is not paid out of revenue, the
payment was not authorised by the provisions of the Road and Railway Transport Act.
With regard to the operations of the
second year, which ended on the 30th
September last, and during which period
the acquisition of goods undertakings was
carried out at an intensive rate, I am
informed that the Board anticipate that
it will not be possible to pay out of
revenue either the interest on the stock,
which falls due to be paid on the 1st
January next, or the interest due on its
borrowings.
As I have mentioned already, transport stock has been issued only as part
201 Road and Railway Bill-
1 DECEMBER 1937

Second Reading
consideration for undertakings transferred to the Board, and I feel sure that
hon. Members will agree that it would
be unjust to the holders of that Stock
if payment of interest were deferred even
temporarily. It will, of course, be
appreciated that interest on transport
stock is cumulative.
It is, therefore, desirable that the
doubts I have already mentioned as to

Adjournment.
UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
SCHEMES.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.'
(Mr. Gordon).
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Minister of Home Affairs and the
Minister of Labour if any attention has
been paid to the question asked by the
hon. and learned Member for Central in
regard to finding work for the 70,000
unemployed. Has the right hon.
Gentleman considered making representations to the Northern Ireland
Transport Board to retain the 36 buses
in Northern Ireland? If not, why not?
If the cost of the building of these buses
in Northern Ireland is from £6 to £10
more than across the water could the
Government not make a 2 per cent. or
5 per cent. allowance? The question
was not answered; instead a smoke screen
was thrown over it. The Parliamentary
Secretary quoted a number of cases
which nobody in this House ever heard
of or is likely to hear of, and the winter
is on us now. The 70,000 are still unemployed and I presume will be
unemployed until the spring when the
seasonal occupations will absorb a number of them.
The sooner the Government take the
unemployment situation into consideration the better. They are endeavouring
to make provision of a kind in the New
Industries Act, but the sooner they make
provision to get some work such as the
widening of the Holywood Arches, the
widening of the Upper Newtownards
Road, and the making of Dee Street
safe for the residents of that area the
better. The sooner they make representations to the local authorities to
carry out useful work the sooner they
will come to the time when at least
10,000 will be taken away from the
unemployed.
I was surprised when I heard the
answer given to the question of the Member for Central, because it is an answer
I have heard given for some years. It
made me think that the Parliamentary
Secretary, in the absence of his chief,
had gone to the files of the Ministry and
taken out a file that was in use four years
ago, because the answer reminded me of
one given four years ago. It certainly
did not refer to the question on the
Order Paper to-day. Christmas is
approaching, and we have got all these
unemployed with us. Yet there is no
hope for them before Christmas, and
there is very little hope of them getting
any additional benefits before Christmas,
although the unemployed in England and
Wales will receive them.
All I have to say to the Government is
this: that the sooner the people of Northern Ireland are allowed to make a
further decision in regard to their representation in this House the better. The
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Labour smiles.
Mr. GORDON: Of course I do.
Mr. BEATTIE: Elections are no
bogey to me. I am not afraid of any
election. I am like the hon. and learned
Member for Central. I come here for
service, not for publicity. Nor do I come
here as one man, because I know that if
I did I could achieve nothing. I come
here to assist each and every Member of
the House to do some useful service on
behalf of the people. So far as the Government side of the House is concerned
I have failed to get any support for my
useful suggestions. If I leave the House
early next year I shall not be able to
say that I, and I only, have done this
or that, that I alone was responsible for
having something established. I will not
be able to use that "I" so well as others,
but one thing I will be able to say is
that I served those who returned me
faithfully and well and without fee or
reward.
Two hours could be usefully spent this
afternoon in trying to devise ways and
means to give the unemployed some assistance before Christmas to tide them over
that time of the year when we are all
thinking of our homes and of the
children. Many homes will be denied.
the right to participate in those joyous
greetings, due to the failure of the Government to provide work or adequate
assistance for the breadwinner of the
home.

May I say in conclusion that the hon.
Member seems to think that we are
not active enough in this House in
endeavouring to help the unemployed
and our people who are suffering in
various ways? Why, we spent the
greater part of last Session in connection
with matters to help our people, and
we have spent almost all of this Session
in endeavouring to assist them. Our
New Industries Bill is an example. It
is hoped and expected that that Bill will
be effective and will result in the
establishment of new industries in
Northern Ireland. That is what we all
want, and that is the only solution, in
my opinion, of the unemployment
problem. As I have said before, we
cannot compel British citizens to come
here and establish new industries, but
what we can do is give them large
inducements to do so, and that in this
Measure and in other ways I maintain
that we have done. We all want to help
our unemployed. Why should we not?
The difference between the Government
and the Opposition is this-we look at
the facts as they are; hon. Members
opposite, I venture to say, do not.
They desire to place the whole responsibility for unemployment in Northern
Ireland on the Government of Northern
Ireland. They cannot reasonably or
fairly do so, I maintain, because they
know as well as I do that a great deal
of the unemployment that we suffer from
is not caused by local conditions or local
circumstances, but is caused by international conditions over which we have no
control.

Oral Answers to Questions.
EMBROIDERY OUT-WORKERS'
WAGES.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware of the conditions under which many embroidery
out-workers carry on their occupations;
whether it is a fact that the average price
for this work is about 2d per hour, in
some cases falling as low as 1d per hour;
whether the work is distributed in many
cases by shopkeepers from whom workers
are obliged to purchase goods or suffer
loss of work, and whether he will take
steps to have the whole matter investigated with a view to ensuring that a
decent wage will be paid and that the
pernicious practice indulged in by shopkeepers will be prohibited.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Major
Shillington): As the hon. Member is
aware wages in this trade are subject to a
statutory minimum fixed by the Linen
and Cotton Embroidery Trade Board.
The rates quoted in the question are considerably less than the minimum rates
so fixed, and if the hon. Member can
furnish me with particulars of the cases
he has in mind I shall have them investigated without delay.
As regards the latter part of the question, if the hon. Member has any
evidence to prove that the provisions of
the Truck Acts are not being observed,
I shall also arrange to have this matter
investigated.
WORKING CONDITIONS IN THE
CINEMA INDUSTRY.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he will set up an
inquiry into the employment of workers
in the Cinema Industry in Northern Ireland to investigate the working conditions and wages paid, whether he is
aware that a similar inquiry is being held
in Great Britain.
Major SHILLINGTON: I am aware
that the Imperial Ministry of Labour is
conducting an inquiry into the wages and
conditions in the Cinema Industry and
I have already taken steps to institute a
similar inquiry here.

paper

on £10 16s 8d; whether he is aware that

Those of us who are brought into contact with this question believe that many
of these people who are brought into the
institution are well cared for, receiving
the proper kind of treatment, under the
proper kind of supervision, and then at
a certain stage they go back to the conditions they lived under before. This
plunges them right back with all convenient speed into the full deadly scope
of the disease itself with the inevitable
result that they die far too speedily.
Their life is not prolonged at all. The
disease is not eradicated. No constructive attempt has been made by a COordinated after-care policy to place the
conditions of these people in the proper

perspective so far as the municipality

It is alleged, and I believe with some
degree of truth, that when these people
come out of the institution they frequently go back to home conditions not
satisfactory in themselves, and the standard they are in receipt of is made up
to the outdoor relief standard. I am
sure the Minister will be the first to

is not sufficient to give these people the
standard of sustenance that thev
require, having regard to the ravages of
the disease. As a matter of fact a case
could be made out for the proposal
that instead of going back to the
normal economic conditions that prevailed before these people went into
the institution they should be put on a
higher scale of income than previously.
Without that higher standard of income
and a well thought out co-ordinated
scheme of after-care treatment, these
people do not stand an earthly chance
of escaping from the fell clutch of the
disease.
I have had representations made to me,
and I am sure other members must have

that there are many patients in the city

Sir DAWSON BATES: May I first of
all say that I am exceedingly glad that
my hon. Friend opposite has raised this
point. A great deal of misunderstanding
has arisen in regard to the so-called
delay in finding a site for a tuberculosis
hospital. Personally, I and my staff
have been considering this matter very
carefully, and may I say that the fact
that there is no site definitely fixed is
not the fault of the Government nor is
it the fault of the authority of which
the hon. Member is also a member.
Some time ago three sites were presented
to the Government for their views, and
to show the divergence of opinion that
existed I would point out that the price
of one site was approximately £15,000
another was
or £16,000, the price of
£80,000, and, as far as I can remember,
the price of a third site was something
like £10,000. That will indicate the
extreme divergence of opinion there was.
་
The object of the Government is, as
far as possible, to ensure that the best
site can be found for this hospital,
because, after all, we have to look 50,
or 60, or 100 years ahead, and we want
to take no hasty action. In fixing a site
there are other matters that have to be
considered. There is the type of the
ground, and there are the facilities for
persons to visit children and friends who
unhappily have to go to the institution.
I want now to say perfectly frankly
that as Minister of Home Affairs I am
not prepared to sanction the payment of
building site value for a site for this
hospital. I believe it is quite possible to
get a suitable site. I had to turn down
the three proposals that were made in
the hope that better sites would be forthcoming. I may add that none of the sites
put up to the Ministry were approved
by the Belfast Corporation's own technical officers, and I hope on the matter
being referred to the Corporation they
will, on further investigation, be able to
get a site which will fulfil what is
wanted.

What we all want is the best site that
will be available. There is no use going
miles into the country. There is a
general prejudice amongst parents in
regard to the taking of their infant
children during the incipient stages into
an institution. We have to overcome
that difficulty and try to induce them to
put the children into this institution, but
they would not be prepared to do that
if it was miles away from their homes. I
only mention this point because I think
the hon. Member who raised this question fully appreciates all the difficulties
that may arise. I have had many helpful
conversations with the Belfast Corporation, and I have undertaken with their
co-operation to do all that I can to help
them to secure the best possible site.
In regard to after-care, we have the

These gentlemen made excavations in

nearly £9 per head for each man,

woman, and child of the population.
Public expenditure is soaring. To-day
almost as much is spent on the administration of the Six Counties as was spent
on the administration of the thirty-two
counties of all Ireland before the Six
Counties were handed over to the Prime
Minister. Official salaries in this
Lilliputian area are of astronomical proportions, and the services rendered by
unimpeachable mediocrity are in inverse

As for the minority here, of course,

foreign graves from Shanghai to Palestine, but when they are alive even
messenger's job in the gift of the ruling

a
The rising cost of living is of
great concern to many thousands
of the population of Northern Ireland.
It is causing acute and widespread
privation, and it is affecting many
working class homes. It is inevitable
that in recovering from depression such
as we have had in recent years there
should be some rise in the cost of living,
but the Government's restrictive economic policies, for instance with regard
to milk, eggs, and meat, are making
those essential articles of nourishment
almost unobtainable by the poorest.
Young children are the worst sufferers.
I cannot raise a pæan of exultation over
this.
The Minister of Finance referred
yesterday to my speech as depressing. It is
very hard to make anything but a
depressing speech in a depressed area.
I do say that every interest in Northern
Ireland is assailed and weakened by the
intrusion of Stormont. Every class save
and except the official salaried class is the
poorer for the administration. Were it
not for the seventeen million golden
sovereigns which the British Treasury
poured into it since 1921 the Northern
Ireland sack could not stand upright.
We are breaking up to-day for the
Christmas holidays. They will be holidays for many Members of this House,
but they will be no holidays for great
numbers of our people to whom you can
hold out no hope whatever
amelioration in their wretched lot.

asked the Minister of Commerce whether

of the crews.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply. I feel
I am speaking for every Member of the
House when I say that we deeply regret
this tragic catastrophe, and sincerely
sympathise with the relatives of those
who lost their lives. The hon. and
learned Member will, however, be aware
that matters relating to merchant shipping are reserved for the Parliament of
the United Kingdom. I suggest, therefore, that the hon. and learned Member
should direct his inquiries to the Board
of Trade, which is the department concerned with such matters.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask whether
the Minister of Commerce can at least
make representations to the Ministry in
London which controls these matters,
seeing that his own Ministry is quite
powerless to take any steps for the protection of Northern Irish sailors?
Mr. ANDREWS: The Ministry of
Commerce can be relied on to do what is
right and proper in the matter.

SUGGESTED INCREASE IN
UNEMPLOYMENT ALLOWANCES.
Mr. MIDGLEY (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Labour whether in
view of the approach of Christmas, the
continuing severe weather and the increasing cost of living, he will consider
the advisability of recommending an increase of 2s in all unemployment
allowances for adults and 1s in respect
of each child, or, alternatively, if he will
ask the Cabinet to sanction the payment
of an extra week's benefit to all unemployed persons during the Christmas
week.
Major SHILLINGTON: As the hon.
Member is aware, benefits and allowances
paid under the Unemployment Insurance
and Assistance Schemes in Northern
Ireland are at the same rates as in Great
Britain, and the Unemployment Assistance Board for Northern Ireland is acting on parallel lines with the Board in
Great Britain in exercising its special
powers to increase allowances in cases
where changes in the prices of commodities create circumstances which need to
Major SHILLINGTON: I am sure
the hon. Member is aware that in connection with these matters we must go
on parallel lines with Great Britain.
Mr. MIDGLEY: What about asking
them to do it?

will arise affecting considerable numbers
of people who are at present unemployed.

Government, in co-operation with the
local authority propose to do their best
at an early stage to facilitate progress in
regard to some relief schemes. In connection with some of these schemes being
undertaken at present some dubiety exists
as to the employment of labour. I had
put down a private notice question which
Adjournment

I cannot bring up in the ordinary course

or Minister of Labour to make a pronouncement to the House and to the
community at large in regard to the unemployed who may be expecting employment through the development of schemes
like the by-pass road.
Different people have come to me and

I should also like the appropriate

the by-pass road that employment on
these schemes will be on the basis of something like justice, having regard to the
economic position of the claimants.
There is a feeling abroad at the present time that some employment in the
city of Belfast is going to be on the basis
of patronage or privilege. We do not
want an extension of that belief or fear
to any Governmental schemes, and I
would welcome, and the community

scheme is going to be on the basis of the

for employment, to the end that those
men in need of employment will get that
much-needed employment without any
discrimination.
